topics.title: Design for a very small working memory
topics.theory: Memory architecture: three stores, about four chunks

situation.text: A product specialist hands you 46 slides for a one-hour onboarding session with eight new customer support staff. Slide 7 alone carries a pricing table, four plan names and three exceptions. Everything on it is accurate and the hour is fixed. The easy move is to keep every slide and talk faster.

items: **Write one sentence** that starts "After this hour they can". Then put every idea in the content on its own sticky note and count the notes that are new to this audience. That count is the real size of the session.
**Sort the notes** into three or four groups and give each group a name the learner would use, such as "which plan the customer is on". A note that fits no group leaves the session.

**Mark what people must carry** in their heads and what they can look up, inside each group. Everything they can look up moves to a one-page handout. Open the handout once during the session so people know where things are.

**Teach one group at a time.** As a working pattern, give five to seven minutes of input, then three to five minutes where people use it: a question, a short case or a card sort. Start the next group only after that.
**Put one new idea on each slide.** If a table has to stay, reveal it one row at a time or highlight the single row you are talking about.

**Spend one minute on the last group** before each new one. Say: "Without looking, tell your neighbour the three plans and who each one is for." There is more on [why recall does more than a recap](t:1.3).
**Check the level with one quick question** on the first group, in the first ten minutes. If an experienced room answers it easily, merge groups, speed up and add harder cases.

why.text: **Working memory holds only a few things.** Working memory is where people hold new information while they think about it. It is small: about three to five things at once. Past that limit people start dropping items, and what is dropped is unlikely to be learned. A group of related details that a person treats as one thing is called a chunk, and a chunk takes up one space. Once ideas are grouped and practised they move into long-term memory, which frees the space again. Experts seem to hold more because their chunks are bigger.

why.title: The magical number 4 in short-term memory
why.found: Reviewed a wide range of studies and concluded that the real limit is three to five chunks. The famous "seven" was a rough estimate.
why.means: Plan for about four new ideas at a time, not seven.

why.text: **The four-idea rule is a rule of thumb.** Be clear about what is research here and what is craft. The limit of about four chunks is on what a person can hold in mind at one moment. "About four new ideas at a time" is a design rule of thumb drawn from that limit. No study sets the number of ideas a session can carry, and the timings in the steps above are practitioner judgement.

**The steps follow from how chunks form.** A group name gives people one handle for several details, so the details stop competing for separate spaces. Using an idea before the next one arrives gives it a chance to settle, which is why the pause for practice matters more than the slide count. The cost is coverage. You will say less in the hour, and the handout has to carry the rest. The advice reverses with expertise. People who already know the field arrive with large chunks, so a slow build of four ideas wastes their time.

try.text: Take one dense block of your own content, about twenty minutes' worth. Write each idea on a sticky note, group the notes into no more than four named groups and move the look-up detail to a handout. Then explain the regrouped version aloud to a colleague who does not know the subject, and ask them to tell you the groups back from memory.

items: **You add slides** to spread the content out, and each slide still carries six ideas. Count ideas per slide, not slides, and cut to one new idea on each.
**Quoting "seven, plus or minus two".** That is the older figure, and later work puts the limit nearer four. Plan for four.
**A group is only a label**, such as "Other things to know". A label with unrelated items under it is not a chunk. Rename it around what the learner does with it, or split it.
**You run the slow build** for a room of specialists. What counts as new depends on the person, and a room of experts can take far more. Ask one question early and change pace on the answer.

items.label: Cowan (2001), The magical number 4 in short-term memory.

quiz.q: Roughly how many chunks can a person hold in working memory at once?
quiz.a: About three to five, so plan for about four. The older figure of seven was a rough estimate.

quiz.q: You have nine policies to cover in a one-hour induction and each has its own slide. What do you change?
quiz.a: Group them under three or four ideas people must leave with. Introduce one group at a time with a short activity for each, and move the look-up detail into a handout.

quiz.q: You run the same session for a team of specialists and they look bored by the slow build. What do you do?
quiz.a: Speed up and add more. What counts as new depends on the person, and experts hold bigger chunks, so they can take far more at once.

topics.tierReason: The small limit on working memory is one of the most replicated findings in memory research, and the checked review puts it at three to five chunks.

topics.title: Cut the load that teaches nothing
topics.theory: Cognitive load, worked examples, expertise reversal

situation.text: You are teaching eight new customer support agents to issue a refund in the billing system. The guide is accurate. The screenshot is on page 3, the six steps are on page 4, and you read the steps aloud while people flip between the two. Half the room gets step four wrong. The content is not too hard. The presentation is using up the thinking space.

items: **Go through the material as a newcomer** would, with a pen. Mark every place where the learner has to work at something that is not the subject: turning pages, hunting for the right spot, decoding a decoration, hearing and reading the same sentence.
**Put the words on the picture.** Number each step on the screenshot at the place where the click happens, so nobody has to hold a step in mind while they search for the button.
**Cut the text to key words** on any slide with a diagram, three to six words a label, and say the full sentences yourself. Do not read out sentences that are also on the screen.

**Show one fully worked example** to people new to the task before they try. Say each decision aloud: "I choose partial refund here because the customer keeps the first month." Then give an example with the last two steps left for them, then a whole one alone. There is more on [how to fade the support](t:2.13).
**Remove what teaches nothing**: stock photos, a logo on every slide, animated transitions, the paragraph that repeats what you have just said.
**Check the level at the start.** Ask who has done this task before. Give those people the problem without the worked example, and a harder case to go on to.
**Test the new version on one newcomer** and watch where they hesitate. Any hesitation that is about the page and not about refunds goes back on your list.

why.text: **Only wasted effort is worth cutting.** Mental effort during learning comes from two places. Some is the real difficulty of the subject. Some is wasted on poor design. Only the second kind is worth cutting, because the first kind is the learning. [Working memory is small](t:1.1), so every unit of effort spent finding the right place on a page is taken from the effort available for understanding refunds.

**Three effects come up constantly in this research.** Beginners learn more from studying worked solutions than from solving problems unaided. Splitting related information across places forces people to hold one part while they find the other. Reading out full sentences that are also on the screen, beside a picture, is thought to overload people. All of this reverses with expertise: support that helps a novice gets in the way of someone who already knows.

**The read-aloud rule has limits.** A meta-analysis of 57 studies found that narration with matching on-screen text did better than narration alone. The gain showed up for people with little prior knowledge, when the material set the pace, when there were no pictures, and when the screen showed key terms and not the full script. So the thing to avoid is a narrator reading whole sentences off a slide that also carries a diagram. A few key words on screen while you talk are fine.

**Example first or problem first is unsettled.** Whether to show an example first or set a problem first is an open question. Example first has the stronger case for people who are new to a subject and learning a procedure, where an unaided attempt would swamp working memory. Problem first is supported by a pooled analysis of 53 studies (Sinha and Kapur, 2021). It did better when learners could bring what they already knew to the problem and a full explanation followed. Those studies were of school and university students learning concepts in maths and science. Younger primary pupils did better when taught first, and so did learners of general skills not tied to a subject. A rule of thumb, and no more than that: go example first when people are new and the goal is to carry out a procedure correctly. Go problem first when they have some background, the goal is understanding, and you have time to teach it properly straight after. You can [turn this into a design sequence](t:2.13) and read about [difficulty that is worth keeping](t:2.19). The step of testing on one newcomer is craft.

try.text: Find one resource you know is hard to follow: a guide, a slide or a screen recording. List what makes people work without teaching them, and label each item with its problem: no worked example, related information split across places, full sentences read aloud, or support pitched at the wrong level. Redesign it. Then watch one newcomer use the new version and note every hesitation.

items: **You strip out the difficulty** that belongs to the subject. Deciding between a full and a partial refund is hard because it is the job. Keep that effort and cut the page turning.
**You try to measure each kind** of load. The different kinds are hard to measure separately. Use the idea as a design guide, not as a measuring tool.
**One level of support** for a mixed room. It will be wrong for someone. Give the experienced people the harder version and let newcomers keep the worked example.
**You remove every word** from the screen because of the read-aloud rule. Key terms on screen helped in the pooled studies. It is the full script beside a diagram that gets in the way.

items.label: Sweller (1988), Cognitive load during problem solving.
Sweller, van Merriënboer and Paas (1998), Cognitive architecture and instructional design.
Kalyuga (2007), Expertise reversal effect and its implications for learner-tailored instruction.

quiz.q: Which kind of mental effort is worth cutting?
quiz.a: The effort caused by the design: decoration, repetition, hunting for the right place. Leave the difficulty that belongs to the subject.

quiz.q: You are teaching a new procedure to people who have never done it. Your plan opens with a problem for them to solve. What do you change?
quiz.a: Show a fully worked example first, then ask them to solve one. An unaided attempt at a new procedure is likely to swamp working memory.

quiz.q: Halfway through a course, the experienced people in the room are getting slower and more irritable with your step-by-step guides. What is going on, and what do you do?
quiz.a: The support has started to get in their way. Take it away for them and give them the harder version.

topics.tierReason: Worked examples, split attention, redundancy and the expertise reversal effect are each backed by a large body of experiments summarised in the three checked sources.

topics.title: Make practice harder in the ways that help
topics.theory: Desirable difficulties: spacing, retrieval, interleaving, generation

situation.text: A software company's sales team has a weekly session on handling objections. Each one ends with a recap slide, people say it was clear, and the scores on the form are high. Two weeks later their manager listens to calls and hears the old answers. The sessions were smooth, and smooth is often the problem.

items: **Swap the closing recap** for an opening recall. Start each session with three questions on last time. People write answers alone, from memory, for two minutes, compare in pairs for two more, then you show the answers. There is more on [how to build these questions in](t:2.24).

**Space the returns.** List the four or five ideas that have to last, and plan to come back to each one later the same day, in the next session and again some weeks on. The longer you need it to last, the longer the gap should be. There is more on [how to schedule the practice](t:5.14).

**Ask before you tell.** Say: "Before I show you ours, write down what you would say to a customer who tells you it costs too much. Ninety seconds." Take two answers without judging them, then teach. A wrong answer is fine.

**Give newcomers blocked practice first**: three cases of the same type in a row until they get it right. Then mix related types in shuffled order, so the first job on each case is to work out which approach fits.
**Tell people why, before the first quiz.** Say: "This will feel harder than a recap, and you will get some wrong. That is the point. Pulling it out of memory is what makes it last."
**Keep the stakes low.** No marks are collected, pairs check each other, and you ask what was hard to recall, not who got it right. This step is craft.
**Judge the change after a delay** by what people can do, not by how the session felt. There is more on [why a delayed check tells you more](t:1.4).

why.text: **Harder practice often lasts longer.** Conditions that feel harder in the moment often make learning last longer. Pulling something out of memory with effort strengthens it more than seeing it again. Four techniques follow from this. Spacing is leaving gaps between practice. Retrieval practice is recalling from memory. Interleaving is mixing related problem types. Generation is attempting an answer before you are given it.

why.title: Test-enhanced learning
why.found: Students either re-read a passage or tested themselves on it. After five minutes the re-readers remembered more. After two days and after a week the self-testers did, even though the re-readers had been more confident.
why.means: Swap the recap for a recall exercise, and expect it to feel worse on the day.

why.text: **There is no single correct gap for spacing.** In one large study the best gap was about 20 to 40 per cent of the time until the test when the test was a week away, and about 5 to 10 per cent when it was a year away. The best gap still grew in days as the test moved further off. Longer goals need longer gaps. The four techniques are not equally well supported. A major review of study techniques gave its top rating to practice testing and spaced practice, and a middle rating to interleaving. Interleaving helps most when the things being mixed are related and easy to confuse. A pooled analysis of interleaving studies advises caution with word lists and explanatory texts.

**Recall feels worse than a recap.** The trade-off is what makes this hard to adopt. A recap feels good because everything on the slide looks familiar, and familiar is easy to mistake for known. A recall question shows people the gaps, so the same session feels worse and may score lower on the form. Learners usually rate the easier method as more effective, and their sense of it is unreliable. Tell the client this before they see the forms. The advice reverses for people who know too little to get through the difficulty. Newcomers may need some straightforward, blocked practice first. The two-minute timings and the low-stakes set-up are practitioner judgement.

try.text: Take a session you already run. Mark where each of the four techniques could go, then rewrite its practice schedule across the following weeks. Write three recall questions on the previous session and say your explanation of why the practice is harder aloud, twice, until it takes under twenty seconds. Run the recall opening at your next session and note which question most people could not answer.

try.title: Words you can use: explaining the harder practice
lines: "We are going to start differently today. Three questions on last week, no notes, on your own."
"You will not get them all. Nobody does, and nothing is being marked."
"I am doing this because trying to remember is what makes it last. A recap feels better and leaves less behind."

items: **You mix problem types** before people can do any one of them. Difficulty only helps people who know enough to get through it. Give newcomers blocked practice first and mix afterwards.

**You interleave things that are unrelated.** Mixing helps most when the items are related and easy to confuse, such as three kinds of objection. Do not shuffle a product quiz with a health and safety quiz and expect a gain.

**You revert to the old way** because people say it worked better. Learners usually rate the easier method as more effective. Explain the reason again and keep going. There is more on [why the feel of a session misleads](t:1.4).
**The quiz turns into a test** with scores read out. People stop attempting answers they are unsure of. Keep it unmarked and checked in pairs.

Cepeda and colleagues (2008), Spacing effects in learning: a temporal ridgeline of optimal retention.
Cepeda and colleagues (2006), Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks.

quiz.q: In the passage study, who remembered more after a week: the students who re-read or the students who tested themselves?
quiz.a: The students who tested themselves, although the re-readers had felt more confident.

quiz.q: Your weekly team session ends with a recap slide and people say it is clear, but little carries over to the next week. What do you change?
quiz.a: Drop the recap. Open each session with a few questions on last week, answered from memory, and mix earlier case types into this week's practice.

quiz.q: You switch to mixed practice and no-notes quizzes. People complain that the old way worked better. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep going and explain why the harder practice is there. Learners usually rate the easier method as more effective, and that feeling is unreliable. Check that newcomers have had enough straightforward practice first.

topics.tierReason: Spacing and retrieval practice are supported by several meta-analyses and got the top rating in a major review of study techniques. Interleaving and generation are supported by one meta-analysis each, with conditions.

topics.title: Do not trust how fluent the room looks

situation.text: You have just run a call-handling day for a customer team of ten. In the afternoon role-plays, which came straight after your demonstration, everyone used the new opening. The forms are warm and the client says, "That clearly worked. Let's roll it out to the other three teams." Three weeks later a team leader tells you the calls sound the same as before.

items: **Write down the one or two things** people must be able to do weeks later, and how you will see each one: a cold role-play, a sample of real calls or a short written recall. Do this before the course.

**Book the delayed check** before the course runs, and put it in the proposal. A week or more after the session is a sensible working gap. That figure is craft, not a research finding. There is more on [how to run the check](t:6.5).

**Warn the client in advance.** Say: "People will do well on the day because they have just watched me do it. I will check again three weeks later with no reminder. Expect a drop. The drop tells us what to fix."
**Record what you see on the day** and label it "performance on the day" in your report. Do not present it as the result.
**Run the delayed check cold.** Use the same task and the same scoring sheet, with no recap, no notes and no demonstration first. Fifteen minutes a person is enough for a short role-play.
**Compare the two sets of scores** line by line. Whatever dropped gets [spaced recall](t:1.3) or a redesign. Whatever held can be left alone.
**Compare on the delayed check only**, when you compare two methods or two versions of a session.
**Teach learners the same test for themselves.** Say: "Close your notes and write down what you remember. Whatever you cannot write, you do not know yet, however familiar the page looks."

why.text: **Performance on the day is a poor guide.** How well people perform during a session is a poor guide to what they have learned. Methods that raise performance on the day often produce the weakest retention, and the reverse. That is the research finding this page rests on, and it is why a method cannot be judged by how fluent people look while it is running.

**A check on the day measures familiarity.** Think about what the afternoon role-play measured. The demonstration was minutes old, the wording was still in people's heads and the prompt sheet was on the table. The job asks for something else: the same behaviour weeks later, with a real customer and nothing to copy. A check on the day cannot tell those two apart. A check after a delay can, because the easy familiarity has worn off by then.

**A confident room says little about next month.** Memory fades without reinforcement, which is the original reason for coming back to material later. People also misjudge their own learning. Easy study feels productive and effortful practice feels worse, yet the effortful kind usually leaves more behind. So warm forms and a confident room are information about how the session felt. They are not evidence about next month.

**The delayed check costs time and flatters less.** There is a cost, and it is as much commercial as practical. The delayed check takes time you have to price in, and it will usually give a less flattering number than the form did. Clients who have been warned tend to read the drop as useful. Clients who have not may read it as failure. The reasoning in the second paragraph and the advice on handling the client are craft.

try.text: Pick a course you know. Find one place where looking fluent has been taken as having learned. Design the delayed check that would show the truth: the task, the scoring sheet, the date and who runs it. Then say the warning to the client aloud, as you would in the briefing call, until you can say it plainly in three sentences without apologising for it.

items: **You quote the forgetting curve** with exact percentages. The curve is the familiar graph of memory dropping steeply and then levelling off. It is an illustration, not a precise law. Describe the shape and leave the figures out.
**A drop on the delayed check** reads to you as a failed session. It is useful information. It shows where to add spaced recall.
**You help during the delayed check**: a nod, a hint, a quick reminder beforehand. Then it measures your prompting. Run it cold and stay neutral.
**You swing to making everything hard.** Only some difficulties help. There is more on [which difficulties help](t:1.3), and on who needs easier practice first.
**The check is planned too late:** after the course, when the budget is spent and diaries are full. Put it in the proposal and book it before day one.

items.label: Soderstrom and Bjork (2015), Learning versus performance: an integrative review.
Kornell and Bjork (2007), The promise and perils of self-regulated study.
Murre and Dros (2015), Replication and analysis of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve.

quiz.q: Why is a fluent session a poor sign of learning?
quiz.a: Performance on the day says little about what people can do later. Methods that raise performance on the day often give the weakest retention.

quiz.q: A client wants to judge your call-handling course on the end-of-day feedback form and the role-play run straight after the demonstration. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Run the same role-play cold a few weeks later and use that result to decide what gets redesigned. Warn the client now that scores will drop, so the drop is read as information.

quiz.q: Your delayed check shows people have lost a good part of what they could do on the day. How do you read it?
quiz.a: As useful information, not as a failed session. It shows where to add spaced recall. Do not respond by making everything hard.

topics.tierReason: The gap between performance during training and lasting learning is documented across many experiments in the checked integrative review.

topics.title: Tell adults why, and start from their problems
topics.theory: Adult learning, used as a rule of thumb

situation.text: Fourteen store managers have been sent by head office to a half-day on the new stock records process. Most have run a shop for ten years. Arms are folded, and one says before you start, "We did this two years ago." Your first slide reads "Records policy, sections one to six".

items: **Phone two or three participants** before the day and spend ten minutes with each. Ask: "What goes wrong with stock records at the moment? What did it cost you the last time?" Collect two real incidents you have permission to use. There is more on [the fuller evidence gathering](t:2.1).
**Open with their problem** inside the first two minutes, in their words. Then give the reason for the session in one sentence that ends with what they will be able to do by the finish.

**Ask what they already do.** Give pairs three minutes: "When a delivery does not match the paperwork, what do you do now, and what works?" Write their answers on a flipchart and use them later by name: "This is the step Priya described."
**Offer two or three real choices**: which case to start with, the order of two modules, their own example or yours. Do not offer a choice over anything that is required.
**Teach each point through a case**, not a policy section. Put the situation first ("Friday delivery, two boxes short, the driver wants a signature"), ask what they would do, then give the rule.
**Ask where they will use it** to close each block: "Write one line. Where does this come up in your shop next week?" There is more on [planning the first use](t:5.2).
**Narrow the choices to two** for people new to the work, and give more direction. They do not yet have problems of their own to start from, so supply a case.

why.text: **Knowles gives useful starting points.** The classic account of adult learning comes from Malcolm Knowles. It says adults are more self-directed, bring experience, care about problems more than subjects and need to know why. These are useful starting points for design.

**They are rules of thumb, not laws.** They describe adult learners more than they explain how learning works. Knowles himself came to treat the adult and child approaches as two ends of one line, each suited to some situations. So an adult who is new to a subject may need a good deal of direction, and that is no insult to them.

**People decide early how much effort to give.** The steps above are craft built on those rules of thumb. The reasoning runs like this. People who were sent to a session spend the first minutes deciding how much effort to give it. A problem they recognise, described accurately, answers that question faster than a list of objectives can. Asking what they already do has two uses. It tells you what you can build on, and it tells you which [mistaken ideas are in the room](t:1.7). Experience cuts both ways.

**Choice has a price.** Every option you offer has to be one you can deliver well, and free choice of content can leave gaps in what a mandatory session has to cover. That is why the choices here are about order and example, never about whether the required material is taught.

try.text: Take the opening of one module you run for a specific audience. Find one real problem that audience has, by asking two of them. Rewrite the first three minutes so the problem comes first, the reason comes second and a choice comes third. Then stand up and deliver it aloud against a timer and record it on your phone. Good looks like this: the problem is stated in under 30 seconds, in words those people would use, and you do not mention the policy by section number.

try.title: A worked example: the first three minutes of a mandatory records session, before and after
lines: Before: "Good morning. Today we cover the records policy, sections one to six. Please hold questions until the end."
After, minute 1: "Morning, everyone. Last month two of you lost an afternoon looking for a signed delivery form. One of you told me you ended up counting a whole stockroom by hand."
"That is the problem we are here to fix. By half past twelve you will be able to record a short delivery in under two minutes and find any form from the last year in under one."

Minute 2: "You have all been handling this for years, so I want to start with what you do now. With the person next to you: when a delivery does not match the paperwork, what do you do, and what works? Three minutes."
Minute 5, after taking four answers on the flipchart: "Keep those in view. Some of them are already what the new process asks for."
Minute 6: "I have three cases from real shops: a short delivery, a missing signature and a return with no paperwork. Which one do you want to start with?"

items: **Experience treated as only an asset.** People bring knowledge to build on and [misconceptions to manage](t:1.7). Ask what they do now, then check it against the method.
**You present these principles as proven** to a client. Say they are a working guide that describes adult learners. Do not call them the science of adult learning.
**You give newcomers free choice** over what to cover and they look lost. Choice needs structure. Offer two options inside a route you have set.
**The "why" is the organisation's reason**, not theirs. "Head office needs accurate data" will not move a store manager. Use the afternoon they lost.
**You ask, then ignore the answer** about what they already do. Write it up, refer back to it and credit the person. Otherwise the question was a ritual, and they will know.

items.label: Knowles and colleagues (2020), The Adult Learner, 9th edition.
Merriam (2017), Adult learning theory: evolution and future directions.

quiz.q: How firmly should you state the principles of adult learning?
quiz.a: As a rule of thumb. They describe adult learners more than they explain how learning works.

quiz.q: You are opening a mandatory records session for experienced staff who did not choose to come. Your first slide lists policy sections one to six. What do you do instead?
quiz.a: Open with a problem they recognise and say why the session matters to their work. Then offer a real choice, such as which case to start with.

quiz.q: You give a group of newcomers free choice over what to cover and in what order. They look lost. What went wrong?
quiz.a: Choice needs structure. Offer a small set of options, such as which case or which example, inside a route you have set.

topics.tierReason: Andragogy is a set of assumptions about adult learners that is widely used in practice. The sources opened describe it and its critics and do not report direct tests of it.

topics.title: Build practice at the edge of ability

situation.text: An account manager with eight years in the job gives a product demonstration that is fine. It was fine three years ago too. Her manager asks you to sharpen it, so she runs the whole 25 minutes for you, you say it went well, and nothing changes.

items: **Watch or record one real run.** Pick a single weakness you can state in a sentence and see in a short stretch, such as "the first 90 seconds do not say what the customer gets". Agree it with the person.
**Cut the drill down to that stretch.** Practise one to three minutes of the task, not all 25.
**Set the level just beyond comfortable.** If every run is clean, it is too easy, so add a constraint. If no run comes close, it is too hard, so remove one.
**Give one note straight after each run**, on that weakness only: "You reached the benefit at 50 seconds. Aim for 20." Save everything else you noticed for another day.
**Run it again with that one change.** Five runs is a good set. Name what improved between the first and the fifth.
**Stop after 15 to 20 minutes** and plan a rest or easier work afterwards. Practice at the edge is tiring, and tired repetition slides back into the comfortable version.
**Raise the difficulty next time**: a colleague interrupts with a question at 30 seconds, or the customer is in a hurry, or the limit drops to 60 seconds.
**Promise the drill and the feedback** when you describe the plan to the client. Never promise mastery from hours alone.

why.text: **Experience by itself does not build expertise.** Improvement comes from practice that is effortful, aimed at a weakness, pitched at the edge of ability and followed by feedback. Running the whole demonstration again fails on every count. Most of it is already good, so most of the time goes on what she can do, and "it went well" gives her nothing to change. Twenty years in a job can be one year repeated.

**The "10,000 hours" figure is a popularisation.** The research behind it was about a particular kind of effortful practice kept up for years, not a count of hours. A later pooling of studies found that deliberate practice explained about a quarter of the difference in performance in games, about a fifth in music and sport, and under one per cent in professions.

**How much deliberate practice explains is disputed.** Ericsson and Harwell (2019) argued that the pooled analysis counted many kinds of structured practice that do not meet the original definition. When they kept only the studies that did, practice time explained 29 to 61 per cent of the difference in performance after correcting for measurement error. So do not read the figure for professions as proof that practice hardly counts at work. It may say more about how loosely practice was measured in those studies.

**The cost of the drill is comfort.** Feedback straight away suits a skill that is still being learned. There is more on [when a delay can help](t:2.27). The set of five runs, the 15 to 20 minute limit and the way of adjusting the level are practitioner judgement, not findings. The trade-off is comfort. A drill on a weakness feels worse than a full run-through, and experienced people can find it exposing, so agree the weakness with them and keep the audience small.

try.text: Choose a skill you are developing yourself, such as opening a session or giving instructions. Record one real attempt and pick one weakness. Design the drill: the stretch, the level and where the feedback comes from. Then do it: five runs aloud, recorded, with one change between each. Listen to the first and fifth back to back and write down the difference you can hear.

items: **Comfortable repetition feels like practice** and is not. If the person can do the drill without errors or effort, change it.
**You give five notes** after one run. The person changes none of them well. One note, on the agreed weakness, then run it again.
**No feedback at all**, or only "good". Without feedback people practise their mistakes. If you cannot be there, a recording and one question to answer when listening back will do.
**The drill runs for an hour.** Practice at the edge is tiring. Keep it short and plan a rest after it.

**You quote a figure as proof:** the under one per cent figure to argue that practice does not matter at work, or 10,000 hours to argue that time is all it takes. Both readings go beyond the research.

items.label: Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Römer (1993), The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance.
Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald (2014), Deliberate practice and performance: a meta-analysis.

quiz.q: What separates deliberate practice from repetition?
quiz.a: It targets one weakness, sits at the edge of ability and comes with feedback.

quiz.q: An experienced presenter wants to improve. She plans to run the whole talk again and ask a colleague how it went. What do you suggest instead?
quiz.a: Pick one weakness, such as the opening. Practise only that part several times, with one specific note after each run.

quiz.q: A manager says the team does not need practice sessions because they all have ten years in the job. How do you answer?
quiz.a: Experience by itself does not build expertise. Comfortable repetition keeps people where they are. Improvement needs effortful practice on a named weakness with feedback.

topics.tierReason: Deliberate practice is well described, but the pooled studies show it explains a modest and very uneven share of performance, and almost none in the professions.

topics.title: Start from what people already know

situation.text: A retailer has changed its phone protection plan, and the new one no longer covers accidental damage. You explain this clearly to sixteen store staff, with a slide. They nod. The following week a mystery shopper hears three of them tell customers that a dropped phone is covered. They went back to the idea they arrived with.

items: **Find out what people already believe** before you design. Ask two experienced staff and one manager: "What do new people get wrong about this? What do experienced people still get wrong?" Write down the three most likely wrong ideas.

**Open with a question** that brings the belief out, answered in writing and alone before any teaching: "A customer drops their phone in week three and the screen cracks. Covered or not? Write yes or no, and why." Allow two minutes, take a show of hands and do not give the answer yet.
**Say what is right in their thinking**: "If you wrote yes, you were right until March. The old plan did cover it."

**Name the wrong idea**, say plainly that it is wrong and explain why: "Many of us still think accidental damage is included. It is not. The new plan covers faults only, and here is the line in the terms."
**Give the correct idea** and have people use it at once. Three short cases in pairs, each needing a covered or not covered decision and the sentence they would say to the customer.
**Check again later with a fresh case** and no warning: at the start of the next session, or a week on through the team leader. Old ideas come back.
**Do the same with experienced groups.** Ask their question first too, and be ready for the wrong idea to be one they teach to others.

why.text: **Unaddressed wrong ideas tend to survive.** New learning is built on what people already know. What they know helps when it is accurate and gets in the way when it is not. A wrong idea that is not addressed tends to survive the lesson. Telling people the right answer is often not enough. It works better to name the wrong idea, say plainly that it is wrong and explain why.

why.title: Refutation text facilitates learning
why.found: Pooled 44 comparisons with 3,869 learners. Texts that named a common wrong idea and refuted it led to more learning than other texts on the same subject, a moderate effect (g = 0.41) that held across many settings.
why.means: Name the wrong idea, say it is wrong and explain why, instead of only presenting the right one.

why.text: **Experienced people may not learn fastest.** How much existing knowledge helps varies a great deal. One pooling of many studies found that people who knew more beforehand still knew more afterwards, but on average they did not gain more from the teaching. Do not assume the experienced people in the room will learn fastest.

**Writing an answer down makes the clash visible.** The written question at the start is craft, and here is the reasoning behind it. A person who has committed to "yes, covered" on paper notices when the answer turns out to be no. A person who only listened can file the new rule beside the old one and never see that they clash. The cost is a few minutes and some discomfort, so the tone matters: most people hold a wrong idea because someone taught it to them. One worry can be set aside. Some trainers avoid naming a myth in case repeating it makes it stronger. That worry has not held up well in later studies. Label the idea clearly as wrong and put the correct idea next to it.

try.text: Before your next session, write down three wrong ideas people are likely to bring. For each, write the question that will bring it out, what is right in it and the case where it fails. Then try your refutation aloud on a colleague: name the idea, say it is wrong, explain why and give the replacement, all in under a minute. Ask them whether any part sounded like blame.

Question that brings it out

Where it fails

"A customer drops the phone in week three. Covered or not, and why?"

The new plan covers faults only. A cracked screen from a drop is not a fault

try.title: Words you can use: correcting an idea without blame
lines: "Hands up if you wrote yes. Thank you. That was the right answer until March, and most of us were trained on it."
"It is no longer true. The new plan does not cover accidental damage."
"Here is why: the plan now covers faults, which means something going wrong inside the phone. A drop is not a fault."
"So the sentence for the customer is: this plan covers faults, and it does not cover drops or spills."
"Three cases on your table. For each one, decide covered or not, and say that sentence to your partner."

items: **You humiliate someone** for a wrong idea. Most people were taught it. Thank them for the answer and say where it came from.

**You teach only the right idea** and never mention the wrong one, in case naming it spreads it. That worry has not held up well in later studies. Name it, label it as wrong and put the correct idea beside it.
**You assume the experienced group** has nothing to unlearn. Experienced groups bring wrong ideas too. Ask them the opening question as well.
**You reveal the answer early**, before people have committed to one. Then nobody finds out what they believed. Get it in writing first.
**You check once, on the day.** Old ideas come back. Put a fresh case into the following week.

items.label: Simonsmeier, Flaig, Deiglmayr, Schalk and Schneider (2022), Domain-specific prior knowledge and learning: a meta-analysis.
Schroeder and Kucera (2022), Refutation text facilitates learning: a meta-analysis of between-subjects experiments.
Swire-Thompson, DeGutis and Lazer (2020), Searching for the backfire effect: measurement and design considerations.

quiz.q: What happens to a wrong idea that the lesson does not address?
quiz.a: It tends to survive, even after a clear explanation of the right one.

quiz.q: You have explained a feedback model clearly and people nod. A week later they are giving feedback the old way. What do you change next time?
quiz.a: Have people commit to their own approach first and see where it fails. Name the wrong idea, say it is wrong and explain why. Then give the model, have them use it, and check again later.

quiz.q: A colleague tells you never to mention a myth in a session because repeating it makes it stronger. What do you do?
quiz.a: Name it anyway. That worry has not held up well in later studies. Label the idea clearly as wrong and put the correct one next to it.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis supports naming and refuting a wrong idea over plain explanation, but how much prior knowledge helps learning varies widely across studies.

topics.title: Know the main theories of learning and what each is good for
topics.theory: A map of learning theories: behaviourist, cognitive, constructivist, social, experiential

situation.text: You are pitching an onboarding course for a retailer's new store staff. Halfway through, the head of learning asks, "Which learning theory is this based on?" You know the course is sound. You are less sure what the choices are, or which answer she is hoping for.

items: **Learn the five families** in one line each. Behaviourist: what people do and what follows it. Cognitive: memory and thinking. Constructivist: people build understanding from experience. Social: people learn by watching and working with others. Experiential: people learn by doing and reflecting.
**List what the course has to produce** and tag each outcome by kind: a routine that must be fluent, facts and understanding, judgement, or the unwritten norms and craft of the job.

**Match method to kind.** For fluency, borrow from behaviourism: practice, feedback, reinforcement. For understanding, borrow from cognitive theory: memory, load, recall. For judgement, borrow from constructivism: problems and discussion. For norms and craft, borrow from social and experiential theory: watching, doing, reflecting.
**Then check the learner** as well as the task. Newcomers need guidance whichever family you borrow from. Keep open, messy problems for people with experience.

**Look for the family that is missing** from your design, and decide whether that is a gap or a fair choice. A course with no watching or shadowing in it may be leaving out how the job is really done.
**Answer the client by activity**, in about thirty seconds, not with one label. The script below shows how.
**Ask what learners are doing** in minute ten when a supplier uses a theory name. Judge the method, not the label.

why.text: **Each theory is a tool for some jobs.** Behaviourism looks at what people do and what follows. Cognitive theory looks at memory and thinking. Constructivism says people build understanding from experience. Social theory says people learn by watching and working with others. Experiential theory says people learn by doing and reflecting. Each explains some kinds of learning well and others badly. A working trainer uses them as tools for different jobs.

**One framework matches theory to learner and task.** One well-known comparison written for course designers matches the theory to the learner as well as the task. It suggests behaviourist methods for facts and set procedures, cognitive methods for applying rules to new problems, and constructivist methods for experienced people facing messy problems. That is a designer's framework, not an experiment, and the tagging method in the steps is craft built on it.

**Activities tell the client more than labels.** The reason to answer by activity is practical. A single label invites the wrong argument, because every family has critics and every real course mixes methods. "Drills with feedback for the till, case discussion for complaints" tells the client what their staff will be doing and why, and it can be checked against the session plan. It also protects you from your own preferences. Trainers who like discussion tend to use it for everything, including routines that only need drilling.

**Kolb's cycle is popular but loosely defined.** Kolb's learning cycle is the best-known experiential model: have an experience, reflect on it, form an idea, try the idea out. It is widely used and loosely defined. A review of the research found it unclear what counts as a concrete experience. There is more on [how to use the cycle](t:1.25). This page is a map. Each family has a large literature behind it, so read further before you claim expertise in one.

try.text: Take one course you know. List its main activities and tag each with the family it borrows from. Note which family is missing and whether that matters for this job. Then answer the client's question aloud, as if in the pitch, in thirty seconds, and record it. Good looks like this: you name activities and the reason for each, and you do not claim that any one theory is the basis of the course.

try.title: Words you can use: answering "What is it based on?"
lines: "No single theory. Different parts of the job need different methods, so I have matched them."
"The till is a routine, so that part is drills with feedback until it is fluent."
"Product knowledge is about memory, so it is short input and recall quizzes spread over the first week."
"Complaints need judgement, so we use real cases and discussion, once people know the policy."
"And the tone of the shop floor is learned from colleagues, so there are two shadowing shifts with things to look for."
"I can show you where each one sits in the session plan."

items: **A theory name sells a product.** Theory names are used to sell products. Ask what the method is, and what learners do with their time.
**"Constructivist" is taken to mean unguided.** It does not mean that. Newcomers need guidance, so teach the basics before you set the open problem.
**You use one family for everything** because it suits your style. Tag the outcomes first and let the kind of learning choose the method.
**You quote Kolb's cycle** as settled science. It is widely used and loosely defined. Use it as a [prompt to add reflection](t:1.25).
**You claim expertise** from a one-page map. Each family has a large literature. Say you draw on several, and read further before going beyond that.

items.label: Ertmer and Newby (1993, reissued 2013), Behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism: comparing critical features from an instructional design perspective.
Kirschner, Sweller and Clark (2006), Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work.
Morris (2020), Experiential learning: a systematic review and revision of Kolb's model.

quiz.q: Name the five families of learning theory.
quiz.a: Behaviourist, cognitive, constructivist, social and experiential.

quiz.q: A client asks which learning theory your course is based on. How do you answer?
quiz.a: By activity, not with one label. For example drills with feedback for a routine, recall quizzes for facts, case discussion for judgement and shadowing for how the team works.

quiz.q: A supplier describes a course for complete beginners as constructivist, meaning people work it out for themselves with no instruction. What do you say?
quiz.a: Constructivist does not mean unguided. Newcomers need guidance. Ask what the method is in practice, because theory names are used to sell products.

topics.tierReason: This is a map of theoretical frameworks for choosing methods. The map itself has not been tested as a practice.

parts.title: Spot the myths
parts.summary: Why brain myths spread, the big ones debunked, and how to test a claim.

topics.title: Know why smart people believe brain myths

situation.text: A supplier's deck for a sales kick-off has a glowing brain on slide 4 and the line "Our method rewires neural pathways for faster learning". Your client's head of sales likes it and wants the line in the opening talk. It sounds scientific, you half remember reading something like it, and you are tempted to let it through.

items: **Treat certain words as a stop sign**: "brain-based", "neuro", "rewires", "hard-wired", a named brain chemical, or a brain image with no reference under it. Until you have seen the source, the claim is unproven.
**Ask for the source in writing.** "Could you send me the study this line is based on? The paper itself, please, not a summary." A supplier who has it will send it the same day.
**Read what the finding showed.** Note who was tested, on what task, how learning was measured and whether the study tested this product or method at all.
**Write the claim and the finding** side by side, one sentence each. The gap between the two sentences is the stretch.
**Ask who gains if you believe it.** A claim that sells something, or flatters the buyer, needs a closer look.
**Decide whether the line stays.** Use the finding at its real size, in plain words, or leave the line out. Tell the client what you can stand behind and offer the replacement sentence.

**Run the same test once a year** on your own slides, website and proposals. Search for "brain", "neuro", "proven" and "science shows", and trace each one. There is a [full set of questions to ask](t:1.11).

why.text: **Most brain myths start from something true.** A neuromyth is a real finding about the brain or learning that has been stretched or distorted. Most are not lies. They start from something true, and they spread because they are plausible and often flattering.

**Careful people still fall for brain myths.** Two findings explain why careful people fall for them. In one experiment, adding irrelevant brain language made weak explanations more satisfying to people without neuroscience training. Experts were not taken in. In a survey of 242 teachers in the UK and the Netherlands, all of them interested in the neuroscience of learning, teachers believed about half of the myths they were shown. Those who knew more about the brain believed more of them.

**Feeling a claim sounds right is no test.** Put together, these say something uncomfortable for a trainer who reads a lot. Interest and general knowledge are not protection, and may make things worse. One possible reading, and it is only a reading, is that people who enjoy the subject meet more claims and find them more believable. Whatever the cause, the practical point holds. You cannot rely on the feeling that a claim sounds right, because brain language is what produces that feeling. The defence is a routine you follow every time: get the source, read the finding and compare it with the claim.

**A myth you repeat carries your authority.** The steps themselves are craft. They cost about an hour for each claim, and now and then an awkward conversation with a client who liked the slide. Against that, a trainer is a trusted source. When you repeat a myth, it spreads with your authority behind it, and the person who checks it later will remember who said it. The same caution has a limit. The findings underneath are real, and it is the stretching that causes the problem, so do not dismiss neuroscience as a whole.

try.text: Take one real marketing claim for "brain-based" training, from a brochure, a conference talk or your own old slides. Trace it back to the finding it rests on and write one sentence on what the finding supports. Then say aloud, as if to the client, why you are leaving the line out and what you would say in its place. Keep it under thirty seconds, with no lecture on neuroscience.

try.title: Words you can use: telling the client

"The study behind it is about students remembering word pairs. It did not test this product, and it did not measure anything in the brain."
"So I cannot stand behind 'rewires neural pathways' in front of your team."
"What I can say is that the programme spaces practice over six weeks, and that is well supported. I would open with that."

items: **A respected person said it**, so you repeat the claim. A trainer is a trusted source, and that is how myths travel. Trace it yourself before it goes on a slide.
**You trust your instinct** because you have read a lot about the brain. In the teacher survey, knowing more went with believing more. Follow the routine anyway.
**You overcorrect and dismiss all neuroscience.** The findings are real. Keep the finding at its true size and drop the stretch.
**You accept a summary**, a blog post or a reference list as the source. Ask for the paper and read what was tested.
**You never check your own materials**, only suppliers. Old slides are where most trainers keep their myths.

items.label: Weisberg and colleagues (2008), The seductive allure of neuroscience explanations.
Dekker and colleagues (2012), Neuromyths in education.
Howard-Jones (2014), Neuroscience and education: myths and messages.

quiz.q: What is a neuromyth?
quiz.a: A real finding about the brain or learning that has been stretched or distorted.

quiz.q: A supplier's sales deck says their method "rewires neural pathways for faster learning". You like the slide. What do you do before using it?
quiz.a: Ask for the study and check what it really showed. If the finding never tested the product, leave the slide out.

quiz.q: You have read a lot about the brain and feel well placed to judge these claims on instinct. Why should you still check the source?
quiz.a: In the teacher survey, those who knew more about the brain believed more of the myths. Brain language makes weak claims sound stronger, so trace each claim back to its finding.

topics.tierReason: The checked studies show that brain language persuades and that interested teachers believe many myths. The remedy on this page, tracing a claim to its source, is sensible practice that has not itself been tested.

topics.title: Drop learning styles and the other big myths

situation.text: A client is briefing you on a programme for twelve new managers. She asks for a questionnaire to sort them into visual, auditory and kinaesthetic learners, with a handout for each group. Her slide template also has a pyramid showing that people remember 10% of what they read and 90% of what they teach. She learned both from a trainer she respects.

items: **Agree with what is true** before you correct anything. Say: "You are right that people have preferences. What the research does not back is teaching each group differently."
**Drop the questionnaire** and say what you will do with the time: "I would put those twenty minutes into practice. Everyone gets the same three things."
**Choose the medium by content, for everyone.** Show a process. Describe a principle in words. Practise a skill.
**Use more than one medium** where it helps understanding, and say so out loud. Otherwise people hear "pictures do not matter".
**Check your own slides, workbook and website** against the table below. Search for each phrase. Most trainers find one or two.
**Replace each myth** with something that holds up. A deleted slide leaves a hole the old claim will fill again. The table gives a replacement for each.
**Answer a myth in under a minute** when it comes up in the room: what is true in it, what is not, what you do instead. Then go back to the session. Do not let it become a debate.
**Check any claim not in the table** before you repeat it. Use the [questions for testing a claim](t:1.11).

why.text: **Matching teaching to style is not worth it.** People do have preferences. What the evidence does not support is sorting people by style and teaching each group differently. The picture is not a clean zero. A 2024 pooling of 21 studies found a small average benefit when teaching matched a person's style. The idea needs matching to help learners of more than one style. Only about a quarter of the measures showed that, and the studies were weak. The authors judged the benefit too small and too rare to be worth the time and cost.

why.title: A meta-analysis of the learning styles matching hypothesis
why.found: Pooled 21 studies with 1,712 learners. Matched teaching gave a small average benefit (g = 0.31), but only 26 per cent of the outcome measures showed matching helping more than one style, and study quality was low.
why.means: Do not spend time sorting people by style. Choose the medium that fits the content.

why.text: **The same goes for other popular ideas.** People are not left-brained or right-brained learners. Brain scans of more than a thousand people showed that each side has its own specialised networks, and gave no sign that a person favours one side overall. The table below lists the other claims a trainer meets most often, with the verdict this site gives each in the Myth file on the home page, where every one is traced to a source. A few sit in other stages: the [10% transfer figure](t:5.1), the [70-20-10 model](t:5.3) and [satisfaction scores as proof](t:6.3).

**Agreeing first lets people drop the myth.** Learning styles persist because the idea is intuitive, flattering and gives people a tidy label. Most of these myths share that pattern, and most [started from something true](t:1.9). That is the reason for the first step. A person who hears "that is a myth" defends the idea. A person who hears "you are right about preferences" can let go of the part that does not hold. The cost of a styles questionnaire is not only the twenty minutes. A label can also give someone a reason to avoid a medium they would learn from. The wording in the steps and the one-minute rule are craft.

try.text: Audit one course, brochure or slide deck for the claims in the table, and rewrite each part that rests on one. Then practise the answer to "But I really am a visual learner" aloud, three times, until it takes about twenty seconds and sounds friendly. Record the third and check that you named what is true first.

items: **You shame someone for believing it.** Most people were taught it by a trainer. Start with what is true in the idea.
**You call learning styles a myth** and stop there. People hear "pictures do not matter". Say that using several media is good practice, for everyone.
**You claim a clean zero** in the evidence against matching. It is not. A small average benefit showed up in weak studies. Say it is too small and too rare to be worth the cost.

**You treat the table as complete.** Related claims need the same care, such as fixed attention spans and big effects from hydration or sugar. Treat each as unproven until you have checked it with the [questions for testing a claim](t:1.11).
**You give a ten-minute lecture** on a myth raised in the room. Give the one-minute answer and offer to send the source afterwards.

quiz.q: What does the evidence not support about learning styles?
quiz.a: Sorting people by style and teaching each group differently. People do have preferences, but matching teaching to them gives too small and too rare a benefit to be worth the cost.

quiz.q: A client asks for a questionnaire to sort the group into visual, auditory and kinaesthetic learners, with a handout for each. What do you offer instead?
quiz.a: No questionnaire. Choose the medium that fits the content, for everyone: show the process, describe the principle, practise the skill.

quiz.q: A participant says, "But I really am a visual learner." How do you respond?
quiz.a: Start with what is true: people do have preferences. Then say that the research does not back teaching each group differently, and that using several media helps everyone. Do not shame them. Most people were taught this.

topics.tierReason: Reviews agree that matching teaching to learning styles is not worth doing, but a 2024 meta-analysis found a small average benefit in weak studies, so the evidence is not a clean nil.

topics.title: Test any learning claim before you repeat it
topics.theory: Evaluating a claim: evidence levels, effect sizes, red flags

situation.text: A client forwards you a vendor brochure on a Wednesday. The headline says the platform "improves learning by 40%". Her message reads, "Looks impressive. Should we buy it? I need a view by Friday." You have two days and no statistics degree.

items: **Write the claim down word for word.** Then write what would have to be true for it to hold: who was tested, on what task, measured how and against what. Check whether the source says so.
**Find out what kind of evidence** it is: a story, one study, several studies, or a pooled analysis of many. Ask the vendor: "Could you send the study behind the 40% figure?"
**Ask "compared to what?".** An effect means little without the comparison. Forty per cent better than no training is a different claim from forty per cent better than the course you already run.
**Ask whether people were grouped at random.** If they were not, something else about the groups may explain the difference.
**Look at the size of the effect**, not only whether it was "significant". Ask for the effect size (d or g) and the number of people.
**Ask how good the pooled studies were**, for a pooled analysis. Many weak studies added together are still weak.
**Check who paid for the research** and who gains from the claim.

**Give your view in three parts**: what the evidence is, what it does and does not show, and what you would do. Suggest a small trial of your own with a comparison group if the decision is expensive. There is more on [how to use a comparison group](t:6.6).

why.text: **Evidence comes in strengths.** A single story is the weakest. One study is better. Findings repeated by others are better still, and a careful pooling of many studies is the strongest common form, as long as the studies in it are sound. Design counts as well as number. An experiment that assigns people to groups at random can show cause, and a correlation cannot. There is a catch with pooling: the [pooled effect for learning styles](t:1.10) is positive, and it rests on weak studies.

**Wording and funding give a weak claim away.** A result can be statistically significant and still too small to matter in practice. The usual warning signs are brain language with no reference, the phrase "brain-based", a claim that flatters the buyer, no comparison group, and a commercial interest that is not declared. The funding point has been measured in medicine. A Cochrane review found that drug and device studies paid for by the maker reported favourable results and conclusions more often than studies with other funding.

**Most real-world effects count as small.** Effect sizes are usually reported as d or g. Both express the gap between two groups in standard deviations, so 0.5 means the average person in one group scored half a standard deviation above the average person in the other. By the old labels 0.2 is small, 0.5 is medium and 0.8 is large. The study cards on this site quote these figures. Do not judge size by those labels alone. Most real-world education programmes produce effects that count as small on that scale, so ask about cost and how widely the method can be used as well.

**The questions weigh a claim, not veto it.** The order of the steps is craft. "Compared to what?" comes early because it is the question that most often ends the matter, and anyone can ask it. The questions also have a cost. Applied without judgement they would reject most of what trainers do, since much useful practice has never been studied. Use them to decide how much weight a claim can bear, and how much money to put behind it.

try.text: Take three competing claims about learning from brochures, conference talks or posts you have seen this month. Rank them by strength of evidence. For each, write one sentence on what would make it trustworthy. Then pick the weakest and say your view aloud in three parts, as you would on a call with the client, in under a minute.

try.title: Words you can use: the reply to the client
lines: "I asked the vendor for the study behind the 40%."
"It is a survey of their own customers, who rated their confidence before and after. Nobody was tested, and there was no group without the platform to compare against."
"So it tells us that users who replied felt more confident. It does not tell us that anyone learned more."
"That does not mean the platform is bad. It means this figure cannot carry the decision."
"If you like the product, I would ask for a three-month trial: one team uses it, a similar team does not, and we test both at the end."

items: **The questions treated as a guarantee.** This is a way of judging. Strong evidence in schools may not carry over to your workplace, so ask who was studied.
**You wave your own favourites through** and test other people's claims. Run your preferred methods through the same questions.
**No evidence read as evidence against.** Some useful practices are simply unstudied. Say "untested" when that is what you mean, and call it craft.

**You dismiss a method** because its effect is "small" by the old labels. Most real-world education programmes come out small on that scale. Weigh the size against cost and how widely the method can be used.
**The word "significant" sways you.** A result can be statistically significant and still too small to matter in practice. Ask for the size.

items.label: Kraft (2020), Interpreting effect sizes of education interventions.
Lundh, Lexchin, Mintzes, Schroll and Bero (2017), Industry sponsorship and research outcome. Cochrane review.

quiz.q: What can a randomised experiment show that a correlation cannot?
quiz.a: Cause. If people were not put into groups at random, something else about the groups may explain the difference.

quiz.q: A vendor brochure says their platform "improves learning by 40%". What do you ask before acting on it?
quiz.a: Compared to what, measured how, and who ran and paid for the study. If the answer is a vendor survey of user confidence with no comparison group, treat it as a story.

quiz.q: A colleague backs a method by pointing to a pooled analysis of twenty studies with a positive result. What do you check?
quiz.a: How good the pooled studies were and how big the effect is. Many weak studies added together are still weak, and a significant result can be too small to matter.

topics.tierReason: This is a professional habit for judging claims. The individual checks are standard research practice, but the routine as a whole has not been tested.

parts.title: The body matters
parts.summary: Sleep, stress and energy across a training day.

topics.title: Protect sleep on multi-day programmes

situation.text: You are checking the timetable for a three-day residential for twelve new managers. The client's draft starts at 08:00, runs sessions until 21:00 and sets a team task that is due at breakfast. Every hour is full, and the client reads that as value for money. Nobody has asked when these people are meant to sleep.

items: **Fix the nights before the content.** Write the last taught minute of each day and the first of the next on the timetable first. A workable pattern is teaching finished by 17:30 and a 09:00 start, which leaves room for dinner, an evening and a full night.
**Take out the overnight work.** No task due at breakfast and no reading handed out at 18:00 for the morning. If the team task matters, give it an hour of timetable on day two.

**Make the evening social, optional and finite**, and say so on day one: "Dinner is at seven. After that the evening is yours. We start at nine tomorrow and I'd like you rested." There is more on [the rules for evenings and alcohol](t:8.14).
**Check how people get there.** Anyone who got up at five to reach the venue has already had a short night. Start day one at 10:30, or keep the heaviest content for day two.

**Open each morning with recall**, 15 to 20 minutes of it, before anything new. Pairs, notes closed: "Write down the three things from yesterday you would use first. Then compare." Fill the gaps you hear. There is more on [why recall beats a recap from you](t:1.3).

**Timetable a quiet gap** of at least 15 minutes with no content in it, after the most demanding session of the day. A walk outside does the job. There is more on [how long a break should be](t:1.14).

**Give the client the reason** in two sentences and promise nothing: "Sleep is when the day's learning settles, so I have kept the nights clear. I can't put a number on what that gains, but the long days are the bigger risk."

why.text: **Sleep helps new memories settle.** A major review describes them being strengthened and reorganised overnight. That may be one reason [practice spread over days](t:1.3) works better than one long sitting: sleep falls between the sessions. There is more on [what else helps memory settle](t:5.13) after a session.

**Too little sleep hurts at both ends.** Pooled studies found that a lost night before learning weakened taking in new material, and a lost night after learning weakened keeping it. The second effect was the smaller one. The authors warn that both are probably overstated, because studies that found nothing were less likely to be published.

why.title: Sleep deprivation and memory
why.found: Two pooled analyses of about fifty years of experiments. Losing a night of sleep before learning harmed memory, and losing a night after learning harmed it less. Both effects shrank once missing unpublished studies were allowed for.
why.means: Protect the nights on a multi-day course, and keep your claims about sleep modest.

why.text: **The studies tested lost nights, not timetables.** That is the research. The timetable advice is craft built on it. The experiments mostly compare a whole lost night with normal sleep, and nobody has tested course timetables directly, so treat the early finish as sensible caution and not as a proven gain. The trade-off is real: you give up three taught hours a day, and the client can see those hours on the invoice. What you are betting is that hours taught to tired people after 18:00 add little, and that a short night puts the morning at risk as well.

**Protecting sleep does not mean ending the evening.** The advice has a limit. On a residential, the evening together is often the reason for taking people away at all. Protecting sleep does not mean sending people to their rooms. It means the programme itself never demands a late night, and people who stay up do so by choice.

try.text: Take the timetable of a real multi-day programme and ignore the content. Mark every place where sleep is cut short: late finishes, early starts, overnight tasks, travel. Mark where demanding sessions run back to back with no quiet gap. Redesign the rhythm. Then say your two-sentence explanation to the client aloud, to a colleague, and ask them to push back with "but we are paying for three full days". Good looks like this: you hold the early finish, and you do not claim a result you cannot show.

try.title: Words you can use with the client
lines: "I've moved the finish to half past five on both evenings. I want to explain why before you see the timetable."
"Sleep is when the day's learning settles. A short night puts today's material at risk and makes tomorrow's harder to take in."
"I can't promise you a number. The studies compare a lost night with a normal one, not one timetable with another."
"What I can say is that the evening sessions were the weakest hours in the plan, and the team task now has a proper hour on day two."
