items: **You inflate the claim** to win the argument. The mechanism is real and easy to overstate. Say what the pooled studies found, and say that timetables have not been tested.
**You quote a popular book** on sleep to the client. Popular books often claim more than the research shows. If you quote anything, quote a research review.
**You cancel the evening** to protect sleep. Social evenings matter on a residential. Keep them, make them optional and give them no task.
**The optional evening is not optional** in practice, because the most senior person stays up and others feel they must. Ask that person beforehand to say goodnight at a sensible hour.
**The morning recall turns into re-teaching**, with you going over day one for 40 minutes. Keep it to 20. People recall first, and you fill only the gaps.

items.label: Diekelmann and Born (2010), The memory function of sleep.
Newbury, Crowley, Rastle and Tamminen (2021), Sleep deprivation and memory: meta-analytic reviews of studies on sleep deprivation before and after learning. Authors' summary.

quiz.q: In the pooled studies, which did more harm to memory: a lost night before learning or a lost night after it?
quiz.a: The lost night before learning. A lost night afterwards also hurt, but less. Both effects are probably overstated.

quiz.q: A client wants a three-day residential with sessions until 9pm and a team task due at breakfast. What do you propose?
quiz.a: End teaching in the early evening, keep the evening social and optional, move the team task into the daytime timetable, and open each morning by recalling the day before.

quiz.q: The client asks you to promise that the earlier finish will improve retention. What do you say?
quiz.a: That you cannot promise it. The experiments compare a whole lost night with normal sleep, and nobody has tested course timetables directly. The early finish is sensible caution, not a proven gain.

topics.tierReason: Sleep's part in memory is well reviewed and pooled studies show a lost night harms learning, but the effects are probably overstated by publication bias and nobody has tested course timetables directly.

topics.title: Take needless stress out of the room

situation.text: Fourteen account managers file in for an assessed workshop. A restructure was announced on Monday. The sales director sits at the front with a scoring sheet, and the first exercise is a timed solo presentation to the whole room. People are polite and very quiet. Nobody is thinking about the content.

items: **Go through your session plan** before the day, with three triggers in mind: public failure, time pressure that serves no purpose, and status threat. Mark each place one appears.
**Remove public failure.** Anything the whole room will see is tried in pairs first. Three minutes in pairs, then volunteers, then everyone else.

**Keep only the job's real time limits**, such as a two-minute opening to a customer call. Everywhere else, give time as a guide: "You have about ten minutes. I'll tell you when there are two left." Take countdown clocks off the screen.

**Reduce status threat.** Mix the groups so nobody works beside their own manager. [Brief the senior person beforehand](t:4.38) to join a group as a participant and to speak last. Move any scoring to a later day.

**Say plainly that mistakes are expected** in the first five minutes: "You will get things wrong this morning. That is what the morning is for." There is more on [how to make that believable](t:1.17).

**Check with the sponsor** what you can truthfully say if something large is happening in the organisation, then say it once: "I know Monday's news is on people's minds. Today is not part of that process." Do not say it unless the sponsor has confirmed it.

**Tell people anyone can step out** without explaining, and say that at the start. Before the session, find out where to refer someone, usually HR, a mental health first aider or the employee assistance programme. You are not a therapist. There is more on [what to do in the moment](t:4.42).

why.text: **Threatened learners take in and recall less.** Stress gets in the way of recalling what you know. A pooled analysis of 113 laboratory studies found that stress just before or during recall made memory worse. Stress before or during learning usually did the same. So a learner who feels threatened is less able to take things in and to show what they know.

why.title: Acute stress and memory: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across 113 laboratory studies with 6,216 people, stress before or during learning usually made memory worse, and so did stress just before or during recall. Stress just after learning usually helped. The effects at recall were larger for emotional material.
why.means: Keep pressure out of the moments when people take in new material or are asked to recall it.

why.text: **When the stress arrives decides the harm.** Timing matters. In the same analysis, stress that came just after learning tended to help memory for what had been learned. So stress is not always harmful. It does the damage when it arrives while people are taking material in or being asked to recall it. A review written for teachers adds two points. Stress can make it harder to update what you already know when new information arrives. It may also push people away from flexible thinking and towards rigid habits. Both matter when the aim of the session is to change how people work.

**The stress findings come from the laboratory.** All of that is laboratory work on short bursts of stress, mostly with students. The steps on this page are sensible practice built on it, and they have not been tested in training rooms. The finding about stress after learning is not a licence to add some at the end of a session.

**An audience and a clock create threat.** The useful distinction is between threat and challenge, and this part is craft. A hard task that people attempt in private, with time to think, is a challenge. The same task done alone in front of a director with a clock running is a threat, and what it measures is nerve. There is one case where the advice turns round. If the job itself is done under pressure, such as a live complaint call, people need to practise with some of that pressure. Add it late, once the skill is in place, and tell people you are adding it.

try.text: Take the plan for one real programme and list every stress trigger in it under the three headings. Design each one out, or write down why it stays. Then stand up and say your opening lines aloud: the sentence about mistakes, the sentence about stepping out, and the sentence about anything happening in the organisation. Record them on your phone. Good looks like this: under a minute in total, a level voice, and nothing promised that you cannot guarantee.

items: **You explain it with detailed claims** about stress hormones. Those are easy to overstate. Describe it in plain terms: people who feel under threat take in less and recall less.

**You promise nothing leaves the room** when the sponsor expects a report on individuals. Agree beforehand what will be reported, and tell the group exactly that.
**You trust a calm face** to mean a calm person. Some people arrive carrying things you cannot see. Say at the start that anyone can step out without explaining, and mean it.

Vogel and Schwabe (2016), Learning and memory under stress: implications for the classroom.

quiz.q: In the laboratory studies, when did stress tend to help memory?
quiz.a: When it came just after learning. Stress before or during learning, or at recall, tended to hurt.

quiz.q: You are running an assessed workshop. The plan is for each person to present alone while the director scores them. What do you change?
quiz.a: Let people rehearse in pairs first, brief the director to join a group as a participant and speak last, and move the scoring to a later day.

quiz.q: A sponsor says a bit of pressure is good for people and asks you to keep the timed, public exercises. How do you answer?
quiz.a: Keep the challenge and remove the threat. Pressure while people are taking material in or recalling it tends to make memory worse, so cut public failure and time limits that serve no purpose. Offer to add realistic pressure late, where the job itself has it.

topics.tierReason: Laboratory studies show that short-term stress around learning and recall usually harms memory, but the steps on this page have not been tested in training rooms and the long-term stress claim was not confirmed.

topics.title: Break before attention drops, and match the break to the work

situation.text: It is 11:40 on a full day with fifteen store managers. You have been on the new stock system for 100 minutes without a break because you are behind. Half the room has slumped. The two people you asked to demonstrate in front of everyone are rigid and making slips they did not make an hour ago. Both groups have stopped learning, for opposite reasons.

items: **Learn the two states** and look for them every 20 minutes or so. Too little alertness looks like slumping, slow answers, phones and people asking you to repeat the instruction. Too much looks like rushing, fast talk, a fixed stare and simple slips.
**When alertness is low, change the activity.** Stand people up, move them to a wall chart, or switch from listening to a paired task. Do not talk louder or push harder.
**Lower the stakes** when it is too high. Let people try in pairs first, give more time, and take away the audience. There is more on [taking needless stress out of the room](t:1.13).

**Plan a break every 90 minutes**, at least, and write each one into the plan as a clock time. That figure is a common working habit, not a research finding. When you are behind, cut content and keep the break. There is more on [what to cut](t:4.31).
**Match the length to what comes next.** Five to ten minutes restores energy before a lighter segment. After heavy thinking, or before it, give more than ten: 15 to 20 minutes.
**Call the break with a return time** and something to do: "Fifteen minutes. Leave the room, get some water, and be back in your seats at five past eleven." Restart on that minute.
**Put water on the tables** and keep the room comfortable. It is cheap and it helps a little. Do not sell it as a concentration aid.
**Look elsewhere for two things:** [where the hard content goes](t:2.14) across the day, and [the slot after lunch](t:4.43).

why.text: **The Yerkes-Dodson curve is a rough guide.** Alertness affects performance. Too little and people drift. Too much and they tighten up. The usual picture is a curve that rises and then falls, known as the Yerkes-Dodson law. It began in 1908 as a narrow finding about the strength of a stimulus and the forming of habits. Later writers restated it in terms of stress, arousal and motivation, and it has been stretched well beyond the original work. Treat it as a rough guide and not a precise law. Its practical use is that it gives you two problems to look for, and their fixes point in opposite directions.

**Short breaks do help energy.** A pooling of 22 study samples found that breaks of ten minutes or less left people with more energy and less fatigue. The effects were small. They did not reliably improve performance, and the gain showed only on less demanding tasks. Longer breaks helped performance more, so after heavy thinking plan more than ten minutes.

why.title: Micro-breaks: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across 22 study samples with 2,335 people, breaks of ten minutes or less raised energy and reduced fatigue by a small amount (d about 0.36 and 0.35, compared with no break). The overall effect on performance was not significant. Longer breaks gave a larger performance gain.
why.means: Use short breaks to restore energy, and give a longer break after the most demanding segment.

why.text: **Rest and water help only modestly.** Rest, water and movement are real conditions for attention. Their effects are modest, and claims that hydration or sugar transform concentration are overstated. The idea that attention rises and falls in regular natural cycles is promising. It is not an established rule for session length.

**A skipped break costs more than it saves.** The rest is craft. For many groups energy is highest mid-morning and lowest straight after lunch, and that pattern varies by person. Breaking early is a judgement about cost. Ten minutes taken at 11:00 is ten minutes lost. Forty minutes taught to a room that stopped listening at 11:00 is forty minutes lost, and it feels like progress because you covered the slides. Be honest about what a short break buys. It lifts energy and mood by a small amount. It does not promise better scores, which is why the heavy segment gets the longer break.

try.text: Take the plan for a real full day. Mark every break with its clock time and length, and write next to each one why it is that length. Then say each break call aloud as you would in the room, with the return time. In your next session, ask a colleague or the client contact to note the time whenever they see three or more people slump. Compare their notes with where your breaks fell.

items: **You push harder when energy drops**: louder voice, faster slides. Change the activity or take the break.
**You skip the break** because you are behind. You then teach the next 40 minutes to a room that is not listening. Cut a segment and keep the break.
**You quote the Yerkes-Dodson curve** as a law. It dates from 1908 and has been stretched well beyond the original work. Call it a rough guide.

items.label: Teigen (1994), Yerkes-Dodson: a law for all seasons.
Albulescu and colleagues (2022), "Give me a break!" A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance.

quiz.q: What did the pooled studies find that breaks of ten minutes or less do?
quiz.a: They raised energy and reduced fatigue by a small amount. They did not reliably improve performance. Longer breaks helped performance more.

quiz.q: It is 11:40. You have run 100 minutes without a break, you are behind, and half the room has slumped. The next segment is the hardest of the day. What do you do?
quiz.a: Break now, for more than ten minutes, with a clear return time. Then cut content to recover the time. Pushing on would mean teaching the hardest material to people who have stopped taking it in.

quiz.q: A client tells you sessions must be exactly 90 minutes because the brain works in 90-minute cycles. How do you answer?
quiz.a: Say the idea of regular natural cycles is promising and not an established rule for session length. A break at least every 90 minutes is a sensible working habit, and you will break earlier when the room needs it.

topics.tierReason: Planning a day around energy is common practice with little direct testing. The one meta-analysis read shows short breaks lift energy but do not reliably lift performance.

topics.title: Use movement where it helps the learning
topics.theory: Exercise, movement and acting things out

situation.text: Sixteen store staff have sat through three hours of slides on the new returns process. Your co-trainer leans over and suggests a "brain gym" routine to "activate both hemispheres". She is right that the room needs to move. The reason she is offering is a myth, and there is a better use for movement sitting unused in the content.

items: **Sort each segment of the session** into one of two kinds: an action people will perform, or an idea they need to understand. The two call for different uses of movement.

**Add a short walk or stretch** for energy between segments, two to three minutes, about once an hour. Say what it is for: "Two minutes to wake ourselves up. Walk to the window and back, or stretch where you are."
**Build the movement into the task**, better still. Put the practice cases on wall charts and send threes round them. Run a paired discussion standing up. People move and the session loses no time.

**Have every person perform it** when the content is an action: process the return on the practice till, lift the box, fit the security tag. Watching your demonstration does not count. As a rule of thumb, each person does it at least twice.

**Offer a seated or still version** every time, in the same breath and as an equal choice: "or stay where you are and coach your partner through it". Ask about access needs before the day. There is more on [designing for this from the start](t:2.23).
**Check the space beforehand.** If sixteen people cannot stand and move between the tables, use the corridor or keep the movement to standing pairs.
**Make no claims about the brain.** If someone asks why you are doing it, say it gives a small lift in energy, and that actions are remembered better when you do them.

why.text: **Movement gives a small lift in energy.** There are two separate reasons to move, and they rest on different evidence. The first is energy. A pooled analysis of studies on a single bout of exercise found that its effect on thinking is real and generally small. Movement helps a little. It is not a method of teaching, and any movement will do.

**Performing an action helps you remember it.** The second is memory for actions. People remember an action phrase, such as "lift the box", better when they perform it than when they only read it, and a large review found this effect is strong. It is less clear that doing beats watching someone else do it. Here the movement has to be the content. A stretch does nothing for the returns process. Processing a return does.

**Keep both claims within their limits.** The acting-out studies used simple action phrases, and complex ideas may not benefit in the same way. Long-term claims about exercise and brain growth are promising and easy to overstate. The "brain gym" claim is the [left-brain, right-brain myth](t:1.10) in another form. A stretch is worth having for the energy. It does not switch on one side of the brain.

**Mixed-up reasons put movement in the wrong place.** The design point is craft. Mixing up the two reasons is how a group ends up doing star jumps in the name of learning while the one physical skill in the session is taught from a slide. There is a cost on the other side too. Movement that people feel pushed into, in front of colleagues, becomes [a small threat of its own](t:1.13). That is why the seated option is offered every time and as an equal.

try.text: Take a real three-hour agenda. Mark each segment as an action or an idea. Add two movement breaks, and choose one point where people will physically do the thing being taught. Then stand up and say your movement invitation aloud, with the seated option in the same sentence. Record it. Good looks like this: under 20 seconds, no claim about the brain, and the seated version sounds like a real choice.

items: **You make movement compulsory.** Not everyone can or wants to move. Offer the seated version every time, without asking anyone to explain.
**You run an energiser** that has nothing to do with the work, and a group of experienced staff finds it childish. Build the movement into the task with wall charts or standing pairs.
**You only demonstrate the action** and move on. Watching you is not doing. Every person performs it.
**You expect acting out** to help with ideas. The studies used simple action phrases, and complex ideas may not benefit in the same way.
**You repeat a claim about hemispheres** or brain growth to sound scientific. Claim a modest lift in energy and nothing more.

Roberts, MacLeod and Fernandes (2022), The enactment effect: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

quiz.q: How big is the effect of a single bout of exercise on thinking?
quiz.a: Real, and generally small.

quiz.q: People have sat for three hours and a co-trainer suggests "brain gym" exercises to "activate both hemispheres". What do you do?
quiz.a: Take a short walk or stretch to reset energy, with a seated option. Do not make the hemisphere claim. It is a myth, and movement gives a modest lift at most.

quiz.q: You are teaching the six steps of a return on the till from slides, followed by a paper quiz. How could movement help the learning itself?
quiz.a: Have everyone process a return on a practice till. When the content is an action, doing it is remembered better than reading about it. Offer a seated role, such as coaching a partner from the checklist.

topics.tierReason: The checked summaries report a small effect of a bout of exercise on thinking and a strong effect of acting out action phrases, with an unclear advantage of doing over watching.

parts.title: Motivation and safety
parts.summary: Motivation, psychological safety, early wins, peer teaching, and skill versus will.

topics.title: Give people choice, progress and connection

situation.text: Forty customer support staff have been booked onto mandatory data protection training at three o'clock on a Friday. Nobody wants to be there. The sponsor expects groans and proposes a leaderboard, with a voucher for the top score.

items: **Open with the value in their terms**, in under a minute. Name a moment from their own job: "A caller says she is the account holder's wife and asks you to read out his new address. By four o'clock you'll know exactly what to say, and why."

**Build in two or three real choices**: which case to work on, in which order, and how to show what they have learned. Offer cases by role, such as phone, chat and back office. A choice only counts if you will accept either answer.
**Set a first task everyone can complete** with some effort inside ten minutes, then raise the difficulty. There is more on [engineering an early win](t:1.18).
**Show people their progress.** Put the five decisions they need to be able to make on a card and have them tick each one off once they have made it correctly on a case.
**Build connection.** Have pairs or threes work a shared problem, ideally a real one from their own queue.
**Cut what the session costs them.** Ask the sponsor for a better slot than Friday at three, shorten 90 minutes to 60, and remove any form that nobody reads.
**Give specific positive feedback** and leave the prizes out: "You asked who was calling before you opened the account. That is the step most people skip."
**Keep rewards for dull but necessary parts**, such as completing the annual declaration by the deadline.

why.text: **People need choice, progress and connection.** Self-determination theory is one of the better-supported accounts of motivation. It says people need three things: a sense of choice, a sense of getting better, and a sense of connection to others. Design for those and people engage more willingly. Motivation also depends on two judgements: whether I expect to succeed, and whether I value the result. You can design for both, and the first steps above do. What a task costs people, in time and effort, lowers motivation as surely as low value does.

**External rewards can backfire.** A pooling of 128 experiments found that tangible rewards reduced people's interest in tasks they already enjoyed, while positive feedback increased it. The finding has a boundary. The analysis covered tasks people already found interesting. The harm came from tangible rewards that people expected, whether given for taking part, for finishing or for reaching a standard. Tangible rewards that came as a surprise showed no effect. None of this says a reward harms motivation for a task people find dull, which is why the last step keeps rewards for those.

**Other researchers read the evidence differently.** Cameron and Pierce pooled about 100 experiments and argued that the harm is small and confined to tangible rewards promised in advance and given regardless of how well people do. Deci and colleagues reply that this analysis mixed dull and interesting tasks. Both sides agree that praise and feedback on performance do no harm.

**The shortage is usually value, not incentive.** What follows is craft. The sponsor's leaderboard treats low motivation as a shortage of incentive. More often it is a shortage of value: people cannot see what the session is worth to them, and it has been put in the worst hour of the week. You rarely need to make the content fun. A prize also changes what people are working for. On a quiz with a voucher attached, the aim becomes the score, and the caller asking for an address is forgotten.

try.text: Take one mandatory, unpopular topic you might be asked to deliver. Reframe it so that people expect to succeed and can see why it matters, without adding rewards. Write down the choices you will offer and how people will see their progress. Then stand up and deliver your value opening aloud, timed. Good looks like this: under a minute, a moment from their job in the first sentence, and no mention of policy, compliance or the regulator until after it.

items: **The choice is not real**, such as "choose any case" when all three are the same. People notice. Offer fewer choices and honour them.
**Points and badges are not neutral.** On a task people already like, a prize they expect can lower their interest in it. There is more on [when game elements help](t:2.22).
**You leave the cost alone.** A long session at a bad hour with a form to fill in lowers motivation whatever you do in the room. Raise it with the sponsor before the day.

**A compliance course:** you apply all this without checking what the record requires. There is separate advice on [doing mandatory compliance courses properly](t:2.30). There is also advice on [the person who resents being sent](t:4.36).

Ryan and Deci (2017), Self-Determination Theory: Basic Psychological Needs in Motivation, Development, and Wellness.

quiz.q: Which three needs does self-determination theory say motivation rests on?
quiz.a: Choice, a sense of getting better, and connection to others.

quiz.q: You are planning mandatory data protection training. The sponsor suggests a voucher for the top score. What do you do?
quiz.a: Start with value and choice. Explain why it matters, let people pick the case closest to their own job, show their progress and have them work in pairs. Keep rewards for parts that are dull but necessary.

quiz.q: People on your coaching course enjoy the practice exercises. A colleague wants to add a prize for everyone who completes them all. What do you say?
quiz.a: Leave the prize out. In the pooled experiments, tangible rewards that people expected lowered their interest in tasks they already enjoyed. Give specific positive feedback, which raised interest.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis of 128 experiments supports the finding on rewards, and the three needs come from a well-developed theory, but the effects depend on the task and the type of reward.

topics.title: Make it safe to be wrong out loud
topics.theory: Psychological safety and the error climate

situation.text: You ask twelve new managers, "What would you have done differently?" Six seconds of silence. Then the same confident person answers, as she has all morning. The others are not short of ideas. They are working out whether it is safe to be wrong in front of this group, with their director two seats away.

items: **Find out where rank sits** before the day, and who will be in the room. Brief any senior person beforehand and ask them to speak last. There is more on [the senior person who takes over](t:4.38).
**Describe a mistake of your own** in the first five minutes. Make it recent, specific, about the topic of the day, and under 30 seconds.
**Frame each early activity as practice** and say it in words: "This is a first go. Nothing is marked." Only say it if it is true.
**Make the first question low risk** and take it through pairs. Give two minutes to compare first guesses, then take one answer from each pair in turn.

**Say how you will invite people in** at the start: "I'll sometimes ask people by name. You'll always have had a minute to think or talk to a neighbour first, and 'pass' is a fine answer." Then keep to it, and accept a pass without comment.

**Treat a wrong answer as useful** when it comes, and say why: "That is the most common first answer, and it shows where the rule is confusing." Then give the right answer clearly. Do not pretend the wrong one was right.

**Raise the risk in stages** across the day: pairs, then threes, then the whole room, then practice in front of others. Build safety before you ask people to take risks, not after. There is more on [running a role-play people do not dread](t:4.29).
**Repair it at once and aloud** if you snap at someone: "That was sharp of me. Your answer points at something worth clearing up."

why.text: **Learning depends on people taking risks.** Psychological safety is a shared belief that it is safe to take a risk in this group: to ask, to admit a mistake, to offer a half-formed idea. Learning depends on exactly those behaviours.

**Units with open leaders reported more errors.** The idea grew out of a study of eight hospital units. The units with more open leaders recorded more drug errors, not fewer, and the likely reason is that people there felt able to report them. A later study of 51 teams in a manufacturing company found that psychological safety went with more learning behaviour. Both are studies of working teams. The moves on this page are craft built on them.

**Safety does not mean being nice.** People still challenge each other, and they do it with respect. The working rule for a trainer is to be firm about the answer and kind to the person who gave it. If you soften the correction to protect feelings, people leave with the wrong idea. If you are sharp, the whole room learns what a wrong answer costs.

**The first wrong answer sets the tone.** The group decides how safe it is from what it sees. It watches what happens to the first person who gets something wrong, so your reaction in that moment carries more weight than anything you announced at the start. The cost of all this is time: pairs before every question add two minutes each. Spend those minutes in the first hour, when the belief is forming, and you can ask the room directly later. [Training that encourages individuals to make errors](t:1.22) and learn from them is covered separately. That is evidence about a practice method for one person at a time, not about how safe a group feels.

try.text: Script the first ten minutes of a real session to build safety. Name each move and the behaviour it is meant to open up. Then deliver it aloud, standing, and record it. Ask a colleague to give you three wrong answers in a row and respond to each one aloud. Good looks like this: your own mistake takes under 30 seconds, every question goes through pairs first, and each wrong answer gets a reason it was useful followed by a clear correction.

items: **You assume safety will appear** by itself. It will not, least of all when senior and junior people share a room. Brief the senior person and ask them to speak last. There is more on [handling rank in the room](t:4.38).

**You call on someone by name** with no warning, and it feels like a trap. Say at the start that you will invite people in, give thinking time or a pair conversation first, and let anyone pass without comment.

quiz.q: What is psychological safety?
quiz.a: A shared belief that it is safe to take a risk in this group: to ask, to admit a mistake, to offer a half-formed idea.

quiz.q: You ask the group a question and get silence. The same two confident people usually fill it. What do you do?
quiz.a: Give everyone a minute to think or to compare first guesses in pairs, then take one answer from each pair in turn. When a wrong answer comes, say what makes it useful and then correct it clearly.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes in, someone gives a wrong answer and you hear yourself say "No, we covered that." What do you do?
quiz.a: Repair it at once. Say that was sharp of you, and that the answer points to a confusion worth clearing up. One sharp remark from the trainer can undo an hour of work, so do not let it stand.

topics.title: Engineer an early win
topics.theory: Belonging, self-efficacy and staying the course

situation.text: It is week three of a twelve-week programme for sixteen new team leaders, and four have stopped coming. You look back at session one: a 90-minute overview, a model of leadership and a reading list. The people who left had decided early that they could not do this, or that the course was meant for someone else.

items: **Choose a first win**: a small, real piece of the job that every person completes in session one, in 30 to 40 minutes. A fair test is whether they would show it to their own manager.

**Size it so that it takes effort** and nearly everyone gets there on a first or second attempt. Try it on someone at the level of your least experienced participant. Have a harder version ready for anyone who finishes fast.
**Cut the overview to make room.** Fifteen minutes on the shape of the programme is enough for session one.

**Show people like them who have succeeded.** Invite a past participant from a similar role for five minutes, or play a short recording. Ask them to say what they found hard in week one. A star performer is the wrong choice.
**Build belonging on purpose** in the first ten minutes: names in use, a paired conversation, then a shared first task. There is more on [running introductions that fit the group](t:4.22).
**Help people read nerves as readiness.** Before the task, say: "If you feel a bit keyed up, good. That is your body getting ready to do something new."

**Make the win visible and name it.** Each person shows their work to a partner, and you tell at least half the room one specific thing they did: "You opened with the purpose of the meeting. That is the part most new leads leave out."
**Say what they can now do** to close session one, and what next week adds to it.

why.text: **A real success builds belief best.** Belief in your own ability to succeed is built from four things: succeeding at something real, seeing people like you succeed, being told you can by someone credible, and how you read your own nerves. The theory says the more dependable the source, the more that belief changes. A real success is hard to argue with. The steps above use all four, with the real success doing most of the work.

**An overview gives no proof of ability.** An overview and a reading list supply none of the four. People leave session one knowing how much there is to learn and with no evidence that they can learn it. For someone who arrived confident, that is fine. For someone who arrived doubtful, the doubt now has twelve weeks of content to feed on.

**Belonging helps those who doubt they fit.** Belonging matters most to people with a reason to doubt it. In a study of US college students, a short exercise that eased doubts about fitting in raised the grades of Black students and made no difference to white students. That is a college study, not a workplace one, so use it as a pointer and not as proof. Who might doubt they fit in your cohort is a matter of judgement: perhaps the only person from the warehouse, or the one promoted last week into a room of people with two years in post.

**A win too easy or too hard backfires.** The size of the task is the hard part, and it is craft. A win that anyone could manage without trying proves nothing, and people can tell. One that a quarter of the room fails does harm in exactly the week you can least afford it. The price is content, since session one covers less. Belonging is cheap to build at the start and expensive to repair later, so that is usually the right trade.

try.text: Design the first win for a course you run or plan to run. Check it against three tests: it is a real piece of the job, everyone can finish it with effort, and it happens in the opening session. Try the task on one person who is new to the subject and time them. Then say your introduction to the task aloud, including the line about nerves, and record it.

"You can now open a meeting so people know why they are in it. Use it this week. Next week we add how to close one."

try.title: The four-line frame for the first win
lines: 1. Why we are meeting: "We're here to decide ..."
2. What we need by the end: "By half past, I'd like us to have ..."
3. What I need from you: "I need each of you to ..."
4. How long it will take: "This is 25 minutes, and we'll finish on time."
Harder version for anyone who finishes early: add the sentence you will use if the meeting drifts.

items: **The win is too easy.** It teaches nothing and can feel patronising. If people finish in two minutes, move straight to the harder version.
**The win is too hard** for some, and they fail in public in week one. Try the task beforehand on someone new to the subject, and have people show a partner before anyone shows the room.
**Your example is the star** of last year's group. People conclude that she is not like them. Choose someone ordinary who struggled at first and says so.
**You praise everyone in general terms.** "Great work, all" is not a credible source. Say what one person did and why it worked.

items.label: Walton and Cohen (2007), A question of belonging.
Bandura (1977), Self-efficacy: toward a unifying theory of behavioral change.

quiz.q: Name the four sources of belief in your own ability.
quiz.a: Succeeding at something real, seeing people like you succeed, being told you can by someone credible, and how you read your own nerves.

quiz.q: You are designing a twelve-week programme. Session one is an overview and a reading list. What do you change?
quiz.a: Put a small real task into session one that everyone can finish and show to a partner. Shorten the overview to make room. People decide early whether they can do this and whether they belong.

quiz.q: Everyone finishes your first-session task in two minutes and someone says "Was that it?" What went wrong, and what do you do?
quiz.a: The win was too easy, so it proved nothing and may have felt patronising. Follow it straight away with a harder version that everyone can still complete with some effort.

topics.tierReason: The four sources of self-belief come from an influential theory paper and the belonging finding from one study of US college students, so the practice of an early win is supported but not directly tested in workplace training.

topics.title: Have learners teach each other

situation.text: Eighteen new starters have joined a software company's customer support team, and there is one of you. Six have worked in support before and twelve have not. There are four procedures to learn by Friday. You cannot sit beside each person, and the experienced six are already bored.

items: **Choose content people can check** against a checklist or handout. Split it into parts of equal size. Here that is the four procedures, each with a one-page checklist.

**Give each person one part** and 15 minutes to prepare. Tell them at the start that they will teach it and be asked questions. Hand out a preparation card: the steps in order, the mistake people most often make, and one question to ask the listener.

**Run the teaching in pairs or threes.** Each person teaches for five minutes while the listener follows the checklist and asks at least two questions. Then swap. Everyone teaches, whatever their experience.

**Give the feedback a structure.** The listener looks for two things, such as "every step covered" and "said why the step matters", and uses a set form of words: "One thing that worked, one thing to try." There is more on [feedback people can act on](t:2.27).
**Walk the room and listen for errors.** Write them down and do not interrupt unless a pair is about to agree on something unsafe. There is more on [watching groups while they work](t:4.26).
**Review the key points** with the whole room for ten minutes. Correct the errors you heard without naming the pairs.
**Hold each person accountable.** Close with a five-question quiz that everyone answers alone, or choose at random who reports back.
**Use the peer instruction pattern** for a quick check on a concept: everyone answers a question alone, discusses it with a neighbour for two minutes, then answers again.

why.text: **Teaching helps the teacher learn.** Preparing to teach, and teaching, deepens learning for the person doing the teaching. Explaining forces you to organise what you know and find the gaps. The benefit rests on a pooling of 28 studies. People who prepared to teach learned more than people who studied with no thought of teaching. People who prepared and then taught gained more again, most of all when the teaching was a real exchange with questions and answers.

why.title: Learning by preparing to teach and teaching: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across 28 studies, preparing to teach improved learning compared with studying without expecting to teach (g = 0.35). Preparing and then teaching improved it more (g = 0.56). Interactive teaching gave larger gains than teaching with no exchange.
why.means: Have people prepare and then teach a partner who can ask questions, not only prepare.

why.text: **Peer instruction and peer feedback both help.** The best-known version is peer instruction, used for ten years in introductory physics at Harvard. Students answer a question alone, discuss it with a neighbour, then answer again. The authors report better grasp of the concepts and better problem solving than before they introduced it. Peer feedback helps too. A pooling of 54 controlled studies in schools and universities found that students who assessed each other's work did somewhat better than students who had no assessment, and somewhat better than students assessed by the teacher. Give it a structure so people know what to look for.

**Everyone must teach, and listeners must ask.** Those findings come from schools and universities. The session design here is craft built on them. Two consequences follow from the research. The gain goes to the person teaching, so the design fails if only the experienced six teach while the twelve listen. Everyone has to take a turn. And because a real exchange added most, the listener's two questions are part of the method and not a courtesy.

**Peers can pass on errors confidently.** There is a cost. The listener gets a rougher explanation than yours would be, and peers can pass on errors with great confidence. That is why the content has to be checkable against a page, and why your review afterwards is not optional. As a rule of thumb, keep peer teaching away from material where a wrong version is hard to spot or costly to act on. Teach that yourself. It also needs [a room where being wrong is safe](t:1.17) in front of peers.

try.text: Design a peer-teaching activity for a real course where each learner teaches a segment to a partner. Write the preparation card and say how you will hold each individual accountable. Then try the format yourself: take one procedure you know, prepare for ten minutes with the card, and teach it to a colleague in five minutes while they ask two questions. Notice what you could not explain. That gap is what the method is for.

items: **Some people coast.** Without individual accountability a group can carry them. Use the quiz answered alone, or choose at random who reports back.
**A pair agrees confidently** on a wrong step. Peer teaching can spread errors. Always review the key points afterwards, and correct errors with the whole group without naming anyone.
**One explains while the other nods.** Swap the roles for the next segment so both teach, and require the two questions.
**You use it with no checklist**, for content where the listener cannot tell a good explanation from a bad one. Teach that yourself and use peers for practice afterwards.

items.label: Crouch and Mazur (2001), Peer instruction: ten years of experience and results.
Kobayashi (2019), Learning by preparing-to-teach and teaching: a meta-analysis.
Double, McGrane and Hopfenbeck (2020), The impact of peer assessment on academic performance: a meta-analysis of control group studies.

quiz.q: In the pooling of 28 studies, which helped more: preparing to teach, or preparing and then teaching?
quiz.a: Preparing and then teaching, most of all when the partner could ask questions.

quiz.q: You set up pair teaching. In one pair, the same person does all the explaining while the other nods. What do you do?
quiz.a: Swap the roles for the next segment so both teach. Close with a short quiz that everyone answers alone, so nobody can coast.

quiz.q: After a peer-teaching round you overhear a pair agree, confidently, on a wrong step. What do you do?
quiz.a: Correct it with the whole group when you review the key points, without naming the pair. Peer teaching can spread errors, so always check the key points afterwards.

topics.tierReason: Meta-analyses support learning by teaching and peer assessment, mostly with school and university students, and the size of the gain depends on how the activity is set up.

topics.title: Check it is a skill problem before you train

situation.text: A sales manager at a software company emails you: "The team isn't logging calls in the CRM. Can you run a refresher?" You could have a session designed by Friday. Then, in passing, she mentions that every one of them logged every call in the last week of the quarter, when the bonus report was run.

items: **Ask the quick test** before you design anything: "Could they do it if their job depended on it?" Ask the manager first. Then ask two or three of the people themselves, because the manager's answer is a guess.
**Ask for the evidence behind the answer**: "Has there been a time when they did it properly?" An audit week or a quarter end tells you more than an opinion does.

**If the answer is yes, say so.** It is not a skill problem and a course will not fix it. Ask four short questions about the environment: do people know it is expected, do they have the tools and the time, does anyone tell them how they are doing, and what happens when they do it and when they do not. There is a [full method for diagnosing the cause](t:2.29).

**Find out exactly what they cannot do** if the answer is no. Ask to watch someone do the task, or to see three pieces of real work. "Which step do people get stuck on?" narrows a course down to an hour.

**Check that "won't" is not hiding "can't".** People who doubt they can do something tend to avoid it, and that looks like unwillingness. Ask one or two people to show you, privately, with nothing riding on it.
**Offer to train the skill part** when the cause is mixed, and say plainly what training will not fix.

**Tell the sponsor in three sentences**: what you found, what you recommend, and what a course would and would not change. Be ready to decline work that will not help. There is more on [turning the request into work that helps](t:9.29).

why.text: **Lack of skill is only one cause.** Poor performance has many causes, and lack of skill is only one. People may not know what is expected, may lack the tools, may get no feedback, or may be rewarded for doing something else. Training aimed at those problems wastes money and costs you credibility. The other topics in this part help people learn. This one comes before them, because it tells you whether learning is the answer. The quick test comes from Mager and Pipe's work on analysing performance problems. The reasoning below is craft.

**The test separates can from does.** The test works because it separates what people are able to do from what they do on an ordinary day. If the team logged every call in bonus week, the knowledge is there. Something about ordinary weeks makes not logging the sensible choice: it takes four minutes a call, nobody looks at the records, and the time comes out of selling.

**Unwillingness is usually a reasonable response.** That is the point about "will". Skill against will sounds like a judgement of character, and managers often hear it that way: they can, so they are lazy. Unwillingness is usually a reasonable response to the situation. The right way is slower, or unrewarded, or quietly punished. Treat "will" as a description of the environment and you will find something to fix. Treat it as a description of people and you will be asked for a motivational session.

**The test has two blind spots.** A person with low confidence can look unwilling, which is why you ask to see the task done. And "they did it once" is weak evidence for a task people perform rarely, because [skills that are not used fade](t:5.17). If the last correct performance was a year ago, check again before you rule training out.

try.text: Take a real request for training, yours or a colleague's. Run it through the quick test and the four environment questions. Decide whether to accept it, reshape it or decline it. Then say your three sentences to the sponsor aloud, to a colleague who plays the manager and replies, "I just want the course." Good looks like this: you name what you found without blaming the team, you offer something that would work, and you stay friendly when pushed.

try.title: Words you can use with the sponsor
lines: "I've had a look, and I don't think a refresher will change this. They all logged every call in bonus week, so they know how."
"What's different in an ordinary week is that it takes four minutes a call and nobody looks at the result."
"Three things would help more than a course: a shorter logging screen, a weekly report you go through with them, and saying out loud that it matters."

items: **The sponsor arrives with the solution** already chosen. Test it gently. A useful opener: "If this worked, what would you see people doing differently?"
**You ask only the manager.** Their answer is second-hand. Speak to two or three of the people and look at real work.
**The manager hears "lazy"** when you report back that the team "can but won't". Describe what in the environment makes the wrong way easier.
**You treat a mixed cause** as all one thing. Train the skill part and say plainly what training will not fix.
**You decline and leave it there.** Declining well means offering what would work.

items.label: Mager and Pipe (1997), Analyzing Performance Problems. Third edition.

quiz.q: What question separates a skill problem from the rest?
quiz.a: Could they do it if they really had to?

quiz.q: A manager asks for a course because the team keeps missing a step in the handover. You learn they did every handover correctly during last month's audit. What do you do?
quiz.a: Treat it as an environment problem. They can do it when they have to, so look at expectations, tools, feedback and incentives, and recommend that fix to the manager in place of a course.

quiz.q: You find the cause is half skill and half a system that makes the right way slower. The sponsor only wants the course. What do you say?
quiz.a: Offer to train the skill part, and say plainly that the course will not fix the system. Recommend the system change alongside it.

topics.title: Aim people at getting better, not at looking good

situation.text: You set a hard pricing-objection exercise for ten account executives and say, "Let's see who can get this right." Three people suddenly need to check their email. One offers to take notes for the group. They are not lazy. They have worked out that the safest way to avoid looking bad in front of colleagues is not to try.

items: **Introduce the task as practice**, in words: "This is practice. Most people need a few goes. Compare your second attempt with your first, not with your neighbour's."
**Build in two attempts** so that improvement has somewhere to show. For example: five minutes for a first attempt, three minutes of feedback from a partner, five minutes for a second attempt.
**Keep a record of the first attempt**, as notes or a phone recording, and have each person compare the second against it. Ask: "What did you change, and what did it do?"
**Praise effort that was well aimed**, and name the method: "You checked the figures before you wrote the summary. That is why it holds up." Leave out any praise for being quick or talented.
**Do not rank people in public.** If you score anything, show each person only their own score, next to their earlier one.
**Ask about the approach** when someone struggles in front of others: "What did you try? What would you change next time?"
**Brief any manager in the room** beforehand not to compare people aloud or pick out the best.
**Leave out the talk about attitude.** Do not promise that believing you can improve changes results.

why.text: **Aiming to improve goes with better results.** People who aim to get better tend to learn more and perform better, in study and at work. A large pooling of studies found that link. The same analysis found that aiming to avoid looking bad went with worse results. Aiming to look good showed no clear link either way. These are associations. They do not prove that changing someone's goal changes their results.

why.title: Goal orientation: a meta-analysis
why.found: A learning goal orientation was positively correlated with learning, academic performance, task performance and job performance. Aiming to prove ability was uncorrelated with them. Aiming to avoid looking incompetent was negatively correlated. Goals set by the situation showed stronger links than goals as a personal trait.
why.means: Set up the task so that the goal in the room is to improve, since the goal a situation creates matters more than the one people arrive with.

why.text: **You control what the task is for.** One detail in that analysis is useful to a trainer. Goals set by the situation showed stronger links than goals as a personal trait. You cannot change what kind of person walks in. You do control what the task appears to be for, and the steps above are all ways of making it about improving: two attempts, a comparison with yourself, private scores. That step from the finding to the practice is craft. A phrase like "let's see who can get this right" does the opposite. It turns practice into a contest, and anyone who expects to lose has a reason to sit out.

**Growth mindset evidence is disputed.** The idea of a "growth mindset" is popular and its evidence is disputed. Two pooled analyses in 2018 found a weak link between mindset and achievement and weak effects of mindset programmes, with possible gains for students at academic risk or from poorer backgrounds. A large US school experiment in 2019 found better grades among lower-achieving pupils after a session of under an hour. A 2023 review of 63 studies concluded that the apparent benefits most likely come from weak study design and bias. All of this research is on school and college students. Do not build a workplace programme on it.

**People must believe it is practice.** There is a limit to the practice framing. People need to believe it. If you call it practice while a manager takes notes at the back, the group will trust what it sees. And practice has to end somewhere. Where people must later be assessed, say when, and keep that separate from the sessions where they are learning.

try.text: Take one hard exercise from a real session. Rewrite its introduction so that it is framed as practice, add a second attempt, and remove anything that ranks people. Then say the introduction aloud and record it. Listen for words that turn it back into a contest: "best", "winner", "who can", "fastest". Next, have a colleague attempt something badly on purpose, and practise responding with a comment on the method.

items: **You say "have a growth mindset".** It does little. Change what the task rewards.

**You put up a leaderboard** to add energy. It can push people towards looking good, or towards hiding to avoid looking bad. There is more on [when game elements help](t:2.22). Show each person their own progress.
**You praise effort with no direction.** "You worked so hard" is wasted if the method was wrong. Name what they did that worked, or what to try next.
**Someone senior scores from the back** while you call it practice. People believe what they see. Move the scoring to another day, or say honestly that this one is assessed.
**You tell clients attitude lifts performance.** Do not promise that attitude alone changes results.

quiz.q: Which goal is most clearly linked with worse results?
quiz.a: Aiming to avoid looking bad.

quiz.q: You introduce a hard exercise and three people hang back and let others do it. What do you change?
quiz.a: Frame it as practice. Say most people need a few goes, remove anything that ranks people, and ask each person to compare their second attempt with their first.

quiz.q: A client asks you to add a "growth mindset" session to a workplace programme to lift performance. What do you say?
quiz.a: Advise against building on it. The evidence is disputed, the effects found are weak, and all of it comes from school and college students. Offer to set up the tasks so the goal in the room is to improve.

topics.tierReason: Aiming to get better is linked with more learning and better performance in a large meta-analysis, but the link is correlational, and the evidence that growth mindset programmes raise results is disputed.

topics.title: Treat mistakes in practice as information

situation.text: A retailer is bringing in a new till system. The course walks twenty store staff through each click so that nobody goes wrong, and the session looks smooth. A week later, on the shop floor, people freeze at the first unexpected screen and call a supervisor. They learned one route through the system, and real customers do not follow it.

items: **Check that the method fits.** You need a training copy or simulator where a wrong entry costs nothing. Complete beginners may need a worked example first, as part of [starting with full support](t:2.13). While people still have to say each step to themselves, [an early stage of learning a skill](t:1.26), keep the task simple.
**Give a short orientation** of five to ten minutes: where things are on the screen, how to undo or go back, and where the help is. Do not give the steps.

**Tell people errors are expected and useful**, and print it on the exercise sheet: "You will hit error messages. That is the point of this exercise. Each one tells you something about how the system works."
**Set a goal but no path** for the task: "Create an invoice any way you can." Give 15 to 20 minutes. Each person works on their own screen.
**Keep your hands off their mouse** when someone is stuck. Ask three questions: "What does the message say? What have you tried? What could you try next?"
**Teach recovery as a skill** in its own right: read the message, undo or go back, and know where to look for help. Have each person write down one error and how they got out of it.
**Review the common errors together** for ten minutes. Put three columns on a flipchart: the error, what it means, and the way out.
**Finish with a task nobody has practised**, and judge the session on how people handle that.

why.text: **Training that welcomes errors came out ahead.** Training that encourages people to make errors and learn from them has been pooled across 24 studies. It came out ahead of training that avoids errors, most of all when people later met a task they had not practised. Two parts of the method did the work: letting people explore actively, and telling them plainly that errors are welcome. It suits skills where the real job will throw up surprises.

why.title: Error management training: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across 24 studies with 2,183 people, training that encouraged errors beat error-avoiding or purely exploratory training by a moderate margin (d = 0.44). The gain was larger after training than during it, and largest on tasks that differed in structure from those practised (d = 0.80).
why.means: Use it when people will face unfamiliar situations, and judge it by later performance, not by how smooth the session looked.

why.text: **Exploration teaches a map, not a path.** That is the research. The reasoning that follows is an interpretation, and the timings in the steps are craft. Click-by-click training teaches a path. It never shows people what the system does when they leave the path, so the first error message at work is also the first one they have ever seen. Exploration puts those messages in front of them while help is close and nothing is at stake. What people take away is a rough map of the system and the habit of reading the message. That is what an unfamiliar task calls for.

**People must hear that errors are welcome.** The statement that errors are welcome matters as much as the freedom to explore. Without it, an error message reads as "I have failed", and people stop and wait for you. With it, the message reads as information. The method fails in a room where mistakes are punished, so it depends on [making it safe to be wrong](t:1.17).

**The cost shows on the day.** The session looks messier, people get through fewer features, and some will be frustrated. In the pooled studies the gain was larger after training than during it. A sponsor watching from the back will prefer the smooth version, so agree beforehand that the session will be judged on later performance.

try.text: Take one step-by-step exercise from a real course. Rewrite it as exploration, with a goal, a five-minute orientation and three written prompts about errors. Then practise the hard part aloud. Ask a colleague to play a stuck learner who says, "Just tell me what to click." Respond with the three questions and nothing else, for two minutes. Good looks like this: you never touch the mouse, and they find the next step.

**You use it with complete beginners** who have no picture of the system at all. They may need a worked example first, as part of [starting with full support](t:2.13). While people still have to say each step to themselves, [an early stage of learning a skill](t:1.26), keep the task simple.

quiz.q: When does the advantage of error management training show most?
quiz.a: When people later meet a task they have not practised.

quiz.q: You run a software session as exploration. It feels messy, and the sponsor watching says the old click-by-click version looked smoother. What do you say?
quiz.a: Say that the mess is expected and ask to be judged on later performance. In the pooled studies the gain showed after training more than during it, and most on unfamiliar tasks.

quiz.q: You are training people on a live payments system where a wrong entry moves real money. Do you still let them explore and make errors?
quiz.a: Yes, on a simulator or training copy and never on the real system. Where an error is dangerous or costly, people still need to practise recovering, somewhere safe.

topics.tierReason: One meta-analysis of 24 studies supports it, with the clearest gain on tasks unlike those practised and a smaller gain during training itself.

topics.title: Use play on purpose, not as a break
topics.theory: Play and playful learning in adults

situation.text: The plan for a sales and support team's away day has "Energiser, 15 minutes" at 13:30. Your co-trainer suggests a ball-throwing name game. The afternoon is about handovers between the two teams, and the game has nothing to do with them. Fifteen minutes of the day are about to be spent on something nobody will mention again.

items: **Write the purpose in one line** before you choose an activity. Use one of three stems: "People will try ... safely", "People will see how ... behaves", or "People will trust each other enough to ...". If you cannot finish the line, you have a break. Call it one, keep it to five minutes and borrow from the advice on [the slot after lunch](t:4.43).

**Pick the form that fits the purpose.** Role-play suits trying a conversation, and there is more on [running a role-play](t:4.29). A simulation or a card game with rules suits seeing how a system behaves. Building something together suits trust and shows how the group plans.

**Rig the activity** so the thing you want to talk about will happen. If the topic is handovers, give each team part of the information and a reason to trade. Run it once with two colleagues for ten minutes to check that it does happen.

**List the play and debrief separately** on the plan, as two lines with clock times. As a working rule from practice, give the debrief at least as long as the play: ten minutes of game, ten of debrief.

**Invite people in, with a way out.** Say: "This next part is a game. You can play or you can observe. Observers have a job: write down every time a team decides something without the information it needs."
**Brief it in under two minutes** with the rules on a flipchart, using [instructions people can follow first time](t:4.24). Stop on time, even if nobody has won. Winning was never the purpose.
**Debrief with three questions**, in this order: what happened, what it shows about work, and what you will do with it. Observers speak first. There is more on [how to run the debrief](t:4.28).

why.text: **Evidence for adult play is thin.** Play lets people try things without real consequences, which lowers the cost of getting it wrong. Supporters of playful learning also say it helps people take risks and think more freely. That has rarely been tested with adults. The evidence for play in adult learning is thin: a 2018 review of playful learning in higher education called adult play under-explored and found no settled line of research. So choosing play is a craft decision, and you should present it to a client as one.

**The debrief has the stronger record.** A pooling of 46 samples found that people and teams who held a structured debrief performed about a fifth to a quarter better than those who did not. Most of those studies were not full experiments. The debrief is where the learning is made explicit, which is why it gets its own line on the plan and at least half the slot.

why.title: Do debriefs improve performance? A meta-analysis
why.found: Across 46 samples with 2,136 people, a debrief improved performance by about 25 per cent compared with no debrief (d = 0.67), or about 21 per cent with three outlying studies removed. Teams and individuals gained alike. Facilitated debriefs looked better than unfacilitated ones, though very few studies had no facilitator.
why.means: Keep time for a facilitated debrief after every playful activity.

why.text: **A game gives everyone one shared event.** The reasoning for a game over a discussion is this. A game gives the whole room one small event that everyone saw ten minutes ago. People can say "we hoarded our cards" far more easily than "my team hoards information", and then make the link to work themselves. The price is time. When a group already trusts each other and has a real case to hand, go straight to the case. When trust is low, play can feel exposing, so the observer role matters more.

try.text: Take one playful activity you already use. Say its purpose line aloud. Then stand up and deliver the invitation and the brief against a timer, twice, until both fit inside two minutes. Write three debrief questions and ask a colleague whether the second one points clearly at their real work.
