items: **Some people find play exposing.** Offer the observer role in the same breath as the invitation, with a real job attached, and accept the choice without comment.
**The game overruns** and eats the debrief. Stop on the planned minute. An unfinished game with a debrief teaches more than a finished one without.
**Play that mocks the content** undermines it. A joke quiz about the new pricing policy tells people the policy is a joke. Keep the tone light and the subject respected.
**The activity shuts someone out.** Check it against the room: mobility, sight, hearing, reading speed, and working in a second language. Change the task, not the person's role in it.

**All you want is people awake** after lunch. Then call it a break or a stretch and keep it short. There is more on [using movement where it helps](t:1.15) and on [the slot after lunch](t:4.43). There is also advice on [play on a residential](t:8.6).

items.label: Whitton (2018), Playful learning: tools, techniques, and tactics.
Tannenbaum and Cerasoli (2013), Do team and individual debriefs enhance performance? A meta-analysis.

quiz.q: In the pooled studies, how much better did people and teams perform after a structured debrief?
quiz.a: About a fifth to a quarter better than those who had none. Most of those studies were not full experiments.

quiz.q: Your co-trainer wants a quiz-show game after lunch "to lift the energy". What do you ask before you agree?
quiz.a: Ask what the game is for and how it connects to the content. If it has a purpose, add three debrief questions and give them as long as the game. If it only lifts energy, treat it as a break and keep it short.

quiz.q: You set up a simulation and one person says they would rather not take part. What do you do?
quiz.a: Accept it without comment and give them the observer role, with a job: noting what happens for the debrief. Joining in has to be a choice.

topics.tierReason: The debrief is supported by a meta-analysis, but research on play itself in adult learning is thin and mostly argument and case studies.

topics.title: Make people curious before you tell them

situation.text: You open a session for a customer support team by reading five learning objectives from a slide. Two people check their phones and one opens a laptop. Nobody in the room is wondering about anything, so nothing you say for the next twenty minutes is the answer to a question they have.

items: **Look inside your content for a question.** Good places are a result that surprises people, two cases that began the same and ended differently, or a common-sense prediction that turns out wrong. The test: you teach the answer in the next twenty minutes.
**Write it as one sentence** that people can guess at. A number, a choice between two options, or "what was different" all work. "Why does communication matter" cannot be guessed at.
**Give a foothold.** Two or three facts of background are enough for people to feel that a sensible guess is possible.
**Make everyone commit.** Thirty seconds alone to write a guess, then ninety seconds in pairs to compare. Take three guesses and write them on the flipchart without saying which is right.
**Say when the answer is coming**, and keep the wait short. "You will have the answer in about ten minutes" holds people. Ten minutes is a craft figure. Do not stretch it across a whole morning.
**Give the answer plainly** and go back to the guesses: "Two pairs said the longer reply. Here is what happened." Then say what it means for their work.

**Repeat the move before each main section** in a smaller form: one prediction, thirty seconds, then the content. There is more on [the whole opening of a session](t:4.21) and on [what you can send before the day](t:2.20).

why.text: **Curiosity needs a gap people can close.** One influential account says curiosity arises when people notice a gap in what they know or understand. If that is right, people need to know enough to notice the gap and to believe they can close it. That is the reason for the foothold, and for choosing a question from inside the content.

**One small study links curiosity to memory.** A laboratory study of trivia questions found that people remembered answers better when they were curious. They also remembered unrelated faces shown while they waited for the answer. Both effects were still there a day later. It is one small study using trivia in a brain scanner, so treat it as a pointer. The timings and the guessing routine on this page are craft.

why.title: Curiosity and memory
why.found: People in a brain scanner saw trivia questions they had rated for curiosity, then waited for each answer while an unrelated face was shown. They later remembered more of the answers they had been curious about, and more of the faces shown while curiosity was high. This is one small laboratory study.
why.means: Open with a question people want answered, and treat the memory benefit as a likely bonus, not a promise.

why.text: **Emotion marks what is worth remembering.** Strong emotion can also narrow attention and crowd out detail, so a shocking opener may be recalled while the point behind it is lost. Aim for interest and stop short of alarm.

**A pressing question of theirs comes first.** The trade-off is three or four minutes at the start, and the cost of being seen to withhold. The advice reverses when people arrive with a pressing question of their own, such as a system that goes live on Monday. Then their question is the gap. Answer it first and do not put a puzzle in the way.

try.text: Rewrite the first three minutes of a session you run so that it opens with a question from inside the content. Deliver it aloud to a colleague and stop after the question. Ask them two things: could they make a guess, and did they want the answer. If either is no, change the foothold or the question and try again.

try.title: A worked example: the first three minutes for 10 customer support staff, on writing replies to complaints
lines: Before: "Good morning. Here are today's five objectives."
After, 09:30: "Good morning. I am going to read you two replies to the same customer. She had been charged twice and had already written in once."
"Reply A is four lines. It says sorry in the first line, says what was done, and says when the refund will arrive."
"Reply B is twelve lines. It explains how the billing system works, quotes the policy, and says sorry at the end."
"One of these replies closed the case. The other brought a second complaint. Both writers were experienced and both were trying to help."
09:31: "On your own, write down which reply brought the second complaint, and one reason. Thirty seconds."
09:32: "Now compare with the person next to you. Ninety seconds."
09:33: Take three guesses with reasons. Write the reasons on the flipchart. Do not react.
09:34: "You will have the answer in ten minutes, once we have looked at what a customer reads first."
09:44: "It was Reply B. Three of your reasons are on this chart already. Here is the fourth."

items: **The gap is too wide** and nobody guesses. A gap that wide feels hopeless. Narrow it with a hint or with two options to choose between, then go to pairs.
**The teaser is unrelated** to the content. A striking story about a mountain rescue grabs the room and then competes with your topic. Find the question inside the content.
**You never give the answer**, or you give it after lunch. People stop trusting your questions. Answer inside the time you promised.
**You react to the first guess**, with a nod or a "not quite". The guessing stops. Write every guess down in the same neutral way.
**You promise a memory boost.** The trivia study was a small laboratory task. Say that an opening question gets attention, and leave the claim there.

items.label: Loewenstein (1994), The psychology of curiosity: a review and reinterpretation.
Gruber, Gelman and Ranganath (2014), States of curiosity modulate hippocampus-dependent learning via the dopaminergic circuit.

quiz.q: What did the trivia study find about curiosity and memory?
quiz.a: People remembered answers better when they were curious. They also remembered unrelated faces shown while they waited. Both effects were still there a day later, in one small laboratory study.

quiz.q: You open with a puzzle. People look lost and nobody will guess. What do you do?
quiz.a: Narrow the gap. Give a foothold, such as a hint or two options to choose between, then let pairs guess. A gap that is too wide feels hopeless.

quiz.q: You have a striking story that would grab the room, and it has nothing to do with today's topic. Do you open with it?
quiz.a: No. A teaser unrelated to the content distracts. Find a question from inside the content, and answer it within the time you promise.

topics.tierReason: The curiosity and memory finding comes from a small laboratory brain-imaging study with trivia questions, and the opening moves on this page have not been tested in training.

topics.title: Let people do it, then make them reflect

situation.text: On the second afternoon of a leadership team's offsite, eight people build a raft and race it across a lake. There is cheering, a group photo, and the coach packs up. At dinner someone asks what the afternoon was for, and nobody at the table can say.

items: **Choose a task that behaves like work.** If the team's problem is changing plans under pressure, the task needs a plan that has to change. Write one line: "This task will show us ...".

**Split the slot before the day.** As a craft rule, the activity gets no more than 60 per cent of the time. In a 60-minute slot that is 35 minutes of doing, 20 of reflecting and 5 to set up a second attempt or a first use at work.

**Stop the activity on time.** Then give two minutes of silent writing before anyone speaks: "Write down one moment when things changed, and what you did." People who think before they talk have something to say.
**Ask what happened.** Stay on facts and sequence: "Take me through it. What happened when the first plan failed?"
**Ask why**, and where the same thing happens at work: "Where do we do that with a customer deadline?" Wait for a real example with a date or a name of a project.
**Ask what each person will do differently**, and have them write it as one sentence that starts "Next time I will".

**Have them try it soon.** Run the task again for ten minutes in the same session if you can. If you cannot, agree the first use in the first week back at work, with a [plan for that first use](t:5.2). There is more on [running the debrief in detail](t:4.28).

why.text: **Experience alone does not teach.** People learn from an experience when they reflect on it and connect it to something they will do. A raft race with no reflection is a good afternoon, and that may be worth having for its own sake, but it should not be sold as training.

**Kolb's cycle is a prompt, not a law.** The best-known model is Kolb's cycle of doing, reflecting, forming an idea and trying again. It is widely used. A 2020 review found the model unclear about what counts as a concrete experience and proposed a revised version that still needs testing. Use the cycle as a prompt for the debrief and not as a law.

**Reflection can beat extra practice.** The reflecting half has better support than the cycle. Ten experiments with more than 4,000 people found that stopping to reflect on what you have done can teach more than extra practice, once you have some experience to reflect on. A pooling of 46 samples found that structured debriefs improved later performance by about a fifth to a quarter (Tannenbaum and Cerasoli, 2013).

why.cite: Di Stefano, Gino, Pisano and Staats (working paper, revised 2023)
why.title: Learning by thinking
why.found: In ten experiments with 4,340 people, reflecting on past experience could produce more learning than extra practice. It helped most early on, once people had enough experience to reflect on, and the gain carried over to related tasks. How people reflected made a difference.
why.means: Stop the activity early enough to reflect, and do it while the skill is still new.

why.text: **Hold the line on stopping to reflect.** The trade-off is uncomfortable. Stopping a task people are enjoying feels like spoiling it, and the group will ask for one more go. The research above is the reason to hold the line: the minutes of reflection may be worth more than the extra practice they replace. The condition matters too. People need some experience first, so with complete beginners let them do enough of the task to have something to reflect on. The 60 per cent split, the silent writing and the three questions are craft.

try.text: Take one activity you run. Write the line "This task will show us ...", then the three questions: what happened, why it matters at work, what next. Ask all three aloud to a colleague who has just done any shared task with you, even a meeting. Notice where you are tempted to answer for them, and wait.

items: **The activity eats the debrief time.** Put a stop time on the plan and tell the venue or the outdoor coach beforehand that you will stop on it.
**Answers stay at "it was fun"** and "good teamwork". Ask for one specific moment and what the person did in it.
**Nobody says what went wrong** in front of colleagues. Reflection needs safety, which comes from [making it safe to be wrong](t:1.17). Start with silent writing and pairs before the whole group.
**Someone suggests sorting people** into "learning styles" from the Kolb model. Do not. There is [evidence against learning styles](t:1.10).
**There is no second attempt.** Insight with no next use fades. Rerun the task, or leave with [a named first use at work](t:5.2).

Morris (2020), Experiential learning: a systematic review and revision of Kolb's model.
Di Stefano, Gino, Pisano and Staats (2014, revised 2023), Learning by thinking: how reflection can spur progress along the learning curve. Working paper.

quiz.q: What did the ten experiments find about reflection compared with extra practice?
quiz.a: Stopping to reflect on what you have done can teach more than extra practice, once you have some experience to reflect on.

quiz.q: The raft-building has overrun and ten minutes are left. The group wants one more race. What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop the activity and use the ten minutes for the debrief. Without it people had a good afternoon and cannot say what they learned.

quiz.q: In the debrief people say "It was fun" and "Good teamwork". What do you ask next?
quiz.a: Ask for specifics: what happened when the plan changed, where the same thing happens at work, and what each person will try on Monday.

topics.tierReason: Structured reflection and debriefing after an activity are supported by a meta-analysis and a set of experiments, while the cycle itself is a widely used model with known gaps and little direct testing.

parts.title: What the learner brings
parts.summary: How skill develops, what people bring with them, and how they manage their own learning.

topics.title: Know the stages of learning a skill
topics.theory: Stages of skill acquisition: from spoken steps to automatic

situation.text: A new starter can log a refund in the ticket system if she reads the steps under her breath and nobody talks to her. Her team lead says she has been trained. Put a customer on the phone at the same time and the whole thing falls apart.

items: **Decide which stage people must reach** before they leave you: can do it with the prompt card, without the card, or while holding a conversation.
**Give the steps in words** at the start, and show them once at normal speed and once slowly. Let people say the steps aloud as they work.
**Keep everything else quiet** while the steps are still spoken. No customer, no clock, no second task. [A very small working memory](t:1.1) has no room for them yet.
**Move to repetition with feedback.** Aim for many short runs on varied cases, not one long run.
**Watch for signs someone has moved on**: the card stays on the desk and the muttering stops. Only then add the second demand, such as talking to a customer while doing it.
**Say what the course will not do**, and say it plainly. Fast, automatic performance comes from weeks of use. Agree with the manager where those repetitions will happen.
**Check accuracy again** once people are fluent. A step that has become automatic with a mistake in it is harder to change than one still being read from a card.

why.text: **Skill is learned in three stages.** Paul Fitts described skill learning in three stages in the 1960s. First people work out what to do, slowly and with errors. Then they join the parts and the errors fall. Finally the skill runs with little attention.

**Practice builds the facts into the procedure.** John Anderson's theory explains the change. A new skill starts as facts about what to do. People hold those facts in working memory and often rehearse them in words. With practice, the facts are built into the procedure itself. They no longer have to be recalled and held, so the spoken rehearsal drops away and the load on working memory falls. After that, practice keeps tuning the procedure: it gets applied more widely, more precisely and faster.

**The stages are lab research, applied here.** The stages and the mechanism are research, drawn from laboratory studies of tasks such as geometry proofs. The step list above is a trainer's application of them. There is no agreed figure for how many repetitions a workplace skill needs, so treat the numbers in the example as starting points.

why.title: Acquisition of cognitive skill
why.found: Sets out a theory in which a skill begins as stated facts that are interpreted step by step, is then compiled into procedures that no longer need those facts held in working memory, and is afterwards tuned by further practice.
why.means: Let beginners talk themselves through the steps, protect them from extra demands, and add the second task only when the talking has stopped.

try.text: Watch someone carry out a task they learned in the last fortnight. Do not help. Note where they read, where they mutter and where they pause. Then say aloud to a colleague, in one minute, which stage the person is in and what practice you would give them next.

**Calling it done at stage one.** Name the stage people reached in your handover to the manager.

**Experts who cannot explain.** People at the automatic stage have often lost the words for what they do. Ask them to demonstrate slowly and write the steps yourself, a way of [drawing out steps experts no longer notice](t:3.17).

items.label: Anderson (1982), Acquisition of cognitive skill. Psychological Review, 89(4).
Huber, Applying Educational Psychology in Coaching Athletes. Excerpt describing the three stages of Fitts (1964) and Fitts and Posner (1967).

quiz.q: What are the three stages of learning a skill, in order?
quiz.a: Working out what to do, joining the parts with fewer errors, and performing with little attention.

quiz.q: A new sales rep can run the product demo from her notes. Her manager wants her to take live customer questions during it tomorrow. What do you do?
quiz.a: Hold the questions back and give her more runs first. While she still needs her notes, the demo is using the working memory that answering questions would need.

quiz.q: A retailer wants store staff to be "fast on the new till" by the end of a two-hour session. What do you say?
quiz.a: Promise accurate use with a prompt card, and agree where the repetitions will happen in the first weeks. Speed comes from volume of practice, which a two-hour session cannot hold.

topics.tierReason: Rests on a well-established theory of skill acquisition read in the original paper. The stage model is from laboratory tasks and the step list is an application that has not been tested in workplace training.

topics.title: Find out who is in the room before you design
topics.theory: Trainee characteristics: motivation to learn, self-efficacy and prior ability

situation.text: Two people sit through the same new-manager workshop. One has asked for it for a year. The other was sent after a complaint and expects to be bad at it. You gave them the same session and you will not get the same result.

items: **Find out three things before you design**: what people can already do, whether they chose to come, and whether they expect to succeed. A short form or a call with their manager is enough.
**Ask about the workplace as well.** Will their manager make time for them to use this?
**Open by showing peers have done it.** A short story or demonstration from a peer does more than telling them they can.
**Say what the training is worth** to them in their own terms: fewer escalations, an easier Monday meeting, a step towards a role.

**Take out avoidable anxiety.** Tell people in the joining note what will happen, whether anything is assessed, and that practice is private. There is more on [what the note should tell learners](t:2.21).
**Give an early task everyone can complete**, then raise the difficulty. There is more on [engineering an early win](t:1.18).
**Name what the session could not change** when you report results. Prior ability and a cold workplace are not fixed by a good afternoon.

why.text: **What trainees bring predicts what they gain.** A meta-analysis of twenty years of training research found that what trainees bring predicts what they take away. Motivation to learn was related to knowledge gained, to skill, and most strongly to using the training afterwards. Belief in your own ability to succeed, measured before training, was related to the same outcomes. General mental ability was the strongest predictor of knowledge gained.

**Motivation goes with control, calm and support.** The same study looked at what sits behind motivation to learn. People who believed outcomes were under their own control were more motivated. Anxious people were less so, and older trainees slightly less. A supportive climate at work went with higher motivation. Motivation still predicted outcomes after ability was taken into account.

**These are correlations between measures, not experiments.** They show what goes together. They do not prove that raising someone's confidence will raise their learning, because people who have done well before tend to be both more confident and quicker to learn. The steps follow the authors' advice to build self-belief early and make the benefits clear. They are not tested one by one. The figures in the card below are correlations, which run from 0 (no link) to 1 (a perfect link). They are not on the same scale as the d values quoted on other pages, so do not compare the two.

why.title: Toward an integrative theory of training motivation
why.found: Pooling 20 years of studies, motivation to learn was related to knowledge (.27), skill (.16) and transfer (.58). Self-efficacy before training was related to knowledge (.30), skill (.32) and transfer (.47). Cognitive ability was related to knowledge (.69), skill (.38) and transfer (.43).
why.means: Find out who is in the room before you design, build belief and show the value early, and check the climate people go back to.

try.text: Ring one manager who is sending people to your next session. Ask the four questions below out loud and write the answers as they speak. Then change one thing in your opening ten minutes because of what you heard, and rehearse the new opening aloud once.

try.title: A worked example: four questions to a sending manager, before a new-manager programme
lines: "Who chose this for them: you, them, or HR?"
"What have they already done that is close to this? Have they run a one-to-one before?"
"If I asked them today whether they will be good at it, what would they say?"
"In the fortnight after, when will they get to try it, and will you ask them how it went?"
What the trainer heard: six of eight were sent, two have never run a one-to-one, most expect to find feedback conversations hard, and the manager had not planned anything afterwards.

What changed: the session opens with a team lead from last year's group describing her first awkward one-to-one. The first practice is a three-minute check-in everyone can do. The manager agrees to ask about it at the next team meeting.

try.title: Words you can use in the first five minutes
lines: "Some of you asked to be here and some of you were told to come. Both are fine."
"Nothing today is marked and nothing goes back to your manager from me."
"By lunch you will have run one short conversation that you could use this week. I will show you one first."
"Maya did this course last spring. I have asked her to tell you what her first try was like."

items: **Blaming the learner.** "They were not motivated" is a finding about the set-up as much as the person. Ask what they were told and what waits for them back at work.
**Pep talks.** Telling people they can do it is the weakest way to build belief. Show a peer, then give a real success.
**Screening people out.** Ability predicts learning. Use that to adjust support and pace, and do not use it to turn people away.
**Someone was sent and resents it.** There is advice on [handling that once the session is running](t:4.36).

items.label: Colquitt, LePine and Noe (2000), Toward an integrative theory of training motivation: a meta-analytic path analysis of 20 years of research. Journal of Applied Psychology, 85(5). Full paper.
Colquitt, LePine and Noe (2000). Abstract on the university record.

quiz.q: In the pooled training studies, which outcome was motivation to learn most strongly related to?
quiz.a: Transfer, meaning use of the training afterwards.

quiz.q: A client says last year's sales course failed because "the reps were not motivated". You are asked to run it again. What do you do first?
quiz.a: Ask how people were told about it, whether they expected to succeed and what their managers did afterwards. Motivation to learn is shaped by anxiety, climate and expected value, which the set-up controls.

quiz.q: Your pre-course form shows half the group expects to be bad at presenting. What do you change?
quiz.a: Open with a peer showing a first attempt and give a short task everyone can complete before anything harder. Belief built on a real success is more dependable than reassurance.

topics.tierReason: Rests on a meta-analysis of workplace training studies read in full. The links are correlations, and the steps apply them without having been tested one by one.

topics.title: Teach people to manage their own learning

situation.text: You launch a four-week self-paced product course for a customer team. Week one looks busy. By week three most people have stalled halfway through module two and nobody has told you why.

items: **Have each person set a goal** at the start, one for the course that is specific and a stretch. "Pass the product check at 90 per cent by the 28th" beats "get through it". If the work is brand new to them, start with a goal about learning it and move to a result goal once the basics are in place, as the advice on [setting a learning goal first](t:1.29) explains.
**Agree the effort in hours** and put it in the diary. Three 30-minute blocks a week, named days. Effort that has no slot does not happen.

**Build short prompts into the course** itself, at the start, in the middle and near the end of each module. A prompt is a question on screen that makes the learner stop and check their goal, their attention or their progress. The worked example below has the wording.
**Plan for the stall.** Ask each person to write what they will do in the week when work gets in the way. There is a [when-and-then form for the plan](t:5.2).
**Show progress against the goal** each week, to the learner first. A count of modules done is enough.
**Check in once at the midpoint**, by message or a ten-minute call. Ask about the goal and the hours.
**Keep study-skills teaching short** and tied to the goal. Teach [the study techniques learners can use](t:5.16) when people need them, not as a separate module.

why.text: **Self-paced learners must steer themselves.** Self-regulated learning is what people do to steer their own learning: setting goals, putting in effort, keeping going, checking how it is going. In a classroom the trainer does much of this for them. In self-paced formats nobody does.

**Four habits went with learning.** A meta-analysis of 430 studies of adults in work-related training asked which of these habits go with learning. Four stood out: the level of the goal people set, persistence, effort, and belief in their own ability. Together they explained 17 per cent of the differences in learning after ability and prior knowledge were taken into account. Planning, monitoring, asking for help and controlling emotion showed no reliable link with learning when measured separately.

**Prompts raised learning in an online course.** Prompts are one tested way to act on this. In an online course, trainees who were asked reflective questions throughout learned more than a control group and fewer of them dropped out. The gain in learning came through spending more time on the material.

**One finding is correlational, one an experiment.** The four-habit finding is correlational. The prompt finding is an experiment in online training. The step list combines both with ordinary practice. The prompts in the worked example are written for that example and are not the wording used in the study.

why.title: Self-regulated learning in work-related training
why.found: Across 430 studies and 90,380 trainees, goal level, persistence, effort and self-efficacy had the strongest links with learning and together explained 17 per cent of the variance after cognitive ability and pre-training knowledge. Planning, monitoring, help seeking and emotion control were not significantly related to learning.
why.means: Put your design effort into goals, time on task and keeping people going. A planning template alone is unlikely to help.

try.text: Take a self-paced course you run or have taken. Write the goal question and three prompts for its first module. Then read them aloud to a colleague and ask whether they sound like a person or a form. Rewrite the ones that sound like a form.

items: **Easy goals.** "Finish the course" asks for attendance. Push for a level and a date.

**Blaming a stall on motivation.** Ask about hours first. Often the diary slot was never protected.

quiz.q: Which four self-regulation habits had the strongest links with learning in work-related training?
quiz.a: Goal level, persistence, effort and self-efficacy.

quiz.q: A client wants to add a 45-minute "how to plan your study" module to the front of an online course with a high drop-out rate. What do you suggest?
quiz.a: Replace it with a specific goal, diary slots and short prompts through the course. Planning by itself showed no reliable link with learning, while prompts raised learning and cut drop-out in an online experiment.

quiz.q: Three weeks into a self-paced course, a learner has done one module of six. What do you ask first?
quiz.a: Ask what goal they set and how many of their planned sessions took place. Effort and persistence are the usual gap, and they are fixed with protected time more often than with new content.

parts.title: Goals, attention and outcomes
parts.summary: What research says about setting goals, kinds of learning outcome, wandering attention, and why people expect to succeed and value the result.

topics.title: Set a learning goal first when the task is new
topics.theory: Goal setting: performance goals, learning goals and the limit for new, complex tasks

situation.text: A software company hires six account managers. On day one the sales director gives them the target: four qualified meetings a week from week two. By Wednesday they are ringing anyone who will pick up and reading the pitch from a sheet. Nobody is practising the discovery questions you taught on Tuesday.

items: **Ask one question about the task**: do people already know how to do it? If they do, set a performance goal. If they are still working out how, set a learning goal.

**Write the learning goal** to be as specific and as hard as a target. "By Thursday, find and write down four questions that get a customer talking about cost" is a learning goal. "Learn about discovery" is a wish.
**Say what happens to the number** out loud, having agreed it with the sponsor. "Your meetings target starts in week four. Until then I am counting the questions you can use."
**Give feedback against the goal.** A tally in the workbook is enough: questions found, questions tried, questions that worked.
**Break a distant goal into near ones**: one for today's practice round, one for the week.

**Switch to a performance goal** when people can do the task without the prompt card, the second of [the stages of learning a skill](t:1.26). Make it specific and hard, with a date: "Three qualified meetings a week by the end of week six."

**Have each person leave with one goal** at the end of a course, of the right kind for the stage they have reached, written into [the plan for first use at work](t:5.2). Tell their manager which kind it is.

why.text: **Specific, hard goals raise performance.** Goal setting is among the most tested ideas in work psychology. Locke and Latham's summary of 35 years of studies reports that a specific, hard goal produces higher performance than telling people to do their best. The pooled effects they cite run from d = .42 to d = .80. The findings cover more than 100 tasks and more than 40,000 people, in laboratories, simulations and workplaces. Goals point attention, raise effort and keep people going. They work best when people are committed and can see feedback on progress.

**Hard outcome goals can hinder new learners.** The limit sits in the same paper. The effect is smaller on complex tasks: d = .41 for the most complex against d = .77 for the simplest. When people do not yet know how to do the task, a hard outcome goal can pull attention away from learning it. Kanfer and Ackerman tested this with US Air Force trainees learning a simulated air traffic control task. A score goal in the first trials did not help, and in Locke and Latham's account it got in the way of learning. A goal given after some practice raised performance for people of high and low ability. Their explanation is attention: early on the task takes all of it, and watching your score takes some away.

**A learning goal beat a target in simulation.** Later work changed the kind of goal and kept the idea of having one. Seijts and Latham describe a business simulation in which people asked to find a set number of strategies ended with almost twice the market share of people given a market-share target. The pages read do not say who took part. Their rule is step one.

**The learning-goal findings are pointers, not proof.** The main goal-setting effect has been found with people in real jobs. The learning-goal findings come from a simulation and from military trainees on a laboratory task, so they are pointers and not workplace proof. The moment to switch and the wording are trainer's judgement.

**This page adds which kind comes first.** The advice on [managing your own learning](t:1.28) asks for a specific stretch goal at the start of a self-paced course, and the studies behind it link the level of goal people set with how much they learn. That holds. This topic adds which kind to set first when the skill is new. [The aim people arrive with](t:1.21) is covered separately. Here you choose the goal you assign.

why.title: Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation
why.found: Summarising 35 years of research, specific hard goals led to higher performance than do-your-best instructions, with pooled effects from d = .42 to d = .80, and smaller effects on complex tasks. Commitment and feedback strengthened it.
why.means: Set specific, hard goals and show progress against them. On a new, complex task, make the goal about finding how to do the task.

try.text: Take a course you will run in the next month. List every goal it sets, including the client's target and your closing action plan. Mark each P for performance or L for learning. For each P that lands before people can do the task without a prompt, write the learning goal that should come first. Then ring the sponsor and agree the date the target starts.

try.title: Words you can use with the sponsor and with the group
lines: To the sales director: "I want them at four meetings a week as much as you do. They will get there sooner if the first three weeks are measured on the call itself."
"Can we agree the number starts in week four, and until then you ask them what they tried on their calls?"
To the group: "For the next three weeks nobody is counting your meetings. I am counting the questions you can use without looking down."
"Your goal for this round is small. Try two of your questions and write down what you heard."
"From week four you have a number. By then you will know how to hit it."

items: **A vague learning goal.** Give it a count and a date, as you would a target.
**Holding the target back too long.** Once people can do the task, a learning goal alone leaves effort on the table. Switch.
**A manager who keeps asking** for the number. Brief them before day one and give them a question to ask in its place.
**A hard goal with a bonus** attached. Locke and Latham note that a very hard goal tied to a bonus for hitting it can hurt performance. Keep early goals away from pay.
**Treating this as settled.** The learning-goal studies used simulations. Watch your own groups and adjust.

quiz.q: In Locke and Latham's summary, how does a specific hard goal compare with telling people to do their best, and where is the effect smaller?
quiz.a: It produces higher performance, with pooled effects from d = .42 to d = .80. The effect is smaller on complex tasks.

quiz.q: A retailer rolls out a new stock system. The area manager wants every store to hit a 98 per cent accuracy target in week one. Staff have had one two-hour session. What do you propose?
quiz.a: A learning goal for the first fortnight, such as each person completing five types of stock adjustment without the card, with the accuracy target starting after that. A hard outcome goal before people know the steps can pull attention from learning them.

quiz.q: At the end of a two-day workshop for new managers you ask everyone to set a goal. One writes "cut team turnover by 10 per cent this year". She has never run a one-to-one. What do you say?
quiz.a: Keep that as the long aim and set a near learning goal for the first month, such as running four one-to-ones and noting which questions got people talking. She does not yet know how to reach the outcome, so the first goal should be about finding out.

topics.tierReason: Rests on a published summary of 35 years of goal-setting research, read in full, plus an article and two technical reports on learning goals. The learning-goal evidence is from a simulation and from military trainees on a laboratory task.

topics.title: Know what kind of outcome you are teaching
topics.theory: Learning outcomes: cognitive, skill-based and affective

situation.text: A client asks for a half-day on handling customer complaints. The draft has three objectives. Read closely, one is about knowing the refund policy, one is about running the conversation, and one is about staff believing that a complaint is worth their time. The plan teaches all three with slides and tests all three with a ten-question quiz.

items: **Sort every objective** into one of three kinds before you design anything. Cognitive: what people know and how they think about it. Skill-based: what they can do. Affective: what they believe, value or feel able to do.

**Split any objective that holds two kinds.** "Understand and apply the refund policy" is one cognitive objective and one skill-based objective. Write both in the form for [objectives you could observe](t:2.11).

**Pick the method by kind.** Knowledge needs explanation, examples and recall. A skill needs a demonstration, practice and feedback, the pattern of [behaviour modelling training](t:2.34). An attitude or a belief in your own ability needs a real success, a credible peer and a reason that matters to the person. There is more on [engineering an early win](t:1.18) and on [what trainees bring with them](t:1.27).

**Pick the measure by kind.** Test knowledge with questions that make people recall or decide. Assess a skill by watching the task done against a checklist, which is [assessing the real task](t:2.25). Ask about confidence and intent directly, on a short scale, before and after.
**Check the three columns line up.** For each objective, the method should give practice at the thing the measure will ask for. Where they do not match, change the method or the measure.

**Tell the client what you will measure**, by kind, and when. Knowledge and skill at the end of the session. Use on the job and belief later, in the follow-up measures: [measuring what people do differently](t:6.4) and [going back later to see what stuck](t:6.5).
**Report by kind.** "Knowledge up, skill reached standard for 14 of 16, confidence unchanged" tells the client far more than a single score.

why.text: **The scheme sorts learning into three kinds.** In 1993 Kraiger, Ford and Salas argued that training evaluation lacked models with theory behind them. They drew on cognitive, social and instructional psychology to build a classification with three kinds of learning outcome: cognitive, skill-based and affective. Each kind has its own suggested measures. A later review by Ford, Kraiger and Merritt says the scheme was built from the learning taxonomies of Bloom, Gagné and Krathwohl. A textbook from the Society for Industrial and Organizational Psychology gives a plain measure for each kind: knowledge of facts and principles, error-free performance of a task, and motivation and confidence.

**The scheme is a classification, not proof.** What this is and is not. The scheme is a way of classifying outcomes, written for workplace training by work psychologists. The summary read does not report an experiment showing that courses sorted this way get better results. Its value is practical: it stops you teaching a skill with a talk, and it stops you claiming a change in behaviour from a quiz.

**One test catches only one kind.** It also fills a gap in the evaluation models. Kirkpatrick's second level is simply called learning, and there is more on [using Kirkpatrick as vocabulary, not proof](t:6.2). This scheme says learning comes in three kinds and a single test will catch only one of them. The affective kind is the one most often left out. A [meta-analysis of web-based and classroom training](t:3.25) reported that too few studies measured affective outcomes to estimate an effect at all.

**The method column is this site's own.** The method column in the steps is this site's application. It draws on other topics: [behaviour modelling for interpersonal skills](t:2.34), [the stages of skill](t:1.26) and the sources of [belief in your own ability](t:1.18). The paper's summary names the kinds and the measures, not the methods.

why.title: Cognitive, skill-based and affective learning outcomes
why.found: Proposes a classification of learning outcomes for training evaluation, drawn from cognitive, social and instructional psychology. It names three kinds of outcome, cognitive, skill-based and affective, and suggests evaluation measures for each.
why.means: Decide which kind each objective is, then choose a measure made for that kind. One end-of-course quiz measures knowledge only.

try.text: Take the objectives for a course you are building now. Sort them into the three kinds and fill in one row of the table below for each. Then show the table to the client or a colleague and talk them through it for two minutes. Notice which kind has no measure.

try.title: Two confidence questions you can use before and after
lines: "How confident are you that you could handle an annoyed customer's complaint by yourself, start to finish? 1 is not at all, 5 is completely."
"In the next two weeks, how likely are you to handle a complaint yourself before calling a manager? 1 is very unlikely, 5 is very likely."
Ask both on paper, with no names if the group is small. Compare the group's answers before, after and at three weeks.

items: **Calling everything "understanding".** If the objective has a verb you cannot watch, you have not yet decided which kind it is.
**Teaching a skill as knowledge.** People can pass the quiz on the four steps and still not be able to run the conversation. Check the method against the measure.
**Skipping the affective kind** because it sounds soft. Confidence before training is [related to learning and to later use](t:1.27). Two questions cost one minute.
**Treating a confidence rating as proof** of skill. [People misjudge their own ability](t:1.4), most of all when new. Report it as belief, next to the observed skill.
**Forcing a whole task** into one box. Many real tasks need all three. Split them and plan each part.

Ford, Kraiger and Merritt (2009), An updated review of the multidimensionality of training outcomes: new directions for training evaluation research. In Learning, Training, and Development in Organizations, 135 to 165.

quiz.q: What are the three kinds of learning outcome in Kraiger, Ford and Salas's scheme?
quiz.a: Cognitive, skill-based and affective. Each has its own measures.

quiz.q: A technology company asks you to prove its new product course worked. The only data is a 20-question quiz with an average of 88 per cent. The stated aim was that reps can run a demo for a customer. What do you tell them?
quiz.a: The quiz shows a cognitive outcome, which is knowledge of the product. The aim is skill-based, so it needs an observed demo against a checklist before anyone can say the course met it.

quiz.q: You are designing a session on giving feedback for new managers. The sponsor says most of them avoid these conversations because they expect them to go badly. Which kind of outcome is missing from a plan made only of a model and a practice round, and what do you add?
quiz.a: The affective kind: belief that they can do it and intent to try. Add an early round everyone can complete, a peer describing a first attempt, and a confidence question before and after.

topics.title: Understand attention and mind wandering
topics.theory: Sustained attention and mind wandering during lectures

situation.text: You are 25 minutes into a product briefing on a video call for 40 customer support staff. Cameras are on and people are looking at the screen. You have no idea how many of them are thinking about their inbox.

items: **Assume some minds are elsewhere** in any stretch of listening, and more of them the longer you talk without a change. Plan for it.
**Cut long inputs into segments**, meaning any input longer than about ten minutes. The length is a judgement, not a research figure, and there is an account of [why there is no fixed span](t:2.14).
**Put recall questions after each segment**, two or three on the material just covered. Everyone answers alone, in writing or in the chat held back until you say "send". Allow two minutes.
**Give the answers straight away** and move on. Mark nothing. The point is the attempt to recall, a case of [making practice harder where it helps](t:1.3).
**Tell people the questions are coming** at the start. "Every eight minutes or so I will stop and ask you three quick questions. Nobody sees your answers."
**Leave room for notes.** Ask people to add one line of their own to the handout after each set of questions.
**Put the content that matters most early**, and ask about it again in the last set of questions.

why.text: **Minds often wander while people listen.** Mind wandering means attention drifting from the task to unrelated thoughts. Researchers measure it by stopping people and asking what they were thinking about. It is common while people listen.

**Attention fell as the lecture went on.** One study filmed 21 undergraduates watching a 40-minute recorded lecture. Every five minutes they rated how well they were attending, and they took a recall test afterwards. Rated attention fell as the lecture went on. In blocks where attention was lower, people recalled less of that block. This is a correlational finding from one lecture and a small group.

**Quizzes between segments reduced mind wandering.** The best-known test of a remedy is by Szpunar, Khan and Schacter. Harvard undergraduates watched a 21-minute online statistics lecture cut into four segments. One group answered a short quiz after every segment. The others did arithmetic or re-read the same questions with the answers. In the second experiment the tested group reported mind wandering at 19 per cent of the checks, against 41 per cent for the group that was not tested and 39 per cent for the group that re-read. The tested group also took more notes, did better on the final test and felt less anxious about it. Re-reading the answers made no difference.

**The studies used students, not workers.** Where the evidence is from. Both studies used university students watching recorded lectures in a laboratory, with 80 people in one and 21 in the other. No opened study tests quiz breaks with adults in workplace training. The steps borrow the method because the mechanism is plausible for any listening task and the cost is two minutes. Treat it as a reasonable bet.

**There is no magic segment length.** [Bradbury's review of attention spans](t:2.14) found no good primary evidence for a limit of ten to fifteen minutes and found that attention varied more with the teacher than with the format. So there is no magic segment length. Attention drifts over an unbroken stretch and a recall task pulls it back. There is separate advice on [arousal and energy, the body's side](t:1.14). This topic covers where the mind goes while the body sits still.

why.title: Interpolated memory tests reduce mind wandering and improve learning of online lectures
why.found: In two experiments with 80 Harvard undergraduates watching a 21-minute online lecture in four segments, a short test after each segment reduced mind wandering (19 per cent of checks, against 41 per cent with no tests and 39 per cent with re-reading, in experiment two), increased note taking and improved learning.
why.means: Break recorded or live input into short segments and put a brief recall quiz between them. Re-showing the key points does not do the same job.

try.text: Take a real input of 30 minutes or more that you will deliver soon: a briefing, a webinar or a section of a workshop. Mark the breaks, write the recall questions and run it. At the end, ask the group one question on paper: "How much of the time was your mind on this, out of ten?" Keep the number and compare it next time.

items: **Trusting faces.** A room that looks attentive tells you about attention at best, and nothing about what will be remembered. There is more on [not trusting how fluent the room looks](t:1.4).
**A recap slide replaces the quiz.** In the study, re-reading the answers did no better than doing nothing.
**Questions that feel like an exam** or are too hard. Keep them short and private. The tested students felt less anxious, and a public score would undo that.
**Quoting a segment length as science.** Five and a half minutes was simply what that experiment used.
**Using quiz breaks to rescue content** that should not be a talk. If people need to practise, let them practise.
**Fidgeting that spreads late** in a long input. In the filmed lecture it rose over time and went with poorer recall. Take it as a prompt for a break.

quiz.q: In Szpunar, Khan and Schacter's second experiment, what happened to mind wandering when students were quizzed after each segment of an online lecture?
quiz.a: It fell to 19 per cent of the checks, against 41 per cent for students who were not tested and 39 per cent for students who re-read the answers.

quiz.q: A client asks you to record a 45-minute compliance update as one video because "people can watch it when they like". What do you propose?
quiz.a: Cut it into short segments with two or three recall questions after each, answers shown at once. The student evidence suggests attention drifts across an unbroken recording and a recall task brings it back, and it costs a few minutes.

quiz.q: A co-trainer says the afternoon session went well because "everyone was looking at me the whole time". You saw no recall and no practice in it. What do you say?
quiz.a: Looking at the speaker shows attention at best, and people can look and be elsewhere. Add a short written recall task next time and judge the session by what people can produce.

topics.tierReason: Rests on two laboratory studies of university students watching recorded lectures and one review of lecture attention. No opened study tests the method with adults in workplace training.

topics.title: Know why people expect to succeed and why they value it

situation.text: A technology company moves its customer success team onto a new forecasting tool and books a day of training. Half the team think it is head office's latest fad. The other half can see the point and are privately sure they will be the slow one in the room.

items: **Ask two questions before the session** on a 1 to 5 scale. "How well do you expect to do at this?" and "How useful will this be in your job?" Add a third in words: "What will this cost you?"
**Read the answers as a two-by-two.** The worked example sets out the four cases.

**Build belief when expectation is low**, with a real early success and a peer who has done it. There is a [method for engineering an early win](t:1.18). Do this before you say anything about why the subject matters.
**Have people work out the use themselves** when value is low. Give five minutes to write, alone: "Where in your next two weeks could you use this? What would it save you or get you?" Then pairs.
**Offer one or two everyday examples** as prompts. "Some people use it for the Monday forecast call."
**Lower the cost you control.** Protect the time, cut the pre-work to what is needed and say what people can stop doing.
**Come back to the written uses** at the close, and carry one into [the plan for first use at work](t:5.2).

why.text: **Effort depends on expectation and value.** Expectancy-value theory says that how hard people try, and whether they choose to take part at all, depends on two judgements. One is whether they expect to do well. The other is how much they value the task. Wigfield and Eccles split value into four parts: how much doing well matters to you, how much you enjoy the task, how useful it is for your plans, and what it costs in effort and in other things given up.

**Expectation predicted grades, value predicted choices.** In their studies the two judgements predicted different things. Expectations and beliefs about ability predicted later grades. Value predicted choices, such as whether a pupil intended to carry on with maths and whether they did. For a trainer, low expectation tends to show as poor performance in the room. Low value shows as people who do not come, do not start the e-learning or do not use the skill afterwards. That reading across to training is this site's.

**Writing about usefulness helped doubtful pupils.** Usefulness is the part of value that has been tested as an intervention. In a randomised field experiment in high school science classes, Hulleman and Harackiewicz asked pupils to write about how the course material connected to their own lives. For pupils who expected to do poorly, this raised interest in science and course grades. A replication in a college course found gains for low-performing students, and a database of replications records its outcome as mixed.

**How people come to see the value matters.** In three laboratory studies with undergraduates learning a mental arithmetic method, telling low-confidence students that the method was useful lowered their performance and interest. Having them write their own reasons helped. Everyday examples raised their interest more than career examples did. Hence steps three to five: belief first, then value in their own words.

**Almost none of the evidence is from work.** Where the evidence is from. Almost all of it is from schools and universities. Wigfield and Eccles studied pupils in school grades one to twelve, mostly European American and from lower-middle and middle-income families. The writing studies used school pupils and undergraduates. No opened study tests the writing exercise with adults at work. The nearest workplace evidence is on [what trainees bring with them](t:1.27), where motivation to learn and belief in your own ability went with learning and later use. The advice on [choice, progress and connection](t:1.16) names the two judgements in one line. This topic is the working method. The two-by-two and the wording are trainer's judgement.

why.title: Promoting interest and performance in high school science classes
why.found: A randomised field experiment with high school science pupils. Pupils who wrote about how the course material related to their own lives showed more interest in science and better course grades, when they had started with low expectations of success. The summary reports the gain for that group only.
why.means: Let people write their own answer to "where would I use this?". Expect the gain among those who doubt themselves, and do not promise it for everyone.

try.text: Before your next course, send the three questions below to every participant. Sort the replies into the four cases. Change your first 15 minutes to suit the largest group. On the day, run the five-minute writing task and collect the uses people wrote.

try.title: The three questions, and the writing task in the room
lines: Before the course: "How well do you expect to do at using the new forecasting tool? 1 is badly, 5 is very well."
"How useful do you think it will be in your own job? 1 is no use, 5 is very useful."
"What will taking part cost you? Think of time, other work and anything you are not looking forward to."

"Now tell the person next to you the one you would try first."

items: **Selling the benefits from the front.** For people who doubt themselves, being told how valuable something is can make things worse. Ask first.

**Blaming low value on attitude.** Sometimes the training is not useful to that person. If several people cannot find a use, tell the sponsor. There is a [full method for diagnosing the cause](t:2.29).
**Ignoring cost.** A course that eats two evenings of pre-work has lowered its own value before it starts.
**Assuming school findings carry over whole.** The size of any effect at work is unknown.
**Asking the questions and changing nothing.** Let people see that the opening reflects their answers.

items.label: Wigfield and Eccles (2000), Expectancy-value theory of achievement motivation. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 25, 68 to 81.
Hulleman and Harackiewicz (2009), Promoting interest and performance in high school science classes. Science, 326(5958), 1410 to 1412.
Canning and Harackiewicz (2015), Teach it, don't preach it: the differential effects of directly-communicated and self-generated utility value information. Motivation Science, 1(1), 47 to 71.
Hulleman, Kosovich, Barron and Daniel (2017), Making connections: replicating and extending the utility value intervention in the classroom. Journal of Educational Psychology. Authors' summary page.
FORRT Replication Atlas, entry for Hulleman and Harackiewicz (2009), listing the 2017 replication with a mixed outcome.

quiz.q: In Wigfield and Eccles's studies, what did expectations of success predict, and what did value predict?
quiz.a: Expectations predicted later performance, such as grades. Value predicted choices, such as whether pupils intended to continue a subject and did.

quiz.q: You are about to open a mandatory course on a new expenses system. The pre-course answers show most people expect to manage it easily and rate its usefulness at 1 or 2. What do you do in the first ten minutes?
quiz.a: Run the short writing task on where it could save them time or trouble, with one or two everyday prompts, then pairs. Their problem is value, not belief, and value people work out themselves holds better than a speech.

quiz.q: A sponsor wants to open a presentation-skills day for nervous graduates with a senior leader explaining how vital presenting is for their careers. What do you advise?
quiz.a: Move the leader to later in the day and open with a short task every graduate can complete. In laboratory studies, telling low-confidence students how useful something was lowered their performance, so build a success first and then ask them where they would use the skill.

topics.tierReason: Rests on a theory paper and intervention studies read in summary or in full. Nearly all the evidence is from school pupils and university students, and none of the opened studies tests the method with adults at work.

parts.title: Plan the programme
parts.summary: Needs, competencies, the shape over time, managers, and what happens before and after.

topics.title: Find the real need behind the request

situation.text: The head of support at a software company emails: "We need a time management course for the team, ideally before the end of the quarter." She has a budget and a date in mind. What she has sent you is a proposed solution. Nobody has yet checked what the problem is, and she is the only person you have heard from.

items: **Write the request down** word for word, with who made it. Under it, write the gap as one sentence: "Now people do X. They should do Y. We know because Z." Leave blank whatever you cannot fill in. The blanks are your list of things to find out.

**Ask the requester five questions** in the first conversation: what are people doing now, what should they be doing, how do you know, what happens if nothing changes, and what has already been tried. The list is craft. There is more on [running the discovery conversation](t:9.3).

**Ask for three kinds of access** before you leave that conversation: the figures she already looks at, covering the last three months, the names of four to six people to talk to, and an hour to watch the work being done.

**Interview for more than one view.** Choose two people who do the job well, two who are typical or newer, and one team leader. Give each twenty minutes and open with "Talk me through the last time this went badly. What happened first?"
**Watch for an hour.** Note each point where someone waits, looks something up, asks a colleague or works round a tool. Write down what you saw before you interpret it.

**Sort what you found into two columns:** skill and knowledge, and everything else, meaning tools, incentives and unclear expectations. There is a [quick test for telling them apart](t:1.20) and a [full method for diagnosing the cause](t:2.29).

**Send the sponsor one page** within a week. Put the gap in terms she cares about, such as cost, complaints, time lost or risk. "Refunds take nine days and should take three" lands better than "people need process training".

why.text: **The request and the real need often differ.** A programme built on an untested request can miss the real problem however well it is made. A short analysis lowers that risk. The request and the real need often differ, so test the request against evidence from several people, then tell the sponsor what you found.

**Research backs analysing first.** A review of the research on workplace training recommends a training needs analysis before anything is built. It should say what needs to be trained, for whom, and in what kind of organisation. A meta-analysis of leadership training found that programmes built on a needs analysis did better than those that were not. That is the research. The five questions, the interview mix and the one-week limit are craft.

**Each person sees only one part.** The reason to go beyond the requester is that each person sees one part of the job. A manager sees the results and the complaints. The people doing the work see the waiting, the missing information and the tool that freezes. Existing figures show how big the problem is but seldom why. You need all three to say what the cause is, and observation is the check on the other two, because people tend to describe the job as it should be done.

**The trade-off is speed.** A sponsor who has budget now does not want a month of study, and a long analysis can lose the work. Keep it to days. For a small, low-cost request where the cause is plain, two conversations and a look at the figures can be enough.

try.text: Take a real request, current or past. Write the gap sentence and mark the blanks. Then list who you would interview, what figures you would ask for and what you would watch. If the request is live, hold one of the interviews this week and write the one-page summary, keeping what was asked for apart from the cause you found.

try.title: A worked example: one-page needs analysis for a software company's support team

head: Heading
What goes on the page
rows: The request
"A time management course for the support team." From the head of support.
The gap
Now: refund requests take about nine days from first contact to payment. Should be: three days. We know because of the support system's own case reports for the last three months.
Who we heard from
Head of support. Two experienced agents, two newer agents and one team leader, twenty minutes each. One hour sitting with the refunds queue.
What we saw
Agents open a refund case within a few hours. Each case then waits about two days for approval from the finance team. Agents chase by message and keep cases open in the meantime.
Cause that training can fix
Newer agents are unsure which calls to take first when the queue is long. A short session on prioritising, with practice on real queues, would cover it.
Cause that training cannot fix
The two-day wait for approval. This needs a change to the approval step, agreed with finance.
What we recommend
A ninety-minute session on prioritising for the eight newer agents. Separately, a conversation between the head of support and finance about approving small refunds the same day.
What we could not check
Whether the nine-day figure is the same across all shifts. The reports do not split it.
Decision needed from you
Go ahead with the short session, and say who will raise the approval step with finance.

items: **The sponsor resists** because diagnosis delays the course. Keep it short, a few days and not a few weeks, and show what it saves. If the answer turns out not to be training, you can [reshape the brief](t:9.29).
**The performance data is missing** or poor. Say so on the page, as in the example, and lean on observation.
**You interview only the sponsor's picks.** Ask for a mix, including someone newer, and ask each person who else you should talk to.
**The cause is mixed,** which is common. Name the part training can fix and the part it cannot, and price only the first.
**The answer is already decided** when you arrive at interviews. Ask about the last real case and write down what people say before you sort it.

items.label: Salas and colleagues (2012), The science of training and development in organizations: what matters in practice. Psychological Science in the Public Interest.
Lacerenza and colleagues (2017), Leadership training design, delivery, and implementation: a meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology.

quiz.q: What does a training needs analysis set out?
quiz.a: What needs to be trained, for whom, and in what kind of organisation. It also separates causes training can fix from causes it cannot.

quiz.q: A head of support asks you for a time management course. You have only spoken to her. What do you do before agreeing?
quiz.a: Write down the gap between what people do now and what they should do. Then gather evidence from more than the requester: three months of existing figures, an hour of observation and four to six short interviews across the team.

quiz.q: Your analysis shows the main cause is a slow approval step in another department, with a small skill gap on top. What do you tell the sponsor?
quiz.a: Name both causes. Say which part training can fix and which part needs a change to the process, and put the gap in terms the sponsor cares about.

topics.tierReason: A research review recommends a needs analysis before training and one meta-analysis links it to better leadership training, but the cause-analysis methods themselves are practitioner frameworks.

topics.title: Define what good looks like in the role

situation.text: A retailer asks for a programme for new team leaders and sends a list: delegation, feedback, rotas, absence, health and safety. It is a pile of topics. Nothing on it tells you what a capable team leader does on a Tuesday morning, so you cannot tell what to teach first or when someone is ready.

items: **Interview people who do the job well.** Talk to two or three of them, and to their managers, for thirty minutes each. Ask "What did you do last week?" and "What do you do that someone three months in does not?" This way of gathering the list is craft.
**Make each item something you could see** the person do: a verb, an object and a standard. "Gives feedback on a specific piece of work within two days" can be seen. "Understands feedback" cannot.
**Cut the list.** Eight to twelve statements for the first level is a workable size from practice. Merge near-duplicates and drop anything nobody mentioned doing.
**Sort into three levels:** foundation, intermediate and advanced. Foundation is what the person must do alone by the end of the first three months. Ask the managers to set that line.
**Order the levels into a path,** so that each one builds on the one before. Check every intermediate statement: which foundation statement does it depend on.
**Test it on two people** in the role. Ask "Is this the job? What is missing? What would you never do?" Change the wording to theirs.
**Show the path on one page** to the learner and the sponsor, and put a review date on it. Then choose content. Each statement becomes [an objective you can observe](t:2.11).

why.text: **A competency model turns topics into a path.** A competency model is a written list of what a capable person in a role knows and can do, usually sorted into levels. It turns a list of topics into a path with a purpose. You can show a learner and a sponsor exactly what capability is being built, and the learner can see where they are on it.

**A published framework is only a starting list.** Published frameworks can speed this up. They also have limits, and they describe a typical role, not this one. Use one as a starting list to react to, then check every line against the people you interviewed.

**The best-known guidance rests on experience, not studies.** The best-known guidance on competency models sets out twenty good practices for building, presenting and using them. Its authors say these come from experience and have not been tested in studies. Treat a competency model as a useful working tool, not as a proven method.

**The insight is in the wording.** A topic such as "delegation" can be covered in an hour and ticked off. A statement such as "hands over a task with the outcome, the deadline and a check-in agreed" tells you what practice to design, what the manager should look for afterwards and what to assess. The trade-off is detail. Every statement you add makes the model more complete and less likely to be read. For a one-off workshop you do not need a full model. Three or four observable statements will do the same job.

try.text: Draft a model for a real role you know. Interview one person who does it well, write eight to twelve observable statements, and sort them into three levels. Read the foundation level aloud to someone in the role and ask whether it is the job. To do this across a whole organisation, [map roles and skills before planning courses](t:9.13).

items: **Models go stale.** Put a review date on the page and look again when the role changes.
**Too much detail** makes a model nobody uses. As a rough guide from practice, if the foundation level will not fit on one page, cut it.
**A framework borrowed from elsewhere** needs checking against the real job. Take it to two people in the role before you design from it.

**A model of only today's job** dates quickly. Good models are tied to what the organisation is trying to do and can look ahead to what the role will need. Ask the sponsor what will change in the role in the next two years.
**The statements drift back into topics,** such as "knows the absence policy". Rewrite each one until you could watch someone do it.

items.label: Campion and colleagues (2011), Doing competencies well: best practices in competency modeling. Personnel Psychology.
Association for Talent Development (2020), Talent Development Capability Model.

quiz.q: What does a competency model list?
quiz.a: The knowledge, skills and behaviours that make someone capable in a role, usually sorted into levels.

quiz.q: A client hands you a published leadership framework and asks you to build the programme straight from it. What do you do first?
quiz.a: Check it against the real job. A published framework describes a typical role, so ask people who do this one well what they actually do, and adjust.

quiz.q: Your draft model for team leaders runs to six pages and the sponsor has stopped reading. What do you change?
quiz.a: Cut the detail. Keep a short list of things you could see a person do at each level, so the path is visible at a glance. If the foundation level does not fit on one page, it is too long.

topics.tierReason: Competency modelling is a widely used professional practice, and the main published guidance says its recommendations rest on experience more than on tests.

topics.title: Shape the programme over weeks, not days

situation.text: A client wants twelve new managers trained in two packed days. The draft agenda covers twelve topics, one after another, forty-five minutes each. Every topic is covered once and never returned to. By the Thursday after, most of the group will be back in their inboxes with nothing booked.

items: **List three to five whole tasks** from the real job, such as "run a one-to-one with someone who is behind on their work". Build the programme around these and not around the topic list.
**Write each task in three versions** that get harder. Version one is simple and fully supported. Version three has the complications of real life: a defensive person, missing information, less time.
**Choose the order on purpose:** simple to complex, concrete to abstract, known to unknown. Write one line saying why the first task comes first.

**Shape it as one core day** and then short sessions. A workable pattern is a day built on version one of each task, followed by four ninety-minute sessions over eight weeks. The two-week gap is a starting point from practice. Stretch the gaps when the skill has to last for many months.

**Bring an earlier task back** to open every follow-up session: five minutes recalling it from memory, with no notes, then the harder version. There is [research on spacing and retrieval](t:1.3) behind this.
**Drill separately only what keeps failing:** a sub-skill such as a calculation people keep getting wrong. Ten minutes, then back to the whole task.
**Put every date in diaries** before the first session, and [tell managers which hours to protect](t:2.4).

why.text: **Joining up is often the hard part.** The shape of a programme over time is a design decision. One approach to complex skills argues that people learn them best by practising meaningful whole tasks of rising difficulty, with part-practice for the pieces. The reasoning is that the hard part of a real job is often the joining up. Someone who has learned twelve topics separately has still never had to decide which one applies in the middle of a conversation.

**Spacing works across a programme too.** Spacing means spreading learning over time with gaps between sessions. There is more on [the research behind spacing](t:1.3) and on [spacing and mixing practice](t:5.14). It applies at the scale of a programme as well as a session. Revisiting the same ideas at greater depth is one way to build it in, which is why each follow-up returns to an earlier case in a harder version.

**What must last longer needs wider gaps.** A large review of spacing studies found that the best gap between sessions grows with the time people need to remember the material. Most of those studies tested recall of words and facts, so applying it to a whole programme is a reasonable extension, not a tested rule. A meta-analysis of leadership training also found better results when sessions were spread out.

why.title: A review of spaced practice
why.found: The review pooled 839 assessments from 317 experiments on verbal recall. Spreading study over time helped later memory, and the gap that worked best grew longer as the delay before the final test grew longer.
why.means: Set the gaps in a programme by how long people need to keep the skill, with longer gaps for learning that must last months.

why.text: **Spreading it out is harder to run.** The cost is real. A spread programme is harder to schedule, loses people along the way and feels less finished than two days away. A block still makes sense when people have travelled far, or when the group itself needs time together. In that case keep the block and add two short follow-up calls. That gives the material at least two more visits.

try.text: Take a set of competencies or a topic list from a real programme. Pick three whole tasks, write a harder second version of each, and lay them out across a realistic period with dates. Then explain the shape aloud to a colleague in two minutes, as you would to a client who asked for two days.
