items: **Clients often want one block.** Offer a shorter event with follow-up sessions, and show the two shapes side by side with the same total hours.
**Whole tasks can overwhelm newcomers.** Simplify the task, do not split it into unrelated pieces. [Start with full support and remove it](t:2.13) as people improve.
**A long programme loses people.** Put every date in diaries before the first session, keep follow-up sessions short, and [ask managers to protect the time](t:2.4).
**Follow-up sessions turn into new topics.** Each one must reopen an earlier task before it adds anything.
**Quoting spacing research as a rule** for programme gaps. It was mostly tested on recall of words and facts. Present your gaps as a reasoned choice.

items.label: Cepeda and colleagues (2006), Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: a review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin.
Lacerenza and colleagues (2017), Leadership training design, delivery, and implementation: a meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology.

quiz.q: What did the large review of spacing studies find about the best gap between sessions?
quiz.a: It grows with the time people need to remember the material. Learning that must last months needs longer gaps.

quiz.q: A client wants twelve topics covered in two packed days, with nothing afterwards. What do you propose?
quiz.a: A shorter event built around a few realistic cases, plus short follow-up sessions over the next weeks that return to those cases in harder versions.

quiz.q: You build a programme around a whole realistic task and the newcomers are swamped in the first session. What do you change?
quiz.a: Simplify the task and add support. Keep it whole. Do not break it into unrelated pieces.

topics.tierReason: Spacing is well supported, but the best gap depends on how long the learning must last and most of that evidence is on verbal recall, and the whole-task claim could not be checked.

topics.title: Give managers a job before, during and after
topics.theory: Stakeholders, managers and the transfer environment

situation.text: You ran a good one-day workshop on handling difficult calls for sixteen customer service staff. Six weeks later the sponsor says nothing has changed. When you ask what the team leaders did afterwards, it turns out nobody told them what the workshop covered. Two of them pulled people out at lunchtime to clear the queue.

items: **Ask the sponsor about the managers** in your first conversation, with two questions: "Who do the learners report to?" and "What have those managers been told?" Get the names. The workplace is part of the design.
**Give each manager three jobs:** set expectations before, release time during, follow up after. Ask for about ten minutes each time.
**Write the jobs on one page,** with the time each takes and words the manager could say. A request with the words supplied is easier to act on than a request to "support your people".

**Agree what support the programme needs** with the sponsor, before you start. Ask the sponsor to send the page under their own name two weeks before the session. If you are external and will not meet the managers, ask for ten minutes on a managers' call to talk it through.
**Write for three audiences.** The sponsor gets the purpose and the measure. The manager gets their three jobs. The learner gets what to bring and what to try afterwards.
**Send managers two lines** the day after the session: what their people practised, and the one question to ask in the next one-to-one.
**Ask each manager for two lines** at week six, on what has changed and what has not. Use the replies in your report, and say in the proposal [which results depend on managers](t:9.6).

why.text: **Trainers control the work environment least.** Transfer means [using at work what was learned](t:5.1) in training. The classic model names three influences on it: the learner, the training design and the work environment. The work environment is the one a trainer controls least, and it is easy to neglect.

**The manager decides what gets noticed.** A learner's manager sets expectations and reinforces them, or fails to. Do not leave that to chance. Give managers specific actions and the words to use. The reasoning is practical. A manager decides what gets time, what gets noticed and what gets praised. If the manager never mentions the workshop, people conclude that the old way is still what is wanted.

**Supportive workplaces go with more transfer.** A meta-analysis of 89 studies found that a supportive work environment goes with more transfer. The link was stronger for open skills such as leadership than for closed skills such as using software. The studies show an association. They did not test a one-page manager guide, which is one practical way to act on the finding.

why.title: What predicts transfer of training
why.found: Across 89 studies, transfer was positively related to a supportive work environment, and to the learner's ability, conscientiousness and motivation. Links were stronger for open skills such as leadership. Results looked better than they were when the same person rated both the support and the transfer.
why.means: Plan manager support most carefully for people skills, and do not rely on learners' own ratings alone to judge transfer.

why.text: **A people skill needs a careful manager brief.** So spend your effort where the finding points. For a people skill, the manager brief deserves as much care as a section of the workshop. For a closed skill such as a new software screen, a shorter note and protected practice time may be enough. Where the manager is new, hostile or absent, the brief will not work, and the learner needs another person to back them.

try.text: Draft a one-page manager guide for a real programme, with what managers do before, during and after, the time each job takes and words they could use. Then say aloud, in under two minutes, what you would tell a managers' call about it. Record it and check that you asked for something specific.

items: **Managers are busy.** Ask for ten minutes, three times, and supply the words.
**Some managers are the problem.** Find another sponsor for those learners, such as the programme sponsor or another senior person, who will set the expectation and ask afterwards what they tried.
**Transfer you cannot influence:** do not promise it. Say in the proposal [what depends on managers](t:9.6).
**You may never meet the managers** if you are external. Ask the sponsor to send the brief under their own name, and ask for ten minutes on a managers' call to talk it through.
**Judging the result from learners alone,** by what they say about their managers. Ratings from one person inflate the link. Ask managers too, and look at a measure the sponsor already tracks.

quiz.q: In the classic model, what three things influence transfer?
quiz.a: The learner, the training design and the work environment.

quiz.q: You are an external trainer and will never meet the learners' managers. How do you still get them involved?
quiz.a: Write a one-page brief with their three jobs: set expectations before, release time during, follow up after. Ask the sponsor to send it under their own name, and ask for ten minutes on a managers' call.

quiz.q: One manager tells her team the workshop is a waste of time. What do you do for those learners?
quiz.a: Find someone else to back them, such as the sponsor or another senior person, who will set the expectation and ask afterwards what they tried.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis links a supportive work environment with transfer, but the link is stronger for some skills than others and the evidence is mostly correlational.

topics.title: Design the before and after, not only the event
topics.theory: The pre, during and post framework

situation.text: You have spent three weeks on the slides and activities for a product knowledge day for a retailer's store staff. The joining email says where to park. Nothing is planned for the week before, and the only thing after is a feedback form. All the effort has gone into the middle third.

items: **Draw three columns** headed before, during and after. Give each column one action for you, one for the learner and one for the manager. An empty box is a decision you have not made yet.

**Before: send three questions** a week ahead, on the three points that matter most. Say "Have a guess if you do not know. Wrong answers are useful." Ask for replies, and keep the whole of the pre-work under fifteen minutes.
**Before: make sure the manager conversation happens.** Ten minutes on what the person will work on. You can use the [brief for managers](t:2.4).
**During: open with the group's answers** to the three questions, shown without names. Then make sure the session answers each one clearly, and say so when it does: "That was question two."
**During: get a plan from each person** before people leave, for [their first use at work](t:5.2).

**After: schedule the follow-up:** a recall quiz, a task to apply at work and a check-in. Give each an owner and a date before the day itself. Time the first one to the first real use of the skill. There is more on [how to schedule the follow-up](t:5.4).
**Tell learners their part** in one short paragraph of the joining email: prepare, use it soon, teach someone, come back to it.

why.text: **The event is the middle of three parts.** A well-run session with no preparation and no follow-up tends to fade. The before sets up what people will pay attention to, and the after is where the skill is first used for real. Both are cheap compared with the day and both are usually left to chance.

**Guessing before learning can improve recall.** Trying to answer questions before learning, even wrongly, can improve what is remembered later, as long as people then meet the right answers. The gain is mostly for the points you asked about. This is a form of [generation, which means producing an answer yourself](t:1.3) before you are given it. That is why the three questions go on the three most important points, and why the session has to answer them by name.

why.title: The pretesting effect
why.found: In five experiments, people who tried to answer questions about a text before reading it did better on a later test than people given extra reading time. This held even for questions they had got wrong at the start.
why.means: Open with a few questions on the points that matter most, then make sure the session answers them.

why.text: **Pre-questions suit facts, not reasoning.** There are limits. Pre-questions work best for clearly stated facts. They help less with questions that need complex reasoning, and most of the evidence comes from students in laboratory studies. Because the gain is mostly for what you asked about, three questions on minor points would pull attention to the wrong places. The fifteen-minute ceiling, the owner-and-date rule and the three-column map are craft. If a group cannot be reached before the day, ask the three questions in the first five minutes in the room.

try.text: Map before, during and after for a real programme, with one action in each phase for you and for the learner. Write the three pre-questions. Then read the joining paragraph aloud and check that it tells a learner what to do, by when, and how long it will take.

try.title: Words for the joining email
lines: "You are booked on the new range day on Tuesday 9th. Here is your part."
"Before: answer the three questions below. It takes five minutes. Have a guess if you do not know. We will use your answers in the first ten minutes."
"1. Which two products in the new range replace ones we already sell?"
"2. What is the one question customers ask most about the warranty?"
"3. A customer wants the cheapest option for a small flat. Which model do you show first?"
"On the day: bring one customer question you found hard to answer this month."
"After: you will get a short quiz before your next shift, and your manager will ask what you tried."

items: **Pre-work that is not used** in the room teaches people to skip it. Open the session with it.
**Follow-up needs an owner and date,** or it does not happen. Book both before the day, not after.
**Long pre-work:** keep it short. Fifteen minutes is a sensible ceiling for most groups (craft).
**Your pre-questions need long reasoning.** Pre-questions work best for clearly stated facts, so ask for a fact, a choice or a number.
**People feel tested** before they have been taught. Say in the email that guesses are expected and that nobody's answers will be shown by name.

items.label: Salas and colleagues (2012), The science of training and development in organizations: what matters in practice. Psychological Science in the Public Interest.
Richland, Kornell and Kao (2009), The pretesting effect: do unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance learning? Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied.
Pan and Carpenter (2023), Prequestioning and pretesting effects: a review of empirical research, theoretical perspectives, and implications for educational practice. Educational Psychology Review.

quiz.q: In the pretesting experiments, did the benefit hold for questions people got wrong at the start?
quiz.a: Yes. People who tried to answer before reading did better later, even on questions they first got wrong, as long as they then met the right answers.

quiz.q: You sent a twenty-minute reading as pre-work. On the day, half the room has not done it. What do you change next time?
quiz.a: Make the pre-work shorter and use it in the room, for example three questions that the session then answers. Pre-work that is never used teaches people to skip it.

quiz.q: The workshop went well. Four weeks later nobody has run the follow-up quiz or the check-in. What was missing from the plan?
quiz.a: An owner and a date for each follow-up step. Without both, follow-up does not happen.

topics.tierReason: A research review supports designing what happens before and after training, and pre-questions have good evidence, but their benefit depends on how they are used and comes mostly from laboratory studies.

topics.title: Design for the kind of programme it is
topics.theory: Programme types: onboarding, leadership development, compliance

situation.text: In one month a client asks you for an induction for new starters, a leadership course and a fire safety refresher. You reach for the format you know: a day in a room, slides, two activities and a quiz. It fits none of the three well, because each one is trying to produce something different.

items: **Name the type before you design anything:** induction, compliance, leadership or technical skill. If a request mixes two, split it into two pieces with their own plans.
**Write one "This has worked when" sentence** that starts with those words and ends with something a person does on the job. Agree it with the sponsor. That sentence is the test you design towards.

**Induction: teach the first week's essentials.** Ask what a new starter must be able to do by Friday of week one, teach that, and spread the rest over the following weeks. Add who they will meet and one real task they can finish. There is a [full design for onboarding](t:2.31).

**Compliance: aim at what people do,** and test that. Have each person show the behaviour in their own workplace. Keep the record of completion as well, since regulated training still requires it. There is more on [the record and the behaviour](t:2.30).
**Leadership: practice on real work,** over months. One skill at a time, tried with the person's own team between sessions, with feedback. There is more on [designing for managers](t:2.8).

**Technical skills: show a worked example,** then give practice with feedback, and remove the support as people improve. There is more on [why worked examples help](t:1.2) and on [taking support away](t:2.13).
**Check the format against the sentence** from step two. If the format could be completed by someone who still cannot do the thing, change the format.

why.text: **Programmes differ in what success means.** Induction succeeds when someone can do the job and feels they belong. Compliance succeeds when behaviour is safe and lawful. Leadership development succeeds when people lead differently. Copy one format across all of them and you design for the wrong test.

**Research backs the induction and leadership advice.** Research supports two of these directly. A meta-analysis of newcomers found that being clear about the role, feeling able to do the job and feeling accepted by colleagues link induction to later performance and staying. A meta-analysis of leadership training found better results with practice, feedback and sessions spread over time. The guidance here on compliance and on technical skills applies general principles of practice and assessment, and the "This has worked when" sentence is craft.

**Naming the type shows where time goes.** The useful thing about naming the type is that it tells you where the time should go. In induction it goes on clarity and people in the first week. In compliance it goes on the few behaviours that matter and on checking them where they happen. In leadership it goes on the gaps between sessions. The same content, such as "how we handle a customer complaint", would be built three different ways depending on which programme it sits in.

**Real programmes mix the types.** Types are a starting point and real programmes blur. A graduate scheme is induction with some leadership in it. A new system launch is technical skill with a compliance edge. When a programme is mixed, write a success sentence for each part and let each part take its own shape. There is separate guidance on [designing for early-career learners](t:2.7).

try.text: Take two programmes of different types that you know. For each, write the "This has worked when" sentence and say how you would check it on the job. Then look at the current format and mark anything a person could complete without being able to do the thing.

items: **Compliance training that only proves attendance** may change little. Decide what people must do differently and test that.
**Induction often overloads week one.** Ask what a new starter must be able to do by Friday and move the rest later.
**Leadership courses are often events** with no practice. Build in a task to try with the person's own team between sessions.
**The sponsor wants the same format** for everything because it is easy to book. Show the success sentence for each programme and ask which format would prove it.
**You drop the completion record** because behaviour matters more. In regulated training you need both.

Lacerenza and colleagues (2017), Leadership training design, delivery, and implementation: a meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology.
Salas and colleagues (2012), The science of training and development in organizations: what matters in practice. Psychological Science in the Public Interest.

quiz.q: What three things did the newcomer meta-analysis link to later performance and staying?
quiz.a: Being clear about the role, feeling able to do the job, and feeling accepted by colleagues.

quiz.q: You are asked to turn the fire safety slide module into something that works. What does the new assessment look like?
quiz.a: People show the behaviour. Each person walks their own exit route and shows where the nearest extinguisher is. A completed module does not count as success.

quiz.q: A client wants the two-day induction format reused for new team leaders. What do you say?
quiz.a: The test of success is different. Leadership development works when people lead differently, which needs practice on real work, feedback and sessions spread over months.

topics.title: Design for people early in their career
topics.theory: Early-career learners: onboarding, graduates and apprentices

situation.text: Ten graduates and apprentices join a software company's customer team in September. Your session on handling incidents says "Escalate anything unusual to the duty manager." Nobody in the room knows who the duty manager is, how you reach one, or what counts as unusual here. None of them asks.

items: **Check what they know before you design.** Ask their line managers what new starters got wrong last year, and ask two people who joined a year ago: "What did you wish someone had told you in week one?" Assume little about the workplace and a lot about their ability.
**Mark every assumption in your material** about how a workplace runs: job titles, tools, who decides, how to raise a problem, how formal an email should be. Each mark needs a sentence or an example.

**Use worked examples and plenty of structure.** Show a finished version first, such as a real escalation message, then have people write their own with the example in view, then without it. There is more on [taking support away](t:2.13).
**Teach the unwritten rules openly.** Give one page: who to ask for what, how to say you are stuck, how long to try alone before asking. Twenty minutes is a workable rule to offer, and it is craft.
**Build belonging and an early win.** Introduce them by name to the people they will work with, and give each [a small real task they can finish](t:1.18) in the first week.
**Involve the line manager or buddy.** Tell them what was taught and what to ask about. There is a [brief for the manager](t:2.4).
**Give a private way to ask questions,** such as a named buddy or a message channel for the cohort only.

why.text: **Seniority and knowledge are different things.** People early in a career are usually beginners in the job, so the guidance for beginners applies: more structure, more examples, and [support that fades](t:2.13). They are often quick, well educated and used to studying. What they lack is the map of the workplace that everyone else stopped noticing years ago.

**Career stage explains more than generation.** There is no good evidence that generations learn in different ways. Age, career stage and experience explain more. You can read [the research on generations at work](t:2.10). So a request to design "for Gen Z" is better answered by designing for capable people who are new to the job.

**Newcomers settle through clarity, confidence and acceptance.** A meta-analysis of 70 samples of newcomers found three signs of settling in: being clear about the role, feeling able to do the job and feeling accepted. These linked what the organisation did, and how much newcomers sought information, to later performance, satisfaction and staying. That is the case for teaching the unwritten rules openly.

why.title: How newcomers settle in
why.found: Across 70 samples, role clarity, self-efficacy and social acceptance carried the effect of an organisation's induction practices and of newcomers' information seeking through to job performance, satisfaction, commitment and staying.
why.means: Design early-career programmes to build clarity, confidence and acceptance, as well as knowledge.

why.text: **Settling in includes asking questions.** Notice that the finding includes how much newcomers seek information. Asking is part of settling in, and asking is what a new person in a room of experts will not do. Making it easy and private to ask is a direct way to act on the research. The limit on all of this is tone. Heavy structure can read as distrust, so tell people why the examples are there and take them away as soon as the work is right.

try.text: Take a session written for experienced staff. Read it aloud to someone who has never worked in that organisation, and ask them to stop you every time they would not know what to do next. Mark each stop. Rewrite the worst one with a worked example.

**A beginner will not ask** in a room of experts. Give them a buddy or a private way to ask.
**Their manager shapes the outcome:** whether any of it is used. [Brief the manager or buddy](t:2.4). There is also a [full onboarding design](t:2.31).

**You design for a generation.** Design for the stage they are at.

quiz.q: Which three signs of settling in did the newcomer meta-analysis identify?
quiz.a: Role clarity, feeling able to do the job, and feeling accepted by colleagues.

quiz.q: Your session for graduates says "escalate anything unusual to the duty manager". Nobody does. What was missing?
quiz.a: The unwritten rules. Say who the duty manager is, how to reach them, what counts as unusual, and give a sample message. Then practise it, with the sample removed the second time.

quiz.q: A sponsor asks you to redesign the apprentice programme "for Gen Z". How do you respond?
quiz.a: Say there is no good evidence that generations learn differently. Design for what they are: capable people who are beginners in the job and new to the workplace.

topics.tierReason: The case for more structure and examples for beginners is well reviewed and depends on prior knowledge, while the advice on belonging rests on correlational studies of newcomers.

topics.title: Design for managers

situation.text: Twelve managers from a technology company file in at 14:00 for ninety minutes on difficult conversations. Most have managed for five years or more. One says, kindly enough, that this is her fourth leadership course. Your plan has forty minutes of slides on a four-box model.

items: **Ask each manager one question** by email, a week before: "Which conversation are you putting off this month?" Build the session from the replies. Start from a problem they have now.
**Keep input to fifteen minutes at most.** Teach one usable thing, such as a way to open the conversation in two sentences, and show it once.

**Practise with their real cases** and spend the bulk of the time on it. In threes, each manager rehearses the opening of the conversation they are due to have, for five minutes, with one person playing the other side and one observing.

**Run feedback in a fixed order:** the person who practised speaks first, then the observer, then the other player, and you last. Then they try the opening again. There is more on [running role-play and skills practice](t:4.29).
**Use their experience.** Before the practice, ask the group: "Who has had a conversation like this go well? What did you say first?" Have them advise each other.
**Set a task to try** with their own team: hold the conversation, by a date they name.
**Follow up,** with [their own manager involved](t:2.4). Before they leave, each person says who will ask them how it went. Spread further sessions over the following months.

why.text: **Managers need practice, not a walk-through.** Managers bring experience, so support aimed at beginners can get in their way. A step-by-step walk through something they already do well wastes their time and their goodwill. They also bring habits, and habits change through practice and feedback on real work. Hearing a model explained does little to change what someone says under pressure on Thursday.

**Leadership training works on average.** A meta-analysis of 335 samples found that leadership training works on average. Programmes did better when they were built on a needs analysis, gave feedback, used several methods including practice, and spread sessions over time. Face-to-face and on-site delivery were also linked with better results.

why.title: A meta-analysis of leadership training
why.found: Across 335 samples, leadership training improved reactions, learning, behaviour at work and results. It was more effective when based on a needs analysis, when it included feedback and practice, and when sessions were spaced, on site and face to face.
why.means: Build a leadership programme from a diagnosed need, with practice and feedback in every session and gaps between sessions.

why.text: **Pooled results do not prove your design.** The meta-analysis pools many kinds of programme. It shows what tends to go with better results, not that any one design will work in your setting. The fifteen-minute limit on input and the question sent a week ahead are craft.

**Real cases persuade sceptics and start the task.** Using their real cases does two jobs at once. It answers the sceptic, because the session is about her conversation and not about a model. It also means the rehearsal is the first attempt at something that will happen, so the task afterwards is already half done. The advice on short input reverses when the skill is new to them. A manager of fifteen years who has never run a redundancy consultation is a beginner at it and needs the worked example first.

try.text: Take a leadership topic and design ninety minutes with no more than fifteen minutes of input. Then deliver the input aloud against a timer, and say the instruction for the practice round as you would in the room. If the input runs over, cut content until it fits.

What happens
Words you say

"Two sentences, then stop talking. Watch."

items: **Experienced people can be beginners** in a new skill. Ask what they have done before, not how long they have managed.
**Status makes it hard to practise** in front of peers. Use small groups of three and [make it safe to get it wrong](t:1.17).
**Models with neat names sell well.** [Check the evidence](t:1.11) before you teach one.
**A manager brings a formal matter** as a case, such as a grievance. Ask them to pick another for practice and to take the first to their HR contact.
**The audience is more senior** than you planned for. Where time is shorter and status matters more, [design for executives](t:2.9). There is a [method for teaching people skills](t:2.34).

Kalyuga (2007), Expertise reversal effect and its implications for learner-tailored instruction. Educational Psychology Review.
Kalyuga and Renkl (2010), Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications: introduction to the special issue. Instructional Science.

quiz.q: According to the leadership training meta-analysis, what went with better results?
quiz.a: A needs analysis, feedback, several methods including practice, and sessions spread over time. Face-to-face and on-site delivery were also linked with better results.

quiz.q: You have ninety minutes with a group of managers on difficult conversations. How do you split the time?
quiz.a: About ten to fifteen minutes of input, then most of the time rehearsing a real conversation each of them is due to have, with feedback. End by planning when they will hold it and who will ask how it went.

quiz.q: A manager of fifteen years says she has "done all this before" and sits back. How do you bring her in?
quiz.a: Start from a problem she has this month and use her experience. Ask her to advise a peer on a real case, then set a task to try with her own team.

topics.title: Design for executives
topics.theory: Executive education: short time, status in the room and learning from peers

situation.text: You have ninety minutes with the executive team of a technology company, on customer complaints. Seven people, phones face up on the table, the chief executive at the head of it. The sponsor's brief says "an update". Nobody in the room wants to be taught, and two of them will be called out before the end.

items: **Agree the one decision or change** the session is for, with the sponsor. Push until it reads as an outcome: "By the end, the team agrees which two complaint types to fix first and who owns each."

**Send a one-page brief** three working days ahead: the purpose, their own data, and the question they will be asked to decide. The page carries the information so that the room time goes on the decision.
**Speak to the most senior person beforehand.** Say: "I would like to hear the others first. Would you give your view last?" There is more on [the senior person who takes over](t:4.38).
**Open with their data or their problem,** in under five minutes. Keep your total input to ten minutes.
**Have them work with each other** while you facilitate. Two minutes writing a view alone, then pairs, then the table. Writing first stops the room from following the first voice.
**End with who will do what,** by when. Write it on a flipchart in their words, read it back, and send a photograph of it the same day.
**Offer each person a private follow-up** of twenty minutes, where they can ask what they would not ask in front of peers.

why.text: **Executives often weigh peers above the trainer.** Executives have little time and much at stake in front of peers. Being seen not to know can feel costly, so [safety to be wrong out loud](t:1.17) is likely to matter more as rank rises. In practice they often give more weight to the views of peers than to those of a trainer. That is why the design has them working with each other and puts you in the role of holding the conversation.

**Research on executives is thin.** These are observations from practice. The research on what works for executives in particular is thin, and you should say so if a client asks what the method rests on.

**Safe teams showed more learning behaviour.** One piece of research does bear on the safety point. A study of 51 teams in a manufacturing company found that teams whose members felt safe to take risks with each other showed more learning behaviour, and that this went with better team performance. It studied ordinary work teams, not executives.

**Room time is for deciding.** The reasoning behind the single purpose is about what an executive team is for. Its scarce resource is time together, and the thing only it can do is decide. Information can travel on a page. A session that spends eighty minutes informing and ten deciding has used the room for the part that did not need it. The private follow-up handles the status problem from the other side: it gives each person somewhere to say "I did not follow the figures" at no cost. If the team truly needs new knowledge before it can decide, split the work. Put the knowledge in a longer brief or in short individual sessions, and keep the room for the decision.

try.text: Design a ninety-minute executive session with one purpose and no more than ten minutes of input. Write the purpose sentence and the one-page brief. Then say your opening aloud, from "Good morning" to the first question, and time it. It should finish inside five minutes.

try.title: A worked example: the one-page brief, sent three working days ahead
lines: Before: "An update on customer complaints for the executive team."
After. Purpose: "By the end of Thursday's ninety minutes, the team agrees which two complaint types to fix first and who owns each."
What you are being asked to decide: two priorities and two owners. Nothing else.
Your data: the five most common complaint types from the last quarter, with volume and time to resolve for each. (Table attached, one page.)
What customers said: three short quotes for each type, taken from the complaints log.
Please read before Thursday and come with your own first and second choice written down.
How the time will run: five minutes on the data, then the team works on the choice. No slides after the first five minutes.
Afterwards: each of you is offered twenty minutes with me in the following week, in private, for any questions.

items: **The most senior person speaks first** and can close the room down. Ask them beforehand to [give their view last](t:4.38). If it still happens, go to two minutes of writing and take other views first.
**You simplify the content.** Do not. Shorten it. One chart with their own figures, not a primer.
**A session with no decision** is soon forgotten. Write the decision and the owners down before people leave.
**Nobody has read the brief.** Give three minutes of silent reading at the start. Do not present it.
**You quote research** as if it were about executives. The study on safety was of ordinary work teams. Describe the advice as practice.

items.label: Edmondson (1999), Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. Administrative Science Quarterly, 44(2). A study of work teams, not of executives.

quiz.q: How strong is the research on what works for executives in particular?
quiz.a: Thin. Most of the advice comes from practice. The psychological safety study often cited was of ordinary work teams, not executives.

quiz.q: You have ninety minutes with an executive team on customer complaints. The sponsor's brief is "an update". What do you do before the day?
quiz.a: Agree with the sponsor the one decision or change the session is for. Send a one-page brief with the data in advance, so the time goes on the decision.

quiz.q: Five minutes in, the chief executive gives a firm view and the others go quiet. What could you have done, and what do you do now?
quiz.a: Beforehand, ask the most senior person to speak last. In the room, have people work in pairs or write their view first, then take views from others before returning to the chief executive.

topics.title: Know the learner's working day before you design
topics.theory: The modern learner and their context

situation.text: Your design for a retailer's store staff has sixty minutes of online pre-work on a desktop computer. Then you visit a store. There is one shared tablet in a break room next to the delivery bay, breaks are fifteen minutes, and nobody has a desk. The design assumed a working day that these learners do not have.

items: **Ask four things about the working day** before you design: when people could learn, where, on what device, and who pays for the time. Get the answers from learners and not only from head office.

**Shadow or interview two or three learners.** Ask: "Talk me through yesterday from when you arrived." "When did you last have ten minutes without being interrupted?" "Where do you read something from head office, and on what?"
**List what interrupts them:** customers, calls, alarms, a shared device, a noisy break room. Note how long the gaps between interruptions are. That length is your maximum piece size.
**Fit the design to what you found:** shorter pieces that can be stopped and picked up, offline or printed versions, sound-free options for a shared space, and protected time on the rota.

**Ask managers to release the time,** and name the amount: "ten minutes at the start of three shifts". Agree it with the sponsor first, since it costs hours. There is more on [what to ask of managers](t:2.4).
**Test with two or three real learners** in the real place, on the real device, before you build the rest. Watch them do it. Do not ask whether they would.
**Write the constraints at the top** of your design document, so that anyone reviewing it can see what the design was fitted to.

why.text: **The working day decides whether people take part.** A design that does not fit the working day is unlikely to be used. Time, place, device and interruptions decide whether people can take part at all. These are facts about a workplace that you can find out in an afternoon, and they often overturn a design that looked sound on paper.

**People are interrupted, not short of attention.** The popular claim of [a fixed, short attention span](t:2.14) is not supported. People are busy and interrupted, which is a different problem with a different answer. If attention were short, everything would need to be tiny. If people are interrupted, pieces need to survive being stopped, and some of them can be long when the time is protected.

**Designing by generation is not supported either.** A meta-analysis of 20 studies and about 20,000 people found that generations differed little or not at all in job satisfaction, commitment and intention to leave. A 2020 report from the US National Academies concluded that generational labels are not a sound basis for managing people. It found that age, career stage, experience and working conditions explain more, and that people within a generation differ about as much as people across generations.

why.title: Generations at work, a meta-analysis
why.found: Pooling 20 studies and 19,961 people across four generations, the differences in job satisfaction, commitment to the organisation and intention to leave were small and in many cases close to zero. The authors concluded that meaningful generational differences probably do not exist for these attitudes.
why.means: Do not build separate designs for age cohorts. Find out about people's roles, experience and working conditions.

why.text: **A label gives you nothing to design from.** Very few studies have tested training by generation at all. Ask about each group's working day, experience and role, and design for those. The interview questions and the test in the real place are craft. Their value is that a label such as "frontline" or "young" tells you nothing you can design with, while "one shared tablet and fifteen-minute breaks" tells you nearly everything.

try.text: Shadow or interview two learners about a normal day, using the three questions above. Say the questions aloud first so they sound like conversation. Afterwards, list three changes your design needs and one thing you must ask the sponsor to pay for.

items: **Mobile-friendly is not enough:** it does not mean a phone is the right place to learn it. A tricky conversation needs practice with a person. A screen reference can sit on a phone.
**Learning in people's own time** has a cost. Say who bears it, and get the sponsor to decide before launch.
**You ask head office** what the stores are like. Go and look, or speak to two people who work there.
**The test group is the keenest** two people at the nearest site. Include one person from a busy store and one who is newer.
**Designing around generations:** do not. There are [other myths of this kind](t:1.10).

items.label: Costanza and colleagues (2012), Generational differences in work-related attitudes: a meta-analysis. Journal of Business and Psychology.
National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2020), Are Generational Categories Meaningful Distinctions for Workforce Management?
Bradbury (2016), Attention span during lectures: 8 seconds, 10 minutes, or more? Advances in Physiology Education.

quiz.q: What did the meta-analysis of generations at work find?
quiz.a: Differences between generations in job satisfaction, commitment and intention to leave were small and often close to zero.

quiz.q: Your design has an hour of online pre-work. You learn the learners work shifts on a shop floor with one shared tablet. What do you change?
quiz.a: Cut it into short pieces that work on that tablet or offline, ask managers to release time at the start of a shift, and test it with two or three real learners.

quiz.q: A client says the content must be in two-minute clips because "people have no attention span now". What do you say?
quiz.a: No good data support a fixed, short attention span. People are busy and interrupted. Find out about their working day and design for interruption.

topics.tierReason: Fitting a design to the working day is sound professional practice with little direct testing, although the two myths the page warns against are well examined.

parts.title: Design the course
parts.summary: Objectives, design models, sequencing and pace.

topics.title: Write objectives you could observe

situation.text: A client sends you the aims for a one-day pricing course for account managers. They read "understand the new pricing tiers" and "be aware of the discount rules". You could run a good day or a poor one against those aims, and afterwards nobody could tell which it was.

items: **Ask the sponsor one question** before you write anything: "Three weeks after the course, what would I see someone doing that they are not doing now?" Write the answer down in their words.

**Turn each answer into one sentence** in the form: who does what, under what conditions, to what standard. Make the conditions the real ones: a customer waiting, no manager to ask, the price list open or closed.

**Test each sentence with one check.** Could two people watch and agree whether it happened? If they could not, change the verb. Replace understand, know and be aware of with choose, explain, log, decide or calculate.

**Keep the list short:** three to five objectives for a day. If you have nine, ask the sponsor which three they would keep if the day became a morning. The rest become reference material or [a job aid](t:5.7).
**Decide how you will assess each objective** before you plan any teaching. Write the task, the materials and the pass standard next to it. There is more on [assessing the real task](t:2.25).

**Lay the plan out as a table** with three columns: objective, practice activity, assessment. Every activity should sit on a row. Cut or change any activity that sits on none, and add practice to any objective that has none.
**Use Bloom's levels to check the pitch.** If the job needs people to choose a tier for a real customer, which is applying, then "list the three tiers", which is remembering, is pitched too low.
**Send the sponsor the objectives** in this form for sign-off. Give learners a plainer version that starts "By the end of today you will be able to".

why.text: **Objectives, activities and assessment share one target.** Designing backwards means choosing the capability first, then the assessment, then the teaching. Objectives, activities and assessment must point at the same target. This is called alignment. When it is missing, people are taught one thing and assessed on another. Backward design and alignment are design frameworks, set out in the sources below. The who, what, conditions and standard form is a craft convention for writing a sentence that can be checked.

**The sentence brings disagreements out early.** The sentence does a second job. The conditions and the standard are where you and the client find out that you disagree. "Explains the price in under two minutes" will draw a reply such as "two minutes is far too long on a call", and that reply is worth more to the design than a signature under "understand pricing". Have that argument while the course is still a page of objectives.

**Bloom's levels are a guide, not a hierarchy.** Bloom's taxonomy is a useful ladder for pitching the level of thinking. The 2001 revision names six levels: remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate and create. Its authors say the levels overlap, so use it as a guide, not a strict hierarchy.

**Tight objectives can narrow the learning.** There is a cost. Tightly specified objectives can narrow learning to what is easy to watch, and higher-order skills are harder to write this way. For judgement, describe the performance in place of a checklist: "decides and gives a reason a senior colleague would accept". The advice also bends for a session whose purpose is a decision, such as a leadership team's strategy day at an offsite. Write the output the group must produce by the end, and treat that as the thing you check.

try.text: Take the aims of a course you are about to run, or one you attended. Rewrite each as an observable objective, then fill in the three-column table for the whole plan. Read each objective aloud to a colleague who does not know the course and ask them, "How would you know this had happened?" If their answer differs from yours, the sentence is not finished.

try.title: A worked example: three weak objectives rewritten as observable ones
lines: The form: WHO does WHAT, under WHAT CONDITIONS, to WHAT STANDARD.
Weak 1: "Understand the new pricing tiers."
Observable 1: "Given a customer's size and usage, the account manager chooses the right tier and explains the price in under two minutes, correctly for all three test customers."
Weak 2: "Be aware of the returns policy."
Observable 2: "At the till, with a customer waiting and no manager to ask, the store assistant decides whether to refund, exchange or refuse, and gets four out of five sample cases right."
Weak 3: "Appreciate the importance of regular one-to-ones."
Observable 3: "In the four weeks after the workshop, the new manager holds a 30-minute one-to-one with each team member and records one agreed action from each."
Check each one: could two people watch and agree whether it happened?
Verbs you can use: choose, explain, demonstrate, list, sort, calculate, write, log, diagnose, repair, decide, present, handle, compare.
Verbs to avoid: understand, know, appreciate, be aware of, be familiar with, learn about.
For judgement, describe the performance: "decides and gives a reason a senior colleague would accept".

items: **You write objectives for the easy-to-watch** and lose what matters. "Lists the three tiers" is observable and is not the job. Check each one against the sponsor's answer to your first question.
**Tight objectives squeeze out judgement.** Where the skill is a judgement, describe the performance and name who would accept it, and leave the route open.
**An objective nobody assesses** is a wish. If there is no time to assess it, drop it or tell the sponsor plainly that the session only introduces it.
**A standard picked from the air,** such as "90 per cent". Ask what a person who is only just competent would do, and set it there. There is more on [checking what a test measures](t:2.26).
**Objectives read off the first slide** in design language. [Open with the problem](t:4.21) in the group's own words and keep the formal wording for the sponsor.

quiz.q: What four parts does a well-formed objective have?
quiz.a: Who does what, under what conditions, to what standard.

quiz.q: A client's aim reads "Understand the new pricing tiers". How do you rewrite it?
quiz.a: As something you could watch. For example: given a customer's size and usage, the account manager chooses the right tier and explains the price in under two minutes, correctly for three test customers.

quiz.q: Your alignment table shows a favourite quiz game that matches no objective, and a discount objective that is tested at the end and never practised. What do you do?
quiz.a: Cut the game or change it so it practises an objective, and add practice for the discount rules. Every activity and every assessment should trace to an objective, and anything assessed should have been practised first.

topics.title: Use design models as checklists, not rules
topics.theory: ADDIE, SAM, Gagné and Merrill, used critically

situation.text: At the kick-off for a product launch course, the client's learning lead says, "We follow ADDIE here, so I need the analysis report signed off before any design starts." The launch is six weeks away. The product team changed the feature list twice last week.

items: **Learn the four models** well enough to say each in one sentence. The table under Try it has them. Two are about running a whole project (ADDIE and SAM). Two are about what one lesson contains (Gagné and Merrill).
**Write the constraints in three lines** at the start of a project: how firm the brief is, how many weeks you have, and who must sign off and how fast they reply.

**Choose how to run the project** from those lines. If the brief is firm and sign-off is formal, work through the phases in order. If the brief is uncertain or still changing, prototype early: build one rough session in the first week and run it for 45 minutes with three people from the audience.

**Hold the plan against ADDIE's five words,** whichever you choose: analyse, design, develop, implement, evaluate. Put a date and a name against each one, so that analysis and evaluation are not forgotten.

**Check each lesson against Merrill's five principles.** Is it built round a real problem? Does it activate what people know, demonstrate, have people apply it, and tie it into their work? Mark any that are missing.

**Run down Gagné's nine events** for a lesson you are unsure of, and note which ones it skips, looking hardest at practice, feedback and recall. Adapt the list to the content and to what the learners already know. A lesson does not need all nine.

**Write four lines saying what you borrowed** from which model and why, in the client's vocabulary. If they know ADDIE, show them where each phase happens in your plan and that you will go round more than once.
**Read the plan again halfway through** and ask of every step what it is for. Skip the ones that do nothing for this project.

why.text: **ADDIE is a checklist, and has critics.** ADDIE (analyse, design, develop, implement, evaluate) is a useful checklist. Its critics say it is dated and less efficient than iterative ways of working. SAM, the Successive Approximation Model, is an iterative alternative that its authors present as simpler. Gagné offers a sequence for one lesson. Merrill centres learning on real problems.

**Treat all four as aids to thinking.** They are descriptions of how to design, and tests of one model against another are hard to find. The case for SAM over ADDIE is made by SAM's own authors, so it is an argument and not a tested result. Choosing between them is therefore craft, and the honest reason for a choice is the project's constraints. You will also meet Kolb's learning cycle. It is influential and [its evidence is contested](t:1.25).

**Blending the models involves no contradiction.** The models answer different questions, which is why blending them involves no contradiction. One project model plus one lesson check covers both the running of the work and the content of each session. A team that argues "ADDIE or SAM" has often missed that neither says what a good lesson contains.

**Each way of running a project costs something.** Each way of running a project has a price. Working in order delays the moment a learner sees anything, so a wrong assumption surfaces late. Iterating needs reviewers who can respond in days, and three rounds will not fit into six weeks if each sign-off takes two. The advice to prototype early reverses when wording must be approved before anyone outside the team may see it, as with some regulated content. There, do the phases in order and test the structure with placeholder text.

try.text: Take one real project, past or coming. Write its three lines of constraints, then say which model or blend you would use. Explain the choice aloud to a colleague in 60 seconds, as if they were the client's learning lead and expected ADDIE. Good looks like this: you named the constraint that drove the choice, and you used their words for the phases.

**The client expects the model** they know. Explain your choice in their terms, and show where each of their phases happens in your plan.
**Kolb's cycle gets taught as proven.** It is [influential and contested](t:1.25), so present it that way.
**The case for SAM over ADDIE** is made by SAM's own authors. Treat it as an argument, not a tested result, and do not tell a client that iteration is proven to be better.
**"Rough" turns into polished.** A prototype with finished slides invites comments on fonts. Keep the first version plain so people react to the content.

quiz.q: Which of the four models covers a single lesson in nine steps?
quiz.a: Gagné's nine events. ADDIE and SAM are ways to run a whole project. Merrill's first principles are five principles centred on a real problem.

quiz.q: A product launches in six weeks and the brief changes every few days. Which approach do you take?
quiz.a: Build a rough version early and test it with a few people, as SAM suggests. Keep the ADDIE phases as a list so analysis and evaluation are not forgotten.

quiz.q: The client's learning lead insists every project "follows ADDIE". Your project needs fast iteration. What do you say?
quiz.a: Explain your choice in their terms. Show where analysis, design, development, delivery and evaluation each happen in your plan, and that you will go round more than once.

topics.title: Start with full support, then take it away

situation.text: Eight new customer support staff start on Monday. By ten o'clock each has been handed a real billing query and told, "Have a go, and shout if you get stuck." Two of them freeze. One works through it with confidence and gets it wrong.

items: **Open with three or four questions** on paper to find out [what people already know](t:1.7). Anyone who gets them all right starts at step 5.

**Break the content into pieces** [small enough to hold in mind](t:1.1) at once. For a procedure, list every check an expert makes and group the checks into steps. Put first whatever the later steps depend on.
**Show one fully worked example.** Do it in front of the group in about five minutes, and at each step say what you are checking and why.
**Hand out a second example** with the first steps done and the last two left for people to finish, in pairs. Then a third with only the first step done.
**Give a fresh problem to solve alone,** with no notes. Follow it with another that looks different on the surface and needs the same steps.
**Remove each support** once people no longer need it. A working rule, which is craft: when most of the group gets two in a row right with a support, the next one goes out without it.

**Reverse the order** when the conditions call for it. If people have some background and the goal is understanding, set the problem first for ten minutes, then teach it fully straight after. There is a [case for useful difficulty](t:2.19).

why.text: **Fading the support is half the method.** A sequence that starts with full support and withdraws it lets a newcomer climb without overload. The reason to withdraw it is the expertise reversal effect: support that helps a beginner holds the same person back once they know more. So the fading is half of the method, and the half that gets forgotten. A worked example that was right in week one is a drag on the same person in week three.

why.title: The expertise reversal effect
why.found: This review brings together studies showing that the teaching methods that work best change with what the learner already knows. Guidance that helps beginners can stop helping, or get in the way, once people know more.
why.means: Check prior knowledge first, start beginners with full support and take each support away as they improve.

why.text: **Struggling first can sometimes work better.** There is a competing finding. Letting people struggle with a problem before teaching can work better under some conditions. One reading is that the two bodies of evidence meet on prior knowledge: struggle is more likely to help people who know enough to learn from it.

**Example or problem first depends on the learner.** Whether to show an example first or set a problem first is an open question, and the right answer depends on the learner. There is more on [the research on worked examples](t:1.2) and on [the case for useful difficulty](t:2.19). Example first has the stronger case for people who are new to a subject and learning a procedure, where an unaided attempt would swamp working memory. Problem first is supported by a pooled analysis of 53 studies (Sinha and Kapur, 2021). It did better when learners could bring what they already knew to the problem and a full explanation followed. Those studies were of school and university students learning concepts in maths and science. Younger primary pupils did better when taught first, and so did learners of general skills not tied to a subject.

**Go example first when people are new.** A rule of thumb, and no more than that: go example first when people are new and the goal is to carry out a procedure correctly. Go problem first when they have some background, the goal is understanding, and you have time to teach it properly straight after. The sequence in Do this is the design. The evidence supports its direction. The step sizes and timings are craft.

try.text: Take one procedure you teach. Write the progression from worked example to solving alone, with what is removed at each stage and the sign that tells you to move on. Then deliver the worked example aloud to a colleague, giving the reason at every step, with a timer running. Good looks like this: under five minutes, a reason for each step, and your colleague can finish the part-worked version without asking you anything.

items: **Support stays in place too long.** It bores experienced people and slows them down. Use the starting check and let those who pass skip ahead.
**Newcomers are left stuck** because struggle first is read as a licence. If people are new and it is a procedure, show the example first.
**Job title decides the starting point.** [Check prior knowledge](t:1.7) with three or four questions at the start.
**The worked example shows the steps** and not the reasons, so people copy it without knowing why. Say the reason at every step, and ask pairs to say it back.
**Every example looks the same.** People then learn the example and not the procedure. Change the surface details by the last stage.

Kalyuga and Renkl (2010), Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications: introduction to the special issue. Instructional Science.

quiz.q: What is the expertise reversal effect?
quiz.a: Guidance that helps beginners stops helping, or gets in the way, once people know more.

quiz.q: You are teaching new starters to check a customer invoice, a fixed procedure. Do you open with an example or a problem?
quiz.a: An example. Show a fully worked invoice, then one part-worked for them to finish, then a fresh one alone. An unaided first attempt would overload people who are new.

quiz.q: Half your group already does the task daily and looks bored by the worked example. What do you do?
quiz.a: Check what they know with a quick test and let those who pass skip to solving problems alone. Support kept too long holds experienced people back.

topics.tierReason: Reviews support strong guidance for beginners that is withdrawn as knowledge grows, and the right amount depends on what the learner already knows.

topics.title: Put the hard content where the energy is
topics.theory: Pacing, attention and the energy curve

situation.text: You are sent the agenda for a full day with a retailer's store managers. It opens at nine with a 40-minute policy update. The hardest case study sits at 13:30, straight after lunch, and a 90-minute talk follows it. By two o'clock half the room is looking at the table.

items: **Print the agenda and mark every block** high, medium or low for how much thinking it asks of the learners. Mark the learners' effort, not yours.

**Sketch the energy you expect** across the day. Trainers commonly find a room sharpest in mid-morning, flattest in the first 45 minutes after lunch and tired in the last hour. That pattern is craft, and there is [science on attention and physical state](t:1.14). Then ask the client what is particular to this group: an early drive, a late shift the night before, a dinner on the first evening of an offsite.
**Move the most demanding block** into the mid-morning slot. Move low-demand items such as policy updates and admin into a short slot in mid-afternoon.

**Break each block into segments** and change the activity between them: listening, then talking in pairs, then doing. As a planning habit, look at any stretch longer than 20 minutes in one mode and write down what the learner is doing during it. The 20 is a prompt to check, not a research limit.

**Plan three moments on purpose:** [the opening](t:4.21), [the slot after lunch](t:4.43) and [the close](t:4.32), which needs 20 minutes on a full day. After lunch, start with something active, such as a recall quiz followed by paired discussion.
**Put breaks in as clock times** and treat them as part of the learning: 15 minutes in mid-morning, 45 for lunch, 15 in mid-afternoon. When you run late, [cut content](t:4.31) and keep the break.
**Write two fallback moves** in the margin for each afternoon block, for when energy dips anyway. Re-order what is left, add a three-question recall task, or take five minutes.

why.text: **There is no fixed attention span.** Attention depends on interest, difficulty and design, and on how well the session is taught. A review of lecture studies found no good data for a limit of ten to fifteen minutes.

why.title: Attention span during lectures
why.found: This review traced the claim that attention falls after ten to fifteen minutes and found it rests mostly on repeated citation, with little sound primary data. The most consistent pattern was that attention varied with the teacher more than with the format.
why.means: Do not plan around a fixed attention limit. Plan for variety that serves the content, and work on delivery.

why.text: **A stopwatch rule has nothing behind it.** That finding changes what you plan with. A stopwatch rule ("switch every ten minutes") has nothing behind it, and it produces changes of activity that serve the clock. What you can control is the order of the day, the mix of activity and your own delivery. Breaking material into segments is widely recommended to help people process it. A pause between segments also gives people time to take stock, which is why a break counts as working time.

**Where energy and logic clash, sequence wins.** Matching demand to energy is craft reasoning. Hard content needs people's full effort, so it goes where they have most to give. The cost is that the best order for energy can fight the best order for logic. If the hard case study needs two ideas taught first, teach them at 09:30 and run the case at 10:15. Where one thing depends on another, [sequence wins](t:2.13) and you manage the energy with activity and breaks instead.

**The usual pattern also reverses for some groups.** Night-shift staff, people who have flown in that morning and a group on [day two of a residential](t:8.10) will not follow it. Ask before you assume.

try.text: Take a full-day agenda, yours or one you have sat through. Mark the demand of each block and the energy you would expect, then re-order it so the most demanding content sits where energy is highest. Talk a colleague through the new order in two minutes and give a reason for each move. If a reason is only "for variety", look at that block again.
