items: **Variety added for its own sake.** An energiser with no link to the content distracts. Make each change of activity do some of the teaching.
**Someone quotes a "ten-minute attention span".** The source is weak. Do not repeat it, and do not design to it.
**Claims of natural attention cycles** of a set length are promising, not settled. Do not fix session lengths by them.
**You push through a dip** to finish the section. Change something: take a short break, switch to a recall or paired task, or re-order what is left.
**The break gets cut** to recover time. The afternoon then costs you more than the ten minutes you saved. Cut a block of content.

items.label: Bradbury (2016), Attention span during lectures: 8 seconds, 10 minutes, or more? Advances in Physiology Education.

quiz.q: What did the review of lecture studies find about the ten to fifteen minute attention limit?
quiz.a: No good data for it. The claim rests mostly on repeated citation, and attention varied more with the teacher than with the format.

quiz.q: Your full-day agenda has the hardest case study straight after lunch. What do you change?
quiz.a: Move the case study to the morning, when energy is higher. After lunch, use something active such as a recall quiz and paired discussion.

quiz.q: It is mid-afternoon, you are halfway through a dense section and the room has gone flat. What do you do?
quiz.a: Change something. Take a short break, switch to a recall or paired task, or re-order what is left. Do not push on at the same intensity.

topics.tierReason: The attention span myth is well examined, but the advice on energy, breaks and placing hard content has only limited support that could be checked.

topics.title: Use problems, cases or enquiry when judgement is the goal

situation.text: A retailer wants its store managers to use better judgement when a customer complaint turns difficult. The current course is one slide of escalation rules and a five-question quiz. Everyone passes the quiz. The same avoidable complaints keep reaching the regional office.

items: **Choose the method** by what people must do. Use a case when they must decide in a situation you can write down in a page, in 20 to 40 minutes. Use a problem when they must also work out what they need to know before they can decide, over an hour or more. Use enquiry when the answer is not known in advance and has to be found in evidence people gather themselves, such as customer calls, store figures or interviews, over days or weeks.
**Check that people have the knowledge** the task needs, with three questions at the start. If they do not, [teach the basics directly first](t:2.13).
**Make at least two answers defensible** when you write the task. Give people a role, a decision to make, and information that is realistic: some of it irrelevant, one useful fact missing.

**Build in the guidance.** For a case or problem, give a time limit and a named output, for example "Choose one response and write your three reasons. You have 15 minutes." For an enquiry, set the question, name the sources, give a one-page template for the findings, and book a checkpoint halfway where you look at the evidence so far.

**Put people in groups** of three or four. Walk round and listen. When a group is stuck, ask a question that points at the evidence and leave the answer to them. There is more on [supporting groups while they work](t:4.26).
**Debrief the reasoning, not only the answer.** Ask each group why they chose as they did and what would have changed their mind. There is more on [debriefing an activity](t:4.28).
**Close by naming the principles** the case shows, and write them where everyone can see. Then give a second, shorter case with different surface details and the same principle underneath.

why.text: **Cases work once people know enough.** Problems and cases suit judgement, because people practise weighing evidence and deciding. They work when people already have enough knowledge to reason with. For newcomers, working things out with little guidance is slow and overloading. Teach the basics directly first.

**Cases build skill but take longer.** Pooled studies of problem-based courses in higher education found a clear gain in skills. Students gained slightly less knowledge, but remembered more of what they did learn. So there is a trade. A case takes 30 minutes to reach a point a slide makes in three. Spend that time where judgement is the goal, and teach plain facts plainly.
**Guidance is what makes the difference.** Discovery with no help did worse than direct teaching. Discovery with feedback, worked examples and prompts to explain did better than other methods.

why.title: Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
why.found: Two pooled analyses covered 164 studies. Discovery with no help did worse than explicit teaching (d = -0.38). Discovery with support such as feedback, worked examples and prompts to explain did better than other methods (d = 0.30).
why.means: Keep the problem or case, and build in guidance, feedback and a debrief.

why.text: **Keep enquiry open and keep the support.** Enquiry is where the guidance is most often dropped, because the point seems to be that people find things out for themselves. The finding above argues the other way: keep the question open and keep the support. The set question, the named sources, the template and the checkpoint in step 4 are that support. They are craft, and applying the finding to a workplace enquiry is a reading across from studies done mostly with students. A second craft point: an enquiry needs a question whose answer you do not already hold. If you know the answer and want people to reach it, write a case and say so.

try.text: Write one case for your subject: the role, the decision, the information and the output you want from groups. Try it on two or three colleagues for 15 minutes, then run the debrief aloud for ten. Good looks like this: they disagreed with each other, they gave reasons you had not written down, and you named no more than three principles at the end.

try.title: A worked example: from a rules slide to a case (store managers, groups of three, 35 minutes)
lines: Before: a slide of six escalation rules and a five-question quiz.
Starting check, 3 minutes: three questions on the refund limits. Everyone needs these to work the case.

The case, handed out on one page: "You are the duty manager on a Saturday. A regular customer wants a refund on a coat bought seven weeks ago, worn once, no receipt. The policy is 28 days. She is loud, and two other customers are filming. Your assistant has already said no."
Realistic clutter in the case: her loyalty card shows four years of purchases. The stock system is down.
The task: "Choose what you do in the next two minutes, and write your three reasons. You have 15 minutes. One person will report."
Two defensible answers: refund as goodwill and note it, or offer an exchange and move the conversation off the shop floor.
Trainer while groups work: listens, and asks only "What do you know for certain here?" and "Who else is affected by what you choose?"
Debrief, 12 minutes: each group gives its choice and one reason. Then to every group: "What would have changed your mind?"
Principles named and written up: move it off the floor first. Back your assistant in public and review the decision in private. Policy sets the default and the manager owns the exception.
Second case, 5 minutes, in pairs: the same principles in a phone complaint about a late delivery.

try.title: A worked example: a guided enquiry brief (12 new managers, two weeks between workshop days)
lines: The question: "Why do new starters in our teams leave in their first 90 days, and what is one thing a manager could change?"
Why it is an enquiry: nobody in the room, the trainer included, knows the answer yet.
Groups: four groups of three, mixed across departments.
Sources each group must use: two conversations with people who joined in the last six months, one with a manager from another team, and the onboarding checklist.
Sources that are off limits: individual HR records and exit interviews.
Template for findings, one page: what we looked at, what we found, what we are still unsure of, the one change we recommend.
Checkpoint, day 6, a 20-minute call for each group: the trainer looks at the evidence so far and asks, "What have you heard that surprised you?" and "What would prove your current view wrong?"
Report on day two: five minutes for each group, then five of questions from the other groups.
Debrief, 20 minutes: where the four groups agree, where they differ, and what each manager will try with their next new starter.
Trainer's close: the principles the findings point to, written up, with what the evidence was too thin to show.

items: **The case has an obvious answer,** so it is a quiz. Rewrite it until two responses are defensible and groups have to give reasons.
**Groups drift.** Give every task a deadline and a named output, and call the time at the halfway point.
**One case is treated as enough.** Several cases beat one, because people generalise from variety. Change the surface details and keep the principle.
**An enquiry launched with too little:** a question and a date and nothing between. Groups collect opinions and present them as findings. Name the sources, give the template and hold the checkpoint.
**The research is mostly from universities** and medical schools. Workplace courses are less studied, so check your own results.

items.label: Kirschner, Sweller and Clark (2006), Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work. Educational Psychologist, 41(2).
Schmidt, Loyens, Van Gog and Paas (2007), Problem-based learning is compatible with human cognitive architecture. Educational Psychologist, 42(2). A reply to Kirschner and colleagues.
Hmelo-Silver (2004), Problem-based learning: what and how do students learn? Educational Psychology Review, 16(3).
Dochy, Segers, Van den Bossche and Gijbels (2003), Effects of problem-based learning: a meta-analysis. Learning and Instruction, 13(5).
Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich and Tenenbaum (2011), Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning? Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(1).

quiz.q: What did the pooled studies find about discovery with no help compared with direct teaching?
quiz.a: Discovery with no help did worse. Discovery with feedback, worked examples and prompts to explain did better than other methods.

quiz.q: You want new starters to practise judgement on complaints, but they do not yet know the escalation rules. What do you do first?
quiz.a: Teach the basics directly. Cases work when people have enough knowledge to reason with. Then give them the case.

quiz.q: You set twelve managers a two-week enquiry into why new starters leave. At the report-back, every group presents its own opinions. What was missing from the design?
quiz.a: Guidance. Name the sources each group must use, give a one-page template for findings and hold a checkpoint halfway to look at the evidence. Finding out with no help does worse than finding out with support.

topics.tierReason: Pooled studies show problem-based and guided enquiry methods help skills and application, but unguided discovery does worse than direct teaching, so the result depends on prior knowledge and on how much guidance you give.

parts.title: Design the experience
parts.summary: Who is in the room, the journey they take, and where it drags.

topics.title: Design for the range of people, not the average
topics.theory: Personas and the myth of the average learner

situation.text: The sign-up list for a spreadsheet course at a software company has 14 names on it. Three people have never written a formula. Four build pivot tables every week and were told to come by their manager. Your course plan assumes someone in between, and nobody on the list is that person.

items: **Get real information before you describe anyone.** Ask for the sign-up list with job titles. Send a three-question form: "What do you do with this now?", "What do you want to be able to do?" and "What would stop you using it?" Book a 20-minute call with one manager and with two of the learners.

**List how these people differ** under four headings: prior knowledge, motivation (chose to come or was sent), context (where and when they will use the skill) and constraints (time, equipment, shift pattern, language). Cross out any difference that would not change something you build.

**Find the heading with the widest spread.** It is usually prior knowledge. Write one persona for each end of it. Add a third only if someone has a different reason for being there, such as the person who was sent. Stop at three.

**Keep each persona to half a page:** a first name, the job, what they can already do written as tasks ("can sort and filter, has never written a formula"), why they are coming, what limits them, and one line in their own words taken from the form or the call.

**Walk each persona through your session plan** one block at a time. Mark each block "keeps up", "lost" or "bored". Any block where one persona is lost or bored for more than about 15 minutes needs a change.

**Make one change for each mark.** For the least experienced person, ask what they need in order to keep up: a primer sent ahead, a worked example, a practice file with the first step done. For the most experienced, ask what keeps them interested: a harder version of the same task, or a skip-ahead challenge. Keep the objective the same for everyone and vary the support and the stretch.
**Offer more than one way** to take in content and to show learning. There is more on [designing for different minds](t:2.23).
**Compare the personas with the people** who came, after the first run. Correct them before you use them again.

why.text: **A design for the average fits few.** Almost nobody is average on every measure, so a design aimed at the average fits few people. One person can be strong on one dimension and weak on another.

**Prior knowledge matters and learning styles do not.** The differences that matter are real ones, such as prior knowledge and context. Learning styles are not among them. [Matching teaching to a preferred style](t:1.10) is not supported by the evidence. Prior knowledge earns the most attention because it changes which kind of help works: [support that a beginner needs](t:1.2) can slow down someone experienced.

**Personas are craft, not a research finding.** Personas themselves are a craft tool borrowed from product design. Treat them as craft, not as a research finding. A named person with a job and a limit is easier to design for than a list of percentages, and walking that person through the plan shows you the exact block where they would be lost.

**Every extra route is more to build.** There is a cost. Every extra route through a session is something to build and to manage in the room, which is why you stop at two or three personas and one change per problem. The advice also reverses in two cases. If the group is one team in one role with similar experience, skip the personas and design for that team. If the spread is so wide that the two ends share almost no tasks, no amount of optional material will hold them together, and the better answer is two courses.

try.text: Take a real course you are about to run. From the sign-up list and one conversation, write two contrasting personas, half a page each. Walk both through the plan and mark every block. Name one design change each persona demands.

try.title: A worked example: two personas for a spreadsheet course, and what each one changes

head: Priya, customer support adviser
Dan, finance analyst
rows: Can already do
Sorts and filters a list. Has never written a formula.
Lookups and pivot tables every week. Self-taught.
Why they are coming
Wants to stop asking a colleague to build her weekly report.
His manager booked the whole team.
What limits them
Dreads tests. Shares a laptop on shift.

In their words

Where the plan fails them

The change

Two hours to write three harder tasks.

items: **Personas invented at your desk.** Invented personas are stereotypes. Ground every line in the list, the form or a call, and delete anything you cannot trace.
**You write six.** Too many personas paralyse the design, because every block fails somebody. Two or three is enough.
**The beginner's change seems a favour** to one person, and you treat it as one. Designing for the edges often helps the middle too. A worked example before the task helps most of the room.
**An unpaid assistant all day:** you use the experienced person as one. They came to learn something as well, so give them the harder task.
**The personas are never checked.** People change between cohorts. Compare them with the room after each run.

CAST (2024), Universal Design for Learning Guidelines, version 3.0.
Pruitt and Grudin (2003), Personas: practice and theory. Conference on Designing for User Experiences.
Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork (2008), Learning styles: concepts and evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3).

quiz.q: Why does a course designed for the average learner fit few people?
quiz.a: Almost nobody is average on every measure. One person can be strong on one dimension and weak on another.

quiz.q: You are designing a spreadsheet course. The sign-up list has complete beginners and working analysts. What do you do?
quiz.a: Build a persona for each end from the list, a short form and a call, then walk both through the plan. Make one change for each, such as a primer and worked examples for the beginners and a skip-ahead challenge for the analysts.

quiz.q: A colleague suggests sorting the group into visual and auditory learners. What do you say?
quiz.a: [Matching teaching to learning styles](t:1.10) is not supported by the evidence. Design for differences that are real: prior knowledge, motivation, context and constraints.

topics.tierReason: Personas and designing for a range of people are widely used design practice with little direct testing in training. The warning about learning styles is well supported.

topics.title: Map every step from first email to follow-up

situation.text: You have planned a two-day course for twelve new managers to the minute. Then the client's coordinator forwards you the invitation that went out last week. It is a calendar entry titled "Mgmt Trng Cohort 3" with a room number on the wrong floor. Nothing at all is planned for the week after.

items: **Draw a table of every step**, one row each, in the order the learner meets them: first hearing about it, the invitation, pre-work, the reminder, arriving, the first activity, the event itself, the last hour, the first day back, the first use, the manager's conversation and the follow-up. Ten to fourteen rows is enough.
**Fill in four columns for every row:** what the learner receives or does, who sends or owns it, what the learner is likely to think or feel, and what could go wrong.

**Collect the real items.** Ask the client for the invitation, the calendar entry and the booking confirmation as they were sent. Read them on a phone, as a learner would, and note what you still do not know at the end.
**Star the moments** that can build or break motivation and belonging. The usual ones are the invitation, arriving, the first activity, the last hour and the first week back.

**Circle every row with no owner**, or an owner who is not you. These are where most of the gaps sit. For each one, write the item yourself or send the owner a draft they can use. [Write the first contact yourself](t:2.20), or at least edit it. [Plan the first ten minutes](t:4.21) of the first session.

**Plan the return to work** as rows of its own: the first use, the manager's conversation and a check-in. There is more on [designing the before and after](t:2.5), [planning the first use at work](t:5.2) and [when to time the follow-up](t:5.4).

**Test the map on two people** who attended last time, or two who are about to. Take 15 minutes each and say: "Talk me through what happened from the moment you first heard about this." Correct the map from what they tell you. Then plan [the high point and the close](t:2.18) of the event itself.

why.text: **The map finds the handovers.** Two fragile parts of a programme are the start and the return to work. If you design only the event, those are left to chance. They are also the parts most likely to belong to somebody else: a coordinator sends the invitation, a manager decides whether the first week back includes any use of the skill. The map is a way of finding the handovers. Mapping a service step by step comes from service design, and using it for training is craft, not a tested method.

**People remember the peak and the end.** People judge an experience largely by its most intense moment and by how it ends. Its length hardly matters. This is about how the programme is remembered and rated. It does not show that people learn more. There is more on how to [plan the high point and the close](t:2.18).

why.title: A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule
why.found: Across 174 effect sizes, ratings given after an experience were strongly related to its peak and its end (r = 0.58). That was about as strong as the link with the average of all moments. The length of the experience had almost no effect.
why.means: Design the high point and the close on purpose, and do not treat good ratings as proof of learning.

why.text: **The trade-off is reach.** You cannot own every row, and a trainer who tries to rewrite the client's booking system will run out of goodwill. Put your effort into the starred rows and offer drafts for the rest. On a one-hour session for a team that already works together, a full map is more than the job needs. Check the invitation and the follow-up and leave it there.

try.text: Map a real course from the first message to the follow-up, using the real invitation and calendar entry. Star the moments that matter and circle the rows nobody owns. Then ring one past participant and ask them to talk you through what happened. Good looks like this: you find at least one row you did not know existed, and every circled row ends up with a name against it.

items: **The map ends with the event.** Intensive formats such as retreats need [a planned "after"](t:8.17) most of all. Add the rows for the return before you finish.
**You treat the map as fact.** It is a guess until you test it with learners, so make the two phone calls.

**You leave the administration to others** and never read it. The administration is part of the experience. A wrong room number or a late invitation sets the tone before you have said a word. Ask to see everything that will be sent.
**The map has forty rows** and nobody acts on it. Keep it to one page and agree three changes with the client.
**A circled row stays circled.** A change with no owner will not happen. Put a name on each one before the meeting ends.

quiz.q: In the pooled analysis of the peak-end rule, how much did the length of an experience affect how people rated it afterwards?
quiz.a: Hardly at all. The peak and the end were related to the rating about as strongly as the average of all moments.

quiz.q: Your two-day course scores well, but people arrive unsure why they were sent and nothing happens afterwards. What do you do?
quiz.a: Map every step from the first message to the follow-up, with an owner for each row. Rewrite the joining message with a reason to come, and plan the return to work, such as a manager conversation and a check-in two weeks later.

quiz.q: Ratings rise after you add a strong closing hour. The sponsor says people are now learning more. What do you say?
quiz.a: The ratings show how the course is remembered. They do not show learning, so check that separately.

topics.tierReason: Journey mapping is a service design practice with little direct testing in training. The peak-end finding is well supported for how experiences are rated afterwards, not for how much is learned.

topics.title: Plan a peak and a proper ending
topics.theory: The emotional arc and experience mechanics

situation.text: You run a 90-minute data protection session for a customer support team. The content is accurate, the exercise works and the forms say "fine". A week later nobody can tell you what happened in it. It ran at one level from the first slide to the last and ended with "Any questions?" while people packed their bags.

items: **Draw the session as a line** across a page, and mark clock times on it. Sketch the shape you want above it: a rise at the opening, one high point about two thirds of the way through, and a close that is planned as carefully as the start.

**Open with a question people want answered**, and [let them guess before you answer it](t:1.24). Write the question down word for word. Give pairs two minutes to guess, take three guesses, then give the answer.

**Set tasks that take effort** but that most people can do. If everyone finishes early, the task was too easy. If people stop trying, it was too hard. Prepare an easier and a harder version of the main task so you can switch in the room.

**Plan one high point** and build towards it: the hardest case, a live demonstration, or the moment people use the skill on a real problem of their own. Give it the longest unbroken block in the session. Introduce nothing new after it.

**Close on purpose.** In a short session, protect the last ten minutes for a short practice and one commitment, written down or said to a partner. Take questions before the close, so they are not the last thing that happens. A full day needs [a longer close](t:4.32).
**Decide now what goes** if you run late, and mark it "cut first" on the plan. [Cut content from the middle](t:4.31) and keep the high point and the close.
**Limit story and challenge** to where they carry the content. Test each one by removing it. If the point still lands without the story, the story was decoration.
**Add one check of learning** that does not depend on how people feel: a task at the end, or a question a week later.

why.text: **The feel of a course is designed.** Emotion affects attention, motivation and memory, so the feel of a course is a design matter. Curiosity arises from a gap between what people know and what they want to know. That is the reason for the guess: a question you answer at once opens no gap. Absorption is more likely when challenge and skill are balanced, though [that link is moderate and correlational](t:8.2).

why.title: Curiosity and memory for answers
why.found: People read trivia questions and rated their curiosity. They spent tokens or waiting time to see answers they were more curious about. One to two weeks later they recalled surprising answers better when they had been more curious.
why.means: Open with a question people want answered, let them guess, then give the answer.

why.text: **Engagement is a means.** A session can be enjoyable and teach little, and interesting but irrelevant material can lower learning. So the high point has to be the content at its most demanding, with the group doing the work. A funny video two thirds of the way in is a peak too, and it may teach nothing.

**A planned shape is a rating effect.** A planned high point and a deliberate close change how people rate and remember the session. That is worth having, but it is a rating effect. Check learning separately. You can read about [the pooled study behind this](t:2.17). The placing and timings here are craft.

**The shape costs you coverage.** The trade-off is that a shaped session covers less. Protecting a long block and a close means something in the middle goes. A short briefing whose only job is to pass on three facts does not need an arc.

try.text: Take one session you run and draw its arc on a single page: where you create curiosity, where you aim for absorption and how you close. Then stand up and say the opening question and the closing two minutes aloud against a timer. Record the close on your phone. Good looks like this: the opening question makes a colleague want to guess, the close ends on what people will do, and "Any questions?" is not your last line.

items: **You add something interesting** that has nothing to do with the objective. Interesting but irrelevant material can lower learning. Keep the story only if the point needs it.
**You reach for points and prizes** to lift the energy. [Game elements can backfire](t:2.22). Put the challenge in the task.
**The session ends on a high** and nothing follows. A big finish with no follow-up is theatre. Tie [the closing commitment to a check-in](t:5.4).
**You run late** and the close is the thing that goes. Cut the block marked "cut first" as soon as you are ten minutes behind.
**The forms improve** and you report that the course now works. Ratings and learning are different measures. Report both.

quiz.q: In the curiosity study by Kang and colleagues, which answers did people recall better one to two weeks later?
quiz.a: Surprising answers to the questions they had been more curious about.

quiz.q: Your data protection session has sound content and feels flat. You have ten minutes to rework the opening. What do you do?
quiz.a: Open with a realistic case and one question people want answered. Let them guess before you give the answer.

quiz.q: You are 20 minutes behind and the planned close is at risk. What do you do?
quiz.a: Cut content from the middle and keep the last ten minutes for a short practice and one commitment. Then check learning separately, because a good ending changes ratings, not what people can do.

topics.tierReason: Single ideas here have support, such as curiosity helping memory and endings shaping ratings, but designing an emotional arc to improve learning in training has little direct testing.

topics.title: Remove the friction that frustrates, keep the friction that teaches

situation.text: The feedback on an onboarding course for new customer support staff says "too hard" in a dozen different ways. Read closely, the comments are about two different things. One is a login that times out. The other is the recall questions at the start of each module. The sponsor wants both gone by next month.

items: **List every point where learners struggle**, from three places: help-desk queries, feedback forms and your own walk-through. Do the walk-through as a newcomer would. Use a fresh account, the standard laptop or a phone, and the real joining emails, and note every place you hesitate.
**Write each point on one line:** where it is, what the learner is trying to do and what stops them.

**Sort each line with one question:** "Is the effort going into the thing we want them to learn?" Recalling, working something out, deciding and correcting an error all teach. Hunting for a file, decoding an instruction, waiting for a page and filling in admin only frustrate.

**Remove the friction that only frustrates** and give each fix an owner: menus that are hard to find your way round, unclear instructions, admin, technical barriers. Put instructions in one place. Show the first step of any task done.

**Keep the friction that teaches:** recall, effort, working it out. Then check each one can be overcome. If most people cannot get there with what they have been taught, add a hint, put a worked example in front of it or shorten the gap since they last met the content.
**Choose example first or problem first** for each new piece of content, using the rule of thumb in the next section.
**Tell learners which difficulty is staying** and why, in the course itself and in two sentences.
**Look again after the changes** at help-desk queries and at scores on practice tasks.

why.text: **Smoothing everything removes the learning too.** Some friction is the effort that builds lasting learning. Some is waste. Confusing the two is a common and costly mistake, because smoothing everything removes the learning along with the annoyance. A polished course can still fail to teach.

**Helpful difficulty feels like learning less.** [The difficulties that help](t:1.3) include spacing, recall from memory, mixing topics and making errors you then correct. A difficulty stops being useful when people lack the background to overcome it. Learners often feel they are learning less under these conditions, which is why they ask for them to be removed. The complaint is honest, and you still keep the questions.

**Problem first or example first is open.** Trying a problem before being taught is one such difficulty. Whether to set a problem first or show an example first is an open question. The case for example first comes from [cutting load with worked examples](t:1.2) and from [starting with full support](t:2.13). Example first has the stronger case for people who are new to a subject and learning a procedure, where an unaided attempt would swamp working memory. Problem first is supported by a pooled analysis of 53 studies (Sinha and Kapur, 2021). It did better when learners could bring what they already knew to the problem and a full explanation followed. Those studies were of school and university students learning concepts in maths and science. Younger primary pupils did better when taught first, and so did learners of general skills not tied to a subject.

why.title: When problem solving followed by instruction works
why.found: A pooled analysis of 53 studies and 166 comparisons. Problem solving followed by instruction did better than instruction followed by problem solving (g = 0.36). The gain was larger when the design followed productive failure principles closely. Pupils in school years 2 to 5 did better with instruction first.
why.means: Consider letting people who have some background attempt a hard, solvable problem before you teach the method, then teach it properly. The studies were of school and university students, not adults at work.

why.text: **The order depends on learner and goal.** A rule of thumb, and no more than that: go example first when people are new and the goal is to carry out a procedure correctly. Go problem first when they have some background, the goal is understanding, and you have time to teach it properly straight after. The sorting question in step three is craft. Some cases will not sort cleanly. A deliberately awkward system in a simulation, for example, teaches if the real system is awkward too.

try.text: Run a friction audit on a real course. Walk through it as a newcomer with a timer running, collect the last month of queries and comments, and sort every point. Decide what to remove and what to protect. Then say aloud, as you would to a group, why one difficulty is staying. Good looks like this: every line has a decision and an owner.

items: **Learners want the useful difficulty removed** too. Explain why it stays, and fix the login the same week so they can see you listened.
**You audit from memory.** You cannot see friction you are used to. Walk through as a newcomer, or watch a real newcomer do it.
**A kept difficulty leaves people stuck.** Confusion that never resolves is not productive. Follow every hard attempt with the answer and an explanation.
**You remove everything on the list** to raise the ease score. The score may rise while the learning falls. Report the two kinds of friction to the sponsor separately.
**Complete beginners get a problem first** while learning a procedure. [Show an example first](t:2.13) and move to problems once they have some footing.

Sinha and Kapur (2021), When problem solving followed by instruction works: evidence for productive failure. Review of Educational Research, 2021.

quiz.q: In the pooled analysis by Sinha and Kapur, which did better on average: problem solving followed by instruction, or instruction followed by problem solving?
quiz.a: Problem solving first, by a moderate margin (g = 0.36). Pupils in school years 2 to 5 did better with instruction first.

quiz.q: Learners complain about four things: a login that times out, instructions spread over three emails, recall questions at the start of each module, and a case with no model answer until they have tried it. What do you change?
quiz.a: Fix the login and put the instructions in one place. Keep the recall questions and the case, and tell learners why they stay.

quiz.q: A sponsor asks you to drop the practice questions because learners say they make the course feel harder. What do you say?
quiz.a: Recall from memory is one of the difficulties that helps, and learners often feel they are learning less under it. Keep the questions, explain why, and check people have enough background to answer them.

topics.tierReason: Effortful practice such as recall, spacing and trying a problem before being taught is supported by pooled studies, but it only helps when learners can meet the challenge, and the friction audit itself is an untested practitioner tool.

topics.title: Build anticipation before the event
topics.theory: Anticipation, priming and what happens before training

situation.text: The joining email for a one-day course is a calendar invite and a car park map. Twelve new managers will arrive on Tuesday knowing the room number and nothing else. Two of them think it is a compliance briefing, and one has been told only that "HR wants you on it".

items: **Write the joining note yourself**, or ask to edit the client's. Send it about a week before, from a named person. Keep it to what someone can read in two minutes, with the practical details at the bottom.
**Start with why this matters to them**, in one or two sentences that use their own situation. Then say one thing they will be able to do by the end of the day.
**Direct people's attention on the day** to the two or three ideas everything else hangs on. Name them in plain words.
**Send one question to think about**, or a task that takes ten minutes at most. Say how you will use it, then use the answers in the first session.

**Have the manager talk to each person** before they come. [Send the manager two questions to ask](t:2.4), such as "What do you want to get better at?" and "Where will you use it first?" Ten minutes is enough.
**Give a first sight** of the people and the place: a photo of you, a photo of the room, and who else is coming.
**Say what the day involves** and what it does not, in a few plain lines. There is more on [how to write those lines](t:2.21).
**Send one short reminder two days before**, with the question repeated. Then stop. Keep everything short.

why.text: **Preparation before training helps learning.** What happens before training affects what people get from it. A pooled analysis looked at five pre-training steps: advice on what to pay attention to, strategies for checking your own understanding, advance organisers, goal orientation and preparatory information. All helped learning. The first two helped most consistently. That is why the note names the ideas to look out for and carries a question people can test themselves against.

why.title: Pre-training interventions and learning
why.found: A doctoral meta-analysis of 359 studies with 37,038 participants. Pre-training interventions had consistently positive effects on learning. Advice on where to direct attention and strategies for monitoring your own learning gave the most consistent gains.
why.means: Before the course, tell people what to look out for and give them a question to check their own understanding against.

why.text: **Anticipation itself is untested.** Whether looking forward to a course changes what people take from it has not been tested directly. Treat anticipation as a reasonable aim, not a proven effect. The research also tested structured steps used with the training itself. A joining email is a looser version, so check your own results.

**Extra messages compete with real work.** The rest is craft. A note from a named person with a photo answers the questions people do not ask aloud: who is this, who else will be there, will I look foolish. The question does a second job for you, because the answers tell you who is in the room before you start. The trade-off is attention. Every extra message before the event competes with people's real work, and pre-work you do not use teaches them to skip the next lot. One note, one question and one reminder is a limit worth keeping.

try.text: Take a real joining email and rewrite it so it says why, names what people will be able to do, tells them what to look out for and asks one question. Read it aloud against a timer. Then send it to one colleague who knows nothing about the course and ask what they now expect. Good looks like this: it takes under two minutes to read, and your colleague can tell you the question and one thing the day is for.

try.title: Before: the joining email as sent
lines: Subject: Mgmt Trng Cohort 3
When: Tuesday, 09:30 to 16:30. Where: Room 2.04.
Parking: see attached map. Lunch provided.

try.title: A worked example: the joining note, rewritten, for twelve new managers on a day about giving feedback
lines: Subject: Tuesday's feedback day: one question to bring
Hello Asha,
You took on a team this year. One of the hardest parts of that job is telling someone, clearly and kindly, what you need them to do differently. Tuesday is a day for practising exactly that.
By half past four you will have planned one real feedback conversation and rehearsed it twice.
Three ideas run through the day, so look out for them: describe what you saw and leave out what you think it means, say the effect it had, and ask before you advise.

One question to bring an answer to: who on your team most needs to hear something from you, and what has stopped you saying it? You will not have to name them. We start the day with this, so please think about it on the way in.
Your manager will find ten minutes with you this week to ask what you want from the day.
What to expect: most of the day is practice in groups of three, with very few slides. Nothing is recorded and nothing is reported back to your manager.
There will be twelve of you, all in your first year of managing a team. I'm Sam, and I'll be running the day. My photo and one of the room are below.
Practical details: Tuesday, 09:30 to 16:30, Room 2.04 on the second floor. Coffee from 09:15. Lunch is provided, so tell me by Friday if you have a dietary need. Parking map attached.
If anything would help you take part, reply to me and I will sort it out.
Sam

items: **The note promises too much:** a day that will change everything. Over-selling sets up disappointment. Promise one thing people will be able to do, and deliver it.
**Pre-work is set and never mentioned** again. Pre-work that is not used is resented. Use the answers in the first 15 minutes, or do not ask.
**The client wants a countdown** of five emails. Too much contact before the event is noise. Offer one note and one reminder.
**The why uses the sponsor's language**, such as "aligning to our leadership framework". Rewrite it as the learner's problem.
**You assume the note worked.** The research tested structured steps used with the training itself, and a joining email is a looser version. Ask at the start who read it and what they brought.

items.label: Mesmer-Magnus (2005), The impact of pre-training interventions on cognitive, skill, and affective learning outcomes: a meta-analytic examination of four decades of research. Doctoral dissertation, Florida International University.
Cannon-Bowers, Rhodenizer, Salas and Bowers (1998), A framework for understanding pre-practice conditions and their impact on learning. Personnel Psychology, 51(2).

quiz.q: In the pooled analysis of pre-training steps, which two helped learning most consistently?
quiz.a: Advice on what to pay attention to, and strategies for checking your own understanding.

quiz.q: The client's joining email is a calendar invite and a car park map. You can add five lines. What do you add?
quiz.a: Why the course matters to this team, one thing people will be able to do afterwards, what to look out for, and one question to bring an answer to.

quiz.q: A client wants a four-week teaser campaign and asks you to confirm it will make people learn more on the day. What do you say?
quiz.a: Telling people what to pay attention to is supported by research. Whether looking forward to a course changes what people learn has not been tested directly. Keep the contact short, because too much before the event is noise.

topics.tierReason: Pooled studies support specific pre-training steps such as attention advice and advance organisers, but whether a joining message or looking forward to a course changes learning has not been tested directly.

topics.title: Tell learners what to expect, and what not to

situation.text: It is 09:40 on a workshop for a software company's sales team about handling price objections. You announce the first practice round in threes. Two people fold their arms and one says, "Nobody told us this was role-play." Another has been waiting for someone to explain the new price list, which is not in your plan at all.

items: **Mark up your session plan for surprises**, meaning anything a reasonable person would not expect: role-play, speaking in front of the group, being recorded, pre-work, a test, a late finish, their manager in the room. Mark what is missing too, such as the topic people assume will be covered.

**Write a preview in five lines.** What happens, with rough proportions ("about two thirds of the day is practice in threes"). What the session does not include. What effort you will ask of people. What they will be able to do at the end. What they will not.
**Say plainly what people tend to dread** and put the safeguards next to it: how long it lasts, who is watching, and whether they can observe first.

**Try the five lines** on two or three people from the group before you send them. Ask: "What do you expect now? Does anything put you off?" Change the wording that worried them without hiding the activity.
**Send the preview** in [the joining note](t:2.20) about a week ahead. [Give managers the same five lines](t:2.4), since they set expectations too.
**Repeat it at the start** in under a minute, then ask: "Is any of that a surprise?" Wait for an answer. Deal with surprises there and then.
**Tell people if the format changes** after the note has gone, as soon as you know, and say what changed.

why.text: **A realistic preview lets people prepare and choose.** The research behind it comes from recruitment, not training. Pooled studies of realistic job previews found that candidates who got one started with lower expectations, and that previews went with fewer leavers and better job performance. Nobody has shown the same for a training course, so treat this as a reasonable borrowing.

why.title: Realistic job previews: a meta-analysis
why.found: A pooled analysis of 40 studies. Realistic job previews went with lower starting expectations, fewer people dropping out of recruitment, lower turnover and higher job performance. Timing, medium and setting changed the size of the effect.
why.means: Give an honest preview of the course, and remember the evidence is borrowed from hiring.

why.text: **Surprise costs you the first hour.** The craft reasoning is about the first hour. A person who is surprised by role-play spends the opening deciding whether to object, and you spend it winning them back. Told a week before, the same person has had time to pick a real case, ask a question or tell you about something that makes the activity hard for them. Being honest about limits also protects your credibility. If the invitation promised mastery, every exercise is measured against a promise the day cannot keep.

**Too many warnings make people brace.** There is a balance to hold. A preview that lists every demand reads as a warning, and people arrive braced. State the hard part once, with its safeguard, and give more space to what people will leave with. The advice bends for one kind of activity. Some simulations depend on people not knowing what is coming. For those, preview the kind of activity and the effort involved, and keep the content back.

try.text: Write a five-line preview for one course: what happens, what it leaves out, what you will ask of people, what they will leave with and what they will not. Then stand up and say it aloud as you would in the first minute of the day, ending with "Is any of that a surprise?" Record it. Good looks like this: it takes under a minute, the hard part is named once without apology, and nothing in it is a promise you cannot keep.

try.title: A worked example: a joining note with the preview in it, for a sales team workshop on price objections
lines: Subject: Thursday's workshop: what it is, and what it is not
Hello Tom,
On Thursday the team spends a day on one moment in a sales call: the customer says the price is too high, and what you say next.
What happens: about two thirds of the day is practice in groups of three, using objections you have heard yourselves. I will show a method in the first hour, and after that it is mostly you.
The practice is role-play, in short rounds of five minutes. Only your group of three sees it. In the first round you can observe before you take a turn. Nothing is recorded and nothing is scored.
What it is not: it is not a briefing on the new price list. Your sales manager is covering that at Monday's team meeting.
What I will ask of you: bring one real deal where price came up and you were not happy with how it went. Expect to say things aloud that feel clumsy the first time.
What you will leave with: a worded response to your three most common objections, practised at least twice each.
What you will not leave with: a script that works on every customer. One day gets you a method and a start, and the habit comes from using it on calls afterwards.
Practical details: Thursday, 09:30 to 16:30, the training room on the first floor. Lunch is provided.
If anything about the day would make it hard for you to take part, reply to me and we will sort it out beforehand.
Sam

try.title: Words you can use: the same preview in the first minute of the day
lines: "Before we start, here is what today is. Most of it is you practising in threes, on objections you brought with you."
"The practice is short rounds, five minutes each, seen only by your three. You can watch the first round before you take a turn."
"We are not covering the new price list. That is Monday's team meeting."
"You will leave with wording for your three commonest objections. You will not leave with a script that works on everyone."
"Is any of that a surprise?"

items: **A preview that warns too much** puts people off. Name the demanding part once, give the safeguard, and move on to what people gain.
**The manager tells the team** it is "a bit of a refresher". Managers set expectations too. [Brief them with the same five lines](t:2.4).
**The plan changes** and the note does not. If the format changes, tell people before the day.
**You send the preview cold** to the whole group. In the recruitment studies, when and how the preview was given changed its effect. Try yours on a few people first.
**The sponsor adds a line** promising mastery. Replace it with what people will leave with and what they will not.

items.label: Phillips (1998), Effects of realistic job previews on multiple organizational outcomes: a meta-analysis. Academy of Management Journal, 41(6). Research on recruitment, not on training.

quiz.q: Where does the research on realistic previews come from?
quiz.a: Recruitment. Job previews went with lower starting expectations and fewer leavers. The idea is borrowed for training, not tested there.

quiz.q: Your workshop includes a role-play, and you know some people dread them. What do you put in the joining note?
quiz.a: Say plainly that there is role-play, how long it lasts, who sees it and that people can observe first. Say what else the day involves and what effort you will ask for.

quiz.q: A sponsor wants the invitation to say people will "master difficult conversations in a day". What do you do?
quiz.a: Rewrite it as what people will leave with, such as a plan for one real conversation, and say they will not leave as experts. Over-promising costs you credibility when the day cannot deliver it.

topics.tierReason: The evidence for realistic previews comes from recruitment. No study of previews given before a training course was opened, so for training this is sensible practice, not a tested method.

topics.title: Use game elements only where they help

situation.text: A retailer is launching a new handset and wants its store staff trained in three weeks. The creative team presents a space theme, points for every module opened, badges and a leaderboard between stores to "drive engagement". The client's brand lead loves it. Nobody has yet said what staff will practise.

items: **Say which behaviour should increase**, as something you could count in practice. "Attempts the opening conversation with five different shoppers" is a behaviour. "Engagement" is a hope.
**Agree what people will practise** before anyone discusses a theme. Write it as one line and get the client to sign it off.

**Use game elements that give clear goals**, feedback and visible progress. Write the goal as one sentence the learner sees. Give feedback on every attempt. Let progress move only when a practice task is passed, never when a page is opened.

**Be wary of competition and of rewards** for tasks people already value. If the client wants competition, pair it with collaboration, such as store teams working towards a shared target, and do not rank individuals in public.
**Tie every element to the objective.** Next to each one, finish the sentence "This makes people do more of ...". If the answer is "logging in", the element is aimed at the wrong thing.
**Test each element by taking it away.** If the practice gets worse without it, keep it. If nothing changes, it is decoration.
**Give people who dislike competing another route** to the same practice.
**Check whether learning improved**, not only activity. Agree the measure before the build: scores on the last and hardest practice task, and what trainers or managers see on the shop floor.

why.text: **Gamification has small positive effects.** A pooled analysis of gamification studies found small positive effects on three kinds of outcome: what people learned (g = 0.49), their motivation (g = 0.36) and their behaviour (g = 0.25). The effect on what people learned held up in the more rigorous studies. The other two were less steady.

why.title: The gamification of learning: a meta-analysis
why.found: Pooled effects of gamification were small and positive: g = 0.49 for cognitive outcomes (19 studies), g = 0.36 for motivation (16 studies) and g = 0.25 for behaviour (9 studies). Only the cognitive effect stayed stable in the high-rigour studies.
why.means: Expect a modest gain at best, and measure learning, not activity.

why.text: **Rewards and leaderboards can backfire.** [Rewards can reduce interest](t:1.16) in tasks people already enjoy. Leaderboards can motivate those near the top and discourage the rest. In the same analysis, a story wrapped round the tasks helped behaviour, and so did competition when it was combined with collaboration. Which design choices help learning itself is not yet settled.

**It helps to separate two kinds of fun.** Fun that carries the practice is built into the task: a clear goal, feedback on each attempt, progress the learner can see, and a story that gives the task a reason. Remove it and the practice gets worse. Decoration sits on top: points for turning up, badges for opening a page, a theme that has nothing to do with the skill. Remove it and the practice is unchanged. The first kind matches the elements in the steps above, and the pooled analysis found that a story round the tasks helped behaviour. The analysis does not show that a more enjoyable session teaches more, so "make it fun" is a sound brief only when the fun is in the practice.

**Decoration is cheap and practice costs more.** The take-away test and the wording of the brief are craft. They exist because a point system counts whatever is easiest to count, and people then do more of that. The trade-off is commercial as much as educational. Decoration is cheap to add and looks good in a demonstration, and practice with feedback on every attempt costs more to build. Say that to the client early, so the budget goes on the attempts and the feedback.

try.text: Take one gamified element you use or have been offered. Write what behaviour it drives and whether that behaviour is learning. Then run the take-away test on paper: describe the practice with the element removed. If you are working with a creative team, write them a brief like the one below and talk them through it aloud before you send it.

try.title: A worked example: a brief for a creative team (launch training for store staff)
lines: What people practise: the first 30 seconds with a shopper who picks up the new handset.
Goal the learner sees: "Find out what this shopper needs in three questions."
Feedback: after each attempt the shopper character reacts, and one line says what the question revealed.
Progress: five shoppers, each harder than the last. A bar fills when a shopper is helped, not when a screen is opened.
Story: a Saturday on the shop floor, opening to close.
Please do not add: points for logging in, a leaderboard between stores, or mini-games unrelated to the conversation.
How we will judge it: scores on the fifth shopper, and what field trainers see in store.

items: **Points for clicking reward clicking.** Attach points and progress to passed practice tasks, or leave them out.
**The first fortnight looks wonderful.** Novelty wears off, so judge the design on later weeks and on practice scores.
**Some people dislike competing.** Offer another route, such as beating your own last score.
**The brief is "make it fun"**, from a client or creative team. Agree what people will practise first, then ask for the goal, the feedback, the progress and the story to be built round that.
**The sponsor's report shows logins** and badges earned. Those are activity figures. Report scores on the hardest practice task beside them.

items.label: Sailer and Homner (2020), The gamification of learning: a meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 32(1).

quiz.q: How large are the effects of gamification on learning?
quiz.a: Small on average. Steadiest for what people learn, less steady for motivation and behaviour.

quiz.q: A creative team proposes a space theme, points for every module opened and a leaderboard between regions. What do you ask for instead?
quiz.a: Ask what people will practise, then for a clear goal, feedback on each attempt, visible progress and a story tied to that task. Points for opening modules reward opening modules, and ranking discourages those near the bottom.

quiz.q: A client says, "Our brand is fun, so the training must be fun." What do you say?
quiz.a: Agree, and put the fun in the practice: a challenge with a goal, quick feedback and a story from their customers' world. Check each element by asking whether the practice would be worse without it.

topics.tierReason: One meta-analysis found small positive effects, steady for what people learn and less steady for motivation and behaviour, and what makes gamification work is still unsettled.

topics.title: Design for different minds from the start
topics.theory: Inclusion, neurodiversity and Universal Design for Learning

situation.text: At the first break of a half-day session for a retailer's store managers, a participant tells you quietly that she cannot follow fast speech, cannot read the small text on your slides and cannot sit still for ninety minutes. You have two and a half hours left, a deck in small type and one long block planned before lunch.

items: **Ask about needs in advance**, in plain words, on the joining form: "Is there anything that would help you take part?" Give examples so people know what they can ask for: slides in advance, captions, a seat near the door, regular breaks, large print. Do not ask why.
**Send materials to everyone two days ahead**, in [a format a screen reader can use](t:3.15).
**Present content in more than one way:** spoken, written, visual. Say each instruction aloud and show it on screen or on a card. Give the key points on a one-page handout as well as on slides.

**Offer different ways to take part** and to show learning. Let people answer by speaking, by writing on a card or in a pair before the whole group. Where you check learning, allow a spoken answer or a written one.
**Build in a break every hour**, a chance to move, and some quiet working time. Five minutes each hour is enough, and a few minutes of silent writing before a discussion gives people time to think.
**Make adjustments normal for everyone.** Send slides to all, caption every video, and say at the start that anyone can stand, move or step out without asking.
**Thank whoever tells you on the day**, act on what you can at once, and ask privately at the next break: "What else would help this afternoon?"
**Add what you learned afterwards** to your standard form and your standard set-up.

why.text: **Planning for range is fairer, usually easier.** Designing for a range of people from the start is fairer, and usually easier, than fixing it for one person on the day. Universal Design for Learning, a widely used framework from CAST, suggests offering several means of engagement, of presenting content and of responding.

**The framework as a whole is unproven.** Many adjustments help everyone. Evidence that the framework as a whole raises learning is still developing. So treat the framework as a sensible checklist, not as a proven method, and judge each adjustment on whether it removes a barrier for someone in your room.

**People often will not ask.** The practical reasoning is about who speaks up. People often will not tell a trainer they have never met that they need something, and they should not have to explain why. An open question with examples makes asking easy. Making the common adjustments standard goes further, because the person who would never ask still gets the slides, the captions and the break.

**Designing for everyone has costs and limits.** There are costs and limits. Sending slides ahead removes surprise, so hold back the answer to an opening question if the session depends on it. More ways of responding take more time to run, so choose them for the moments that matter most. Designing for everyone also does not replace an individual adjustment. Some people need something specific that no general design supplies. This is separate from [learning styles](t:1.10): the aim is access and choice, not matching teaching to a supposed type.

try.text: Take one session you run. List three points where a different way of taking part would cost you nothing, and build them in. Then write the question for your joining form with four examples, and say your opening line about breaks and moving aloud until it sounds ordinary. Good looks like this: nobody would need to ask permission, or give a reason, to use any of the three.

try.title: A worked example: the joining form and the opening line
lines: On the joining form: "Is there anything that would help you take part? For example: slides in advance, large print, captions on videos, a seat near the door, regular breaks, a quiet space at lunch. You do not need to say why."
In the joining note: "Slides and the handout are attached, two days ahead, for everyone. There is a five-minute break every hour."
Said at the start: "We break for five minutes every hour. If you need to stand, move about or step out before then, just do it. You don't need to ask me."
Said before a discussion: "Take two minutes on your own first and jot down a thought. Then we'll talk in pairs."
Said privately at the break: "Thank you for telling me. I'll slow down, and here is the handout in large print. What else would help this afternoon?"

items: **The form asks about conditions.** Do not ask people to disclose a diagnosis. Ask what would help, and take the answer without a reason.
**A colleague gets the label wrong** and calls this catering for [learning styles](t:1.10). Do not confuse the two. The aim is access and choice.
**The Equality Act 2010 sets duties** in the UK to make reasonable adjustments. This is general information, not legal advice.
**You decide the standard set-up** covers everyone. Designing for everyone does not remove the need for individual adjustments. Some people will still need something specific, so keep asking.
**You name the person** when you make an adjustment in front of the group. Handle it quietly, and where you can, change it for the whole room.

items.label: CAST (2024), Universal Design for Learning Guidelines, version 3.0.
Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork (2008), Learning styles: concepts and evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3).

quiz.q: What three things does Universal Design for Learning suggest offering in more than one way?
quiz.a: Engagement, how content is presented, and how people respond.

quiz.q: At the first break a participant tells you they cannot follow fast speech or read the small text on your slides. What do you do?
quiz.a: Slow down, give them the slides or a handout now, and ask privately what else would help. Next time, send materials ahead and ask about needs on the joining form.

quiz.q: A colleague drafting the joining form suggests asking people to list any conditions or diagnoses. What do you write instead?
quiz.a: Ask what would help them take part, with examples such as slides in advance, captions or regular breaks. Do not ask for a diagnosis or a reason.

topics.tierReason: Universal Design for Learning is a widely used framework and the topic also covers legal duties. Direct evidence that the whole framework raises learning was not confirmed.

parts.title: Assess and give feedback
parts.summary: Checking what people can do, fairly, and telling them what to do next.

topics.title: Test little and often

situation.text: A two-day course for new customer support staff ends with a 30-question test at four o'clock on day two. A third of the group gets the refund questions wrong. At half past four everyone goes home, and you now know exactly what you should have re-taught on day one.

items: **Check where people start.** Put four to six questions on paper at the opening, or send them two days before. No names and no marks. Sort the answers into three piles: most know it, mixed, few know it.
**Decide what each pile will change** before the day. Write it in the plan: "If most know the refund limits, drop the 20-minute recap and go straight to cases."

**Add one short check to every segment**, two to five minutes each. Vary the form: three questions answered from memory with notes closed, pairs explaining one idea aloud while you listen, or everyone holding up one to four fingers for options A to D.
**Write two lines for each check** in your plan. What it measures. What you will do if most people get it wrong, including where the ten minutes will come from.
**Keep the stakes low and say so.** "This is not marked and I am not collecting names. It tells me what to teach next." Do not record scores for checks during the course.
**Let people finish a recall check** before you [go through the answers](t:2.27). Then give the answers straight away and ask who wants one explained again.
**Start each later session with three questions** on the one before, [answered from memory](t:1.3).
**Keep the end assessment for the judgement** at the end. [Match it to the objectives](t:2.11), and report that result to the client, not the checks along the way.

why.text: **A check must change what happens next.** Assessment has three purposes: to find the starting point, to guide learning while it happens, and to judge it at the end. The middle one is often called formative assessment. It is widely seen as a strong lever on learning, though estimates of its size vary. The lever only moves if the result changes what happens next, which is why step 4 asks you to decide your response in advance. In the room you will not have time to think of one.

**A recall check teaches as it measures.** Every test is also a learning event, because [recalling strengthens memory](t:1.3). A short quiz teaches as it measures. So a check earns its minutes twice, and it must be recall from memory to do so. A check that people answer by looking at their notes tells you they can find the page.

**A test pays off days later.** The benefit of a test shows up later, not at once. In one well-known experiment, students who reread a passage recalled more five minutes afterwards. Students who were tested on it recalled more after two days and after a week. Rereading also made people more confident, without the lasting memory to match.

why.title: Test-enhanced learning
why.found: Students read prose passages, then either reread them or took recall tests with no feedback. After five minutes the rereaders recalled more. After two days and after one week the tested group recalled substantially more.
why.means: Swap some review time for short recall quizzes, and judge them by what people remember next week.

why.text: **Checks cost time and need low stakes.** Two things follow for a trainer, and both are craft readings of that result. A recap at the end of the day will feel better to the room than a quiz, and [the feeling is a poor guide](t:1.4). And checks cost time: five checks of four minutes is 20 minutes of content you must cut. That is the trade. The low stakes matter for a separate reason, also craft. People only show you what they do not know when being wrong costs them nothing. Where a result has to be recorded, as in certified or regulated training, keep that for the end assessment and keep the checks during the course apart from it.

try.text: Take a course you run or are designing. Add three low-stakes checks and write, for each, what it measures and what you will do with the result. Then stand up and say the low-stakes framing aloud until it sounds like you, and run one three-question check with a colleague or two: notes closed, two minutes, answers straight after.

items: **A check nobody acts on** is wasted. Decide in advance what you will do if most people get it wrong.
**Graded quizzes raise the stakes** and lower honesty. Do not record names or scores for checks during the course, and tell the client why.
**"Does that make sense?"** is used as the check. Nods measure confidence. Ask a question people must answer from memory.

**The answers are given too soon,** while half the group is still writing. Let people finish first. Feedback timing matters and sometimes a delay helps, and there is a [rule of thumb for choosing](t:2.27).
**The check asks people to recognise** the right option when the job needs them to recall it unprompted. Match the form of the check to how the knowledge is used.

items.label: Black and Wiliam (1998), Assessment and classroom learning. Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy and Practice, 5(1).
Roediger and Karpicke (2006), Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3).

quiz.q: In the Roediger and Karpicke experiment, which group remembered more after a week?
quiz.a: The group that was tested. The group that reread did better only at five minutes, and felt more confident than their later memory justified.

quiz.q: Your opening check shows most of the room already knows the first section. What do you do?
quiz.a: Drop or shorten that section and spend the time on what they do not know. A check is only worth running if it changes what you do next.

quiz.q: A client wants every in-course quiz scored and reported to managers. What is the risk, and what do you suggest?
quiz.a: Higher stakes make people less willing to risk being wrong, so the checks stop showing what people really know. Keep checks during the course unrecorded and report the end assessment.

topics.tierReason: Testing strengthens later memory in controlled studies and a large review found learning gains from frequent feedback, but the gain depends on acting on the results and the size of the formative assessment effect is debated.

topics.title: Assess the real task, not a quiz about it

situation.text: A software company certifies its internal facilitators with a 20-question multiple-choice quiz. All of them pass. Nobody has watched any of them run a room, and the first person to see them do it will be a group of forty new starters.

items: **Write what the person must do** in real life, in one sentence, [with the conditions](t:2.11). "Runs a 15-minute activity with a group of eight, gives the instructions once and debriefs it."

**Set a task close to real life**, as close as you safely can. In order of preference: the real task watched live, the real task recorded, a simulation with a briefed colleague playing the other part. Use a simulation where the real task is unsafe, rare or would put a customer at risk.

**Write the criteria as a rubric:** a table of three to five criteria, each with a description of what you would see or hear at each level. Choose criteria that carry the substance of the work. "Kept to time" may belong. "Used the slide template" does not.
**Test the rubric before you use it.** Two assessors mark the same recording separately, then compare. Where they disagree, rewrite the level description until they do not.
**Send the rubric a week ahead** to the people being assessed, with the task and the time limit.
**Have two observers on the day** write down what was said and done, mark separately, then take five minutes to compare and agree.
**Give each person their result** [against the rubric the same day](t:2.27). Offer anyone at "not yet" a second attempt on the criterion they missed.
**Budget for the time** [when you scope the work](t:2.33). Twelve people at 15 minutes each, plus ten minutes between them for marking, is five hours for two observers.

why.text: **Only watching shows a performed skill.** A written test cannot certify a skill that is performed. Authentic assessment measures someone doing something close to the real task, in place of answering questions about it. The quiz in the situation above shows that people can recognise good facilitation described in words. Whether they can do it is a separate question, and only watching answers it.

**People practise what the rubric rewards.** A rubric makes the criteria explicit, so people know what good looks like. Check that assessors agree by comparing marks on a sample. A review of rubric research concluded that the criteria are what matter most. Criteria that count trivial things pull attention away from the substance of the work. People practise what the rubric rewards, so a rubric that counts eye contact and slide numbers will get you eye contact and slide numbers.

**The rubric tells people what to practise.** Sending the rubric in advance can feel like handing out the answers. For a performed skill it is not, and this is craft reasoning. Knowing that "plays back the customer's problem in the customer's words" is on the sheet does not let anyone do it without practice. It tells them what to practise.

**Realism is not validity, and it costs.** Two limits. A realistic task is not valid by default: ask the same questions of it as of any test, which are [what the score means](t:2.26) and what follows from using it. And realism costs. It takes observer time, and realistic tasks are harder to mark consistently than a quiz. The advice reverses where the real task is itself recall. If someone must know the refund limit from memory at the till, a short closed-book quiz is the authentic test of that.

try.text: Pick one real skill you teach and design the assessment: the task, the conditions, and a rubric with four criteria at three levels. Then test it. Record a colleague doing the task for five minutes, mark the recording separately from a second person, and compare. Count the criteria where you differed and rewrite those descriptions.

try.title: A worked example: rubric for a recorded sales conversation (first meeting, 20 minutes)

head: Criterion
Not yet
Meets the standard
Strong

Starts on the product. The customer is not asked how long they have or what they want from the call.
States the purpose and checks the time available. Asks what the customer wants from the call.
