A specific next step is agreed, with a date and who will do what.
The customer proposes or confirms the step in their own words. A second contact is named.

try.title: A worked example: certifying 12 internal facilitators by observation, in place of a quiz
lines: Before: a 20-question multiple-choice quiz, taken online.
The real task, in one sentence: runs a 15-minute activity with eight colleagues, gives the instructions once and debriefs it.
The assessment task: each person runs a 15-minute segment of their own course with a real group of eight volunteers.
Rubric, four criteria at three levels: instructions, handling questions, the debrief, keeping to time.
Three weeks before: two observers mark one recorded segment separately. They differ on "handling questions" and rewrite that row.
One week before: the task, the time limit and the rubric go to all twelve.
The day: 09:30 to 15:30, twelve slots of 25 minutes with a lunch break. Fifteen minutes to run the segment and ten for the observers to mark and compare.
During each segment: both observers write what was said and done, with times. Each marks alone before they talk.
16:00: each person gets ten minutes with one observer, the marked rubric and one thing to change.
Anyone at "not yet" on a criterion: a second 15-minute attempt within two weeks, marked on that criterion only.
Cost to plan for: two observers for a day, plus half a day to build and test the rubric.

items: **Observation costs time,** and it is the first thing cut. Budget for it [when you scope the work](t:2.33).
**A rubric that rewards the trivial** will be gamed. Read each criterion and ask whether a poor performer could score well on it.
**Nothing is observed** because the real task is unsafe or rare. Use a simulation with a briefed colleague.
**A realistic task is assumed valid.** Ask [what the score means](t:2.26) and what follows from using it.
**The rubric goes live untested.** Two assessors should mark the same recording separately first. Where they disagree, rewrite the level description until they do not.

items.label: Messick (1995), Validity of psychological assessment. American Psychologist, 50(9).
Brookhart (2018), Appropriate criteria: key to effective rubrics. Frontiers in Education, 3:22.

quiz.q: According to the review of rubric research, what matters most in a rubric?
quiz.a: The criteria. Criteria that count trivial things pull attention away from the substance of the work.

quiz.q: A client certifies its facilitators with a multiple-choice quiz. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Watch each person run a short segment with a real group. Two observers mark against a shared rubric that was sent out in advance.

quiz.q: Two assessors mark the same recorded sales call and disagree on "finding the need". What do you do?
quiz.a: Rewrite the level descriptions for that criterion until they agree, then try it on another recording. Do this before the rubric is used for real.

topics.tierReason: Performance assessment with a rubric is established professional practice, but no study comparing it with written tests for certifying a skill was opened.

topics.title: Check the test measures what you think it does

situation.text: The end-of-course test for a customer service team comes back with an average of 92 per cent, and the sponsor wants the figure in the board report. Then a team leader mentions that the top scorer is the person whose calls she most often has to take over. Nobody has asked what the test measures.

items: **Say what a high score means** by finishing this sentence in writing: "A high score on this test means the person can". If you cannot finish it, or the ending is "remember what was on the slides", you have found the first problem.
**Look at who scores highest and lowest** and ask what each group has in common. Set the scores beside something else you know about the same people, such as a team leader's view or observed calls.

**Read every question** looking for things that move the score and are not the skill. The usual three are reading load, cultural references and test technique, such as the longest option being the right one.

**Check alignment in a table.** List [the objectives](t:2.11) down the side and put each question against the one it tests. Look for objectives with no questions, questions with no objective, and questions on things that were never taught.
**Check reliability.** Two assessors mark the same five pieces separately, then compare. Where they differ, rewrite the criterion and try again on five more.
**Reason the pass mark.** One way, which is craft: ask what a person who is only just competent would score, and what a wrong pass would cost.
**Ask how the scores will be used.** Who sees them, what happens to someone who fails, and what the test rewards people for studying.
**Fix the largest threat first**, then try the new version on five or six people before it goes to everyone.

why.text: **Validity and reliability are different questions.** Validity is whether an assessment measures what it claims to. Measuring the wrong thing accurately is still useless. Reliability is whether it gives consistent results across assessors and occasions.

**The two can pull against each other.** Realistic tasks are often harder to mark consistently. The easy way to make markers agree is to simplify the task until there is one right answer, and each step that way can take the test further from the job. A practical position, which is craft: accept [a realistic task](t:2.25), then work on agreement with clear level descriptions and a second marker on a sample.

**Validity depends on how scores are used.** Validity is not a fixed property of a test. In Messick's account it is a judgement about what the scores mean and how they are used, and it includes the consequences of using them. Content, links to other measures and consequences are all evidence for the same question.

**Higher stakes need more checks.** That is why step 7 is on the list. The same quiz can be sound for one use and unsound for another. As a check on what to re-teach tomorrow, a rough ten-question quiz may be good enough. As the basis for deciding who is signed off to handle complaints alone, the same quiz needs far more behind it. The higher the stakes of the decision, the more of these checks you should run. For [a low-stakes check during a course](t:2.24), steps 1 and 4 are usually enough.

try.text: Take one assessment you use or have sat. Work through the first four steps and write down each threat you find, with the evidence and a fix. Then explain the biggest one to a colleague in a minute, as you would to a sponsor who is pleased with the scores.

try.title: A worked example: reviewing a customer service end test (25 written scenarios, pass mark 80 per cent)

head: Check
What we found
Threat
Fix
rows: What a high score claims
"Can handle a difficult call." The test is read and written. Nothing is spoken.
The test and the claim do not match.
Change the claim to "knows the policy", and add [an observed call for the handling skill](t:2.25).
Who scores highest
The strongest readers, whatever their service skills. Two people with English as a second language scored lowest and are rated well on calls.
Reading load drives the score.
Shorten each scenario to under 80 words. Play six of them as audio.
Things that are not the skill
In most questions the longest option is the correct one. One scenario depends on knowing a TV quiz show.
Test technique and a cultural reference.
Even out the option lengths. Replace the reference.
Alignment
A large block of questions on product history, which is in no objective. None on the escalation decision, which is objective two.

Cut the history questions to two. Write six escalation scenarios.
Reliability
Two markers scored the same five free-text answers. They gave different marks on more than half.
The result depends on who marks.
Write a three-level description for the free-text answers. Mark five more and compare again.
Pass mark
80 per cent, because the last course used it.
A mark that was picked, not reasoned.
Ask three team leaders which questions a just-competent agent must get right. Set the mark from that.
Use and consequences

High stakes on a weak measure, and it rewards cramming.
Until the fixes are in, report pass or not yet only, and keep the score out of probation decisions.

items: **High scores are reported as success.** High scores on a poor measure tell you nothing. Check what the test measures before the figure goes into a report.
**The pass mark is picked,** not reasoned. Ask what a person who is only just competent would score, and what a wrong pass would cost.
**Assessment shapes what people study.** Look at what yours rewards, and change it if the answer is memorising slides.
**Marker agreement is taken as proof** the test is good. Two markers can agree perfectly on a test of the wrong thing. Check validity first.
**The test covers what is easy** to write questions about. Build it from the objectives, starting with the one that is hardest to test.

items.label: Messick (1995), Validity of psychological assessment. American Psychologist, 50(9).
Biggs (1996), Enhancing teaching through constructive alignment. Higher Education, 32.

quiz.q: What is the difference between validity and reliability?
quiz.a: Validity is whether an assessment measures what it claims to. Reliability is whether it gives consistent results across assessors and occasions.

quiz.q: On your customer service test, the best readers score highest whatever their service skills. What do you change?
quiz.a: Cut the reading load: shorter scenarios, some played as audio. Reading is affecting the score and it is not the skill being tested.

quiz.q: Everyone passes the end test with over 90 per cent and the sponsor is delighted. What do you check before reporting it as success?
quiz.a: What the test measures. Check it matches the objectives, that nothing other than the skill drives the score, and that the pass mark was reasoned. High scores on a poor measure tell you nothing.

topics.tierReason: Validity, reliability and alignment are core professional principles of assessment set out in theory papers, not practices tested by experiment.

topics.title: Give feedback people can act on

situation.text: A new manager has just practised a difficult conversation in front of two colleagues. You say, "That was really good. Maybe a bit more structure next time." She nods and thanks you. In the next round she does exactly the same thing, because nothing you said told her what to change.

items: **Say where people are heading** before the practice starts. Name the one or two criteria you will watch for, taken from the objective or [the rubric](t:2.25).

**Write down what was said and done** while you watch, in the person's words, with rough times. Record evidence and leave the verdicts for later. "02:10, 'this is not a telling-off'" is a note you can use. "Bit vague" is not.

**Ask the person first:** "What went as you meant it to, and what would you change?" After [a practice round in threes](t:4.29), the person who practised speaks first, then the observer, then the other player, and you speak last.

**Give your feedback in three parts.** Where they are heading. How they are doing against that, with one thing that worked and one gap, each tied to something you wrote down. What to do next, as one change they can make today.
**Keep to the one or two points** that would change the result most.
**Comment on the task and the method**, not the person. "The opening had no example" is about the work. "You are a natural" is about the person.
**Give time to act on it.** Have them redo only the part that changes, for a minute or two, in the same session.

**Do not repeat the point more firmly** if the person disagrees. Read back what you wrote down, ask how they saw it, and agree on what happened before you discuss what it means. Then offer a test: try it the other way for a minute and ask the other player how it landed. The decision stays with them.

why.text: **Feedback on the task beats praise.** The most useful feedback answers three questions: where am I going, how am I doing, and what next. Feedback about the task and the process helps. Praise of the person is among the least effective kinds.

**Feedback is not always good.** A pooled analysis found that it improved performance on average, yet more than a third of feedback interventions made performance worse. Feedback worked less well as it pulled attention away from the task and towards the self.

why.title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance
why.found: A meta-analysis of 607 effect sizes and 23,663 observations. Feedback improved performance on average (d = 0.41), but over one third of feedback interventions reduced it. Feedback became less effective as it moved attention from the task towards the self.
why.means: Keep feedback on the task and the next step, and leave out comments on the person.

why.text: **Disagreement pulls attention to the person.** That finding is the reason for steps 2 and 8, though the steps themselves are craft. A disagreement is the moment attention is most likely to slide to the person, who is now defending themselves. Going back to the written note and then to a one-minute test puts you both back on the task. It also allows for the chance that they are right.

**When to give feedback has no single answer.** A review of the feedback research (Shute, 2008) found the timing studies in conflict, with many field studies favouring immediate feedback and many laboratory studies favouring a delay. Its working guidelines are to give feedback straight away when the task is hard for the person, or is a procedure they are still learning. Consider holding it back when the task is easy for them, or when the aim is for them to apply an idea somewhere new. The review presents these as provisional and says the point about applying ideas needs more research. A reasonable reading for a training room: correct a new procedure [while it is being practised](t:1.6). [Let people finish a recall quiz](t:2.24) or a case before you go through the answers. Both fit the review, and neither is settled.
**Fairness belongs here too.** Fair assessment [removes barriers](t:2.16) that have nothing to do with the skill, so the result [reflects what the person can do](t:2.26).

try.text: Take a weak piece of feedback, such as "Great job" or "Needs work". Rewrite it in the three parts, with one clear next step. Say it aloud to a colleague in under a minute and record it. Ask them to disagree, and answer without repeating your point. Listening back, mark any sentence about the person.

try.title: A worked example: feedback to one person after a practice round (new manager, a conversation about missed deadlines)
lines: Before, as first given: "That was really good. Maybe a bit more structure next time."

Trainer's notes from the three-minute round: 00:20 "Thanks for making time." 00:50 "I want to talk about how things are going generally." 02:10 "This is not a telling-off." 02:40 other player: "So is there a problem or not?"
Trainer asks first: "Priya, what went as you meant it to, and what would you change?"
Priya: "I kept it friendly. I think I took a while to get to it."
Where she is heading: "The aim we set was that he knows by the end of the first minute what the conversation is about, with one example."
What worked: "You opened by thanking him for his time and your tone stayed level throughout. He stayed in the conversation."
The gap: "At fifty seconds you said 'how things are going generally'. No deadline was named in the three minutes. At 02:40 he asked, 'So is there a problem or not?'"
What next: "Write one sentence that names the two missed deadlines and the dates. Say it straight after your thank-you. Then stop and let him answer."
Second attempt: "Take two minutes to write it. Then run just the first minute again with the same partner."
After the second attempt, to the other player: "What was different for you that time?"
After, written on her sheet: "Aim: he knows the issue in the first minute. Worked: level tone, he stayed with you. Change: name both deadlines in your second sentence."

try.title: Words you can use: when the person disagrees
lines: Priya: "I don't agree. If I open with the deadlines he'll get defensive. He's sensitive, and I know him."
Do not say: "Trust me, it works better." Or the same point again, slower.
Trainer: "You know him and I don't, so that matters. Can I check what we both saw? I wrote that at 02:40 he asked, 'So is there a problem or not?' Is that how you remember it?"
Priya: "Yes. But that was the role-play, not him."

Trainer: "Fair. So we agree on what happened, and we read it differently. You think naming it early will put him on the defensive. I think not naming it left him guessing. We can test that in two minutes."

Trainer: "Run the first minute twice. Once your way, once with the deadlines in your second sentence, in your own words and as gently as you like. Then we ask Dan which one he would rather be on the end of."
After both runs, to the other player: "Dan, what was each one like to hear?"
If Dan prefers the direct version: "Priya, what do you make of that?" Let her draw the conclusion.
If Dan prefers her version: "Then keep your opening. What would make sure he still leaves knowing about both deadlines?"

If she still disagrees: "That's your call, and it's your conversation to have. The aim stays the same: he leaves knowing which deadlines and what happens next. Tell me on the follow-up call how it went."
What the trainer does not do: argue it out in front of the group, or mark her down for disagreeing.

items: **Feedback only works with safety,** where people feel [safe enough to hear it](t:1.17). In a new group, say beforehand what you will comment on.
**Marking by judgement carries bias.** Use rubrics and compare notes with another assessor.
**Too much feedback at once** is not used. Pick the one or two points that would change the result most.
**There is no second attempt.** Feedback given as people pack up cannot be acted on. Cut a point from the content and keep two minutes for the redo.
**Praise drifts to the person:** "you are a natural, but". Say what in the work was good, and quote the moment.

items.label: Hattie and Timperley (2007), The power of feedback. Review of Educational Research, 77(1).
Kluger and DeNisi (1996), The effects of feedback interventions on performance: a historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory. Psychological Bulletin, 119(2).

quiz.q: In the Kluger and DeNisi meta-analysis, what share of feedback interventions made performance worse?
quiz.a: More than a third. Feedback helped on average, and worked less well as it pulled attention from the task towards the self.

quiz.q: You have told a new manager her practice conversation needs a clearer opening. She says, "I disagree. If I am that direct he will get defensive." What do you do?
quiz.a: Do not repeat the point. Read back what you wrote down, agree on what happened, then have her run the first minute both ways and ask the other player how each one landed. This keeps attention on the task, and the choice stays with her.

quiz.q: People are practising a new procedure step by step and one person keeps making the same error. Do you correct it now or at the end?
quiz.a: Now. Give feedback straight away when someone is still learning a procedure. A delay suits easier tasks, or a recall quiz or case that people should finish first.

topics.tierReason: Feedback improves performance on average across many studies, but more than a third of feedback interventions made performance worse, so the result depends on what the feedback points at.

topics.title: Know what training can do, on average
topics.theory: Training effectiveness: what the pooled workplace studies show

situation.text: In a scoping call a finance director asks you whether training works at all, or whether people just enjoy a day out. You need an honest answer in two sentences, and you need to avoid promising the average.

items: **Answer the question directly.** On average, well-designed training in organisations works, and the pooled effects are medium to large.
**Give the comparison with the number.** The main meta-analysis pooled comparisons between groups and left out studies that only measured one group before and after.
**Say what was measured.** The average was about the same for what people felt, what they learned, what they did at work and what the organisation got. Far fewer studies measured the last of those.
**Do not promise the average** for this programme. Results varied with the training method and with the kind of skill.
**Move the conversation from whether to how.** The research review that sits beside the meta-analysis says what happens before and after the session matters as much as the session.
**Offer three commitments** that follow from it: [a needs analysis first](t:2.1), methods built on sound principles of learning, and [a plan for use](t:2.4) and [evaluation afterwards](t:2.5).
**Write the claim into the proposal** in the same careful words.

why.text: **Training's average effect is medium to large.** Arthur and colleagues pooled 397 results from studies of training in organisations. The average effect was d = 0.60 for reactions, 0.63 for learning, 0.62 for behaviour at work and 0.62 for organisational results. The authors call this medium to large. The method used and the kind of skill trained were both related to how well training worked.

**Read the figures with their limits.** They compare groups, and the paper says little about what the comparison groups received. The results figure rests on 26 studies and the learning figure on 234. Team training was excluded, and so were trainee factors such as motivation and ability. Only 22 of the 397 results reported a needs analysis, too few to show whether one helps.

**Good design reaches beyond the session.** Salas and colleagues reviewed the wider research for a general audience. Their conclusion is that training works when it is designed well, and that the design reaches beyond the session: analyse the need and prepare the climate beforehand, use sound instructional methods and build the right mindset during, and check transfer and evaluate afterwards. It is a narrative review and gives no pooled number.

why.title: Effectiveness of training in organizations
why.found: A meta-analysis of training in organisations. Sample-weighted average effects were d = 0.60 for reaction measures (15 studies), 0.63 for learning (234), 0.62 for behaviour (122) and 0.62 for results (26). Single-group before-and-after studies were excluded.
why.means: You can say training works on average and by a worthwhile margin. Say what was compared, and do not carry the average over to one programme.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play a sceptical finance director. Give your answer to "does training work?" aloud in under 40 seconds, using the lines below as a base. Record it. Listen back for any sentence that sounds like a guarantee and say it again without one.

try.title: Words you can use with a sceptical sponsor
lines: "Fair question. The short answer is yes, on average, and by a decent margin."
"The best pooled study covers a few hundred results from workplaces. Trained groups came out ahead of comparison groups on learning, on what people did at work, and on business results."
"Two cautions. That is an average, and it hides a wide spread. And fewer studies measured business results than measured learning."
"What separates the good programmes is mostly outside the session: whether the need was checked first, and whether anyone made room for people to use it after."
"So I will not promise you the average. I will tell you what has to be in place for this one to work, and how we will know."

try.title: A worked example: what you can and cannot claim

head: You want to say
Supported
Say it like this
rows: Training works.
Yes, on average, for organisational training against comparison groups.
"Pooled studies show a medium to large average effect."
It changes behaviour, not only knowledge.
Yes on average. 122 studies measured behaviour.
"The average effect on behaviour at work was about the same as on learning."
It pays back.
Thinly. 26 studies measured results.
"Some studies show business results. We should measure yours."
Our programme will deliver a 0.6 effect.
No. Averages do not transfer to one case.
Do not say it.
A needs analysis makes it work better.
Recommended by the research review. Too few studies in the meta-analysis to tell.
"The research review recommends it, and it lowers the risk of training the wrong thing."

items: **Quoting d = 0.62** to a client with no comparison. A number without "compared with what" invites the wrong reading. Use words unless they ask.
**Treating four similar averages as proof** that happy learners perform better. The paper did not test that link, and [reactions and learning are only loosely related](t:6.2).
**Forgetting what was left out.** These studies are of individual training with a comparison group. Team training and before-and-after studies are not in the average.

items.label: Arthur, Bennett, Edens and Bell (2003), Effectiveness of training in organizations: a meta-analysis of design and evaluation features. Journal of Applied Psychology, 88(2). Abstract.
Arthur, Bennett, Edens and Bell (2003). Full paper, read for what was compared and what was excluded.

Salas, Tannenbaum, Kraiger and Smith-Jentsch (2012), The science of training and development in organizations: what matters in practice. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 13(2). Publisher's summary.

quiz.q: In the main meta-analysis of training in organisations, how did the authors describe the average effect?
quiz.a: Medium to large, at about d = 0.6 on reactions, learning, behaviour and results.

quiz.q: A sales director asks you to put "training improves results by 0.6" in the proposal. What do you do?
quiz.a: Decline, and write that pooled studies show a medium to large average effect against comparison groups, with fewer studies of business results. An average across hundreds of programmes is not a forecast for one.

quiz.q: A client says the session is all that matters and wants to skip the needs check and the follow-up to save money. What do you say?
quiz.a: Say that the research review puts as much weight on what happens before and after as on the session. Offer the smallest version of each, not none.

topics.tierReason: Rests on a meta-analysis of workplace training read as abstract and full paper, and a research review read in the publisher's summary. The scripts are practitioner wording.

topics.title: Run a performance diagnosis

situation.text: A sales director asks for a refresher course because the team is not using the new product pitch. They were all trained on it three months ago.

items: **Pin down the gap** in something you can count or watch. Ask: "What are people doing now, what should they be doing, and how do you know?" There is more on [analysing the gap](t:2.1).

**Check six causes, in this order:** expectations, feedback, tools and resources, incentives, skills and knowledge, capacity and motives. Check the first four first. They belong to the organisation and a course cannot fix them.
**Ask one plain question for each cause.** The worked example below gives them. Write down evidence, not impressions.

**Talk to people at three levels:** the sponsor, two or three line managers, and four to six of the people doing the job. Include one or two who already do it well. Add whoever owns the tools and the pay plan. Allow 30 minutes each.
**Watch the work:** three to five calls or meetings, live or recorded. Ask for data the client already holds, such as usage reports.
**Write one page:** the gap, what you found under each cause, a verdict in two sentences, and a fix with a named owner for each cause that matters. Say which part training can fix.
**Talk the sponsor through the page first.** Pass each non-training fix to its owner, such as sales operations or the HR partner.

**Offer the diagnosis on its own**, as a small piece of work: two to three days of your time across two weeks, a fixed fee, one page and a one-hour readout, with no commitment to buy the course afterwards.

why.text: **The six causes follow Gilbert's model.** This is practitioner method. The six-cause list follows Thomas Gilbert's Behavior Engineering Model, set out in his book Human Competence. The model sorts causes into those in the work environment and those in the person. Chevalier (2003) presents it as a systematic way to find what is getting in the way of performance. Winiecki (2015) points out that it has been reworked so often that versions differ. So choose one list and keep to it.

**Diagnosing this way is untested.** None of these sources tests whether diagnosing this way leads to better results. There is a research case for [analysing the need first](t:2.1). The framework gives you a fixed order of questions.

**A paid diagnosis buys you access.** There is a [quick version of this check](t:1.20), and advice on what to offer [when the cause is not skill](t:9.29). The practical problem is who pays. If you are external, nobody has agreed to give you access until the course is sold. A small paid diagnosis gives you a reason to ask for interviews and data, and makes "this is mostly not a training problem" a finding the client paid for. If the client will not buy it, do the small version: three 30-minute calls and one data export. Mark every cause you could not check as "not checked".

try.text: Take a request you have had, or one from a past job. Fill in the six causes on one page from what you already know. Mark each line "known" or "guess". Then record yourself giving the two-sentence verdict aloud, as you would to the sponsor.

try.title: A worked example: one-page diagnosis for a software company's sales team that is not using the new product pitch

head: Cause

rows: Gap
What happens now, and what should?
The new pitch is used on about one call in five that we heard. The target is every first meeting with a qualifying customer.
Sales director confirms the target in writing.
Expectations
Do people know exactly when to use it?
Reps say it is optional. Two managers say it is required.
Sales director states the rule at the team meeting. Managers repeat it.

Each manager reviews one recorded call per rep each fortnight.

try.title: Words you can use: offering the diagnosis
lines: "Before I quote for the course, I would like to spend two weeks finding out why the pitch is not being used."
"I will talk to a few reps and managers, listen to some calls and look at your usage data."
"You get one page. It says what is causing the gap, what training can fix and what it cannot, and who would need to act on the rest."
"It is a fixed fee, and you are free to stop there."
"If the answer is a course, the course will be smaller and aimed at the right thing. If it is not, I will have saved you the cost of one."

items: **The sponsor wants the course** whatever you find. Train the skill gap, and put the other causes in writing with an owner beside each.
**People say what is safe.** Interview them without their manager and report themes, never names.
**The finding points at the sponsor.** Describe the system: "the rule has not been stated", not "you never told them".
**The diagnosis grows.** Hold to the days you agreed.
**A cause you cannot fix:** you find one, such as pay. Name it and hand it over.

items.label: Chevalier (2003), Updating the Behavior Engineering Model. Performance Improvement, 42(5).
Winiecki (2015), Comparing a few behavior engineering models. Performance Improvement, 54(8).
Gilbert, Human Competence: Engineering Worthy Performance, tribute edition. Pfeiffer, 2013.

quiz.q: Which four of the six causes belong to the organisation and not the person?
quiz.a: Expectations, feedback, tools and resources, and incentives.

quiz.q: A support manager asks for a course on a new ticketing system. Agents were trained last month and still use the old one. You have two days. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the six questions of a few agents, a manager and whoever owns the system, and look at usage data. You are checking whether the old system is still switched on, expected or simply faster before you assume a skill gap.

quiz.q: Your diagnosis finds the main cause is the commission plan. The sponsor says, "Fine, but can you still run the course?" What do you do?
quiz.a: Offer to train only the part that is a skill gap, and put the commission finding in writing with the owner named. That way nobody later judges the course on a result it could not have produced.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner frameworks in the tradition of Gilbert's Behavior Engineering Model. No test of the method was opened.

topics.title: Do compliance training properly
topics.theory: Compliance training: the record and the behaviour

situation.text: A client needs every member of staff through data protection training by the end of the quarter. Everyone clicks through the current hour-long module, and the same mistakes keep happening.

items: **Ask the client's compliance or risk owner** which rule this training serves, what an auditor or regulator would ask to see, and what has gone wrong recently. Do not guess the law yourself.
**Write two aims side by side.** One is the record: proof that named people were trained on a dated version. The other is the behaviour: the two or three things people must do so the risk falls.
**Target by risk.** Everyone gets a short core. Roles that handle the risk every day get more time, real cases and practice.
**Build the test from job situations**, with wrong answers that are real mistakes. Set the pass mark with the compliance owner.

**Offer a test-out** where the rule allows it. People take the scenario test first. Those who pass skip the teaching and still get a record. Ask the compliance owner first, because some rules may require the training itself.
**Keep refreshers short:** 10 to 15 minutes on changes and on recent errors. The client sets the interval.
**Agree the record before launch:** who, which version, the date, the result, and a copy of the material as delivered.
**Report completion and behaviour separately:** completion to whoever answers to the auditor, and a behaviour measure, such as incidents or spot checks, to whoever owns the risk.

why.text: **You need the record and the behaviour.** The auditor needs evidence and the business needs fewer incidents. [Completions alone say little](t:6.7). In regulated training the record is still something the client may be asked to produce.

**The HSE says employers must train everyone.** The Health and Safety Executive says employers must give everyone who works for them clear instructions and information, and adequate training and supervision. That includes contractors and self-employed people. It asks for particular attention to new recruits, people changing jobs and young employees. Its guidance on work equipment says training should cover how the equipment is used, the risks and the precautions. Training may need refreshing at suitable intervals, with no fixed period given, and should normally happen in working hours at no cost to the employee.

**The ICO expects training, records and follow-up.** The Information Commissioner's Office sets out what it expects when it audits data protection training. All staff are covered. Induction training comes before a person has access to personal information, and within a month of starting. Refreshers happen at appropriate intervals. Completion is monitored and followed up. The organisation keeps copies of the material and records of who received it. An end assessment can carry a minimum pass mark. The ICO calls these ways to meet its expectations, not mandatory steps, and says the guidance is under review. This is general information, not legal advice.

**Neither body prescribes these design choices.** Risk-based targeting, testing out and short refreshers are design practice. Neither body prescribes them. The HSE leaflet on training does give five steps that fit: decide what training is needed, set priorities, choose methods, deliver it, and check that it worked.

try.text: Take one compliance module you have sat through. Write the two aims for it: the record, and the two or three behaviours. Then write one scenario question and read it aloud to a colleague. See whether they can answer without the module.

quiz.q: What two aims do you write side by side for compliance training?
quiz.a: The record: proof that named people were trained on a dated version. The behaviour: the two or three things people must do so the risk falls.

quiz.q: A client wants to let experienced staff skip the annual module if they pass a test first. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the client's compliance owner whether the rule allows it, and get the answer in writing. If it does, build the test from job scenarios and keep a record for those who test out.

quiz.q: Completion is at 98 per cent and the same data protection mistake happened twice last month. The client says the training is working. What do you say?

topics.title: Design onboarding that gets people productive
topics.theory: Onboarding: first day, first week, first 90 days

situation.text: A new account manager spends week one in back-to-back presentations from every department. In week five they still cannot run a customer call alone, and their manager asks what the induction was for.

items: **Agree what "productive" means** with the hiring manager, as things you could watch. For example: runs a renewal call alone, or forecasts their accounts within the agreed margin. Set a date for each.
**Work back from those into three milestones** at 30, 60 and 90 days. Each one is something the person can do, not something they have attended.

**Send the first-week timetable before day one**, with the name of their buddy and what to bring. Ask IT for accounts and equipment to be ready. A first day spent waiting for a password is remembered.
**Give day one four jobs:** meet the manager and the buddy, get systems working, see the real work being done, and complete one small real task before going home.

**Teach only what the person needs** in week one in order to start. The same point comes up in [designing for the kind of programme](t:2.6). Put everything else on a dated list across the 90 days, close to when it will be used.
**Give the manager a written part:** a 30-minute one-to-one every week, and a review at each milestone against the agreed list. There is more on [manager briefs](t:2.4).
**Give the buddy a part too:** one shadowing session in week one, and a standing 15 minutes twice a week for the first month for the questions nobody wants to ask the manager.
**Ask the new starter at 90 days** what they needed earlier and what could have waited. Change the plan for the next person.

why.text: **The test is doing the job unaided.** Most of this is practitioner judgement about order and load. The test of an onboarding plan is how soon someone can do the job without help, so the plan is written as milestones the manager can check.

**Clarity, confidence and acceptance carry induction.** One piece of research shapes the aims. A meta-analysis of 70 samples of newcomers found that three things carried the effect of an organisation's induction through to later performance, satisfaction and staying: being clear about the role, feeling able to do the job, and feeling accepted by colleagues. It is described under [designing for people early in their career](t:2.7). That is why day one includes a real task and a buddy as well as information. The study is about what goes with good outcomes across many organisations. It did not test a 30-60-90 plan.

**The manager matters more than the programme.** You can design a good first week and have it undone by a manager who cancels the one-to-ones. If you are external, you rarely control that. Write the manager's part down, get the sponsor to send it, and build the milestone reviews into the manager's diary before the person starts.

try.text: Pick a role you know. Write three things a person in it should be able to do alone by day 90, each as something you could watch. Then explain the plan aloud, in two minutes, as if to the hiring manager. If you find yourself listing sessions, go back to the milestones.

items.label: Bauer and colleagues (2007), Newcomer adjustment during organizational socialization: a meta-analytic review. Journal of Applied Psychology.

quiz.q: What three things did the newcomer meta-analysis find carried induction through to later performance?
quiz.a: Being clear about the role, feeling able to do the job, and feeling accepted by colleagues.

quiz.q: Six department heads each want an hour with new starters in week one. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask each what the new starter must be able to do with their department, and when that first comes up. Give them a slot near that date, and keep week one for what the person needs in order to start.

quiz.q: A manager says they are too busy for weekly one-to-ones with a new hire. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask for the three milestone reviews as a minimum and move the weekly questions to the buddy. Tell the sponsor in writing, because the plan depends on someone checking progress.

topics.title: Design for scale

situation.text: Your one-day workshop went well with twelve people. The client now wants it delivered to 600 staff in four countries by eight facilitators you have never met.

items: **Decide what is fixed** and what is local before you write anything else. Fix the outcomes, the practice tasks, the assessment and the timings of the main blocks. Leave the examples, the stories and the opening to the facilitator.

**Write the facilitator guide as the product.** At scale the guide is the design, and your own delivery is one instance of it. You can see [a page of a facilitator guide](t:3.20) and [the handover from the facilitator's side](t:9.31).

**Pilot twice.** Run the first pilot yourself to fix the design. Have someone else run the second from the guide alone while you watch and say nothing. Every question they ask you afterwards is a gap in the guide.

**Train the facilitators in three passes.** They take the workshop as participants. They teach back one segment each and get feedback. They co-deliver once with someone already signed off. There is more on [sign-off by observation](t:5.10).
**Plan the waves.** Start with one site and two facilitators. Fix what breaks, then widen. Leave a week between the first two waves for changes.

**Control versions.** Keep one master set. Print the version number and date in the footer of every page and slide. Release changes in numbered batches with a short change note. There is more on [the filing and versioning](t:3.18).
**Hold a 30-minute facilitator call every week** for the first month, then monthly. Ask two questions: what did you change, and what did people get stuck on.
**Check for drift.** Observe a sample of sessions against the fixed elements, and compare assessment results by facilitator.

why.text: **Research on scaling training is thin.** This is practitioner judgement. [Research on train-the-trainer is thin](t:5.10), and there is little research on how to scale a training design.

**Some variation helps and some breaks it.** A design that lives in your head varies every time someone else delivers it. Some variation helps: a facilitator who uses their own examples is more believable than one reading yours. Some variation breaks the design, such as cutting the practice to make room for more talk. So you separate the two in writing. What you fix is whatever the outcome depends on. What you leave open is whatever makes the session belong to that room.

**Scale also changes what the client is buying.** A head of learning buying for 600 people is asking how you will keep session 40 as good as session 4, what it costs per person, and what happens when a facilitator leaves. Pilots, sign-off and version control are your answers. They also take time, and that time belongs in the quote.

quiz.q: Why run the second pilot with someone else delivering from the guide alone?
quiz.a: It shows where the guide is not enough. Each question they ask is a gap to fill.

quiz.q: A local facilitator wants to drop the afternoon practice and add a talk from the regional manager. What do you do?
quiz.a: Say no to cutting the practice, because it is a fixed element the outcome depends on. Offer the regional manager ten minutes at the opening, which is local.

quiz.q: Assessment results from one facilitator's sessions are well above everyone else's. What do you do?
quiz.a: Watch one of their sessions before drawing a conclusion. They may be doing something worth copying, or marking to a different standard, and the numbers alone cannot tell you which.

topics.title: Choose group size and staffing
topics.theory: Group size, feedback time and when to add a facilitator

situation.text: You quoted for twelve. A week before the workshop the client says, "We have had a lot of interest. Can we make it twenty?"

items: **Start from the promise.** If the session promises that each person will practise the skill and get feedback from a trainer, the limit is feedback time.
**Do the sum.** Count the minutes of practice time in the day. Divide by the length of one observed turn, including feedback. That is the number of turns one trainer can watch.

**Use this example to check your own.** A turn of six minutes with four minutes of feedback is ten minutes, so one trainer watches six turns an hour. A day with three hours of practice gives 18 watched turns. Twelve people get one each with some to spare. Nine people get two each.

**Set your position before the client asks.** For a skills workshop with trainer feedback, a common practitioner ceiling for one trainer is 12, or 16 with less feedback each. State it in the proposal with the reason.
**Add a second facilitator** when the sum does not work, when groups will be in separate rooms, or when the content may upset people and someone may need to step out with a participant.
**Change the design as numbers change.** The table below shows how.

**Plan for wrong numbers on the day.** If six turn up where twelve were expected, run pairs and lengthen the debriefs. If twenty turn up, cut one activity, keep the practice, and say aloud what has changed.
**Give three options** when the client wants to add people: a second facilitator, a second date, or the same day with less individual feedback. Say what each one costs them.

why.text: **The group-size numbers are working figures.** All of this is practitioner judgement. There is little research on the best group size for workplace training, and the numbers here are working figures that experienced trainers use. Check them against your own sum.

**Input scales and watched practice does not.** The reasoning is simple arithmetic. Input scales well: sixty people can hear a ten-minute explanation as easily as six. Practice with feedback does not scale, because a trainer can only watch one conversation at a time. So the more a session depends on watched practice, the smaller the group one trainer can serve. A session that is mostly discussion or planning can take more people.

**Adding people looks free to the client.** Group size is also the first place a client tries to save money, because adding people looks free. Showing the sum changes the conversation. The client can see that eight more people means either less feedback for everyone or a second trainer, and can choose.

try.text: Take a session plan you have. Add up the practice minutes and do the sum for 8, 16 and 30 people. Then rehearse aloud, with a colleague playing the client, your answer to "Can we make it twenty?" Record it and listen for whether you gave a reason and a choice.

**Trios become fours** to save time. The fourth person waits longest and practises least. Add a round or keep to threes.
**A second facilitator arrives unbriefed.** [Give them the guide](t:4.17), the checklist and their groups before the day.
**Small groups feel exposed.** With six, say at the start how practice will work and let people choose their own case.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: In a skills workshop with trainer feedback, what sets the limit on group size?
quiz.a: Feedback time: how many practice turns one trainer can watch in the practice minutes available.

quiz.q: Your day has two hours of practice and each watched turn takes ten minutes. Sixteen people are booked and each has been promised trainer feedback. What do you do?
quiz.a: One trainer can watch twelve turns, so four people would miss out. Bring a second facilitator, shorten the turns, or tell the client the promise has to change.

quiz.q: Six people arrive for a workshop planned for twelve in trios. What do you do?
quiz.a: Drop the trios and run the practice in pairs or in front of the group, with longer debriefs. Tell the group they will get more individual feedback than planned.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement. The group sizes are working figures, not research findings.

topics.title: Teach interpersonal skills by showing, practising and giving feedback

situation.text: You have 60 minutes to teach a sales team how to handle a price objection. The current session explains a model on slides.

items: **Choose one skill small enough to perform** in three minutes. Write its three to five key points as rules that say what to do and why, such as "Ask what they are comparing the price with, so you answer the real objection."
**Show the key points first.** Then show a model: a live demonstration with a colleague, or a two-minute video. Keep the key points off the screen while the model runs.
**Show a poor version** as well as a good one. Ask which key points were missing.
**Give one quiet minute** for each person to picture using the points in a conversation they have coming up.
**Have people write their own practice scenarios** from real customers.
**Practise in threes:** one person plays the seller, one plays the customer from the scenario, one observes with the key points on a card. Rotate. There is more on [running the role-play](t:4.29).
**Give feedback after each turn** against the key points only. The person who practised speaks first, then the observer, then you. Then the person retries the weakest point.
**Close with a goal and a manager.** Each person writes when they will next use the skill. Their manager, briefed beforehand, asks about it within a week.

why.text: **The method has four parts.** This method is called behaviour modelling training: describe the key points, show a model, let people practise, and give feedback.

why.title: A meta-analysis of behaviour modelling training
why.found: The review pooled 117 studies. Effects were largest on learning outcomes, smaller on behaviour at work and smaller again on results. Knowledge gains faded with time. Skill and job behaviour held or grew. Skill grew most when key points were given as rules and when training time was longest. Transfer was greatest with models of both good and poor behaviour, practice scenarios written by trainees, instructions to set goals, managers who were also trained, and rewards and sanctions for the skill at work.
why.means: Write the key points as rules, show a poor example beside the good one, let people practise on their own cases, and plan the goal and the manager's part before the session.

why.text: **Two steps rest on a later summary.** Most steps above follow one of those findings. Two come from a later summary of this research and not from the meta-analysis itself: keeping the key points off the screen during the model, and picturing the conversation before practising.

**The findings are patterns across many studies.** They show what went with better results and do not promise that one feature will work in your session. The smaller effect on results at work is a reminder that [what managers do afterwards](t:2.4) carries weight.
**If you cannot reach managers, use a card.** If you are external and cannot reach the managers, send each participant home with their goal on a card and one question for their manager to ask.

try.text: Write the key points of a short interpersonal skill as rules. Then record yourself on your phone modelling it twice with a friend: once well, once with two points missing. Check that a stranger could name what was missing.

quiz.q: In the 2005 meta-analysis, which outcome faded over time and which held or grew?
quiz.a: Knowledge faded. Skill and behaviour at work held or grew.

quiz.q: You have prepared ten practice scenarios for a session on giving feedback to a team member. A co-trainer suggests the managers write their own. What do you do?
quiz.a: Let them write their own, and keep two or three of yours for anyone who is stuck. Trainee-written scenarios went with better transfer in the meta-analysis.

quiz.q: A sponsor wants the demonstration video to show only a perfect conversation, in case the poor one gives people bad ideas. What do you say?
quiz.a: For a skill people must adapt to different customers, showing a poor version beside the good one went with better transfer. Offer to make the poor one an ordinary, realistic mistake and to name what is missing straight after.

parts.title: Enablement programmes
parts.summary: How enablement differs from training, and how to plan it, launch a product, train retail staff and partners, coach through managers and run a large event. Mostly professional practice, and labelled as such.

topics.title: Know what enablement is

situation.text: A client introduces herself as head of sales enablement and asks what you would do about ramp time in her new markets. You have designed courses for years and you are not sure what she is asking you for.

items: **Learn the working definition.** Enablement is a standing service that gives customer-facing people what they need to sell or serve: content, training, coaching and tools. It is judged on commercial results, not on courses delivered.

**Set it beside training.** Training is one of the four things enablement supplies. A course has an end date. Enablement runs all year and changes whenever the product, the price or the market changes.

**Find out who owns it** in this client. Ask three questions in the first meeting: who does the enablement lead report to, who writes the product messaging, and who owns the sales system and its data.

**Draw the client's map on one page.** Put the enablement team in the middle. Round it put product marketing (messaging and launch content), sales operations (systems, data, targets), sales managers (coaching) and the learning team (platform, leadership programmes).

**Ask which commercial measure** the work is tied to before you propose anything. Typical ones are ramp time, win rate and sales of a new product. All three are defined in the table below. Then ask who can give you the figures. There is more on [how to measure against them](t:6.14).
**Name which of the four supplies** you are providing in every proposal, and who provides the other three. A workshop with no content, coaching or tool behind it is a training event.

why.text: **This topic is professional practice.** There is no agreed academic definition of enablement and very little research on it. The academic study below says as much.

**Where enablement sits varies by company.** The description above is the common working one in technology companies. Titles and reporting lines vary a great deal. It may sit under the sales leader, operations or marketing, and in a small company it is one person. So ask, and draw the map.

**Speak in sales results, not course hours.** The difference from training matters to you for a practical reason. An enablement lead is measured on a sales figure and has a calendar driven by launches and quarters. If you talk about learning objectives and course hours, you are answering a question she did not ask. If you talk about what sellers will be able to say and do by a date, and how you will both know, you are speaking her language.

why.title: Sales enablement: conceptualizing and developing a dynamic capability
why.found: An ethnographic study built mainly on 41 in-depth interviews with people who design or run sales enablement. It notes that empirical research on enablement is lacking and proposes a process model of how firms build it as a capability.
why.means: Treat what you read about enablement, including this page, as practice. Nobody has yet tested which enablement set-up produces better sales results.

try.text: Record yourself for two minutes explaining to a friend outside the industry what enablement is and how it differs from training. Use four of the terms below. Play it back, note where you hesitated, and record it again.

try.title: Terms you will hear in the first meeting

head: Term
Plain meaning
rows: Enablement
The ongoing supply of content, training, coaching and tools to people who sell or serve customers.
Sales enablement
Enablement for the sales team. Some clients say revenue enablement when it also covers customer success and partners.
Field
The sellers and technical specialists who talk to customers, as opposed to head office.
Channel or partners
Other companies that sell or fit the client's product: resellers, distributors, retailers.
Product marketing
The team that decides how a product is described and to whom. Usually the source of launch content.
Sales operations
The team that runs the sales system, targets and reports. Sometimes called revenue operations.
Quota
The sales target a seller must reach in a period.
Pipeline
The deals in progress, by stage.
Ramp time
How long a new seller takes to reach an agreed level, such as a first deal or full quota.
Win rate
The share of deals pursued that are won.
Playbook
A written guide to selling one product or to one kind of customer.
Battlecard
One page on how to answer a named competitor.
Sell-in and sell-out
Sell-in is what the retailer buys from the client. Sell-out is what shoppers buy from the retailer.

items: **Promising a commercial result** that training alone cannot deliver. Say which part of the result your work can move and what else has to be true.
**Assuming the learning team** is your client. The budget often sits with sales or marketing. There is more on [who buys training](t:9.1).
**Using the client's terms loosely.** Ramp time has a different definition in every company. Ask for theirs and write it down.
**Treating enablement as a new name** for product training. The client will ask about content, coaching and tools as well.

items.label: Peterson, Malshe, Friend and Dover (2021), Sales enablement: conceptualizing and developing a dynamic capability. Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science, 49(3).

quiz.q: What four things does enablement supply?
quiz.a: Content, training, coaching and tools.

quiz.q: A client asks for a two-day product course for sellers in three new markets. Her own target is ramp time. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask how she defines ramp time and what slows new sellers down today, then propose which of content, training, coaching and tools you would supply. A course alone answers a smaller question than the one she is measured on.

quiz.q: You have sent a proposal to the learning manager and heard nothing for three weeks. What do you check?
quiz.a: Check who owns the budget and the result, which is often the sales or enablement lead. Ask the learning manager for an introduction and bring them with you, because they still own the platform.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner description of a working discipline. The one academic study opened says research on enablement is lacking.

topics.title: Plan a sales enablement cycle

situation.text: It is October. The client's enablement lead has next year's budget to defend and a list of forty requests from product teams. She asks you to help turn it into a plan the sales leader will accept.

items: **Start from the client's fixed dates**, not from the content. Mark the financial year, quarter ends, the sales kick-off (the annual meeting that opens the sales year), known product launches and the busiest selling weeks.
**Protect selling time.** Agree with the sales leader how many hours a seller may spend in training each quarter and where. A common rule is nothing live in the last two weeks of a quarter.

**Sort every request into four layers.** The annual plan holds the few themes for the year. Launches are tied to a product date. In-quarter campaigns push one skill or message for four to six weeks. Always-on resources are what a seller can look up at any time.
**Give each quarter one campaign.** If the list has three, ask the sales leader to choose. Everything else goes to always-on or to next quarter.
**Write one line per launch and campaign:** what sellers will do differently, by when, and which figure should move.
**Name an owner and a review date** for every always-on resource. A playbook with no owner is out of date within two releases.
**Leave one month in four free** of new live training. Use it for manager coaching and for fixing what the last campaign showed.
**Review the plan with the sales leader** each quarter. Use the guidance on [sequencing a programme over weeks](t:2.3) when you shape each campaign.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. There is little research comparing one way of planning an enablement year with another.

**Sellers skip training near quarter end.** The reasoning is about attention and timing. Sellers are paid on a quarterly target, so anything that takes them off the phone near quarter end will be skipped or resented. A plan built round their calendar gets attended.

**The four layers stop two common failures.** Without a campaign layer, each product team sends its own training and sellers receive a dozen unrelated asks a month. Without an always-on layer, every question becomes a request for a session. Sorting also gives the enablement lead a fair way to say no, part of [deciding what not to train](t:9.14).

**Build a measure into every line.** The research on sales training is thin, as the review below shows. That is a reason to build a measure into each line of the plan. There is more on [which figures to use](t:6.14).

why.title: Sales training: a state of the art and contemporary review
why.found: A review of 56 articles on sales training published from 1985 to 2014. Most were surveys and only two were experiments. Findings on effectiveness were generally positive but mixed, and several studies reported sellers returning to old habits once back in the field.
why.means: Do not tell a client that sales training is proven to raise sales. Plan the follow-up, and agree a figure to watch for each campaign.

**Always-on becomes a dumping ground.** If a resource has no owner and no review date, do not publish it.
**Nobody agrees the figure to watch** until the campaign is over. Agree it in the planning meeting, as part of [agreeing what success looks like](t:9.6).

quiz.q: What are the four layers of an enablement plan?
quiz.a: The annual plan, launches, in-quarter campaigns and always-on resources.

quiz.q: Three product teams each want a live session for all sellers in the last fortnight of the quarter. What do you do?
quiz.a: Move all three out of that fortnight and ask the sales leader to pick one as next quarter's campaign. Sellers will not give attention at quarter end, and three unrelated asks compete with each other.

quiz.q: A playbook written for last year's release is still the top search result on the sales portal. What do you do?
quiz.a: Find or appoint an owner, then update or retire it this week. Give every always-on resource a named owner and a review date so this does not recur.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement on planning. The one research review opened shows that evidence on sales training is thin.

topics.title: Get a team ready for a product launch

situation.text: The launch date is public and will not move. The product team changed the pricing yesterday, half of what you have been told is under embargo, and 400 sellers, 60 partner firms and a retail chain all need to be ready on the same morning.

items: **Agree what ready means**, per audience, in one sentence each. For a field seller: can explain who the product is for, run the three-minute demo and answer the five likeliest questions.

**Get the embargo rules in writing** from the launch owner, the person at the client who is accountable for the launch. An embargo is a ban on sharing a fact before a set date. List who may know what, from which date, and what must never appear in a file sent outside the company.

**Split content into stable and volatile.** Customer problems and the audience rarely change late. Price, names, dates and screenshots do. Build the stable part first and keep volatile facts on one sheet that everything else points to.
**Set a content freeze date** and a change rule. After the freeze only the launch owner can approve a change, and each change is logged with a version number and date.
**Plan the cascade**, the order in which each group is briefed, in waves. The core team first, then regional leads and managers, then field sellers, then partners and retail as the embargo allows.
**Build in practice, not only briefings.** Every seller should say the pitch aloud and be heard by a manager or peer before launch day. There is a [format for the practice](t:2.38).
**Run a readiness check a week before.** Use a short spoken or recorded pitch, not only a quiz. Report the result by region to the launch owner.
**Staff the first two weeks after launch.** Collect field questions daily and answer them in one place.

why.text: **Launch readiness is professional practice.** There is little research comparing one launch plan with another.

**One study favours confidence over pressure.** One piece of research does bear on what the training should do. A study that tracked industrial salespeople through two product launches found that sellers who felt positive about selling the new product and confident that they could sell it formed stronger intentions and grew sales faster. Pressure from others to sell it worked less well, and it weakened the other two effects. That fits the craft view that a launch needs practice until sellers feel able. It is one study in one setting.

**Keep each changing fact in one place.** Separating stable from volatile content is what makes a moving product manageable. A price on forty slides means forty edits. A price on one sheet is changed once.

why.title: Motivating salespeople to sell new products
why.found: A longitudinal study of industrial salespeople across two launches, using surveys and daily sales records. Positive attitudes to selling the new product and self-efficacy built selling intentions and faster sales growth. Perceived pressure from others was less effective and weakened those effects.
why.means: Spend launch training time on practice that builds confidence with the product. Do not rely on telling sellers how important the launch is.

try.text: Write the one-sentence definition of ready for a launch you know. Then, standing up, give a colleague the two-minute briefing you would give regional leads four weeks out: what is fixed, what may change, what they must not share. Ask them to repeat back the embargo rule.

items: **The date is fixed**, so scope gives. Decide early what you will drop if the product changes two weeks before launch, and tell the launch owner.
**Embargoed facts leak** through file names, screenshots and speaker notes. Check all three.
**The readiness check becomes a quiz** on features. Test the conversation, because that is what ready means.

**Partners and retail are told last** and trained least. Plan their wave from six weeks out. The guidance on [retail and frontline staff](t:2.39) and [partners and resellers](t:2.40) covers how to train them.

items.label: Fu, Richards, Hughes and Jones (2010), Motivating salespeople to sell new products: the relative influence of attitudes, subjective norms, and self-efficacy. Journal of Marketing, 74.

quiz.q: Which kinds of launch content tend to change late?
quiz.a: Price, names, dates and screenshots. Keep them on one facts sheet that other content points to.

quiz.q: Two weeks before launch the product team renames a feature. Your decks are frozen and half are translated. What do you do?
quiz.a: Log the change, get the launch owner's approval, update the facts sheet and issue a new version number to every market. Because volatile facts sit in one place, the stable content and its translations should need few edits.

quiz.q: A regional lead asks to forward the manager briefing deck to a reseller a week early. What do you do?
quiz.a: Say no and point to the written embargo list. Send the partner version on the date the embargo allows.

topics.title: Turn product knowledge into customer conversations

situation.text: The product manager has sent a 60-slide deck listing every feature. Sellers sat through it last quarter, passed the quiz, and still open customer calls by reading out the feature list.

items: **Pick the three or four features** that matter most to the customers these sellers meet. Leave the full list as a reference document.

**Ask which customer has the problem.** For each one, put the same question to the product manager and two good sellers: which customer has this problem, and how do they describe it in their own words.

**Write a conversation guide for the feature**, not a description. Use the six main headings from the worked example below: who cares, the problem, a question to ask, how to say it in one sentence, proof, and the likely objection.
**Get the proof from the client.** Use only customer stories and figures the client has approved for use. If there is none, write "no approved proof yet" and tell the launch owner.
**Show the conversation done well and badly.** A two-minute recording of each is enough. Say what the rule is behind the good one.
**Have every seller practise aloud** in threes: seller, customer, observer. Give the customer a card with a role and one objection. Four minutes, then two minutes of feedback, then rotate.
**Ask sellers to write one real account** where they will use the guide this week, and tell their manager which.

why.text: **The research supports the direction only.** Two bodies of research support the direction of this topic. Neither tested a conversation guide as such.

**Selling knowledge is closely linked to performance.** A meta-analysis of what predicts sales performance, covering studies from 1982 to 2008, found that selling-related knowledge had the strongest link with performance of the drivers it examined, followed closely by how well sellers adapt to the customer. Selling-related knowledge there means more than knowing the product. It includes knowing customers and how to present a solution to them. These are associations, not experiments.

**The practice method is behaviour modelling.** The practice method in steps 5 and 6 is behaviour modelling: show the skill, state the rule, practise, get feedback. There is a [full guide to behaviour modelling](t:2.34). A meta-analysis of this method covered 117 studies. Published summaries of it report clear gains in knowledge and skill and smaller gains in behaviour back at work. They also report that transfer was better when learners saw poor examples as well as good ones, worked on scenarios they wrote themselves and set goals for use on the job.
The six headings are craft.

why.title: Drivers of sales performance: a contemporary meta-analysis
why.found: Synthesising studies from 1982 to 2008, five drivers were significantly related to sales performance. Selling-related knowledge was the strongest (standardised beta .28), then adaptiveness (.27), role ambiguity (negative, .25), cognitive aptitude (.23) and work engagement (.23).
why.means: Teach product knowledge in the form sellers use it: tied to customers and adapted to the person in front of them.

try.text: Take one feature of a product you know and write its guide. Then run the three-person practice with two colleagues and record it on a phone. Listen for the moment the seller stops asking and starts listing. That is the point to coach.

try.title: A worked example: one feature rewritten as a conversation guide (invented helpdesk software)
lines: Feature as the product team wrote it: Rules engine routes inbound email to queues by keyword, sender and language.
Who cares: the support team leader with more than ten agents and one shared inbox.
The problem in their words: "Messages sit unread because everyone assumes someone else has picked them up."
Ask: "When an email arrives in the shared inbox today, how does it get to the right person?"
Listen for: forwarding by hand, a morning triage rota, complaints about slow first replies.
Say it in one sentence: "Each message goes straight to the team that can answer it, so nobody has to sort the inbox."
Show: the 90-second demo. One email in French about a refund lands in the right queue. Stop there.
Proof: the approved customer story in the reference library. Do not quote figures that are not in it.
Likely objection: "We tried rules in our old system and they broke."
Reply: "What broke them? ... Here you can test a rule on last week's messages before you switch it on."
Next step: offer to set up two rules on their own inbox in a 30-minute session.
Do not say: anything about features not yet released.

items: **The guide becomes a script** and sellers read it out. Practise with different customer cards so they have to adapt.
**Proof gets invented in the room.** Only approved stories and figures may be used, and the guide should say where they are.
**The quiz tests the feature list.** Assess the conversation, as the advice to [assess the real task](t:2.25) sets out.
**The product team wants everything covered**, all sixty features. Offer the reference document for the rest and hold the session to a few.
**Role-play customers go easy.** Give them a written objection.

items.label: Verbeke, Dietz and Verwaal (2010), Drivers of sales performance: a contemporary meta-analysis. ERIM report, published in 2011 in the Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science.
ScienceForWork, summary of Taylor, Russ-Eft and Chan (2005), A meta-analytic review of behavior modeling training.
QIC-WD, summary of behaviour modelling training research, including Taylor, Russ-Eft and Chan (2005).

quiz.q: In the meta-analysis of sales performance drivers, which driver had the strongest link with performance?
quiz.a: Selling-related knowledge, with adaptiveness close behind.

quiz.q: A product manager insists sellers must be trained on all sixty features before launch. You have 45 minutes. What do you do?
quiz.a: Agree the few features that matter most to these sellers' customers and build conversation guides for those. Put the full list in a reference document, because sellers need to be able to hold a conversation, not recite a catalogue.

quiz.q: In practice, a seller answers the customer's first question with four minutes of features. What do you do in the feedback?
quiz.a: Play back or describe the moment they stopped asking, and have them redo the opening with the question from the guide. One specific correction followed by a second attempt does more than a general comment.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis links selling-related knowledge and adaptiveness with sales performance, and behaviour modelling research supports the practice method. The guide format is craft.

topics.title: Train retail and frontline staff
topics.theory: Training at the point of sale

situation.text: A phone maker wants store staff to explain its new handset well. The staff work for a retail chain, sell forty other products, get no time off the floor, and a third of them will have left by spring.

items: **Find out what the retailer allows** before you design. Ask who may enter the store, when, for how long, and whether staff may use their own phones for training.
**Design for minutes.** Plan one session of ten minutes before opening or at a quiet time, and follow-ups of two or three minutes. Assume nobody will do an hour.

**Choose one customer conversation to improve.** For a handset it might be the first thirty seconds when a shopper picks it up. Apply the advice to [know the learner's working day](t:2.10) and spend an hour on a shop floor first.

**Put the knowledge on a job aid** at the point of sale: a pocket card or a card behind the display. Three customer questions, three things to show, one line on who the product suits. There is more on [building a job aid](t:5.7).
**Practise on the floor** with the real product. Show it once, have each person do it once with a colleague as the shopper, and give one piece of feedback.
**Hand over a two-minute refresher** for the store manager or team leader to run at the weekly briefing. They are there every week and you are not.
**Plan for turnover.** Every new starter should be able to get the same ten minutes from the team leader and the card, without you.

**Agree how it will be checked.** Combine the retailer's sell-out figures (what shoppers bought), a short observation by the brand's field trainer on a store visit and, if the client uses it, mystery shopping against a checklist you helped write. In mystery shopping a paid visitor poses as a shopper and scores the visit.

why.text: **Research on floor sessions is scarce.** Most of this is practitioner know-how from field trainers. There is little research on ten-minute floor sessions or pocket cards in retail.

**The constraints do the designing.** Store staff are employed and managed by the retailer, so the brand cannot instruct them to attend anything. Time on the floor is the retailer's money. High turnover means a one-off visit trains people who will soon be gone, which is why the job aid and the team leader matter more than the visit.

**Be careful with mystery shopping as proof.** A study using large data sets from three retail chains found that mystery shoppers' scores had no substantial relationship with what real customers said or with sales. A mystery shop can still tell you whether staff did a specific, visible thing, such as offering the handset to hold. Do not report it as a measure of customer satisfaction.

why.title: Do mystery shoppers really predict customer satisfaction and sales performance?
why.found: Using large-scale data from three service retail chains, mystery shopper assessments showed no substantial correlation with customer evaluations or with sales performance. Customer satisfaction measures were related to sales.
why.means: Use mystery shopping to check whether a trained behaviour happened. Use customer feedback and sell-out figures for the result.
