quiz.a: They had no substantial relationship with real customers' evaluations or with sales.

quiz.q: A client wants a 45-minute product course for staff in 300 stores owned by a retail chain. What do you propose?
quiz.a: A ten-minute floor session, a pocket card and a two-minute refresher run by team leaders, agreed with the retailer first. The staff are not the client's employees and the retailer will not release 45 minutes.

quiz.q: Three months after your store visits, a field trainer reports that most of the staff she meets are new. What do you do?
quiz.a: Check that team leaders have the card and the ten-minute plan and are using them with new starters. With turnover this high the lasting training is whatever the store can run itself.

topics.title: Train partners and resellers

situation.text: Your client sells through 200 reseller firms. Their sellers carry six competing brands, do not report to anyone at the client, and opened last quarter's training email at a rate nobody wants to say aloud.

items: **Ask how partners make money** from this product, putting the question to the client's partner manager. Training that helps a reseller win or keep a deal gets attention. Training that helps the vendor does not.
**Segment the learners.** A partner's sellers, technical staff and owner need different things. Write one line for each on what they must be able to do.

**Make certification mean something.** Tie each level to a benefit the partner values, such as deal registration (the right to log a deal with the vendor and have it protected from other partners), a better discount tier, leads or a listing in the partner directory. Agree this with the partner manager, who owns those benefits.
**Assess the job, not attendance.** A seller records a five-minute pitch. A technical person completes a set-up in a test environment. Apply the advice to [assess the real task](t:2.25).
**Keep it short and findable.** Put a 20-minute core path on the first screen of the portal, with search, no more than three clicks to any item, and a date on every page.
**Give partner managers a part.** They mention the next certification step in each quarterly review and run a short session at the partner's own team meeting.
**Set an expiry.** Certification lasts a year or until a major release. Send a short update module when the product changes, not the whole course again.
**Report to the client by partner firm**: who is certified, at what level, and whether certified partners register more deals. Say plainly that the last figure is a comparison, not proof of cause.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. What is published on partner training and certification is mostly vendor articles and analyst marketing. There is little independent research.

**Nobody can make partners attend.** The reasoning starts from authority. With employees, a manager can require attendance. With partners nobody can, so the programme has to be worth a busy seller's time on its own terms. That is why benefits and the partner's commercial interest come before content.

**A certificate has to signal something.** Certification works here as a signal as much as a course. It tells the client which partners can be trusted with leads, and it tells customers who is competent. A certificate earned by clicking through slides signals nothing.

**Keeping it current is the harder half.** Partner portals fill with material from past releases, and a seller who finds one wrong price stops trusting the rest. There is more on [how completion is tracked](t:3.14).

**Incentives need care.** Rewards paid to another company's staff can conflict with that company's policies and, in some sectors, with rules on inducements. That is a legal question. Ask the client's legal team.

quiz.q: Why can you not design partner training the way you design employee training?
quiz.a: Partner staff do not work for the client and cannot be told to attend, so the training must be worth their time commercially.

quiz.q: A client wants every partner seller to complete a four-hour course by the end of the month. Completion so far is very low. What do you suggest?
quiz.a: Cut the required part to a 20-minute core path and tie the longer certification to a benefit such as deal registration. Partners give time to what helps them win business.

quiz.q: A partner seller tells you the portal still shows last year's pricing. What do you do?
quiz.a: Have it removed or corrected that day and check every page for a date and an owner. One wrong fact makes partners distrust the rest of the portal.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement. No checkable research on partner or reseller training was found.

topics.title: Coach through sales managers

situation.text: The workshop on discovery questions went well. Four weeks later deal reviews sound exactly as they did before: the manager asks for the close date and the amount, and nobody mentions the customer's problem.

items: **Decide where reinforcement will happen** before you design the workshop. In sales the two places that already exist are the deal review and the joint customer call.
**Brief managers first.** Run a 60-minute session for them a week before their teams are trained, so they see the skill, try it and know what to listen for.
**Give each manager one page.** Three questions to ask in every deal review for the next six weeks, and three things to listen for on a joint call. No more.
**Have managers practise the coaching conversation** with each other, aloud. Ten minutes in pairs using a real deal. There is more on [how to ask and wait](t:5.5).
**Ask for a small, countable commitment**: two deal reviews per seller and one joint call per seller in six weeks, using the page.
**Teach managers to separate coaching from inspection.** In a coaching review the manager asks about the customer first and the forecast last, or holds the two on different days.
**Check in with managers at week 3.** Fifteen minutes as a group: what they heard and what sellers found hard.
**Report to the sales leader** how many reviews and joint calls happened. If managers are not doing it, that is the finding. There is more on [the manager's wider role](t:2.4).

why.text: There is some direct research here, and it carries a warning.

**Coaching skill mattered more than frequency.** A study in one pharmaceuticals company followed 1,246 sales representatives in 136 teams for a year. Managers whose coaching skill had been rated higher in a training exercise had teams that got closer to their annual sales goals, partly because those teams were clearer about their role. Coaching more often did not help by itself. Where the manager's skill was low, more frequent coaching went with lower goal attainment.

**Teach managers the skill first.** That is one company and an observed link, not an experiment. It still changes the brief. Telling managers to coach more may do harm. They need the skill first, which is why the manager session comes before the sellers' workshop and includes practice. The [wider evidence on workplace coaching](t:5.5), and its gap on line managers, is covered separately.

**Use the meetings managers already hold.** The rest is craft. Deal reviews and joint calls already happen every week, so reinforcement costs no extra meetings. Managers have their own targets and will not read more than a page.

why.title: Does coaching matter? Managerial coaching skill, frequency and sales goal attainment
why.found: Among 1,246 sales representatives in 136 teams at a pharmaceuticals organisation, tracked for a year, managers' coaching skill was related to their representatives' annual sales goal attainment, partly through team role clarity. When coaching skill was low, more frequent coaching was associated with lower attainment.
why.means: Build managers' coaching skill before asking for more coaching. Count coaching conversations, and also listen to how they are done.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play a seller with a real or invented deal. Run a five-minute coaching deal review using the page below and record it. Count how many of your turns were questions. Then swap.

try.title: A worked example: the manager's page for six weeks after a discovery workshop
lines: In every deal review, before the forecast, ask:
1. "What problem is this customer trying to fix, in their words?"
2. "Who else there has that problem, and have we spoken to them?"
3. "What question will you ask on the next call that you have not asked yet?"
Then wait. If the seller does not know, the next step is a call to find out, not a guess.
On a joint call, stay quiet and listen for:
1. Did the seller ask before presenting?
2. Did the customer do at least half the talking in the first ten minutes?
3. Did the seller say the problem back and get a yes?
Afterwards, within the hour: "What went well? What would you do differently? One thing from me."
Your commitment: two deal reviews and one joint call per seller by the end of week 6.
Week 3: fifteen minutes with the other managers to compare notes.

items: **The manager takes over** the joint call. Agree beforehand that the seller leads and the manager only steps in to save a deal.
**Coaching turns into forecast inspection.** Separate the two in time or in order.
**You have no access** after the workshop. Ask for the week 3 call in the proposal, and if you cannot have it, give the enablement lead the agenda to run.
**Managers get the page without practice.** Reading three questions is not the same as asking them and waiting. Keep the ten minutes in pairs even if the session is cut.

items.label: Dahling, Taylor, Chau and Dwight (2016), Does coaching matter? A multilevel model linking managerial coaching skill and frequency to sales goal attainment. Personnel Psychology.

quiz.q: In the pharmaceuticals study, what happened when low-skill managers coached more often?
quiz.a: More frequent coaching was associated with lower sales goal attainment.

quiz.q: A sales leader says, "Just tell my managers to do a coaching session with everyone each week." What do you say?
quiz.a: Propose a manager session with practice first, then a small commitment of two deal reviews and one joint call per seller. The one study on this found that frequent coaching by unskilled managers went with worse results.

quiz.q: On a joint call you are observing, the manager answers the customer's questions and the seller goes quiet. What do you do afterwards?
quiz.a: Ask the manager what they wanted the seller to learn from the call and agree a rule for the next one: seller leads, manager listens. Reinforcement only happens if the seller does the skill.

topics.tierReason: One large study in a single company links managers' coaching skill, not frequency, with sales goal attainment. The one-page method is craft.

topics.title: Run a large event or kick-off

situation.text: The sales kick-off has 150 people in a hotel ballroom, a chief executive who wants forty minutes, six breakout rooms and you as lead facilitator. Twelve people is what you are used to.

items: **Agree one aim for the half day** with the sponsor, in a sentence that names what people will do afterwards. Cut anything that does not serve it.

**Use the main stage** for what only it can do: direction from leaders, a customer voice, shared energy. Keep each main-stage item to 20 minutes or less and put a two-minute pair conversation after each.

**Put the practice in breakouts** of 20 to 25, each with a room host. Print the room on the badge. Allow ten minutes to move 150 people and seat them, with signs at every turn and a host at each door.
**Write a run sheet to the minute** and a one-page host guide. The guide gives the aim, the timings, the exact instructions to read out, and what to do if the room finishes early or late.
**Brief the hosts twice.** Forty-five minutes by video a week before, to walk the guide and try the activity. Fifteen minutes in the room on the morning, to check equipment and agree signals.
**Run a producer's desk.** One person, not you, watches the clock, cues speakers with countdown cards at five, two and zero minutes, and messages hosts on one group chat.
**Rehearse in the room the evening before**, with microphones and slides: the opening, every handover and the close.
**Close on the main stage** with one action each, said to a neighbour, and tell people what happens next and when.

why.text: **This is craft learned by running events.** There is little research on how to structure a kick-off.

**Scale changes what goes wrong.** With twelve people you can see confusion and repair an instruction. With 150 a vague instruction produces 150 versions, so wording has to be written down and tested. There is more on [how to word an instruction](t:4.24). A five-minute overrun on stage is five minutes lost in six rooms at once.

**Practice belongs in breakouts, not on stage.** The main stage is a poor place to practise a skill, because most people are watching. It is a good place to give direction and to let people feel part of something. Breakouts do the opposite job. The room host is the person who makes the practice happen. There is more on [briefing people who deliver under your name](t:9.20).

**The timetable sets the room's energy.** Energy in a big room follows the timetable more than the facilitator. Long runs of speakers flatten it. Short items, pair conversation and a change of room lift it. There is more on [where to put the demanding work](t:2.14).

try.text: Read the first three minutes of your opening aloud in the largest room you can get into, standing, with a microphone if there is one. Then read the breakout instruction to two colleagues without explaining it, and watch whether they do what you meant.

items: **A senior speaker overruns.** Agree the countdown cards with them beforehand and tell them the break is what gets cut.
**Hosts improvise the instruction** and rooms do different things. Give them the words and ask them to read them.
**Questions from the floor are inaudible.** Use roving microphones or collect questions on cards.
**The breakout is a discussion** about the skill. Make it practice of the skill, in threes, with a customer card.
**Nothing follows the event.** Book the first manager deal reviews before the kick-off, as the guidance on [coaching through sales managers](t:2.41) sets out.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: How long should you allow to move 150 people from a ballroom to breakout rooms and seat them?
quiz.a: About ten minutes, with signs and a host at each door.

quiz.q: The chief executive is at 28 minutes of a 20-minute slot and still talking. What happens?
quiz.a: The producer shows the zero card as agreed, and you step to the side of the stage ready to thank them. You then shorten the pair conversation or the break, because breakout practice is the part that serves the aim.

quiz.q: At 10:15 a host messages that her room has finished the first round early and people are on their phones. What do you tell her?
quiz.a: Start round two now and use the early-finish line in the host guide, a harder customer card. Keeping rooms on the same activity matters more than keeping them on the same minute.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement from running large events. No research on kick-off design was found.

parts.title: Leadership and management programmes
parts.summary: How to design, staff, sponsor and judge a manager programme that runs over months, with practice on real work, coaching skill and a careful view of feedback tools.

topics.title: Design a first-time manager programme
topics.theory: The first-line manager programme: components spread over six to twelve months

situation.text: A software company has promoted sixteen people into their first management job in the last year. Most were engineers or support leads a few months ago. The people director asks you for a two-day new manager course. You know that two days will not change how sixteen people run their teams.

items: **Reshape the request in the first meeting.** Say: "Two days will give them the ideas. What changes how they manage is trying things on their own teams for some months, with someone asking how it went. Can I show you what that looks like for the same sixteen people?"

**Diagnose before you choose content**, by [finding the real need behind the request](t:2.1) and [running a performance diagnosis](t:2.29). Interview six of the new managers, four of their own managers and a few team members. Ask each the same question: what do new managers here get wrong in their first year. Choose five or six skills from the answers.

**Build the spine from seven components.** A kick-off with the sponsor. Short workshops four to eight weeks apart, one skill each. An assignment on the manager's own team after every workshop. Peer groups of four that meet between workshops. A monthly conversation with the participant's own manager. One point where the team's view is gathered. A close where each person reports to the sponsor.

**Order the skills** by when a new manager first needs them. One-to-ones and clear expectations come first because they happen every week. Feedback comes before the hard conversation, which needs both the skill and some trust in the cohort. Use the guidance on [sequencing a programme over weeks](t:2.3) when you set the gaps.

**Keep each workshop to a day** or a half day. Give no more than a quarter of the time to input and spend the rest on practice with the managers' own cases, as the guidance on [designing for managers](t:2.8) and [showing, practising and giving feedback](t:2.34) describes.
**State the time cost in plain hours** and get the sponsor to protect it. In the outline below it is five days in the room across the year, and between one and two hours a month outside it.

**Choose the length from the client's calendar.** Six months suits a small cohort and four skills. Twelve months lets every participant go through one full round of goal setting, performance reviews and pay conversations while they still have the group behind them.
**Write the measures before the first session.** The guide to [measures at three, six and twelve months](t:2.49) shows how.

why.text: **One piece of research supports the shape.** The rest is practitioner judgement.

**Pooled studies favour practice spread over time.** The research is the meta-analysis already described under [designing for managers](t:2.8) and [what the evidence says about retreats](t:8.8). Pooling 335 samples, Lacerenza and colleagues found that leadership training works on average. Programmes went with stronger effects when they were built on a needs analysis, gave feedback, used several methods including practice, spread their sessions over time, and were run on site and face to face. That is a pattern across many different programmes. It did not test a twelve-month design against a two-day course, and it cannot tell you that this mix of components is the right one.

**Teach each skill just before it's needed.** The mix itself is a convention among large employers. The reasoning behind it is about timing. A first-time manager's year has its own calendar, from the first one-to-ones to the first person who is not performing. A skill taught months before it is needed has faded by the time it is used, which is the point made about [skills that go unused](t:5.17). A programme spread over the year can put each workshop a few weeks ahead of the moment.

**The assignment is what holds the components together.** With it, every workshop ends in something the manager does with a named person on their team, the peer group hears how it went, and the manager's own manager asks about it.

why.cite: Lacerenza, Reyes, Marlow, Joseph and Salas (2017)
why.title: A meta-analysis of leadership training
why.found: Across 335 samples, leadership training improved reactions, learning, behaviour at work and results. Needs analysis, feedback, several delivery methods including practice, spaced sessions, an on-site location and face-to-face delivery went with stronger effects.
why.means: Start from a diagnosed need, put practice and feedback in every session and leave gaps between sessions. The study does not test any one programme outline, including the one on this page.

Then stand up and present it in four minutes to a colleague who plays a people director with a budget for two days. Good looks like this: you name the hours, you name the five or six skills and where each came from, and you do not apologise for the length.

items: **The client cuts the peer groups** and the manager conversations to save time, after accepting the twelve months. What is left is six workshops. Show the sponsor that the cut items cost under two hours a month and carry the practice.
**Workshops drift to ten weeks apart** because diaries are full. Book all dates before kick-off and have the sponsor send them.

**The hard conversation is scheduled first** because it is what the client worries about most. People will not rehearse a real case in front of strangers. Leave it until the cohort has practised together at least twice.

items.label: Lacerenza, Reyes, Marlow, Joseph and Salas (2017), Leadership training design, delivery, and implementation: a meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 102(12). Abstract on the University of Central Florida repository.

quiz.q: Name four of the seven components of the first-time manager programme on this page.
quiz.a: Any four of: a kick-off with the sponsor, spaced workshops, an assignment on the manager's own team, peer groups, a monthly conversation with their own manager, a point where the team's view is gathered, and a close with the sponsor.

quiz.q: A people director agrees to twelve months but wants to drop the peer groups and the monthly manager conversations because "people are busy". What do you do?
quiz.a: Show that those two items cost under two hours a month and are where the practice gets talked about and noticed. Offer to shorten a workshop before you cut them, because without them the programme is six separate events.

quiz.q: The client wants the workshop on the hard performance conversation to come first, in month one. What do you say?
quiz.a: Recommend that it comes after feedback has been practised and the cohort has worked together a few times, because people will not rehearse a real case with strangers. If one manager has an urgent case now, arrange help for that person through their own manager and the people team.

topics.tierReason: One meta-analysis read in summary supports spacing, practice, feedback and needs analysis. The mix of components, the order and the twelve-month outline are practitioner judgement.

topics.title: Choose who is on it and how the cohort works
topics.theory: Nomination, cohort size and mix, and the people who are not chosen

situation.text: The people director sends you sixteen names for the new manager programme. Three of them have managed for six years. Two were told on Friday that they are "going on a course". One head of department has put nobody forward. And an engineer who was not picked has already asked her manager what she did wrong.

items: **Write the entry rule** before you look at names. For a first-time manager programme a workable rule is: in a first people-management role, appointed in the last 18 months, at least three direct reports, and their own manager has agreed to a monthly conversation. Agree it with the sponsor and publish it.

**Prefer entry by role** to entry by nomination. If everyone appointed in the window comes, nobody has been chosen and nobody has been passed over. Keep nomination for programmes with scarce places, such as one for people thought ready for a bigger job.

**Make any nomination open.** Ask each nominating manager for three sentences: why this person, why now, and what the nominator will do to support them. A small panel reads them together: the sponsor, a people partner, and you as adviser without a vote.
**Check the list against everyone eligible.** Compare by function, site, sex and working pattern. If part-time managers or one office are missing, ask why before the list goes out.

**Set the size at 12 to 16** for one trainer. Sixteen gives four peer groups of four and still works if two people leave the company. Above sixteen, practice in threes needs a second facilitator, as the guidance on [group size and staffing](t:2.33) explains.
**Mix functions on purpose.** Put engineering, support, sales and product managers in the same cohort, and build peer groups so that no two members share a team or a boss.

**Keep reporting lines out of the room.** A manager and someone who reports to them should not be in the same cohort. Brief the participants' own managers for 45 minutes before kick-off, giving them [a job before, during and after](t:2.4).
**Have each participant hear it first** from their own manager, with a reason, and then receive the sponsor's invitation. Use the wording below.

**Decide what happens to everyone else** and say it on the same day. Eligible people who missed this cohort get the date of the next one. Experienced managers are offered a part, such as hosting a peer group or telling a story at a workshop.
**Set one attendance rule** and have the sponsor state it: miss two workshops and you move to the next cohort.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study was opened for this page on how to pick a cohort, and the numbers here are working conventions.

**A place is read as a verdict.** The reasoning starts from what a nomination tells people. In most companies a place on a leadership programme is read as a verdict. Those who get one hear that they are valued, or that they are thought to need fixing. Those who do not hear the opposite. A written rule and a plain reason take most of the guesswork out of it. They also make it less likely that someone arrives having been sent, the problem of [the person who was sent](t:4.36).

**Less visible people get overlooked.** Checking the list against the eligible group is a fairness habit. Nominations follow visibility, so people who work part time, sit in a smaller office or have a quiet manager are easier to overlook. You are not the decision maker. You can still ask the question, and the people team will know what the organisation's own policies require.

**Mixed cohorts are a trade.** Managers from one function share examples and jargon, which makes cases quicker to set up. Managers from several functions speak more freely about their own boss, hear how other parts of the company work, and leave with people they can ring. For a first-time manager programme the second usually matters more, because the skills are the same in every function.

try.text: Take a programme you know, or the sixteen names above. Write the entry rule in four lines. Then say aloud, to a colleague playing each part, the three conversations in the first artefact: to a participant, to someone who is not on it this time, and to an experienced manager.

try.title: Words you can use: three conversations a participant's manager needs to have
lines: To a participant: "You've been managing the team since March, and everyone who has taken on a team this year is on this programme. It runs for twelve months, about a day every two months, plus a small group that meets in between."
"My part is half an hour with you each month to hear what you're trying. I've put those in the diary. The invitation from the sponsor comes on Thursday."

To someone not on it this time: "The programme is for people in their first management job who started in the last 18 months. You are not in that group, and that is the only reason. It says nothing about how you are doing."
"If you want to move into management, let's use our next one-to-one to look at what would get you ready. The next cohort starts in September."

To an experienced manager: "This one is built for people in their first year, so it would repeat a lot for you. We would like your help with it. Would you host one of the peer groups for the first two meetings, or come to the feedback workshop and tell them about a conversation you got wrong?"

items: **A department head uses the programme** to deal with a manager who is failing. Ask before the list is final whether anyone on it is in a formal performance process. If so, that is a matter for their manager and the people team, and the programme should not be presented as the remedy.
**People learn from a calendar invitation** that they are on it. Hold the invitations until every participant's manager has confirmed the conversation has happened.
**Nobody tells the people not chosen** anything. Silence is read as a verdict too. Give their managers the wording.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What cohort size does this page suggest for one trainer, and why sixteen in particular?
quiz.a: Twelve to sixteen. Sixteen divides into four peer groups of four and still works if two people leave.

quiz.q: Two participants tell you at kick-off that they only found out on Friday and do not know why they were picked. What do you do?
quiz.a: Give the entry rule to the room in one sentence so everyone hears the same reason, then ask the sponsor or people partner to make sure their managers speak to them this week. Next time, hold the invitations until every manager has confirmed the conversation.

quiz.q: A director wants to nominate a manager with six years' experience because "he needs it more than anyone". What do you say?
quiz.a: Point to the entry rule, which is for people in their first 18 months, and ask what the director wants to change about this manager's work. If it is a performance concern, that belongs with the director and the people team. Offer the experienced manager a part in the programme only if the director is content for him to be seen as a contributor.

topics.title: Give the sponsor a real job
topics.theory: The senior sponsor's part at the start, in the middle and at the end

situation.text: The chief technology officer has agreed to sponsor the new manager programme. Her assistant offers you ten minutes at the kick-off for a few words of welcome. Nothing else is in her diary, and she has not seen the outline.

items: **Ask for 30 minutes with the sponsor** four weeks before kick-off. Bring one page that lists every date you need her for and what she does at each. For a twelve-month programme, ask for about eight hours in total.
**Agree the reason in her words.** Ask: "If this works, what will be different in your teams a year from now?" Write down two or three answers. These become her opening and the basis of the measures.

**Have her do two things before kick-off**, the two things only she can do. She signs the invitation. And she tells the participants' own managers, who report up to her, that the monthly conversation is part of their job this year.

**Give her 20 minutes at kick-off** and no slides. She says why the company is doing this now, tells one story from her own first year as a manager that includes a mistake, and says what she expects. Ten minutes of questions follow. Then she leaves, so the room can work without rank in it, the point made about [the senior person who takes over](t:4.38).

**Book one drop-in of 45 minutes** in the middle, around month four. Peer groups send questions in advance. She also reads a one-page progress note at three and six months and replies to the cohort in a few lines.

**Ask her to remove one obstacle** the cohort raises. It might be a standing meeting that clashes with every workshop, or a rule that stops new managers seeing their own team's pay data. One visible fix is enough.
**Give her counts** she can act on. Tell her how many manager conversations happened in each department. Do not report on named participants.

**Book 90 minutes at the close.** Each participant tells her one change they made and how they know. She asks questions and makes no assessments. Afterwards she decides with you whether a second cohort runs and what changes.
**Write her words for her.** Two days before each appearance, send five lines of talking notes. Busy sponsors use what they are handed.
**Agree what she will not do**: turn up unannounced at a workshop, ask you what an individual said, or use the close to rank people.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study opened for this page tested what a programme sponsor should do. There is research on [support from a learner's own manager](t:2.4), and a sponsor is a different role.

**Only the sponsor can expect managers' support.** The line manager helps one participant use the skill. The sponsor holds two things nobody else has. She can say why the company is spending the time, with the authority to be believed. And she manages, directly or one level down, the people whose support the participants need. A trainer can ask a head of department to hold a monthly conversation. The sponsor can expect it.

**A sponsor's opening signal soon fades.** A sponsor who only opens the programme sends a signal that fades within a few weeks. By month four the participants are busy, two workshops have been moved, and some of their managers have quietly stopped asking. That is the moment a second appearance earns its place.

**The limits protect the practice.** People will only rehearse a real conversation, or admit to a peer group that they avoided one, if they trust that it stays there. A sponsor who hears detail about individuals, or who judges people at the close, ends that trust for this cohort and the next. If the sponsor changes job or goes quiet during the year, there is advice on [handling a change of sponsor](t:9.36).

try.title: Words you can use: the sponsor's talking note for kick-off
lines: "We promoted sixteen of you this year because you were good at your last job. Managing is a different job, and we have not helped people learn it before."

"In my first year as a manager I avoided telling someone his work was not good enough for four months. By the time I did, the whole team knew, and he was the last to hear. I would like you to be quicker than I was."
"I expect three things. Come to every session. Try each thing on your own team before the next one. And tell your peer group the truth about how it went."
"Your managers know this is part of your job this year. I have asked each of them to give you half an hour a month on it."
"I will be back in month four to hear what is getting in your way. What would you like to ask me now?"

items: **The sponsor sends a deputy** to kick-off. Ask for a three-minute recorded message from her as well, and move the drop-in earlier so the cohort meets her by month two.
**She stays for the whole day** of kick-off to show commitment. Thank her, and explain that people rehearse more honestly without her there.
**She asks about the strong ones**, and asks you who they are. Say that you report on the cohort as a whole, and that she will hear from each of them herself at the close.
**The obstacle the cohort raises** is one she cannot or will not fix. Ask her to say so plainly and give the reason. People accept a clear no better than silence.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Which two things, before kick-off, can only the sponsor do?
quiz.a: Sign the invitation, and tell the participants' own managers that the monthly conversation is part of their job this year.

quiz.q: At month six your notes show that manager conversations have stopped in one department. The sponsor asks which participants are affected. What do you give her?
quiz.a: The count for that department and the name of the department head, who reports up to her. You do not name participants, because the sponsor's job is to speak to the managers and the participants need to trust that you do not report on them.

quiz.q: The sponsor wants to score each participant's presentation at the close and send the scores to their managers. What do you say?
quiz.a: Ask her to listen and ask questions instead, and explain that people will present a safe story if they know they are being ranked. If she needs a view on readiness for promotion, that comes from their own managers through the normal talent process.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement. No study was opened on what a programme sponsor should do.

topics.title: Build practice on real work between sessions
topics.theory: Assignments on the participant's own team, peer groups and action learning sets

situation.text: The feedback workshop in month five went well. Six weeks later you open the next workshop by asking who gave the piece of feedback they planned. Five hands go up out of sixteen.

items: **End every workshop with one assignment** on the manager's own team. Make it small, dated and written down. For example: "By 14 March, give one piece of corrective feedback to someone on your team, using the opening line you rehearsed today. Write down what you said and what they said." There is a [method for planning the first use](t:5.2).
**Have each person say aloud** to their peer group who it will be with and when. Their own manager hears the same plan in the monthly conversation.
**Form peer groups of four or five** at kick-off and keep them fixed for the programme. They meet for 75 minutes between workshops, without the trainer. Put every date in diaries on day one.
**Give the groups a guide** with clock times and two roles, a host and a timekeeper, which rotate. Each meeting takes two cases of 30 minutes. The guide below sets the order.

**Protect the questions round.** For ten minutes the group may only ask questions, and nobody gives advice. If someone starts with "have you thought of", the timekeeper says "question or suggestion?" and they rephrase.
**Teach the format in the room** before the groups run it alone. At kick-off, run one full case in each group for 30 minutes while you walk round and coach the timekeepers.
**Ask each group for a three-line note** after every meeting: who came, the two topics in a few words, and one question for the trainer. Everything else stays in the group.
**Open the next workshop in peer groups** with ten minutes: what you tried, what happened. Then take two examples to the whole room. This is what makes the assignment count.

**Use an action learning set** when the sponsor also wants business problems worked on. Each person brings one larger problem from their own area, returns to it at every meeting and reports what they did since the last one. Sit in on the first two meetings as facilitator.

why.text: The evidence for these methods is thin, and this topic is craft.

**One review found gains, on weak evidence.** One review was opened for this page. Leonard and Marquardt gathered 21 articles, theses and dissertations that tried to measure the effects of action learning. Their summary says the studies point to gains in broad leadership skills, with collaborative leadership and coaching named in particular. It lists things that went with success, among them questioning, taking action, learning from group members, a safe environment and the presence of a coach. The same summary says plainly that very little rigorous research on action learning has been done. It is a review of a small and mixed set of studies, read here in summary.

**No study of trainer-free groups was read.** No study of trainer-free peer groups inside a manager programme was opened. The general case for [learners teaching each other](t:1.19) is made separately, and the pooled finding that leadership programmes with practice and feedback do better is covered under [designing for managers](t:2.8).

**Someone has to ask how it went.** The rest is reasoning from practice. The assignment exists because a skill rehearsed once in a workshop has not yet met a real person with real feelings. The peer group exists because someone has to ask how it went, and a group of peers asks more honestly than a trainer who is there for one day in sixty.

**Questions come before advice for a practical reason.** Advice arrives fast, fits the adviser's team and lets the presenter off thinking. Ten minutes of questions usually changes what the presenter believes the problem is. The review's mention of a coach is one reason to stay with each group for its first full round.

try.text: Find three colleagues and run one case round from the guide below, with a real work problem of your own and a timer on the table. Take the timekeeper role in a second round. Notice how hard the group finds it to ask without advising, and practise saying "question or suggestion?" until it comes out lightly.

"What does this person think the problem is?"

items: **Groups stop meeting by month four.** The three-line note is your early warning. If one is missing, ring the host that week and ask what got in the way.
**The meeting turns into a moan** about senior management. The guide's last step fixes this if it is kept: each person leaves with a next step that is theirs to take.
**A case names a team member** and concerns their health, conduct or pay. Tell groups at kick-off to describe the situation without the name, and to take anything formal to their people partner.
**The assignment is vague**, such as "think about your feedback style". If it has no person and no date, rewrite it before people leave the room.

items.label: Leonard and Marquardt (2010), The evidence for the effectiveness of action learning. Action Learning: Research and Practice, 7(2).

quiz.q: In the peer group guide, what is the group allowed to do in the ten minutes after a case is presented?
quiz.a: Ask questions only. No advice and no stories of their own.

quiz.q: By month four, one peer group has not sent its three-line note twice running. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ring the host that week, ask what got in the way and help them fix a date. A group that misses two meetings rarely restarts without someone asking, and the dates may clash with something the sponsor can move.

quiz.q: A participant says the peer group is pleasant but "we just swap tips". What do you change?
quiz.a: Sit in on their next meeting for one case and coach the timekeeper to hold the questions round. Tips arrive before the problem is understood, and ten minutes of questions usually changes what the presenter thinks the problem is.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement. The one review opened says itself that rigorous research on action learning is scarce, and no study of trainer-free peer groups was opened.

topics.title: Teach managers to coach
topics.theory: Coaching as a manager's skill: a half-day practice design

situation.text: A support team lead takes every problem her team raises back to her own desk. She tells you she has no time to coach because she spends the whole day answering their questions.

items: **Define the skill narrowly.** In a ten-minute conversation, the manager helps a team member reach their own next step by asking, and says so when they switch to telling. The [shape of the coaching conversation](t:5.5) is covered separately. This topic is about getting sixteen managers to practise it.

**Start with their own habit.** Ask each manager to write down the last question a team member brought them and what they said back. Ask for a show of hands: who gave the answer. Most hands go up, and that is your opening.

**Show it twice**, following the method of [showing, practising and giving feedback](t:2.34). With a co-facilitator or a recording, play a two-minute version where the manager solves the problem and a two-minute version where the manager asks. Ask the room what was different and write their words on the flipchart.

**Hand out a card with three questions** and one rule. "What have you tried? What are your options? What will you do, and by when?" The rule: ask at least two questions before you give a view, and if you give one, ask first: "Can I tell you what I think?"

**Practise in threes for three rounds**: coach, team member and observer. Eight minutes of conversation and four of feedback, then rotate. The team member brings a real problem of their own, so the coach cannot know the answer. The observer counts questions and statements. Feedback follows the order set for [running a role-play](t:4.29).

**Teach when to stop coaching.** Give each table six situation cards to sort into coach, tell or teach. A customer outage in progress is a tell. A new starter who has never seen the system needs teaching. A conduct matter is neither, and goes to the people team.

**Set the assignment**: three ten-minute coaching conversations in the next four weeks, inside one-to-ones that already exist. Each manager notes their first question and what the person decided, and takes one conversation to their peer group.
**Come back to it.** At the next workshop, run one more round in threes with a harder case: the team member who says "just tell me what to do".

why.text: **The design on this page is practitioner judgement.** The research that bears on it sits in two other topics, and both carry a caution.

**Most coaching evidence is about trained coaches.** As the guidance on [coaching with questions, not answers](t:5.5) reports, pooled studies find that workplace coaching has positive effects, but most of that evidence is about trained coaches. One of the two meta-analyses there left out managers coaching their own staff. A manager also judges the person's work, which makes an honest answer harder to give.

**One study links unskilled coaching to worse results.** The study described under [coaching through sales managers](t:2.41) is the closest to this situation. In one sales organisation, managers with higher coaching skill had teams that came closer to their goals. Where skill was low, coaching more often went with worse results. That is one company and an observed link. It is still the reason this design asks for three careful conversations and a second practice round, and does not ask managers to coach every day.

**Outside sales the setting changes.** A sales manager has the deal review, a meeting that already exists and has a number attached. A support or engineering manager has the weekly one-to-one and the question that arrives at the desk or in a chat message. So the practice has to be short enough to fit an interruption, and the manager has to learn to notice the moment. That is why the session opens with the last question each manager was asked.

try.text: Ask a colleague to bring a real problem from their week. Coach them for eight minutes using only the card, and record it. Listen back and count your questions and your statements. Then mark every question that was advice in disguise, such as "have you thought about asking finance?". Do it again with a second colleague and compare the counts.

items: **Managers ask leading questions** and count them as coaching. Have the observer mark any question that contains the answer.
**The workshop teaches a model** with a name and four boxes, and people remember the name. Keep to three questions on a card.

**Someone coaches when they should tell.** A new starter asked "what are your options?" about a system they have never seen learns only that the manager is unhelpful. The card sort is there for this, and there is an explanation of [why beginners need more direction](t:1.26).

**The client asks for a count** of coaching conversations as a target, and asks you to do it. Report the count as activity, and point to the finding, under [coaching through sales managers](t:2.41), that frequency without skill may do harm.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What is the one rule on the card?
quiz.a: Ask at least two questions before you give a view, and if you have a view, ask first whether you can share it.

quiz.q: In a practice round a manager asks, "Have you thought about escalating it to the product team?" The observer counts it as a question. What do you do?
quiz.a: Point out that it is a suggestion with a question mark on it, and ask the manager to try again with "What are your options?". Leading questions keep the thinking with the manager, which is the habit the session is trying to change.

quiz.q: A participant says her team is too new for coaching and she has to tell them everything. What do you say?
quiz.a: Agree that people who lack the knowledge need telling or teaching, and that choosing well is part of the skill. Ask her to pick the one or two people on her team who do know enough, and to hold her three conversations with them.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement. The supporting research on coaching is reported in 5.5 and 2.41, and neither tested this workshop design.

topics.title: Use feedback tools with care
topics.theory: 360-degree feedback and personality questionnaires: what each can and cannot do

situation.text: A vendor has offered the people director a 360-degree survey and a personality profile for every participant, at a discount if both are bought. She would like them added at month six. Sixteen new managers, most with teams of three or four, would each receive two reports.

items: **Ask the purpose of each tool.** Say: "What will a participant do differently after reading this report, and who will help them?" If nobody can answer, leave the tool out.

**Know what a 360 is.** The manager, their boss, their peers and their direct reports rate the manager on a list of behaviours, and a report sets the views side by side. It can show a manager how their behaviour lands with different groups.

**Set conditions before you agree** to a 360. It is for development only, and plays no part in pay, promotion or a place on the programme. The report belongs to the participant. Raters are told in writing who sees what. Scores from a group are shown separately only when enough people answered. A common working threshold is three or more.

**Budget a one-to-one debrief** of 45 to 60 minutes for every participant, with someone trained in the tool, before or as the report is handed over. The debrief ends with one or two goals, and the participant chooses what to share with their own manager.
**Use something lighter for small teams.** With three direct reports, nobody is anonymous. A five-question team pulse, reported only when four or more answer, does the job at less risk.

**Tell two kinds of personality questionnaire apart.** Trait questionnaires place a person along several scales. Type tools sort a person into one of a fixed set of categories. If the client wants one, prefer a trait measure and use it only to open a conversation about how people differ.

**Ask any vendor for the technical manual** and for an independent review of the tool. Ask who is qualified to give the feedback. In the UK the British Psychological Society sets standards for people who use psychological tests.
**Refuse when the conditions cannot be met.** The table below lists when. Treat every report as personal data, following the rules on [learner data and privacy](t:9.24).

why.text: **None of the sources tested this setting.** Three research sources were read in summary for this page, along with one official page. None tested these tools inside a first-time manager programme.

**Feedback from all sides brings small gains.** On 360 feedback, Smither, London and Reilly pooled 24 studies that followed people over time after multisource feedback. Ratings improved, and the improvement was generally small. The authors argue that some people gain more than others. Improvement is more likely when the feedback shows that change is needed, when the person is open to feedback and sees a need to change, and when they set suitable goals and act on them. That is the case for the debrief and the goals.

**Feedback about the self helps less.** The research on [feedback people can act on](t:2.27) adds a warning: feedback helps less as it draws attention from the task towards the self. A 360 report is many pages of other people's ratings of you. Applying that finding to 360 reports is an inference made here, which the study did not test.

**Personality links to leadership are modest.** On personality, Judge and colleagues pooled 222 correlations from 73 samples using the five-factor model. Four of the five traits were related to leadership across studies, with extraversion the most consistent, at a correlation of about 0.3. Those are modest links across large groups. They do not let you predict how one new manager will do.

**Type tools rest on weaker ground.** A review by Stein and Swan examined the theory behind the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, that each person has a true type on four either-or pairs. It concluded that the theory does not agree with known data, cannot be properly tested and contradicts itself in places. That is one critical review, read in summary.
The rater threshold, the debrief length and the refusal list are practitioner conventions. No source was opened for them.

why.title: Does performance improve after multisource feedback?
why.found: A meta-analysis of 24 longitudinal studies. Improvement in ratings from direct reports, peers and supervisors over time was generally small. The authors propose that improvement is more likely for some recipients, for example when feedback shows change is needed, and when the person sets suitable goals and takes action.
why.means: Do not expect a 360 report to change behaviour unaided. Pay for the debrief, end it with one or two goals, and have someone ask about them.

why.title: Personality and leadership
why.found: A meta-analysis of 222 correlations from 73 samples, organised by the five-factor model. Extraversion was the most consistent correlate of leadership. Neuroticism, openness and conscientiousness were also related, and agreeableness only weakly.
why.means: Traits have modest links with leadership across groups. Use a trait report to start a conversation, never to sort or select the people in a cohort.

try.title: Words you can use: setting conditions and saying no
lines: "I'm happy to include a 360 if we can agree four things: it is for development only, the report belongs to the participant, every person gets an hour with a trained debriefer, and nobody's scores go on file."

"Most of this cohort have three or four direct reports. Their teams will know they can be identified, and they will answer politely. For those managers I would use five team questions and only report when four or more people reply."
"On the personality profile, I would not make it part of the programme. The evidence for sorting people into types is weak, and people remember the label long after they forget the caveats."
"If the group would enjoy it, we could offer a trait questionnaire as an optional extra, with a qualified person giving the feedback, and keep the results with the participant."
"I can't run a 360 during the reorganisation. People will read it as part of the decision about their jobs, whatever we say."

items: **Reports arrive with no debrief booked**, by email on a Friday afternoon. Hold release until every participant has a debrief date.

**The type label sticks.** Months later a manager says "she's an introvert, so I didn't ask her to present". If a type tool has been used, say at the time that it describes a preference on the day and decides nothing.

**The 360 is run again** at month twelve to prove the programme worked. Raters who know about the programme tend to rate kindly, so report it as one view among several, as the guide to [judging a leadership programme over a year](t:2.49) sets out.

quiz.q: What did the Smither, London and Reilly meta-analysis find about improvement after multisource feedback?
quiz.a: Across 24 longitudinal studies, improvement in ratings over time was generally small, and more likely for people who saw a need to change, set goals and acted.

quiz.q: A client wants 360 results sent to each participant's line manager "so they can support them". What do you do?
quiz.a: Say no to sending the report, and offer that each participant shares one or two goals from the debrief with their manager. The report belongs to the participant, and raters answer less honestly once they know it reaches the boss.

quiz.q: Half your cohort have teams of three. The client still wants a 360 for everyone. What do you propose?
quiz.a: A five-question team pulse for managers with small teams, reported only when four or more people answer, and the 360 only where there are enough raters in each group. With three direct reports nobody is anonymous, so the answers will be polite and of little use.

topics.tierReason: Two meta-analyses and one critical review, each read in summary, carry the claims about what 360 feedback and personality measures can show. The conditions and thresholds are practitioner convention.

topics.title: Judge a leadership programme over a year
topics.theory: Measures at three, six and twelve months, and their limits

situation.text: It is month two. The finance director has asked the sponsor what the company is getting for sixteen managers' time. She forwards the question to you with one line: "What will we be able to say in December?"

items: **Agree the measures with the sponsor** before kick-off, as part of [deciding what you will measure](t:6.1). Frame them as three plain questions. Are the managers doing the things. Are their teams noticing. Is anything changing for the business.

**Take a baseline** in the month before the programme starts. Send a five-question team pulse to every participant's team. Ask the people team for the last twelve months of leavers from those teams, using the method for [getting data from the client](t:6.12).

**Report activity and first use** at three months. Count workshops attended, assignments done, peer group meetings held and manager conversations held. Add each participant's own account of one thing they tried, with an example. Label all of it as activity, because you should [not mistake activity for learning](t:6.7).

**Look for behaviour at six months** that other people can see. Repeat the team pulse. Ask each participant's own manager three questions about what they have observed. Score one rehearsed conversation per participant against a short rubric at the month-five workshop, which shows what people can do on the day.

**Repeat the pulse at twelve months**, a third time. Count leavers from participants' teams and among the participants themselves, beside the year before. Ask their managers whether each person is ready for a larger team, and treat the answer as opinion.

**Use the next cohort as a comparison** where you can. Managers who are eligible but start later give you teams measured over the same months without the programme, an approach to [separating the effect of training](t:6.6).

**Interview four to six participants** using the [Success Case Method](t:6.13), including one or two for whom little changed. Their stories show how the programme worked where it did, and what blocked it.
**Report counts, and keep people unnamed.** Sixteen managers and about seventy team members are small numbers. Say "four leavers against six the year before", and list what else changed in the year.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study of how to evaluate a single leadership programme was opened for this page. The pooled finding described under [designing for managers](t:2.8) says leadership training improves results on average across many programmes. It cannot tell a finance director whether this one did.

**A manager's results arrive late, through others.** The difficulty is that a manager's results arrive through other people and arrive late. A new manager who starts holding proper one-to-ones in month two may keep someone who would have left in month ten. Nobody will ever see the resignation that did not happen. Meanwhile pay, a reorganisation or one unpopular product decision can move retention more than any programme.

**Pair quick measures with slow ones.** So the plan pairs fast, close measures with slow, distant ones. Assignments done and conversations held tell you within weeks whether the programme is running as designed. The team pulse tells you at six months whether teams notice a difference in specific behaviours. Leavers and readiness ratings come last and prove least by themselves.

**State each measure's weakness in the report.** Each measure has a known weakness, and the report should state it. Team members rating their own manager tend to be kind, and kinder when they know the manager is on a programme. Readiness ratings come from managers who have given time to the programme and want it to have worked. A rubric score shows what someone can do in a rehearsal. Read together, and set beside a few honest cases, they give a sponsor enough to decide on a second cohort.

**Keep the effort in proportion.** There is advice on [matching evaluation to the stakes](t:6.11). If someone asks for a return figure, guides to [showing the value](t:6.8) and [the cost and benefit case](t:6.15) show how to build one and how far to trust it.

lines: 1. I have a one-to-one with my manager at least every two weeks.
2. I know what is expected of me this quarter.
3. In the last month my manager gave me feedback I could act on.
4. When I bring a problem, my manager helps me think it through.
5. I would tell my manager if I had made a mistake.

items: **Nobody takes a baseline**, and at twelve months there is nothing to compare with. Send the first pulse before kick-off, even if the rest of the plan is not settled.
**Only two people answered a pulse**, and the team's results are shown to the manager. Set the threshold at four and show nothing below it.
**The sponsor asks for scores** by participant. Report the cohort as a whole, and by department only where a department has enough people to hide in.
**The report claims the credit** when retention improves. Put the pay round and any reorganisation beside the figure, and use the later cohort as a comparison if you have one.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Which measures does this page suggest reporting at three months, and how should they be labelled?
quiz.a: Attendance, assignments done, peer group meetings and manager conversations held, with each participant's account of something they tried. They are labelled as activity.

quiz.q: At twelve months, four people have left participants' teams against six the year before. The sponsor wants to tell the board the programme cut attrition by a third. What do you advise?
quiz.a: Report the counts as they are, with the pay round and other changes beside them, and say the direction is encouraging. With numbers this small, two people is not a rate, and several things besides the programme moved in the same year.

quiz.q: The team pulse rose on every question at six months. A colleague says that proves the managers have changed. What do you check before agreeing?
quiz.a: Check how many people answered each time and whether teams knew their manager was on the programme, since both push scores up. Set the pulse beside the rubric scores, the managers' observations and a few interviews before you draw a conclusion.

parts.title: Service and customer teams
parts.summary: Enablement for the support, customer success and renewals teams who look after customers after the sale, and how to measure it.

topics.title: Enable the teams who look after customers after the sale
topics.theory: Enablement for support, customer success and renewals teams

situation.text: A software client's head of support asks for your help. She has sixty agents on two sites and a product release every six weeks. "They sat the same launch training as sales," she says. "It was forty minutes on how to pitch. On release day they had two hundred tickets about a setting nobody had shown them."

items: **Find out which teams the client has**, because titles vary. Support answers problems as they arrive, by phone, chat or ticket. Customer success looks after named accounts so that customers use what they bought. Renewals or account managers handle the contract when it comes up. Ask who leads each and what each is measured on.

**Learn their calendar before you plan anything.** Support has no quarter end. Its peaks follow releases, incidents and billing dates, and the queue must be covered every hour. Customer success works to customer review meetings. Renewals works back from each contract date, often starting three or four months ahead.
**Meet whoever builds the support rota.** Ask which hours are quietest and how many agents can be off the queue at once. That number sets your group size and session length.

**Define good with the team leads**, using the method for [defining what good looks like](t:2.2). Start from the quality scorecard if one exists. If not, read or listen to ten good conversations and ten poor ones with two leads, and write down five behaviours you can observe.

**Sort the work into the four layers** used to [plan a sales enablement cycle](t:2.36), changed to fit. Release readiness happens every release. One skill campaign runs each quarter. The knowledge base is the always-on layer, with a named owner for every article. New starters follow a path.

**Deliver in pieces that fit the rota.** Run a 30-minute session three or four times across shifts with eight to ten agents each time. Practise on real tickets and recorded calls with customer details removed.

**Work through the team leads.** Most already review a sample of each agent's conversations and hold a weekly one-to-one. Give leads one page for the campaign: what to listen for and one question to ask. It is the service version of the deal review used to [coach through sales managers](t:2.41).

**Ask for a seat** in the release process. Support needs the known issues, the steps to diagnose them, what to say when there is no fix yet and who to escalate to. They need it a week before release day.
**Let customer contacts choose the next campaign.** Each month, ask for the top five reasons customers got in touch. The reason that is common and handled worst is next quarter's skill.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No research on enabling support or customer success teams was opened for this page.

**An agent in training is a customer waiting.** The [plan for a sales enablement cycle](t:2.36) is written for sellers, and two things differ here. The first is time. A seller chooses when to make calls. An agent is on a rota, and every agent in a training room is a customer waiting longer. Training that ignores this gets cancelled on the day by a team lead watching the queue.

**Agents need to know what breaks.** The second is the content. Sales material teaches people to open a conversation and make a case. Service work is diagnosis and explanation, often with a customer who is already annoyed. Agents need to know what breaks and what to say when they do not yet have an answer. The product knowledge is also wider, since a customer can ask about anything, and it changes with every release. That is why the knowledge base carries more weight here than any course, as the guidance on [job aids in the flow of work](t:5.7) argues in general.

**Customer success is its own audience.** Customer success and renewals sit between the two worlds. Their conversations are planned, like a seller's, and their aim is that the customer stays. Treat a renewals team like a small sales team with a rolling calendar. Treat customer success as its own audience and ask what a good customer review meeting looks like.

try.text: Ask someone who works in a support or service team to give you twenty minutes. Ask the three questions from step 3 and step 9: the quietest hours, how many people can be off the queue at once, and the top five reasons customers get in touch. Then say aloud, in two minutes, how you would fit one skill campaign into their next quarter.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Name two things a support team needs from release readiness that a sales team does not.
quiz.a: Any two of: the known issues, the steps to diagnose them, what to say when there is no fix yet, and who to escalate to.

quiz.q: A head of support offers you every agent for a full day in the week after a release. What do you say?
quiz.a: Thank her and ask for 30-minute blocks across shifts in a quieter week. The week after a release is the busiest for tickets, and a full day off the queue will be cancelled or resented.

quiz.q: Team leads say they have no time to reinforce the campaign skill. What do you try?
quiz.a: Fit it into what they already do: one thing to listen for in the conversations they review anyway, and one question in the weekly one-to-one. Give them a single page and a 60-minute session of their own before the agents are trained.

topics.title: Measure service enablement
topics.theory: Service measures, their limits and where the data lives

situation.text: You ran a quarter's campaign teaching support agents to diagnose a problem fully before answering. The head of support rings. Average handling time has gone up by forty seconds a contact and the finance team has noticed. She asks whether the training made things worse.

items: **Choose one result measure before the campaign**, one that fits what you are teaching. A diagnosis campaign should move repeat contacts and reopened tickets. A campaign on handling upset customers should show in quality scores and in satisfaction.

**Pair it with a counter-measure**, and say in advance which way each is expected to move. If agents diagnose properly, handling time may rise while repeat contacts fall. Write that sentence in the plan so nobody is surprised later.

**Get each definition in writing** with its date. First-contact resolution is the usual trap. In one company it means the customer did not get in touch again within seven days. In another it means the agent ticked a box. Ask which.

**Find where each figure lives** and who owns it, using the table below, then request it using the method for [getting data from the client](t:6.12). Service data usually sits across a ticketing system, a telephone or chat platform, a survey tool and the team leads' quality records.
**Record a baseline by team** for the quarter before. Where contact volumes are seasonal, also ask for the same quarter a year earlier.
**List what else moved the figures** in the period: a difficult release, an outage, new starters joining, a change to the survey, a change in the kinds of contact coming in.

**Use the quality score** on the campaign skill as your leading indicator. Before you rely on it, have two team leads score the same five conversations and compare. If they disagree, fix the scorecard first.

**Report the pair together**, by team, as a trend. Where sessions were rolled out shift by shift, the later shifts give you a comparison, as the guidance on [comparison groups and attribution](t:6.6) explains. Claim what the guidance on [measuring enablement by business results](t:6.14) allows: training is one contributor.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No source was opened for the measures on this page. They are described as support and customer success teams commonly use them, and every client defines them a little differently.

**Chasing one measure can harm customers.** Service measures come in pairs because each one can be improved in a way that harms customers. Handling time falls if agents rush people off the phone. First-contact resolution rises if agents stop logging the second call. Speed measures and quality measures pull against each other, and a campaign that improves one will often cost a little of the other. Deciding in advance which trade you are making turns an awkward phone call into an expected result.

**Ask who answered and what they rated.** Customer satisfaction scores need two questions asked of them. One is how many customers answered, because a score from a small share of contacts can swing on a handful of replies. The other is what the customer was rating. Someone who waited a week for a refund may give a low score to an agent who handled the conversation well. The score reflects the product, the policy and the wait as well as the person.

**Training can claim renewal least.** Renewal is the figure the business cares about most and the one training can claim least. It arrives up to a year after the conversations that shaped it, and it moves with price, product and the customer's own fortunes. Customer success teams often keep a health score for each account, built from usage and contact history. It moves sooner than renewal, but it is the client's own formula, so ask what goes into it.

**The quality score depends on the scorer.** The quality score is the measure closest to the training, which is its strength and its weakness. It shows whether agents are doing what was taught. It depends on who is scoring, which is why step 7 comes before any report.

try.text: Take the situation at the top of this page. Ring a colleague, or record yourself, and give the head of support your answer in two minutes. Good looks like this: you say what the campaign was expected to do to handling time, you ask for repeat contacts and reopened tickets for the same weeks, and you offer to bring both to finance on one page.

lines: "This quarter we are teaching agents to diagnose fully before they answer."
"We expect repeat contacts on the top three problems to fall. That is the result we are aiming for."
"We expect handling time to rise a little, because a full diagnosis takes longer. If it rises by more than a minute, we will look at why."

items: **One measure is reported alone.** Handling time without repeat contacts, or satisfaction without the number who answered, invites the wrong conclusion.

**The definition changes during the quarter** because the ticketing system was reconfigured. Keep the definition and its date in the report, as the guidance on [measuring enablement by business results](t:6.14) advises.
**Agents learn what the scorecard rewards** and say the phrases without doing the diagnosis. Have leads score what the agent found out as well as what they said.
**Asked to show training raised renewals.** Offer the nearer measures now and the renewal figure when it arrives, with the other causes beside it.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Why should average handling time always be read with a second measure?
quiz.a: Because it falls when agents rush customers. A quality score or repeat contacts shows whether the shorter contact still solved the problem.

quiz.q: After your diagnosis campaign, handling time is up forty seconds and finance is unhappy. What do you ask for?
quiz.a: Repeat contacts and reopened tickets for the same teams and weeks, and the quality scores on diagnosis. If fewer customers are coming back, the extra forty seconds is buying fewer contacts overall, and you can show both on one page.

quiz.q: A client says first-contact resolution rose from one quarter to the next and credits your training. What do you check before you accept the credit?
quiz.a: Check how the figure is defined and whether that changed, and what else happened in the quarter, such as a quieter release. If it rests on an agent ticking a box, ask for repeat contacts as well, since those come from what customers did.
