parts.title: Change and pilots
parts.summary: Training tied to a go-live date, and testing a programme on a small typical group before it goes to everyone.

topics.title: Train for a system or process change
topics.theory: Go-live readiness: role-based tasks, a sandbox, super users and floor support

situation.text: A retailer is replacing its stock and ordering system in 60 stores on Monday 1 March. The project manager sends you a 140-slide deck of screenshots and asks for "a two-hour session for everyone", to run in January.

items: **Get the facts of the change** from the project team. You need the go-live date and whether it is phased, which roles are affected, what each role does differently on day one, and what is not built yet. There is more on [planning the change and explaining why](t:9.15).

**Build a role-by-task list.** For each role, write the five to eight tasks people will do in the first week, ordered by how often they happen and how much an error costs. Train those. Rare tasks go into [job aids](t:5.7).

**Ask for a sandbox**, which is a practice copy of the system with realistic made-up data and logins that work. Ask for it at least three weeks before go-live. If there will be none, say plainly that you can offer demonstration and screenshots only, and that people will be less ready.

**Recruit super users**, one for each store, team or shift. Ask for volunteers and choose for patience over technical skill. Train them two weeks before everyone else, in more depth. Teach them to explain why a step is done and to help without taking the mouse. Agree with their managers that they are released from normal duties in the first two weeks.

**Time the end-user sessions** for the two weeks before go-live. Run 90 minutes, hands-on, in groups of eight to ten. Each person completes their own role's tasks in the sandbox. Close with a short observed task as a readiness check.
**Write one job aid per task**, on one page. Test each on someone who has not been trained. Put it at the workstation and date it.

**Plan floor support** for the first two weeks. Super users are on shift and visible. Hold a 15-minute call each day where they report problems. Keep one list of known issues and fixes where everyone can see it, and update job aids within a day.

**Track readiness by role and site**: trained, passed the readiness task, super user named. Report it to the project every week, in line with [tracking progress where everyone can see it](t:9.21). Afterwards, run a clinic for rare tasks such as the month-end count, and set up training for new starters.

why.text: **Most of this is practitioner judgement.** Two points have some research behind them.

**Train close to go-live, or it fades.** The first is timing. The guidance on [planning refreshers before skills fade](t:5.17) reports that skills which are not used fade, fastest for procedures with many steps. System tasks are exactly that kind of skill. Training in January for a March go-live means most of it has gone by the day it is needed. Two weeks is this site's working figure.
The second is super users, where the evidence is thin.

why.title: How clinician super users influence others during the implementation of electronic health records
why.found: The authors followed two hospital units for about nine months as a new records system went live. One unit had volunteer super users. The other had super users appointed for their technical skill. The volunteers were more proactive, explained the reasons behind steps and shared what they knew widely. The appointed ones tended to wait to be asked and to show a step without the reasoning. Clinicians on the volunteers' unit rated their own proficiency higher at follow-up. Super users on both units sometimes passed on workarounds.
why.means: Prefer volunteers, and train super users in how to help as well as in the system. It is one hospital, two units and 43 clinicians, with self-rated proficiency, so treat it as a pointer.

why.text: **Roles share a system but few tasks.** The rest is reasoning. A buyer and a store supervisor share a system and almost no tasks, so one session for everyone wastes most of each person's time. The sandbox matters because procedures are learned by doing them, with errors that cost nothing, the idea behind [treating mistakes in practice as information](t:1.22). This is a different job from [preparing a team for a product launch](t:2.37). There the audience has to talk about something new. Here they have to operate it on Monday morning with customers waiting.

try.text: Take a system you use at work. Write the role-by-task list for one role: the tasks someone new would do in their first week. Then teach the top task to a colleague in ten minutes, hands-on, with them at the keyboard and your hands off the mouse.

quiz.q: What is a sandbox?
quiz.a: A practice copy of the system with realistic made-up data, where people can do their real tasks and make mistakes at no cost.

quiz.q: The project manager wants all training finished eight weeks before go-live "to get it out of the way". What do you say?
quiz.a: Propose training super users three weeks before and everyone else in the final two weeks, with a readiness check. Procedures that are not used fade quickly, so training eight weeks early would mostly be gone by go-live.

quiz.q: A store manager offers her most technical team member as super user. He is quick with systems and short with colleagues. Another supervisor has volunteered. Who do you choose?
quiz.a: The volunteer, with extra system practice in the super user day. The one study opened here found volunteer super users explained more and shared more, and patience is harder to train than the system is.

topics.title: Run a pilot before you roll out
topics.theory: Piloting a programme: who to pilot with, what to watch, what to change and the decision

situation.text: A client wants a new manager programme to reach 300 managers in five countries from January. It has never been run. The sponsor says, "Run the first cohort and we will call it the pilot," and has invited her twelve keenest people.

items: **Agree in writing the pilot's purpose**, what the pilot is for. List three to six questions it must answer and the decision that follows: go, go with changes, or stop. For example: "Does the practice on day two fit in the time?" and "Do managers use the one-to-one structure in the following fortnight?"

**Set the bar before you run it.** Write what you expect to see for each question, such as "at least 10 of 12 complete the practice task to the standard" and "each block runs within ten minutes of plan".

**Choose a typical group** of 8 to 16. Mix keen and sceptical people, sites and experience, and include at least one person who works remotely or on shifts. Tell them it is a pilot and that their views will change the programme.
**Pilot the whole route.** Include the invitation, the preparation, the platform, the manager briefing and the follow-up. Many failures happen outside the room.

**Put an observer at the back** with a sheet. They note planned and real timings, where an instruction had to be repeated, where energy dropped, what was asked and every error in the materials. The facilitator cannot do this while running the session. There is more on [being watched while you work](t:4.44).

**Collect four kinds of evidence.** Timings. Performance on the practice tasks. Participants' views, from the form filled in before the close and a 15-minute group conversation with three questions: what would you cut, what was missing, what would stop you using this. Then, two to three weeks later, what managers and participants report was used.

**Sort every finding** into fix, change, leave or park. Fix errors and unclear instructions at once. Change the design where two kinds of evidence agree. Leave single opinions, matters of taste and difficulty that is there on purpose, [the friction that teaches](t:2.19).

**Hold the decision meeting within two weeks**, for 45 minutes, with the sponsor, the learning partner and the facilitator. Leave at least three weeks before the next cohort so that changes can be made. Record the decision, then update the [facilitator guide](t:3.20) and the [version number](t:3.18).

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study was opened that tests piloting a training programme against launching without one.

**A pilot is a test of the design.** A first cohort with a hopeful label is something else, and the difference shows in three places. The questions are written down in advance. The group is chosen to be typical. And someone is free to watch. Without those, the pilot produces a warm feeling and a few typing corrections.

**Keen volunteers flatter a programme.** They forgive slow passages, do the preparation and say kind things on the form. The 300 who follow will include [people who were sent](t:4.36), people on poor connections and people whose managers never mention it again. A pilot group with some of those in it tells you what the rollout will be like.

**Restraint in changes is the less obvious half.** Twelve people will give you forty comments. If you act on all of them, the second cohort gets an untested programme, which is another pilot. The rule of two kinds of evidence is a judgement call that keeps changes to what the pilot showed.

**Be honest about what a pilot proves.** Twelve people and no comparison cannot show that the programme works, a question of [separating training's effect from everything else](t:6.6). It can show that the programme runs, that people can do the tasks by the end and that some of it is used afterwards. It can also give you [the baseline and the measures](t:6.1) for the evaluation that follows. If the rollout is staggered, later groups can serve as a comparison for earlier ones.

try.text: Take a session you are about to run for the first time. Write three pilot questions and the bar for each. Ask a colleague to observe with a sheet ruled into four columns: time planned, time taken, what happened, change needed. Afterwards run the 15-minute group conversation aloud with whoever attended, and say nothing in defence of the design.

items: **The sponsor fills the pilot** with enthusiasts. Ask for a mix and explain why: the rollout will not be made of volunteers.

**The group performs for someone senior** when the sponsor or a senior leader sits in. Brief them using the advice on [the senior person who takes over](t:4.38), or ask them to join the decision meeting instead.
**The pilot is quoted as proof** of impact by the client after it goes well. Say what twelve people can and cannot show, and point to the evaluation plan.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What four kinds of evidence does a pilot collect?
quiz.a: Timings, performance on the practice tasks, participants' views, and what participants and managers report was used two to three weeks later.

quiz.q: After the pilot, one confident participant says the role-play was patronising and should go. The observed scores show eleven of twelve met the standard in it. What do you do?
quiz.a: Leave it in, and note the comment. It is a single view against the performance evidence, and the rule is to change the design only where two kinds of evidence agree.

quiz.q: The pilot's bar was ten of twelve to standard and nine made it. The sponsor says, "Close enough, call it a success and roll out." What do you say?
quiz.a: Report it as a narrow miss with its cause, which was skipped preparation, and propose going ahead with that one change and a check after cohort 2. Moving the bar afterwards removes the point of setting it, and the cause is cheap to fix.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement. No study was opened that tests piloting a training programme.

stages.name: Make the materials
stages.question: How do we build slides, media and e-learning that teach?

parts.title: Slides, visuals and story
parts.summary: What the research on words and pictures says about slides and charts.

topics.title: Judge every slide by what it asks of the learner

situation.text: You have inherited an eight-slide deck for a 20-minute briefing to a software company's support team, on the new way to escalate a ticket. It uses the brand template, has a neat flow diagram, and the product lead called it polished. At the last briefing three people asked which step was new. A slide can look finished and still give the learner no help.

items: **Print the deck as thumbnails**, six to a page. Beside each slide, finish this sentence in pen: "On this slide the learner has to...". If you cannot finish it, the slide is there for you or for the sponsor.

**Check selecting.** Look at each slide for three seconds, then look away and say which part you were meant to look at. If you cannot say, mark one part with a highlight, a circle or an arrow and turn the rest pale grey. If a slide has three things to point at, build it in three clicks.
**Check organising.** Group related items under a short label, number the steps, and draw a sequence as a sequence, left to right or top to bottom. A list of seven becomes two or three groups.

**Check connecting.** Find the thing on the slide that the learner already uses at work: a real screen, a real ticket, a term their team says. If there is none, swap the generic example for one of theirs.

**Circle every element that helps with none** of the three, such as the logo on each slide, the stock photo and the paragraph you will say anyway. There is more on [how to cut them](t:3.2) and where they go.

**Adjust for who is coming.** For newcomers, keep the labels and the step-by-step build. For experienced people, show the whole process at once, drop the labels they know, and mark only what has changed.

**Judge it in use.** Ask a colleague to present three slides aloud while you sit as far from the screen as the back row will be. After each slide, write down what you think the point was and compare it with theirs.

why.text: **Learners must select, organise and connect.** The leading theory of learning from words and pictures is Richard Mayer's multimedia learning theory. It rests on three ideas. People take in pictures and words through separate channels. Each channel holds little. Learning needs active work by the learner: selecting what matters, organising it, and connecting it to what they already know.

**The learner sees the slide only briefly.** Design either supports that work or gets in its way, which is why the audit sentence starts with the learner. "Looks professional" is a judgement made on a still slide, by someone who already knows the content and has as long as they like. The learner meets the slide for the first time, for a few seconds, while also listening to you. The three checks put you in that seat.

**What helps also changes with expertise.** Labels and step-by-step support that a newcomer needs can slow down someone who already knows the subject. So there is no single correct version of a slide, only a version for this group. There is more on [how small working memory is](t:1.1) and on [cutting the load that teaches nothing](t:1.2).

**The audit routine is craft, not research.** The three ideas and the point about expertise come from research. The thumbnail audit, the three-second look and the back-row test are craft: ways to apply the theory that nobody has tested as a routine. There is a cost to accept. A slide built for the room is a poor document to email afterwards, because the explanation was in your voice. Plan [a handout people will use](t:3.19) for that job.

try.text: Take a deck you will present in the next month and audit it on paper with the sentence from step 1. Then present three of its slides aloud to a colleague, who writes down the point of each one as you finish it. Good looks like this: their sentence matches yours for all three, and they can say where on each slide they were looking.

items: **The house template fights you** with a logo on every slide, a fixed title bar and small grey text. Change what you can, and ask the brand team for a plain layout for teaching slides.
**You highlight everything.** Three highlights on one slide select nothing. Keep to one at a time and build the rest.
**A deck built for new starters** goes to experienced people unchanged. What helps a newcomer may be redundant for an expert, so strip back the support they no longer need.
**The sponsor approved it** on a laptop, reading at their own pace. It can still fail in the room. Judge it while someone talks over it, and show the sponsor that version.

items.label: Mayer (2020), Multimedia Learning, 3rd edition. Cambridge University Press.
Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler and Sweller (2003), The expertise reversal effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1).

quiz.q: In multimedia learning theory, what are the two channels people use to take in a slide?
quiz.a: One for words and one for pictures. Each holds little at a time.

quiz.q: You are reviewing a slide with a process diagram, a paragraph and a stock photo. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep the diagram and highlight the step being discussed. Remove the photo. Say the paragraph aloud or move it to the handout, because neither helps the learner select, organise or connect.

quiz.q: A deck that works well for new starters is going to a room of experienced engineers. What do you check?
quiz.a: Whether the labels and step-by-step support are now redundant. What helps a newcomer can slow an expert, so show the whole and mark only what has changed.

topics.tierReason: The multimedia design principles rest on a large body of experiments, but their benefit depends on the learner's prior knowledge and most studies use short lessons.

topics.title: Cut what does not serve the point

situation.text: Slide 5 of the escalation deck has a flow diagram of seven boxes, a 90-word paragraph that repeats the diagram, and the logo. You hear yourself reading the paragraph aloud. The support team finished reading it ten seconds ago and are waiting for you to catch up.

items: **Write the point of the slide** in one sentence in your notes. Every element is now judged against that sentence.

**Go through the slide element by element** and ask: if I delete this, is the point harder to understand? If the answer is no, it goes. The usual candidates are the logo on every slide, the stock photo, decorative icons and background music on a video.

**Move the words you cut.** Full sentences go into your speaker notes, because you will say them. Detail people need later goes into the handout. Keep a list of what moved where, so you can show the sponsor that nothing was lost.
**Replace any sentence left on screen** with a label of two to five words or a key term. Do not narrate full sentences that are also on the screen, above all beside a diagram.

**Put each label on the picture**, on or right beside the part it describes, and delete the separate key. Reveal the label at the moment you talk about that part, so words and picture arrive together.
**Mark the one essential thing** with an arrow, a highlight or bold type. On the process slide, that is the new step.
**Find the interesting aside**: the cartoon, the history of the helpdesk, the joke slide. Ask whether anyone needs it to do the task. If not, cut it from the slides and from the handout.
**Leave captions and transcripts alone.** They are an access need and are not what these cuts are about.

why.text: **Extra text and decoration often hinder learning.** The four main principles have names you will meet in the research. Coherence means cutting what is off the point. Signalling means marking what matters. Redundancy means not narrating a full script that is also on screen. Contiguity means keeping words beside the picture they describe and showing them together. The instinct to add more text, more decoration and more "engaging" extras often gets in the way of learning. The same idea applies to [cutting load across a whole session](t:1.2).

**Irrelevant extras tend to lower learning.** Interesting but irrelevant material tends to lower what people learn. A 2020 meta-analysis of 58 studies found this on average, with more harm on paper than on screen. That is the evidence behind cutting the fun but pointless bits. For material that passes quickly, narration with graphics can beat on-screen text with graphics.

why.title: Keep it coherent: a meta-analysis of the seductive details effect
why.found: Across 58 studies with more than 7,500 students, people who learned with interesting but irrelevant extras scored lower than people who learned without them. The harm was greater on paper than on screen, and greater when the extra stayed in view beside a useful diagram.
why.means: Cut the joke, photo or music that does not serve the point, above all on handouts and beside diagrams.

why.text: **Reading out key terms can help.** The redundancy principle is narrower than "never read out what is on the screen". A meta-analysis of 57 studies found that narration with matching on-screen text beat narration alone, and did no worse than text alone. The benefit came when learners had little prior knowledge, when the material set the pace, when no pictures were present, and when the screen showed key terms and not the whole script. The harm is thought to come when a full script competes with a diagram for the eyes.

**Moving material makes cutting easier.** Cutting is hard because every item on the slide is true and cost someone effort. The author sees what is lost. The learner only pays, in attention, for what is left. Step 3 is the way through: moving material to the notes and the handout lets you clear the slide without arguing that the content is worthless. A [story or example that carries the point](t:4.4) is not an irrelevant extra. The principles and the two meta-analyses are research. The element-by-element test and the list of what moved are craft.

try.text: Take the most crowded slide you own and redesign it, naming the principle behind each change. Then present both versions aloud to a colleague, one minute each, and ask after each what the point was. Good looks like this: you never read from the new slide, and they give the point back in one sentence.

items: **Stakeholders ask for content** to be added back. Offer a handout, and show them your list of what moved where.
**A colleague objects to captions**, saying they break the redundancy principle. They do not. Captions and transcripts are an access need, so keep them.
**You teach principles as fixed laws.** These findings are averages and they come with conditions. Say "on average" and give the conditions.
**You lean on the findings** for a full day in a training room. Most studies of irrelevant extras used lessons of 6 to 12 minutes, and less is known about longer sessions.
**The emailed deck makes no sense** without you. That is the right result for the room. Send the handout, not the slides.

Sundararajan and Adesope (2020), Keep it coherent: a meta-analysis of the seductive details effect. Educational Psychology Review, 32(3). Washington State University's summary of the paper.

quiz.q: What does research find about interesting but irrelevant extras?
quiz.a: On average they lower what people learn. A 2020 meta-analysis of 58 studies found this, with more harm on paper than on screen.

quiz.q: A stakeholder asks you to put the full paragraph back on the slide beside the diagram. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep the diagram with short labels, explain it in speech, and offer the paragraph as a handout. Full sentences beside a diagram compete with it for the eyes.

quiz.q: A colleague says the captions on your video break the redundancy principle and should come off. What do you say?
quiz.a: Keep them. Captions and transcripts are an access need. The redundancy problem is a full script on screen competing with a diagram while you narrate.

topics.tierReason: Cutting irrelevant material, cueing and avoiding read-aloud text are backed by many experiments and a meta-analysis, but the effects vary with format, subject and learner, and most studies use lessons of a few minutes.

topics.title: Make charts honest and quick to read

situation.text: Slide 4 of the escalation deck is headed "Escalation data". It is a 3D bar chart of six support teams in six colours, with the axis starting at 80. Team A's bar stands four times taller than Team F's. The figures behind them are 92 and 83 out of 100, and someone from Team F will be in the room.

items: **Write the one sentence** the chart has to show, before you open the charting tool. "Half of bounced escalations are missing the account number" is a sentence. "Escalation data" is a label. If you cannot write the sentence, you do not need a chart.
**Pick the form from the comparison.** As a working rule, use bars to compare amounts, a line for change over time, and a table when people need exact figures.
**Start every bar chart at zero.** A line chart may start somewhere else, but say so on the axis. Label both axes, with units.
**Take off whatever carries no information**: the 3D effect, shadows, the background fill, heavy gridlines, the border.

**Make every bar mid-grey**, then give the one bar that matters a dark shade. Write the category and the value on or beside each bar and delete the legend. Sort the bars from largest to smallest unless the order means something, as months do.
**Check it without colour.** Print it in black and white. If the meaning has gone, add direct labels or vary the line style. Check the contrast of the text against its background.
**Say under the chart what was counted**, over what period and how many: "50 escalations returned to the sender, March". A percentage with no count behind it cannot be judged.
**Show the chart to someone** for five seconds and ask what it says. If their sentence is not your sentence from step 1, change the chart.

why.text: A visual should make the point faster and more truthfully than words. If it does not, it is decoration.

**Drawing choices can make data mislead.** The same data can mislead or clarify, depending on how it is drawn. A cut-off axis makes a small difference look large. A 3D effect distorts the size of the bars, and six colours leave the reader hunting for the one that matters.

**A bar makes its claim through length.** The reasoning behind the zero rule is that a bar makes its claim through length. Cut the axis and the lengths no longer match the numbers, whatever the labels say. A line makes its claim through direction, which is why it can start elsewhere if the axis says so. An honest redraw sometimes takes your point away. If the gap between teams almost vanishes once the bars start at zero, the gap was small, and that is what the data says. In the worked example the team comparison is dropped for that reason and a different chart takes its place.

**Zero can flatten a change that matters.** There is a trade-off. Starting at zero can flatten a small change that does matter, such as a two-point shift in a rate the business watches closely. Then put the number in the headline, or use a line with a clearly labelled axis, or give a table. This page is convention and craft. The one source on it supports checking colour contrast.

try.text: Find a chart in a deck you will use, or in a report a client has sent you, and redraw it with the eight steps. Show both versions to a colleague for five seconds each and ask them to say aloud what each one claims. Good looks like this: for the new one they give your sentence without prompting, and they can tell you what was counted.

**Colour alone carries the meaning**, and some people cannot tell the colours apart. Check contrast, and add labels where colour carries meaning.
**It reads only on your laptop**, and not from the back row or on a phone. Design for both. There are [minimum sizes for projected slides](t:3.22).

quiz.q: Where should the axis of a bar chart start?
quiz.a: At zero. Label any other scale clearly.

quiz.q: You inherit a 3D bar chart in six colours with the axis starting at 80. What do you do?
quiz.a: Redraw it as flat bars from zero, in grey, with the one bar that matters in a dark shade and labelled directly. If the difference disappears when drawn from zero, it was small, so check the chart still has a point.

quiz.q: Your chart uses a red line and a green line for two teams. What do you change?
quiz.a: Label each line directly, or vary the line style, so the meaning does not depend on colour alone. Some people cannot tell the colours apart.

topics.title: Put the claim in the headline and the evidence below

situation.text: The escalation deck has slides headed "Background", "Escalation data", "New process" and "Summary", most with five bullets underneath. After the last briefing you asked three people what the main message was and got three different answers. Each of them had built a point out of the bullets, and none was the one the product lead intended.

items: **Take each slide and say its point** aloud: "The point of this slide is that...". Write down the words that follow. That sentence is the headline. Two points means two slides. No point means the slide goes.

**Edit the headline into a full sentence** with a verb, until it fits on two lines at the [type size for projected slides](t:3.22). Put it top left. "New process" becomes "The new route adds one step: fill in three fields before you escalate".

**Delete the bullets and show the evidence** for that sentence underneath: a chart, a screenshot, a diagram, a photo of the real thing, a customer's words. Use a picture where you can. Where the evidence is words, keep it to a few short lines.
**Move what the bullets said** into your speaker notes. You will say it.
**Read only the headlines aloud, in order.** They should sound like a short argument a colleague could follow with their eyes shut. Where it jumps, a slide is missing or in the wrong place.
**Give the run a shape**: the situation, what makes it a problem, and what resolves it. For a training deck, add a slide that sets up the learners' practice.
**Cut every slide that stalls the argument.** The agenda becomes one spoken sentence. The summary becomes a last slide that states what you are asking people to do, and it stays up during questions.

why.text: **A sentence headline does the audience's work.** A topic label over bullets asks the audience to assemble the meaning. A sentence headline does that work for them and leaves room for evidence. It also does something for you. Writing the claim forces you to have one, and many label-and-bullet slides exist because the author had not yet decided what they were saying.

**People tend to follow a story better.** People tend to follow and remember a narrative more easily than a list of points. You can read about [telling a story in the room](t:4.4). Experts often structure explanations badly because they have forgotten what it was like not to know. There is more on [the steps experts no longer notice](t:3.17).

**One study backs the whole approach.** The best-known test compared two versions of one technical talk with 110 engineering students. The claim-and-evidence slides led to better understanding, fewer misconceptions and better recall later. The comparison slides broke several design principles at once, so the study supports the whole approach. It does not show how much the headline alone adds.

why.title: How slide design affects audience comprehension
why.found: 110 engineering students saw the same technical talk with one of two slide sets. Those who saw claim-and-evidence slides understood more, held fewer misconceptions, reported less mental effort and recalled more at a later test than those who saw default topic-and-bullet slides.
why.means: Rewrite topic labels as short claim sentences and replace bullets with the evidence, shown as a picture where you can.

why.text: **A claim can be wrong or disputed.** There is a price. A claim can be wrong, and a sponsor can disagree with it, where nobody argues with "Background". Better to find that out when you send the headlines for review than in the room. The approach reverses in two cases. Reference material is for looking things up, so leave it as labelled tables that are easy to scan. And when you want the group to reach the conclusion themselves, put the question in the headline and give the claim after they have answered. The study is research on the whole approach. The headline test and the two reversals are craft.

try.text: Take a run of five topic-and-bullet slides from a deck you own and convert them. Then stand up and say only the headlines to a colleague, in order, in under a minute, and ask them to tell you the argument back. Good looks like this: they can, and they name what you want people to do at the end.

quiz.q: Your slide is headed "Customer complaints" and has five bullets. How do you rebuild it?

parts.title: Choose the medium
parts.summary: Picking and combining media from the objective, not from fashion.

topics.title: Pick the medium after the objective

situation.text: The email from a retailer's operations director reads: "We want a ten-minute video on handling angry customers, for all 400 store staff, by March." The budget line already says video. Nobody has yet said what a member of staff should do differently at the till.

items: **Do not argue with the video.** Reply with one question: "When this has worked, what will someone at the till do that they don't do now?" Turn the answer into [an objective you could observe](t:2.11).

**Name what that objective needs.** The common answers are practice with feedback, discussion, or reference at the moment of use. Handling an angry customer needs practice with feedback. Knowing the refund limits needs reference.

**Write the constraints as numbers**: how many people, how many sites, which devices and what bandwidth they have on shift, any access needs, the budget, the date, how often the content will change and who will update it.
**Weigh live against self-paced.** Live gives discussion and feedback on the spot. Self-paced lets people choose the time and the speed. Ask which of those the objective cannot do without.
**Shortlist two options** that meet the need inside the constraints. For each, estimate the cost to make, the cost to run per person, and the cost to update each time the content changes.
**Choose, and record each option you rejected**: write one line on each and why. The client will ask.

**Take it back in the client's terms**, and keep their medium where it earns a place: "A three-minute video to show one good conversation, then 30 minutes of paired practice run by each store manager, with a checklist."
**Do not judge it on the pilot** if the medium is new to the organisation. Look at the second or third group, once it has stopped being a novelty.

why.text: **Choosing the medium first bends the objective.** Each medium has real strengths, and the objective should decide between them. When the medium is chosen first, the objective gets bent to fit it, and that is expensive to undo. A ten-minute video can show what a calm reply sounds like. It cannot hear the learner try one.

**A named medium usually hides a real need.** Clients name a medium because it is the part they can picture and buy. Behind "a video" there is usually a real need: reach 400 people, say the same thing to all of them, and do it without closing stores. Treat that need as a constraint and you can honour it while changing the medium. That is why step 1 is a question and step 7 keeps some video in the answer.
**Novelty often inflates early results.** A new medium often shows inflated results that fade once the novelty wears off. That misleads buying decisions, and it is the reason for step 8.

**Fixed constraints pick the medium first.** The order reverses when a constraint is truly fixed. If there is no paid time off the shop floor and no manager free to run practice, the constraints pick the medium first. Then narrow the objective to what that medium can do, and tell the client plainly what it will not achieve. The sequence on this page is craft. There is more on [the research argument about media and method](t:3.7) and on [immersive technology](t:3.10).

try.text: Take three objectives from your current work. For each, name what it needs, choose a medium, and write one line on each alternative you rejected. Then say your recommendation for one of them aloud, in under a minute, to a colleague playing the client who wants the video. Good looks like this: you ask the till question first, and the client's own medium still has a job in your answer.

quiz.q: A brief arrives as "we want a video" on handling angry callers. What do you do?
quiz.a: Go back to the objective. Handling a caller needs practice and feedback, so propose paired role-play with a short checklist. Keep video for modelling one good call.

quiz.q: A supplier recommends its own app for a course whose content changes every month. What do you check?
quiz.a: What the objective needs, what each update will cost, how many people will use it and who can access it. Cheap to make can be dear to maintain.

topics.tierReason: Choosing the medium from the objective is standard design practice backed by argument and by media comparison research, not a method tested directly.

topics.title: Blend on purpose, and keep microlearning for what it suits

situation.text: A one-day product course for a software company's sales team runs from 09:30 to 16:30. Slides on features fill the morning, and practice on customer cases gets 40 minutes at four o'clock. Then the head of sales forwards an article and suggests replacing the whole day with five-minute clips.

items: **List every block of the current course** with its minutes. Mark each one T for telling or P for practice, discussion and feedback. Add up the two columns.

**Move the telling into pre-work**, and cap it. Thirty to forty-five minutes in total is a workable limit, split into two or three pieces. If the content will not fit, cut content. Do not lengthen the pre-work.
**Build in a check**: a five-question quiz due the day before, and one thing to bring, such as a live account. Say how both will be used: "We start at 09:30 with your account. There is no recap."
**Open the live session with a task** that needs the pre-work, inside the first fifteen minutes. Pair people who did it with people who did not. Do not re-teach it.
**Spend the live time on practice**, discussion and feedback. There is more on [doing this in online sessions](t:4.10).

**Add short units after the event** for two jobs only: reminders, and help at the point of use. Give each a single job and a first line that says where it fits in the whole. Time the first one to the first real use of the skill, when you [schedule the follow-up](t:5.4).
**Give complex, joined-up skills a longer format.** The test is whether the parts happen together in the real job. In a negotiation they do. In a list of product codes they do not.
**Write one line for each part** saying what it is for. A part with no job comes out.

why.text: **Flipping only pays if live time changes.** Blending means each mode does what it does best. Flipping moves content before the session so the scarce live time is used for interaction. The logic is that any gain comes from what you do with the time you free. Move the reading out and lecture anyway, and you have only made the course longer.

**Expect a modest gain from flipping.** A 2019 meta-analysis found flipped classes beat lecture-based teaching by a small margin, and by less in the larger studies. Checking the pre-work, for example with a short quiz, may add a little.

why.title: Does the flipped classroom improve learning and satisfaction?
why.found: Pooling 272 comparisons of flipped and lecture-based teaching, learning was a little better in flipped classes (Hedges' g = 0.35). In the 90 adequately powered studies the gain was smaller (g = 0.24). Satisfaction rose only slightly, and the authors suspect publication bias.
why.means: Flip to free live time for practice, check the pre-work was done, and promise a modest gain.

why.text: **Short units suit reinforcement and performance support.** They are a doubtful fit for complex skills, because the parts of a complex skill have to be practised together. That limit is a design judgement more than a research finding. For microlearning, a 2025 review of 40 studies reports mostly positive results for knowledge, engagement and satisfaction. How strong those studies were is not clear, so treat the support as early.

**Flipping moves time into the learner's diary.** Flipping has a cost that is easy to miss. It moves time out of the course and into the learner's own diary. Ask [their manager to protect it](t:2.4). If people have no paid time to prepare, as with many shop-floor staff, do not flip. Put fifteen minutes of quiet reading at the start of the session. The cap on pre-work, the opening task and the no-recap rule are craft.

try.text: Take a single-mode course you know. Do the T and P count, redesign it as a blend, and write the one-line job for each part. Then read your pre-work message aloud to a colleague and ask what they think happens if they skip it. Good looks like this: most of the live time is marked P, and their answer is "I'd be lost in the first task".

quiz.a: A small one (g = 0.35), and smaller still in the larger studies (g = 0.24).

quiz.q: You open a flipped session and half the room has not done the pre-reading. What do you do?
quiz.a: Run the planned task that uses it, and pair people who read it with people who did not. If you re-teach it, nobody will do the pre-work next time. This is craft advice.

quiz.q: A manager proposes turning a negotiation skills course into five-minute clips. What do you say?
quiz.a: Use clips for reminders and for help at the point of use. Keep the skill itself in a longer format, because its parts have to be practised together.

topics.tierReason: Flipping shows a small average gain that shrinks in the better-powered studies, and the microlearning research is recent and of uncertain quality.

topics.title: Buy a medium for the method it makes possible

situation.text: A supplier is demonstrating a fire-safety app to a retailer's learning manager. It has a leaderboard, an animated mascot and a slide saying it "improves learning outcomes". The manager turns to you, in front of the supplier, and asks what you think.

items: **Write down the objective and the methods** it needs, before any demo. For fire safety that might be a demonstration, hands-on practice with an extinguisher, and recall spread over the following weeks.
**Ask one question in the demo:** "What does this let our people do that a workshop, a video or a printed card can't?" Write the answers down as verbs: rehearse, get reminded, be tested.
**Sort each feature into method or wrapper.** Practice, feedback, spacing and simulation are methods. Graphics, points, mascots and newness are wrappers.
**Ask whether a cheaper medium could carry** each method. If one could, get both prices.

**Question any evidence the supplier shows.** Ask: "Compared with what? Did both groups get the same teaching method?" If the app group had spaced quizzes and the classroom group had none, the result is about the quizzes.
**Buy for the method** and write it into the order: "Bought for spaced quiz reminders on staff phones." That sentence is what you review the purchase against next year.
**Design the method well inside the medium**: which questions, how often, what feedback. Keep live whatever the medium cannot do, such as handling a real extinguisher.
**Ignore what was spent last year.** Headsets bought then are not a reason to use them now.

why.text: **A medium does not teach by itself.** One side of a long debate, argued by Richard Clark, holds that media are vehicles: they deliver instruction and do not cause learning. The method teaches. The other side, argued by Robert Kozma, replies that a medium's capabilities can make methods possible that would otherwise be impractical. So do not expect a medium to teach by itself.

**Many studies comparing media find no difference.** That usually means the method mattered, not the medium. It is also useful news for a buyer. If two media carry the same method equally well, you are free to choose between them on cost, access and upkeep.

**The two sides give you two questions.** Clark's tells you where to look: at what the learner does. Kozma's tells you what is worth paying for: a method you could not otherwise run. Sending a recall question to 400 phones on a schedule is hard to do with a workshop. That is a real capability and it is the thing to buy. The mascot is not.

**The method-first rule has a limit.** A good method in a poor medium still suffers: practice on an app that crashes, or feedback on a screen too small to read. Once the method is settled, the quality of the medium matters again. The debate is a scholarly argument, and the finding of no difference comes from research. The sorting and the questions are craft. The same test applies to [virtual reality](t:3.10) and to [adaptive tools](t:7.2). There is more on [the wider choice of medium](t:3.5).

try.text: Take a real proposal or product page for a learning tool and sort its features into methods and wrappers. Then ask a colleague to play the supplier, and put the two questions from steps 2 and 5 to them aloud. Good looks like this: you finish with one sentence that starts "We would buy this for...", or with a clear reason not to buy.

**A poor medium:** a good method in it still suffers. Try the tool on the devices and the connection staff really have.

**Nobody designs the method** after you buy for it. An app full of weak questions carries a weak method, so budget time for the content.

quiz.q: What were Clark's and Kozma's positions?
quiz.a: Clark: the method teaches and the medium only carries it. Kozma: a medium's capabilities can make methods possible that would otherwise be impractical.

quiz.q: A supplier says its app will improve fire-safety learning. What do you ask?
quiz.a: What it lets people do that a workshop cannot. Buy it for that method, such as spaced quiz reminders on a phone, and keep the extinguisher practice live.

quiz.q: A study finds no difference in results between the online and classroom versions of a course. What do you conclude?
quiz.a: That the method probably mattered more than the medium. Choose between them on cost, access and which methods each makes possible.

topics.tierReason: This is a reasoned position taken from a long-running academic debate. It guides buying decisions but has not been tested as a practice.

topics.title: Offer print or self-pacing for dense reading
topics.theory: Screen versus paper, reading versus listening, handwriting versus typing

situation.text: A client's compliance lead wants a forty-page policy read on screen in a timed 45-minute session. She also wants laptops banned from the room, because "handwriting is better for memory". One of the twelve managers attending uses a screen reader.

items: **Sort the reading.** Dense informational text, such as a policy, a specification or a contract, is where the medium makes a small difference. A story or a case narrative is not.
**Send dense text ahead** as an accessible PDF, at least three working days before. Offer print in the same message: "Reply by Thursday if you'd like a printed copy."
**Time yourself reading it** and tell people how long to allow. Let them read at their own pace, in their own time.
**Take timed reading out of the session.** Use the time for three scenario questions that people answer with the policy open in front of them.
**Put paper copies on the tables** if the reading has to happen in the room, as well as sharing the file, and let people finish. Do not put a countdown on the screen.
**Give a transcript as a choice** with audio and video. Do not ask people to follow the text while the audio plays.
**Let people take notes their way**, by pen or keyboard, as they prefer. If the worry is email, set a rule about [what screens are used for](t:4.39). Do not ban screens outright.
**Answer the handwriting claim with the finding** and its conditions when a client quotes it, and do not teach the claim as fact yourself. The worked example gives wording.

why.text: **Paper has a small edge over screens.** Reading comprehension can be slightly worse on screen than on paper. One meta-analysis of 54 studies found a small advantage for paper (g = -0.21 for screens against paper). The gap was larger when reading time was limited than when people set their own pace. It showed for informational text, and not for stories alone. It also grew over the years studied, so do not assume that familiarity with screens removes it.

why.title: Paper against screens: a meta-analysis of 54 studies
why.found: Across 54 studies, people understood text slightly better on paper than on screen (g = -0.21 for screens against paper). The gap was larger under time limits than with self-paced reading, and it showed for informational text but not for stories alone.
why.means: For dense reading, offer print or let people read in their own time, and do not treat the difference as large.

why.text: **The handwriting claim has not held up.** The well-known claim that handwriting beats typing for memory has not held up. Two direct repeats of the original study found no consistent difference in test scores between people who wrote by hand and people who typed. The original explanation, that typing leads to word-for-word copying which harms learning, was not reliable in the repeat either. The fair summary is that neither tool has been shown to be better.

**Listening while reading adds very little.** Adding audio to text helps less than you might expect. A review of 30 studies found only a very small overall benefit from listening while reading (g = 0.18 against reading alone), and no reliable benefit when people read at their own pace. Offer the transcript as a choice, not as something to follow alongside the audio.

**Small effects do not justify a ban.** What the three findings share is size. Each effect is small or absent, and each depends on conditions. A ban is a large act with a certain cost: to the person with a screen reader, to the fast typist, to the person who cannot read their own handwriting. Set a small and uncertain gain against that and the ban does not pay. Self-pacing is different. It costs you nothing, the paper gap was smaller with it, and it is in your hands. That is why the steps take reading out of timed sessions before they say anything about paper. The figures are research. Offering both formats, the three working days and the open-policy questions are craft.

try.text: Take three "medium X is better" claims you have heard, including the handwriting one. For each, state the size of the effect and when it holds. Then say your reply to the laptop ban aloud to a colleague playing the client. Good looks like this: in under a minute you give the finding, its conditions and what you will do, and you do not tell the client she is wrong.

**Print has an access cost** for some learners, including anyone who uses a screen reader or needs to enlarge text. Always send the accessible file as well.
**You quote one of these findings** as a headline. Give its conditions too: how small it is, what kind of text, and whether time was limited.
**You swap one ban for another** and insist on print. The paper advantage is small and does not justify a rule.

quiz.a: No consistent difference in test scores. Neither tool has been shown to be better.

quiz.q: A client wants a forty-page policy read on screen in a timed session. What do you offer?
quiz.a: A printed copy or a PDF to read beforehand at each person's own pace, with the session used to apply it. The paper advantage is small, and it is largest when reading time is limited.

quiz.q: A client wants to ban laptops because "handwriting is better for memory". What do you say?
quiz.a: That the claim did not hold up when the study was repeated. Let people choose pen or keyboard.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis of 54 studies found a small advantage for paper that depends on time pressure and the kind of text, and the handwriting claim has not held up in direct repeats.

topics.title: Design the handoffs between media

situation.text: A programme for twelve new managers has a twelve-minute video, a half-day workshop and a quiz a week later, made by three different people. The video teaches "the four steps", the workshop slides call them "the feedback model", and the quiz asks about "stages". At the workshop, four people have not watched the video, because nothing told them they would need it.

items: **Draw the programme as a row** of boxes, one per piece, and number the gaps between them. The gaps are what you are designing.
**Choose a pattern** and write it above the row: content then live, live wrapped by self-paced work, or short units spread over time.
**Write the last twenty seconds** of the piece before each gap. Say what to do next, by when, and why now: "In the workshop you will use these four steps on your own case, so bring one."
**Then write the first ten minutes** of the piece after it, so that it uses what the last piece produced. The workshop opens by asking for those cases.
**Give every piece something to carry forward**: a case, a score, a draft, a question. If nothing travels across a gap, the two pieces are not joined.

**Make a one-page glossary** with the terms, the names of the steps, and the running case and its characters. Every author works from it. Check that difficulty rises from piece to piece and does not jump.
**Check nothing is left with no link** to the rest. For each piece, ask which later piece uses it and which earlier piece it uses. A piece with no answer to either gets a link or gets cut.
**Name one person who owns the joins.** Before launch they go through the whole programme in order, as a learner would.

why.text: **Learners should experience one programme.** If the pieces do not refer to each other, they experience a pile of separate assets, however good each one is.

**Blends tend to break at the handoff.** In practice the handoff is a common place for a blend to break: instructions are missing, or the next piece does not use the last. The likely reason is ownership. Each author is briefed on a piece and judged on that piece, so the gaps belong to nobody. A handoff takes minutes to write, but only once someone has the job.

**A deadline alone is easy to ignore.** The "why now" matters most for self-paced pieces, which compete with the working day. "Watch this before Thursday" is easy to put off. "Bring one case, because you will work on it in the first ten minutes" gives a reason and a consequence.

**Research says little about handoffs.** Research on blended design is thin on this point. A 2017 review of 20 studies names four design challenges: building in flexibility, getting people to interact, supporting how they learn, and creating a good climate for learning. It does not test handoffs as such, so treat this page as practitioner advice. You can map the whole route [from first email to follow-up](t:2.17). This topic covers the joins between the teaching pieces.

try.text: Take a blended programme you run or have attended. Write the handoff for each gap: the closing words and the opening move. Then read the handoffs aloud, in order, to a colleague who has not seen the programme, and ask what they would do after each one. Good looks like this: every time, they can tell you the next action and the reason for it.

The wrong answers

try.title: A worked example: the one-page glossary every author works from
lines: The four steps: 1 Describe what you saw. 2 Say the effect. 3 Ask for their view. 4 Agree the change.
Always "the four steps". Never "model", "stages" or "framework".
The person receiving feedback is "your team member". Not "the employee" and not "the report".
Running case: Priya, a new team lead, and Tom, who has missed two deadlines.
The video uses Priya and Tom. The workshop demonstration continues their story. The quiz uses a new case of the same kind.
Difficulty: the video shows a cooperative Tom. Workshop round 2 has a defensive one. The quiz includes one borderline case.

items: **An unconnected quiz** follows a great video, and it teaches little. Make the quiz use the video's case and its words.
**Different authors drift in terms.** Keep the glossary, and check each piece against it before sign-off.
**The handoff lives only in email**, and emails go unread. Put it in the last twenty seconds of the piece as well.
**One piece gets replaced** and the joins on both sides break. When anything changes, re-read the handoff before it and the one after.
**Measuring across media is harder**, so plan it early. There is more on [deciding what to measure](t:6.1).

items.label: Boelens, De Wever and Voet (2017), Four key challenges to the design of blended learning: a systematic literature review. Educational Research Review, 22.

quiz.q: Name the three patterns for combining media.
quiz.a: Content then live, live wrapped by self-paced work, and short units spread over time.

quiz.q: Your programme has a video, a workshop and a quiz made by three different people. Learners say the parts feel unrelated. What do you do?
quiz.a: Write the handoff between each pair: what to do next, and why now. Make the workshop use what the video taught, and agree one glossary so the terms match.

quiz.q: You are scripting the last twenty seconds of a pre-workshop video. What goes in them?
quiz.a: The handoff. For example: "In the workshop you will use these four steps on your own case, so bring one."

topics.tierReason: Writing handoffs between media is sound professional practice, but no study read tests it directly.

topics.title: Use immersive technology for what it does best

situation.text: A warehouse client bought twelve headsets for an open day last year, and they have sat in a cupboard since. The operations director now wants "something in VR" in the new-starter programme. The first idea in the meeting is a virtual tour of head office.

items: **Put each task through one test.** List the tasks in the programme and ask of each: is real practice dangerous, rare, costly or impossible to stage? A racking unit starting to fail passes. A tour of head office does not.
**Say so if nothing passes**, and recommend a simpler method with the two costs side by side. There is more on [choosing a medium](t:3.5).
**Design the method before the scenery** for a task that passes: what the person has to notice, the decisions they make, and the feedback they get on each.
**Keep each headset session short.** Around ten minutes is a working rule, not a research figure.
**Brief people for three minutes first**: what they will see, how the controls work, and "Take it off at any point if you feel unwell. You don't need to ask."
**Debrief for ten minutes straight afterwards**, out of the headset: what did you notice first, what did you do, what will you do on shift. There is more on [debriefing an activity](t:4.28).
**Offer an alternative to everyone** at the start, such as the same scenario seated with a tablet. Do not wait for someone to ask. They join the same debrief.
**Test what people can do afterwards** as well as whether they enjoyed it, and compare the cost with the simpler method you could have used.

why.text: **It suits what you cannot practise for real.** Immersive technology earns its place where real practice is unsafe or impractical: emergencies, heights, costly equipment, difficult conversations. It lets people rehearse in a setting close to the real one.

**The measured gains are modest.** A meta-analysis of 48 studies in schools and universities found a small overall advantage for immersive virtual reality over computer-based or traditional resources (g = 0.38). The size of the gain depended on what it was compared with. A meta-analysis of workplace training found that virtual reality did better than the alternatives it was tested against, and that the fit between the task and the technology mattered while the type of headset or controller did not.

why.title: More presence, less learning
why.found: Fifty-two students learned from the same science simulation on a desktop or in a headset. Those in the headset reported much more presence but learned less (d = 0.80 in favour of the desktop), and brain-activity measures suggested higher cognitive load.
why.means: Do not assume that a more immersive version teaches better, and test learning as well as enjoyment.

why.text: **More immersion can mean less learning.** In one experiment, students felt more present in a headset and learned less than on a desktop. That is a single experiment, so hold it as a warning. The practical point is that feeling present is easy to mistake for learning. People come out of a headset impressed, which is why step 8 asks you to test what they can do.

**The headset is still only a medium.** There is an explanation of why [the method inside it does the teaching](t:3.7), and that is why step 3 comes before any talk of graphics. The brief and the debrief carry much of the method. Without them a scenario is an experience, and nobody has said what to take from it. The fit test in step 1 matches what the workplace meta-analysis found about task and technology. The session length, the timings of the brief and debrief, and the offer of an alternative are craft.

try.text: List three skills in your field that cannot be practised safely for real. For each, say whether immersion would add anything a role-play could not. Then deliver the three-minute brief aloud to a colleague, including how to stop. Good looks like this: afterwards they could tell someone else what they will see, how the controls work and how to opt out.

items: **Some people feel sick in headsets.** Say so in the brief, keep sessions short and have the alternative ready.
**Novelty inflates early results**, as with [any medium new to an organisation](t:3.5). Judge the scenario on a later group.
**Content dates** and is costly to update. Ask what a change to the scenario costs before you commission it.
**More immersion can mean less learning.** In one experiment, students felt more present in a headset and learned less than on a desktop. Test what people can do.
**The headsets are already bought**, so someone insists they are used. [Money spent is not a reason](t:3.7).

items.label: Coban, Bolat and Goksu (2022), The potential of immersive virtual reality to enhance learning: a meta-analysis. Educational Research Review, 36.
Howard, Gutworth and Jacobs (2021), A meta-analysis of virtual reality training programs. Computers in Human Behavior, 121.
Makransky, Terkildsen and Mayer (2019), Adding immersive virtual reality to a science lab simulation causes more presence but less learning. Learning and Instruction, 60.

quiz.q: What did the 2019 experiment comparing a headset with a desktop find?
quiz.a: Students in the headset reported much more presence and learned less than those on the desktop.

quiz.q: A client has bought headsets and wants "something in VR" for a course on writing clear emails. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask what must be practised that is dangerous, rare, costly or impossible to stage. Nothing here is, so recommend a simpler method and show the cost comparison. Keep the headsets for a task that fits.

quiz.q: Two people in the group cannot wear a headset. What do you do?
quiz.a: Give them the alternative you planned, such as a seated tablet version, and include them in the same debrief.

topics.tierReason: Meta-analyses find a small average gain from immersive virtual reality that varies with what it is compared with, and single studies show it can also reduce learning.

parts.title: Build video, audio and e-learning
parts.summary: Storyboards, production, interactivity and tracking.

topics.title: Storyboard before you produce anything

situation.text: You have spent a day recording a six-minute screen walkthrough of the new returns process for a retailer's store staff. In the edit you find that the till screen appears before anyone has said what a return code is. Then the subject expert watches it and asks for a step to be added in the middle. Every fix means recording again.

items: **Write the viewer and the objective** at the top of a page: "After this, a new store assistant can process a return without a receipt." One piece has one objective. If you have written two, make two storyboards.
**List the points in a beginner's order**, as five to eight plain sentences. Each sentence becomes one frame, or two at most. Check that no sentence uses a term an earlier one has not introduced.

**Draw a table with four columns**: picture, words spoken, on-screen text, interaction. Fill one row per frame. For the picture, a stick figure or a note such as "till screen, Refund button circled" is enough.
**Write the narration to be spoken.** Use "you", short sentences and the words staff use on the shop floor. Read every line aloud and rewrite any line you stumble over.

**Check each row across.** The picture should show what the words are saying at that moment, and the on-screen text should be a few key words, not the narration again. There is a list of [the tests to apply](t:3.2).
**Time it.** Read the whole narration aloud against a timer and write the running time beside each frame.

**Make a rough version.** Put a photo or screenshot of each frame into slides and record the narration on your phone. Show it to one person who does not know the subject, without explaining anything. Ask them to tell you back what to do, and note where they hesitate.

**Send the storyboard and the rough version** to the subject expert and the sponsor with a reply date and three questions: "Is anything wrong? Is anything missing that a beginner needs? What can come out?" Record nothing until you have a written yes from both.

why.text: **Changes cost least on paper.** Changes are cheap on paper and expensive in the edit. Moving a frame on a storyboard takes a minute. Moving it after recording means new narration, new screen captures and a new edit. The storyboard is where you decide what is on screen, what is said and what is cut.

**An expert's raw material is not a script.** It is organised the way the expert thinks about the subject, and it has to be reorganised for someone who does not know it. There is more on getting [the missing steps out of the expert](t:3.17).

**The four-column method itself is untested.** The tests you apply to each frame come from research on learning from words and pictures: [the underlying theory](t:3.1) and [the design principles drawn from it](t:3.2). The method on this page is production craft. Nobody has tested the four columns or the rough version against another way of working.

**A storyboard moves the argument earlier.** Most sponsors cannot judge a script, and nearly everyone can react to pictures with words beside them. A storyboard moves the argument about content to the point where it costs least. The trade-off is half a day of planning when you would prefer to be recording. For a thirty-second clip, a list of points and one read-aloud will do. The advice reverses when you are filming an expert at work in order to study what they do. Record first, then storyboard the teaching version from what you saw.

try.text: Take a two-minute teaching segment from real work and storyboard it in the four columns. Then stand up and read the narration aloud to a colleague while they follow the picture column with a finger. Good looks like this: it runs within ten seconds of two minutes, you did not stumble, and your colleague can say what the viewer should be able to do afterwards.

try.title: What the read-aloud caught
try.text: In the first draft, the till screen came second and the return code third. A colleague from another department stopped at "type the return code" and asked what that was. The two frames were swapped on paper in under a minute, before anything was recorded.

items: **Nobody reviews the storyboard.** It then saves nothing, because the expert's corrections arrive after filming. Get it agreed by the subject expert and the sponsor before you record, with a date for replies.
**You storyboard only the main path** of a piece that branches. Give every branch its own rows, including the feedback the learner sees after a wrong choice.
**The narration sounds stiff** though it reads well. That is written English. Read the script aloud before recording, and replace any phrase you would not say to a colleague across a counter.
**The storyboard is drawn too well.** People then comment on the drawing, and you become reluctant to change it. Keep it rough enough that throwing a frame away costs nothing.
**The expert adds content** during the review. For each addition, ask which frame it replaces and whether a beginner needs it to meet the objective at the top of the page.

items.label: Mayer (2020), Multimedia Learning, 3rd edition. Cambridge University Press.
Clark and Mayer (2023), e-Learning and the Science of Instruction, 5th edition. Wiley.

quiz.q: What goes in each frame of a storyboard?
quiz.a: The picture, the words to be spoken, any on-screen text and any interaction.

quiz.q: You read your storyboard aloud to a colleague. They point out that frame four uses a term frame two has not yet introduced. What do you do?
quiz.a: Swap the frames on paper and read it through again. Catching this before recording is what the storyboard is for.

quiz.q: The sponsor wants to skip the storyboard and "fix it in the edit" to save time. What do you say?
quiz.a: That changes are cheap on paper and expensive in the edit. Offer a rough version, still frames with narration recorded on a phone, that they can review before anything is filmed.

topics.tierReason: Storyboarding and rough versions are standard production practice with little direct testing. Only the conversational narration point has a research base.

topics.title: Get the sound right and keep videos short

situation.text: A software company sends you the recording of its forty-minute onboarding session for new customer-support staff. It was filmed on two cameras in a glass-walled meeting room and the picture is sharp. The presenter's voice bounces off the glass, and the one thing new starters ask about most, how to escalate a ticket, is at minute 27.

items: **List the questions the video must answer**, one per line, in the learner's words: "How do I escalate a ticket?" Each question becomes its own video. A forty-minute session usually holds five to seven.

**Choose the room for its sound.** Pick a small room with carpet, curtains and soft chairs. Avoid glass walls and bare meeting rooms. Close the door, turn off the air conditioning if you can, and silence phones.

**Put the microphone close.** Clip one to the speaker's clothing about a hand's width below the chin, or stand a desk microphone a hand span from the mouth. A laptop microphone across the table is the usual cause of echo.
**Record twenty seconds and listen back** on headphones before you record the rest. Listen for echo, hum and rustling clothes. Fix what you hear and test again.
**Record each video on one point.** Say the question in the first ten seconds and stop when it is answered. Six minutes or less is a common working guide.

**Show the screen, object or task** for most of the running time. Put the presenter on camera only where a person adds something, such as a demonstration with their hands or a difficult conversation being modelled.
**Watch each video with its question** in front of you and cut what does not serve it: the welcome, the agenda, the story about last year's conference.
**Publish them as separate files**, each titled with its question, so people can pause, replay and skip to the one they need. Add [captions and a transcript](t:3.15) to each.

why.text: **The sound advice comes from experience.** Poor sound makes a video hard to follow, however good the pictures. That claim is production experience, not a research finding. The studies behind this page do not test audio quality. The reasoning is simple enough: in most teaching video the words carry the content, so a viewer who is straining to hear has little attention left for it.

**Short parts ease the load on memory.** A long video in one piece also overloads working memory. Breaking material into short parts that the learner starts one at a time is called segmenting, one of [the multimedia design principles](t:3.2). A face on screen can add social presence. It can also pull attention from the content, which is why the presenter appears only where a person adds something.

**The six-minute figure measured watching time.** The usual figure on length comes from a 2014 study of 6.9 million viewing sessions in four online university courses. People watched nearly all of a video under six minutes and far less of longer ones. That study measured how long people watched, not what they learned, so use it as a guide to attention.

why.title: How video production affects student engagement
why.found: Using 6.9 million viewing sessions from four online courses, the authors found that shorter videos held viewers much better and that informal talking-head videos held them better than polished studio ones. Engagement meant time watched and whether people tried the questions afterwards. Learning was not measured.
why.means: Keep each video to a few minutes and one point, and do not spend on studio polish.

why.text: **Split by question, not by the clock.** Cutting forty minutes into seven slices of six gives you seven fragments that still wander. The gain comes from each video having one job and a title that says what it is. The advice reverses for a recording kept as a record of a live event, for people who missed it. Leave that long, add a list of times and topics beside it, and do not treat it as the teaching version.

try.text: Record and edit one short teaching video from your own work, on one question, under six minutes. Run the twenty-second sound test on headphones first. Then check the finished video against two tests. Is it one segment on one point? Is [everything in it on that point](t:3.2)? Play it to one person on their phone, with the sound on and then with captions only, and ask what they would now do differently.
