try.title: A checklist: the twenty-second sound test
lines: Room: small, carpet, soft chairs, door closed, no glass wall behind the speaker.
Microphone: clipped a hand's width below the chin, cable tucked inside clothing.
Noise: air conditioning off, phones silent, laptop fan not beside the microphone.
Record twenty seconds of the real script at normal speaking volume.
Listen on headphones, not the laptop speaker.
Echo: move to a softer room or hang coats behind the camera.
Rustling: move the clip away from a collar, a lanyard or long hair.
Hum: find the source and switch it off, or move.
Test again after every change, then record.

items: **The video goes out without captions.** Add captions and a transcript to every one. There is more on [why captions matter for access](t:3.15).
**Nobody is told** that you use an AI-generated voice or presenter. Check the quality and tell learners. There is more on [checking AI output](t:7.7).
**The budget goes on studio polish.** In the 2014 study, informal talking-head videos held viewers better than studio ones. Spend the money on a microphone and the time on the script.
**You quote "sound first"** as a research finding. It comes from production experience. The studies behind this page do not test audio quality, so say so if a client asks.

**You quote the six-minute figure** as proof of learning. It measured watching time in university online courses. Use it as a guide to attention, and check learning with a question or a task after the video.

items.label: Brame (2016), Effective educational videos: principles and guidelines for maximizing student learning from video content. CBE Life Sciences Education, 15(4).
Guo, Kim and Rubin (2014), How video production affects student engagement: an empirical study of MOOC videos. Proceedings of the first ACM Conference on Learning at Scale.
Clark and Mayer (2023), e-Learning and the Science of Instruction, 5th edition. Wiley.

quiz.q: What did the 2014 study of 6.9 million viewing sessions measure?
quiz.a: How long people watched, not what they learned. Videos under six minutes were watched nearly to the end.

quiz.q: You have a forty-minute recording of a whole session, with echoing sound. What do you do with it?
quiz.a: Remake it as short videos, each on one question, recorded with a clip-on microphone in a soft room. Add captions and a transcript to each.

quiz.q: A client offers a studio budget for presenter-led videos. Where do you spend it?
quiz.a: On sound, not polish. Show a presenter only where a person adds something, because informal videos held viewers better in the 2014 study.

topics.tierReason: Short, segmented video with learner control has supporting studies, but the length guidance comes from watching data, not learning, and the audio-first advice is production experience.

topics.title: Build interactions that make people think

situation.text: A retailer's data-handling module is forty screens of "click next", with a drag-and-drop on screen 22 to break it up. Every member of store staff has completed it. Last month an assistant still read a colleague's mobile number to a caller who sounded friendly.

items: **Write the decision and the common mistake** for each objective: the decision the person makes at work and the mistake people most often make. Ask a store manager or the subject expert for three real cases. These are your raw material.
**Label each of the existing screens.** Go through them and mark each one: recall, decide, apply, or only moves the page on. Delete or merge every screen in the last group.

**Write each case as a scenario**: two or three sentences with real detail, then "What do you do?" Offer three options: the right action, the common mistake and a tempting half-measure. Leave out joke options, because they turn the question into a guess between two.
**Write feedback for every option** in two parts. First what happens next, then why. "Correct" on its own teaches nothing. There is more on [feedback people can act on](t:2.27).

**Put the decision before the explanation** for people who already do the job, so they find out what they do not know. For complete beginners, show one worked case first. There is more on [why worked examples help beginners](t:1.2).

**Ask people to answer first** for facts they must hold in their head: ask them to choose or type the answer before it is shown. Bring the same point back later in the module inside a new case. There is more on [why recall helps](t:2.24).
**Keep any branching small.** As a working rule, use two or three decision points and let the branches rejoin. Draw the tree on one page before you build a screen.

**Choose the authoring tool last**, once you know what interactions the objectives need. Then check every interaction with a keyboard and a screen reader, as set out in the [steps for building accessibly](t:3.15).

why.text: **Useful interaction makes people think.** Interaction for its own sake adds load without learning. The useful kind makes people think: retrieve something, make a decision, see the result. There is more on [why recall helps](t:2.24) and on [the research behind it](t:1.3). The method on this page, from the three options to the two-part feedback, is design craft built on that research.

**Judge an interaction by the thinking.** The test is what happens in the learner's head, not their hand. A click-to-reveal keeps the hand busy and asks nothing of memory or judgement. A drag-and-drop is no better or worse than the thinking it demands. Matching terms to definitions that are printed on the same screen is copying. Putting the five steps of a procedure in order from memory is recall.

**Starting from the tool lets templates decide.** Choosing an authoring tool comes after deciding what interaction the objective needs. Start from the tool and you build what its templates make easy, which is usually the reveal and the drag-and-drop.

**The trade-off is writing time.** A good scenario takes far longer to write than a reveal, so you will have fewer screens. Ten screens with three real decisions will usually serve the learner better than forty with none. The advice reverses for content people only need to look up, such as a price list or an escalation contact. Do not wrap that in interactions at all. Make it a page they can search, or [a job aid](t:5.7).

try.text: Take one click-through screen from a real module and rebuild it as a decision, with three options and two-part feedback for each. Then read the scenario aloud to a colleague, ask them to choose, and read them the feedback for their choice. Good looks like this: they had to stop and think before answering, and at least one wrong option was something a real person would do.

try.title: A worked example: from click to decision. Scenario: "A caller says she is from the delivery firm and needs your colleague Sam's mobile number to rearrange a drop-off. She is friendly and in a hurry. What do you do?"

items: **A drag-and-drop or a click-to-reveal** feels engaging and often asks for no thought. For each one, ask what the learner has to work out. If the answer is nothing, cut it.
**Branching multiplies the work.** Each new decision point can double the screens. Keep the tree to two or three decision points and let the branches rejoin.
**The wrong options are silly**, so the right one is obvious. Take every wrong option from a mistake someone has really made.
**The feedback says "Incorrect, try again"** and the learner clicks until something turns green. Show the consequence and the reason for the option they chose, then move on.
**The scenario is mouse-only:** it works with a mouse and nothing else. Check it with a keyboard and a screen reader. There is more on [the accessibility standard to build to](t:3.15).

items.label: GOV.UK Service Manual, Testing for accessibility. Supports the check with a keyboard and a screen reader.

quiz.q: What three things can a useful interaction ask of the learner?
quiz.a: To recall something, to decide, or to apply what they know.

quiz.q: A module has a click-to-reveal showing five facts about data handling. How do you rebuild it?
quiz.a: As a scenario. A caller asks for a colleague's phone number. The learner chooses a reply, sees what happens next, and reads why the safer choice was right.

quiz.q: Your branching scenario has grown to thirty screens and the deadline is close. What do you do?
quiz.a: Cut the tree to two or three decision points and let the branches rejoin. Then check it with a keyboard and a screen reader.

topics.tierReason: Asking learners to recall and giving feedback that explains are both well supported, but how much an interaction helps depends on what it makes the learner do.

topics.title: Choose tracking that fits what you need to measure
topics.theory: Standards and platforms: SCORM, xAPI, cmi5

situation.text: The IT lead at a software company emails you: "Is your course SCORM compliant? We need the package by Friday." The course is product training for 60 field sales reps, and half of it is a practice app they will use on their phones between customer visits, often with no signal. You are not sure what you need to track, or what their platform can hold.

items: **Write down the decisions** someone will make from the data, before you answer. For example: "Sales managers chase reps who have not finished before launch day." If nobody will decide anything from a figure, do not record it.
**List the three or four things** you need to record against those decisions. Completion and a score are often two of them.

**Ask IT four questions.** Which standards and versions does the platform accept: SCORM 1.2, SCORM 2004, xAPI or cmi5? Does it have, or connect to, a learning record store? What reports can managers see without asking IT? How do we get our content and our records out if we leave?

**Match the standard to the need.** Completion and a score for content inside the learning management system: SCORM is enough. Activity outside it, such as a mobile app, a simulation or offline work: xAPI, with a learning record store to hold it. xAPI content that is launched from the learning management system: cmi5.

**Test in the first week.** Publish a one-screen package in the agreed standard and version and ask IT to upload it. Check that it launches, records what you expect and shows up in the manager's report.
**Publish to an open standard** and keep the source files, so the content can move to another platform. File them with a version number, as part of [keeping one current version](t:3.18).

**Write one paragraph on what you record**, why, who sees it and how long it is kept, and send it to the client's data protection contact. There is more on [collecting only the data you need](t:9.24).

why.text: **The three standards do different jobs.** SCORM is the long-standing reference model for packaging e-learning and reporting progress to a learning management system. Its most recent release, SCORM 2004 4th Edition, dates from 2009. xAPI records learning activity in many more settings, such as mobile learning, simulations and offline work, and keeps it in a learning record store. Version 2.0 became an IEEE standard in 2023. cmi5 is a set of rules for using xAPI with a learning management system. It covers how content is launched and how results are reported.
**SCORM is still widely used.** The body that created it says newer specifications are overtaking it, and US defence guidance now recommends xAPI and cmi5 for new e-learning.

**Platform names are market labels.** Suppliers tend to describe a learning management system as built around administration and a learning experience platform as built around the learner. These are market labels, not standards, so check what each product records. The wrong choice quietly limits what you can measure later.

**Decide now what you will want recorded.** The descriptions above come from the bodies that publish the standards. The advice on what to track is craft. "Is it SCORM compliant?" is a question about plumbing, and the answer is nearly always yes. The harder question is what you will want to know in six months, because a standard that cannot record it cannot be made to later. The trade-off runs the other way too. xAPI can record almost anything, which tempts people to record everything, and every extra record is more work and more personal data to look after. If the client has an older platform and no budget to change it, do not force the issue. Record completion there and measure practice another way, such as [a manager's observation](t:6.4).

try.text: Take a real programme of yours, or the field sales case below. Write the decisions first, then the three or four things you would record, then the standard that can hold them. Finish by drafting the reply to IT with your four questions. Good looks like this: every item you record has a named person who will act on it.

parts.title: Accessibility, experts and upkeep
parts.summary: Building to a professional standard that lasts.

topics.title: Build to WCAG 2.2 AA from the start

situation.text: It is a week before a council launches its induction module for new managers. The project plan still has a line that reads "Accessibility: after launch". A manager who uses a screen reader starts on Monday. The module has a silent video, pale grey text and a drag-and-drop that needs a mouse.

items: **Put the target in the brief** on day one: "Built to WCAG 2.2 level AA." Ask the client which legal duties apply to them, and whether any learner has told them about an access need.

**Fix the template** before you build a screen. Set real heading styles, a clear text size and a visible outline on whichever button has keyboard focus. Check text colour against its background with a free contrast checker. Level AA asks for a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for ordinary text.
**Give every meaningful image a text alternative**: one sentence on what the image tells the learner, not a description of how it looks. Mark decorative images so a screen reader skips them.
**Never use colour as the only signal.** Put the word "Correct" or a tick beside the green, and label the lines on a chart directly.

**Unplug the mouse** and go through every screen with the Tab, Enter, Space and arrow keys. You must be able to reach every control, see where you are, operate it and leave it. Replace a mouse-only drag-and-drop with a question that asks for the same thinking through a list or buttons.
**Caption every video and provide a transcript.** Correct automatic captions by hand, starting with names and product terms.
**Use plain language and a predictable layout**: the same controls in the same place on every screen, and one term for one thing.

**Test before each release.** Run an automated checker, then spend ten minutes per module with the screen reader built into your computer or phone. If you can, ask someone who uses assistive technology every day to try it.

why.text: **AA is the usual target.** WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, groups its tests under four principles. Content must be perceivable: people can see or hear it, or get an alternative. It must be operable: it works with a keyboard. It must be understandable: plain language and a predictable layout. And it must work reliably with assistive technology such as a screen reader. WCAG 2.2 is the version that UK government guidance now points to. Its success criteria are graded by level. Government services are asked to meet all the A and AA criteria, so AA is the usual target.

**Building access in early usually costs less.** Building access in from the start is usually cheaper and easier than adding it later. Most access decisions live in the template and in the choice of interaction, so a drag-and-drop chosen in week one has to be rebuilt in week six. Access is also wider than sight and hearing. It includes attention, memory and processing. There is more on [designing for the range of people](t:2.16) and [for different minds from the start](t:2.23).

**UK law depends on who the client is.** In the UK, what the law asks depends on who you work for. The accessibility regulations for public sector bodies require their websites, intranets and public-facing apps to meet WCAG 2.2 AA and to publish an accessibility statement. Some bodies and some content are exempt, for example live audio and video. The GOV.UK guidance lists the exemptions.

**Employers still owe reasonable adjustments.** Those regulations do not cover private companies. Employers still have a duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled workers, under the Equality Act 2010 in Great Britain and the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 in Northern Ireland. GOV.UK lists training opportunities among its examples. This is not legal advice. Ask the client which duties apply to them.

**The build order here is craft.** The standard and the legal position above come from official guidance. The build order on this page is craft. The trade-off is that some interactions you like will have to be simplified or dropped, and captions take time.

try.text: Take one real module or deck. Unplug the mouse and work through it with the keyboard, then turn on your computer's screen reader and listen to two screens with your eyes closed. Check for the four common failures: text alternatives, contrast, keyboard use, and colour as the only signal. Fix what you find and run both tests again.

**You guess at the law:** you assume it does or does not apply. Legal duties vary. Check which apply to you and to the client, and ask the client to confirm.
**Accessibility is left to the end.** By then the fixes are rebuilds. Put the target in the brief and the template.
**You offer a separate "accessible version"**, such as a text-only document. It goes out of date and gives some learners a poorer course. Build one version that works for everyone.

topics.title: Write so it can be translated later

situation.text: A software company wants its customer-support onboarding course in German, French and Japanese by next quarter. You open the source files. Labels are drawn into every diagram, each button is sized to fit its English word, and the running example is a cricket team "on a sticky wicket".

items: **Ask the sponsor about other languages** at the start of every project: "Could this ever be delivered in another language?" If the answer is maybe, build as below. It costs little now and a great deal later.

**Keep every word as live, editable text.** Draw nothing into an image. Put numbered points on a diagram and the labels in a text list beside it. For screenshots of software, plan to capture them again in each language.
**Leave room for text to grow.** Size buttons, labels and headings to take at least twice the English length, leave about a third spare in boxes of body text, and do not fix the height of a text box.
**Write plainly.** Use short, complete sentences and one term for one thing. Take out idioms, sporting metaphors and jokes. Write dates in full, as in 17 November 2026, and give units and currencies.
**Choose examples that work in most places**, such as queuing at a shop or a late delivery. Where an example has to be local, mark it "replace locally" so the reviewer in each country swaps it.
**Build a glossary** of 20 to 40 key terms before translation starts. Give each a plain meaning and a rule: translate, or keep in English because it is a product name or a button label.
**Keep sound and picture separate.** Record narration as its own track so it can be re-recorded, keep captions as text files, and do not time animations tightly to the English words.
**Book a native speaker** who knows the job to review each language in the final layout. Ask them to check terms against the glossary, examples, tone and anything that is cut off or overlapping.

why.text: **Unprepared content is costly to adapt.** Prepare the content so it can be adapted, then translate it. The first step is called internationalisation and the second localisation. Localising is more than translating: examples, images and references have to work in the new setting. Content not prepared for this is costly and error-prone to adapt later.

**Translated text grows, short labels most.** Text usually gets longer when translated from English, and short labels grow the most. W3C guidance quotes IBM figures of two to three times the length for strings of up to ten characters, and about 1.3 times for passages over 70 characters. Some scripts also need taller lines. That is why the button is the first thing to break, and why a fixed-height box clips the bottom of a line.

**Every language multiplies each fix.** Those figures are from published guidance. The rest of this page is craft. The reason to prepare early is multiplication. A label drawn into a picture is one fix in English. Once the course is in three languages it is three fixes, by three people, with three chances of error, and again at every update.

**Plain writing can feel flat at home.** There is a trade-off. Writing without idiom or humour can feel flat to a home audience. Many English-language cohorts already include people working in their second language, and they benefit from the plainer version too. The advice reverses for a one-off session for one local team that will never travel. There, local references and shared jokes help, so use them. Norms about directness and hierarchy also change what works in a room. There is more on [adjusting for the cultures in the room](t:4.7) and [delivering across countries and languages](t:9.27).

try.text: Take one piece of your own content, a module or a ten-slide deck. Go through it with a pen and mark everything that would obstruct translation: words inside pictures, tight buttons, idioms, local examples, short date formats, terms used two ways. Redesign the three worst. Then read one page aloud to someone whose first language is not English and ask them to stop you at anything they had to work out.

items: **Machine translation goes out unchecked.** It needs human review, by someone who knows the job as well as the language.
**A joke is translated** word for word. Humour rarely survives. Cut it from the source, or ask the local reviewer to write their own.
**Only the words are translated**, and the examples are not. A reviewer who is only asked about language will leave the cricket in. Ask them to look at examples, images and tone as well.
**The review happens in a spreadsheet** of text strings. Clipped buttons and overlapping labels only show in the final layout, so review there.

**The English is updated after translation** and the other versions are forgotten. Keep a note of which version each language was made from. There is more on [keeping one current version of everything](t:3.18).

quiz.a: Two to three times the length for strings of up to ten characters, on the IBM figures W3C quotes. Passages over 70 characters grow to about 1.3 times.

quiz.q: A diagram in your course has English labels drawn into the picture. What do you change before translation?
quiz.a: Put numbered points on the image and the labels as editable text beside it, with spare room for longer words.

quiz.q: A client plans to machine-translate the course the week before launch with no check. What do you ask for?
quiz.a: A review by a native speaker and an agreed glossary of key terms. Ask them to look at the examples and any humour as well as the words.

topics.title: Draw out the steps experts no longer notice
topics.theory: Working with subject experts and the expert blind spot

situation.text: You are building onboarding for new support engineers at a software company. The senior engineer who knows the escalation process best sends you two hundred slides and says "it is all in there". You have one hour of her time this month, and the first new starters arrive in five weeks.

items: **Ask for a different kind of hour:** "Could I sit with you while you handle two real tickets, and ask questions as you go?" Choose one routine case and one awkward one.
**Agree the scope with the sponsor** before the session: what a beginner must be able to do in the first week. Read enough of the slides to know the vocabulary, and no more.
**Ask the expert to do the task** while talking through it. Record it if she agrees. If not, take notes in two columns: what she did, and what she said.

**Ask three questions at each step:** "What are you looking at?", "How do you know it is right?" and "What would make you stop?" Add a fourth where it fits: "What does a new person usually get wrong here?"
**Write the task as numbered steps** the same day. Include the steps she did and did not mention, and mark each one of those. At every decision point, write the cue she uses to decide.
**Reorganise the material for someone new.** Put the commonest case first, hold the exceptions for later, and define each term where it first appears.

**Check back.** Spend 30 minutes walking the expert through your written steps and ask: "What have I got wrong? What is missing?" Then ask a newcomer to follow the steps while you watch. Where they stall, a step is still missing.

**Agree one version before you build.** If a second expert does it differently, put the two versions side by side in front of both, or in front of the person who owns the procedure. Credit the experts in the materials.

why.text: **Experts skip steps without noticing.** Experts have automated much of what they know and lose sight of what newcomers do not know. Their explanations skip steps. This is often called the expert blind spot, or the curse of knowledge. You are there to surface what the expert no longer notices and put it in an order a beginner can learn. Transcribing their slides does neither.

**Expertise can mislead you about beginners.** In one study, trainee teachers with more advanced maths were more likely to assume pupils must master equations before word problems. Pupils' real results point the other way. Knowing a subject well can mislead you about how a beginner learns it.
**Cognitive task analysis studies expert thinking.** The structured version of this is called cognitive task analysis: you study how an expert thinks and decides, not only what they do.

why.title: Cognitive task analysis-based training: a meta-analysis
why.found: Training built on a structured analysis of how experts think and decide beat training built on other ways of gathering content, with a large average effect (Hedges' g = 0.871). The number of studies was small and results varied a good deal by method and setting.
why.means: Do not build from the expert's slides alone. Watch them work and question them about the decisions they make.

why.text: **Watching catches what an interview misses.** There are more than a hundred named methods for drawing out expert knowledge, and little evidence on which works best. So the steps on this page are craft: watch, ask, write down, check back. The reason to watch and not only interview is that an automated step is hard for its owner to report. Ask an expert how she does the job and you tend to get the version in the manual. The three questions aim at what the manual leaves out: what she looks at, how she judges it, and when she stops. The cost is an hour or two of an expensive person's time. When the content is facts or policy, with no skilled performance to observe, an interview and the documents will do.

try.text: Interview someone on a skill they know well, at work or at home. First ask them to tell you the steps and write those down. Then watch them do it and ask the three questions aloud at each step. Find at least three steps they left out the first time. Finish by reading your written version back to them and asking what is wrong with it.

items: **Experts disagree.** If you build from one version, the other expert will tell the learners it is wrong. Reconcile them before you build.
**The expert will want everything in.** Ask of each item whether a beginner needs it in the first week. Offer a "later" list so nothing feels thrown away.
**You take more expert time** than you agreed. Book one observed session and one check-back, arrive prepared, and credit them in the materials.
**You choose an elaborate method.** There are more than a hundred named ones and little evidence on which works best. Keep yours simple: watch, ask, write down, check back.
**You observe only the routine case.** Much of what an expert knows shows when something goes wrong, so include one awkward case, or ask her to talk you through the last one she remembers.

quiz.a: Training built on a structured analysis of how experts think and decide beat training built on other ways of gathering content. The average effect was large, from a small number of studies with varied results.

quiz.q: An expert hands you two hundred slides and says "it is all in there". What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask to watch them do the task while they talk it through. Ask what they are looking at, how they know it is right and what would make them stop. Write down the steps they did not mention, then reorder the material for a beginner.

quiz.q: Two experts give you different versions of the same procedure. What do you do?
quiz.a: Reconcile them before you build. Put the differences in front of both, or the person who owns the procedure, and agree one version.

topics.title: Keep one current version of everything
topics.theory: Asset management, versioning and the toolchain

situation.text: It is 08:40 on the morning of a manager induction. Your co-facilitator opens "Induction deck FINAL v3 (new).pptx" from an email you sent in March. The exercise on slide 14 quotes a leave policy that changed in June. There are four versions of the deck in three folders, and nobody is sure which is current.

items: **Give each course one home:** one shared folder with three subfolders called Current, Working and Archive. Only approved files live in Current, and there is only ever one of each.
**Name every file the same way:** course, item, version number, date. For example, "Induction deck v2.1 2026-11-17". Write the date year first so files sort in order. Never use the word "final".
**Decide what the numbers mean.** A change to what is taught moves the whole number, from v2 to v3. A correction moves the decimal, from v2.1 to v2.2.
**Put a control line** on the first slide or page of every asset: version, date, owner and next review date. Put the version in the footer of anything printed.
**Keep a register on one sheet:** asset, version and date, owner, review date, status. A course usually needs ten to fifteen rows.
**Approve by moving.** When a new version is approved, move it into Current and move the old one to Archive in the same minute. Then update the register.

**Share by link, never by attachment.** The briefing email to facilitators links to the Current folder. On the morning, each facilitator checks the control line against the register before the room fills.

**Build templates** for the deck, the workbook and the facilitator guide that already meet your design and access standards, covering [accessibility from the start](t:3.15) and [type size and contrast on slides](t:3.22). Put a diary entry on each asset's review date for its owner: 30 minutes to decide whether it is still right, still used, or ready to retire.

why.text: **Materials need upkeep, like a library.** Materials that nobody can find or trust go out of date, and someone ends up teaching from last year's deck. Treat your materials as a library that needs upkeep. Templates make work faster and more consistent, and carry good practice with them.

**A wrong version is found too late.** This is craft. No study compares filing schemes for training materials. The reasoning is about where the cost of a mistake falls. A wrong version is found in the room, in front of learners and sometimes the client, when nothing can be done about it. Ten minutes of filing at approval is cheap against that.

**A link always opens the latest file.** Link, do not attach, because every attachment is a copy you no longer control. A link to the Current folder always opens the latest file. The control line on the first slide is the backstop for the copies that escape anyway.

**Schemes like this fail by weight.** If the rules take more effort than the mess they prevent, people stop following them, and rules nobody follows are worse than none because everyone assumes the files are in order. Start with the folder, the name and the control line, and add the register when you have more than one course. The rules also apply only to what is approved for delivery. In the Working folder, mid-build, drafts can be as untidy as you like. Some clients will require you to keep files in their own system, and there is more on [working inside the client's tools](t:9.30). Use the same naming and the same control line there.

try.text: Take a real set of materials, your own or a client's. Create the three folders, find the current version of each asset, rename it, add the control line and fill in the register. Then test it: ask a colleague to find the current workbook from a cold start and time them. Under a minute is good. Write one sentence on how a stale asset would be found and retired, and who does it.

parts.title: Materials for the room
parts.summary: The printed and physical things a face-to-face session runs on: the workbook, the facilitator guide, wall materials and slides people can read.

topics.title: Write a workbook people will use

situation.text: You hand out a printed copy of the slides. By lunch most copies are closed on the table, and at the end of the day half are left in the room.

items: **Give the workbook two jobs** and design for both. During the session it is where people work. Afterwards it is where they look things up. A copy of the slides does neither.
**Build it from the activities**, in session order. Give each activity its own page with the same layout: the task in one or two lines, the model or example, space to write, and a short notes box.
**Number every page in large type** and call the numbers out: "Turn to page 6." Put the page number on the matching slide.
**Leave real room to write.** Handwriting needs more space than you expect. Give at least a third of each working page to boxes or ruled lines, with lines about 8 to 10 mm apart.

**Move the detail to a reference section** at the back: the full model, definitions, the long table you cut from a slide. There are two reasons it should come off the screen: [how small working memory is](t:1.1) and [cutting what does not serve the point](t:3.2).
**End with an action page:** what I will do, with whom, by when. This is the page you need when you [plan the first use at work](t:5.2).
**Design for cheap printing.** A4, black and white, body text at 11 or 12 point, bold headings, no grey fills. Staple or wire-bind it so it lies flat on a table.
**Fill in one printed copy by hand**, start to finish, with a pen. Fix every box that was too small and every instruction you had to read twice.

why.text: **People remember what they produce.** This is practitioner judgement, not a research finding. The reasoning rests on two ideas from Stage 1. People remember what they produce more than what they are handed. [Working memory is small](t:1.1), so detail belongs on paper they can return to.

**People can start without waiting for you.** A workbook built from activities also protects the session. If the task and the space to do it are on the page, people can start without waiting for you to repeat the instruction, and a group that falls behind can catch up. When the projector fails, the day still runs.

**People keep the pages they filled in.** Afterwards, the pages people filled in are the ones they keep, because their own words are in them. The printed model on page 14 matters less than the three lines they wrote beside it about their own team.

try.text: Take one activity from a session you know. Make its workbook page. Print it, give it to someone who was not there, and ask them to do the task with no help from you. Watch where their pen stops.

try.title: A worked example: contents page for a one-day workshop for new managers, "Giving feedback that helps"
lines: Page 1. Today at a glance: times, outcomes, who is in the room
Page 2. What I want from today (fill in before 09:45)
Page 3. Activity 1: the best and worst feedback I have received
Page 4. The four-part feedback model, with one worked example
Page 5. Activity 2: spot the four parts in two written examples
Page 6. Activity 3: prepare my real conversation
Page 7. Activity 4: practice in threes, with the observer's checklist
Page 8. Activity 5: when it goes badly. Three replies to plan for

Back cover. Trainer's contact details and the date of the follow-up call

try.title: A worked example: page 6, filled in by a participant (their handwriting shown in quotation marks)
lines: ACTIVITY 3: PREPARE MY REAL CONVERSATION. 10 minutes, on your own.
Think of one person in your team you need to give feedback to in the next two weeks.
Who (initials only): "R.T."
1. What I saw or heard. Facts, no opinion: "Two client reports sent late in October, on the 3rd and the 17th. No warning either time."
2. The effect it had: "I found out from the client. We looked disorganised and I could not cover for it."
3. The question I will ask: "What got in the way on those two?"
4. What I will ask for: "Tell me the day before if a report will be late."

items: **The workbook is the slide deck** with lines beside it. People read ahead and stop listening. Build pages round tasks.
**Writing boxes are two lines deep.** Nobody can fit a real answer. Test with a pen.
**It runs to forty pages.** People feel they have failed if they do not finish. Cut it to the pages you will use, plus reference.
**Confidential details go into a book** that gets left on a train. Ask for initials only, and say why.
**Page numbers drift apart** on slides and workbook after an edit. Check them last, after every change.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What two jobs does a workbook have?
quiz.a: A place to work during the session, and a reference afterwards.

quiz.q: A sponsor asks you to print the slides as the handout to save time. What do you do?
quiz.a: Offer a short workbook built from the activities, with the detail from the slides in a reference section at the back. People use pages they have written on, and it takes little longer to make.

quiz.q: In the test print, your colleague cannot fit their answer in the box on page 6 and asks you what question 3 means. What do you do?
quiz.a: Enlarge the box and rewrite the question until it needs no explanation. If one tester stumbles, a room of twelve will.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement. No research on workbook design was opened.

topics.title: Write a facilitator guide someone else can deliver from

situation.text: You are ill on the morning of a workshop. A colleague steps in with your slides and a page of your notes that says "Do the angry caller exercise, about 40 minutes."

items: **Write for a capable trainer** who has never seen the session and cannot ring you. That reader knows how to run a room. They do not know what you meant.
**Start with one page** that sets up the day: purpose, outcomes, who it is for, group size range, room layout, kit list, and the timetable with clock times.
**Give every activity the same block**, with the same fields in the same order: time, method, purpose, what to say, what to watch for, materials, and what to do if short of time.

**Write each activity's instructions word for word**, because small changes in set-up change what groups do. There is more on [wording instructions people can follow](t:4.24). Write the rest of what you say as points, so the facilitator uses their own voice.
**Write the debrief questions out in full**, in order. Add the answers you are listening for and the common wrong turns. There is more on [debriefing an activity](t:4.28).
**Mark each block "keep" or "can cut"**, and say which outcome it serves. A facilitator running 20 minutes late needs to know what to drop without asking.
**Put the slide number and workbook page** beside each block. Add the version number and date to the footer of every page. There is more on [keeping one current version](t:3.18).
**Test it cold.** Ask someone to deliver one block from the guide while you watch in silence. Each time they stop, guess or ask, the guide needs another line.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement, not a research finding.

**Without a guide, timing and debrief are lost.** A guide is how a session outlives the person who designed it. Without one, each new facilitator rebuilds the session from the slides. They keep the parts that are easy to see, which is the content, and lose the parts that are not, which is the timing, the set-up and the debrief.

**Script the instructions, leave the stories open.** The split between exact wording and points is deliberate. Instructions fail when they are improvised: people start the wrong task, or the right task in the wrong groups. Stories and explanations fail when they are read out. So the guide scripts the first and leaves the second open. Writing down what to watch for passes on the thing that otherwise takes years to learn, which is what the activity looks like when it is going wrong.

**The client's learning team may ask for it.** It is also the document a client's learning team will ask to see if they plan to deliver the session with their own people. [Designing for scale with many facilitators](t:2.32) starts from it.

**The guide is not your session plan.** A facilitator guide is a different document from [the session plan you run from](t:4.33). The plan is your own running order. The guide is written for someone else. There is more on [being the person who receives one](t:9.31).

try.text: Take a 20-minute activity you have run. Write its block in the format below. Give it to a colleague, leave the room for ten minutes while they read it, then have them deliver it to you. Say nothing until the end.

try.title: A worked example: one page of a guide. Customer service workshop, block 4 of 7: "The angry caller". Keep. Slides 14 to 16, workbook page 7. Version 1.3, 17 November 2026

head: Time
Method
What to say
What to watch for
rows: Input, whole group
Points: most angry callers want two things, to be heard and to know what happens next. Show the three-step reply on slide 14: name it, own it, next step. Give one example from your own experience.
Keep it to five minutes. If people start telling their own stories, say you want those in a moment.
Demonstration with a volunteer
Say exactly: "I need one volunteer to be an angry caller. Read the card and give me a hard time for one minute. Everyone else, tick each of the three steps on page 7 when you hear it."
Pick someone who will not overplay it. If nobody offers, play the caller yourself and ask a confident participant to reply.
Set up trios

Say exactly: "In threes. One of you is the caller, one the agent, one the observer with page 7. Two minutes of call, two minutes of feedback, practiser first. Then swap. Three rounds. Caller cards are on your table. Who is the first agent in each group? Hands up."
Do not start until a hand is up in every trio. A group of four runs four shorter rounds.
Practice in trios
Call the swaps at four and eight minutes. Otherwise stay quiet. Stand where you can hear two groups.
Agents who jump to the fix and skip "name it". Callers who make it impossible. Step in only for the second.
Debrief, whole group
Ask in this order: "Agents, which step was hardest to say?" "Callers, what did the agent do that calmed you?" "What will you say differently on your next real call?"
Listening for: naming the feeling felt awkward, and it worked. If people say it sounds false, ask the callers how it felt to hear.
If short of time
Cut the demonstration and run two rounds, not three. Do not cut the debrief.

items: **The guide is a script** from start to finish. Facilitators read it out and the room hears it. Script the instructions only.
**It describes content and not timing.** Put a clock time on every block.
**"Debrief the activity" with no questions.** Write the questions and what a good answer sounds like.
**Written after the first delivery** and never updated. Note changes on your copy during each session and revise the master that week.
**It only fits the group size** you had. State the range, and what to change at each end.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Which part of a facilitator guide should be written word for word?
quiz.a: The instructions for each activity. The rest is written as points.

quiz.q: A colleague delivering from your guide is running 20 minutes late before lunch and cannot reach you. What should the guide already tell them?
quiz.a: Which blocks are marked "can cut" and what each "keep" block is for. Then they can drop the right thing and protect the practice.

quiz.q: In a cold test, your colleague sets up the trios correctly and then asks the group, "So, how was that?" The debrief goes flat. What do you change?
quiz.a: Write the debrief questions into the guide in full and in order, with the answers to listen for. A general prompt was all they had.

topics.title: Prepare flipcharts, cards and wall materials

situation.text: The key model was on slide 9. By the afternoon nobody can remember the third step, and you have clicked back to it four times.

items: **Decide what must stay visible all day:** the timetable, the outcomes, the main model, the question list. Those go on the wall. A slide disappears when you move on.

**Prepare flipchart sheets the day before.** Write the headings and any diagram. Leave the parts the group will fill in blank. Pencil light notes for yourself in the corner, which nobody else will see.

**Write large and dark.** As a working rule, make letters at least 3 cm tall, and larger in a deep room. Use black or dark blue for text and keep red and green for marks and underlines. Six or seven lines to a sheet is plenty.
**Check your sheets from the furthest chair** before people arrive. If you have to squint, rewrite.
**Make cards** for anything people sort, rank or act out. One idea per card, in marker, readable at arm's length. Number each set on the back and bring a spare.
**Write role cards in four lines:** who you are, what you want, what you will say first, and what you will only say if asked. The example below shows one.
**Ask the venue about the walls** in advance: what may go on them and what they are made of. Bring your own low-tack tape and tack, and a second flipchart stand if you can.
**Photograph every sheet** before you take it down. Send the photographs to the group within two days, in session order.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement, and the sizes are working rules. Test them in the room you are given.

**Wall materials do something slides cannot.** They stay. A model on a flipchart is there when someone needs it at three o'clock, and you can point to it without stopping the session. Sheets the group has filled in also show progress, which matters on a long day.

**Cards put the work in everyone's hands.** Cards and printed cases change who is doing the work. When a group has to sort twelve cards into an order, every person can reach in and move one. The same task on a slide becomes a conversation between you and the two most confident people.

**Walls and cards survive a failed projector.** There is a practical reason too. A session that runs from walls, cards and a workbook does not stop when the projector fails or the room has no screen. When you [rehearse what could go wrong](t:4.13), you are asked to carry a version that needs no technology, and this is that version. On a retreat or in an unusual venue it may be the only version.
**This covers preparation, not use or packing.** This topic covers preparing the materials. There is more on [using flipcharts and walls during the session](t:4.18), and on [the kit to pack](t:4.19).

items: **Your back is to the room** for minutes at a time while you write. Prepare the sheet, or write a few words and turn round.
**Pale pens and small writing.** Yellow, orange and light green cannot be read from the back. Keep them for highlighting.
**Tape takes paint off the wall.** Ask first, test in a corner, or use stands and windows.
**A card set has one missing.** Number them and count them back in.
**Sheets are binned at the end** and the group's work goes with them. Photograph first.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What belongs on the wall and not on a slide?
quiz.a: Anything people need to see all day, such as the timetable, the outcomes and the main model.

quiz.q: You arrive to find the projector does not work and the technician is an hour away. What do you do?
quiz.a: Start on time from the prepared flipcharts, cards and workbook. Draw any model you need on a fresh sheet, and move slide-only detail to the reference pages.

quiz.q: The venue says nothing may be stuck to the walls. What do you do?
quiz.a: Bring or borrow extra flipchart stands, and use windows or tables for group work if the venue agrees. Decide this before the day, because the layout of the room changes.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement. The sizes are working rules to test in the room.

topics.title: Make slides readable from the back of the room
topics.theory: Type size and contrast for projected slides

situation.text: You say "You probably cannot read this at the back" and carry on. The slide looked fine on your laptop.

items: **Find out the room** before you set the type: how far the back row sits from the screen, how large the screen is, and whether the lights stay on. If you cannot find out, design for a long room and a small screen.
**Set minimum sizes and hold to them.** As working practice on a standard widescreen slide: body text at 24 point or more, headings at 32 or more, and nothing under 18, labels and sources included.

**Use the size limit to edit.** If the text will not fit at 24 point, the slide has too much on it. Cut it, split it, or move it to the workbook. There is more on [cutting what does not serve the point](t:3.2).

**Choose strong contrast** between text and background: very dark on very light, or the reverse. Check the pair with a contrast checker. Avoid text on photographs unless you put a solid panel behind it.
**Pick a plain typeface** in a regular or medium weight. Thin weights and narrow faces break up when projected.
**Label charts directly** and at the same minimum size. A legend in 10 point defeats the chart. There is more on [making charts quick to read](t:3.3).
**Do not rely on colour alone** to carry meaning. Add a label, a shape or a position.

**Test it.** On your laptop, view the slide in the slide sorter at about a quarter of full size. If you cannot read it there, the back row will struggle. Then check in the real room, lights on, from the last chair.

why.text: **A fixed minimum gives you something to check.** The sizes are practitioner judgement, not a standard, and the right size depends on the screen and the distance. A fixed minimum is still useful, because it turns "design for the back row", the advice on [making charts honest and quick to read](t:3.3), into something you can check.

**On contrast there is a published reference point.** The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, part of [building for accessibility from the start](t:3.15), ask at level AA for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 between text and its background. Large text, meaning 18 point or 14 point bold, may drop to 3 to 1. The purpose is that people with moderately low vision can read the text without extra tools. The guideline is written for web content, not for projection. Treat 4.5 to 1 as a floor for slides and aim well above it. A projector in a bright room shows less contrast than your laptop does.

**People who cannot read the screen give up.** Readable slides are partly an access matter and partly a matter of respect. Someone who cannot read the screen stops trying. And a client judging a trainer who used to be a designer will look at the slides first.

try.text: Open a deck you have used. Find the smallest text on each slide and write the size beside it. Fix the three worst. Then project the deck, or put it on a television, and read every slide aloud from the far wall with the lights on.

**Grey text on white** looks elegant on a laptop and vanishes on a projector. Use near-black.
**A screenshot of software** carries tiny text. Crop to the part you are discussing and enlarge it.
**You shrink the type** to fit one more line. Move the line to the next slide.
**You test in a dark office** and deliver in a room with windows. Test with the lights on.

items.label: W3C, Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum). WCAG 2.2.

quiz.q: What contrast ratio does WCAG ask for at level AA for normal-sized text?
quiz.a: At least 4.5 to 1. Large text may be 3 to 1.

quiz.q: A comparison table will only fit on the slide at 14 point. What do you do?
quiz.a: Put the full table in the workbook and show only the two or three cells you are talking about, at 20 point or more. People cannot read and listen to a dense table at once in any case.

quiz.q: The client's brand template uses pale grey text on white. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep the brand colours for panels and accents and set the text in near-black, then show the client both versions projected. Most agree once they see it from the back of the room.

parts.title: The client's learning technology
parts.summary: The systems a large client already owns, what each one does, and how to get a programme loaded, tested and signed off on them.

topics.title: Know the learning technology you will meet
topics.theory: The client's learning systems: what each does and who owns it

situation.text: On the kick-off call the platform owner says, "We will host the module on the learning management system, surface it in the experience platform, run the live sessions through the classroom integration, and you should check the library first." You write down four terms and nod.

items: **Ask for the map in week one.** "Which systems will this programme touch, and who owns each one?" Draw it on one page and send it back to be corrected.

**Start with the learning management system.** It is the record. It holds the catalogue, enrols people, assigns mandatory courses, tracks completions and produces the compliance report. It takes its list of people, managers and job details from the HR system. There is more on [why you never keep a rival record](t:9.30).

**Ask about a learning experience platform** as well. Where one exists it is the front door for learners: search, recommendations and pathways that pull content from several sources. Some clients have one product that does both jobs.

**Check the content library** before you propose anything. Many large companies pay a yearly licence for thousands of ready-made courses. Ask for a login or a title list and search it for your subject. If the library already covers the general knowledge, use those titles as preparation and spend your custom time on the client's own cases. Say in the proposal that you have done so.

**Ask whether a skills platform is used.** It holds the skills framework and each person's skills profile, and content is often tagged to skills there. There is more on [working with the client's skills data](t:9.46).

**Ask which authoring tool the client licenses.** If their team will edit your module later, build in their tool and hand over the source files. Ownership of those files is a contract point, one of [the terms to put in writing](t:9.9).

**Ask about the virtual classroom tool.** Find out whether breakout rooms, polls and whiteboards are switched on, whether attendance passes to the learning management system automatically, and what the recording rules are. There is more on [designing live virtual sessions](t:4.10).

**Ask what reports each system produces** and who can run them. That decides what you can measure without extra work, and it is part of [getting the data you need](t:6.12) from the client. There is more on [the tracking standards the systems use](t:3.14) to talk to each other.

why.text: **Vendors use the labels loosely.** This is practitioner knowledge. Product categories overlap and vendors use the labels loosely, as noted under [choosing tracking that fits your measures](t:3.14), so ask what each system at this client does and records. No study was opened for this topic.

**The client cannot adopt your preferred tool.** A head of learning is constrained by this set of systems more than a supplier usually sees. The platforms are bought on contracts that run for years. They are connected to the HR system, to single sign-on and to reporting, and each connection took a project to build. She cannot adopt your preferred tool for one programme, and she should not. What she needs from you is work that fits what is there.

**The content library changes the commercial conversation.** The client has already paid for general courses on feedback, presentation skills, project management and hundreds of other subjects. A supplier who proposes a custom module on one of those is asking her to pay twice, and it suggests you did not look. Custom work earns its fee where the library cannot reach: the client's own products, customers, processes and judgement calls. Building on the library shows respect for money already spent.

**Each system has its own owner and queue.** Ownership matters because each system has a different person behind it, with a queue and a lead time. The learning operations team usually runs the learning management system. IT often owns the virtual classroom tool. The HR systems team owns the people data. There is more on [the loading itself, from packaging to sign-off](t:3.24).

Then run a ten-minute call aloud with a colleague playing the platform owner, and ask your questions without reading them. quiz.q: Which system is normally the record of who completed what?

quiz.q: A client asks for a custom e-learning module on giving feedback. You find twelve feedback courses in their licensed content library. What do you propose?

quiz.q: The client's design team wants to update your module themselves next year. They license a different authoring tool from yours. What do you do?
quiz.a: Build in their tool, or agree in writing before you start how source files will be handed over in a form they can edit. A published package alone cannot be changed.

topics.title: Get your content on to a client's platform
topics.theory: Packaging, testing, completion rules and sign-off

situation.text: The module is finished on Friday and the launch email is due on Monday. The platform owner replies that uploads need ten working days, the package is in a version the platform does not accept, and in her test it marked itself complete the moment it opened.

items: **Ask for the loading requirements in writing** in week one, from the platform owner: accepted formats and versions of [the tracking standards](t:3.14), file size limit, supported browsers and devices, the lead time and who signs off. Put the dates on [the programme plan](t:9.18).

**Send a test package early.** Build a three-screen dummy in the same authoring tool with the same publishing settings, and ask for it to be loaded weeks before the real content is ready. It proves that the package opens, tracks and resumes.

**Agree the completion rule in one sentence** and write it down. For example: "Complete when every screen has been viewed and the final check is passed at 80% or more." Agree which fields are reported, such as completion, pass or fail, score and time. Track only what will change a decision. There is more on [choosing what to track](t:3.14).

**Test the real package yourself** before you hand it over. Run it in a test player and read what it reports. Then ask for it to be loaded in the client's test area, and go through it as an ordinary learner.

**Test the awkward routes.** Close it halfway and come back. Fail the check and retake it. Finish on a phone. Open it on a work laptop on the client's network, with video and outside links. There is more on [working under the client's security rules](t:9.30).

**Run the accessibility checks before upload**, using [the accessibility level you build to](t:3.15) as the standard. Go through with the keyboard only. Check captions and transcripts, colour contrast and text at 200% zoom, and listen to one screen with a screen reader. Ask whether the client has its own accessibility sign-off.

**List everything else the platform must hold** for a blended programme. Live sessions set up as events. Enrolment and joining messages. How attendance is marked. The feedback form. The rule for completing the whole programme, such as the module plus two sessions plus an assessed task.

**Agree the sign-off chain.** The content owner approves what it says. The platform owner approves the technical test. The learning partner approves the messages. Then release it to five people a few days early and check that their records appear in the report before the full launch.

why.text: **The figures are assumptions to check.** This is practitioner judgement, with one product page for the test player. Lead times and rules differ by client, so the figures here are starting assumptions to check.

**Faults are cheap to fix when found early.** A module that works on your laptop has passed one test out of several. The client's platform is a different player, behind a firewall, on managed devices, with its own settings for what counts as finished. The usual faults are dull and predictable: the wrong version of the standard, a completion rule that fires too early or never, a resume that loses the learner's place, video that the network blocks. Each is quick to fix when found three weeks out and painful when found on launch day.

**A test player does not prove conformance.** Rustici Software, which maintains a widely used test player called SCORM Cloud, says on its site that the free account lets you import SCORM, AICC, xAPI and cmi5 courses and see completion, pass or fail status, score and time, along with debug logs. The same page is clear about the limit. The player shows how content behaves. It does not prove strict conformance to a standard, and it is not the client's platform. Test in both.

**Assume three to four weeks to launch.** As a working assumption, allow three to four weeks from the first test package to launch in a large company, and ask the platform owner for her real figure. Most of that time is waiting in a queue, and you can keep designing while it passes.

try.text: Take any e-learning module you can get, or build a three-screen one. Run it in a test player and write down what it reports when you close it halfway, when you fail and when you pass. quiz.q: In the client's test area your module shows as complete as soon as it opens. Launch is in two weeks. What do you do?

parts.title: What the evidence says about medium
parts.summary: The pooled comparison of online and classroom teaching, and the Clark and Kozma debate read from the original papers.

topics.title: Know whether online training works as well as the classroom
topics.theory: Web-based against classroom instruction: the pooled comparison

situation.text: You have proposed a two-day face-to-face programme for 30 new managers at a software company. The head of people replies: "Our platform can deliver the same content for a fraction of the cost. Why would I take them out of work for two days?" You sell rooms for a living, so your answer has to stand up to a sceptic.

items: **Split the programme by kind of outcome** before you answer. Knowledge, skill, and belief or relationships each get a separate answer. There is more on [the three kinds of outcome](t:1.30).
**Concede the knowledge.** Say plainly that for facts and concepts, online teaching has done as well as a classroom when both use the same methods. Offer to move that part online.

**Compare methods, not media.** List what each version contains: explanation, practice, feedback, time, and how much control the learner has. If the room version has three practice rounds and the online one has none, talk about that.

**Ask about practice and feedback for skills:** what the online version gives, and who watches. The pooled evidence on skills is thin, so make the case from the method, [showing, practising and giving feedback](t:2.34), not from a study of media.

**Say what the comparison studies barely measured:** confidence, trust and working relationships. Make your case from [the case for and against a residential](t:8.7) and [what the evidence says about retreats](t:8.8), and call it a judgement.
**Ask whether people will choose** the online course or be assigned to it. The result changed when people were assigned at random.
**Propose the split as a table** in the proposal, with the reason beside each row. There is more on [choosing a medium for each objective](t:3.5).

why.text: **Web and classroom tied when methods matched.** Sitzmann, Kraiger, Stewart and Wisher pooled studies that compared web-based instruction with classroom instruction. Their summary reports four things. Web-based instruction was 6 per cent more effective than the classroom for teaching declarative knowledge, meaning facts and concepts. The two were equally effective for procedural knowledge, meaning how to do something. Trainees were equally satisfied with both. And when the web and classroom versions used the same instructional methods, they were equally effective for declarative knowledge. The authors read this as support for Clark's argument that [the medium itself adds nothing](t:3.7). Web-based instruction was 19 per cent more effective when learners had control, the course was long and people practised with feedback.

**The headline figure is a small effect.** The full paper gives the detail behind those lines. It covers 96 reports from 1996 to 2005, with 19,331 people in 168 courses. The 6 per cent figure is the authors' way of expressing an effect of d = .15 in favour of the web. With the same methods on both sides the effect was d = .04. Courses that mixed web and classroom beat classroom alone, d = .34 for declarative and d = .52 for procedural knowledge.

**Three limits matter for you.** Most of the studies were of university students. Employees made up about 15 per cent of the courses. Second, in most studies people picked their own course. In the studies that assigned people at random, the classroom came out ahead, d = -.26 for declarative knowledge. People who choose to learn online may be more motivated or more able. Third, only 12 studies measured procedural knowledge, and too few measured attitudes to give any estimate.

**A later review found much the same.** A later review for the US Department of Education reached a similar place. Across 50 comparisons, mostly in higher education and medical training, students taught online did modestly better than those taught face to face. The gain was larger for blends, and the authors warn that blended courses often had more learning time and more teaching elements, so the medium should not get the credit.

**The method does the work, not the room.** So the evidence does not say a room teaches facts better. It says the method does the work, and it is nearly silent on the outcomes a retreat is sold for. How you put that to a buyer is craft.

why.title: The comparative effectiveness of web-based and classroom instruction
why.found: A meta-analysis of 96 reports. Web-based instruction was 6 per cent more effective than classroom instruction for declarative knowledge (d = .15), equal for procedural knowledge and equal for satisfaction. With the same methods in both, the two were equally effective for declarative knowledge. Most samples were university students.
why.means: Do not claim the classroom teaches knowledge better. Compare the methods each version allows, and make the case for the room on practice, feedback and outcomes these studies did not measure.

try.text: Take a face-to-face programme you are proposing or running. List its objectives and fill in the table below for each one. Then say your answer to "why not online?" aloud to a colleague in under a minute, starting with what you would move online.

lines: "For the policy and process content, you are right. The research says online does as well when the teaching is the same. I would move that online and save you half a day."
"What the platform version does not have is practice with someone watching. That is what changes how a manager handles a hard conversation."

"So my proposal is one and a half days in the room, not two, with the knowledge done beforehand."

items: **Quoting "online is better"** as the study's finding. The edge was small, for knowledge only, and reversed when people were assigned at random.
**Quoting "there is no difference"** for everything. Skills had few studies and attitudes had almost none.
**Comparing a rich classroom design** with a page-turning e-learning module. That compares methods. Say so.
**Forgetting the date.** The pooled studies end in 2005 and 2008. Live video classrooms and current platforms were not what they tested.

quiz.q: In Sitzmann and colleagues' meta-analysis, what happened to the difference between web-based and classroom instruction when both used the same instructional methods?
quiz.a: It disappeared. The two were equally effective for teaching declarative knowledge.

quiz.q: A retailer wants to replace a one-day product course for store staff with a 40-minute e-learning module and asks whether learning will suffer. The course is half product facts and half practising how to recommend a product to a customer. What do you say?
quiz.a: The product facts can go online with recall questions and little risk. The recommending practice needs rehearsal and feedback from a person, so keep that live or build it into store time with a manager.

quiz.q: Your own marketing draft says "face-to-face training is proven to be more effective than online learning". Do you keep the line?
quiz.a: No. The pooled comparisons found no advantage for the classroom on knowledge when methods were the same. Say what the room makes easy, which is observed practice, feedback and time together, and promise that.

topics.title: Read the media and method debate at source
topics.theory: Clark (1983, 1994) and Kozma (1994) in their own terms

situation.text: A supplier sends a white paper. Learners who used its mobile app scored higher on a product test than a group taught in a classroom. Your client forwards it with one line: "Should we switch?" You have a stake too, because you sell the classroom.

items: **Hold Clark's position in one sentence.** Media are vehicles that deliver instruction, and no medium in itself has been shown to improve learning. When a study shows a gain, look for a difference in method or for novelty.

**Hold Kozma's reply in one sentence.** The better question is under what conditions a medium influences learning, which depends on what it can do, the method that uses it, and the thinking and social activity that learning needs.
**Run Clark's first check** on any comparison study you read. Was the method the same on both sides: the same content, practice, feedback, time and teacher? If not, the study compared methods.
**Apply his second check.** How long did the study run, and was the medium new to the learners? An early gain may be extra attention that fades.
**Then ask Kozma's question of the medium.** What can it do that the other cannot? Which method uses that? Which part of learning does it support?
**Ask about cost and reach separately.** Clark accepts that a medium can change what instruction costs and who it reaches. That can be a good reason to buy.
**Turn the same checks on yourself.** The room is a medium. It does not teach. Say which methods it makes easy.
**Write the client a verdict** in two or three sentences that names the method, not the medium. There is more on [the buying test this leads to](t:3.7).

why.text: **Clark found no benefit from any medium.** Clark's 1983 review looked at the meta-analyses and studies of his day and concluded that there was consistent evidence of no learning benefit from any specific medium. He wrote that media are vehicles for instruction, and compared them to the truck that delivers groceries without changing what we eat. Where studies had shown gains, he pointed to two rival explanations that had not been controlled: the instructional method, and novelty.

**Gains shrank with one teacher or longer studies.** He gave figures for both. In college courses, the advantage for computer-based teaching was .51 when different teachers taught the two versions and .13 when one teacher taught both. In secondary schools, the effect of computer teaching was .56 in studies lasting four weeks or less and about .2 after eight weeks. Both are effect sizes from the reviews he summarised, for computer-based against conventional teaching.

**Kozma asks when media influence learning.** Kozma answered in 1994. His summary says he restates the question as one about conditions: when do media influence learning? He argues that the capabilities of a medium, and the methods that use them, should be considered together with the mental and social processes by which people build knowledge. He illustrates this with a computer project and a video project. Clark replied in the same journal that year. His summary restates the claim that media do not influence learning or motivation.

**Clark tells you how to read a study.** Kozma tells you how to design. The debate is an argument about research design, built on studies in schools and colleges, with no workplace samples named in the pages read. The modern test with some working adults in it is [the meta-analysis comparing web and classroom](t:3.25), which found no difference for knowledge once methods were the same. The checks in the steps are this site's way of putting both positions to work.

why.title: Reconsidering research on learning from media
why.found: A review of meta-analyses and media comparison studies. It found consistent evidence that no specific medium brings a learning benefit, and attributed reported gains to uncontrolled differences in instructional method and to novelty. With one teacher for both versions, the college advantage for computer teaching fell from .51 to .13.
why.means: Before you accept that a medium improved learning, check whether the method was the same on both sides and whether the gain lasted.

try.text: Find one real claim that a medium improves learning: a supplier's case study, a platform's research page or a line in your own marketing. items: **Citing Clark to dismiss every technology.** He accepts that media change cost and reach, and Kozma shows how a capability can make a method practical.
**Citing Kozma to justify any purchase.** His question has three parts. If nobody can name the method and the kind of thinking it supports, the capability is decoration.
**Exempting your own medium.** If you sell face-to-face work, the same two checks apply to your claims.
**Treating old school studies** as the last word on current tools. The logic of the checks holds. The effect sizes are from the early 1980s.

quiz.a: Uncontrolled differences in instructional method, and novelty.

quiz.q: A supplier shows you a pilot in which sales reps who used its virtual reality headset for objection handling outscored reps who watched a recorded webinar. The headset group practised aloud and got feedback. What do you tell the client?
quiz.a: The pilot compared practice with feedback against watching, so it shows the method working. Ask what the headset allows that a cheaper way of practising with feedback would not, and price that.

quiz.q: A client says "Clark proved the medium does not matter, so we will use whatever is cheapest". The objective is for engineers to diagnose faults on equipment that is costly to take out of service. How do you answer?
quiz.a: Cheapest is fine only if it can carry the method the objective needs, which here is repeated practice on realistic faults. Ask Kozma's question: which medium makes that practice possible at all, and choose on that.
