stages.name: Run the room
stages.question: How do we facilitate, in person and online?

parts.title: Hold the room
parts.summary: Presence, questions, group dynamics and story.

topics.title: Slow down and use the pause

situation.text: You are two minutes into opening a day for a software company's sales team. You have read all three aims in one breath, your mouth is dry and you can hear yourself speeding up. Last week a colleague told you not to worry about the words, because communication is "93 per cent non-verbal".

items: **Cut the opening to fit.** For a two-minute opening, write no more than about 250 words. If the script is longer you will have to rush to get through it, so cut words until it fits at an easy pace.
**Mark the pauses on your notes** with a slash: after each aim, after each key point and after every [question you ask](t:4.2). Three or four in the first two minutes is enough.
**Pause at each slash:** close your mouth and stop for two slow breaths, about three seconds. Look at one person, then another. Keep your eyes off your notes and the screen.
**Slow down.** Nerves speed you up, so aim for a pace that feels a little too slow to you. It will sound normal to the room. Finish each sentence before you move or click.

**Vary pace and volume on purpose.** Underline one sentence in each section, the one people must remember, and say it slower and slightly quieter than the rest. Move briskly through set-up and housekeeping.
**Stand still for the underlined sentence**, with both feet planted. Walk between points, not during them.
**Say to yourself "I am excited"** when you feel nervous before you start. Do not try to calm down. Then say your first rehearsed line.
**Rehearse the first two minutes aloud**, standing, until you can say them without notes. There is a [five-minute voice warm-up](t:4.20), and more on [what goes into an opening](t:4.21).

why.text: **A pause gives people time to think.** Presence is the composure and attention that let you hold a room. It comes from preparation and practice more than personality. A pause gives people time to think and signals confidence. That much is craft, and the reasoning is simple. The pause is the only moment when the listener is not also taking in your next sentence. If you rush on, the important point gets the same few seconds as the housekeeping.

**When you teach, words carry the content.** The "93 per cent" figure adds 38 per cent for tone of voice to 55 per cent for the face, leaving 7 per cent for words. Those weights come from 1960s experiments on how people judge liking and disliking. Their author says they apply only when someone is talking about their own feelings or attitudes. When you teach, your words carry the content. So get the words right first, then work on how you say them.

**Calling nerves excitement beat calming down.** The advice on nerves is research. Nerves and excitement feel alike in the body. In one set of experiments, people who told themselves they were excited before singing, speaking in public or doing maths performed better than people who tried to calm down.

**Pausing means cutting content.** There is a cost. A slower pace with pauses covers less, so the content has to shrink, and there is an [order for cutting it](t:4.31). The advice also reverses in places. A pause before you have made the point clear only leaves people confused for longer. And slow is not the aim everywhere. A session delivered at one careful speed is as flat as one delivered in a rush, because it is the contrast that marks the important sentence.

try.text: Record three minutes of a real session on your phone. Watch it once with the sound off and listen once with your eyes shut. Count the pauses of two seconds or more. Then ask a colleague to watch it and name one place where you rushed. Mark that place with a slash, deliver the three minutes again aloud, standing, and record it a second time. Good looks like this: at least four pauses that you chose, and no "um" or "OK" filling them.

try.title: A worked example: the same opening, unmarked and marked
lines: Unmarked, as first delivered. About 20 seconds, with no stops:

"OK so today we've got three aims, first we'll look at why deals stall at the pricing stage, then we'll practise a way of replying to a price objection, and then you'll plan how to use it on a live account, so, let's get going."
Marked for delivery. A slash is two slow breaths. The line in capitals is said slower and slightly quieter.
"Good morning. / Today has three aims."
"One. We'll look at why deals stall when the price comes up. /"
"Two. You'll practise a reply to a price objection, on each other. /"
"Three. YOU WILL LEAVE WITH A PLAN FOR ONE LIVE ACCOUNT. / /"
"Which of those matters most to you this quarter? Tell the person next to you. One minute."
What changed: the words are almost the same. The marked version takes about 45 seconds, and each aim gets its own silence.

items: **You fill the pause** with "um", "OK?" or "right". Close your mouth and breathe in through your nose. A recording will show you which filler is yours.
**You slow everything down** and the session goes flat. Keep the slow pace for the sentences you underlined and let the rest move.

**Body-language claims:** someone claims to read what a room thinks from posture and gestures. Be wary. If you want to know what people think, ask them, using the [checks for reading the room](t:4.14).

**You use room habits on camera** and assume they work. On camera you lose most of your movement and most of the room's reactions, and a silence can look like a frozen screen. Say what the pause is for ("Take ten seconds on that") and practise online delivery separately.
**You perform a personality** that is not yours. A quiet trainer who pauses well holds a room as surely as a loud one.

items.label: Mehrabian (1981), Silent Messages: Implicit Communication of Emotions and Attitudes.
Brooks (2014), Get excited: Reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement.

quiz.q: Where do the figures behind "93 per cent non-verbal" come from, and when do they apply?
quiz.a: From 1960s experiments on how people judge liking and disliking. Their author says they apply only when someone is talking about their own feelings or attitudes.

quiz.q: You are five minutes from starting and your heart is racing. What do you do?
quiz.a: Tell yourself you are excited. Do not try to calm down. In experiments, people who did this performed better. Then say your rehearsed opening lines, slowly.

quiz.q: You have just made the most important point of the morning and you can feel yourself about to rush on. What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop for two slow breaths, standing still, and look round the room. The pause gives people time to take the point in.

topics.tierReason: Slowing down, pausing and rehearsing are standard presentation practice with little direct testing in training rooms. Only the step on reading nerves as readiness has an experiment behind it.

topics.title: Ask, then wait

situation.text: You have just explained a feedback model to ten new managers. You say "Any questions?", wait about a second, say "No? Good" and click to the next slide. At the break you overhear two of them asking each other what the second step meant.

items: **Decide on telling or drawing out** for this moment. Tell when the group lacks the facts, such as a new pricing rule. Draw out when they have experience to work with, such as a hard conversation they have had.
**Write your questions into the session plan** word for word, three to five for each hour. A question made up on the spot tends to come out long, double or closed.
**Ask one open question at a time**, and make it specific: "What would make this hard to use on Monday?" Say how much you want back: one example, or one sentence.
**Count to five after asking**, in your head, before you say anything. Stand still and look round the room. Do not rephrase and do not add a second question.
**Give pairs a minute first** for a hard question, so everyone has thought before anyone speaks: "Take a minute with the person next to you, then I'll take three answers."
**Wait again after an answer**, counting to three, before you respond. Then follow up before you judge: "Say a bit more about that" or "Who sees it differently?"

**Thank the person for a wrong answer**, keep the part that is right and put the rest to the group: "That fits the first case. Does it hold for the second?" This matters because it keeps it [safe to be wrong out loud](t:1.17). If it is a fact people must not leave with wrong, such as a price or a safety step, give the right answer yourself straight after.
**Replace "Any questions?"** with a question that expects some: "What is still unclear about step two? Tell your neighbour, then I'll take two."

why.text: **Presenting and facilitating do different jobs.** Presenting sends content to an audience. Facilitating draws learning out of a group. A skilled trainer knows which the moment needs.

**A longer wait gets longer answers.** In studies of school lessons, teachers usually waited about one second after a question. When they waited three to five seconds, answers got longer, more pupils answered and pupils asked more questions. Most people wait far too little.

why.title: Wait-time and rewards as instructional variables
why.found: From five years of recorded primary science lessons, teachers waited about one second for an answer and replied within about a second of getting one. When both waits were stretched to three to five seconds, pupils gave longer answers, offered more answers unprompted, asked more questions and sounded more confident.
why.means: Count to three in your head after you ask and again after someone answers, and expect to adapt this for adults.

why.text: **Treat three seconds as a starting point.** This research comes from school classrooms, not workplace training. Treat three seconds as a starting point, not a rule. A long silence after an unclear question only adds confusion, so make the question clear first. The advice here on wording questions and replying to wrong answers is craft.

**One second only suits the fastest thinkers.** The reasoning for the wait is that a one-second gap tells the group the question was a courtesy. Only the fastest thinkers can answer in that time, so the same few people do. Five seconds lets slower and more careful people reach an answer. The price is time. Each real question costs a minute or two, so ask fewer and make each one count. The advice reverses when the group has no experience to draw on. Asking beginners to guess a fact wastes their time, so tell them the fact and then ask what they would do with it.

try.text: Write three open questions for your next session or meeting. Say each one aloud. After each one, count to five before you speak, and count to three after each answer. Ask a colleague to time your waits if you can. Afterwards, note who spoke that usually does not. Then practise the wrong-answer lines below aloud, with a colleague feeding you wrong answers, until the reply comes without a wince.

try.title: Words you can use when an answer is wrong
lines: Partly right: "Thank you. The first half fits: you'd describe what you saw. Let's test the second half. Does anyone see a risk in adding why you think they did it?"
Right for a different case: "That works when the person already knows there's a problem. What about when it will come as a surprise?"
Wrong, and it matters: "Thanks for going first. That's a common reading, and it isn't what the policy says. The limit is two days, not five. I'll put it on the flipchart."
Wrong, and you can't see why: "Talk me through how you got there." Then work with the reasoning.
Off the question: "That belongs in this afternoon's session, and I've written it up so we don't lose it. For now, what would you say in the first ten seconds?"
Later, to the room: "That answer helped us. It showed where the model gets misread."
Avoid: "No." "Not quite." "Anyone else?" said flatly while you look away.

items: **Silence feels longer to you** than to the room. Count in your head and keep your face relaxed.
**You answer your own question**, and the group learns to wait for you. Hold your answer back until they have had a go.
**You praise every answer** with "Great!" The group starts answering for your approval, and the one answer you do not praise stands out. Say "thank you" and follow up.
**The same few people answer** everything. Use the [moves for someone who talks too much](t:4.34). If nobody answers at all, use the [moves for a silent group](t:4.35).

**Only the questions you ask** are covered in this topic. There is separate advice on [handling the questions the group asks you](t:4.30), including the one you cannot answer and the hostile one, and on the [questions to ask after an activity](t:4.28).

items.label: Rowe (1972), Wait-Time and Rewards as Instructional Variables: Their Influence on Language, Logic, and Fate Control.
Rowe (1987), Wait Time: Slowing Down May Be a Way of Speeding Up. American Educator.
Tobin (1987), The Role of Wait Time in Higher Cognitive Level Learning.
Stahl (1994), Using "Think-Time" and "Wait-Time" Skillfully in the Classroom.

quiz.q: In the school studies, how long did teachers usually wait after a question, and what changed when they waited three to five seconds?
quiz.a: About one second. With the longer wait, answers got longer, more pupils answered and pupils asked more questions.

quiz.q: You ask the group a question and nobody has answered after five seconds. What do you do?
quiz.a: Check the question was clear and ask it again in one short sentence. Then give people a minute to write or talk in pairs before you take answers. There is a full [order of moves for a silent group](t:4.35).

quiz.q: A participant gives an answer that is wrong, in front of the group. What do you do?
quiz.a: Thank them, keep the part that is right and put the rest to the group as a question. A flat correction teaches them, and everyone watching, to stop offering answers.

topics.tierReason: School classroom studies, pulled together in a published review, link waits of three seconds or more to longer and more frequent answers. None of the summaries read covers adults in workplace training.

topics.title: Manage the group, not only the content

situation.text: It is eleven o'clock on a day for twelve store managers from a retailer, sitting at three tables. One man has answered your last four questions. Two people by the window have not spoken since the introductions. At the back table a disagreement about the rota policy is getting sharper.

items: **Watch the group** as well as the content. Sketch the seating on your session plan and put a tick by a name each time that person speaks to the room. Look at it every ten minutes or so: who has spoken, who has not, and who has stopped looking up.

**Build structure in before the day.** Plan each main discussion in three steps: write alone for a minute or two, compare in pairs for three, then one point from each pair. The same structure fixes most problems once they appear.
**Change the structure when one person dominates**, before you speak to them. There is a full [order of moves for someone who dominates](t:4.34).

**Give each person a visible part** in group tasks. Have everyone write their own answer first, or give out roles such as scribe, timekeeper and reporter, and rotate them at each task. There is more on [forming groups](t:4.25) and on [supporting groups while they work](t:4.26).

**Bring quiet people in** without putting them on the spot. During pair work, stand near them and listen. If they say something useful, ask quietly: "Would you be willing to say that to the room in a minute?" Then invite it.

**Sort a disagreement** by what it is about. If it is about ideas, keep it going and make it useful: write both views on a flipchart and ask what each would need in order to work. If a remark is about a person, step in at once with "Let's stay with the issue", and deal with the rest in private. There is more on [conflict between two participants](t:4.41).

**Use the breaks.** Anything you need to say to one person, say away from the room: "You have a lot of experience with this, and I need to hear from the others too. Can you help me by holding back for the next task?"

why.text: **Group dynamics do not sort themselves out.** The well-known model of forming, storming, norming and performing says a group first gets acquainted, then argues, then settles how it will work, then works well. It is a useful lens. It was built from a review of about 50 earlier studies, many of them of therapy groups, and not from new data on work teams. Real groups do not move through the stages so neatly.
**A visible part keeps everyone contributing.** People tend to contribute less in a group than alone. Giving each person a visible part counters that. The rest of this page is craft.

**Structure carries no blame.** Structure comes before a word to the person because structure carries no blame. Writing alone and then talking in pairs gives the quiet people a turn and the dominant person a limit, and nobody has been corrected in front of colleagues, which keeps it [safe to be wrong out loud](t:1.17). The trade-off is pace. A small group that is talking freely and evenly does not need three steps for every question, so leave it alone.

**This topic gives the general approach.** Each hard case has its own topic with the order of moves and the words to say: [the person who talks too much](t:4.34), [the silent group](t:4.35), [the cynic](t:4.36), [the expert](t:4.37), [the senior person who takes over](t:4.38), [side conversations](t:4.39) and [conflict between two people](t:4.41).

try.text: Pick three situations that you have met or dread, from [the person who talks too much](t:4.34) to [conflict between two participants](t:4.41). For each, write the first thing you would change in the structure and the first sentence you would say. Role-play one with a colleague, aloud, with them playing the difficult part. Then, in your next real meeting, keep a tick sheet of who speaks for twenty minutes and see what it shows that you had not noticed.

items: **Norms about speaking up** and silence [differ between cultures](t:4.7). Listen in on pair work before you decide that a quiet person has switched off.
**Publicly correcting someone** costs the whole room, because everyone watching learns what happens to people who get it wrong. Use the break.

**A large group:** do not raise your voice to hold it. Use more structure: pairs, tables and a signal for attention. There is more on [group size and staffing](t:2.33) and on [forming groups and moving people](t:4.25).

**Asking people by name:** name people only after they have had time to prepare an answer, by writing alone or talking in a pair. Say in advance that you will ask people by name, and let anyone pass. That keeps it [safe to be asked](t:1.17) and avoids [putting anyone on the spot in public](t:1.13).

**Giving the loudest person the pen** has a cost. The scribe decides what gets recorded, and the job can feel like a punishment. Offer the job and do not impose it. There is more on [handling the person who talks too much](t:4.34).

items.label: Tuckman (1984), This Week's Citation Classic: Developmental sequence in small groups. The author's own account of the 1965 paper.

quiz.q: What was the forming, storming, norming and performing model built from?
quiz.a: A review of about 50 earlier studies, many of them of therapy groups. It was not built from new data on work teams, so use it as a rough lens.

quiz.q: One person has answered your last four questions and the others have stopped trying. What do you do first?
quiz.a: Change the structure. Everyone writes an answer alone, then compares in pairs, and you take one point from each pair. Speak to the person only if that does not work, following the [order of moves for a dominant voice](t:4.34).

quiz.q: In a group of five, two people have left the task to the other three. What do you change?
quiz.a: Give every person a visible part. Each writes their own answer before the group talks, or each takes a named role. People put in less when their part cannot be seen.

topics.tierReason: The stage model is a synthesis of older studies used as a lens, and the steps for handling a group are professional practice. The social loafing research behind individual accountability could not be opened in this run.

topics.title: Use a story to make the point concrete
topics.theory: Storytelling and the curse of knowledge

situation.text: You are training a software company's support team to write better ticket notes. You have said "handover errors come from assumed knowledge" three times, in three different ways. Fourteen people are nodding politely and nobody has written anything down.

items: **Write the point first**, in one sentence a participant could repeat. The story is there to serve that sentence.
**Find a short, true story** that shows the idea. Look in your own work, or ask the client while you prepare: "Tell me about a time this went wrong."

**Make it concrete, in four beats**: a person, a place and time, what happened, and what it cost. Include one exact detail, such as the words someone wrote. Keep it to about 150 words, which is roughly a minute spoken.
**Say the point it makes**, out loud, straight after the story. Do not leave it implied.
**Use an analogy** from something the group already knows: "Write the note you would leave for a house-sitter who has never seen your boiler."
**Hand it to the group**: "Where has something like this happened to you? Two minutes with your neighbour." Their own cases are closer to their work than yours.
**Test the story** on someone outside the subject and ask them what the point was. If they retell the story and miss the point, change it or cut it.
**Keep a bank of stories**: one line for each, the point it serves and when you last used it. Retire the stale ones.

why.text: **People recall stories better than essays.** A well-chosen story makes an abstract point concrete and easier to remember. A meta-analysis found that people understood and recalled stories better than essays.

why.title: Stories against essays: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across more than 75 samples and over 33,000 participants, stories were understood and recalled better than essays. Results varied a great deal between studies and there were signs of publication bias.
why.means: Use a short story to carry an abstract point, and do not expect every story to help.

why.text: **Experts forget what newcomers lack.** People who know a subject well find it hard to set that knowledge aside and judge what a newcomer will follow. This is called the curse of knowledge. The practical guard is to test your explanation on a newcomer. There is a method to draw out [the steps an expert no longer notices](t:3.17). The curse also explains why repeating the abstract version fails. The sentence is clear to you because you already hold the cases behind it. The group does not, and the story gives them one.

**A rule of thumb: concrete ideas last.** Practitioner writing on communication suggests that ideas which last tend to be concrete, unexpected and to carry some feeling. Treat that as a rule of thumb. The four beats, the length and the story bank on this page are craft as well.

**One vivid case proves nothing general.** The strength of a story is also its risk. A vivid case can stick harder than the evidence, and one case proves nothing general. The authors of the story meta-analysis warn against forcing all content into story form, so use a story where it fits the point. A procedure with eight steps is better as a checklist. A group of experts may find a beginner's cautionary tale patronising, so with them, ask for their cases before you offer yours.

try.text: Pick one abstract idea you teach. Write a story for it in four sentences: a person, a place, what happened, and the point. Tell it aloud to a colleague, timed and without notes, and ask what they think they will remember tomorrow. If they give you the point, keep the story. If they give you only the detail, rework the last line and tell it again.

try.title: A worked example: from rule to story, for a support team

head: Beat
What the trainer says
rows: The abstract version
"Handover errors come from assumed knowledge."
A person
"Picture a support agent. Good at her job, eighteen months in."
A place and time
"It's Friday, ten to six. She is handing a ticket to the weekend team before a week's leave."
What happened, with the exact detail
"Her note says: 'Customer wants the usual fix.' The weekend agent has never spoken to this customer. He spends forty minutes working out what the usual fix is, and applies the wrong one."
What it cost
"On Monday the customer's finance team can't send invoices, and the account manager spends the morning on the phone."
The point, said out loud
"She knew exactly what she meant. That was the problem. Write the note for a stranger."
The analogy
"Think of the note you'd leave a house-sitter who has never seen your boiler."
Over to the group
"Where has a note like that caught you out? Two minutes with your neighbour."

items: **A vivid story can stick harder** than the evidence. Do not use one case to prove a general claim. Say "here is one case" and give the evidence separately.
**The story gets a laugh** and nobody remembers what it was for. Say the point at the end, and test it on an outsider.
**Every story makes you the hero.** A story where you got it wrong is easier to listen to, and it makes it [safer for others to admit mistakes](t:1.17).
**Other people's stories** need their permission. Change names and details that would identify a client or colleague. This is part of your [professional ethics as a trainer](t:4.16).
**The story grows** each time you tell it. Time it now and then, and cut it back to a minute.

items.label: Mar and colleagues (2021), Memory and comprehension of narrative versus expository texts: a meta-analysis. Psychonomic Bulletin and Review.
Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber (1989), The curse of knowledge in economic settings: an experimental analysis. Journal of Political Economy.

quiz.q: What is the curse of knowledge?
quiz.a: People who know a subject well find it hard to set that knowledge aside and judge what a newcomer will follow.

quiz.q: You have explained a principle twice and the group still looks blank. What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop repeating the abstract version. Tell a short true story with a person, a place and what happened, then say the point in one sentence.

quiz.q: You have a funny story that always gets a laugh, but people rarely remember what it was meant to show. What do you do?
quiz.a: Change it or cut it. A story belongs in the session only if people take away the point. If you keep it, say the point out loud at the end.

topics.tierReason: One meta-analysis found stories are understood and recalled better than essays, but the studies varied widely, showed signs of publication bias, and tested texts, not a trainer's spoken stories.

topics.title: Set up the room before you plan the session
topics.theory: The learning environment: physical, virtual and hybrid

situation.text: You arrive thirty minutes before a session for twelve new managers. A long boardroom table fills the room, there is no free wall space and the projector screen is at the far end. Your plan has four table-group tasks and a wall of sticky notes.

items: **Ask about the room before you design.** Send the organiser five questions: how big the room is and whether the furniture moves, how much wall space there is and whether paper may be stuck to it, where the screen is, how light and how noisy it gets, and how people get in. Ask for a photo.

**Arrange seating for the activity** that takes most of the time. Use small tables of four or five for group work, with the side facing the screen left empty. Use a horseshoe for discussion with up to about 16 people. Keep rows for a short one-way briefing.
**Draw the room.** Mark where groups work, where you stand, where the flipcharts go and what the person in the worst seat can see.
**Arrive at least forty minutes early** and move the furniture. Aim to be set fifteen minutes before the start, so you can greet people, which is part of [how you open a session](t:4.21).

**Check that everyone can see and hear**, and can get in. Sit in the back seat and read your smallest slide, which should be [readable from the back of the room](t:3.22). Ask someone to stand at the back while you speak from the front. Then go through the access checklist on this page.
**Check temperature and noise** when you arrive. Find out who at the venue can change them and put their number in your phone.
**Change the activity** if the furniture cannot move. Around a fixed boardroom table, use pairs and tasks at flipchart sheets on the walls or windows in place of table groups.
**Treat the platform as the room** when you are online. Set up the breakout rooms, shared documents and sound before people join, as you would for any [live online session](t:4.10).

why.text: **The room changes how content lands.** The same content lands differently in a well or badly arranged space. Layout signals what kind of session this is: rows say "listen", small tables say "work together".
Research on learning spaces is mostly from schools and universities. For workplace training, treat this as informed practice.

**A room works on the trainer too.** One university study compared the same course, with the same lecturer, in a room with round tables and a room with rows. In the round-table room the lecturer talked less and led more discussion, although he meant to teach both groups the same way. It was one course with about forty students, so take it as an illustration. What it illustrates is that a room works on the trainer as well as the group. If you find yourself lecturing more than you planned, look at the furniture.

**The room sets limits you cannot argue with.** Ask before you design because the room sets limits you cannot argue with on the day. Tables decide whether groups can form. Wall space decides whether work can stay in view on [flipcharts and walls](t:4.18). The gap between groups decides whether they can hear themselves. Every layout also has a cost. Small tables take more floor than rows, so the room holds fewer people. A horseshoe suits talk across the room and is awkward for group work. Rows are the right choice for a twenty-minute briefing to sixty people. Choose for the main activity and accept the cost for the rest.

try.text: Draw the room for your next session. Mark where groups work, where you stand and what people can see. Send the five questions to the organiser today. On the day, time your set-up, then sit in the worst seat and have someone speak your opening line from the front while you listen.

try.title: A room access checklist
lines: Before the day: ask everyone, in the joining instructions, what would help them take part. Include food and prayer needs.
Microphone: if the room has one, use it, even if you think your voice carries. Ask about a hearing loop and whether it works.
Questions from the floor: repeat each one before you answer, so the whole room and anyone lip-reading has heard it.
Writing: large, dark letters on flipcharts. Do not use red against green to carry meaning.
Routes: walk the step-free route from the entrance to the room, the toilets, lunch and the fire exit yourself.
Seating: let people choose where to sit. Leave space at a table for a wheelchair and keep some chairs near the door.
Standing activities: give a seated version as part of the instruction.
Quiet space: find a room or corner where someone can step out, and say where it is in your opening.
Lighting: avoid glare on the screen and do not stand in front of a bright window. Keep the lights up enough to read and to see your face.
Printed copies: have paper copies of the slides and of any text on screen, including two in large print.
Breaks: fewer and longer, with a clear statement that anyone can step out at any time.

items: **You accept the room** as you find it. Venues set rooms for meetings, not for training. Move the furniture, and put it back at the end.
**You skip the checks** at a venue you know. Go through the access checklist on this page for every venue, including ones you have used before. Lifts break and rooms get swapped.
**The room is too hot** or too loud and you carry on. Call the venue contact as soon as you notice, and no later than the first break.
**You plan wall work** and the venue does not allow tape. Ask beforehand. There is more on [what may go on the walls](t:4.18) and on [preparing the materials](t:3.21).
**A venue for a residential:** you are choosing and briefing it. That is a bigger job with a site visit. There is separate advice on [choosing and briefing the venue](t:8.11).

items.label: Whiteside, Brooks and Walker (2010), Making the case for space: three years of empirical research on learning environments. EDUCAUSE Quarterly.

quiz.q: In the university study of one course taught in two rooms, what changed in the round-table room?
quiz.a: The lecturer talked less and led more discussion, although he meant to teach both groups the same way. It was one course with about forty students, so it is an illustration.

quiz.q: You arrive to find one long boardroom table, and your plan has four group tasks. What do you do?
quiz.a: Push the table to the wall if you can and set four clusters of chairs. If it cannot move, switch the group tasks to pairs and to tasks at flipchart sheets on the walls or windows.

quiz.q: A participant asks a question from the back and half the room cannot hear it. What do you do?
quiz.a: Repeat the question before you answer, so the whole room and anyone lip-reading has it. Use the microphone if the room has one.

topics.tierReason: Room set-up is professional practice. The one study read is a small comparison in a single university course, with nothing on workplace training.

topics.title: Train the team together when the work is done together

situation.text: At a software company, escalations keep getting lost between the support team and the on-call engineers. The client sends five people from five teams on a one-day teamwork course. They enjoy it. On Monday each goes back to a team that was not there, and the handover is the same as before.

items: **Find where work passes between people** by asking the client. List the three moments where coordination fails, such as a shift handover or an escalation, and pick one.

**Train the team together** where the work is done as a team. Bring the people who do that task into one session, including the team lead and the people on the other side of the handover. Plan cover for their work. Half a day is often enough for one task.
**Practise the team's real tasks.** Build the practice from a recent real case with the customer's details removed. Do not use an abstract teamwork game.
**Run the task once** the way the team does it now, for about fifteen minutes. You and one team member observe and write down what was said and what was left out.

**Debrief as a team** for fifteen to twenty minutes. There is a set of [questions to ask in a debrief](t:4.28). The lead speaks last, as with any [senior person who might take over](t:4.38). End with one or two changes, such as a fixed order for the handover note.
**Run it again with the changes**, and give each person a turn at another role. The support agent plays the on-call engineer and the engineer plays the agent.

**Practise communication, handovers and speaking up**, with the words. Each person says aloud once: "I'm not sure about this. Can we check before we go on?" The lead practises the reply: "Thank you. Let's check."
**Agree to debrief after real work too**: ten minutes after the next real escalation, with the same questions. Put the first one in the diary before people leave.

why.text: **Team skills are different from individual skills.** A team has to coordinate, share a picture of the task and back each other up. Those are learned by practising together.

**Team training has a moderate, positive effect.** A meta-analysis of 93 results from 2,650 teams found that team training had a moderate, positive effect on how teams think, feel, work together and perform. A later meta-analysis of 129 healthcare studies found the same direction. A third found that teams and individuals who debriefed did about 20 to 25 per cent better than those who did not.

why.title: Does team training improve team performance?
why.found: Pooling 93 results from 2,650 teams, team training had a moderate, positive effect on team thinking, attitudes, teamwork and performance. Training content, team stability and team size changed the size of the effect.
why.means: Train teams on their real work, and expect better results from stable teams with focused content.

why.text: **Whole team versus a few is untested.** These studies compare team training with none. They show that what is trained, how stable the team is and how big it is all change the result. They do not test whether training the whole team beats training a few members, so treat that step as sound reasoning.

**Swapping roles shows what a handover lacks.** Swapping roles is craft with a plain logic. People write a poor handover because they have never been the person receiving it, and ten minutes on the other side shows them what was missing. The same logic tells you when to train individuals. If the gap is something one person does alone, such as product knowledge, train the people who lack it. If the membership changes every shift, there is no fixed team to train, so teach everyone the same handover routine. That is reasoning too, not a tested rule.

try.text: For one team you train, list the three moments where coordination fails. Design practice for one, using the plan below as a pattern. Then say the briefing for the first run aloud to a colleague in under a minute, and ask them to tell you back what the team is about to do.

quiz.q: What did the meta-analysis of 93 results from 2,650 teams find?
quiz.a: Team training had a moderate, positive effect on how teams think, feel, work together and perform. What was trained, how stable the team was and its size all changed the result.

quiz.q: A client asks for a teamwork day for one person from each of six teams. The real problem is poor shift handovers. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Train one whole team at a time on its own handover: practise it, swap roles and debrief. Say that this is sound reasoning. The studies do not test whole teams against a few members.

quiz.q: In a team practice, the junior members say nothing while their manager is in the room. What do you do?
quiz.a: Have everyone write their view before anyone speaks, and take the manager's last. Before the next session, brief the manager to ask before telling, as you would any [senior person who takes over](t:4.38).

topics.tierReason: Meta-analyses show team training and debriefs improve team results, but they compare training with no training, and do not test whether the whole team must attend together.

topics.title: Adjust for the cultures in the room

situation.text: At a software company's sales kick-off you have fourteen people from six country offices, and nine of them are working in their second language. You show a new pricing approach and ask "Who disagrees with this?" At home that question starts a ten-minute argument. Here nobody speaks.

items: **Find out who is in the room**: where they work, which languages they work in, and how senior they are to each other. Ask the client, and ask a local colleague what to watch for.
**Send the discussion questions** and any reading two or three days ahead, so people working in a second language can prepare what they want to say.
**Vary how people contribute**: two minutes writing alone, three minutes in pairs, then the group. Ask each pair for one concern, and say it need not be their own.
**Say exactly what you are asking for**: "I want to hear the problems with this. Disagreeing with me is the task."
**Speak plainly and avoid idiom.** Use short sentences, put each instruction on a slide as well as saying it, and slow down. Do not get louder.

**Check that the task has landed** without asking "Is that clear?", which gets a polite yes. Ask pairs to tell each other what they are about to do, one of the checks for [instructions people can follow first time](t:4.24).

**Plan for rank.** Where a manager and their own team are in the same group, have everyone write first and take the senior person's view last. There is more on [the senior person who takes over](t:4.38).
**Add time.** Working in a second language is tiring. As a working rule, allow about a quarter more time for discussion tasks and keep every break you planned.

why.text: **Not every group will challenge the trainer.** Groups differ in how directly people speak, how they treat rank, and what silence means. A method that assumes everyone will challenge the trainer does not travel.

**Most variation in values is within countries.** Models that score countries on cultural dimensions are widely used and criticised for treating a country as one culture. A meta-analysis of 558 studies that used the best-known model found that about 80 per cent of the variation in cultural values lies within countries, not between them.

why.title: Does country equate with culture?
why.found: A meta-analysis of 558 studies using Hofstede's framework found that about 80 per cent of the variation in cultural values sits within countries. The authors conclude that country is often a weak stand-in for culture.
why.means: Find out about the people in the room. Do not predict a person from a passport.

why.text: **National trait lists misjudge many people.** That finding shapes the approach on this page. If most of the variation is inside countries, a list of national traits will be wrong about many of the people in front of you. So ask about these particular people, and design activities that work across the range. Someone who will argue with you in public and someone who never would can both write a concern on a card. This is craft built on the finding. The study did not test it.

**Use country guides for questions, not predictions.** Books that place countries on scales are practitioner guides. Use them for questions to ask, not for predictions about a person. The extra steps cost time and some spontaneity. With a group that is already arguing freely, drop the written step and let them go.

try.text: Take one discussion activity. Add a written step and a pair step before the group step. Then record yourself giving the instruction for it, and listen for idiom, long sentences and speed. Record it again until a colleague who has not seen the plan can tell you the task back after one hearing.

items: **Guessing someone's culture from their name** is a mistake. Ask where they work and which language they would like the materials in.
**Working in a second language** is tiring. Slow down, and simplify the sentences without simplifying the ideas.
**Humour and examples may not travel.** Try them on a local colleague first.
**You treat silence as agreement.** Collect views in writing before you conclude anything.

**A group that stays silent** whatever you try has [its own order of moves](t:4.35). There is also advice on delivering in [another country or through an interpreter](t:9.27), and on [writing materials that will be translated](t:3.16).

quiz.q: In the meta-analysis of 558 studies, how much of the variation in cultural values lay within countries?
quiz.a: About 80 per cent. Country is often a weak stand-in for culture.

quiz.q: You ask a group from six countries "Who disagrees with this?" and nobody speaks. What do you do?
quiz.a: Have everyone write one concern on a card and compare in pairs. Each pair reads out one concern that is not their own. Say plainly that you want to hear the problems.

quiz.q: A colleague warns you that people from one country "never challenge the trainer". How do you use that?
quiz.a: As a question to ask, not a prediction about anyone. Find out about the people who are coming, and build in written and paired steps so nobody has to challenge you in public to take part.

topics.tierReason: The advice is facilitation practice with no direct test. The evidence read supports only the caution against judging people by country.

parts.title: Teach online
parts.summary: Remote and hybrid sessions on their own terms.

topics.title: Design against video-call fatigue

situation.text: A client has moved your six-hour classroom day for sixteen customer success managers online, with the timetable unchanged. By half past two the cameras are going off one by one and the chat has gone quiet. Two people have messaged you to say they have a headache.

items: **Rebuild the timetable.** As a working rule, cut any live block longer than about forty minutes and put a gap of at least ten minutes after it. Move one-way input to pre-work, which [keeps live time for interaction](t:4.10). If the client allows, spread a full day across two or three shorter sessions.
**Make faces smaller.** In the first five minutes, suggest people shrink the call window or sit further back, so nobody spends an hour in close-up eye contact.
**Suggest people hide their own image**, and show them how. Most platforms have the option on the menu of your own video tile. Find it on the client's platform before the day.

**Build in movement and audio-only stretches.** Give each session one task away from the screen, such as a ten-minute paired phone call taken while walking. At each change of block, ask everyone to stand up for a minute with cameras off.

**Reduce what people must watch at once**: faces, chat and slides. Use one at a time. When you ask people to type in chat, stop talking. When you want them to listen to each other, stop sharing the slide.
**Give people a choice about cameras**, and say it out loud: "Cameras are your choice. I'd like them on in the small groups if you can. While I'm presenting, off is fine."
**Check people are with you** in other ways. Ask for an answer in chat or a poll every few minutes, so a dark square is not your only signal when you are [reading the room](t:4.14).
**Ask the client for meeting-free gaps**: keep the half hour before and after each session free of other video meetings.

why.text: **The four causes are likely, not proven.** One researcher proposes four likely causes of video-call fatigue: too much close-up eye contact, seeing yourself constantly, sitting still, and the extra effort of sending and reading non-verbal cues. He says the four have not yet been tested directly, so treat them as likely, not proven. Each has a design answer.

why.title: A scale for video-call fatigue
why.found: The authors built a 15-item questionnaire covering general, social, emotional, visual and motivational fatigue, and tested it with 2,724 people. People with more frequent, longer and more closely packed video meetings reported more fatigue. This is survey data, so it shows a link, not a cause.
why.means: Shorten live blocks and put gaps between them.

why.text: **The fatigue comes from the setting.** Do not read it as a lack of effort from the learner. In survey data, more frequent, longer and closely packed video meetings go with more fatigue, which is why the steps shorten the blocks and protect the gaps. The forty-minute figure is a working rule, not a research finding.

**Each answer has a price.** Cameras on may help connection and may cost energy. Cameras off lowers the load on the learner and takes away most of your cues, so you have to replace them with chat and polls. Shorter sessions over more days are kinder and harder to schedule, and some clients will say no. When that happens, keep the single day and put your effort into the gaps, the audio-only tasks and the pre-work. For a half-hour call with four people who know each other, most of this is unnecessary.

try.text: Take an online session that left people tired. Against each of the four causes, write one change. Then, as a working rule, cut any live block longer than about forty minutes and put a gap after it. Last, say your first five minutes aloud on a test call with a colleague, including where to find the option to hide their own image, and ask whether they could follow it.

items: **You require cameras on all day.** Cameras on may help connection and may cost energy. Let people choose, and ask for them only where it matters most.
**You talk while people type.** Asking people to follow chat and slides at once splits their attention and adds [load that teaches nothing](t:1.2). Stop talking while they read or type.
**You read a dark square** as someone not trying. Ask for a response in chat or a poll before you conclude anything.
**The break becomes email time** on the same screen. Say what the break is for, and put the return time on a slide.
**You call the four causes proven** when you present them to a client. They have not been tested directly. Say they are likely, and that the survey data shows a link, not a cause.

items.label: Bailenson (2021), Nonverbal overload: a theoretical argument for the causes of Zoom fatigue. Technology, Mind, and Behavior.
Fauville and colleagues (2021), Zoom Exhaustion and Fatigue Scale. Computers in Human Behavior Reports.

quiz.q: Name the four proposed causes of video-call fatigue. Have they been tested?
quiz.a: Close-up eye contact, seeing yourself, sitting still, and the effort of sending and reading non-verbal cues. They have not yet been tested directly, so treat them as likely.

quiz.q: A client asks you to run your six-hour classroom day online with the same timetable. What do you change?
quiz.a: Break it into short live blocks with gaps, move one-way input to [pre-work before the live session](t:4.10), add an audio-only or walking task, and make cameras optional during input.

quiz.q: A participant keeps their camera off all afternoon. What do you do?
quiz.a: Nothing about the camera, if you gave people the choice. Check they are with you another way, such as an answer in chat or a poll.

topics.tierReason: The four causes are a theoretical argument that its author says has not been tested directly, and the supporting evidence read is survey data.

topics.title: Build connection, thinking and direction online

situation.text: A six-week online course for 24 new managers at a technology company is ten videos and a discussion forum. In week two, three people have posted. The tutor's last message was the welcome on day one.

items: **Audit the course against the three presences**: social, cognitive and teaching. For each, write what a learner would see this week that shows it. A blank line is your answer.

**Help people seem real to each other.** In week one, ask each person for a short introduction in a set form: name, team and one case from their own work, in about 100 words. Reply to each within a day and use names when you reply.
**Put people in fixed groups** of five or six for the whole course, each with its own thread. A post to five people gets read. A post to 24 often does not.
**Set tasks that make people think** and discuss, with two deadlines: "By Wednesday, post one case from your own work where this failed. By Friday, reply to one other person with a question."
**Bring discussion to a conclusion.** On Friday afternoon, post a summary: what the group concluded, one question still open, and two or three contributions credited by name.
**Be visibly there**, to a pattern you announce. As a working rule, post at set times each week, reply to first posts within a day and sum up each discussion.
**Block the time in your diary** before the course starts. Time yourself in week one and tell the client what the course needs each week.
**Find the weakest of the three** and add one move to strengthen it. Then measure the learning yourself with [a task you assess](t:2.25).

why.text: **The framework names three kinds of presence.** A widely used framework, the Community of Inquiry, says good online learning needs three kinds of presence working together. Social presence is people coming across to each other as real. Cognitive presence is people working ideas out through discussion. Teaching presence is someone designing, guiding and steering. The framework was built to describe written, discussion-based courses in universities.
**Weak courses give no reason to talk.** The common weak pattern is a set of content, a tutor who rarely appears, and no reason for learners to talk to each other.

why.title: Learning in communities of inquiry: a review
why.found: The authors reviewed the studies that used the framework up to 2008. Few measured learning, and those that did mostly used a single survey question on how much students felt they had learned. They concluded the evidence did not show deep learning arising from the model.
why.means: Use the three presences as a design checklist, and measure learning yourself.

why.text: **Posting has to pay the learner back.** The steps on this page are craft, organised by the framework. Their logic is cost and return. Posting to a forum costs a learner time and some exposure, and "post your thoughts" offers nothing back. A task about their own work makes the post worth writing. A required reply means somebody will read it. A Friday summary shows the discussion went somewhere. Remove any one of these and posting stops paying.

**Few studies behind it measured learning.** The framework is widely used and has its critics. A 2009 review found that few studies had measured learning at all, and most relied on students rating their own learning. So use it to spot what is missing, and do not tell a client it proves anything. Its scope is limited too. It describes courses that run in writing over weeks. For a live online session, use the advice on [keeping live time for interaction](t:4.10). A reference library that people dip into when they are stuck is a job aid, and it needs no community. There is more on [building a job aid](t:5.7).

try.text: Audit an online course for the three presences. Add one move to strengthen the weakest. Then write the Monday post for one week and record it as a two-minute video in one take, as you would post it. Watch it back and check that the task, both deadlines and the time of your summary are all said.

items: **A forum needs a reason** to post. Give a task about the learner's own work, with a deadline and a required reply.
**Presence takes facilitator time.** Budget for it, and agree the weekly hours with the client before the course starts. Presence that relies on spare moments tends to stop by week three.
**You reply to every post** at length, and the learners stop replying to each other. Answer first posts briefly with a question, then step back until the summary.
**You oversell the framework:** you tell the client it guarantees deep learning. The 2009 review concluded the evidence did not show that. Measure the learning yourself.
**The framework fits written courses** that run over weeks. For a live online session, use the advice on [keeping live time for interaction](t:4.10).

items.label: Garrison, Anderson and Archer, Critical thinking and computer conferencing: a model and tool to assess cognitive presence. A paper by the framework's authors that sets out the three presences.
Rourke and Kanuka (2009), Learning in communities of inquiry: a review of the literature. Journal of Distance Education.

quiz.q: What are the three presences in the Community of Inquiry framework?
quiz.a: Social: people come across to each other as real. Cognitive: people work ideas out through discussion. Teaching: someone designs, guides and steers.

quiz.q: Your online course is ten videos and a forum with no posts. What do you change first?
quiz.a: Give the forum a task: post one case from your own work and reply to one other person with a question. Then post your own summary of what the group concluded at the end of the week.

quiz.q: A client says this framework proves that discussion forums produce deep learning. What do you say?
quiz.a: It does not. A 2009 review found that few studies measured learning, and most relied on students rating their own. Use the three presences as a design checklist and measure the learning yourself.

topics.tierReason: It is a widely used framework from university online discussion, and a review found very little direct measurement of whether it leads to learning.

topics.title: Keep live time for interaction

situation.text: A two-hour webinar on handling price objections for a software company's account managers has ninety minutes of slides and ten minutes for questions. Forty people join. By the half-hour mark the chat is silent and a third of the names have gone from the list.

items: **Move anything one-way to pre-work**: a twenty-minute recording or a two-page read, sent a week ahead with one question to answer. Open the live session with a poll on it, so that doing the pre-work counts.

**Cut the live session** to what needs people together, and cap the group at a size where everyone can practise. Ninety minutes with a five-minute break carries two or three skills. Write it as a run sheet with a column for the producer, like the one below.

**Use each tool for a purpose**: polls, chat, breakout rooms and shared documents, to get people thinking. A poll makes people recall or commit to an answer. Chat lets everyone answer at once. Breakouts are for discussion and practice. A shared document holds what a group produces.

**Talk for about six minutes at most** without the group doing something, as a working rule. In chat, ask people to type and hold: "Don't press enter until I say." Everyone sends together and nobody copies the first answer.

**Give each breakout a clear task**, a named reporter and a time, in groups of three or four. There is more on [how to give the instruction](t:4.24), and the breakout checklist on this page covers the mechanics. Use pairs before whole-group discussion.

**Have a second person run the technology**, as producer. Send them the run sheet, walk through it on a fifteen-minute call the day before, and agree a private channel outside the platform, such as phone messages.
**Open the room fifteen minutes early**, with a question on the slide for people to answer in chat as they arrive. Start on the minute, as you would when you [open any session](t:4.21).

**Plan for failure.** Have a dial-in number, the organiser's phone number and a task people can do alone while you reconnect. It helps to [rehearse what could go wrong](t:4.13). With no producer, simplify: chat and one other tool, rooms assigned in advance, and a participant asked to watch the chat for you.

why.text: **Live time is scarce.** Spend it on what needs real-time interaction. If a live session has no interaction, it should not be live. A recording handles one-way input better, because people can pause it, replay it and watch it when they are fresh.

**Live online did slightly better than self-paced.** The research is on formats, not on this advice. One meta-analysis found live online learning did slightly better than self-paced online learning on what people learned, and no clear difference from the classroom. Another found blended courses beat classroom teaching, but those courses also gave people more time and more interaction, so the mix alone may not be the cause. The run sheet, the six-minute rule and the producer's role are craft.

**The producer frees your attention for learners.** The producer matters because your attention is the limit. You get fewer cues online, so you need all of your attention for the learners. Each latecomer to admit, poll to launch and microphone to fix takes it away for half a minute, and the group feels the gap. The trade is coverage. An interactive ninety minutes carries far less content than ninety minutes of slides, which is what the pre-work is for. The advice reverses for a one-way announcement to three hundred people. Record it, or run it as a webinar with questions, and do not call it a workshop.
**Fatigue shapes the plan as well.** The [reasons video calls tire people](t:4.8) explain the break at the midpoint and stopping the screen share while people talk.

try.text: Redesign an online session so every live minute is interactive. Move the rest to pre-work. Write the result as a run sheet with a producer column. Then rehearse the first ten minutes on a real call, with a colleague as producer: the arrival question, the opening, the poll and the type-and-hold chat. Good looks like this: you never touch a control yourself, and you never have to ask whether people can see your screen.

try.title: A breakout checklist
lines: Give the whole instruction before you open the rooms: the task, what to bring back, the time, who speaks.
Show the task on a slide and paste the same words into the chat, so people can still read it inside their room.
Groups of three or four. Pairs stall if one person drops out, and five is too many for everyone to speak.
One shared document per room, with the link in the chat and the room number at the top of the page.
Each room names a spokesperson before it starts on the task. Suggest a rule, such as the person whose first name comes first in the alphabet.
Give a time call into every room at the halfway point and at one minute to go.
Producer before the session: build the rooms, check the links to the shared documents, agree how you will reach each other privately.
Producer during: open the rooms on your word, send the time calls, move anyone left alone into another group, let latecomers in.
Producer throughout: watch the chat and the waiting room, and tell you if a room asks for help.
You: visit two or three rooms with your camera on, listen for a minute, and leave unless you are asked something.
On return: one point from each spokesperson, in room order, with no repeats.

items: **A breakout room sits in silence** because it did not have a clear task. Fix the instruction so that [people can follow it first time](t:4.24).
**You get fewer cues online.** Ask people what they are thinking, by poll or in chat. There is more on [reading the room](t:4.14).
**Few people did the pre-work**, so you teach it again live. Next time nobody will do it. Run the poll, give a three-minute recap, and put people who watched it with people who did not.
**You and the producer miss cues** from each other. Agree the cue words in the walk-through: "Poll one, please" and "Rooms open, please".
**The tools become the point.** Chat, one kind of poll and breakouts are enough for ninety minutes.

items.label: Martin, Sun, Turk and Ritzhaupt (2021), A meta-analysis on the effects of synchronous online learning on cognitive and affective educational outcomes. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning.
Means, Toyama, Murphy and Bakia (2013), The effectiveness of online and blended learning: a meta-analysis of the empirical literature. Teachers College Record.

quiz.q: What did the meta-analysis find when it compared live online learning with self-paced online learning and with the classroom?
quiz.a: Live online did slightly better than self-paced online on what people learned. There was no clear difference from the classroom.

quiz.q: You visit a breakout room. Nobody is talking and nobody is sure what the task is. What do you do differently next time?
quiz.a: Give the whole instruction before you open the rooms, show it on a slide and paste the same words into the chat. Have each room name a spokesperson before it starts.

quiz.q: You are running a live session alone. Two people are stuck in the waiting room and one cannot hear, while you are mid-explanation. What does this tell you to change?
quiz.a: Get a producer. Someone else lets people in, sorts the sound and watches the chat, so you can attend to the learners.

topics.tierReason: The design advice is practitioner convention. The studies read compare formats of online learning and do not test interaction against lecture in a live session.

topics.title: In hybrid, design for the remote person first

situation.text: Six people from a leadership team are round a table in the office and four are on a screen at the far end. The room talks for ten minutes. Then someone turns to the screen and asks whether the people online have anything to add. One of them has had a hand up for six minutes.

items: **Decide whether hybrid is the right format.** Ask two things: can the remote people hear every voice in the room, and can they get a turn without waving? If you cannot make it fair, run it all online.

**Sort the sound first.** Keep one microphone and one set of speakers live in the room, such as a conference speakerphone in the middle of the table for up to about six people. Every other device in the room has its microphone muted and its speakers off.

**Sort the view.** Put the remote faces on a large screen beside you, not at the far end of the table. Point a camera at the faces in the room. Share slides through the call, and use a shared document in place of the flipchart, which remote people cannot read or write on.

**Appoint a voice for the remote group:** give one person in the room the job of speaking up for them. They watch the chat and the raised hands and interrupt you: "Sam has a hand up." Change the person every hour. With more than about four remote people, add [a producer to run the technology](t:4.10).

**Design the remote experience first.** Plan each activity for the people on screen, then adapt it for the room. Give remote people a voice early and often: each question goes to them first, after thinking time, and remote groups report back first. Say at the start that you will do this, and let anyone pass.
**Pair people so that the sound works.** Pair room with room and remote with remote, or mix them only where each in-room partner has a headset and a separate corner or room.
**Check sound and sightlines** from the remote end. Thirty minutes before the start, join a test call from another room or ask a remote colleague to join, and have someone speak from every seat.
**Build recall questions into self-paced parts**, spread the work over weeks and keep a fixed weekly rhythm, which is how you [space and mix the practice](t:5.14).

why.text: **Remote people easily become spectators.** Hybrid is hard to do well, because remote people easily become spectators. A review of 47 studies found that remote students often feel left out, take part less and struggle to signal that they want to speak. Designing for them first is a practical answer. It has not been tested head to head.

why.title: Synchronous hybrid learning: a review
why.found: Reviewing 47 studies, the authors found that hybrid sessions widen access but are hard to teach. Remote students often feel excluded and are more passive, and sound quality is decisive. Most studies were case studies and only one was an experiment.
why.means: Plan the remote experience and the sound first, and check both from the remote end.

why.text: **Without rules, the room wins by default.** The reasoning is about defaults. In a mixed session the room wins without anyone meaning it to. People there can catch your eye and start talking in the gap, and people on screen cannot. So the rules have to lean the other way: remote first for questions, remote first for reports, and a named person whose job is to interrupt for them. Sound comes before everything else because the review found it decisive, and because a remote person who cannot hear the room often cannot tell you so.

**The research on hybrid sessions is young.** Most of it is case studies from universities, with very few comparisons. The set-up on this page is craft, and it has a cost. The room moves more slowly. Sometimes the fair answer is a different format. If one person would be remote for a day of physical practice, offer them another date. If the room has no decent microphone, put everyone on their own laptop in separate places.
**People drop out of self-paced study easily.** Spacing, recall and a facilitator who shows up at regular times are sensible ways to keep them going. This is practice advice, not a tested finding.

try.text: Take one hybrid session you have coming up. For each activity, write what the remote people will see, hear and do. Then join a test call from another room and check the sound and the view yourself. Ask a colleague to speak at normal volume from every seat, and note the places you cannot hear.

try.title: Words you can use to put the remote group first
lines: At the start: "Four of us are on screen and six are in the room. I'll come to the people on screen first each time, because it's harder to get a word in from there. You can always pass."
"Maya is watching the chat and the hands for this hour. Maya, interrupt me."
"In the room, one conversation at a time, please. The people online can't hear a side chat."
Asking a question: "Take a minute to note an answer. I'll come to Sam and Priya on screen first, then the room."
Repeating: "For those online, Jo's point was that the budget is fixed until April."
Reporting back: "Breakout room one first, then room two, then the pairs in the room."
Checking: "Online group, how is the sound? Type a number in chat, one for poor up to five for clear."

items: **If you cannot make it fair**, run it all online.
**Room microphones decide** whether remote people can take part. A laptop microphone at one end of a table will miss the far seats. Test from the remote end.
**Side conversations in the room** shut out the people on screen, who cannot hear them. There is more on [dealing with side conversations](t:4.39). Put it in the [working agreement](t:4.23).

**Two devices on the same call** in one room cause echo and a feedback howl. Keep one microphone and one set of speakers live in the room. Anyone else who joins from the room wears a headset or goes somewhere else. Test it with two laptops before the day.
**You ask "anything from online?"** at the end of each discussion. That makes the remote group an afterthought. Go to them first.

items.label: Raes, Detienne, Windey and Depaepe (2020), A systematic literature review on synchronous hybrid learning: gaps identified. Learning Environments Research.

quiz.q: What did the review of 47 studies of hybrid teaching find about remote students?
quiz.a: They often feel left out, take part less and struggle to signal that they want to speak. Sound quality is decisive.

quiz.q: Six people are in the room and four are on screen. You want pair work. How do you pair them?
quiz.a: Room with room, and remote with remote in breakout rooms. Mix them only if each in-room partner has a headset and a separate corner or room.

quiz.q: Two people in the room open their laptops and join the call, and a howl starts. What do you do?
quiz.a: Have them mute their microphones and speakers at once. Keep one microphone and one set of speakers live in the room. Anyone else joining from the room wears a headset or goes somewhere else.

topics.tierReason: A review documents the problems of hybrid sessions, but the research is mostly case studies and the remote-first remedy has not been tested.

parts.title: Judgement and recovery
parts.summary: What experienced trainers do when the plan stops working.

topics.title: Know why a tip works before you use it

situation.text: Over coffee, a colleague with twenty years in the room gives you her rules: always start with an icebreaker, always end on a quiz. Tomorrow you have eight engineers who have worked together for six years and who groaned through the last icebreaker they were given. You need a way to decide which of her rules to take into that room, and in what form.

items: **Write the tip down** as it was said, in one line. "Always start with an icebreaker." Keep the word "always". It is the part you are about to test.

**Name the principle** that would make it work, in one sentence that starts "This works because". For the icebreaker: "This works because people speak more easily once they have spoken once." Give yourself one minute. If you cannot finish the sentence, write "habit" next to the tip.
**Name the conditions the tip needs**: group size, whether people know each other, how much time there is, what kind of content it is. "Needs strangers, and five spare minutes."
**Sort the tip** into one of three piles: it rests on research you can point to (use the [test for any learning claim](t:1.11)), it is craft with a reason you can state, or it is habit.
**Adapt it for the group** in front of you. Keep the principle and change the form. For the eight engineers: no game, and a two-minute paired question about the topic by minute three.

**Try a habit tip once** before you adopt or drop it. Decide beforehand what you will watch, such as how many people speak in the first ten minutes, and write what you saw in [your review the same day](t:4.15).
**Keep a one-page tip sheet** with three columns: tip, principle, limit. Read it when you design, and add a line each time a tip fails you.

why.text: **A tip you understand you can adapt.** A tip you copy breaks when conditions change. Tips reach you stripped of their conditions, because the person passing them on has usually worked in the same kind of room for years and no longer sees what the tip depends on. The word "always" tells you the conditions have been left out.

**Some craft is sound, some superstition.** Most of what keeps a room running has never been tested in a study. That does not make it worthless. Some craft lore is sound and some is superstition, and the test is the one you [apply to any learning claim](t:1.11). Call it the tip plus principle test. Say the tip, then name the principle that would make it work and the conditions it needs. If you can do that, keep the tip and adapt it. If you cannot, treat it as habit until you have seen what it does.

**Not every tip needs a trial.** There is a trade-off. Testing every tip is slow, and a tip that costs nothing and can do no harm, such as giving the restart as a clock time, does not need a trial. Spend the effort on tips that cost room time or put people on the spot. The advice also bends when you are new. If a senior colleague's rule is the only guide you have for tomorrow, use it, watch what it does, and look for the principle afterwards.

**The craft topics name their principles.** Use this test on the craft topics in this stage. The trainer's craft (from [working as a pair](t:4.17) to [looking after your voice and energy](t:4.20)), Run a session (from [opening a session](t:4.21) to [writing a session plan](t:4.33)) and Difficult moments (from [the person who talks too much](t:4.34) to [the client sitting at the back](t:4.44)) are practitioner judgement and are labelled as craft. Most give an order of moves and the words to say, and name the principle they lean on. Try the move, keep the reason, and change the wording until it sounds like you.

try.text: Ask an experienced trainer for the five tips they rely on most. For each one, say aloud to them the principle you think lies behind it, and ask when it has let them down. Write the tip, the principle and its limit in one line each. Good looks like this: you could finish "This works because" for at least three of the five without help, and you came away with one limit you would not have guessed.

try.title: The test applied to eight common tips

head: Tip

rows: Always start with an icebreaker.

Keep the principle. Open with a paired question on the topic.
Never turn your back on the room.
Your voice goes into the flipchart and you stop seeing people.
Keep. Write, turn round, then talk.
Tell them what you will tell them, tell them, then tell them what you told them.
Signposts help people follow the structure.
Half sound. Keep the signpost at the start. At the end, [ask them to recall it](t:2.24).
Nobody can concentrate for more than twenty minutes.

Treat the number as habit, not a finding. Change what people are doing often and [watch the room](t:4.14).
Put the hard content in the morning.

Often sound. The advice on [pacing and the energy curve](t:2.14) says where it holds.
