items: **Experienced people defend their habits.** Ask "What is that for?" and "When has it not worked?". Do not ask whether it is right.
**You break a rule** because it feels old-fashioned. Break a rule only when you can say what it was for, and what will do that job in its place.
**Your own favourites escape the test.** Put the three moves you are proudest of on the tip sheet first.
**The practical detail gets lost** when you keep the principle. "People speak more easily once they have spoken once" still needs a question, a time limit and a start by minute three.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

items.label: The outline draws on earlier modules and gives no separate source.

quiz.q: What is the tip plus principle test?
quiz.a: Say the tip, then name the principle that would make it work and the conditions it needs. If you can, keep the tip and adapt it. If you cannot, treat it as habit until you have seen what it does.

quiz.q: A colleague says you must always open with an icebreaker game. Your group is a team of eight who have worked together for years. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep the principle, which is that people speak more easily once they have spoken once, and drop the game. Open with a paired question on the topic.

quiz.q: A senior trainer tells you nobody can concentrate for more than twenty minutes. How do you treat that?
quiz.a: As habit, not a finding. The principle is that attention drifts when nothing changes. Change what people are doing often and [watch the room](t:4.14).

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement. No research source was checked for this page.

topics.title: Rehearse what could go wrong

situation.text: It is ten past nine and the projector says "no signal" while twelve store managers watch you press buttons. An hour later someone says, "This is the third course on this and nothing ever changes." After lunch the main activity gets blank looks. None of these is rare, and each one goes better if you have already said your first sentence out loud.

items: **Take ten minutes the evening before.** Write at the top of a page: "The session went badly. Why?" List every reason you can think of for three minutes without judging them.
**Circle the three most likely.** Pick at least one about timing, because timing goes wrong more often than technology. The usual three are one about time, one about equipment and one about a person.
**Write the first sentence for each**, the one you would say to the room. Only the first sentence. "The projector has given up, so here is what we will do."
**Stand up and say each sentence aloud** three times. Then say what you would do in the next two minutes.

**Prepare one physical thing for each failure**: the six key slides printed, one set per table, and the main model already drawn on a flipchart. There is more on [preparing flipcharts and wall materials](t:3.21) and on [what to carry in your kit](t:4.19). On your plan, mark the exercise you would cut and the one you would shorten, following the [order for cutting content live](t:4.31).

**Set a limit for fixing equipment.** Give the group a two-minute paired task, try one fix, and if it has not worked when you call time, run from the paper version. Ask the venue for help at the break, not in front of the room.
**Protect people's dignity first** when it happens, yours included. Do not blame the venue, the client or a participant in front of the room. Say what happens next and when the break is.
**Note which failure came up** afterwards, and whether your sentence worked, in [your review of the session](t:4.15). Keep the list. The same three tend to return.

why.text: **These are predictable situations, not rare accidents.** A plan for recovery matters as much as the plan for the session, and good improvising rests on preparation. The trainers who look calm when the projector dies have usually thought about it beforehand.

**The pre-mortem is adapted from Gary Klein.** The pre-mortem comes from Gary Klein, who describes it as a team exercise at the start of a project. Everyone assumes the project has failed and writes down why. He cites earlier research suggesting that imagining an event has already happened helps people find reasons for it. Using it alone before a session is an adaptation, and the rest of this page is craft.

**The first words are the hardest to find.** The reason for rehearsing only the first sentence is practical. When something goes wrong in front of a group, the opening words are the hardest to find, and an apology or a complaint about the venue tends to fill the gap. A sentence you have already said aloud gives you a few seconds to think about the rest. Writing a full script for every failure does the opposite. It makes you rigid, and the real event never matches the script. Three failures and three sentences is enough.

**This topic is the rehearsal.** The recoveries have their own topics: [running late](t:4.31), a [question you cannot answer](t:4.30) or a hostile one, [a cynic](t:4.36), [conflict between two people](t:4.41), [someone upset](t:4.42) and a [flat slot after lunch](t:4.43). There is also a plan for [incidents on a residential](t:8.15).

try.text: Run a pre-mortem on a real session you have coming up. List three likely failures, write the first sentence for each, then stand and say all three aloud while recording on your phone. Good looks like this: each sentence is under fifteen words, none contains an apology or blames anyone, and each ends with what the group will do next.

try.title: A worked example: a pre-mortem for a one-day workshop with 12 store managers

head: What goes wrong
First sentence I will say
What I prepared
rows: The projector fails at the start.
"The projector has given up, so we will work from paper. Turn to your neighbour: what is the hardest conversation you have had with a member of staff this month? Two minutes."
Six key slides printed, one set per table. The conversation model drawn on a flipchart before people arrive.
The case study runs twenty minutes over.
"We have spent longer on that than I planned, and it was worth it. I am dropping the second case so we still finish at half past four."
Second case marked "cut" on my plan. The practice round marked "never cut".
One person argues with every point.
"You have seen this go wrong before, and I want to hear that properly. Can we take it at the break at quarter to eleven?"
A note to find them first at the break and ask what happened last time, as you would with [a cynic or someone who was sent](t:4.36).
The main activity gets blank looks.
"I did not set that up clearly. Stop for a moment and I will show you one."
A finished example of the task output on a flipchart, covered until needed when you [set up the activity](t:4.24).

items: **You plan for ten disasters** and arrive tense. Over-planning can make you rigid. Stop at three and trust the topics that cover the rest.
**You prepare for the projector** and not for the clock. Timing goes wrong more often than technology. Mark in advance [what you would cut](t:4.31).
**You spend eight minutes** under the table with a cable while the group watches. Set the paired task first and hold yourself to the limit.
**You apologise four times.** Say it once, say what happens next, and move on. Repeated apology keeps the group's attention on the fault.
**You blame the venue:** you say "the venue promised this would work". It may be true. It still costs you standing with the group, and the venue staff are the people you need at the break.

items.label: Klein (2007), Performing a project premortem. Harvard Business Review, September 2007.

quiz.q: Where does the pre-mortem come from, and how was it meant to be used?
quiz.a: From Gary Klein, as a team exercise at the start of a project. Everyone assumes the project has failed and writes down why. Using it alone before a session is an adaptation.

quiz.q: The projector dies ten minutes into your session. What do you do?
quiz.a: Give the group a paired task and try one fix for a couple of minutes. Then run from the printed key slides and the flipchart. Do not blame the venue in front of the room.

quiz.q: It is the night before a new workshop and you have ten minutes. How do you use them?
quiz.a: Imagine the session went badly and write the three likeliest reasons. Prepare one thing for each: a printed back-up, an exercise marked to cut, a line to say.

topics.tierReason: The pre-mortem is a practitioner technique described in a magazine article. The research behind it was not opened and was not done on training sessions.

topics.title: Change the plan when the room tells you to

situation.text: You are twenty minutes into explaining a new pricing model to fourteen people from a sales team. Nobody is writing. Two people are looking out of the window, and your last question got no answer at all. There are eleven slides left in this section and your plan says to keep going until 10:45.

items: **Mark three checkpoints on your plan** before the session, one at the end of each long explanation. Next to them write two signs that would make you stop, such as "nobody writing" and "same two people answering".
**Look on purpose.** Every few minutes, sweep the room and count: who is writing, who is looking up, who has stopped joining in. Your [walk round during group work](t:4.26) is the best view you get.
**Act only on a repeated sign:** when you see it in several people or see it twice, not on one yawn. Stop and say so without blame: "I may have lost you."

**Ask, do not guess.** Use a check that needs no words: "Hold up one to five fingers for how clear this is. Five is 'I could explain it to someone else.'" Or give one minute: "Write down the part that is least clear."

**Make the smallest change** that answers what you were told. Mostly fours and fives: carry on. Threes: work one example together. Ones and twos: drop the next slides and go back. Clear but flat: change what people are doing, or take the break five minutes early.

**Say what you are changing** and what it does to the time. "I am going to skip the next two slides and we will do one together on the flipchart. We still finish at half past four." If content has to go, there is an [order for cutting content](t:4.31).
**Check about twice as often online**, by poll or in chat, because you can see far less. "Type a number from one to five in chat for how clear that was."
**Write one line in the margin** about what you changed and why. It feeds [your review the same day](t:4.15).

why.text: **Pressing on costs more than checking.** The plan is a guess to be revised against what the room tells you. Delivering the plan while the room switches off is a failure, even if every slide was shown. The costs are lopsided. A finger check takes thirty seconds. Pressing on through eleven slides nobody is following costs the whole section, and often the practice that depended on it.

**Be modest about reading people.** Cues are easy to misread and may [differ between people and cultures](t:4.7). Folded arms can mean a cold room. A person looking at the table may be thinking hard. That is why the steps above separate seeing from concluding: what you see tells you to ask, and what people answer tells you what to change. Asking is a safer check than guessing.

**Fast reading is unproven for trainers.** The idea that experienced people read a situation quickly comes from studies of firefighters, paramedics, pilots and chess players. Research on teachers noticing what a class is doing comes mostly from schools. Neither has been shown for trainers of adults at work, so treat reading the room as a skill to practise, not a proven method. The checkpoints and thresholds on this page are craft.

**A lively room is not proof of learning.** There is a limit to what the room can tell you. It can tell you about attention and confusion. It cannot tell you what will last. A [lively, fluent room is not proof](t:1.4) that people will remember or use any of it. Read the room to steer the session, and use [a recall check](t:2.24) to find out what was learned.

try.text: Before your next session, write down two signs that would make you stop and one check question you would ask. Stand up and say the stop line and the check question aloud until they sound like you, then say the sentence that announces the change and the finish time. Afterwards, note whether you used them and what you changed in [your review of the session](t:4.15).

**You take a warm room** as proof it worked. [Attention is not learning](t:1.4). Run the recall check anyway.

quiz.a: Studies of firefighters, paramedics, pilots and chess players. It has not been shown for trainers, so treat reading the room as a skill to practise.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes into an explanation nobody is writing and two people are looking out of the window. What do you do?

quiz.q: The room is lively, people are nodding and the client says it is going brilliantly. What can you conclude?

topics.title: Review your own sessions

situation.text: You have run the same one-day workshop on handling complaints for five years. The feedback forms are always kind. The closing summary has run out of time on every run you can remember, and the role-play still takes ten minutes to get going. Nothing has changed because nothing was ever written down.

items: **Put fifteen minutes in your diary** straight after each session, before you travel. The review has to happen the same day, while you can still remember which minute things went wrong.
**Write three lines**: what worked, what did not, and why. Spend most of the time on "why". "Ran out of time" is not a cause. "The plan has no slack after lunch" is.
**Add three clock times**: when you planned to reach the first break, lunch and the close, and when you got there.
**Pick one weakness to work on** next time and write the change into the session plan itself, not into a notebook. "Cut exercise 5. Close starts 16:10."

**Ask a peer to watch thirty minutes** every third run or so, and give them one thing to look for. "Count how many different people speak in the debrief." Or: "Time how long I wait after each question." Ask for the count before their opinion.
**Swap cases** with two or three other trainers, 45 minutes once a month. Each brings a session that went wrong, what they did, and what they would do now.
**Sit in someone else's session** as a learner, twice a year. Note one move to borrow and one moment when you, as a participant, did not know what you were meant to be doing.
**Hold the review together** the same day if you [work with a co-trainer](t:4.17).

why.text: **Experience alone does not reliably turn into expertise.** Reflection helps. There are two kinds: adjusting while it happens, and learning afterwards. The second kind has been tested. A meta-analysis found that people and teams who held a structured debrief did about 20 to 25 per cent better than those who did not.

why.title: Do debriefs improve performance?
why.found: Pooling 46 samples and 2,136 people, debriefs improved performance by about 20 to 25 per cent compared with no debrief (d = 0.67). The effect held for teams and individuals, and in real and simulated settings.
why.means: Review each session in a set format with a clear focus, and act on one point.

why.text: **A solo written review is untested.** Be clear about what that supports. The debrief studies cover teams and individuals in many fields. A trainer's own written review is a reasonable extension, not something those studies tested. The idea of reflecting while you work comes from Donald Schön, who studied five professions, none of them teaching or training. It is a way of describing practice, not a tested method.

**Reviewing cases builds the experience experts use.** Experts decide fast by drawing on experience. Reviewing cases, your own and other people's, is a deliberate way to add to that store. The format here is craft and each part has a reason. Three lines, because a review you will write when tired beats a full form you will skip. One weakness, because changing a move in front of a group takes attention and you have little to spare while delivering. A peer with a single thing to count, because your own review can only contain what you noticed, and the habits that hold a session back are usually the ones you no longer see.

try.text: Set the routine up now. Put fifteen minutes in your diary after each of your next three sessions. Write the three lines each time, and name one weakness to work on across all three. If you can, say the review aloud into your phone on the way out and write it up from that. Good looks like this: by the third session the plan has changed in at least one place and you can say what that change did.

**You list six things to fix** and fix none. Pick one, and leave the others on the list for later runs.
**You rely on feedback forms.** They tell you little about what people learned. You can [ask better questions on them](t:6.3).
**A vague request to a peer:** you ask them to "see what they think". You get general praise. Give them one thing to count.
**You forget what newcomers find hard** as you improve, which is [the curse of knowledge](t:4.4). Sitting in a session as a learner is the corrective.

topics.title: Look after yourself, and know your professional limits

situation.text: It is Thursday in the third week of delivering four days and travelling on the fifth. At the break a participant describes a dispute with her manager and asks whether she has a legal case. You are tired, you like her, and you have an opinion. The same afternoon someone asks which coaching course they should buy, and you happen to run one.

items: **Set your own limit on delivery days** before the diary fills. Choose a number of days in a row and a number in a week, for example three in a row and a clear day after any two-day programme. The figures are yours to choose. What matters is choosing them when you are rested.
**Say the limit when you take bookings**, as a plain fact about how you work. "I deliver up to three days in a row, then I need a day before the next group."
**Plan recovery after delivery days**: keep the next morning free of calls, and do the travel and admin then. There is more on [looking after yourself during the days themselves](t:4.20).
**Write your scope in three lines**: what you advise on, what you refer on, and who you refer to. Keep the list of places to point people on your phone.
**Use one fixed sentence** when a question falls outside the first line, and do not add a view. "That is outside what I can advise on. Acas or your union rep would be the place to start."

**Say what stays in the room** at the start of each session, and where that stops, as part of [agreeing how the group will work](t:4.23). Before the day, ask the client what their safeguarding duties are and who you would report a concern to, so that your promise matches what you may have to do.
**Declare any interest in what you recommend**, in the same breath as the recommendation. "I should say I run a course like that myself, so weigh what I say. Here are two others to look at."
**Find one peer** you can talk cases through with, once a month, with names and employers left out.

why.text: **Facilitating is tiring work.** A tired trainer is likely to notice less and have less patience, and noticing and patience are most of the job. Recovery belongs in the plan for that reason. A limit decided in advance and stated as policy is also far easier to hold than one negotiated with a client who is asking for a favour.

**Professional bodies publish codes of conduct.** The CIPD Code of Conduct and Ethics, in force since 1 January 2023, asks members to refer on work outside their expertise, protect confidential information, act honestly and disclose conflicts of interest. It applies to CIPD members. This page gives general principles and is not legal advice. There is more on the [UK bodies and rules you work under](t:9.8).

**An offhand opinion is taken as advice.** The reasoning behind the fixed sentence is craft. The person at the front of the room is assumed to know things, so an offhand opinion from you can be taken as advice and acted on. You heard one side of the dispute for three minutes at a coffee table. Pointing her to someone who can hear all of it is the more useful thing to do, even though it feels like less. The same reasoning covers conflicts of interest. A group trusts your recommendations because it assumes you gain nothing from them. When you do gain, say so and let people weigh it.

**State the limit on confidentiality early.** Confidentiality has a limit, and it is better stated at 09:40 than discovered at 15:00. If you promise that everything stays in the room and then hear something you have to pass on, you break either the promise or your duty.

try.text: Write three lines: what you advise on, what you refer on, and who you refer to. Then stand and say the referral sentence and the declaration sentence aloud five times each, until neither sounds like an apology. Ask a colleague to put two out-of-scope questions to you without warning and answer each in one breath.

try.title: Words you can use: taking a booking and opening a session
lines: To a client asking for five days a week for six weeks: "I deliver up to three days in a row. I can do three days a week for the six weeks, or we bring in a second trainer and I brief them."

At the start of a session: "What people say in here stays in here. The one exception is anything your organisation has asked me to pass on, such as a risk of harm to someone. Then I would speak to the person I have agreed with them, and I would tell you first."

items: **A participant in distress** needs referral, not coaching. You can follow the [steps and the words to use](t:4.42).
**Selling a follow-on product** from the front of the room is a conflict of interest. If the client wants the next course mentioned, let the client mention it.
**Safeguarding duties may apply.** Ask the client before the day what theirs are and who you would report to.
**You agree to a sixth week** because the client is pleasant. State the limit, then offer a second trainer or a slower schedule.
**You give "just a quick view"** on a legal, medical or financial question. A quick view from the trainer is still heard as advice. Use the fixed sentence.

quiz.q: What four things does the CIPD Code of Conduct and Ethics ask of members, as listed on this page?
quiz.a: Refer on work outside your expertise, protect confidential information, act honestly and disclose conflicts of interest.

quiz.q: At the break a participant asks whether she has a legal case against her manager. What do you say?
quiz.a: That it is outside what you can advise on, and where she could start, such as Acas or her union rep. Do not offer a view.

quiz.q: A client asks you to deliver five days a week for six weeks. What do you do?
quiz.a: State your limit on delivery days in a row and build recovery time into the schedule, or propose a second trainer. A tired trainer is likely to notice less and have less patience.

topics.title: Co-facilitate without tripping over each other

situation.text: You and a colleague are running a two-day programme together. In the first hour you both answer the same question, she adds "just one thing" to each of your segments, and neither of you is watching the clock.

items: **Meet for thirty minutes before the day** and walk through the plan. Put one name against every segment as lead. The other person is support for that segment.
**Say what support does.** The usual jobs are watching the room, keeping time, writing on the flipchart, handing out materials, and dealing with latecomers or the technology.
**Agree three signals.** One for time, such as five fingers held low for five minutes left. One for "I would like to add something", such as a raised pen. One for "move on".

**Set the rule for adding.** Support speaks when the lead invites it: "Anything to add, Tom?" One point, half a minute. If the lead says something wrong, pass a note, unless the error would send an exercise the wrong way.
**Decide who goes to a participant** in difficulty. It is the support person, so the lead can keep the room going. There are [steps for when someone is upset](t:4.42).
**Hand over out loud and swap places**: "That is the model. Tom will take you into the practice." The outgoing lead moves to the side and sits down.
**Take two minutes together at each break**: time, energy, anyone you are worried about, any change to the next segment.
**Debrief for fifteen minutes the same day.** Each says one thing to keep and one to change, first about the session and then about how you worked together. Write the changes into the plan.

why.text: **Two trainers need an agreement.** This is practitioner judgement. Two trainers can give a group more attention, a change of voice and cover when something goes wrong. Without an agreement they give the group two people competing for the floor, and clients notice.

**Participants need to know who leads.** The main idea is that the floor has one owner at a time. Participants need to know who to look at and whose instruction to follow. The spoken handover and the change of position tell them. A support trainer who stays standing at the front, nodding, is still half leading.

**The rule on adding is strict on purpose.** "Just one thing" is nearly always meant kindly and nearly always reads as a correction. Being invited in sounds like teamwork. Saving a point for the break costs nothing.
**The debrief is where a pair improves.** The discipline of [reviewing your own sessions](t:4.15) applies here with one addition, which is that you talk about the partnership as well as the content.

try.text: With the colleague you will work with, run a ten-minute stretch of your session aloud, to an empty room if need be. Include one handover in each direction and one invited addition. Use the signals for real. Then hold the fifteen-minute debrief, standing, with a timer. If you finish with no "one thing to change" about how you worked together, you were being polite. Go round once more.

**Looking at your phone or laptop** while in support tells the room the segment does not matter.

**If you are the junior** of the pair, ask for the agreement anyway. It protects you most.
**Skipping the debrief** because the day went well is how small irritations become next month's problem.

quiz.q: In a co-facilitated session, when does the support trainer add a point?
quiz.a: When the lead invites it. One point, kept to about half a minute.

quiz.q: Your co-trainer gives the group a wrong time for the exercise, twenty minutes when the plan says ten. You are in support. What do you do?
quiz.a: Use the signal to add and correct it when invited, or say "Can I check one thing on timing?", because this error would send the exercise wrong. Smaller slips go on a note.

quiz.q: A participant leaves the room upset while your colleague is leading. What do you do?
quiz.a: As support, you follow the participant and your colleague keeps the room working. You agreed that beforehand, so neither of you has to decide in the moment.

topics.title: Use flipcharts and walls

situation.text: By 11:00 you have filled six flipchart sheets. Nobody past the second row can read them, three are in pale green, and they are in a pile on the floor because the venue will not allow anything on the walls.

items: **Ask the venue about the walls**: what may go on them and how. Many forbid tape or tack on painted surfaces. Bring your own fixings, and use windows, doors or spare flipchart stands if walls are off limits.
**Write big.** Letters about as tall as your thumb is long, in lower case print. Six to eight lines on a sheet. Then walk to the back seat and read it, as you would when [setting up the room](t:4.5).
**Use black or dark blue for words.** Keep colour for headings, underlines and boxes. Do not use pale colours for text, and do not rely on red against green to carry meaning.

**Draw charts in advance**, every one you know you will need: the agenda, exercise instructions, the model, and a parking sheet. Pencil your own prompts faintly in a corner. Only you can see them. There is more on [preparing sheets and cards before the day](t:3.21).
**Put the parking sheet by the door** with sticky notes beside it. Go through it before the close. There is more on [parking an off-topic issue](t:4.30).
**Record what people say in their words**, and check: "Have I got that right?" Write, turn round, then talk. Do not speak to the paper.
**Number and title each sheet** and hang them in order round the room, so the day builds up on the walls.
**Photograph every sheet in order** at the end, and check each photo is readable. Ask the group before you share any sheet that has names or sensitive comments on it. Send the photos within two days.

why.text: **A chart on the wall stays visible.** This is practitioner judgement. The reasoning draws on one idea: [people can hold very little in mind](t:1.1) at once. A slide disappears when you click on. A chart stays on the wall, so the group can look back at the agenda, the model and its own earlier answers without having to remember them.

**Charts also show whose session it is.** A sheet in the participants' own words, written in front of them, tells them their thinking is the material. That is why you check your wording with the speaker.
**Prepared charts are quicker and neater.** Drawing charts in advance saves time in the room and gives you neat, readable sheets for the things that matter most, such as exercise instructions.

**Everyone should get the same information.** The size and colour rules are about access as much as neatness. Someone at the back, someone with poor sight or someone who is colour-blind should get the same information as the person at the front.

try.text: Do this on your feet with real paper. Draw the instruction chart for one of your exercises, hang it, and read it from six metres away. Then ask a colleague to talk for three minutes about a problem at work while you record their points on a second sheet, checking your wording with them twice. Photograph both sheets on your phone and see whether you can read them on the small screen.

**Take every sheet with you** or destroy it. Client material left on a hotel wall is a confidentiality problem. There is more on [confidentiality and your professional limits](t:4.16).

quiz.q: Which colours do you use for words on a flipchart?
quiz.a: Black or dark blue. Other colours are for headings, underlines and boxes.

quiz.q: A participant makes a long point and you write up a neat four-word version of it. They frown. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask "Have I got that right?" and rewrite it in their words. The chart should record the group's thinking, not your version of it.

quiz.q: You arrive and the venue tells you nothing may be fixed to the walls. Your plan has eight wall charts. What do you do?
quiz.a: Use windows, doors and spare flipchart stands, and lay group charts on tables. Ask about walls before the day next time, as part of the [questions for setting up the room](t:4.5).

topics.title: Pack a trainer's kit

situation.text: The venue promised pens, a clicker and a cable. There are two dry markers, no clicker, and the screen takes a connector your laptop does not have. You start in twenty-five minutes.

items: **Keep one bag packed all the time.** Restock it the evening after a session, when you know what ran out, and not the night before the next one.
**Pack in four groups** so you can check quickly: the room, the technology, the paper, and you.

**Carry your session in three forms.** The deck on your laptop, a copy on a memory stick as a PDF, and the key slides printed. When you [rehearse what could go wrong](t:4.13), you are asked for a version that needs no technology, and this is it.
**Bring your own supplies**: markers, tape and sticky notes, even when the venue says it supplies them. Test every marker.
**Count activity materials against the plan** the night before: one set for each group, plus one spare.
**Ask the venue in writing** what it will provide, including the connector on the screen. Bring adaptors anyway.
**Unpack in the same order every time** on arrival: screen and sound first, then walls, then tables. Find out where the first-aid kit and the nearest first-aider are.
**Put your name and number** on the bag and on the clicker.

why.text: **Your kit will differ from this one.** This is practitioner judgement, and the list below is one working trainer's version. Yours will change with your sessions.

**A missing cable costs your set-up time.** The principle is that small failures in the first twenty minutes cost more than they should. A missing cable does not only delay the slides. It uses up the time you had set aside to move the furniture, check sightlines and greet people as they come in, and that [work of setting up the room](t:4.5) is part of the session. A packed bag buys that time back.

**The night before is too late to restock.** Restocking straight after a session is the habit that makes it work. The evening before a job is when you find that the sticky notes ran out last week and the shops are closed.

**Printed slides can still run the day.** Carrying three forms of the deck sounds like too much until the first time a client laptop refuses your memory stick or a hotel screen will not wake up. With printed key slides and a flipchart you can still run the day. Knowing that also does a good deal for your nerves. There is more about nerves under [presence and vocal delivery](t:4.1).

try.text: Run a timed set-up drill. Take the packed bag to a meeting room or your kitchen, start a timer, and go from closed bag to ready to start: screen connected, first chart hung, pens tested, handouts laid out. Aim for fifteen minutes. Then shut the laptop and deliver the first five minutes of your session aloud using only what is in the bag. Note what you reached for and did not have.

items: **A kit spread over three bags** and a car boot is not a kit. If it does not fit in one bag, cut it.
**Do not count on venue wifi** for anything the session depends on. Download videos and files beforehand.
**Check what you may plug in.** Some sites require electrical items to be tested before they are used.
**Participant lists and feedback forms** carry personal data. Keep them in the bag and do not leave them in the room.
**A new activity** needs its own materials list. Add it to the bag check for that day only.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: When do you restock the kit bag?
quiz.a: The evening after a session, when you know what ran out.

quiz.q: The screen in the room will not connect to your laptop and you start in ten minutes. What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop trying at five minutes to go, hand out or hang the printed key slides and run from the flipchart. The first minutes with the group matter more than the slides.

quiz.q: The venue has emailed to say pens, flipcharts and a clicker are all provided. What do you pack?
quiz.a: The same bag as always, including your own tested markers, tape and clicker. Venue supplies are often worn out, and discovering that at 9:10 costs you your set-up time.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement from the training room. No study was opened for this topic and none tests this sequence.

topics.title: Look after your voice and energy on a multi-day run

situation.text: It is the third morning of a five-day programme. Your voice is rough, you slept badly in the hotel, and you snapped at a fair question yesterday afternoon.

items: **Travel the evening before day one**, and get there in time to eat and sleep. There is a case for [protecting the learners' sleep](t:1.12). Protect your own in the same way.
**Warm up your voice for five minutes** before the room fills. Hum, slide gently from low notes to high, then say your opening lines aloud at full volume.
**Keep water within reach** and sip through the day. Take a drink each time the group starts a task.

**Give the group most of the talking** when you design the day. As a working rule, do not speak for more than ten to fifteen minutes at a stretch, and plan the hour after lunch so that they talk and you listen.
**Never shout over a working room.** Use a signal to get attention, such as a raised hand or a chime, and wait. Ask for a microphone for large groups or noisy rooms.
**Take your own break at every break.** Five minutes outside or somewhere quiet, away from participants, before you answer anyone's questions. Eat a proper lunch, sitting down.
**Sit down while groups work.** Wear shoes you can stand in for seven hours.

**Cap evening preparation at thirty minutes**: lay out tomorrow's charts, write three lines on today as your [review of your own session](t:4.15), then stop. Keep one evening completely free on a five-day run.

why.text: **This routine is not medical advice.** This is a routine that working trainers use. It is practitioner judgement and it is not medical advice. If your voice stays hoarse, or you are unwell, see a pharmacist or your GP.

**Delivery is physical work.** The case for [planning recovery and limiting consecutive delivery days](t:4.16) is made elsewhere. This topic covers the days themselves. Delivery is physical work: hours of standing, projecting your voice and paying close attention to a dozen people. On day one you have reserves. By day three, what the group gets depends on how you spent days one and two.

**Talk less and the voice lasts.** The most effective single change is in the design. A trainer who talks for five hours a day will lose their voice whatever they drink. One who talks for ninety minutes, spread across the day, usually will not. The sessions tend to be better for it as well, since the earlier stages argue for practice over input throughout.

**Patience runs out before the voice does.** The sharp reply on day three is often the first sign. The quiet five minutes at each break are there to prevent it, even though it feels unfriendly to step away from a group that wants to chat.

try.text: Before your next delivery day, do the five-minute warm-up, then record the first two minutes of your opening, standing, at the volume the room needs. On the day, ask a colleague or use a phone timer to log how many minutes you speak in each hour. Afterwards, read the log aloud to yourself and name one block where the group could have done the talking.

rows: Breakfast, sitting down. Phone away.

In the room. Charts up. Five minutes of humming and opening lines aloud.
Voice warm before the first hello.
Opens. Ten minutes of input, then the group works.
Short stretches of talk.
Break. Five minutes outside alone, then back for questions.
Recover first, then be available.

items: **Coffee and alcohol in the evening** both cost sleep. On a residential, decide your rule on alcohol before you arrive.
**Clearing your throat hard** and talking over noise both strain a tired voice. Sip water and wait for quiet.
**Rewriting tomorrow's session** at eleven at night rarely improves it. Make one change and go to bed.
**Spending every break and meal** with participants is generous on day one and a mistake by day three.
**If your voice is going**, change the plan for the next day so that groups carry more of it, and tell your co-trainer.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: As a working rule, how long do you speak at a stretch?
quiz.a: No more than ten to fifteen minutes, with the group doing most of the talking across the day.

quiz.q: It is the break on day three and a participant wants to talk through a problem at length. You are tired and your voice is rough. What do you do?
quiz.a: Say you will be with them in five minutes, take your quiet break first, and then give them your attention. A short recovery protects the rest of the day for everyone.

quiz.q: Your voice is hoarse at the end of day two of five. What do you change for day three?
quiz.a: Redesign day three so that groups do more of the talking and your input is shorter, use a signal and not volume to get attention, and warm up before the start. If it does not improve, see a pharmacist or GP.

parts.title: Run a session
parts.summary: The moves that make up a face-to-face session, from the first ten minutes to the last fifteen, each with wording or a timetable you can use.

topics.title: Open a session

situation.text: It is 09:30. Twelve new managers are sitting with their coats on and two are still on their phones. Your first slide lists six objectives. What you do in the next ten minutes shows them whether today is something done to them or something they do.

items: **Be ready fifteen minutes before the start**: room set, first slide up, notes closed. Greet people at the door and learn four or five names before you begin.

**Start on the advertised minute**, even if two people are missing. Say "It's half past nine, so let's start." Latecomers get a nod and a chair. Do not recap for them. There is a [full account of handling late arrivals](t:4.40).
**Say who you are in two sentences** and why the day exists in one. Name the problem in the group's own terms. Keep your biography short and off the screen.

**Get every person speaking** inside the first five minutes. Give pairs a question about the topic, allow two minutes, then take three answers. There is an explanation of [why speaking early matters](t:1.17), and more on [opening with a question](t:1.24).
**Give the shape of the day** as clock times: breaks, lunch and finish. Write them on a flipchart that stays up all day.
**Cover housekeeping in under a minute**: the fire exit and assembly point, whether an alarm test is planned, and the toilets. Ask the venue for these before the day.
**Agree how the group will work**, using the [four-minute version of that agreement](t:4.23), then start the first real task. Aim to be in it by minute fifteen.
**Keep the same order with 30 people.** Pairs still work. Take four answers, and leave names to the table groups.

why.text: **This opening has not been tested.** This is craft. Nobody has tested this opening against another one in a training room, and the timings are practitioner judgement.

**The first task sets the pattern.** The reasoning is about precedent. A group works out how much it is expected to do from what it is asked to do first. If the first fifteen minutes are you talking, people settle into listening and you spend the morning pulling them out of it. A two-minute paired question costs little and sets the pattern for the day.

**Starting on the minute rewards the punctual.** Starting on the minute rewards the people who came on time, and it makes your break times believable later. Giving clock times for lunch and the finish removes a small, constant worry. People with a train to catch or a child to collect stop wondering and start listening.
**Objectives on a slide are your language.** Open with the problem in theirs, and show the objectives later if the client wants them shown.

try.text: Stand up, start a timer and deliver your opening aloud, three times. Record the third on your phone. Good looks like this: it finishes inside ten minutes, you talk for no more than six of them, the paired question comes by minute three, and you do not look at notes. When you listen back, mark every filler phrase and any apology.

try.title: A worked example: the first ten minutes for 12 new managers, on a day about giving feedback

head: Time
What happens
Words you say
rows: Start on the minute, standing, title slide only
"It's half past nine, so let's start. Good morning. I'm Sam. I've trained managers for ten years, and before that I was one, not very well at first."
Why today exists

"You've all taken on a team in the last year. Today is about one part of that job: telling someone, clearly and kindly, what you need them to do differently. You'll practise it twice, once on a real case of your own."
Paired question
"Before anything else, turn to the person next to you. Tell them about one piece of feedback you were given that helped you. What made it useful? Two minutes, both of you. Go."
Walk the room, listen, give a time call
"Thirty seconds. Swap over if you haven't yet."
Take three answers. Write key words on the flipchart
"Let's hear three. What made it useful? Thank you. Keep those in mind. We'll build on that list in a few minutes."
Shape of the day, pointing at the flipchart
"Here's the day. Break at quarter to eleven. Lunch at half twelve for 45 minutes. Another break at half two. We finish at half past four, and I will keep to that."
Housekeeping
"No alarm test is planned, so if it sounds, it's real. Out of that door, down the stairs, meet in the car park. Toilets are along the corridor on the left."
Bridge to the working agreement
"One more thing before we start work, which is how we'll work together today."

items: **You wait for latecomers.** The people who were punctual learn that the times are loose. Start, and let the late ones catch up from their partner.
**The opening runs to 25 minutes.** The cause is nearly always round-the-room introductions or your own story. Time it in rehearsal and cut your biography first.

**A senior person wants to speak.** Agree it beforehand: two minutes on why this matters to the business, then they hand over to you by name. If they keep going, there are moves for [the senior person who takes over](t:4.38).
**The plan cannot change**, yet you ask each person what they want from the day. Only ask if you can act on the answers.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: By when should every person in a group of 12 have spoken?
quiz.a: Inside the first five minutes, usually through a paired question.

quiz.q: It is 09:30 and three of twelve people have not arrived. The client contact suggests waiting ten minutes. What do you do?
quiz.a: Start on time with the paired question, which latecomers can join without a recap. Waiting teaches the group that your times are loose, and it costs you the break times later.

quiz.q: A director asks to open the day with a welcome. What do you agree beforehand?
quiz.a: Two minutes on why the training matters to the business, then a handover to you by name. An unplanned welcome can take fifteen minutes and set a listening mood before you have begun.

topics.tierReason: Craft. This rests on practitioner judgement. No study of this practice was opened for this page.

topics.title: Run introductions that fit the group size

situation.text: Twenty people, and you ask for "name, role and one thing you want from today". The first person takes forty seconds. The eighth takes two minutes. At 10:05 nothing has been taught and the back row has stopped listening.

items: **Do the sum first.** Round-the-room introductions take about a minute a head once you count the handover between speakers. Twelve people is twelve minutes. Thirty people is half an hour.
**Decide what the introductions are for**: names, who does what, or what people need. Pick one or two. That choice sets the format.

**Up to 8 people: go round** the room with a strict form. Name, role, and one sentence answering a question about the topic. Model it yourself in fifteen seconds first, because people copy the length of the first answer.
**From 9 to 16: pairs or threes** talk for three minutes on the question. Then each person says only their name and role to the room, ten seconds each.

**From 17 to 40: people introduce themselves** at their tables. The room hears one line per table. Add a wall chart: on arrival each person writes their name, team and one question on a sticky note and puts it on a flipchart. Read it at the first break and refer to it.
**For 100: no spoken introductions** to the room. Map the room with hands ("Hands up if you manage people. Keep it up if it's more than ten."), then give two minutes with a neighbour.
**Put first names on tent cards**, which are folded cards that stand on the table. Write in thick marker on both sides. With 30 or more, use badges as well, since people move between tables.
**Skip names and roles** if the group already knows each other, and keep the topic question.

why.text: **Introductions take longer than planned.** This is craft, and the main point is arithmetic. New trainers plan five minutes for introductions and spend twenty, then lose the time from the practice at the end of the day.

**A long round also gives little back.** Trainers commonly notice that people waiting for their turn are rehearsing their own line and hear little of anyone else's. So the round costs a minute a head and most of the names are gone by the break.

**Pairs get everyone talking with little exposure.** Pairs and threes change that. Speaking to one person is easier than speaking to a room, so everyone talks early with little exposure, which is the condition needed to [make it safe to be wrong](t:1.17). The wall chart gives you what you wanted from "one thing you want from today" without spending room time on it, and it is still on the wall at three o'clock when you need an example.

try.text: Stand and say your own model introduction aloud against a timer, five times, until it lands between 12 and 18 seconds every time. Then run the 12-person version with two or three colleagues or friends: give the paired question, call time, and take names and roles. Good looks like this: you gave the instruction once, your model answer set the length, and the whole thing took under five minutes.

head: Group
Format
Time
What the room hears
rows: Round the room: name, role, one sentence on the topic question. Trainer models first
3 minutes
Everyone, 20 seconds each
Pairs for 3 minutes on the question. Then name and role only, round the room

items: **An introduction becomes a career history.** Step in kindly at the first breath: "Thank you. I'll stop you there so we hear everyone."
**The "fun fact about yourself"** puts people on the spot and has nothing to do with the work. Ask about the topic.
**The most senior person goes first** and sets a formal tone. Start with pairs, or start the round on the other side of the room.
**You skip introductions with strangers** to save time, then ask them to practise in threes at eleven. People need each other's names before they practise together.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Roughly how long do round-the-room introductions take per person?
quiz.a: About a minute each, once handovers are counted.

quiz.q: You have 30 people, a 09:30 start and the first exercise planned for 09:45. The client wants everyone to introduce themselves. What do you do?
quiz.a: Run introductions inside table groups and hear one line per table, with a sticky-note wall chart for names and questions. A full round would take about half an hour and push the exercise past ten o'clock.

quiz.q: In a group of 8, the first person speaks for two minutes. What should you have done, and what do you do now?
quiz.a: You should have modelled a fifteen-second answer first, because people copy the first length they hear. Now thank them, restate the form in one line, and ask the next person to keep to it.

topics.tierReason: Craft. This rests on practitioner judgement. No study of this practice was opened for this page.

topics.title: Agree how the group will work

situation.text: Mid-morning, a participant starts describing a problem with a colleague and then stops. "Is any of this going back to our manager?" The room looks at you. You have not agreed an answer with the client, and you have not said anything to the group.

items: **Ask the client before the day** what they expect to hear afterwards. Offer themes with no names attached, and get the answer in an email. If the client wants individuals assessed, that is a different event and the invitation must say so.

**Make the agreement straight after the opening**, in the room, and keep it to four minutes. For a one-day course, propose the agreement on a flipchart you wrote beforehand. Asking a room of strangers to invent ground rules takes fifteen minutes and produces the word "respect".

**Cover five things**: confidentiality, what gets reported to the client, phones and laptops, questions, and timekeeping around breaks. Add the right to watch a practice round before joining in, which is worth promising in advance when you [tell learners what to expect](t:2.21).
**State the limit on confidentiality plainly.** You can speak for yourself. You cannot guarantee what other participants do, and you would have to act if you heard about serious harm.
**Ask for changes, then ask for agreement**: "What would you add or change? Can everyone work with that?" Look round the whole room and wait, as you do [whenever you ask a question](t:4.2).
**Leave the sheet on the wall.** When you need it later, point at it: "We said phones away during practice."
**Keep your own side.** Restart and finish at the times you gave, and report only what you said you would.

do.title: Words you can use: a four-minute working agreement
lines: "Before we start, here's how I suggest we work today. It's on the flipchart, and you can change it."
"First, what's said here. You'll be talking about real people in your teams. Use the situation and leave out the name. What you hear from each other stays in this room."
"I'll keep to that myself. I can't promise it for everyone here, so share what you're comfortable sharing. And if someone told me about serious harm, I couldn't keep that to myself."
"Second, what your company hears from me. I'll tell them who attended and the general themes that came up. No names against comments, and nothing about how any one of you did in practice."
"Third, phones. Away during practice, please, because your partner deserves your attention. If you're waiting for a call you must take, tell me now and step out when it comes."
"Fourth, questions. Ask as we go if something is unclear. If it's a bigger issue I'll write it on this sheet headed 'Parked' and we'll come back to it before we finish."
"Fifth, time. I'll start and finish when I said I would. In return, please be back from breaks at the time on the clock."
"Last, the practice. Nobody is made to perform in front of the room. You can watch the first round before you have a go."
"What would you add or change? ... Can everyone work with that? Good. It stays on the wall."

why.text: **Trainers call this contracting.** This is craft. Trainers call it contracting, and nothing here has been tested as a method. There is a [fuller version for residentials](t:8.3), with levels of depth and a free pass.

**A limited promise beats a vague one.** People decide how honest to be in practice from where they think their words will go. Most will not ask about reporting aloud, so you answer the question before it is asked. A vague answer is worse than a limited one. "Themes, no names" is a promise you can keep, and "everything here is confidential" is one you cannot.

**The sheet does the reminding for you.** An agreement made at 09:40 also gives you something to point at in the afternoon. When you remind someone about a phone, you are pointing at a sheet the group accepted. That is easier to hear than a telling-off from you.
**Proposing suits one day with strangers.** Proposing is right for a single day with strangers. An intact team, or a group together for several days, has more at stake and the time to write its own.

try.text: Record yourself saying the agreement aloud, standing, without notes. Then deliver it to one colleague and ask them to interrupt as a wary participant: "So will my manager hear how I did?" Answer aloud, on the spot. Good looks like this: under four minutes, and a reporting sentence nobody could mishear.

items: **You promise total confidentiality.** You cannot deliver it. Say what you will do and where the limit is.
**The list grows to ten rules.** Nobody remembers ten. Keep five or six and drop the ones you would never enforce.
**The client asks how someone did** after the course. Go back to the email: you agreed themes. Offer the themes, and suggest the manager asks the person directly.
**A phone rule with no reason** and no exit gets ignored by the busiest people. Give the reason and the way out together.
**Latecomers miss the agreement.** Point them to the sheet at the first break and check they can work with it. There is more on [handling late arrivals](t:4.40).

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Name the five things a working agreement for a one-day course should cover.
quiz.a: Confidentiality, what is reported to the client, phones and laptops, questions, and breaks or timekeeping.

quiz.q: A week after a course for a software company's team leads, their director emails: "How did Alex get on?" You agreed themes only. What do you reply?
quiz.a: Say that you agreed with the group, and with the client beforehand, to report attendance and themes without names, and send the themes. Breaking that once would undo the trust the next group gives you.

quiz.q: You have a one-day course with 14 strangers and a colleague suggests the group writes its own ground rules. What do you do?
quiz.a: Propose five lines on a prepared flipchart and invite changes, which takes about four minutes. Group-written rules suit an intact team or a multi-day event, where there is time and more at stake.

topics.tierReason: Craft. This rests on practitioner judgement. No study of this practice was opened for this page.

topics.title: Give instructions people can follow first time

situation.text: You say, "OK, so in your groups, have a chat about the case and think about what you'd do, and we'll come back in a bit." Chairs turn. At every table the first thing anyone says is, "What are we meant to be doing?"

items: **Write every instruction word for word** before the day. Put the task, the time, the grouping and the output on a slide or flipchart that stays visible while people work.

**Get attention before you speak.** Stand still in the same spot each time, say "Eyes up here for a minute, please", and wait for quiet. Use the same spot and the same words all day. This is your attention signal. Never talk over the room.
**Say why, in one sentence.** People put more into a task when they can see what it is for, which is the point of [telling adults why](t:1.5).
**Give the task as one action** with a verb: "Write the first two sentences of your reply." If the task is new to them, show a thirty-second example.
**Give the time twice**, as a length and as a clock time: "Eight minutes, so until ten past."
**Give the grouping and the output**: who with, where, and what you will ask for at the end.
**Ask one person to say it back**, as your check: "Jo, so I can check I explained that properly, what are you about to do?" Pick someone at ease in the group. "Is that clear?" only ever gets a nod.
**Hand out materials and move people last.** Say "Off you go", start the timer, and walk past every group in the first two minutes.

why.text: **Unclear instructions often sink an activity.** This is craft, in an order many trainers arrive at by getting it wrong. Instructions are the first thing to coach when you [teach others to train](t:5.10), and unclear ones are a common reason an activity fails.

**The order does most of the work.** Paper in someone's hand wins against a voice from the front, so anything said after the handout is lost. People who are standing up and finding a group are not listening either. That is why materials and movement come after the last word.

**Spoken instructions do not stay in mind.** Spoken instructions pass once and are gone, and there is an explanation of [how little people can hold in mind](t:1.1) at a time. The flipchart holds the instruction for them. One task with one output is easier to hold than "discuss and think about".

**The say-back is the only real check.** Nobody wants to be the person who admits they did not follow, so a room will nod at "Is that clear?" and then ask each other. Frame the say-back as a test of your explaining, which it is.

try.text: Pick a real activity. Stand, record yourself giving the instruction on your phone, and keep it under ninety seconds. Play it back against the eight steps and tick each one you hear. Then give the instruction live to a colleague who has not seen the activity and ask them to say back what they would do. If they miss anything, rewrite and record again.

try.title: A worked example: one instruction, before and after (a customer support team of 12)
lines: Before: "Right, I'm going to give out this case study, here you go, pass those along. Have a read and get into groups, threes or fours, and discuss what went wrong and what you'd do. Take ten minutes or so. Oh, and someone make notes."
What goes wrong: the paper arrives first, so people read and stop listening. The group size is loose. There are two tasks and no output. Nobody knows when it ends.
After: "Eyes up here for a minute, please." (Wait for quiet.)
"You've seen the four steps for answering a complaint. Now you'll use them on a real email, because spotting the steps is easier than writing them."
"Your task: read the customer's email, then write the first two sentences of your reply. Only the first two."
"You have eight minutes. That takes us to ten past eleven."
"You'll work in threes, with the people at your table."
"At ten past, I'll ask each three to read their two sentences aloud."
"It's all on the flipchart: first two sentences, eight minutes, threes, read aloud."
"Jo, so I can check I explained that properly, what are you about to do?" (Jo says it back. Fill in anything missing.)
"Here are the emails, one each. Off you go." (Hand out the paper now. Start the timer. Walk to the furthest table first.)

items: **Something remembered after "Off you go"** gets called across the noise. Half the room misses it. Stop everyone with your attention signal, say it once, and restart.
**The task has three stages** and you give them all at once. Give stage one, let them do it, then stop the room for stage two.
**The instruction slide disappears** when you click on. Put the instruction on a flipchart, or leave the slide alone until the task ends.
**The say-back embarrasses a nervous person.** Choose someone who has already spoken easily, and say that you are checking yourself.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: In the instruction sequence, when do you hand out the materials?
quiz.a: Last, after the say-back check and just before you say "Off you go".

quiz.q: You have set a case exercise. Two minutes in, you walk round and find two of four groups doing the wrong task. What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop the whole room with your attention signal and give the task and output again, pointing at the flipchart. Two groups wrong means the instruction failed, so fixing it table by table would waste more time.

quiz.q: You ask "Is that clear?" and everyone nods, but the groups start slowly and look at each other. What do you change next time?
quiz.a: Ask one person to say the task back before anyone moves, framed as a check on your explanation. A nod tells you nothing, because nobody wants to admit they did not follow.

topics.title: Form groups and move people

situation.text: You say "get into groups of four". Twelve people look at each other. Friends pair up fast, two people are left standing in the middle, and three minutes have gone before anyone starts.

items: **Choose the size for the task.** Pairs for thinking aloud and first attempts. Threes for practice with an observer. Fours for a case that needs several views. Avoid five or more unless the group is making something physical.

**Decide groups before the day** when it matters who is with whom: role-play threes, people from different teams, or keeping a manager apart from someone who reports to them. Write the groups on a flipchart.
**Count off for quick mixing.** Count up to the number of groups you want, not the size of each group. For four groups from twelve people, count one to four round the room.
**Point to where each group will meet** before anyone stands: "Ones by the window, twos at the door."
**Mix in other ways**: line up by years in the job and cut the line into threes, put coloured dots on name cards before people arrive, or say "find two people you haven't worked with yet today".
**Let people choose their own partners** for the first task of the day, when neighbours are enough, and whenever the material is personal, such as a real case from their own team.
**Mix after the first break** and again after lunch, so nobody spends the day with one partner.

**Budget the time.** Turning to a neighbour takes ten seconds. New threes in the same room take one to two minutes. Going to a breakout room takes three or four minutes each way. Keep any task shorter than fifteen minutes in the main room.

why.text: This is craft. The group sizes and timings are rules of thumb from practice.

**Size decides how much each person talks.** In a pair working for ten minutes, each person speaks for about five. In a group of six, it is under two, and one person usually says very little. People tend to [put in less as a group grows](t:4.3).

**Left to choose, people stay put.** Left to choose, people sit and work with those they arrived with. That is comfortable, and it means the experienced people never meet the new ones. It also leaves someone standing alone while the room watches, which is a small humiliation you can prevent by assigning.

**Movement has a cost and a benefit.** It lifts energy, which helps in the [dips in energy across the day](t:2.14), and it uses minutes that new trainers rarely plan for. Layout matters too. Small tables with chairs on three sides, often called cabaret style, let people work in fours and still see the front. There is more on [setting the room](t:4.5).

try.text: Stand in an empty room, or your kitchen, and give the count-off instruction aloud for 12 imaginary people making four groups. Point to each corner as you name it. Do it until it takes under twenty seconds with no correction. Then try it for real at your next team meeting or family gathering of six or more: move people into threes with one instruction, and time how long it takes them to settle.

quiz.q: When you count off to form groups, what number do you count up to?
quiz.a: The number of groups you want, not the size of each group.

quiz.q: A retailer's store managers and their area managers are in one session, and the next task is practice in threes on a real staffing problem. How do you form the threes?
quiz.a: Assign them beforehand so that no store manager practises with their own area manager, and post the threes on a flipchart. People hold back when the person who appraises them is in the conversation.

quiz.q: You have a seven-minute discussion task and two breakout rooms down the corridor. Where do the groups work?
quiz.a: In the main room. Walking to a breakout room and back takes about as long as the task, and you cannot see or hear groups that have left.

topics.title: Watch and support groups while they work

situation.text: The groups are working, so you sit down and look through your notes for the next section. One table finished after three minutes and is talking about the weekend. Another has spent six minutes on the wrong question. You find out both when you ask for reports.

items: **Stand still and look** for the first thirty seconds. Check that every group has started. Say nothing.
**Walk past every group once** in the first two minutes, starting with the one furthest from you. You are checking one thing: are they on the right task.
**Stand where you can see every face** after that, usually a corner or the side wall. Do not stand over a group. People start performing for you when you do.
**Listen for material.** Write down exact phrases you can use in the debrief, with the table they came from. Note any misunderstanding that more than one group shares, and who has not spoken.
**Step in for four reasons only**: the wrong task, a group going round in circles for more than a couple of minutes, one person shut out, or something unkind. Otherwise stay out.
**Get down to their eye level** when you do step in, and ask "Where have you got to?" before you offer anything. Leave as soon as they are moving again.
**Call time twice**, at halfway and near the end, and say where they should be: "Four minutes left. You should be on the second question by now."

**Have an extension ready** for a group that finishes early. An extension is a harder follow-on question on the same material. Tell a group that is behind which part to drop. To end, say "Finish the sentence you're on", then use your [attention signal for giving instructions](t:4.24).

why.text: This is craft. It rests on what experienced trainers do and has not been tested as a method.

**Group time is working time for you.** It is when you learn what people have understood, and it is your only source for the specific moments [a good debrief is built on](t:4.28). A trainer who spent the task reading notes has to open the debrief with "So, how did that go?"

**Staying out is deliberate.** The moment you answer a group's question, the thinking stops and the conversation turns to face you. Asking where they have got to keeps the work with them, and it often shows they were closer than they thought.

**A marker tells groups whether to hurry.** Time calls with a marker let groups pace themselves. "Four minutes left" alone tells them the time. Adding where they should be tells them whether to speed up. You are asked to [change the plan](t:4.14) when the room tells you to, and the walk round is where the room tells you.

try.text: Ask two or three friends or colleagues to discuss any question for six minutes while you practise. Stand where you can see them all. Do not speak for the first two minutes. Write down three phrases word for word. Give a halfway call and a one-minute call aloud, each with a progress marker. Afterwards, read the three phrases back and ask whether you caught them accurately.

quiz.q: Name the four reasons to step into a working group.
quiz.a: They are on the wrong task, they are stuck in circles, one person is shut out, or something unkind is happening.

quiz.q: A group waves you over and asks, "Is this the right answer?" What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask what they think, or what the customer in the case would make of it, and then step away. If you supply the answer, their thinking stops and the group starts working for your approval.

quiz.q: Four minutes into an eight-minute task, one group has finished and the others are halfway. What do you do?
quiz.a: Give the finished group the extension you prepared, such as taking the hardest objection and writing a reply. Then make your halfway call to the room so the others know where they should be.

topics.title: Take reports from groups without losing the room

situation.text: Four groups have worked on the same case. You ask each to present. The first takes seven minutes and covers nearly everything. The other three repeat it with apologies. Twenty-five minutes later most of the room is looking at a phone.

items: **Choose the report format before the activity** and say it in the instruction. It changes what groups produce.
**Do the sum.** "Five minutes each" for four groups is twenty-five minutes with handovers. For six groups it is over half an hour, and if all had the same task, most of it is repetition.

**Default to one point per group**: "One point from each group, the one you most want the others to hear. Nothing we've already had." Go round once, then ask for anything still missing. Start with a different group each time.

**Harvest on a flipchart**, which means collecting answers from the whole room onto one list. Ask a narrow question, such as "What did you decide to say first?" Write the group's own words, key words only, large enough to read from the back. Ask "Who had something different?" There is more on [writing on a flipchart](t:4.18).

**Use a gallery walk** when groups have made something on paper. Put the sheets on the walls like pictures in a gallery. Everyone walks round for six minutes with a pen and marks one idea to borrow and one question. Take the questions standing at the sheets.

**Take reports when each group's case differed**, because the others have not seen it. Give a form and a limit: ninety seconds, covering the case in one sentence, what we decided and why. Run a visible timer.
**Send one person from each group** to the next table to report for two minutes, for speed with larger numbers. Every report happens at once.
**Close it yourself.** Name two patterns you heard, link them to the next section and move on. Do not teach each point again.

why.text: This is craft. The timings are from practice.

**A report-back is for the room.** The useful test is what the other groups need to hear, which is rarely everything a group discussed. Presenting in turn fails on that test. One person talks while eleven listen, the later groups have nothing new, and reporters tend to narrate their discussion when the room only needs the conclusion.

**Choosing one point makes groups think.** One point per group forces a choice, and choosing the most useful point is itself a small act of thinking about the content. The gallery walk gets people on their feet and reading each other's work at their own speed, which suits the [afternoon dips in energy](t:2.14).

**Who holds the pen matters.** If you turn each contribution into your own phrase, the list becomes yours and people stop offering. Writing their words, and checking "Have I got that right?", keeps the list theirs.

try.text: Tape a sheet of paper to a wall and practise harvesting. Ask one or two people to give you points on any easy question, such as what makes a good team meeting. Write each in their words while you stay half turned to them, and ask "Who had something different?" after each. Then walk four metres back and check you can read it. Record it and listen for how often you rephrased what they said.

quiz.q: Why does "each group presents for five minutes" fail when all groups had the same task?
quiz.a: It takes about twenty-five minutes for four groups, and the later groups mostly repeat the first.

quiz.q: Six groups at a sales kick-off have each drawn an account plan on flipchart paper. You have twelve minutes. How do you take reports?
quiz.a: Run a gallery walk: sheets on the walls, six minutes walking with a pen to mark one idea to borrow and one question, then take questions at the sheets. Six presentations would take over half an hour.

quiz.q: During a harvest, a participant gives a long answer and you write a neat summary in your own words. They look unconvinced. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask "Have I got that right? Which words would you use?" and rewrite it. A list in your wording becomes your list, and people offer less.

topics.title: Debrief an activity

situation.text: The role-play ends and the room is buzzing. You ask, "So, how was that?" One person says "Good, yeah." Another says "A bit awkward." You say "Great" and click to the next slide.

items: **Plan the debrief** when you plan the activity and write the questions into your session plan. As a starting rule from practice, give it at least a third of the time the activity took.
**Begin with one minute of silent writing**: one thing that worked, and one moment that was harder than expected. Then everyone has something to say.

**Ask first about what happened**, and ask for specifics: "What exactly did you say in the first thirty seconds?" The people who did the task speak first, then the people they did it with, then observers.
**Move to what it means**: "Why do you think that worked?" Bring in the model you taught here, and correct anything that is wrong.
**Move to work**: "Where does this come up in your week?" Then to action. Each person writes one sentence they will say or one thing they will do.

**Feed in what you heard** while walking round, using the [notes you made while groups worked](t:4.26): "At this table I heard, 'Help me understand what's behind that.' What happened next?" Raise mistakes without naming anyone.
**Record on a flipchart in two columns**, what worked and what to try next, in their words.
**Speak last.** Add at most two points the group missed.

why.text: **One paper defines what counts as a debrief.** There is more on [the three questions and the meta-analysis](t:1.25) that supports debriefing. That paper also says what counted as a debrief, which is the useful part when you run one.

**A debrief that counts has four features.** The authors only counted a debrief if it had four features. Participants worked things out for themselves instead of being told. The purpose was improvement, with no judging or appraisal. The talk was about particular events. And the information came from more than one source, such as several team members or an observer. The steps above are built to meet those four: writing first, exact words, observers, and the trainer last.
The order of questions, the one-third rule and the two-column flipchart are craft. They have not been tested.

why.title: Do team and individual debriefs enhance performance?
why.found: Pooling 46 samples and 2,136 people, debriefs improved performance by about 25 per cent on average, or about 21 per cent with three outlying studies removed. Facilitated debriefs showed larger effects than unfacilitated ones, on little data. Video and similar aids added no meaningful benefit.
why.means: Ask before you tell, keep it about specific moments, bring in observers, and keep judgement out of it.

try.text: Run a five-minute debrief with two friends or colleagues, and record the sound. First give them a three-minute task, such as one persuading the other to change a weekend plan. Then debrief aloud: what was said, why it worked or did not, what each would do next time. Listen back and count your own talking time. Aim for under a third. Check that you asked for exact words and that each person finished with one thing to do.
