**"How did that feel?"** as the opener gets one-word answers. Ask what was said.
**The debrief turns into a critique** of one person's round. Move it to the situation: "That customer brief was the hardest one. What would any of us do with it?"

deeper.text: One meta-analysis supports debriefing and defines what counts as one. The order of questions and the timings on this page are craft.

items.label: Tannenbaum and Cerasoli (2013), Do team and individual debriefs enhance performance? A meta-analysis. Human Factors, 55(1).

quiz.q: In the 2013 meta-analysis, which four features did a discussion need in order to count as a debrief?
quiz.a: Participants working things out themselves, a developmental and non-judging purpose, a focus on specific events, and more than one source of information.

quiz.q: A practice exercise for a customer team overran by ten minutes. You have five minutes for a debrief you planned at fifteen. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep a short version: one silent minute to write, one question on what was actually said, and one sentence each on what they will do. Dropping it altogether loses the part that the evidence supports.

quiz.q: In a debrief, an observer starts listing everything one colleague did wrong. What do you do?
quiz.a: Thank them, ask for one thing to keep and one to try, and widen it to what anyone would do with that case. A debrief is for improvement, and one person being judged in public shuts the rest of the room down.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis of 46 samples supports holding a facilitated debrief built on self-discovery and specific events. The order of questions and the timings on this page are practitioner judgement.

topics.title: Run a role-play that people do not dread

situation.text: You say "now for some role-play" and watch shoulders drop. Someone jokes about leaving early. Their last one was in front of the whole room, with a colleague playing an impossible customer for laughs.

items: **Call it practice.** Say in the invitation that the day includes it, as part of [telling learners what to expect](t:2.21), and say at the start that nobody is made to perform in front of the room.
**Work in threes**: one person practises, one plays the other party, one observes. Run all the threes at once. The noise gives each group privacy.

**Give each role a written brief** of half a page. The practiser's brief gives the situation and the goal. The other party's brief says how to behave: "Push back twice. If you are asked a good question, answer it honestly. Do not make it impossible."
**Demonstrate first for two minutes**, with a volunteer or co-trainer, and leave in one clear flaw. The room gives you feedback from the observer sheet.
**Keep rounds short**: four minutes of conversation and three of feedback. Three rounds, rotating clockwise, so everyone practises once.
**Give the observer a sheet** with three things to watch for, tied to the steps you taught. They write exact words and stay out of the conversation.

**Fix the order of feedback**: the practiser first, then the observer, then the other party on how it felt. You speak last. Each gives one thing to keep and one to try. There is more on [what makes feedback usable](t:2.27).

**Call the changes for the whole room**: "Stop there, wherever you are. Three minutes of feedback, practiser first." Then [debrief the activity](t:4.28) with everyone. Run a second set later on participants' own real cases.

why.text: The format here is craft. There is little research comparing threes with other arrangements.

**People rarely dread the practice.** They dread the audience, and a partner who improvises. Threes working at once remove the audience. Written briefs remove the improvising: without one, the other party either gives in at once or turns into a caricature, and neither teaches anything.

**The observer role earns its place twice.** The observer supplies the second source of information that [a good debrief needs](t:4.28). Watching a skill from outside is also often when the steps make sense.

**There is research on the wider method.** Behaviour modelling training means showing a skill, having people practise it, and giving feedback. A published summary of a 2005 meta-analysis reports large effects on knowledge and skills, and smaller ones on behaviour at work. It reports better transfer in three conditions: when people saw poor examples as well as good ones, when experienced learners wrote their own practice scenarios, and when key points were taught as rules to apply, not scripts to copy. That supports the flawed demonstration and the second set on real cases.

try.text: Run one full round with two colleagues or friends, with you as timekeeper. Read the set-up aloud, hand out two short briefs, call "Stop there" at four minutes and run the feedback in order. Good looks like this: nobody asks what to do, the observer reads from the sheet, and the round is done in eight minutes.

**The observer joins in** or coaches during the round. Remind them their turn comes at the end.
**Someone would rather not take part.** Offer the observer role for the first round, then ask again privately.

deeper.text: The research below is about behaviour modelling training in general. The format in threes, the timings and the observer sheet are craft.

items.label: Paul (2021), Umbrella summary: Behavior modeling training. Quality Improvement Center for Workforce Development. A plain-language summary of Taylor, Russ-Eft and Chan (2005), A meta-analytic review of behavior modeling training.

quiz.q: In a three, what is the order of feedback after a round?
quiz.a: The practiser first, then the other party, then the observer, each with one thing to keep and one to try.

quiz.q: A sales manager tells you her team hates role-play and asks you to drop it from a negotiation course. What do you offer?
quiz.a: Practice in threes with written briefs and an observer, all groups at once, and nobody in front of the room. What the team dislikes is the audience and the improvising, and a negotiation course with no practice will not change what they do.

quiz.q: During round two you see an observer leaning in and telling the practiser what to say. What do you do?
quiz.a: Go over, say quietly that their turn is in the feedback, and point at the sheet. The practiser needs an uninterrupted attempt, and the observer's notes are what make the feedback specific.

topics.tierReason: Craft. The format rests on practitioner judgement. A research summary of behaviour modelling training supports showing, practising and feedback in general, and the paper itself was not read.

topics.title: Handle questions

situation.text: A hand goes up in the middle of your explanation and you do not know the answer. Ten minutes later someone folds their arms and says, "With respect, this would never work in our team." The room goes quiet to see what you do.

items: **Say at the start how questions work**: ask when something is unclear, and bigger issues go on the parked sheet. Put question points in your plan after each input as well as at the end.
**Take a question in three moves**: listen to the end, pause, and repeat it in one sentence for the room. Answer briefly, to everyone. Then check with the asker: "Does that cover it?"
**Ask for questions so you get some.** "What questions do you have about the second step?" works better than "Any questions?" There is more on [the wait after you ask](t:4.2).
**Say so when you do not know**, and say when you will. Write the question on the flipchart and send the answer when you promised. You can also ask the room whether anyone has dealt with it.

**Do not defend against a hostile question.** Agree with the part that is true, ask for the specific case, answer that briefly and move on. Allow one exchange and one follow-up in front of the room, then offer the break. There are separate moves for [the person who stays cynical all day](t:4.36).

**Wait for a breath** when a question is really a speech. Use their name, sum up the point in a sentence, check it and thank them. Then take one other view and move on. If the same person does it repeatedly, there are steps for [the person who talks too much](t:4.34).
**Park an off-topic issue.** Keep a flipchart sheet headed "Parked", which many trainers call the car park. Write the question in the person's words and say when you will return to it.
**Clear the parked sheet before the close.** Answer each item, pass it to the client, or say it is outside today's scope.

do.title: Words you can use
lines: Asking for questions: "What questions do you have about the second step? Take a moment."
Repeating for the room: "The question is whether this works on a first call as well as a renewal."
The one you cannot answer: "I don't know. I'd be guessing, and I'd rather not. I'll find out and email all of you by Friday." (Write it up.)
Using the room: "Has anyone here dealt with that? What did you do?"
The hostile one: "You may well be right that it wouldn't work as it stands. Which part wouldn't fit your team?"
After their answer: "That's a real constraint. Here's how I'd adapt the first step for it. Let's see whether it holds up in the practice."
If it carries on: "I want to do that justice, and I want to keep us to time. Can you and I pick it up at the break?"
The speech: "Dev, let me check I've got your point. You're saying the targets make this impossible. Is that it? Thank you. Let's hear one other view, then I'll move us on."
Parking: "That matters, and it's bigger than today. I'll write it on the parked sheet in your words, and we'll come back to it at four."
Coming later: "That's coming at two o'clock. Hold me to it."

why.text: This is craft. The wording is one trainer's and you should change it until it sounds like you.

**Groups judge how you handle not knowing.** In most trainers' experience, a group judges you more by how you handle not knowing than by how much you know. A confident guess that someone later finds to be wrong costs you the rest of the day. "I don't know, and I'll find out by Friday" costs nothing, provided the email arrives.

**The room watches how you take disagreement.** A hostile question is watched by everyone else as a test of whether it is safe to disagree here, the climate that makes it [safe to be wrong out loud](t:1.17). If you flatten the person, the room learns to keep quiet. There is also usually something true inside it. "This wouldn't work in our team" is often accurate information about workload, targets or a manager, and those conditions decide [whether training gets used](t:5.1).
**Parking only works if you come back.** A parked sheet nobody returns to shows the group it was a way of shutting people up.

try.text: Write three hostile questions about your own subject on cards. Ask a colleague to fire them at you with attitude, in random order, while you stand. Answer each aloud in under thirty seconds and record it. Good looks like this: your first words agree with something, there is no "but" in the first sentence, and you finish with a question back or a clear move on. Do the same with one question you cannot answer.

items: **You give a five-minute answer** to something one person cares about. Give the one-line answer and offer the rest at the break.
**You argue to win.** Even if you do, the rest of the room has stopped asking.
**You promise an answer by Friday** and forget. Photograph the flipchart before you leave the room.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What must happen to every item on the parked sheet before the session closes?
quiz.a: It is answered, passed to the client, or named as outside the day's scope.

quiz.q: During a product session for a software company's sales team, someone asks about a pricing rule you have not been briefed on. What do you say?
quiz.a: Say you do not know and will not guess, write the question up, and give a time by which you will send the answer to everyone. A wrong answer about pricing would travel to customers, and a kept promise builds more trust than a bluff.

quiz.q: A participant says, arms folded, "We tried this two years ago and it failed." What is your first move?
quiz.a: Agree that it may well have, and ask what happened. The answer usually tells you about real conditions at work, and the room is watching to see whether disagreement is safe.

topics.title: Keep time and cut content live

situation.text: It is 14:50 on a full day. Your plan says the final practice should be starting. You are one section behind, with an hour and forty minutes left and about two and a half hours of material.

items: **Tag every segment before the day.** Must: the day fails without it. Should: it makes the day better. Could: good if there is time. As a rule of thumb, the musts should fill no more than two thirds of the working time.
**Make practice, debriefs and the close musts.** Most of your own input is a should or a could.
**Write the short version** next to each should and could: drop it, halve it and how, or move it to a handout.
**Write clock times down the left** of the plan and mark three or four checkpoints: "By 11:00 I am starting the card sort." At each one, compare. If you are more than ten minutes behind, cut now.
**Keep a clock in view**, where you can see it without looking at your wrist. A small travel clock on your table works. Use a visible timer for activities.

**Cut in this order**: your own stories, second examples and slides. Then full report-backs, which become [one point per group](t:4.27). Then a could. Then a round of practice. Do not cut the debrief, the breaks or the close.
**Cut silently.** Never say "we've run out of time, so I'll skip this". Say nothing, or say "The sheet on that is in your pack."
**Give break restarts as clock times** and begin on that minute. A starting pattern from practice: 15 minutes mid-morning and mid-afternoon, and 45 to 60 minutes for lunch.

why.text: **Adjust the rules to your own pace.** This is craft. The two-thirds rule and the break lengths are judgement, and you should adjust them as you learn your own pace.

**Running over costs you the close.** Running over is the failure a client sees most easily. It also falls on the wrong part of the day. The close holds the [plan for first use at work](t:5.2), so a trainer who runs out of time loses the most useful fifteen minutes and keeps the slides.

**Choose your cuts while you are calm.** Plans are nearly always too full, because they are written as if instructions, moving chairs and questions took no time. Tagging makes you say what the day is for while you are calm. A cut chosen the night before is better than one chosen at 14:50 with twelve people watching. The same case applies to [rehearsing what could go wrong](t:4.13).
**Talking faster does not recover time.** People take in less, and the next activity starts with a confused room. Breaks stay because they count as [part of the learning](t:2.14).

try.text: Tag your next plan and write the short versions. Then rehearse one cut aloud: deliver the last minute of the segment before it and the first minute of the segment after, as though the cut piece had never existed. Record it. Good looks like this: no apology, no mention of time, and a join a participant would not notice. Practise the break call aloud as well: "Back at five to eleven by that clock."

items: **Everything is tagged must.** Ask of each segment whether the day would fail without it. If the client insists on content, agree the tags with them before the day.
**A guest speaker overruns.** Agree their slot and a hand signal beforehand, and stand up when the time is reached.
**You shorten the practice** and keep every slide. Cut your talking first.
**A late start loses ten minutes** and you push everything back. Cut a could or shorten a should in the first hour instead.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What do the tags must, should and could mean?
quiz.a: Must: the day fails without it. Should: it improves the day. Could: worth doing only if there is time.

quiz.q: At your 11:00 checkpoint you are twelve minutes behind, and the next segment is tagged could. What do you do?
quiz.a: Cut it now and say only that the handout is in the pack. Waiting in the hope of catching up moves the problem to the afternoon, where the cuts would fall on practice and the close.

quiz.q: It is 16:10 on a day that ends at 16:30, and your last practice round has one group still to go. What do you do?
quiz.a: Let that group finish its conversation, skip your recap, and start the close by 16:15. The close carries the first-use plan, and finishing late breaks the finish time you promised that morning.

topics.title: Close a session

situation.text: At 16:27 you reach the last slide. "We're nearly out of time, so, any questions? No? The forms are by the door. Thanks, everyone." People are zipping bags before you finish the sentence.

items: **Give the close fifteen minutes** in the plan, tag it must, and start it at the planned minute whatever is unfinished.
**Take questions first** and clear the [parked sheet of off-topic issues](t:4.30), for about three minutes. Questions belong before the end, not at it.
**Do the feedback form next**, in the room, in silence, for three minutes. A form filled in while leaving gets a row of ticks.

**Then recall.** Workbooks closed, each person writes from memory the three things they most want to keep, and compares with a neighbour. There is an explanation of [why recalling beats being told again](t:2.24).

**Then plan first use.** Each person writes one sentence on when and where they will use it, in the form used to [plan the first use at work](t:5.2), and says it to a partner. The partner asks what might get in the way.
**Say what happens next** in under a minute: what you will send and when, any follow-up date, and what their managers have been told.
**Finish with a round.** Each person says the first thing they will do, in five words or fewer. You go first to set the length. With 30 people, do this at tables.
**Thank them, name the time and stop.** Stay in the room for fifteen minutes afterwards for anyone who wants a word.

why.text: **Two parts rest on research.** The order is craft. Two parts borrow from research covered elsewhere on this site: the [when-and-where plan for first use](t:5.2), and the finding that [endings shape how a session is rated](t:2.18) and remembered.

**People leave with whatever came last.** Whatever happens last is what people walk out with. If the last act is a form or a question from one person about parking, that is the note the day ends on. Put the questions and the form first and the day ends on each person saying what they will do.

**A summary makes you do the remembering.** Your own summary is the weakest way to close. When you list the key points, you are the one doing the remembering. Three minutes of recall from memory makes them do it, and the comparison in pairs fills gaps without you.

**Ending on time keeps your agreement.** Ending on time is part of the agreement you made in the first ten minutes. People have trains and children to collect. Five minutes over, with half the room watching the clock, is worth less than nothing.

try.text: Deliver the whole close aloud, standing, against a timer, to a colleague or an empty room. Speak your lines and wait in silence where the group would be working. Record it. Good looks like this: your own words add up to under five of the fifteen minutes, you know your final sentence by heart, and you stop after it.

items: **You introduce a new idea** in the last ten minutes because it was left over. It will not be remembered and it pushes out the plan for first use. Send it afterwards.
**The round turns into speeches.** Go first, in five words, and keep the pace with a nod to the next person.

**A senior person wants to close** the day. Give them one minute before the final round, so the last voices are the participants'. Agree this with them beforehand, as you did when you [opened the session](t:4.21).
**At 16:15 you are mid-activity** and tempted to finish it. Stop the activity. The close is the must.
**You pack up** while people fill in forms. Sit still. They take the form as seriously as you appear to.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: In the 15-minute close, what comes last?
quiz.a: A short round in which each person says the first thing they will do.

quiz.q: It is 16:15, your close is due to start and the group is halfway through a discussion they are enjoying. What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop the discussion with one closing remark and start the close. The recall and the first-use sentence are worth more than the end of the discussion, and finishing late breaks your agreement with the group.

quiz.q: The client asks you to end with their feedback form so that everyone completes it. How do you fit it in?
quiz.a: Put the form three minutes into the close, done in silence in the room, and finish with first use and the round. Everyone still completes it, and the day ends on what people will do.

topics.title: Write a session plan you can run from

situation.text: Your plan is the slide deck and a list of headings in a notebook. At 11:20 you cannot tell whether you are ahead or behind. The role cards for the next exercise are still in your bag.

items: **Use one page, turned sideways**, as a table with five columns: clock time, activity, method and grouping, materials, purpose. If you cannot write a segment's purpose in a few words, cut the segment.
**Place the fixed points first**: start, finish, lunch and two breaks. Then the opening and the fifteen-minute close. A day from 09:30 to 16:30 leaves about five hours of working time.

**Put the hardest practice mid-morning**, and something active and undemanding straight after lunch, following the [energy curve of the day](t:2.14). Mark the low-energy times on the plan, usually the first half hour after lunch and mid-afternoon.
**Add two recall points**, one after lunch and one in the last hour. Both are done from memory, with notes closed. There is an explanation of [why recall from memory helps](t:2.24).
**Add up your own talking.** As a starting rule from practice, keep it under a third of the working time, with no input longer than twenty minutes before the group does something.
**Tag each row must, should or could**, and mark your checkpoints, as you do to [keep time and cut content live](t:4.31).
**Add two or three minutes** to every activity for the instruction and the moving about. Leave ten minutes in the day unallocated.

**Write each activity's instruction on a card**, in the [order for giving instructions](t:4.24). Pack materials in plan order. Then walk the plan aloud once against a clock, and keep a printed copy on your table.

why.text: This is craft. The format is one that works for many trainers, and the proportions are judgement.

**You must find your place in seconds.** A plan you run from has a different job from a design document. You need to find your place in three seconds, standing, mid-sentence. That means one page, large type and clock times. Durations make you do sums while you are meant to be listening.

**Each column answers a live question.** Each column answers a question you will otherwise face live. Method and grouping tells you who is talking and whether people need to move. Materials stops the hunt through a bag while twelve people wait. Purpose is what you consult when you have to cut, and it lets a co-trainer or the client see why each piece is there.
**The page shows an over-full day early.** Writing it this way shows up an over-full day before the group does. If the times do not add up on paper, they will not add up in the room.

try.text: Write a one-page plan for a 90-minute session you could give. Then stand up and walk it through against a clock. Say the first sentence of each segment and every instruction in full, and move to where you would stand. Mark each place you ran over or hunted for something. Good looks like this: you can find your place from standing in three seconds, and every row has a purpose you can say aloud.

items: **The plan becomes a four-page script.** You will not read it in the room. Keep one page and put the wording on instruction cards.
**The plan follows the slides.** Write the activities first and add slides only where a row needs one.
**No slack anywhere.** One long question and the day is late. Keep the ten spare minutes and the could rows.
**Times were never tested aloud.** Activities with real people run longer than they do in your head, so walk it through.
**The plan stays in your bag.** Put it beside the clock, where a glance takes in both.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What are the five columns of the one-page session plan?
quiz.a: Clock time, activity, method and grouping, materials, and purpose.

quiz.q: You are planning a day for a customer team and the client asks for the new policy briefing at 13:15, straight after lunch. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Open the afternoon with a short recall task in pairs and place the briefing mid-afternoon in a short slot. Straight after lunch is a dip, so it suits something active and undemanding, not twenty minutes of listening.

quiz.q: You add up your draft plan and find you are talking for three of the five working hours. What do you change?
quiz.a: Turn inputs into tasks, such as comparing two examples before you give the rule, and move reference content to a handout, until your talking is under about a third. Skills are built in the practice rows, and those are what the long inputs are squeezing.

parts.title: Difficult moments
parts.summary: Ladders of response, from light to firm, for the hard moments with people, with the words to say and whether to act in the room or at the break.

topics.title: The person who talks too much

situation.text: Twenty minutes in, one sales manager has answered every question. The others have stopped trying, and two of them are looking at you to see what you will do about it.

items: **Change the structure before you say anything** to the person. Give everyone two minutes to write an answer alone, then put them in pairs, then take one point from each pair in turn. Most over-talking stops here.
**Move nearer to the talker**, and turn your body and your eyes to the other side of the room when you ask the next question.
**Thank and redirect, in the room**: "Thanks, Dev. Let's hear from someone we have not heard from yet." Say it warmly, then wait, as you do [after asking any question](t:4.2).
**Interrupt a long turn at a breath**, with their name and a summary: "Dev, let me stop you there so I can hold on to that. Your point is that discounting starts too early. Who sees it differently?"

**Have a quiet word at the break** if it carries on. Start with what they bring, then ask for help: "You know this area well and I want the room to get the benefit. I also need to hear from the quieter people. Would you hold your answer until two others have spoken?"
**Offer them a job** that uses the energy, such as keeping time or summing up at the end of a discussion. Offer it. Do not impose it.
**Set a rule for everyone** as the last rung: "For this round, each person speaks once before anyone speaks twice."

why.text: **Use the least public move that works.** This is practitioner judgement. No study tests this ladder. The order follows one idea: use the least public move that works. A change of structure costs the talker nothing. A remark in front of colleagues costs them something, and [publicly correcting one person](t:4.3) costs the whole room.

**Treat over-talking as enthusiasm.** Most people who talk too much are keen, nervous, or used to being the one who knows. Very few are trying to spoil the session. If you treat it as enthusiasm you usually keep them on your side, and the quiet word works because it gives them a part to play with nobody watching.

**Keep talk about behaviour for the break.** Act in the room when other people are being shut out right now. Keep anything about the person's behaviour for the break. If the next break is an hour away and the structure change has not worked, make a break: "Let's take five minutes."

try.text: Rehearse this aloud. Ask a colleague to play someone who answers every question and to keep going until you stop them. Run three minutes of discussion and use rungs two to four. Record it on your phone. Listen for whether your interruption used their name, summed up their point and passed the question on within ten seconds. Then say the break-time line to them face to face and ask how it felt to hear.

items: **Handing the talker the pen** and making them the scribe is something some trainers do. That has a risk. Whoever writes decides what gets recorded, and being made scribe can feel like a punishment. If you use it, check the sheet shows the group's points and not only theirs.
**A joke at their expense** gets a laugh and loses you a participant. Keep your tone level and friendly.
**Starting with the rule for everyone** makes the whole group pay for one person. Do not start there.
**Only the talker did the pre-work**, as sometimes happens. Then the problem is the rest of the room, and the moves are those for [the silent group](t:4.35).
**Count your own talking time first.** If you speak more than they do, start there.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What is the first rung of the ladder for someone who talks too much?
quiz.a: A change of structure: everyone writes alone, then pairs, then one point from each pair.

quiz.q: A participant has answered six questions in a row. You have tried pairs and you have asked for new voices. The break is in ten minutes. What do you do?
quiz.a: Hold on until the break and have the quiet word there: name what they bring, then ask them to wait until two others have spoken. Anything about a person's behaviour is better said in private.

quiz.q: You ask the loudest person to scribe. Ten minutes later the flipchart shows only their own three points. What do you do?
quiz.a: Go back to the group and ask what is missing from the sheet, then add it in their words. Next time take the pen yourself or rotate it, because the scribe controls the record.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement from the training room. No study was opened for this topic and none tests this sequence.

topics.title: The silent group

situation.text: You ask a good question. Twelve retail team leaders look at the table. You count to five, and then to five again, and nobody says a word.

items: **Check the question first.** If it was long, vague or had two parts, ask it again in one short sentence and put it on the screen or the flipchart.
**Wait properly**, giving the full [wait after a question](t:4.2). Then lower the cost of answering: "Take one minute and write down your answer. Nobody will see it."
**Go to pairs**: "Compare what you wrote with the person next to you. Two minutes." Walk round and listen. You will hear whether they have answers.
**Collect from pairs, not from individuals**: "Give me one thing your partner said." Reporting someone else's point is easier than owning your own.
**Ask a question that needs no words** if the room is still flat. A show of hands, one to five fingers as a way of [reading the room](t:4.14), or a sticky dot on a scale on the wall.
**Say what you see** and ask about it: "It has gone quiet, and I can't tell if that is thinking, tiredness or me losing you. Talk to your neighbour for one minute about which it is, then tell me."
**Ask one or two people alone** at the break: "Is there something about today or this group that I should know?" Then ask the organiser the same thing.

why.text: **Only the wait has research behind it.** This is practitioner judgement. The [wait itself has classroom research](t:4.2) behind it. The rest is craft that trainers pass on.

**Silence has several causes.** Silence has several causes and the ladder tests them in order of how easy they are to fix. The cheapest cause is your question. Next comes the risk of [being wrong in front of colleagues](t:1.17), which writing and pairs reduce. After that come causes you cannot see from the front: the group heard bad news this morning, their manager is in the room, they were told to attend, or the content is aimed at the wrong level. You find those out by asking, and people will tell you at the break what they would never say in the room.

**The first six rungs single nobody out.** Stay in the room for the first six rungs. They are all changes to the task and single nobody out. Go to the break when you suspect the reason is about people or about the organisation.

**A silent room may work well in pairs.** One caution. A group that is silent in front of the whole room may be working hard in pairs. If the pair talk is lively, the session is fine. Stop asking the whole room and run more of the day in small groups.

try.text: Run this with three or four colleagues or friends. Brief them to stay silent whatever you ask in the first minute. Ask your question, wait five full seconds, and then go down the ladder aloud: the written minute, the pairs, one thing your partner said. Have one person time your waits with a phone. Afterwards ask them at which rung they would have started talking in a real session.

It has gone quiet, and I can't tell if that is thinking, tiredness or me losing you. One minute with your neighbour: which is it?
At the break: Is there something about today or this group that I should know?

items: **Answering your own question** teaches the group that waiting works. Hold the silence, then change the task.
**Do not pick on someone** by name to break the silence. Name people only after they have had time to prepare, as part of [managing the group](t:4.3).
**Jokes about the quiet** ("Don't all speak at once") put the blame on the group.
**Silence can mean thinking.** If people are writing or looking up and away, give them longer.
**Norms about speaking up differ** between groups and [the cultures in the room](t:4.7). Written and paired steps work across most of them.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: When a group is silent, what do you check before anything else?
quiz.a: The question. Ask it again in one short sentence and put it where people can see it.

quiz.q: Nobody answers when you ask the whole room, but when you set a pair task the room is loud and busy. What do you do?
quiz.a: Run more of the session in pairs and small groups and collect from pairs. The group can do the thinking. It is the whole-room setting that is stopping them.

quiz.q: You have tried writing, pairs and a show of hands and the room is still closed. The organiser is in the corridor at the break. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the organiser, and one or two participants privately, whether something about today or the group explains it. The cause is probably outside the session, and you need to know it before you change the plan.

topics.title: The cynic, and the person who was sent

situation.text: Arms folded, chair pushed back. "We did this two years ago with the last lot and nothing changed." Next to him sits someone whose manager booked her on the course without asking.

items: **Deal with resistance before it appears.** In your opening say: "Some of you chose to be here and some of you were told to come. Both are fine. All I ask is that you look for one thing that is worth your afternoon."
**Ask for the doubts early** and write them up: "What have you seen in training like this that did not work?" Keep the sheet on the wall and come back to it.
**Take the cynical remark as information** when it comes. Find the true part and ask for detail: "You have seen three sales methods come and go. What happened to the last one?"
**Widen it to the group** so it does not become a duel: "Who has had a different experience? Who has had the same?"
**Set a test** in place of an argument: "Don't take my word for it. Try it in the next exercise and tell me where it breaks."

**Speak to the person alone** at the break: "I get the sense this is not where you would choose to be today. What would make the rest of it useful to you?" Offer a real choice about how they take part.
**Be plain and private** if the remarks are stopping others: "It is fine to disagree with this. I need you not to make it harder for other people to try it. Can we agree on that?"

why.text: **The opening line gives back some choice.** This is practitioner judgement, with one link to research covered elsewhere on the site. Adults engage more when they [know why something matters to them](t:1.5) and [have some choice](t:1.16). A person who was sent has had neither, so the opening line gives back a little of both.

**The cynic is often right about the past.** Programmes do get launched and dropped. If you defend the training you are arguing with their experience, and you will lose. If you ask what happened last time, you learn what the follow-up needs to avoid, and the room sees you can take a challenge.

**The cynic may speak for others.** A cynic may also be saying what others think. Sometimes the complaint is that training is the wrong answer to this problem, a real possibility that calls for [checking it is a skill problem](t:1.20). Note it and take it to the client afterwards, without naming the person.
**Content in the room, behaviour at the break.** Rungs one to five belong in the room because they are about the content. The last two are about a person's behaviour and belong in the break.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play the cynic and give them three lines to throw at you, such as "This is common sense", "Head office has no idea what we do" and "I was told to come". Stand up and answer each aloud, using the pattern of true part, question, then test. Record it. Listen for any sentence where you defended the course, and say that reply again without the defence.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: Opening: Some of you chose to be here and some of you were told to come. Both are fine.
Opening: What have you seen in training like this that did not work? I'll write them up.
In the room: That is a fair point. What happened to the last one?
In the room: Who has had a different experience?
In the room: Don't take my word for it. Try it in the next exercise and tell me where it breaks.
At the break: What would make the rest of today useful to you?
At the break: It is fine to disagree. I need you not to make it harder for others to try it.
To the client afterwards: Several people doubted the follow-up, because of what happened last time.

items: **Trying to win them over** in front of the group is a mistake. The more attention the doubt gets, the more of the session it takes.
**Avoid "I hear you, but".** People hear only what comes after the "but".
**Check what the client has agreed** before you tell anyone they are free to leave. Attendance may be a condition of their job or of a certificate.
**A named individual's attitude** is not yours to report to their manager unless you said at the start that you would. It breaks the confidence that [professional ethics ask you to keep](t:4.16).

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What do you say in the opening to people who were sent?
quiz.a: That some chose to come and some were told to, that both are fine, and that you ask them to look for one thing worth their time.

quiz.q: A participant says: "We did this two years ago and nothing changed." What do you do?
quiz.a: Agree with the true part and ask what happened last time, then ask who has had a different experience. You gain information for the follow-up and avoid defending the course against their own history.

quiz.q: After two private conversations one person is still making remarks that put others off practising. What do you say, and where?
quiz.a: At the break, in private: it is fine to disagree, and you need them not to make it harder for others to try it. Ask for their agreement to that and nothing more.

topics.title: The expert in the room
topics.theory: Participants who know more than you

situation.text: You are training a software company's support team on a new escalation process. One engineer has run the platform for six years and corrects your second slide.

items: **Find out who the experts are** before the day. Ask the organiser: "Who in the group knows this area deeply?" At the start, ask the room for a show of hands on years of experience.
**Acknowledge the expert early**, in public, without handing over the session: "Priya has run this platform for six years. I'll be asking her to keep me honest on the detail."
**Ask them for cases, not for theory**: "Priya, where have you seen this go wrong on a live account?" A case adds to your session. A lecture replaces it.
**Say so in one breath** when they correct you and they are right: "You're right, thank you. Let me fix that." Change it on the flipchart and carry on.
**Do not bluff** when you are not sure: "I have not come across that. I'll check at the break and come back to it." Then come back to it, out loud.
**Name both views and test them** when it is a difference of view: "There are two schools on this. Here is why the course uses this one. Let's try both on the next case."

**Ask for their help at the break** and set a limit: "I want your experience in the room. I also need the group to work things out before they hear the answer. Could you hold back for the first few minutes of each exercise, then add what we have missed?"

why.text: **Your authority comes from running the process.** This is practitioner judgement. The thinking behind it is that your authority in the room comes from running the process well. It does not come from knowing more than everyone present. A trainer who competes with an expert on content usually loses, and loses the group's trust on the way.

**Give the expert a way to contribute.** An expert who is named and used tends to relax. One who is ignored will keep proving what they know. Asking for cases gives them a way to contribute that helps the others, because real examples from their own workplace are what the group will remember.
**Your quick admission sets the example.** Admitting a mistake quickly also shows the group the behaviour you want from them. People take risks when they see [errors handled without fuss](t:1.17).

**Correct in the room, ask at the break.** The correction and the admission happen in the room, at once, because the group heard the error. The request to hold back happens at the break, because it is about how one person takes part.

try.text: Ask a colleague who knows a subject better than you to sit in while you explain it for five minutes, standing up. Their brief is to correct you twice, once fairly and once on a matter of opinion. Practise the two replies aloud: the fast admission, and "two schools, let's test both". Record it and check that neither reply ran longer than fifteen seconds.

items: **Never bluff.** One invented answer costs more than ten honest gaps.
**The expert becomes a second trainer:** do not let this happen. If the group starts looking to them after every question, take the questions to pairs first.
**Expert detail can bury beginners.** If the answer is beyond what the group needs, say: "That is the advanced version. Let's take it at the break for those who want it."
**A would-be expert:** someone who only believes they are the expert gets the same ladder. Ask for a case and let the case do the work.
**The material is wrong:** if the correction shows this, tell whoever owns the design the same day.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Where does a trainer's authority come from when someone in the room knows more?
quiz.a: From running the process well, not from knowing the most.

quiz.q: An experienced participant corrects a figure on your slide and you can see they are right. What do you do?
quiz.a: Say "You're right, thank you", correct it where everyone can see, and move on. A quick admission keeps trust and shows the group how to handle being wrong.

quiz.q: The expert answers every exercise question before the group has thought about it. What do you do?
quiz.a: At the break, ask them to hold back for the first few minutes of each exercise and then add what was missed. In the room, send questions to pairs first so there is thinking time.

topics.title: The senior person who takes over

situation.text: The sales director has joined your workshop for her regional managers. Each time you ask the group a question she answers it, and each time she finishes, the room agrees with her.

items: **Brief them before the day.** Ask for ten minutes by phone and make three requests: speak last, ask before you tell, and say at the start that you want to hear disagreement.
**Agree what you will do** if it goes wrong, in the same call: "If I think the room is waiting for your view, I'll ask you to hold it. Is that all right with you?"
**Decide together how much they attend.** Opening the day and returning for the conclusions is often better than sitting in all of it.
**Use structure in the room.** Everyone writes first, then you take a round and say in advance: "Sam, I'll come to you last." Seat them at the side, not at the head of the table.
**Do not mix one senior with juniors** in group work. Put them with the people closest to their own level, or ask them to visit groups as someone to consult.
**Hold them gently and in public** when they take over: "Sam, hold that thought. I'd like two more views before yours."
**Remind them of the agreement** at the break: "The room is waiting to hear what you think before they speak. In the next session, could you ask two questions before you give a view?"
**Propose that they step out** if nothing changes: "People will be more candid in the practice without you. Would you come back at three for their conclusions?"

why.text: **The briefing makes the other moves possible.** This is practitioner judgement. The advice on [designing for executives](t:2.9) warns that the most senior person can close a room down by speaking first, and the advice on [taking needless stress out of the room](t:1.13) says to have senior people go second. Neither works reliably on the day unless the person has agreed to it beforehand. The briefing is the move that makes the others possible.

**Senior people rarely mean to take over.** They are used to being asked for a decision, and silence feels to them like a gap they should fill. Most are glad to be told what would help. The briefing gives them a job, which is to draw their people out. It also lets you step in later without that looking like a challenge to their rank, which is far easier for a new trainer when the person has already said yes.

**Only two moves belong in the room.** The first three rungs happen before the day. Structure and the single holding line belong in the room. Everything else is for the break, and never in front of their team.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play a director. First, make the briefing call for real, on the phone, using the three requests and the "if I think the room is waiting" line. Then run a five-minute discussion with two more people, in which the director answers first every time. Say the holding line aloud at least twice. Afterwards ask the director how each one landed.

try.title: Words for the briefing call
lines: Thanks for making time. I want your team to get the most from having you there.
People tend to wait for the most senior person and then agree. So I have three requests.
One. In discussions, would you speak last? I'll come to you at the end of each round.
Two. When you do come in, start with a question before you give your view.
Three. In the first five minutes, would you say that you want to hear where people disagree, with each other and with you?
If I think the room is waiting for your view, I'll ask you to hold it. Is that all right with you?
For the practice after lunch, I'd suggest you step out and come back at three to hear what they concluded.
Is there anything you want me to know about the group before we start?

items: **If you cannot get the call**, use the sixty-second version at the door before the start. Speak last, ask first.
**A group of their own staff:** do not seat them in a small one and expect an honest practice round.
**A senior person who stays silent** all day can worry the room as much as one who talks. Ask them to say something encouraging at the start and at the end.
**If they are also the client**, the advice on [being watched by a client or observer](t:4.44) applies too.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What three things do you ask a senior person to do when you brief them?
quiz.a: Speak last, ask before telling, and say at the start that they want to hear disagreement.

quiz.q: A director will attend your workshop for her own team. You have a week. What do you do first?
quiz.a: Ask for a ten-minute call and brief her: the three requests, and agreement that you may ask her to hold her view. Moves made in the room work far better when she has agreed to them beforehand.

quiz.q: During a discussion the most senior person answers before anyone else for the third time. You briefed them yesterday. What do you say?
quiz.a: "Sam, hold that thought. I'd like two more views before yours." Then at the break, remind them of the agreement in private and ask for two questions before each view.

topics.title: Side conversations and phones

situation.text: Two people at the back table are whispering through your explanation. A third has her phone under the desk, and a fourth has opened his laptop to his inbox.

items: **Cover phones and calls in the opening.** State break times as clock times so people know when they can check messages, and say: "If you need to take a call, step out. You don't need to ask."
**Leave a short side conversation alone.** People are often helping each other, translating, or reacting to what you just said.
**Stop talking if it goes on.** Pause mid-sentence, look at the slide or your notes, and wait. The quiet usually ends it without a word from you.
**Move beside their table** and carry on teaching from there.
**Bring it into the room**, lightly and without sarcasm: "Let's have one conversation. Is there something from that side worth sharing?"
**Turn several conversations into the task.** If that many have started, [the room is telling you something](t:4.14): "Take two minutes with your neighbour on what you make of this so far."

**Ask and do not accuse** at the break: "You two were talking a fair bit. Have I missed a question?" For a phone: "It looks like something is going on at work. Do you need ten minutes to sort it out? I'd sooner you did that and came back properly."
**Make a timed request of everyone** if devices are pulling the whole room away: "For the next forty minutes, lids down and phones face down. Then a ten-minute break for messages."

why.text: **Start with what costs nobody anything.** This is practitioner judgement. The ladder starts with the room and your own behaviour, because those cost nobody anything. It ends with a request to everyone, because a rule aimed at one person in public is a correction, and there is more on [what a public correction costs](t:4.3).

**Side talk is information before it is misbehaviour.** Two people whispering may be confused, bored, or ahead of you. A room full of it means the input has gone on too long. So the early rungs give the talk somewhere to go.

**Clear breaks remove most phone checking.** Phones are different. Participants have jobs that carry on while they are with you. Clear break times and permission to step out remove most of the checking under the table. What is left is usually one person with a real problem at work, and ten minutes outside serves them better than two hours half present.
**Side talk shuts out remote people.** In hybrid sessions this matters more, because talk in the room that [the remote people cannot hear](t:4.11) shuts them out.

try.text: Practise the pause. Ask two colleagues to start whispering one minute into a three-minute explanation that you deliver standing. Stop mid-sentence and wait, looking at your notes, until they stop. Then do it again and use the line "Let's have one conversation". Record both and time the silence. Most people find they waited under three seconds the first time.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: Opening: Breaks are at 10:45, 12:30 and 15:00. Messages can wait until then.
Opening: If you need to take a call, step out. You don't need to ask.
In the room: Let's have one conversation. Is there something from that side worth sharing?
In the room: Take two minutes with your neighbour on what you make of this so far.
At the break: You two were talking a fair bit. Have I missed a question?
At the break: Do you need ten minutes to sort that out? I'd sooner you did that and came back properly.
To everyone: For the next forty minutes, lids down and phones face down. Then ten minutes for messages.

items: **Do not ban devices outright.** A phone or laptop may be how someone takes notes, reads the slides at a larger size or translates, which is part of [designing for different minds](t:2.23).
**Someone may be on call** for work or for a person they care for. Ask about this at the start: "Is anyone on call today?"
**Staring at the talkers** until they notice turns the room against you. Look at your notes.
**Do not catch a whisperer out** with a content question. It is a public correction in disguise.
**The same pair talks all day:** split the groups for everyone at the next activity by [numbering off into new groups](t:4.25).

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What do you say about calls in your opening?
quiz.a: That anyone who needs to take a call can step out without asking, and when the breaks are, as clock times.

quiz.q: Two people have been whispering for a minute while you explain a model. What is your first move?
quiz.a: Stop talking, look at your notes and wait. The silence usually ends it, and nobody has been corrected in public.

quiz.q: Halfway through the afternoon, four separate side conversations have started. What do you do?
quiz.a: Treat it as a message from the room and turn it into a two-minute pair task on what they make of the content so far. Then shorten or change the input that caused it.

topics.title: Late arrivals and people who leave early
topics.theory: Protecting the start and the close

situation.text: It is 9:30 and eight of fourteen people are in the room. At 9:50 the door opens twice. At lunch, three people tell you they have a train at four.

items: **Fix what you can beforehand.** Joining instructions give two times: "Coffee from 9:15, we start at 9:30." They also give the finish time and ask people to say now if they must leave before it.
**Start on time, with a soft start.** The first five minutes are a paired question on the screen, which a latecomer can miss. Introductions and the key content begin once it is done.
**Keep going when someone walks in late**: nod, point to a seat near the door with a handout on it, and carry on. No recap, no joke, no comment.
**Catch them up** at the next pair task: "Ana, would you bring Tom up to date in two minutes?" Or do it yourself while the groups work.
**Give the restart as a clock time** after breaks, write it up, and begin at that time with something worth being there for.
**Ask someone who is late three times** at the break: "You have missed the start of the last two sessions. Is something getting in the way? The next part builds on the piece before lunch."

**Ask in the opening who leaves early:** "Does anyone need to leave before 4:30?" If several do, move the close. Run [the first-use plan](t:5.2) before they go, and use the last stretch for optional extra practice.
**Close with a single early leaver** on their own at the last break: "Before you go, tell me the first thing you will try, and when."

why.text: **Punctual people and the close need protecting.** This is practitioner judgement. Two things are being protected. One is the people who arrived on time, who learn from a late start that the stated time is not the real one. The other is the close, and there is more on [how to close a session](t:4.32). It is where people [plan their first use at work](t:5.2), and it is the first thing to be lost when people drift away.

**The soft start solves a real conflict.** If you wait, you punish the punctual. If you launch into the main content, a third of the room misses it. A short opening task that matters a little, but not too much, lets you begin on time and still have everyone present for the important part.
**Saying nothing to a latecomer is deliberate.** They already know. A remark costs them standing in front of colleagues, and a recap makes everyone else sit through the material again.
**Design handles most lateness.** Nearly all of this is done by design and in the room. Only the repeated case goes to the break.

try.text: Stand up and deliver your opening five minutes to an empty room or a colleague, as a soft start: greet, put the paired question up, give the instruction, then begin properly. Have the colleague walk in ninety seconds late and practise carrying on without a break in your sentence. Then say the three-times-late line aloud until it sounds like concern and not a telling-off.

try.title: A worked example: a soft start and a moved close for a one-day workshop

head: Time

rows: Coffee. Paired question already on the screen.
Early arrivals have something to do.
Start. Pairs discuss the question for four minutes.
On time for those present. Latecomers miss little.

items: **Latecomers placed straight into a group** that is mid-task slow the group. Give them two minutes with you first.
**Where attendance counts towards a certificate** or a compliance record, note what was missed and tell the organiser. That rule is the client's to apply, not yours.
**If half the group is late**, the cause is the venue, the travel or the invitation. Ask, and tell the client.
**Finishing late to make up** for a late start breaks your promise to the people with trains. Cut content instead.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What is a soft start?
quiz.a: Beginning on time with a short paired task that latecomers can miss, and starting the introductions and main content once it is done.

quiz.q: A participant comes in twenty minutes late while you are explaining the first model. What do you do?
quiz.a: Nod, point to the seat by the door and carry on. Catch them up during the next pair task, so they are not embarrassed and nobody else hears the content twice.

quiz.q: At 9:40 three people tell you they must leave at 15:50, and your close is planned for 16:15. What do you do?
quiz.a: Move the first-use plan and close to 15:30 and use the time after 15:50 for optional practice. The close matters more than the last exercise.

topics.title: Conflict between two participants

situation.text: Two store managers disagree about a rota policy. The second exchange is sharper than the first. On the third, one says: "That is typical of your branch." The rest of the table goes still.

items: **Decide which kind of conflict it is.** A disagreement about ideas is useful and you should keep it going. A remark about a person is where you step in.
**Slow down an argument about ideas.** Write both positions on the flipchart as "View A" and "View B", with no names on them. Ask each person to state the other view to that person's satisfaction.
**Bring in the group**: "Who has a case that supports A? And B?" The two are no longer facing each other.

**Stand to break their line of sight** if it heats up, and say: "Let me pause you both. Both views are on the chart. I'm going to move us on, and we can come back to it after the break if it still matters."
**Change the structure.** Give a short task done alone, then form new groups by numbering off round the whole room, so the two are apart and nobody has been moved by name.
**Speak to each one separately** at the break, and briefly: "That got sharp. Are you all right? Is there anything I need to know to make this afternoon workable?"
**Name a repeated personal remark once**, plainly: "Paul, that was about Ana, not about her point. Challenge the idea, not the person."

**Stop an abusive or discriminatory remark** at once: "That is not acceptable in this room." Call a break. Speak to the person it was aimed at and then to the person who said it. Write down what was said, and tell the client contact the same day.

why.text: **Some conflict cannot wait for privacy.** This is practitioner judgement. The advice on [managing the group](t:4.3) says to deal with conflict early and in private where you can. This topic adds which parts cannot wait for privacy.

**Keep the argument, lose the heat.** A room with no disagreement is usually a room being polite, so the early rungs keep the argument and take the heat out of it. Writing the views on a chart moves them off the two people and on to the wall.

**A personal remark is dealt with publicly.** A personal remark is different. Everyone heard it, so everyone needs to see it dealt with, in a few words. One flat sentence and a change of activity is enough.

**You are not a mediator.** A dispute that started before your session belongs to their managers. Your job is to make the room workable for the hours you have. For abusive or discriminatory remarks the client will have its own conduct policy, and your part is to stop it, look after the person, record what happened and pass it on.

try.text: Rehearse with two colleagues. Brief them to argue about something trivial and to make it personal on the third exchange. Practise standing between them and saying the pause line aloud, then the "challenge the idea" line. Do it three times, with them escalating faster each time. Ask them afterwards whether your voice stayed level. That is the thing to work on.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: Ideas: Let me get both of these on the chart. View A is... View B is...
Ideas: Before you reply, tell me her point in a way she would agree with.
Ideas: Who has a case that supports A? And B?
Heating up: Let me pause you both. Both views are on the chart. We'll come back to it after the break if it still matters.
Personal: That was about Ana, not about her point. Challenge the idea, not the person.
Unacceptable: That is not acceptable in this room. We'll take ten minutes.
At the break, to each: That got sharp. Are you all right? Is there anything I need to know for this afternoon?

items: **While tempers are up**, do not take a side on the content, even if one of them is right. Come back to it later with a case.
**If you have a working agreement** from the opening, point to it. If you have none, this is the reason to [agree how the group will work](t:4.23) next time.
**A serious incident:** tell the organiser about it yourself. Do not leave them to hear it from a participant.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Which kind of disagreement do you keep going, and which do you stop?
quiz.a: Keep a disagreement about ideas going. Step in when a remark is about a person.

quiz.q: Two participants are arguing hard about a policy. Nothing personal has been said. What do you do?
quiz.a: Write both positions on the flipchart without names and ask each to state the other's view, then ask the group for cases. This keeps a useful argument and takes it off the two people.

quiz.q: One participant says of another: "That is typical of people like you." What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop it at once with one flat sentence and call a break. Speak to each privately, starting with the person it was aimed at, write down what was said, and tell the client contact that day.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement from the training room. No study was opened for this topic and none tests this sequence.

topics.title: When someone is upset

situation.text: You are running a feedback exercise with new managers. In one of the trios a woman has stopped talking and is crying quietly. Her partners are looking at you.

items: **Keep your voice and pace steady** and do not draw the room's eyes to her. If you are speaking, carry on for a sentence and move so that people look away from her table.
**Give the group something to do**: "Take five minutes in your pairs on the next question." Or call the break early.
**Go to her quietly**, or ask your co-facilitator to. Get down to her level and speak low: "Would you like to step outside for a minute? I can come with you, or you can go on your own."
**Outside, say little**: "Take your time. You don't need to explain." Then offer choices: "What would help? A few minutes alone, some water, someone to sit with you, or to head home?"
**Ask whether she would like a colleague** with her. Fetch that person and no one else.

**Listen if she wants to talk.** Do not probe, advise or tell a story of your own. If it is about work or health, point to help she already has: her manager, HR, an employee assistance line if her employer has one, or her GP.
**Leave the way back open**: "Come back whenever you are ready, or not at all. Nobody will ask." To the group, say one line or nothing: "Sara is taking a few minutes. Let's carry on."
**Check in at the next break**, and agree what is passed on: "I won't mention this to anyone unless you want me to."

why.text: **This is first response, not counselling.** This is practitioner judgement. It is not counselling and it is not medical advice. The advice on [your professional limits](t:4.16) says a participant in distress needs referral, not coaching, and the advice on [taking needless stress out of the room](t:1.13) says to give everyone a way to step out. This topic is the minute in between.

**Cover first, then privacy, then choice.** People cry in ordinary workshops, about feedback, change, redundancy, or something from home that the exercise touched. Usually what they want most is not to be watched. So the order is cover first, then privacy, then choice.

**Your limits are the point of the topic.** You are there to make the next ten minutes bearable and to leave the person in charge of what happens. You are not there to find out what is wrong or to fix it.

**Danger overrides privacy.** There is one exception to keeping it private. If you believe someone may be in danger, say so to them, stay with them or have someone else stay, and tell the client's named contact. If the danger is immediate, call 999. On a residential, [the duty-of-care plan](t:8.5) should already name who does this.

try.text: Practise the words, because they are hard to find in the moment. With a colleague playing the participant, say the cover instruction to an imagined room, walk over, crouch and say the step-outside line at low volume. Then say the three corridor lines. Swap roles so you hear them from the other chair.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: To the room: Take five minutes in your pairs on the next question.
To the person, quietly: Would you like to step outside for a minute? I can come with you, or you can go on your own.
Outside: Take your time. You don't need to explain.
Outside: What would help? A few minutes alone, some water, someone to sit with you, or to head home?
Outside: Is there someone here you'd like with you?
If it is beyond you: That sounds hard, and it is outside what I can help with. Who do you have that you could talk to?
The way back: Come back whenever you are ready, or not at all. Nobody will ask.
To the room: Sara is taking a few minutes. Let's carry on.
At the break: I won't mention this to anyone unless you want me to.

items: **If you are the only trainer**, set a task of ten minutes, not two, and stand in the doorway where you can see the room and the corridor.
**Do not discuss it** with the group, and do not let the group discuss it. Move on to the next activity.
**If your exercise caused it**, look at the design afterwards. There is more on [telling people in advance](t:2.21) what an activity will ask of them and letting them observe first.
**What you tell the client contact:** only what the person has agreed to, unless you think someone is at risk.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What comes first when someone becomes upset: going to them, or setting the group a task?
quiz.a: Setting the group a task, or calling a break. It takes the room's attention away before you go over.

quiz.q: A participant leaves the room in tears during a feedback exercise. You have a co-facilitator. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep the room working and ask your co-facilitator to follow, offer privacy and ask what would help. The person chooses whether to return, and the group is told one line at most.

quiz.q: In the corridor, a participant starts to tell you about a serious problem at home and asks what you think she should do. What do you say?
quiz.a: That it sounds hard and is outside what you can help with, and ask who she has that she could talk to, such as her GP or an employee assistance line. Listening is fine. Advising is beyond your role.

topics.tierReason: Practitioner judgement about the first few minutes. It is not counselling or medical advice, and no study was opened for it.

topics.title: The slot after lunch

situation.text: It is 13:40. Lunch was sandwiches and pastries in a warm room. You are four slides into the afternoon's main model and two people have their chins on their hands.

items: **Design the slot before the day.** Planning around energy is covered under [breaking before attention drops](t:1.14) and [putting hard content where the energy is](t:2.14). Applied here: no input in the first twenty minutes after lunch. Put an activity there in which people talk, move and make something.
**Change the room during lunch.** Open a window, turn the lights up, turn the projector off if the first task does not need it.
**Restart at the stated time** with a task that begins on people's feet: "Find someone you have not worked with yet and go to a flipchart."
**Stop talking and get them talking** if energy drops during input: "Turn to your neighbour. Two minutes. Where would this fail in your team?"
**Next rung: get people up.** A vote by standing along a wall, or a walk round the charts to add a comment. Both [use movement where it helps the learning](t:1.15). Offer a seated way to take part.
**Next: name it, take a short break.** "We have hit the afternoon dip. Five minutes of fresh air, back at 14:25."
**The firm rung is to cut.** Drop the rest of the input and go straight to practice. Move the heavy piece to tomorrow morning, or to a handout with a recall question at the next session.
**Afterwards, write what you would move** next time in your plan, as part of [reviewing your own sessions](t:4.15).

why.text: **The fixes for this hour are judgement.** There is a separate account of [what is known about energy](t:1.14) across the day. The rest of this topic is practitioner judgement about one hour that goes wrong often.

**Enthusiasm cannot rescue a badly placed slot.** The dip is predictable, so most of the answer is design. A trainer who puts the hardest slides at 13:30 and then tries to rescue the room with enthusiasm is solving the wrong problem. People who are standing, talking and writing on a chart stay awake without being asked to.

**Each rung costs more time than the last.** The ladder for the day itself moves from changing who is talking, to changing what bodies are doing, to stopping. Each rung costs more time than the one before. Cutting content feels like failure, but material delivered to a room that is half asleep has not been delivered.

**Raise a problem lunch with the organiser.** All of this happens in the room, with one exception. If lunch itself is the problem, because it is heavy, late or too long, raise it with the organiser at the afternoon break for tomorrow, or before the next booking.

try.text: Take the first thirty minutes after lunch from a session you run and deliver the restart aloud, on your feet: the instruction that gets people up, the task and the time call. Then rehearse the rescue. Start explaining a slide, stop yourself at one minute and say the pair question. Record it and listen to how long you take to hand over to the room. Aim for under twenty seconds.

try.title: A worked example: the first hour after lunch, twelve new managers

head: Time
What happens
Why
rows: Lunch. Trainer opens the windows and puts four flipcharts round the room.
Cooler room, and the task is ready.
Restart, standing. New pairs go to a flipchart.
People move before they sit.
Pairs list the three hardest conversations they had this month.
Their own material. Everyone talks.
Walk round. Each pair adds a tick to the two they share most.
Movement, and a group result.
Sit. Trainer gives ten minutes of input on the conversation model, using the top-voted case.
Input is short and tied to their case.
Practice in threes, round one.
Doing, not listening.
Two-minute stretch, then round two.
A planned pause before the dip returns.
Groups report one thing to keep and one to change.
Leads into the afternoon break at 14:45.

items: **Do not show a long video** in a darkened room at 13:30.
**An energiser with no link** to the content can feel like being made to play. There is more on [using play on purpose](t:1.23).
**Do not say they look tired.** Say the session has hit the dip and change something.
**Standing activities need a seated version**, said as part of the instruction and not as an afterthought.
**A very long lunch** does not fix the dip. It shortens the afternoon.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What should not happen in the first twenty minutes after lunch?
quiz.a: Input from the trainer. Use an activity in which people talk, move and make something.

quiz.q: At 13:50 you are halfway through explaining a model and you can see people drifting. What do you do first?
quiz.a: Stop talking and set a two-minute pair question on the content. It changes who is doing the work at the lowest cost in time.

quiz.q: It is 14:20, you have tried pairs and a standing vote, and you still have twenty minutes of slides left. What do you do?
quiz.a: Take a five-minute break, then cut the slides and go straight to practice. Move the remaining input to the next morning or to a handout.
