topics.title: The client or an observer sitting at the back

situation.text: The client's head of learning has come to see the pilot. She sits behind the group with a laptop. Twice she adds a comment from the back, and the participants keep glancing round at her.

items: **Ask in advance who is coming** and why. They may be there to assess you, to see the content, or to watch their own people. The answer changes what you agree.
**Offer the better option first**: "People behave differently when they are watched. Would you join a table and take part?"

**Agree the terms if they will observe.** They sit at the side, not behind the group. They stay out of small-group work. Comments come to you at breaks. They do not report on how individuals performed.
**Introduce them at the start** and say why they are there: "Jo is from the learning team. She is here to see how the course runs, not to assess anyone."
**Then teach the room.** Do not look to the back for approval or aim your examples at them.

**Thank them and bridge** if they comment from the back: "Thanks, Jo. Let me take that into the next exercise." If you want their view, ask for it at a moment you choose: "Jo, what does the business need from this?"
**Ask for the change at the break**: "It helps the group if comments come through me. Could you pass me a note and I'll bring it in?"
**Ask them to step out** if the room has gone quiet because of them: "The group has been careful since the practice started. Could you leave us for the role-plays and come back for the debrief?"

why.text: **Participants turn careful and the trainer performs.** This is practitioner judgement. An observer changes a room in two ways. The participants become careful, most of all in practice, because nobody wants to get it wrong in front of the person who reports to their director. And the trainer starts performing for one person at the back and stops attending to the fourteen in front.
**Both problems are mostly solved before the day.** An observer who has been told where to sit, what they are watching for and when to speak is rarely a difficulty.
**The introduction matters more than it seems.** Left unexplained, a stranger taking notes will be assumed to be assessing the participants. One sentence removes that.

**Bridge in the room, ask at the break.** The bridging line is for the room, where a client has to be treated with respect in front of their own staff. The request to change, and the request to step out, are for the break. Afterwards, ask for fifteen minutes of feedback on two things you chose, so the observation is useful to you too.

try.text: Ask a colleague to sit behind you with a laptop while you run ten minutes of a real session for two or three others. Their brief is to type throughout and to interrupt once. Practise the introduction, then the bridging line, without turning your body to the back. Afterwards ask the others how often you looked at the observer. Then say the step-out request aloud to your colleague, face to face.

try.title: A message to send an observer before the day
lines: Thanks for coming on Thursday. A few things will help the group get the most from it.
If you can, join a table and take part. People are more open with a fellow participant than with an observer.
If you would prefer to watch, please sit at the side by the window, not behind the group.
I'll introduce you at the start and say you are there to see the course, not to assess anyone.
During the practice rounds, please stay at your seat. People find it hard to try things with someone listening in.
If you spot something, pass me a note or catch me at a break and I'll bring it in.
Please don't share how individuals did with their managers. I have told the group that practice is private.
Could we have fifteen minutes at the end? I'd value your view on the pace and on the afternoon exercise.

items: **A senior observer:** one who is also the most senior person present needs [the briefing for a senior person](t:4.38).
**If they correct a participant directly**, step in with the bridge at once and raise it at the break.
**Typing behind people is distracting** whatever is being typed. Ask for handwritten notes, or a seat at the side.
**If you promised private practice** to the group, check that the observer has agreed to that before you say it.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What do you say when you introduce an observer to the group?
quiz.a: Who they are and why they are there, including that they are not assessing the participants.

quiz.q: The client arrives unannounced five minutes before the start and sits behind the group with a laptop. What do you do?
quiz.a: Go over and ask, kindly, for a seat at the side and for comments to come to you at breaks, then introduce them to the group. A short word at the door prevents most of the trouble.

quiz.q: Since the observer arrived, the role-plays have gone flat and people are choosing safe examples. What do you do?
quiz.a: At the break, ask the observer to step out for the practice rounds and come back for the debrief. People will not risk getting it wrong in front of someone who may report on them.

parts.title: Teach and coach in the room
parts.summary: What the trainer does while teaching: a short input, a demonstration, feedback during practice, a split room, and sessions that are shorter or longer than a day.

topics.title: Give a ten-minute input

situation.text: It is 10:15 and twelve new managers are waiting for the part where you teach them something. Your deck for this slot has fourteen slides and a model with five boxes. The plan gives you ten minutes before the practice starts.

items: **Write the one point as a sentence** the group could repeat at lunch. If the sentence needs "and", you have two inputs. Choose one and put the other on a handout.

**Open with a question** before you tell them anything. Give pairs one minute on a question from their own work, then take two answers. You hear [what they already know](t:1.7), and they have a reason to listen to yours.
**Say the point by minute three**, in plain words, and write it on a flipchart as you say it. It stays up for the rest of the session.
**Give one example from their world**: a named role, a day, the actual words someone said. Then give the same example done properly. One pair of examples is enough.

**Show it.** Draw a simple picture on the flipchart while you talk, or act out thirty seconds. Keep to key words on the paper and do not read sentences off a slide, which adds [load that teaches nothing](t:1.2).

**Check with a question** that makes people use the point. Give them a fresh case and ask what is wrong with it. One minute in pairs, two answers, and correct anything that is off. Then bridge to the task in one sentence and give the instruction in [a way people can follow first time](t:4.24).

**Cut before the day, on paper.** The history of the model goes. So do your second and third examples, the exceptions, the names of researchers and any slide you would say "just quickly" about. Put what matters from that pile on a one-page handout.

**Rehearse aloud against a timer.** The group talks for about three of the ten minutes, so you have seven. As a rough guide, a minute of unhurried speech is about 130 words, which gives you around 900.

why.text: **Ten minutes is a convention, not research.** This is craft. Ten minutes is a working length that many trainers settle on. It is not a research finding about attention spans, and the advice on [writing a session plan](t:4.33) allows up to twenty. The order is practitioner judgement too.

**One point is what people can hold.** The reasoning starts with [how little a person can hold](t:1.1) in mind at once. One point with one example and one picture fits. Five boxes do not, and people leave able to name the model and unable to use any of it.

**The opening question does two jobs.** It tells you where to pitch the next eight minutes: if both answers show the group already has the point, you shorten the input and go to the practice. It also makes people curious about the answer before you give it, which is the argument for [making people curious before you tell them](t:1.24).

**A nodding room tells you nothing.** The check matters because a room that nods has told you nothing. You can read [why a clear explanation feels like learning](t:1.4) to the people hearing it. A fresh case that people have to judge shows you in one minute whether the point has landed, while you can still fix it. A check that asks people to repeat your sentence back only tests their hearing.

**Cut what the task does not need.** New trainers from a design or subject background usually find the cutting harder than the delivery. Everything in the deck is true and took effort to make. The test is whether a person needs it to do the task that follows. If not, it is a handout.

try.text: Take a real input you are due to give, or the one below. Stand up, start a timer and deliver it aloud to a colleague, or to your phone on record. Leave real silence where the pairs would talk. Good looks like this: you finish inside ten minutes, the point is said and written by minute three, your own voice fills no more than seven minutes, and your colleague gets the check question right without help. Listen back and strike out every sentence that did not serve the one point.

try.title: A worked example: ten minutes on giving feedback, minute by minute (12 new managers)

head: Minute
What you do
Words you say
rows: Question first, in pairs
"Think of a time a manager told you to 'be more professional' or 'step up'. Tell your neighbour what you did differently the next day. One minute."
Take two answers
"What did you change? ... So mostly nothing, because you couldn't tell what they meant. Keep that in mind."
Say the one point and write it up: "Say what a camera would have seen"
"Here is the whole of the next few minutes in one line. Before you give your view, say what a camera would have seen."
The example, done badly
"A support team lead says to Ali: 'You need to be more careful with customers.' Ali now knows she is unhappy. He doesn't know which customer, which day, or what careful means."
The same example, done properly
"Second go. 'Ali, on Tuesday you told the billing customer her refund would arrive on Friday. The screen said the Friday after. She rang back twice.' Now they are both looking at the same thing."
Draw the picture: a line down the flipchart, "My opinion" on the left, "What a camera saw" on the right
"Left side: careless, unprofessional, bad attitude. Those are my opinions. Right side: Tuesday, the refund date, two calls back. Start on the right."
Say why, once
"People argue with an opinion. It's much harder to argue with Tuesday. And the person can fix a date. They can't fix 'careless'."
Check, in pairs. Write the sentence on the flipchart
"Here's a new one. 'Your reports are always late and it's affecting the team.' Which side of the line is that? What would you say instead? One minute."
Take two answers and correct
"What did you get? ... Yes. 'Always' is the giveaway. Which report, due when, and when did it arrive?"
Bridge and instruction for the task
"You've seen one done. Now you'll write one. Think of something you need to raise with someone in your team. Write only the camera sentence. Three minutes, on your own, until 10:28."
Timer on. Walk round and read over shoulders
Nothing. The input is over.

items: **You run two inputs** back to back and call it one. If your point sentence has "and" in it, split it and put a task between the halves.
**The opening question becomes a discussion.** Take two answers and stop. Say "Hold that, we'll come back to it" and move on.
**Your old job is the example.** Use one from theirs. Ask the client for two real situations before the day and change the names.
**Half the room fails the check.** Do not repeat the explanation louder. Give a second example, shorter than the first, and check again with a new case.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: In a ten-minute input, by which minute should the one point be said and written up?
quiz.a: By minute three, after a one-minute question in pairs and two answers.

quiz.q: You are briefing a software company's sales team on a new pricing rule. The product manager has given you 22 slides for a ten-minute slot. What do you do?
quiz.a: Write the one thing a seller must say differently on a call, build the ten minutes around that with one example and a check, and put the rest on a one-page handout. Twenty-two slides in ten minutes would leave people recognising the rule and unable to apply it.

quiz.q: You ask your check question after an input to retail team leaders. Both pairs you call on get it wrong. What do you do?
quiz.a: Give one more short example and ask a new check question before starting the task. Two wrong answers mean the input missed, and practice built on a misunderstanding wastes the next half hour.

topics.title: Demonstrate a skill

situation.text: You say "let me show you what I mean" and ask for a volunteer. The volunteer plays the customer for laughs. Eight minutes later the room has enjoyed it and nobody can say what they were meant to notice.

items: **Choose a slice of the skill** you can perform in two to three minutes. Write its three or four key points as short rules, the method used for [teaching interpersonal skills by showing](t:2.34), and put them on a flipchart.

**Prepare your partner.** Use a co-trainer, or ask one participant at the break before, in private, and give them a written brief of a few lines. Nobody is made to perform in front of the room, so a volunteer is someone who has already said yes and knows what to do.
**Tell the room what to watch for** before you begin, and give them a job. Split it: "This side, write down my first sentence. That side, count the questions I ask."
**Show it well, once**, at the speed of real life. Do not stop to explain. Commentary in the middle breaks the thing people need to see whole.
**Name the key points afterwards.** Ask "What did you see?" first, then point to each rule on the flipchart and say where it happened: "The question came here, before I offered anything."

**Label any poor version you show.** Say "This one has two of the points missing. Spot which." Keep it under a minute and make it the ordinary mistake, played straight. With people new to the skill, show the good version first.

**Let people try straight away.** Within two minutes of the demonstration ending, every pair should be saying the first two sentences aloud. The full [practice in threes](t:4.29) can come later. The first attempt cannot wait.

**Use the same order for a task** on a screen or at a till. Do it once at working speed, do it again slowly while saying each step and its reason, then take your hands away and let them do it while you watch.

why.text: **Staging decides what the room sees.** This is craft about how to stage a demonstration. The research on the wider method lives with [teaching by showing, practising and giving feedback](t:2.34). Its meta-analysis found better transfer when people saw poor examples as well as good ones, and better skill when key points were given as rules. This topic is the staging: what to do so that the room sees what you meant to show.

**People copy what they watch, flaws included.** That is the argument for labelling. An unlabelled poor version, or a good one with an accidental slip, gets remembered as "what the trainer did". The [role-play that people do not dread](t:4.29) uses a demonstration with one planned flaw, and it works there because the room has been told to hunt for it with the observer sheet.

**Beginners cannot tell what matters.** Telling people what to watch for is a way of [cutting the load that teaches nothing](t:1.2). A live conversation has dozens of things going on. Someone new to the skill cannot tell which three matter, so they watch your manner and miss the question you asked. A job to do while watching points their attention at the right ten seconds.

**A first try shows people the gap.** Trying straight away is judgement from practice. The reasoning is that a demonstration leaves people feeling they could do it, which is [not the same as being able to](t:1.4). Thirty seconds of saying the words shows each person the gap while the model is still fresh. The order of good before poor and the two-minute limit are working rules. Nobody has tested them.

try.text: Pick one skill you teach. Write the brief for your partner, then perform the whole five-minute plan with a colleague while a phone films you. Do the good version, name the points aloud to the empty chairs, do the labelled poor version, and say the hand-over line. Good looks like this: the good version runs under two and a half minutes, you did not explain during it, each key point can be heard on the recording, and the poor version would be recognised by someone who does the job. Ask your colleague which points they would have named without your help.

try.title: A worked example: a five-minute demonstration plan (a retailer's store staff, 10 people, when the item a customer wants is out of stock)

head: Time
What happens
Words you say
rows: Set-up. Key points are on the flipchart: say what you can do first, ask what it is for, put one alternative in their hand
"Watch this once. Window side, write down the first thing I say to the customer. Door side, count my questions. Beth is the customer, and she has a brief."
The good version, at real speed, with the product in your hand. No commentary
"I can get that for you by Thursday, or I've something here today. What are you using it for? ... For a week's walking, then this one will do the job. Have a feel of the weight."
Name the points. Ask, then point at the flipchart
"What did you see? Window side, my first words? ... 'I can.' I started with what I could do. Door side, how many questions? ... Two, and both came before I picked anything up."
The poor version, labelled, 40 seconds, played straight
"Now the same customer again. Two of the three points are missing. Spot which." Then, to Beth: "No, sorry, we're out of that size. You could try online?"
The room names what was missing
"Which two? ... Yes. I led with 'no', and I never asked what it was for. I've said that sentence myself on a busy Saturday."
Hand over to pairs for a first attempt
"Your turn, now, while it's fresh. Turn to your neighbour. The one nearer the door is staff. Say your first two sentences to a customer who wants something we haven't got. Thirty seconds, then swap."
Pairs are talking. Walk round and listen for "I can"
Nothing.

try.title: A worked example: the brief you give your partner beforehand
lines: Thank you for doing this. It takes five minutes and you only need to follow these lines.
You are a customer who wants the walking boot in a size 6. We do not have it.
Round one: be an ordinary, pleasant customer. If I ask what the boots are for, say a week's walking in the Lakes next month.
If I offer you something else, look at it and say "maybe". Do not buy and do not walk off.
Round two, straight after: same customer. I will do it badly on purpose. When I say "try online", say "oh, OK" and turn away.
Please do not make it funny or difficult. The room needs to see a normal customer.
You will not be asked for feedback and nobody will comment on how you played it.

items: **Your partner improvises a difficult customer** and the demonstration turns into a rescue. Stop, smile, say "Let's take that again from the top", and point at the brief.
**The poor version becomes a comedy.** People laugh and decide they would never do that. Use the mistake they make every week.
**You make a real slip** in the good version. Name it yourself in the review: "I missed the question there. Did you catch it?" It becomes a labelled example.
**You demonstrate, then give input:** twenty minutes of it before anyone tries. Move the input before the demonstration, or cut it.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: When is it safe to show a poor version of a skill?
quiz.a: When you label it before you start and tell the room what to look for. With people new to the skill, show it after the good version.

quiz.q: You are about to demonstrate a discovery call to a software company's sales team and planned to ask for a volunteer on the spot. What do you do instead?
quiz.a: Ask one person privately at the break before, and give them a short written brief on how to play the customer. A surprised volunteer improvises, and it puts someone in front of the room who did not agree to it.

quiz.q: Your demonstration for new managers went well, and the plan now has a fifteen-minute input before the practice in threes. What do you change?
quiz.a: Put a thirty-second first attempt in pairs straight after the demonstration, then give the input. People should say the words while the model is fresh, and the attempt shows them what they cannot yet do.

topics.title: Give feedback during practice

situation.text: A round ends in the three you have been watching. The seller looks up at you. You have about a minute, two colleagues are listening, and what comes out is "Really good. Maybe slow down a bit. But great." The seller nods and learns nothing.

items: **Tell the three you will sit in** on their round, before it starts. Sit low, outside their triangle and out of the practiser's eyeline. Write exact words against the key points you taught, and nothing else.

**Keep the speaking order** set for [a role-play practice round](t:4.29): the person who practised speaks first, then the observer, then the other player, and you last. While they talk, choose your two things. If someone has already said one of them, confirm it in five words and use your time on the other.

**Plan the four minutes.** About 45 seconds for the practiser, 45 for the observer, 30 for the other player, a minute for you and 45 seconds for a second attempt. In a three-minute slot, cut the second attempt to one sentence said again.
**Give one thing to keep.** Quote their words and say what you saw happen next: "You said 'what are you comparing us with?' and she talked for a full minute."

**Give one thing to change**, as an action for next time. "After she answers, ask one more question before you mention the discount." Then stop. You can read [why the comment stays on the task](t:2.27) and off the person.
**Ask for a second attempt at once.** Name the line to start from: "Take it again from where she says it's too expensive. Thirty seconds." Afterwards, say in one sentence what was different.

**Stop a round in the middle** for three reasons only: the practiser is stuck and sinking, they are repeating the same mistake, or the other player has left the brief. Say "Pause there", give one instruction, name the line to restart from and say "carry on". Twenty seconds at most.
**Do the sum on feedback time**, as set out for [group size and staffing](t:2.33), and tell the room which three you will watch in each round. Do not give feedback on a round you did not hear.

why.text: **Only the content of feedback is researched.** This is craft. What good feedback contains has research behind it, set out under [feedback people can act on](t:2.27): it should say how the person did against the goal and what to do next. The timings, the wording and the second attempt on this page are practitioner judgement.

**People can act on one instruction.** One thing to change is a limit set by the next attempt. A person about to try again can hold one instruction and act on it. Given four, they try to do all of them, do none of them well and decide they are bad at this. The other three things you noticed are not lost. If two groups share them, they belong in [the debrief of the activity](t:4.28), with no name attached.
**Your view sounds like the answer.** You speak last because the room treats your view as the answer. If you go first, the practiser's own account is never heard, and the observer agrees with you.

**The last thing seen is the improvement.** The second attempt is where the feedback gets used. Without it the practiser carries a comment out of the room. With it they have done the better version once, in front of two colleagues, and the last thing those colleagues saw was the improvement. That is most of what stops a public correction from flattening someone. The [climate that makes the rest safe](t:1.17) is covered separately.

try.text: Ask two colleagues or friends to hold a three-minute conversation in which one asks the other for a favour they will resist. Give them one key point to aim for, such as "ask a question before you argue". Sit outside, write exact words, then give your feedback aloud inside one minute and ask for a thirty-second second attempt. Record the sound. Good looks like this: you quoted at least one sentence word for word, you gave one keep and one change, the change was something to do, you said nothing about the person, and the retry happened.

try.title: Words you can use: stopping a round and correcting in front of peers
lines: Before the round: "I'm going to sit in on this one. I'll be writing, so ignore me. I'll come in last when you do the feedback."
Stopping mid-round: "Pause there, both of you. Nadia, you've explained the price three times. Try a question. Go back to 'I can't get that signed off' and carry on."
When the other player has gone off the brief: "Pause. Ken, the brief says push back twice and then answer honestly. From your last line, please."
Your turn in the feedback: "Two things from me. One to keep, one to change."
The keep: "You said, and I wrote it down, 'what would make this an easy yes?' He leaned in. Keep that sentence."
The change: "After he answered, you went back to the features. Next time, repeat his answer to him before you say anything else."
The second attempt: "Take it again from his answer. Thirty seconds. I'm listening for you saying it back."
After the retry: "That time he said 'exactly'. That's the difference."
When they start to apologise: "No need. It's the step most people miss in a first round, which is why we do a second."
When they disagree with you: "Fair enough. Try it my way for thirty seconds and tell me what you notice."

items: **You give a list.** If you hear yourself say "and another thing", stop. Write the rest in your notebook for the debrief.
**Your keep is general praise.** "Good rapport" tells them nothing. If you have no quote, you were not writing enough during the round.

**The whole round was weak** and you cannot find a keep. Look for a choice they made: "You stayed in the conversation when he pushed back twice." It must be true. Then pick the one change that would move the most.

**Someone goes quiet or red** after your comment. Do not add reassurance in front of the others. Have a private word at the break and ask how it landed. If it is more than embarrassment, there is advice on [what to do when someone is upset](t:4.42).

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: In a three, who speaks before the trainer in the feedback after a round, and in what order?
quiz.a: The person who practised, then the observer, then the other player. The trainer speaks last.

quiz.q: You are watching a new manager practise a difficult conversation. Ninety seconds in, she has repeated the same explanation three times and her partner is stonewalling. What do you do?
quiz.a: Say "Pause there", give one instruction such as asking a question, name the line to restart from and let them carry on. She is repeating a mistake, which is one of the three reasons to stop a round, and twenty seconds from you gives her a better attempt to finish on.

quiz.q: After a round with a retailer's team leaders you have four points written down, and the observer has already made one of them. You have a minute. What do you say?
quiz.a: Confirm the observer's point in a few words, give one quoted thing to keep and one action to change, then ask for a thirty-second second attempt. Save the other points for the whole-room debrief if more than one group shares them.

topics.tierReason: This rests on practitioner judgement about what a trainer says after a practice round. The research on what makes feedback usable is in 2.27 and is applied here, not tested.

topics.title: Teach a mixed-level group

situation.text: A software company's customer team of twelve is in the room. Four joined last month. Four have done the job for ten years. You pitch the morning at the middle, and by 10:15 the new people are lost and the experienced ones are answering email under the table.

items: **Find out the spread before you design.** Ask the organiser for each person's time in the role, or send three questions a week ahead to [find out who is in the room](t:1.27). On the day, a line-up by years in the job shows the room its own range in two minutes, and is one way to [form groups and move people](t:4.25).

**Use pre-work to lift the floor.** Send the new people twenty minutes of basics: the key terms, one worked example, the screen they will be using. Mark it optional for everyone else. Assume a third will not have done it, and put a one-page summary on the tables.
**Say the range out loud** in the opening and say how the day deals with it.
**Keep the shared input short**, as for [a ten-minute input](t:4.45), and pitch it at the newer people. Give the experienced ones the depth on paper to read if they choose.

**Set one task at three levels** on the same case, with the same time and the same kind of output so the report-back works for everyone. The first level is a worked example to complete. The second is the bare case. The third adds a complication. Recommend a level by experience and let people choose.

**Group on purpose** and change it through the day. For a first attempt at something new, put like with like, so the newer people are not watched by experts. For a case that needs know-how, mix them, and give the experienced person a defined part such as playing the customer.

**Ask experienced people for help** and keep it small. Ask before the day or at a break, in private. Give one specific job per half day: bring a real case, play the hard customer for one round, or tell the room for three minutes what the process leaves out. They still get their own full practice turn and your feedback.

why.text: **One task cannot suit both ends.** This is craft. It applies one research idea, set out under [cutting the load that teaches nothing](t:1.2): support that helps a newcomer gets in the way of someone who already knows the work. That is called expertise reversal. A worked example saves a beginner from drowning. The same worked example makes an expert read through steps they do in their sleep. So one version of the task cannot be right for both ends of this room, and levels are the practical answer. No study of tiered tasks in workplace training was read for this page.

**This is range planning on the day.** There is a design case for [planning around the range](t:2.16) and not the average. This topic is what that looks like at ten in the morning with both ends in front of you. There is separate advice on the different problem of [a single expert who knows more](t:4.37) than you do.

**Helpers were sent to learn too.** The limit on helping jobs is about fairness as much as learning. There is a case for [people teaching each other](t:1.19). But they were sent to learn too, and their employer is paying for their place. If they spend the day as your assistants, they leave with nothing new and say so on the form. One job per half day, asked for and not assigned, keeps it a contribution.

try.text: Take a task from a session you run and write it at three levels. Then stand and say two things aloud to a colleague, recorded: the sentence in your opening that names the range, and the instruction that offers the three levels. Ask your colleague to say back which card they would pick and why. Good looks like this: neither statement makes the first level sound like the slow table, the instruction takes under ninety seconds, and your colleague could choose without asking a question. Then rehearse aloud the private request to an experienced person, with your colleague playing someone a little reluctant.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: In the opening: "Some of you started last month and some of you have done this for ten years. I've planned for that. A lot of the work today comes at three levels, and you pick the one that stretches you."

Giving the task: "Three cards, same customer, same fifteen minutes. If you've done fewer than ten renewal calls, I'd start with card one. If you do them every week, card two. If you could do them asleep, card three has a twist. Your choice. Everyone finishes with an opening line to read out."

Asking an experienced person, in private, before the day: "You've handled more of these than anyone in the room. Would you be willing to bring one real account, with the names changed, for the group to work on after lunch? Ten minutes of your time. Say no if you'd rather not."
Setting the limit: "That's the only thing I'll ask. The rest of the day is for you, and I've got a harder case for your table at eleven."
In mixed threes: "Rosa, you're the customer for this round. Play it as it really happens. Please don't tell them what to say. They need to find it."
To the experienced table: "You four have twenty minutes on your own. The question is: which renewal did you lose that you still think about, and what would you do now?"
At the break, to a newer person: "How's the pace for you? Too fast, about right, or too slow?"

items: **You pair newcomers with experts** for the whole day. The expert does the task and the newcomer watches. Mix for some tasks only, and give the expert a part that is not "do it for them".
**A remedial table:** the first level gets treated as one. Call the levels by card number, hand all three to every table, and never announce who took which.
**An experienced person starts teaching** the room unasked. Thank them, use one point, and offer a slot: "Could you hold the rest for your three minutes after lunch?"
**You pitch everything at the top** to keep the experts interested. The new people fall behind in the first hour and stop asking. Pitch the input low and put the stretch in the task.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What does expertise reversal mean for a task given to a mixed-level group?
quiz.a: Support that helps a newcomer, such as a worked example, slows down someone experienced. One version of the task will not suit both ends, so set it at more than one level.

quiz.q: A retailer sends eight team leaders to a session on handling complaints. Three have been in post a month and two have fifteen years behind them. The organiser suggests the two veterans "help you run the practice". What do you agree?
quiz.a: Ask each veteran, in private, for one specific job in the day, such as playing the customer for one round, and plan a harder case and a full practice turn for them as well. They were sent to learn too, and a day spent as unpaid assistants gives them nothing.

quiz.q: It is 10:20 in a session for a technology sales team. The four newest people are silent and two senior sellers have their laptops open. What do you change for the next task?
quiz.a: Set it at three levels on the same case and let people choose, with the newer people starting from a worked example and the senior sellers getting a complication. The one pitch in the middle has lost both ends, and levels give each a task at the edge of what they can do.

topics.title: Adapt for a short session and for a multi-day course

situation.text: A sales director says, "We can give you ninety minutes at the Tuesday team meeting. Can you do the one-day course in that?" A month later the same company asks for three days with its new managers. Your only plan is the one-day version.

items: **Do not shrink the day** for a short session. Choose one slice of the skill and [one objective you could observe](t:2.11). Tell the client in a sentence what ninety minutes will and will not do.

**Know what never gets cut**: every person speaking in the first five minutes, one round of practice with feedback, a debrief, and a close with [a first-use sentence](t:5.2). Cut these first: round-the-room introductions, a full working agreement (keep two lines on confidentiality and reporting), second examples, the history of the model, full report-backs and most of the slides. A session of 60 to 90 minutes has no break.

**Use rough proportions** for 90 minutes: five to open, ten of input, five to demonstrate, thirty of practice, ten to debrief, fifteen for a second attempt on a real case, ten to close and five spare. For 60 minutes, drop the second attempt and take five from the practice.

**Move the rest outside the session**, by [designing the before and after](t:2.5). Send ten minutes of pre-work and a one-page follow-up, and give the manager one question to ask in the next team meeting.

**Give each day one question** it answers and its own arc when the course runs three to five days. Day one builds the base and the group. The middle holds the hardest and longest practice. The last day is the participants' own real cases and their plans.

**Open with recall every morning** after the first. Fifteen minutes, from memory, notes closed, in pairs: what yesterday covered and one thing they would now do differently. The reasons are under [making practice harder in ways that help](t:1.3). Then give the day's times.

**Close every day properly.** The final day gets the full twenty-minute close. Other days get ten to fifteen: recall, one question for tomorrow written on a card, and the finish time kept. Fill in the feedback form in the room before the last close, not after.

**Reduce new content day by day**, change the groups each morning, and protect the evenings. Fifteen minutes of preparation is the most to ask. There is more on [what sleep does for a multi-day course](t:1.12), and on [your own stamina](t:4.20).

why.text: **The proportions are untested working rules.** This is craft. The proportions and the day shapes are working rules from practice and nobody has tested them. Three ideas are borrowed from topics that do rest on research: [recall after a gap](t:1.3), [proper endings](t:2.18) and [sleep and memory](t:1.12).

**Shrinking the day cuts the practice.** A short session fails when it is a long one played fast. The input survives, because it is the part the trainer controls, and the practice goes. The group hears about the skill and never tries it. Choosing one slice turns that round. Ninety minutes is enough for twelve people to try one thing twice and decide where to use it. It is not enough to form a habit, and the honest thing is to say so to the client and plan the follow-up with them.

**One trainer hears three of twelve turns.** The practice sum for [group size and feedback time](t:2.33) still applies. In thirty minutes one trainer can sit in on three of the twelve turns, so tell the client that before the day.

**Long courses fill up with content.** Over several days the risk runs the other way. There is so much time that the trainer fills it with content, and day three opens with a room that has forgotten day one. The morning recall is the cheapest fix.

try.text: Stand up with a colleague playing the client and say, in under thirty seconds, what your ninety-minute session will and will not do. Record it. Good looks like this: one skill named, one honest limit, one follow-up asked for, and no apology. Then walk the ninety-minute plan aloud against a clock, saying the first sentence of each segment and each instruction in full. Mark where you ran over. Last, deliver a day-two morning recall aloud, with silence where the pairs would talk, and check it fits fifteen minutes.

items: **The client adds topics:** they ask you to "just cover" three more in the ninety minutes. Offer them as a handout or a second session. Say that each added topic comes out of the practice.
**You skip the close** because the session is short. In ninety minutes the first-use sentence is most of what will carry into the week. Keep ten minutes.
**You do the remembering for them** when day two opens with "So, yesterday we covered...". Close your notes and ask them.
**You save the real cases** for the last afternoon of a five-day course and run out of time. Start real cases no later than the second half of the course.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Name the four things that are never cut from a session of 60 to 90 minutes.
quiz.a: Everyone speaking in the first five minutes, one round of practice with feedback, a debrief, and a close with a first-use sentence.

quiz.q: A retailer gives you 60 minutes with 12 store staff before opening and asks for "the whole customer service day". What do you offer?
quiz.a: One slice of the skill with a short input, one round of practice, a debrief and a close, plus a one-page follow-up and a question for their manager to ask. The whole day at speed would be all input and no practice, and people would leave having tried nothing.

quiz.q: It is the second morning of a three-day course for new managers. You planned to start with new content because day one overran. What do you do first?
quiz.a: Run the recall from memory in pairs, even if you shorten it to ten minutes, then start the new content. It shows you what did not stick from day one, and building on forgotten material costs more time than the recall takes.

parts.title: Difficult moments online
parts.summary: The awkward moments of a live call, with the words and the back-up plan for each.

topics.title: When nobody speaks or cameras are off

situation.text: Fourteen people from a customer team are on the call. Nine squares show initials. You ask a question, count to nine, hear nothing and answer it yourself. Twenty minutes later you have done that four times and decided the group does not care.

items: **List the ordinary reasons** before you assume disengagement. An open-plan office. A weak connection that drops with video on. A shared kitchen table. A sixth call of the day. Lunch. The delay while someone finds the unmute button. None of these is about you.

**Set up how people respond** in the first three minutes. Say that short answers go in the chat, that a raised hand means "I'd like to speak", and that cameras are their choice. There are [reasons for leaving cameras to them](t:4.8).
**Get every person to do something** in the first two minutes. One word in the chat is enough. It proves the chat works and sets the pattern.

**Ask one question at a time**, put it on the screen, and say how to answer it: "One line, in the chat." For a question that needs thought, ask everyone to type and hold, then send together on your word. Count to ten before you speak again.

**Read the chat aloud by name**, then invite: "Amira, you wrote 'the handover'. Would you say a bit more, or pass?" Say in the opening that you will do this. The person has already prepared an answer by typing it, and they can always pass.
**Use answers that need no words.** A poll, a number from one to five in the chat, or a reaction button tells you where the room is in fifteen seconds.

**Move to small rooms.** Pairs or threes for four minutes, with the question pasted into the chat before the rooms open. Name who goes first: "Whoever's first name comes earliest in the alphabet starts." Ask for one line per room in the chat afterwards.

**Say what you see without blame** if it stays quiet, and ask with numbers. Then check privately with one person or the organiser at the break. The same moment in a room is [the silent group](t:4.35).

why.text: **The video-call research is about fatigue.** This is craft. The research this site has on video calls is on [why remote learning tires people](t:4.8), and it is about fatigue, not participation. What follows is practitioner judgement.

**Online, typing is easier than speaking.** In a room you can see twelve faces and tell thinking from boredom. Online you have lost most of that, so a silence that would last four seconds in a room feels like a refusal. It is usually smaller than it feels. Speaking on a call has a higher cost than speaking in a room: you have to find the button, you cannot see whether someone else is about to start, and your voice arrives alone into quiet. Typing has almost no cost. That is why chat first and voice second gets answers where an open question gets none.

**Polite rooms stall without a first speaker.** Naming who speaks first in a small room removes the stall where three polite people each wait for the others. It sounds trivial and it saves the first minute of every room.

**Cameras are a separate question from engagement.** People with cameras off may be listening closely, and people with cameras on may be reading email on the same screen. If you need faces for a particular task, such as practice in pairs, ask for that task and give the reason. A rule for the whole session mostly makes people tired.

try.text: Run a ten-minute call with two or three colleagues and ask them all to keep cameras off and stay muted unless asked. Record it. Do four things aloud: the set-up lines, one type-and-hold question, one read-back by name with the offer to pass, and one small room with the first speaker named. Good looks like this: every person had typed something inside two minutes, you never answered your own question, and your longest wait was at least ten seconds. Listen back for the moments you filled a silence.

Reading back: "Tom says 'customers hear the date and stop listening'. Tom, what happens next on those calls? Or pass."

Before rooms: "You'll be in threes for four minutes. The question is in the chat now. Whoever's first name comes earliest in the alphabet speaks first. When you're back, one line per room in the chat."
Asking for cameras for one task: "For the next ten minutes you'll practise in pairs, and it's easier with a face. If you can turn your camera on for that, please do. If you can't, that's fine."
Naming it: "I can't see most of you, which is fine, so I'm going on the chat. Type 1 if you're with me, 2 if I've lost you, 3 if you need five minutes."
At the break, in a private message: "Is there anything about today or this group I should know?"

items: **Cameras on for everyone:** you tell the group to turn them on. Some cannot, and now they feel told off. Ask for a named task, give the reason, and accept no.
**You call on someone cold.** They were on mute making tea, and everyone hears the silence. Only invite people who have typed something, and offer the pass.
**You answer your own question** after four seconds. Count to ten with your own microphone muted if you have to.
**Chat, slides and voice at once:** you are running all of them. Stop talking while people type. There is a [cost to splitting attention](t:1.2).
**The numbers are mostly 2.** Thank them, go back one step, and give a shorter example. Do not ask who is lost.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Before a small room opens online, what two things should every person already have?
quiz.a: The question pasted in the chat, and the rule for who speaks first.

quiz.q: Ten minutes into an online session for a software company's sales team, you have asked two open questions and nobody has unmuted. Eleven of fourteen cameras are off. What do you do next?
quiz.a: Ask the next question as type and hold in the chat, send together, then read two answers back by name with the offer to pass. Typing costs people far less than unmuting, and cameras off tells you little about whether they are listening.

quiz.q: A client asks you to make cameras compulsory for an online session with retail managers, some joining from the shop floor. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Leave cameras to each person and ask for them only during the pair practice, giving the reason. A blanket rule tires people and shames those who cannot comply, and the chat and small rooms give you better evidence of who is following.

topics.tierReason: This rests on practitioner judgement about running a quiet call. The fatigue research in 4.8 informs the advice on cameras and nothing here has been tested directly.

topics.title: When the technology fails

situation.text: You are twenty-five minutes into a product session for twenty sellers. Your slide stops moving. The chat says "we can't hear you" three times. You click things, say "can you see my screen now?" to nobody, and four minutes go by.

items: **Write a failure plan on one page** before any online session. List what could fail, the first move, the back-up, who does it and the words. Send it to your producer and the client contact.

**Set up the back-up kit.** A second device signed in to the call, with its microphone and speaker off so it does not howl, as [the hybrid design advice warns](t:4.11). The slides as a PDF with the producer. The dial-in number on paper. The organiser's mobile number. Every room task in a document ready to paste. A charger plugged in.

**Give the producer a defined job**: host rights, letting people in, rooms and polls, watching the chat, helping individuals in private messages, and taking over the moment you drop. With no producer, make the client contact a co-host and brief them for five minutes before the start.
**Say what happens if you vanish**: tell the group in the opening. Two sentences. People who know the plan stay on the call.
**Use a two-minute rule.** Try the simple fix once. If it has not worked in two minutes, switch to the back-up and stop fiddling. Say what you are doing in one line.

**Give the group work** before you fix anything. Keep one holding task ready that fits any point in the session: write for two minutes on the last point, then post it in the chat. The producer can run it without you.

**Do not stop the room** for one person's problem. The producer handles it by private message with two fixes, leaving and rejoining or switching to phone audio. If neither works, send that person the materials and offer a catch-up.

**Agree when you would stop** with the client beforehand. A common line is ten minutes without a working call. Then end cleanly, and email within the hour with what was covered, what is left and when it will be finished.

why.text: **The time limits are yours to adjust.** This is craft, and the two-minute and ten-minute limits are conventions for you to adjust. There is a general case for [rehearsing what could go wrong](t:4.13). This topic is the online version, written out.

**Groups forgive a failure quickly.** What they remember is the trainer troubleshooting aloud while twenty people wait. The two-minute rule exists because fixing things feels like progress from the inside. Each next click seems likely to work, and five minutes pass. A fixed limit, decided when you were calm, makes the choice for you.

**A task turns the gap into recall.** Giving the group a task first changes what the gap is. Two minutes of writing about the last point is the [useful kind of recall](t:1.3), and nobody is sitting in silence. You come back to a chat full of answers and carry on from them.

**The producer is the largest single difference.** One person cannot teach, watch the chat, run rooms and repair a connection together. If the budget has no producer, a briefed co-host from the client still covers the one thing that matters most, which is that someone can speak to the group when you cannot. Say so in your proposal when you price online work.

try.text: Rehearse a failure on purpose. On a test call with your producer or a colleague, start delivering a segment aloud, then leave the call mid-sentence without warning. They say the holding line and set the task. You rejoin from your second device and pick up. Time it from drop to your first sentence back. Good looks like this: the group had a task inside thirty seconds, you were back inside two minutes, and neither of you said "can you hear me?" more than once. Then swap, and practise saying the lines from the table aloud until you do not need to read them.

items: **You narrate the repair.** "Let me just try... no... hang on." Mute yourself, let the producer give the task, and fix it in silence.
**The call howls** because your second device is signed in with the sound on. Check it is muted with the speaker off before anyone joins.
**The back-up has never been used.** Test the phone dial-in and the producer's copy of the slides in the technical check, on the real platform.
**You run without a producer** and nobody else has host rights. If you drop, the call may end for everyone. Always give one other person co-host rights.
**After a failure you rush** to make up the time. Cut a "should" from the plan, the way you [keep time and cut content live](t:4.31), and keep the pace.

quiz.q: What is the two-minute rule?
quiz.a: Try the simple fix once, and if the problem is not solved inside two minutes, switch to the back-up and stop trying to repair it.

quiz.q: You are running an online launch briefing for 20 sellers with no producer. The client's enablement lead is on the call. What do you arrange before the start?
quiz.a: Make the enablement lead a co-host and brief them for five minutes on the holding task and the line to say if you drop. Someone must be able to speak to the group and keep the call open when you cannot.

quiz.q: Halfway through an online session for a customer team, one participant types that her sound keeps cutting out. The rest are fine. What happens?
quiz.a: You carry on, and the producer messages her privately with two fixes, rejoining or phone audio, and sends the materials if neither works. Stopping nineteen people for one connection costs the room more than it saves her.

topics.title: When someone dominates, disrupts or is upset on a call

situation.text: You are training fifteen people from a customer team on a new product. One person unmutes after every point. Another is filling the chat with jokes about the release. Then, after a small room on difficult customers, a third camera goes dark and a private message arrives: "sorry, need a minute".

items: **Change the structure** before you speak to anyone, as advised for [the person who talks too much](t:4.34). Move from open microphones to chat first. "Everyone type an answer. Then I'll ask three people to say more." Most over-talking ends there.

**Thank and redirect by name** when a person keeps unmuting, then use raised hands and take them in order. If it carries on, send a private message that starts with what they bring and asks for one thing.
**Check where a private message is going** before you press enter. Sending it to everyone is the classic mistake. Write each one as if the client might read it.

**Treat a busy chat as energy first.** Give it a job: "Put those in the chat as questions and I'll take three at half past." If it is sniping, reply to that person privately. If it spreads, set a chat rule for everyone with an end time. There is matching advice on [side conversations in a room](t:4.39).
**Never mute a person silently** for what they are saying. Mute for noise, and say so. Removing someone from the call is for abuse only. The producer does it, and you tell the client the same day.

**Never name upset on the main call.** When someone seems upset, give the group a task or call the break. Then send one private message that asks for nothing. There is a room version for [when someone is upset](t:4.42), and the same rule holds: say little and offer choices.
**Offer a private room** with you or your co-facilitator, and let them decide. Do not move anyone into a room without asking. If they leave the call, message once and leave it.

**Follow up the same day**, by direct message or email. For the person who was upset: no need to explain, what was covered, and when you are free. For the person who talked a lot: thanks, and one request for next time. Go to the organiser only if you are worried about someone's safety, and say only that they left early.

why.text: **The in-room reasoning carries over.** This is craft. The in-room versions are [the person who talks too much](t:4.34), [side conversations and phones](t:4.39) and [when someone is upset](t:4.42), and the reasoning there carries over. This page covers what changes on a call.

**Online you lose your body and see less.** Two things change. You lose your body. In a room you can stand next to the talker, turn away, or walk over and crouch by someone's chair. Online, the private message and the small room are the nearest things you have to those moves, so you need the wording ready. And you see less. Someone can be close to tears behind a dark square, and the only sign is a camera going off or a name leaving the list. So the check-in has to be a message that is easy to ignore.

**Reporting is limited by what you agreed.** The limit on going to the organiser comes from [the working agreement with the group](t:4.23). You told the group what would and would not be reported. A person who left a call upset has not agreed to their manager hearing about it. The exception is the one you stated in that agreement: a real worry about harm.

try.text: Set up a call with two colleagues. One plays the person who unmutes after every point. Deliver three minutes of any content aloud and practise the thank-and-redirect line twice, then type and send the private message while you keep talking. Next, the second colleague turns their camera off and types "need a minute". Say the task line to the group aloud, then send the private message. Record the call. Good looks like this: you never said the upset person's name on the main call, both private messages went to the right person, and the group had a task within fifteen seconds.

lines: To the person who talks a lot: "Tom, you know this product better than most of the call and it's helping. I need to hear from the quieter ones too. Could you hold back until two others have answered, then add what we've missed?"
To the person sniping in the chat: "I can see the release has been a sore point. I'd like to hear it properly. Can you and I talk for five minutes at the break?"
To someone who seems upset: "No need to reply. Take whatever time you need. I'm here at the break if you'd like a word."

To the organiser, only if you are worried about someone: "Rosa left the session early today. It might be worth someone checking in with her."

items: **A private message goes to everyone.** Do not delete it and pretend. Say aloud, "That was meant for one person, apologies," and move on. It is the reason to write every message kindly.
**You mute the dominant person** without a word. They notice, and so does everyone else. If you must, say why, and make it about noise or time.
**You move an upset person** into a room to be kind. They did not ask, and now they are alone with a trainer. Offer, and wait for a yes.

**The session is being recorded.** Tell people at the start, and pause the recording for practice and for anything personal. Check what your platform saves. On some, a saved chat can include private messages.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: When is it acceptable to tell the organiser that a participant left an online session upset?
quiz.a: Only if you are worried about the person's safety, and then you say only that they left early and that a check-in might help.

quiz.q: On a call with a software company's sales team, one senior seller has unmuted after each of your last five points. What is your first move?
quiz.a: Change the structure to chat first, with raised hands taken in order, before saying anything to him. Most over-talking stops when the open silence goes, and it avoids correcting him in front of colleagues.

quiz.q: During an online session for new managers, one camera goes off straight after a small room on a difficult conversation, and the person types to you, "sorry, need a minute". What do you do?
quiz.a: Give the group a short written task without mentioning her, then send one private message that needs no reply and says you are there at the break. She may or may not be upset, and a message that is easy to ignore leaves the choice with her.

topics.tierReason: This rests on practitioner judgement. It carries the room advice in 4.34, 4.39 and 4.42 on to a call, and none of it has been tested.

stages.name: Make it stick
stages.question: How does it survive the return to work?

parts.title: Get it used at work
parts.summary: Transfer, follow-up and coaching.

topics.title: Treat transfer as a design problem

situation.text: In March a customer support team of twenty learned a new handover routine for shift changes. The feedback forms were glowing and everyone did well in the practice. In April the team lead tells you nobody uses it. The client's first suggestion is to run the course again.

items: **Write one sentence before you design anything,** saying what people should be doing differently at work a month after the course. Make it [something a manager could see](t:2.11). "At each shift change, the outgoing agent talks through open tickets using the three-line handover." Design back from that sentence.

**Ask the client three questions** at the briefing, one for each of the three influences. The learner: "Can they do any of this already, and do they want to?" The design: "What does the real task look like on a bad day?" The workplace: "When in the week will they have time to do it, and which manager will expect it?" There is more on [the manager's part in transfer](t:2.4).

**Do not rerun a course** that has not transferred. Speak to five or six participants and two of their managers, fifteen minutes each. Ask participants: "Talk me through the last time you could have used it. What happened?" Ask managers: "When did you last see it used, and when did you last ask about it?"
**Sort what you hear into three columns,** learner, design and workplace, with the evidence under each. Mark the weakest.
**Fix the weakest influence** before you touch the content. If it is the workplace, the fix belongs to the client, so take the evidence to the sponsor with one specific request.
**Get evidence of use from someone else,** not from the learner: a manager's observation, a record in the system, a sample of real work.

**Practise on varied cases** if people will meet situations the course did not show them, and say so in the objectives. There is more on [designing practice that transfers](t:5.2) and on [why far transfer is hard](t:5.18).

why.text: **Transfer often fails, but no percentage fits.** Transfer means people using at work what they learned on the course. It is the point of training and it often fails. You will hear that only 10 per cent of training transfers to the job. That figure traces to a 1982 magazine article, which opened with a training director's guess and gave no data. A 2011 review found no behavioural evidence behind it. No single percentage fits all training, so do not quote one. The problem behind it is real.

**Transfer is linked to learner and workplace.** A meta-analysis of 89 studies found transfer was linked to the learner's ability, conscientiousness and motivation, and to a supportive workplace. These links were stronger for open skills such as leadership than for closed skills such as using software. Results looked better than they were when the same person rated both the training and its use, which is the reason for step seven.

why.title: Transfer of training: a meta-analytic review
why.found: Across 89 studies, transfer was positively related to cognitive ability, conscientiousness, motivation and a supportive work environment. Most links were stronger for open skills such as leadership than for closed skills such as software. Links were inflated when one source supplied both measures in the same setting.
why.means: Check the learner, the design and the workplace, and get evidence of use from someone other than the learner.

why.text: **New situations have to be designed for.** Applying a skill to a similar situation is easier than applying it to a new one. The second has to be designed for, and there is an explanation of [why far transfer is hard](t:5.18).

**The workplace is the easiest part to neglect.** The steps for diagnosing a failed course are practitioner craft. The research supports the three influences. It does not give a set method for checking them. The craft reasoning is about where trainers look. The course is the part you control, so it is the part that gets redesigned when results disappoint. The workplace is the part you do not control and the easiest to neglect. Asking the workplace question at the briefing is far easier than raising it afterwards as an explanation for failure. If your interviews suggest people never could do the task, the question has changed, and that calls for [a full performance diagnosis](t:2.29).

try.text: Take a programme that did not transfer. Write one sentence on each of the three influences, with the evidence you have for it. Mark the weakest and write the one change you would make there. Then say aloud, as if to the sponsor, the two sentences in which you would report it. Good looks like this: each sentence names evidence, not opinion, and the change is something a named person could do this month.

items: **The workplace is easy to neglect.** A supportive one is linked to more transfer. Ask about time and [the manager's part](t:2.4) at the briefing.
**Blaming the learner** is the easy answer. Check the design and the workplace before you settle on it.
**The 10 per cent figure:** do not quote it. Say what you saw change at work instead.
**You take the participants' own word** that they are using it. Results look better than they are when the same person rates both the training and its use. Ask a manager, or look at the work.

quiz.q: What are the three influences on transfer?
quiz.a: The learner, the training design and the workplace.

quiz.q: In a kick-off meeting the client says: "We all know only 10 per cent of training transfers." What do you say?
quiz.a: That the figure began as a guess in a 1982 magazine article and has no data behind it. Agree that the problem is real, then ask what they want to see people doing at work a month after the course.

quiz.q: A team liked the course and did well in the practice. A month later nobody uses the new routine. What do you check?
quiz.a: The workplace. Ask a few participants and their managers what got in the way, such as no time in the shift or a manager who never asks about it. The learner and the design look sound, so changing the course will not fix it.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis of 89 studies links transfer to the learner, the training and the workplace, but the links vary with the kind of skill and with how transfer was measured.

topics.title: Plan the first use at work before people leave

situation.text: It is 16:10 on a day about giving feedback, with twelve new managers. Your plan says "action planning, 5 min" and you are fifteen minutes behind. The usual ending is "any final questions?" and a feedback form, and people go home with a warm, general intention to be better at this.

items: **Start in the design, not the close.** Practise on tasks that look like the job: real cases, the real form or system, and the usual time pressure. Vary the examples, with more than one kind of customer, problem or setting, so people do not learn a single case by heart.
**Protect ten minutes for the first-use plan** inside [the 20-minute close](t:4.32). If you are running late, [cut content from the exercise before it](t:4.31).

**Minute one: give the instruction** and show your own example on the flipchart. "Think of the first time in the next two weeks when you will be in the situation we practised. Write one sentence: when that happens, I will do this." Leave the frame "When ___ happens, I will ___" on show.
**Minutes two to four: people write alone,** in silence. Walk round. Where you see a vague plan, ask quietly: "When exactly? What is the first thing you will say?"

**Minutes five to eight: work in pairs,** two minutes each. One reads their plan aloud. The partner asks one question: "When exactly will that be, and what could stop you?" The writer adds a second line for the obstacle, in the same form.

**Minutes nine and ten: date and send.** Each person writes the date of the first use, photographs the card and sends it to their manager from their phone, with one line: "This is what I am trying first. Please ask me about it on Friday." If phones are not allowed, collect the cards and send them yourself with each person's agreement. That gives [the manager a job after the course](t:2.4).
**Tell the group when someone will ask** how it went, and who. That is part of [scheduling the follow-up](t:5.4).

why.text: **Build transfer into the whole course.** Practice across varied examples helps people apply a skill in new settings more than repeating one example. Transfer should be built into every part of a course, not added on the last afternoon. The first-use plan is the last link in that chain and cannot repair a day of practice that looked nothing like the job.

**If-then plans make follow-through more likely.** A specific if-then plan makes follow-through more likely than a general intention. A meta-analysis of 94 tests found a medium to large benefit for people who added such a plan to a goal, compared with holding the goal alone.

why.title: Implementation intentions and goal achievement
why.found: Across 94 independent tests, people who formed an if-then plan reached their goals more often than people who only held the goal. The effect was medium to large (d = .65). The plans helped people get started and stay on course.
why.means: Have each person write one when-and-where plan for first use before they leave the room.

why.text: **The if-then evidence comes from other fields.** The if-then evidence comes from health, study and laboratory goals, not from training courses. Treat the plan as a well-supported bet borrowed from another field.

**A named moment does the remembering.** The partner question, the photograph and the timings are craft. The reasoning goes like this. "I will give better feedback" has no moment attached, so on a busy Friday there is nothing to remind the person that this is the time. A plan that names Friday's one-to-one does that remembering for them. The partner's question brings out the obstacle while there is still time to plan for it, and it means one other person has heard the plan said aloud. Sending it to the manager turns a private note into something that somebody will ask about. The advice on variety has a limit. As a rule of craft, newcomers need to get one example right before variety helps them. That is the case for [starting with full support](t:2.13).

try.text: Take a course you know that ends with questions and a feedback form. Write a ten-minute close for it: the instruction you would give, one example plan in the form "when X happens, I will do Y", and how the plan reaches each manager. Then stand and give the instruction aloud against a timer. Good looks like this: under a minute, your own example included, and the partner question said word for word.

**The plan lists five things.** Ask for one situation and one action. A second plan can wait until the first has been used.

**Prior knowledge changes what transfers.** As a rule of craft, newcomers need to [get one example right](t:2.13) before variety helps them.

quiz.q: What form should a first-use plan take?
quiz.a: When X happens, I will do Y. It names the moment and the action.

quiz.q: In the close, a participant writes: "I will communicate better with my team." What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask them to name the moment and the action. For example: "When Monday's team meeting ends, I will ask each person for one thing that is blocking them." A general intention is followed through less often than a specific plan.

quiz.q: You are running twenty minutes late and the last item on your plan is the first-use plan. What do you do?
quiz.a: Cut content from the exercise before it and keep ten minutes for the plan. People write it before they leave the room, and it goes to their manager.

topics.title: Use 70-20-10 as a reminder, not a formula

situation.text: A technology company's people strategy says learning should be "70 per cent experience, 20 per cent social, 10 per cent formal". In the budget meeting the finance lead reads that line aloud and proposes cutting the course budget by 70 per cent. Everyone looks at you.

items: **Say where the numbers came from,** in two sentences, without scorn. "Those figures come from successful executives in the 1980s looking back on what had shaped them. They describe where those people said they learned, and a 2018 review found the evidence for the 70 weak."

**Offer the rewrite straight away,** so you are not only taking something away. Replace the ratio with its intent: "Most development happens in the work. We will design stretch tasks, feedback and peer support, and keep courses where a skill needs teaching."

**Sort the skills into two lists.** On one, skills people can pick up safely by doing the work with feedback. On the other, skills that need teaching first: new knowledge, a method nobody would discover alone, anything where a mistake on a live customer is costly. Courses stay for the second list.

**Design the on-the-job part for one role,** on one page: a stretch task (work a little beyond what the person can do now) with a date, twenty minutes to reflect on it afterwards, and feedback from someone who saw the work.

**Design the social part with names** against it: [coaching inside the existing one-to-one](t:5.5), a peer to compare notes with every fortnight, and [a community of practice](t:5.8) where one already has a reason to exist.
**Give each piece an owner.** The manager agrees the stretch task. The person books their own reflection time. You supply the one-page template and the three reflection questions.
**After a quarter, check what happened:** which stretch tasks were done, who gave feedback, and what the person can do now that they could not do before.

why.text: **The model is a reminder, not a formula.** The numbers come from Center for Creative Leadership research in the 1980s, in which successful executives looked back on the events that had shaped them. The ratio itself was set out later, in a 1996 planning guide by Lombardo and Eichinger. A 2018 review found the evidence for the 70 per cent claim weak and the studies behind it inconsistent. The model is a useful reminder and not a validated formula.

**Memories of learning cannot set a budget.** The finance lead's argument fails on its own terms. The figures began as people's memories of where their development happened. They were never a measure of where money was spent or of what a pound produces in each place, so a budget cannot be read off them. The Center for Creative Leadership itself says well-designed courses strengthen the other two parts. The model's own home does not treat it as a case for cutting formal training.

**Experience alone does not build expertise.** What the model gets right is the reminder that most learning happens outside courses. The catch is that experience alone does not build expertise. Without reflection and feedback it levels off. That is why steps four and five matter more than the argument about percentages. An organisation that cuts courses and designs nothing in their place has not moved to learning from experience. It has stopped doing one thing and started hoping about another.

**Designed experience costs managers' time.** The two-list sort and the one-page plan are craft, not something the research on this model prescribes. They also carry a cost you should name to the client. Designed experience takes managers' time, and that time is harder to budget for than a course fee.

try.text: Take a "70-20-10 strategy", or the line from the situation above. Rewrite it so the intent survives and the false precision goes. Then say your two-sentence account of where the numbers came from aloud to a colleague, and ask them to push back as the finance lead would. Good looks like this: you stayed calm, you did not call the model a myth, and you ended on an offer.
