topics.title: Schedule the follow-up
topics.theory: Spaced reinforcement after the event, relapse prevention and coaching cycles

situation.text: In March you ran a day on a new quoting process for fourteen people in a sales team, and it went well. You sent the slides round at 30 days. By June nobody mentions the course. Most of the team wrote their first real quote under the new process in week three, with nothing from you in front of them, and by day 30 several had already gone back to the old way.

items: **Ask the client about first use** before the course, with one question about each participant or team: "When will they first do this for real?" Time the first follow-up to that moment, not to the calendar. Send a prompt two or three days before the first real use, and check within a week after it.
**Name the owners before the course runs.** For each contact, write who sends it, who chases the replies and who records them. An unowned prompt does not get sent.

**Ask what will pull people back** to old habits, in the close. Each writes a plan for it in the form "when X happens, I will do Y", the same form as [the first-use plan](t:5.2). That is relapse prevention: naming the obstacles in advance and planning what to do when they come.

**Build contacts from recall and a task:** every one has two or three recall questions answered from memory, plus one task done on live work. Do not send a summary. There is more on [what goes into a follow-up](t:5.15).

**Set up check-ins** with a manager or coach. Fifteen minutes inside an existing one-to-one is enough, built on one question: "Where have you used it, and what got in the way?" There is more on [the manager's part after a course](t:2.4) and on [coaching with questions](t:5.5).
**Put short prompts beside the work,** where the skill is used, such as a line in the meeting template or a card beside the till. There is more on [building a job aid](t:5.7).

**Place the later contacts by the work** as well. The familiar pattern of about 30, 60 and 90 days is a convenient default. Move each date to sit just before the skill is next needed, and [plan a refresher](t:5.17) for anything used rarely.

**Build the follow-up before you leave** if you are external and lose access after the event. Write the manager's step into the contract, hand the client a ready-made follow-up pack with the recall questions, the task and the dates, and include one 30-minute call at about 30 days.

why.text: **A good event can fade without follow-up.** A well-run event with no follow-through is likely to fade. [How fast it fades](t:5.17) depends on the kind of task and how well it was learned in the first place. Follow-up is part of the design.

**Time prompts to first use, not the calendar.** Be plain about the dates. The 30, 60 and 90 day pattern is a practitioner convention, not a research finding. The [research on skill decay](t:5.17) says skills that are not used fade, fastest for procedures with many steps. That points to the first real use as the moment that matters. A prompt that arrives two days before someone's first live quote reaches them when they have a reason to care and a task to try it on. A prompt on day 30 may reach a person who has not yet needed the skill, or one who met the moment in week three and has already reverted.

**Relapse prevention plans for obstacles in advance.** Relapse prevention means naming the obstacles in advance and planning what to do when they come. Regular check-ins keep the new behaviour in view while it becomes routine.

**The research does not test this schedule.** The dates and the check-in format are practitioner craft. The research behind this page supports follow-up in the workplace and if-then plans in general. It does not test this schedule. Timing to first use means finding out when that is, which takes a conversation with the client. When you cannot find out, calendar dates are a fair fallback.

try.text: Design a follow-up plan for a real programme. Start by writing when each group will first use the skill for real. Then for each contact write the recall questions, the task, who sends it and who chases. Include a step for relapse. Finish by reading the first prompt aloud as if you were the person receiving it at their desk. Good looks like this: it takes under two minutes to answer and it could not be answered by opening the slides.

topics.title: Coach with questions, not answers
topics.theory: Coaching and mentoring as a skill

situation.text: Two weeks after a course, a customer success manager says to her team lead: "The client rejected the onboarding plan. What should I do?" The team lead, who tells you she supports the learning, answers in four seconds: "Send them the revised plan today and copy me in." It is quick. Next week the same person is back at her desk with the next question.

items: **Choose coaching, mentoring or teaching:** take a breath and decide which the moment needs. The test is whether this person could find a workable answer with what they already know. If yes, coach. If they lack the knowledge, teach. If your own experience is what would help, mentor, and say that is what you are doing. If it is urgent or about safety, tell them.
**Agree the goal.** "What do you want to have sorted by the end of this conversation?"
**Ask where things stand now.** "What did they say, exactly?" "What have you tried so far?"

**Ask what the options are.** "What could you do?" Then ask "What else?" at least once before you offer an idea of your own. If you do add one, offer it as one more option: "Can I add one to your list?"
**Ask what the person will do,** and when. "Which will you do, and by when?" Then: "What might get in the way?"
**Listen, and wait.** [Let a silence run for several seconds](t:4.2) before you speak. The second and third options usually arrive after the pause.
**Close by saying when you will ask** about it. "I will ask you on Friday how the call went." Keep it to ten minutes inside [a one-to-one you already hold](t:2.4).

why.text: **Coaching draws the answer out of the person.** Mentoring shares experience. Teaching passes on knowledge. A common structure for a coaching conversation, set out in Whitmore's Coaching for Performance and known as GROW, runs through goal, reality, options and will. Will means what the person will do. Some versions call the last step way forward.

**Workplace coaching helps, but the studies are few.** Two meta-analyses find that workplace coaching has positive effects on skills, performance, wellbeing and how people pursue their goals. The studies are few. One of the two looked only at coaching by trained internal or external coaches and left out managers coaching their own staff, so the evidence for manager coaching is thinner. Coaching is also a common way to follow up after a course.

why.title: Does workplace coaching work?
why.found: Pooling 17 studies of coaching by internal or external coaches, the authors found positive effects on skills, on attitudes and on results. Internal coaches did better than external ones. Face-to-face and online coaching did not differ, and nor did longer and shorter programmes. Coaching by line managers was left out.
why.means: Offer coaching as follow-up with some confidence, and do not assume a manager's coaching will work as well as a trained coach's.

why.text: **Telling teaches people to bring you problems.** The rest is craft reasoning. Telling is faster today. It also teaches the person that the way to solve a problem is to bring it to you, so the next one arrives at your desk as well. Asking costs five minutes now, and the person leaves with a plan they chose and a little more practice at thinking it through. "What else?" earns its place because the first option people give is usually the obvious one, often the one they were already unhappy with.

**The advice reverses in three cases.** A beginner who does not know the options cannot be asked for them. Anything urgent or about safety needs a clear instruction. And a manager is not a neutral coach: she also judges the person's work, which can make open answers harder to give. A manager who has always told will need to say what she is doing differently, or the questions will feel like a test.

try.text: Run a ten-minute coaching conversation on a peer's real goal. Ask a third person to count your questions and the times you gave advice. Then ask the peer where you could have waited longer. Good looks like this: no advice before the second "What else?", at least one silence of five seconds that you did not fill, and an action with a day attached.

try.title: A worked example: a five-minute coaching conversation (illustration)
lines: Team member: "The client rejected the onboarding plan. What should I do?"
Manager: "That is frustrating. What do you want to have sorted by the end of this conversation?"
Team member: "What I send back to them by Friday."
Manager: "Where do things stand? What did they say, exactly?"
Team member: "That eight weeks is too long. Their launch is in six."
Manager: "What have you tried so far?" Team member: "Nothing yet. The email came this morning."
Manager: "What could you do?" Team member: "Cut the training sessions from four to two."
Manager: "What else?" She waits. Six seconds pass.
Team member: "I could ask which parts they need live for launch and move the rest to afterwards."

Manager: "Which will you do, and by when?" Team member: "Call this afternoon and ask what has to be live at launch. Send a two-phase plan on Thursday."
Manager: "What might get in the way?" Team member: "If I cannot reach her today. Then I will email the question and book ten minutes tomorrow."
Manager: "Good. I will ask you on Friday how the call went."
What to notice: the manager gave no advice, and the plan the team member chose was her third option, not her first.

topics.title: Make the new behaviour easy to start and easy to repeat

situation.text: Three weeks after a course, all ten people in an account team agree that logging every client call matters. The log has four entries. Opening it takes six clicks, nobody has mentioned it since the course, and the team is measured on calls made per day.

items: **Pick one behaviour** and make it specific enough to see. "Keep better records" becomes "log each client call in one line".

**Ask what the behaviour depends on,** using three questions. Can they do it? Does the working day give them the time and the tools? Do they want to? Ask two or three people: "What makes this hard on a normal Tuesday?"
**Attach it to something that already happens.** "After the Monday meeting, I will send the three actions." "When I put the phone down, I will open the log." Each person writes their own sentence.
**Make the first step small.** One line in the log, not the full record. If it takes more than about half a minute, shrink it again.
**Remove one obstacle,** and do it in the room where you can: a template, a shortcut, a reminder at the point of use. Have everyone pin the log to their toolbar before they leave.
**Have someone notice when it happens.** A manager or a peer saying "I saw you did that" is enough. Ask the team lead to mention the log by name at the weekly meeting for the first month.
**Tell people what to expect:** it will feel like effort for a good while, and one missed day does not undo it. "If you miss one, log the next call."

**Come back at about four weeks.** If it has stopped, ask what the workplace does when people do it. When the new way is slower and people are measured on speed, take that to the manager. There is more on [how the workplace affects transfer](t:5.1).

why.text: **Knowing is not doing.** One widely used model, known as COM-B, says behaviour depends on capability, opportunity and motivation together. A course usually addresses the first. The steps above are aimed at the other two: the cue, the shortcut and the smaller first step change opportunity, and being noticed feeds motivation. In the account team, capability was never the gap.

**Habits form by repetition in one setting.** Habits form when an action is repeated in the same setting until the setting prompts it. In one study, 96 volunteers repeated a chosen eating, drinking or activity behaviour daily for 12 weeks. The time to become close to automatic ranged from 18 to 254 days. Among the people whose progress could be tracked well, half took longer than about two months. In the same study, missing a single day did not noticeably set people back.

why.cite: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts and Wardle (2010)
why.title: How are habits formed
why.found: 96 volunteers repeated a self-chosen eating, drinking or activity behaviour daily for 12 weeks and rated how automatic it felt. Time to near-peak automaticity ranged from 18 to 254 days. Missing one opportunity did not materially affect the process.
why.means: Plan support for months, not weeks, and tell people one missed day does not undo the habit.

why.text: **The timings are only a rough guide.** The behaviours in that study were simple health actions that people chose for themselves, so treat the timings as a rough guide for workplace skills. A behaviour an employer has asked for, done among interruptions, may well behave differently, and nobody has measured it here.

**Anything that makes starting cheaper helps.** Attaching the behaviour to something that already happens is an if-then plan. There is [evidence for if-then plans](t:5.2). Shrinking the first step and having someone notice are craft. The reasoning is that a new behaviour competes with an old one that costs no effort at all, so anything that lowers the cost of starting helps it survive the first busy week. The trade-off is that a one-line log is less useful than a full record. Accept that at the start and ask for more once the line is routine.

try.text: Take one behaviour from a course you run. Write the cue, the small first step and one obstacle to remove. Then do the first step yourself with a timer running, and say the cue sentence aloud to a colleague as you would ask a participant to. Good looks like this: the first step takes under half a minute, and the obstacle is something you can remove before people leave the room.

items: **Someone quotes a fixed number** of days for a habit. There is no fixed number. Popular figures of a few weeks have no support in the study above.

**The workplace punishes the new behaviour,** and it stops. When the new way is slower and people are measured on speed, they will drop it. Raise that with the manager. There is more on [the workplace side of transfer](t:5.1).
**Too many new behaviours at once** and none of them happen. Pick one per person.
**The cue is vague,** such as "when I have a moment". Tie it to an event that happens anyway: a call ending, a meeting closing, a laptop shutting.

items.label: Lally and colleagues (2010), How are habits formed: modelling habit formation in the real world.
Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006), Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis of effects and processes.

quiz.q: In the model this page uses, what three things does behaviour depend on?
quiz.a: Capability, opportunity and motivation, together.

quiz.q: A participant asks: "How many days until this becomes a habit?" What do you say?
quiz.a: That there is no fixed number. In one study of simple health behaviours it took from 18 to 254 days, and half of the people tracked well took longer than about two months. Missing one day did not noticeably set people back.

quiz.q: Three weeks after the course everyone agrees that logging client calls matters, and nobody is doing it. What do you change?
quiz.a: Make it easy to start. Attach it to a cue such as putting the phone down, shrink the first step to one line, remove an obstacle with a pinned shortcut, and have the team lead notice when it happens.

topics.tierReason: If-then planning has meta-analytic support and one field study tracked habit formation, but that study used self-chosen health behaviours and the time taken varied widely.

parts.title: Keep learning going
parts.summary: Job aids, communities, alumni and new trainers.

topics.title: Build a job aid when a course is the wrong tool
topics.theory: Learning in the flow of work

situation.text: A retailer's store staff refund an item without a receipt about twice a month. Each time, the person on the till has forgotten the steps, calls a supervisor over, and the queue grows. The area manager asks you for a refresher course. These people are stuck in the middle of a task. They need the answer at the till.

items: **Ask when people need this.** There are five moments: learning it for the first time, wanting to learn more, applying it, fixing a problem, and coping with a change. For the last three, build a job aid before you consider a course.

**Check that looking it up is safe.** If there is no time to look anything up, as in an emergency response, the skill has to be in the head. Train and rehearse that, with [practice past the first correct run](t:5.14) and [planned refreshers](t:5.17), and do not replace it with a card.

**Decide which kind you are building.** A planner is read just before or just after the task, such as a checklist before a renewal call. A sidekick is used during the task, such as steps beside the till.

**Watch one competent person do the task** and write down what they do, in the words they use. Then ask "Where do new people go wrong?" and "When do you have to call someone?" There is more on [the steps experts no longer notice](t:3.17).

**Write it to be scanned.** One page. Numbered steps that each start with a verb. Button and screen names exactly as they appear. Each decision written as "If this, do that". A name or number to call when it goes wrong. Keep it to about nine steps. If it needs more, split it into two aids.

**Test it on someone** who has never done the task. Hand it over, say nothing and watch. Every place they stop, re-read or ask you a question is a fix. Repeat with a second person after you have made the changes.
**Put it where the work happens:** inside the tool, on the machine, at the till. Introduce it in a two-minute huddle at the start of a shift.
**Name an owner and a review date** on the aid itself. That is part of [keeping one current version](t:3.18).

why.text: **Three of the five moments happen during work.** The five moments come from a framework by Gottfredson and Mosher: when something is new, when people want more, when they must apply it, when something goes wrong, and when things change. The last three happen during work. It is a practitioner model and has not been tested as a whole.

**A findable checklist can beat a remembered course.** At those three moments a checklist that can be found is often more use than a course that has to be remembered. A course does not change how often a task comes up, and a task done twice a month gives memory little to hold on to. A job aid puts the steps in the workplace instead.

**Planners and sidekicks are written differently.** A standard book on job aids, by Rossett and Schafer, splits them into two kinds. Planners are used just before or after the task and sidekicks during it. Deciding which you are building changes the writing. A planner can carry reasons and reminders. A sidekick can carry only the next action.

**A job aid carries steps better than judgement.** The format advice is craft: one page, verbs first, the words of the job. So is the silent test, which is the step most often skipped. There is a cost to weigh. Reading a card takes seconds and can look hesitant in front of a customer, so train a task done many times a day until it is fluent, and keep the card for the exceptions. A job aid also carries steps better than judgement. Where the hard part is deciding what the customer needs, people still need practice with feedback.

try.text: Take a task people do rarely and get wrong. Decide whether they need a planner or a sidekick, draft the aid on one page and say where it will live. Then hand it to someone who has never done the task and watch without speaking. Good looks like this: they finish without asking you anything, and you can name the owner and the review date.

try.title: A worked example: a sidekick job aid clipped beside the till screen (an invented store's process)
lines: REFUND WITHOUT A RECEIPT. About three minutes. Version 3.
1. Say: "I can sort that out for you. Without a receipt the refund goes onto a gift card. Is that all right?"
2. Check the item is one we sell and can go back on the shelf. If not, go to step 9.
3. Press RETURNS, then NO RECEIPT.
4. Scan the barcode on the item.
5. If the screen shows MANAGER APPROVAL, call the duty manager on 201 and wait. Do not press CANCEL.
6. Ask for the customer's name and postcode and type them in.
7. Press GIFT CARD. Swipe a new card from the drawer. Hand it over with the first slip.
8. Attach the second slip to the item and put it in the returns crate under the till.
9. If you cannot refund it, say: "I can't do this one at the till, but the duty manager can look at it with you now." Call 201.
Step does not match the screen? Tell the duty manager today.
Owner: store operations lead. Next review: when the till software changes, or in six months.

items: **Nobody can find it.** A job aid nobody can find is useless. Put it at the point of work and check a month later that it is still there.
**It replaces a skill** that must be in the head. An emergency response leaves no time to look anything up. Train and drill those.
**It goes out of date.** A card with one wrong step teaches people to distrust the whole card. Give it [an owner and a review date](t:3.18), and review it whenever the system changes.
**It grows into a manual.** Hold it to one page and move the background elsewhere.
**It uses the system's language.** The expert writes "initiate a non-receipted return" and the staff say "refund with no receipt". Use the staff's words.

items.label: Association for Talent Development (2018), Learning at the moment of need.
Rossett and Schafer, Job Aids and Performance Support: Moving from Knowledge in the Classroom to Knowledge Everywhere, 2nd edition.

quiz.q: Name the five moments of need, and say which three happen during work.
quiz.a: New, more, apply, solve and change. Apply, solve and change happen during work.

quiz.q: A team runs a month-end report once every four weeks and forgets the steps each time. The manager asks you for a half-day course. What do you propose?
quiz.a: A one-page checklist placed inside the reporting tool. The need comes up during the task, and a course would be forgotten by the next month-end too.

quiz.q: You wrote a clear job aid and saved it on the intranet. Three months later nobody uses it. What do you check first?
quiz.a: Where it lives. A job aid nobody can find is useless, so move it to where the work happens. Then check that it is still current.

topics.tierReason: The five moments of need and job aids are practitioner models and guidance. No experimental test of them was opened.

topics.title: Grow a community of practice, do not announce one

situation.text: Leadership announces a "Facilitators' community" and sets up a channel with 140 members added on day one. The launch message gets a few thumbs-up. Three weeks later the launch message is still the most recent post, and the sponsor asks you why nobody is engaging.

items: **Find a shared problem** before you find members. Talk to five or six practitioners for 15 minutes each and ask "What did you struggle with last month that a colleague has probably already solved?" Start where three people name the same thing.

**Invite five to eight people** in person or by direct message. Leave the channel for later. Say what the problem is, what you are asking for and when it ends: "Six sessions, 30 minutes, every other Thursday. Then we decide whether it is worth keeping."
**Fix the rhythm before the first meeting.** Same slot each fortnight, in diaries for all six sessions. A group that has to find a date each time stops meeting.

**Use one format: a case clinic.** One person brings a half-finished piece of work and takes five minutes to say where they are stuck. The group asks questions for ten minutes, then offers ideas for ten. The person closes by saying what they will try.

**Seed the first two or three cases:** bring them yourself or arrange them, and make one of them your own unfinished work. People judge how safe it is by what the first person shows. There is more on [making it safe to be wrong](t:1.17).
**Keep one running page:** the problem, what was suggested, and at the next session what happened when the person tried it. Store it where members already work.

**Hand over the agenda** by the fourth session. Ask "Who has something for next time?" and rotate who hosts. Then step back to tending: reminders, the notes page, a quiet word with anyone who has gone silent.

**Let it grow by invitation.** Members bring a colleague when a session would help that person. At session six, ask each member what they have used in their own work, and decide together whether to continue, change or stop.

why.text: **Most communities need cultivating.** A community of practice is a group of people who share a concern for something they do and get better at it by interacting regularly. That description comes from Wenger-Trayner and Wenger-Trayner, who developed the idea. Some communities organise themselves. Most need cultivating, and an announcement alone does not make one.

**An announcement supplies only the domain.** All three parts are needed: a shared domain, a real community and a developing practice. This explains the silent channel. The announcement supplied a domain, in name. It supplied no community, meaning people who know each other well enough to ask a question that shows a gap. It supplied no practice, meaning the cases, tools and ways of working the group builds together. Starting with six people and one problem builds the second and third parts first.

**Unfinished work invites help, and help teaches.** The steps above are craft, including seeding the first cases and stepping back. The thinking behind unfinished work is that a finished piece invites applause and an unfinished one invites help, and the learning is in the help. The fixed end date matters too. People agree to six sessions more readily than to something with no end, and a group that chooses to continue belongs to its members.

**An invited group can look like a clique.** There is a trade-off. A small invited group can look like a clique, so say from the first message that it will open up once it is useful. The advice also reverses in one case. If practitioners already meet informally and it works, do not formalise it. Ask what they need, which is usually a protected slot and a sponsor who leaves them alone.

try.text: Design the launch conditions for one community: its domain, its rhythm and how safety will be built. Then say your invitation aloud to one real person this week. Good looks like this: the invitation names one problem, asks for a fixed number of sessions, and takes under 30 seconds to say.

items: **Nobody tends it.** A community needs a named person with about an hour a fortnight to send the reminder, keep the notes and chase the next case. Agree who that is before session one.
**Newcomers are pushed to contribute.** People often watch and listen before they join in. Let them, and do not call on them.
**The sponsor counts posts.** Measure usefulness instead. Ask members what they have used in their own work and report that.
**A manager sits in** and people stop showing unfinished work. Agree at the start that the sponsor gets a quarterly summary and no seat.
**It drifts into show and tell.** Finished work gets polite praise and nobody learns much. Hold the rule that cases are unfinished.

items.label: Wenger-Trayner and Wenger-Trayner (2015), Introduction to communities of practice.

quiz.q: What three parts does a community of practice need?
quiz.a: A shared domain, a real community and a developing practice.

quiz.q: A director asks you to launch a facilitators' community with a new channel and an announcement. What do you suggest?
quiz.a: Start smaller. Find a few people with a shared problem they care about, set a regular meeting, make it safe to bring half-finished work, and let them invite others once it is useful.

quiz.q: A community has 200 members and plenty of posts. The sponsor asks whether it is working. How do you find out?
quiz.a: Ask members what they have used in their own work. Post counts show activity and say little about usefulness.

topics.tierReason: Communities of practice are an influential framework with long use in organisations. No controlled test of the launch steps was opened.

topics.title: Keep graduates involved

situation.text: Twelve new managers finish a six-month programme with a certificate and a group photo. The chat group goes quiet within a fortnight. Four months later the next cohort starts, you want two people to help with the practice sessions, and you are not sure who would say yes.

items: **Plan what happens after the last session** before the programme starts, and put it in the timetable the group sees on day one. An ending that was always part of the plan gets diary space.

**Book one date before people leave,** in the last session: a one-hour case clinic six weeks later. Each person brings one real case. Take three in full at 15 minutes each and collect the rest in a closing round.
**Give every contact something new** that is worth an hour: a fresh tool, a harder case, or one graduate's account of what happened when they used the method.

**Form peer groups of three** in the last session and have each group agree its own first date in the room. Suggest 30 minutes a month and one question: "What are you working on, and where are you stuck?"

**Invite graduates to help the next cohort** with a specific, small ask. One hour, one date, one job: observe a practice round and give feedback, or explain how they used one technique and take questions.
**Brief each helper for 15 minutes** beforehand. Tell them what the new group is practising, what to watch for, and to give feedback on one thing.
**Offer mentoring as an opt-in** for both sides: one graduate, one new learner, three conversations of 30 minutes. Write a start date and an end date into the offer.

**Keep a short list** of who came, who offered and what each person is willing to do. Tell people you are keeping it and [hold only what you need](t:9.24). [Ask for consent](t:9.25) before you use anyone's story or results as proof.

why.text: **Past learners can keep the learning in use.** The last session does not have to be the end of your contact with the group. A network of past learners can keep the learning in use and supply new teachers. This is practice wisdom and not a research finding.

**Graduates stay for what is useful now.** The reasoning is that graduates stay in touch for what is useful to them now. Loyalty to the programme fades quickly. So each contact has to solve a current problem, which is why the case clinic comes first and the newsletter never arrives. Dates booked in the room matter for the same reason. Once people are back at work the programme competes with everything else in the diary.

**The teaching evidence comes from students.** Teaching newer learners can deepen the graduate's own learning. The study below is the reason to give helpers an active job. Note what it studied: students learning material, compared with students who studied without expecting to teach. Using it for graduates of a workplace programme is a reasonable step and an untested one. There is more on [learning by teaching](t:1.19).

why.title: Learning by teaching
why.found: A meta-analysis of 28 studies compared students who prepared to teach, or prepared and then taught, with students who studied without expecting to teach. Both groups learned more, and those who went on to teach learned most. Teaching with real interaction helped more than teaching without it.
why.means: When graduates help a newer cohort, have them explain and answer questions, not only sit in.

why.text: **The cost is the graduate's time.** The cost is the graduate's time, which belongs to their team and their manager. Keep each ask to an hour and tell the manager what it is for. The advice has a limit as well. A half-day skills workshop does not need an alumni plan. [One scheduled follow-up](t:5.4) is enough, and anything more is your wish to stay in touch and not their need.

try.text: Design a plan that gives graduates a reason to stay connected and a way to contribute. Then say the ask aloud, as you would in the last session, and time it. Good looks like this: under 30 seconds, one date, one job, and an easy way to say no.

try.title: Words you can use: asking a graduate to help with the next cohort
lines: The ask: "The next group reaches the feedback practice on the 14th. Would you come for an hour, from two until three, watch one round and tell them what you noticed? You did this six months ago, so they will listen to you."
The way out: "If the date doesn't work, say so. There will be another one."

The briefing: "They are practising the opening sentence of a difficult conversation. Watch for whether they say what they saw before they say what they want. Pick one thing per person and tell them that."
To their manager: "I've asked Sam for one hour on the 14th to coach the new cohort. It is useful practice for Sam too. Is that all right with you?"
Afterwards: "Thank you. What did you notice about your own practice while you were watching?"

items: **You send a newsletter** and call it a network. A mailing list is not a community. People stay for contact with each other, so put your effort into the clinic and the groups of three.
**The ask is too big.** "Would you like to be a mentor?" has no end. "One hour on the 14th" gets a yes.
**Graduates sit in with no job.** It does little for them or for the new group. Give them something to explain, a question to answer or a round to give feedback on.
**The same two keen people help** every time. Ask others directly and by name. People who would never volunteer in a group often say yes to a personal request.
**A client wants to use graduates** as proof. [Get each person's consent](t:9.25) before anything about them is used.

items.label: Kobayashi (2019), Learning by preparing-to-teach and teaching: a meta-analysis.

quiz.q: In Kobayashi's meta-analysis of learning by teaching, which students learned most?
quiz.a: Those who prepared to teach and then taught. Teaching with real interaction helped more than teaching without it.

quiz.q: Two graduates offer to help with your next cohort. What do you ask them to do?
quiz.a: Something active and small: explain a point, answer questions or give feedback in a practice session, for about an hour. Sitting in does little for them or for the new group.

quiz.q: A client wants to put three graduates' results in a brochure. What do you do first?
quiz.a: [Ask each graduate for consent](t:9.25) before anything about them is used as proof.

topics.tierReason: Alumni programmes are professional practice with no direct studies found. Only the learning-by-teaching step has research behind it, and that comes from students.

topics.title: Teach others to train, and sign them off

situation.text: Your half-day session on giving feedback is booked eleven times next quarter and you can deliver five. A colleague will take the rest. She presents well, knows the subject, has your slides and has watched you run it once. The client would like her to run it alone next week.

items: **Write the standard before you train anyone.** List eight to ten things you could see or hear in the room, and mark two or three as must-haves: the parts that do the teaching. That list is your observation sheet. Give it to the new trainer on day one.

**Hand over the reasons with the material.** Spend 60 to 90 minutes walking through [the facilitator guide](t:3.20). For each section say what it is for, what she may change and what she may not, and what the evidence does and does not show.

**Let her watch you deliver once:** the whole session, with the sheet in her hand, noting where you did each item. Debrief for 20 minutes the same day. Ask "What did you see me do that is not in the guide?"
**Watch her deliver one part,** starting with the 20-minute practice activity. Over the next one or two runs she takes more parts and you take fewer. There is more on [working as a pair](t:4.17).
**Give feedback within the hour,** on one thing at a time. She speaks first. Then you name one thing to keep and one thing to change, each tied to something you saw or heard.
**Run a certification observation.** She delivers the whole session to a real group. You sit at the back, say nothing and fill in the sheet.

**Decide against the sheet.** Signed off means every must-have was seen and no more than two other items are marked "not yet". Otherwise the decision is "not yet", with the gaps named and a date for one more observed run. Write it down: trainer, session, date, observer, decision. Both of you sign it. The sign-off covers this session only.

**Keep the standard alive.** Observe each signed-off trainer once in their first three months, then once a year and after any large change to the session. Hold a 45-minute call each quarter for everyone who delivers it, to compare what they have changed and why.

why.text: **Hand on the caveats with the material.** Trainers learn the craft by watching, guided practice and feedback. Teaching people to teach multiplies your reach. It is also how standards spread or slip, so hand on the evidence and the caveats with the material.

**The train-the-trainer research is thin.** The research here is thin and comes mostly from health and social care. One review found that train-the-trainer programmes usually improved knowledge or practice. Programmes that mixed interactive methods with written materials looked best, and the right mix is still unclear.

why.title: Does train-the-trainer work?
why.found: A systematic review found 18 studies in health and social care. Thirteen reported better knowledge, clinical behaviour or patient outcomes, three a possible effect and one none. The studies were too varied to pool and carried a moderate risk of bias.
why.means: Build your handover from interactive practice plus materials, and check the result by observing, since the evidence will not do that for you.

why.text: **Sign off on what you have seen.** Everything else on this page is craft, including the must-haves, the threshold of two and the yearly check. The reasoning runs like this. Someone can describe a session well and run it badly, so you sign off on what you have seen. A sheet she has held since day one keeps the decision about the standard. Must-haves protect the parts that are cut first under time pressure. Practice is always the first to go, because slides are easier to run than a room of people trying something.

**Reasons protect the practice from being cut.** A trainer who has only the slides will keep the slides. One who knows why the practice is there will cut a slide to save it. The cost is your time: the handover takes three or four of your own delivery days, so put it in the plan and the price. An experienced trainer who is new to your session can skip some of the watching. Do not skip the observation. If the date cannot move, deliver it together.

try.text: Design a short train-the-trainer plan for one session of your own. Say how you would observe, give feedback and judge readiness. Then practise the hard part. Watch a colleague deliver for 20 minutes, or use a recording of yourself, and fill in a sheet. Give the feedback aloud in two minutes. Good looks like this: they spoke first, you named one thing to keep and one to change, and each was tied to something you saw.

items: **Quality drifts as more people deliver.** Each trainer makes small, sensible changes. Observe again on a schedule and hold the quarterly call.
**You hand over a script.** A script produces readers, not trainers. Hand over reasons, and ask her to replace your stories with her own.
**Nobody budgeted time to observe.** Put the observed runs in the plan and the price before you agree the handover.
**You sign off on a rehearsal,** or because you like her. Sign off only on a whole session with a real group, against the sheet.
**Your feedback lists nine points.** She will remember none of them. Choose the one that matters most and leave the rest for the next run.

items.label: Pearce and colleagues (2012), The most effective way of delivering a train-the-trainers program: a systematic review.

quiz.q: What did the Pearce review of train-the-trainer programmes find?
quiz.a: Of 18 studies in health and social care, thirteen reported better knowledge, behaviour or patient outcomes. The studies were too varied to pool and carried a moderate risk of bias.

quiz.q: A new trainer has watched your session once. The client wants her to run it alone next week. What do you do?
quiz.a: Have her deliver one part while you watch, and give feedback on one thing. She runs the whole session only after you have seen her do each part. If the date cannot move, deliver it together.

quiz.q: Six months after a handover, you find the new trainer has cut the practice activity to fit in more slides. What went wrong, and what do you do?
quiz.a: She was given the slides without the reasons. Explain why the practice is there, observe her again, and keep time in the budget for observing.

topics.tierReason: One systematic review in health and social care found most train-the-trainer programmes helped, but the studies were varied, carried a moderate risk of bias and could not be pooled.

topics.title: Curate what exists before you create more

situation.text: The head of support at a software company asks you for a new course on giving feedback, for her eight team leads. In the first hour of looking you find a chapter in the company's own manager handbook, a recorded talk by one of their directors and several good articles outside. Writing a course from nothing would take weeks, and most of it would repeat what is already there.

items: **Search before you write,** with a time limit of 60 to 90 minutes. Look inside first: the handbook, the learning platform, recordings. Ask three experienced people "What do you send a new colleague on this?" Then look outside.

**Judge each source on four points.** Is it accurate, and does it agree with the client's own policy? Is it current? Is it at the right level for these people? Can they get through it in about 15 minutes? Drop anything that fails one.
**Choose three to five** and put them in order: where to start, the core, and one that stretches. For each, write one line on why it is there and how long it takes.

**Add what is missing.** That is usually the client's context, a task on real work and a check. "Read the second, then rewrite the feedback you gave last week" turns reading into practice. The check can be a ten-minute conversation with a manager.

**Credit every source and respect its licence.** Link to outside material, and do not copy it into your pack unless you have permission or a licence. Keep a note of where each item came from and on what terms you are using it.
**Put a review date** and a reviewer's name at the top. There is more on [keeping one current version](t:3.18). At each review, open every link and re-read each source against current policy.
**Tell the person who asked** what you found: what exists, what the gap is, and what you will build to fill it. Often the gap is practice with feedback, which no reading supplies.

why.text: **Curation is judgement, not a list of links.** Making new content is slow and costly. Selecting and arranging good existing material can meet the need faster, if someone exercises judgement over it. A list of links is not curation. The value is in the selection, the order and the task that makes people use it.

**The learner's time is the scarce thing.** This is craft and the reasoning is about attention. Material on most workplace subjects is plentiful. The learner's time is scarce. Twelve links hand the sorting to the person least able to do it, who does not yet know which source is sound. Three sources in order, with a reason for each, do that sorting for them. The task matters most. Without one, a curated set is a reading list, and reading on its own changes little.

**Curation has costs, and sometimes you build.** There are costs. Curated material was not written for this audience, so the voice shifts between sources and the examples come from somewhere else. You also depend on other people keeping their pages up. That is why the context paragraph and the review date carry so much weight. And sometimes the advice reverses. Build new when what exists contradicts the client's policy, when the subject is the client's own product or process and nothing outside covers it, or when the need is a skill that takes practice. Even then, build only the gap.

**UK copyright's teaching exception is narrow.** UK copyright law has a narrow exception for copying to illustrate a point in teaching. Official guidance says the use must be non-commercial, fair and acknowledged. If your training is commercial, do not assume it covers you. Link to the material, or get permission or a licence. This is general information and not legal advice.

try.text: For one topic you are asked about often, pick three existing sources. Write one line on why each is there and one task that uses them. Then give the set to one person and ask them afterwards what they did with it. Good looks like this: they did the task and can tell you which source helped.

quiz.a: Search what exists and judge each source for accuracy, currency and level. Choose a few, put them in order, and add what is missing: the client's context, a task and a check.

topics.title: Build a culture where learning is expected
topics.theory: Learning culture and the learning organisation

situation.text: The director of a 60-person software company asks you to build a learning culture and already has a quote for a learning platform. The values poster says "We learn from our mistakes". Last quarter a product launch slipped by a month and nobody has discussed why. Half the training budget went unspent because no one could find the time.

items: **Look at what leaders do** and ignore the posters for now. Over one week, find out three things. What happened the last time something went wrong? Who was praised last month, and for what? When did a leader last say "I got that wrong" in front of their team?
**Ask five people in one team:** "When did you last learn something at work, and what made it possible?" Listen for whether they had time, permission and a reason.
**Pick one routine and nothing else:** a 20-minute review after each project. Three questions. What did we expect? What happened? What will we do differently?
**Brief the leader to go first.** Ask her to name one decision of her own that she would make differently, in a sentence, before anyone else speaks. Agree the sentence with her beforehand.
**Run the first review yourself** to set the form. Facts before opinions. Talk about decisions and conditions, and keep names out of it. End with one to three actions, each with an owner.

**Put the notes where they get read** by the next project team, such as the top of the next project's kick-off document. Open every review by reading the actions from the last one and asking what happened to them.

**Have leaders say what they are learning:** two minutes at the monthly all-hands, covering one thing learned and one thing that went wrong. Have them credit by name a person who shared something useful, and say what it was.

**After six reviews, check two things.** Were the actions done? Are problems being raised earlier? Then decide on a second routine. The survey in the Garvin article is a good prompt for that conversation.

why.text: **A trainer cannot install a culture.** Culture is what people do repeatedly and what is rewarded. A trainer cannot install it. A trainer can help leaders change a few routines. A routine puts learning in the diary, which gives people time and permission at once, and a leader going first changes what is seen to be rewarded. There is more on [making it safe to be wrong](t:1.17).

**The learning organisation is an untested framework.** The "learning organisation" is an influential management idea. One well-known article, by Garvin, Edmondson and Gino, breaks it into three parts: a supportive environment, concrete learning processes, and leaders who reinforce learning. The article comes with a survey for scoring each part. Treat a score as a prompt for discussion and the idea as a direction. It is a framework and not a tested method.

**The review routine is the best-supported step here.** Research on debriefs, also called after-action reviews, finds that teams and individuals who hold them perform better than those who do not. Be clear about what that supports. The studies measured the performance of people who debriefed. They did not measure culture. So the evidence backs the routine, and the larger claim that routines add up to a culture is reasoning.

why.title: Do debriefs improve performance?
why.found: A meta-analysis of 46 samples compared people and teams who held debriefs with control groups who did not. Debriefs improved performance by roughly a fifth to a quarter (d = 0.67). The effect was similar for teams and individuals and in real and simulated settings.
why.means: Start with a short, structured review after each project, with a clear focus and the right people in the room.

why.text: **Reviews with undone actions do harm.** The rest is craft, and it carries a risk. A review whose actions are never done teaches people that speaking up is pointless, and it teaches that faster than having no review. Hence reading the last actions first. The advice also has a condition. If the leader will not go first, or has punished candour before, do not launch reviews across the company. Start with one team whose leader will, and let others see it.

try.text: Ask three people in one team when they last learned something at work and what made it possible. Then run a 20-minute review of a recent piece of your own work with one or two colleagues, aloud, using the three questions. Go first with something you got wrong. Good looks like this: it ends on time with no more than three actions, and each has a name beside it.

lines: Project: onboarding a new customer's support team onto the product. Review held two days after go-live. Six people, 20 minutes.
Last review's actions: the shared test account was set up. The handover template was not started. Carried forward with a new owner.
We expected: go-live in six weeks, with the customer's administrators trained in week four.
What happened: go-live took nine weeks. Training ran in week four as planned, before the customer's data had been loaded, so people practised on sample data and had forgotten the steps by go-live.
The director: "I held the training date because it was in the contract. I should have moved it when the data slipped."
Do differently 1: training is booked relative to the data load and not to a calendar week. Owner: project lead.
Do differently 2: [a one-page job aid](t:5.7) for the three administrator tasks goes out at go-live. Owner: training lead.
Do differently 3: the handover template gets written this month. Owner: support manager.
These notes are pasted at the top of the kick-off document for the next onboarding project.

items: **The answer offered is a platform.** A learning platform is not a culture. It does nothing about time, permission or what gets rewarded. Start with the routine.
**Reviews hunt for blame.** That teaches people to hide. Keep to the three questions, talk about decisions and conditions, and have the leader start with a mistake of their own.
**You promise a culture** by the end of the year. Change takes years. Promise a start: one routine, running in one team, with its actions followed up.
**Reviews happen only after failures.** Then the invitation itself becomes bad news. Review the projects that went well too, and ask the same three questions.
**The survey score becomes a grade.** Use it once, to pick what to talk about.

items.label: Garvin, Edmondson and Gino (2008), Is yours a learning organization?
Tannenbaum and Cerasoli (2013), Do team and individual debriefs enhance performance? A meta-analysis.

quiz.q: What three parts does the Garvin, Edmondson and Gino article give for a learning organisation?
quiz.a: A supportive environment, concrete learning processes, and leaders who reinforce learning.

quiz.q: A director asks you to build a learning culture and suggests buying a learning platform. What do you propose?
quiz.a: One routine: a 20-minute review after each project, with the director going first and naming something she got wrong. A platform is not a culture, and debriefs are the best-supported step.

quiz.q: A team's project reviews have turned into arguments about who was at fault, and people have stopped speaking. What do you change?
quiz.a: Refocus the review on three questions: what did we expect, what happened, what will we do differently. Ask the leader to start with a mistake of their own. Reviews that hunt for blame teach people to hide.

topics.tierReason: The learning organisation is a management framework. The one routine the page starts with, a short review after each project, has meta-analytic support.

parts.title: Practice and consolidation
parts.summary: How to schedule practice so it lasts.

topics.title: Leave time for memory to settle

situation.text: A software company's induction week for new support staff runs from 09:00 to 17:30, Monday to Friday, with a new topic every hour and reading set each night. The test is on Friday morning and everyone revises on Thursday night. They pass. Three weeks later the team leads tell you that nobody can remember the escalation procedure.

items: **List what has to last** and for how long. Mark the items people must still have in three months. Those are the ones the timetable must come back to. Move what can be looked up into [a job aid](t:5.7).
**Put new material in the mornings** and practice on it in the afternoons. As a working limit, plan no more than three or four new topics a day.

**Start each day with recall** for ten minutes. Notes closed. "Write down three things from yesterday that you would need on a live call." Then two minutes comparing in pairs before anyone opens a folder. There is [research on recall](t:1.3) behind this.
**Avoid teaching similar things back to back.** If two procedures are easy to mix up, such as a refund and a credit note, put them on different days.
**Protect sleep.** Finish evening sessions early and set no overnight work, because [sleep helps memory settle](t:1.12).

**Space the returns** to match how long the memory has to last. For something needed for months, come back to it after days and then weeks: the next morning, the end of the week, week three, week eight. There is more on [scheduling the follow-up](t:5.4) and [adding a follow-up layer](t:5.15) after people have left the room.
**Replace the Thursday-night revision** and the single Friday test with the short morning recall and a later check in week three, on the job. This is [testing little and often](t:2.24).
**Show the client each gap's purpose.** Annotate the timetable so that every space has a purpose written beside it and the recall that follows it.

why.text: **Memories settle over time, and sleep helps.** Memories are stabilised over time, and sleep helps. How much it helps depends on what was learned and when the sleep comes. The gaps between practice give that time, which is one likely reason spreading practice works.

**Do not build a design on reconsolidation.** Recalling something makes it easier to recall later. One proposed reason is that a recalled memory is stored again. That idea, called reconsolidation, is less settled in people than it is often made to sound, so do not build a design on it. New learning can also disturb recent learning, and gaps may reduce that. This is the thinking behind keeping similar procedures on different days.

**Longer-lasting memories need longer gaps.** A large review of spaced practice, by Cepeda and colleagues, found that the best gap grows with how long the memory has to last. For something people must keep for months, space the sessions by days or weeks and not by hours. The same finding has a second edge. For something needed only tomorrow, such as the running order of a one-off event, a short gap is enough. Cramming works for Friday, which is why the crammed week keeps passing its own test.

**The price of a roomy week is coverage.** That is the insight to take to a client. The Friday test measures what is fresh and says little about week three. That is [the gap between performance and learning](t:1.4). The price of a week with room in it is coverage. Fewer new topics fit, so something has to leave, move to a job aid or come later. The numbers in the steps, such as ten minutes and three or four topics, are craft. The principle under them is the research.

try.text: Take a crammed schedule you have run or attended. Redesign its rhythm so memory has time to settle. Then explain the new version aloud in two minutes to a colleague playing the client who asks "Why is there less in it?" Good looks like this: you can say what each gap is for and which recall follows it, and you do not mention sleep stages.

items: **You oversell sleep.** Keep what you tell a group modest. Say that it helps, and leave sleep stages out.
**You add gaps and nothing else.** Gaps without recall are just gaps. Each one needs a moment afterwards when people retrieve the material.
**Clients read white space** as wasted time. Show them what each gap is for and what recall follows it, written on the timetable.
**The gaps fill up.** An "optional" evening session or a pre-read appears in every space you made. Name the free time as part of the design and defend it.
**The morning recall becomes you re-teaching** yesterday. Make people retrieve first, with notes closed, and correct only what they got wrong.

Dunlosky and colleagues (2013), Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques.

quiz.q: According to a large review of spaced practice, how does the best gap between sessions relate to how long the memory must last?
quiz.a: The best gap grows with it. For something people must keep for months, space sessions by days or weeks and not by hours.

quiz.q: A client wants five back-to-back days with a new topic each hour and revision on Thursday night. How do you change the rhythm?
quiz.a: New material in the mornings, practice in the afternoons, ten minutes of recall at the start of each day, and similar procedures on different days.

quiz.q: You add gaps between sessions and nothing else. A month later people remember little. What was missing?
quiz.a: Recall. Gaps without recall are just gaps. Bring people back to the material by having them retrieve it.

topics.title: Space and mix the practice, then stop drilling

situation.text: A retailer's new store staff drill one till procedure, a card refund, fifty times in a row. By the end of the hour they are quick and the manager is pleased. On Saturday, with a queue, a customer wants an exchange and half the group starts a refund.

items: **Sort the practice into four kinds,** because each has its own rule: facts and concepts, related procedures that get confused, basics that must be automatic, and rare procedures that are costly to get wrong.

**With newcomers, begin with a short block.** Each procedure three or four times with the steps in front of them, until each person has done it right once. This is [starting with full support](t:2.13).
**Then mix related tasks.** Put the three procedures on cards, shuffle them, and have people draw one at a time, so they must first decide which procedure applies.
**Tell the group why before you start:** "This will feel slower and messier than doing one thing over and over. That is expected. Mixed practice tends to last longer."
**Stop drilling facts and concepts** once people can do it. A workable rule is each person getting each item right twice. Then stop, even if there is time left.

**Use the time saved for later sessions,** and put them in the calendar before people leave. Set recall at widening or regular intervals over days and weeks: ten minutes two days later, and again the next week. Pitch the questions so most people can answer with effort.
**Drill to automatic only the basics** that free up thinking, such as finding a customer record or the keyboard shortcuts used on every sale.
**Keep practising a rare, high-stakes procedure,** such as an emergency response, past the first correct run and [put refreshers in the calendar](t:5.17).

why.text: **Mixed practice often produces better learning later.** Blocked practice looks better during the session. Mixed practice often produces better learning later, though the benefit depends on the material. It is strongest when the things being learned are easy to confuse with each other. One way to read that is that mixed practice makes people choose which procedure applies, and the till on a Saturday asks for the same choice. Fifty refunds in a row never ask it. There is [research on spacing and mixing](t:1.3) behind this.

**Spend spare time on a later session.** Practising past the point of first success helps a lot a week later, and the advantage shrinks over the following weeks. The time is better spent on a later, spaced session than on more repetition now.

why.title: What overlearning buys
why.found: In two experiments 218 students learned geography facts or word definitions, some to a low level and some well past the first perfect run. One week later the overlearners recalled far more. Tested up to nine weeks later, most of that advantage had gone.
why.means: For facts and definitions, stop once people have it right, and spend the saved time on a later session.

why.text: **The advice to stop covers facts and concepts.** The advice to stop is for facts and concepts, which is what the study behind it tested. Procedures that are rarely used and costly to get wrong are a different case. A meta-analysis of overlearning (Driskell, Willis and Copper, 1992) found that practice past first mastery had a moderate overall effect on retention. The size depended on how much extra practice there was, the type of task and how long people had to retain it. Pair the extra practice with scheduled refreshers. There is more on [planning refreshers before skills fade](t:5.17), and in the aviation case study, where emergency drills are repeated on a fixed cycle.

**Mixed practice feels worse in the room.** The rule of "right twice" and the card shuffle are craft. The trade-off is how the session feels. Mixed practice is slower and produces more errors in the room, so the group and the manager watching both think it went worse. Plan to explain it to both.

try.text: Design a spaced, mixed practice plan for a real skill, and say when you stop drilling. Then run ten minutes of it with two colleagues: shuffle the cards, say the explanation aloud first, and apply your stop rule. Good looks like this: nobody knew which task was coming next, you stopped when the rule said to, and the next two sessions have dates.

**You mix everything.** Mixing does not suit all material. In one meta-analysis it helped with pictures and maths problems and did worse than blocking for word lists. **"Stop drilling" applied to an emergency.** Do not apply it to first aid, fire response or any emergency procedure. Stopping at the first success is the wrong advice there.

quiz.q: A group drills one procedure fifty times in a row and looks excellent by the end of the hour. The manager is pleased. What do you change for the next run?
quiz.a: Mix three related procedures until each person gets each right twice, then stop. Bring them back for ten minutes two days later and again the next week. Blocked practice looks better in the session than it lasts.

quiz.q: You are designing practice for a fire response. A colleague quotes this topic and says to stop at the first correct run. What do you say?
quiz.a: That advice is for facts and concepts. For a rare, high-stakes procedure, practise past the first correct run and [put refreshers in the calendar](t:5.17).

topics.title: Add a follow-up layer to any format

situation.text: You run a two-day leadership offsite, a four-part webinar series for a sales team and a self-paced course. Each one ends on a thank-you slide. Six weeks after the webinars the sponsor asks what people are doing differently, and you have nothing to show her.

items: **Write down what follows each format,** three things: a recall question, a task to apply, and a review. If you cannot name all three, the format is not finished.

**Put dates on them.** Time the first one to the first real use and not only to the calendar. If the sales team's renewal calls start in ten days, the first message lands in nine. There is more on [scheduling the follow-up](t:5.4), including the 30, 60 and 90 day pattern.

**Fit the delivery to the format.** After a retreat, [a cadence of short calls](t:8.17). In a webinar series, open each webinar with two recall questions on the last one, then send messages after the final one. In a self-paced course, spaced quizzes that arrive after completion. After a single talk, one message from the sponsor with a question and a task.
**Write every message before the event.** Each is under 60 words and has one recall question to answer from memory and one small task with a day attached.
**Use the channel people already open,** and send from someone they would reply to. A team's own chat and their manager's name beat a new platform and a no-reply address.
**Sell the layer with the event.** Put it in the proposal as part of the product and the price, with the dates.

**Plan for no access afterwards** if you are a supplier, by doing three things. Agree in the contract who on the client side sends the follow-up. Give them the messages already written and dated. Book one 30-minute review call before the event ends.
**Check whether it is being used.** Count replies to the recall questions and ask who did the task. If replies fall, send fewer messages.

why.text: **Spacing and recall are a sound bet.** Spacing and recall have helped across many ages, materials and settings, so they are a sound bet for any format. Few studies test them after a retreat or a webinar series. Without follow-up, expect much of the content to fade.

**The three parts stay constant.** How the follow-up is delivered depends on the format: a cadence of calls after a retreat, spaced quizzes in a self-paced course. What stays constant is the three parts. Recall brings the content back. The task moves it into work. The review gives people a date by which someone will ask. That last one is craft reasoning, and it is often what gets the task done.

why.title: Spaced questions by email
why.found: In a randomised trial 115 medical students were emailed short case questions with explanations on one of two topics, repeated over several months. They learned their emailed topic better than the other group did. About nine months later the gain had lasted for one topic and not the other. The authors could not separate spacing from simply seeing more content.
why.means: Send short spaced questions through a channel people already use, and check whether the gain lasts.

why.text: **Spaced messages do not guarantee retention.** Read that study with its limits. The gain lasted for one topic and not the other, and the authors could not say whether spacing or extra exposure did the work. So check your own results and do not promise a client that spaced messages guarantee retention.

**The trade-off is attention.** Every message spends some of it, and a muted channel delivers nothing. A few good messages do more than a daily drip. Questions sent by message also suit facts better than judgement, so for judgement lean on the task and the review call. And some formats need no layer. A talk meant only to inform, with nothing for people to do differently, can end when it ends.

try.text: Take one format you run that stops at the end. Design its follow-up in full: what, when and how spaced. Write the messages. Then read each one aloud. Good looks like this: each takes under 20 seconds to say, asks one question that cannot be answered by scrolling up, and sets one task with a day.

lines: Week one, sent the day before the first renewal calls: "Morning all. From memory, no scrolling: what are the three questions we open a renewal call with? Reply in the thread. Then use them on one call tomorrow and tell us which question got the longest answer."
Week three: "Quick one. A customer says 'we're happy as we are'. What was the response we practised? Reply in the thread. This week, try it once and post what the customer said next."
Week six: "Last one before our review call. Without looking it up, what goes in the follow-up email after a renewal call? Reply here. Then bring one email you actually sent to the call on the 12th."
Week eight, the review call, 30 minutes: each person shows one call or email where they used the method and one place it did not work. The manager hears it. You note what to change in the series.
The measure: replies in each thread, and how many people brought an example to the call.

items: **You rely on a spaced-repetition tool** for everything. These tools suit facts better than judgement. For judgement, use a task on real work and a conversation about it.
**You send too much.** Too many messages get muted. Use a few, spread over weeks, each with one question and one task.
**Selling follow-up after the event.** By then the budget is closed and attention has moved on. Put it in the proposal as part of the price.

**You have no access** once the event is over. Agree in the contract who on the client side sends the follow-up, hand over the messages written and dated, and book the review call before the event ends.
**The messages only re-send content.** A link to the slides asks nothing of anyone. Every message asks a question people answer from memory.

quiz.q: What does a follow-up layer contain?
quiz.a: Recall, a task to apply and a review, each with a date.

quiz.q: You are an outside supplier and will have no contact with learners after the event. How do you still get follow-up to happen?
quiz.a: Agree in the contract who on the client side sends it, hand over the messages already written and dated, and book one 30-minute review call before the event ends.

quiz.q: Your follow-up sends a message every day. By week two nobody replies. What do you change?
quiz.a: Send fewer. Too many messages get muted. Use a few messages spread over weeks, each with one recall question and one small task, in the channel people already open.

topics.tierReason: Spacing and recall are well supported in education, but a follow-up layer after workplace formats has little direct testing, and the one trial opened gave mixed results.

topics.title: Teach learners how to study

situation.text: Six new starters in a sales team have a product certification exam in four weeks. They show you how they are preparing: the product guide, read twice, highlighted in three colours. They tell you they feel ready.

items: **Show it before you explain it.** Half the group re-reads one page twice. The other half reads it once, turns it over and writes down everything they can recall. Each person privately predicts their score out of ten. Run a short quiz two days later and let each person compare prediction with result.
**Teach self-testing as the main method.** Close the page. Write or say what you remember. Then open it and correct yourself in a different colour. The step people skip is closing the page.
**Teach spacing.** The same total study time, split across several days, with each session starting by recalling the last one. There is [research on spacing](t:1.3) behind this.
**Teach explaining in your own words.** After each section ask "Why is that true?" and "How does this connect to what I already know?" and answer aloud or in writing, without copying.
**Have them teach someone else.** Ten minutes explaining one product feature to a colleague, who then asks two questions. There is more on [learning by teaching](t:1.19).

**Say why effortful study works** better than it feels: "Re-reading feels good because the page looks familiar. Familiar is not the same as being able to produce it in front of a customer. Testing yourself feels worse because it shows you the gaps, and that is the point of it."

**Help each person build a routine** they will keep. Ten minutes, tied to something they already do, written as when, where and what. "After the morning stand-up, at my desk, five questions from my cards."

**Have them plan, check and review** their own study. On Fridays, two minutes: what did I test myself on, what did I get wrong, what will I do next week. There is more on [managing your own learning](t:1.28).

why.text: **Learners rely on the low-value methods.** Re-reading and highlighting are what learners say they rely on, and a major review rates both as low value. It rates self-testing and spaced practice highest. Explaining in your own words comes in the middle, with less evidence behind it. Learners need to be told this, because easy study feels productive.

why.title: Which study techniques work
why.found: A review of ten study techniques rated practice testing and spaced practice as high utility, because they help across ages, materials and real classrooms. Self-explanation and mixed practice were rated moderate. Re-reading, highlighting and summarising were rated low.
why.means: Teach self-testing and spacing first, and tell learners plainly that re-reading and highlighting do little.

why.text: **Choosing by feel picks the weaker method.** The reason telling is not enough is that the feeling is strong. A page read twice looks familiar, and [familiarity passes for knowing](t:1.4). Self-testing produces the opposite feeling, because it shows people what they cannot yet recall. So someone choosing by feel will pick the weaker method every time. The demonstration in step one is there to let people catch the gap between their prediction and their score. It is a classroom illustration and not an experiment. With six people it may not come out as expected. If it does not, say so, and show them the review's ratings instead.

**Study skills outlast your course.** A learner who knows how to study can keep using these techniques long after your course. That is the case for spending session time on it. The cost is that the time comes out of content. It earns its place when there is an exam or a lot of self-study ahead. For a half-day workshop where the practice happens in the room, a two-minute mention is enough. The routine advice, ten minutes tied to an existing habit, is craft.

try.text: Write a personal plan for consolidating what you have learned from this site. Choose techniques you will keep up. Then teach it: explain self-testing aloud to a colleague in three minutes and have them try it on one page. Good looks like this: your plan fits in ten minutes a day, names when and where, and your colleague closed the page before writing.
