try.title: A worked example: the fifteen-minute demonstration, and what you say
lines: Set-up: one page from the product guide, about 400 words. Six people, split into two groups of three.
Group A: "Read this page twice, carefully. You have six minutes."
Group B: "Read it once. Then turn it over and write down everything you can remember. Six minutes in total."
Everyone: "On a sticky note, write the score out of ten you expect on Thursday's quiz on this page. Fold it and keep it. Nobody else will see it."
Two days later: ten short questions, marked by each person themselves.
Then: "Open your sticky note. Compare what you predicted with what you got. Talk to the person next to you about the gap, if there is one."
To close: "Scores are yours and I am not collecting them. What I want you to notice is which way of studying felt better on Tuesday, and whether that feeling was right."

items: **People return to highlighting under pressure.** The week before the exam is when the old habit comes back. Plan that week in advance, with the same short slots.
**The plan is too ambitious.** An hour every evening is dropped by Wednesday. Ten minutes of self-testing tied to something people already do is more likely to last.
**You teach these techniques by lecture.** Model them in your own sessions: start with recall, space the returns, and have people explain to each other.
**The demonstration embarrasses someone.** Keep predictions and scores private, and let people mark their own.
**Self-testing slides into recognising.** People flip the card too soon and think "Yes, I knew that." Have them say or write the answer in full before they check.

items.label: Dunlosky and colleagues (2013), Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques.
Kobayashi (2019), Learning by preparing-to-teach and teaching: a meta-analysis.

quiz.q: In the Dunlosky review, which study techniques were rated high and which low?
quiz.a: Practice testing and spaced practice were rated high. Re-reading, highlighting and summarising were rated low.

quiz.q: Your learners say re-reading works for them because they feel well prepared afterwards. How do you show them otherwise?
quiz.a: Run the comparison. Half re-read a page twice, half read it once and write down what they recall. Each person predicts a score, and a quiz two days later shows the gap between feeling and result.

quiz.q: A learner shows you a study plan with an hour of self-testing every evening. What do you say?
quiz.a: Cut it to something they will keep, such as ten minutes tied to an existing habit. A plan too ambitious is dropped.

topics.tierReason: A major review rates self-testing and spaced practice as high utility and re-reading and highlighting as low, mostly from studies of students. Whether teaching the techniques builds a lasting habit is less tested.

parts.title: Fading and transfer
parts.summary: Why skills fade, why they do not travel far, and what to do about both.

topics.title: Plan refreshers before skills fade

situation.text: Store staff were trained in March on what to do when a customer collapses. Everyone passed. It is now November, nobody has needed it, and the manager assumes they still can.

items: **List the skills from the course.** Mark each one that is used rarely and is costly to get wrong.
**Ask when every skill is next used** for real. If the answer is this month, the job is the practice and no refresher is needed.
**Practise the marked skills further:** past the first correct run in the original session, then set a refresher date before people leave. There is more on [the extra practice](t:5.14).
**Refresh a rarely used procedure** within about six months, as a rule of thumb, and sooner when the stakes are high.
**Run the refresher as doing,** from memory, before any reminder.
**Make the refresher match the real moment:** the real kit, the real place, the same people.
**Score accuracy, not only speed.** People stay quick longer than they stay correct.
**Give the refresher an owner** on the client side and put it in a shared calendar. Record what was missed and adjust the next gap.

why.text: **Unused skills fade, and by a lot.** Skills that are not used fade, and the loss is large. A meta-analysis of 53 articles found almost no loss straight after training and a loss of about 1.4 standard deviations after more than a year without practice or use.

**Some things faded faster.** Cognitive tasks decayed more than physical ones. Accuracy decayed more than speed. Loss was greater when people had to recall than when they only had to recognise, and it was much smaller when the retention test resembled the conditions of training, though that last comparison rested on very few results. Too few studies reported extra practice past first mastery for this analysis to judge it. A separate meta-analysis of overlearning found a moderate benefit for retention.

**Accuracy is lost sooner than speed.** A 2025 meta-analysis of procedural skills, covering 457 reports, puts rough timings on this. Accuracy fell by about 0.08 standard deviations a month and speed by about 0.06. On average, half of what was gained in training had gone after about six and a half months for accuracy and about thirteen months for speed.

**The six-month rule is this site's reading.** The size and pattern of decay are research. The six-month rule of thumb is this site's reading of that average. It is not a tested schedule, and decay varies with the task and with how well it was first learned.

why.title: Factors that influence skill decay and retention
why.found: A meta-analysis of 189 results from 53 articles. Skill loss grew with the length of non-use, from d of about -0.01 straight after training to about -1.4 after more than 365 days. Physical tasks decayed less than cognitive tasks and speed less than accuracy.
why.means: Find the skills that will sit unused, and schedule practice for them before the loss shows up in a real event.

try.text: Pick one procedure you were trained in more than six months ago and have not used since. Without looking anything up, perform it or talk it through aloud to a colleague while they check against the written steps. Count what you missed.

quiz.q: In the skill decay meta-analyses, which fades faster: speed or accuracy?
quiz.a: Accuracy.

quiz.q: A software company trains its on-call engineers once a year on a recovery procedure they use perhaps twice a year. The last incident went badly. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Add a short hands-on refresher at about the halfway point, done from memory on a test system before any reminder. A rare, costly procedure is exactly what fades, and attempting it shows what has gone.

quiz.q: A client asks for a six-monthly refresher on a task their staff do every day. What do you say?
quiz.a: Say it is not needed, because daily use keeps the skill up. Spend the time on the rare tasks from the same course.

topics.title: Know why far transfer is hard

situation.text: A sales team spends a happy afternoon on a negotiation game about trading spice routes. The debrief is lively. On Monday a customer asks for a discount and every one of them gives it away as before.

items: **Write down the real moment** you are training for in one sentence.

**Compare your practice task with that moment** on six points: the subject matter, the place, the time gap, the purpose, whether people are alone or with others, and the format (spoken, written, hands-on).
**Count the points of difference** between practice and the real moment.
**Close the gaps you can.** Use their product, their price list, their customer's words. If the real thing is a phone call, practise by phone.
**Plan for the gaps you cannot close.** Time is the usual one: add [a first-use plan](t:5.2) and a refresher.
**Follow any far-off exercise the same day** with practice on the real task, if you keep one for energy or insight. Do not expect the exercise to carry over unaided.
**Test with a case that differs** from practice on the point that matters. If people only succeed on the case they rehearsed, you have near transfer and should say so.

why.text: **Far transfer means a different situation.** Near transfer is using what you learned in a situation much like the one you practised in. Far transfer is using it somewhere that differs in important ways.

**"Far" can mean six different things.** Barnett and Ceci reviewed a century of argument over whether far transfer happens. Their answer is that the argument stalled because researchers compared unlike things. "Far" can mean a different subject, a different place, a long delay, a different purpose, a different social setting or a different format, and studies rarely said which. They proposed a taxonomy of nine dimensions, three describing what is transferred and six describing the context. They argue that a single effect size for far transfer makes no sense.

**Each difference from the job is a risk.** Their reading of the evidence is balanced. Transfer under some conditions is well supported. For many of the conditions people care about most, the tests have not been done. For a designer, each dimension on which practice differs from the job is a risk to manage.

**The six-point design check is untested.** The taxonomy is a research framework for classifying studies. Using its six context dimensions as a design check is this site's application and has not been tested as a method. There is more on [the workplace side of transfer](t:5.1).

why.title: A taxonomy for far transfer
why.found: A review arguing that a century of debate about far transfer made little progress because the dimensions of transfer were not specified. It offers a framework of nine dimensions for classifying studies, and concludes that evidence for transfer under some conditions is substantial while many key conditions remain untested.
why.means: Describe how far your practice is from the job, dimension by dimension, and close the gaps that matter.

items: **Selling general gains.** "Builds critical thinking" or "improves resilience" from a single exercise is a far transfer claim on nearly every dimension. Promise the specific behaviour you practised.
**Realism for its own sake.** Match only the dimensions that change what people have to think and do.
**Calling it transfer** when the test repeats the practice case. Change one thing that matters.
**Dropping every game.** A far-off exercise can earn its place as a way in. It needs real-task practice straight after.

quiz.q: Why, according to Barnett and Ceci, did a century of debate about far transfer make little progress?
quiz.a: Researchers did not specify the dimensions along which transfer can occur, so they compared unlike studies.

quiz.q: A client wants a raft-building afternoon at an offsite to improve how the team runs project handovers. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep the raft only if real handover practice follows the same day, on their own projects and in their own format. The raft differs from a handover on almost every dimension, so little will carry over unaided.

quiz.q: After your course, reps handle the rehearsed objection well and fail on a new one. What does that tell you, and what next?
quiz.a: You have near transfer only. Add practice on varied objections and test with one they have not seen.

stages.name: Prove it worked
stages.question: How do we measure it and make the case?

topics.title: Decide what you will measure before you design
topics.theory: Evaluation planning, baselines and success measures

situation.text: Three weeks after a two-day course for twelve new managers, the HR director emails: "Can you send me something that shows it worked?" You have twelve feedback forms and an attendance sheet. Nobody counted anything before the course, so there is no starting point to compare with, and it is too late to get one.

items: **Ask what people will do differently** in the first scoping conversation, before any design: "If this works, what will people be doing in three months that they are not doing now? Where would that show up in figures you already keep?" Write the answer down in the sponsor's own words.
**Turn the answer into measures**, two or three of them. Aim for one behaviour you can count people doing and one result the client already tracks. With more than three, nobody collects them.
**Write five things for each measure:** exactly what is counted, where the figure comes from, who pulls it, where it stands today, and the date of the second count.
**Take the baseline before learners hear** that a course is coming. Count over two to four weeks, so that one odd week does not set the starting line.
**Build a stand-in you can count now** if the sponsor has no data: a two-week tally kept by managers, or a sample of 20 records pulled by one named person.

**Ask what figure would count as success:** "What would you need to see at the second count to say this was worth doing?" There is more on [having that conversation in full](t:6.8). Where the sponsor will not name a figure, record the direction and say so.
**Put the measures table in the proposal** as its own page, with the name of [the person who owns each data source](t:6.12). Scale the [effort to what is at stake](t:6.11).
**Check the design against the table.** Every behaviour measure should have practice time in the course. If a measure has none, change the course or drop the measure.

why.text: **A figure needs a baseline beside it.** You cannot show a change without a starting point. That is logic, not a research finding, and the method here comes from the practitioner handbooks on evaluation. A figure taken after the course has nothing beside it, so the reader cannot tell a gain from the level things were already at.

**Choosing measures first sharpens the design.** Deciding the measures first also sharpens the design, because it forces agreement on what the programme is for. It is the same discipline as [designing backwards from objectives](t:2.11), applied to the whole programme. The conversation often shows that two sponsors want different things. One wants fewer calls to HR and the other wants better survey scores. It is far cheaper to find that out in week one than in the results meeting.

**Late measures favour what is easy.** Measures chosen late favour what is easy to collect, which usually means attendance and form scores. Measures chosen early can be awkward ones, because there is still time to set up the counting.

**A baseline can also change the brief.** If the count shows that most managers already do the thing, the problem is smaller than the sponsor thought, or it sits somewhere else, which is a job for [a performance diagnosis](t:2.29). The trade-off is time. A full table is too much for a one-hour awareness session, and there is guidance on [how little is enough there](t:6.11).

try.text: Take one real programme you are scoping or have just run. Fill in the table below for it: two or three measures, the source, the owner, today's figure and the date of the second count. Then read it aloud to a colleague playing a finance director and ask them one thing: "Which of these would you not believe, and why?" Rewrite the row they pick.

Your people partner will count how many one-to-ones include it in September, before anyone is told about the course, and count again eight weeks after it. We will report both figures, with anything else that changed in between."

items: **The sponsor has no data.** Help them find a stand-in they can count now, such as a two-week tally by managers or a sample of records. A rough baseline is far better than none.
**Measures are chosen after the course.** They will favour what is easy. Agree them at proposal stage, and if you were brought in late, take a baseline in the days before the first session.
**Nobody owns the data.** A measure with no named person behind it is not collected. Agree [who owns each source](t:6.12) and who can pull it.
**The baseline is taken late**, after the course is announced. People who know they are being counted change what they do. Count first, announce second.
**You pick a measure too big** for the course to move alone, such as staff turnover. Keep it as context with no target, as in the last row of the example.

quiz.q: What do you need in order to show a change?
quiz.a: A baseline: a record of where things stood before the programme, taken before learners knew a course was coming.

quiz.q: At proposal stage the sponsor says, "We will send a feedback form afterwards." What do you ask for?
quiz.a: Agreement on what will change if the programme works, two or three measures of it, a count of where each stands now, and who collects what and when. Then write it into the proposal as a table.

quiz.q: The sponsor has no data on the behaviour you want to change. What do you do?
quiz.a: Find a stand-in you can count before the course, such as a two-week tally by managers or a sample of 20 records. Record it now so there is something to compare with later.

topics.title: Use Kirkpatrick as vocabulary, not proof

situation.text: The feedback forms from a one-day course for a software company's sales team average 4.7 out of 5. The sales director forwards the summary to the board with the line "Level one and level two both passed, so the course worked." The second level was a ten-question quiz taken at 16:45 on the day.

items: **Draw four columns on one page** in the planning meeting: reaction, learning, behaviour, results. Sort every piece of evidence the client already collects into a column. Most of it will land in the first two.
**Say each column's limits aloud:** what each filled column can and cannot tell you. For example: "These scores tell us people rated the day highly. They do not tell us anyone can do the task."
**Plan a separate measure for each level** you need. Never infer one level from another. A high reaction score is not evidence of learning, and a passed quiz is not evidence of use at work.
**For learning, swap the end-of-day recall quiz** for a realistic decision or task, set several days or more after the course. That is what LTEM tiers 5 and 6 ask for.

**For behaviour, name one thing** a manager could see, and have someone other than the learner check it about six weeks later. There is more on [measuring what people do differently](t:6.4) and on [going back later to check](t:6.5).
**Add the question the levels leave out:** what helped and what got in the way. [The Success Case Method](t:6.13) is built around it.

**Size the plan to the stakes**, using [three levels of evaluation effort](t:6.11). A one-hour briefing may need a usefulness question and a short decision check. A year-long programme needs behaviour and results.

why.text: **The levels are not a causal chain.** The four-level model is the dominant framework and a useful vocabulary. The levels are often wrongly treated as a causal chain. How much people liked a course relates only weakly to what they learned. Evaluation often stops at reaction and learning, the levels furthest from what a sponsor is paying for. People can also [mistake a session that felt easy](t:1.4) for one they learned from.

**Critics say the levels leave things out.** Critics go further than the causal chain. Holton argued the four levels are a list of outcomes, not a model, because they leave out what sits between a course and a result, such as motivation and the workplace. Bates added that the levels tell you whether training worked but not how to make it work better. Kirkpatrick's reply was that the levels are meant to be practical.

**Studies of reaction forms disagree.** The evidence on reaction forms is not all one way. One meta-analysis found that ratings of usefulness were a better guide to learning and to use at work than ratings of enjoyment. A later one found no difference between the two. Neither supports reading a happy room as a trained one.

why.title: How the levels of training evaluation relate to each other
why.found: This meta-analysis split reactions into enjoyment and usefulness, and split learning into immediate, retained and demonstrated skill. Ratings of usefulness were more strongly related to learning and to performance on the job than ratings of enjoyment were.
why.means: If you use a reaction form, ask whether the content is useful for the job, and still measure learning and behaviour separately.

why.text: **LTEM grades evaluation methods in eight tiers.** Will Thalheimer's Learning-Transfer Evaluation Model, known as LTEM, offers a second vocabulary. It has eight tiers. His page on the model says the lower tiers are methods that are inadequate for validating learning success, and that the upper half can be used to validate efforts to create transfer. The current version is 13, released on 31 October 2024. The first table under Try it gives the tiers as his 2018 report describes them.

**Trainers control only the first two levels.** The steps above are craft built on that research. Evaluation stalls at the first two levels for a plain reason: the trainer controls them. A form and a quiz can be finished before you leave the building. Behaviour and results need the client's managers and the client's data, so they have to be arranged before the course, when the client is still keen. That is why the four columns belong in the planning meeting.

try.text: Take a real evaluation that rested on a feedback form. Sort its evidence into the four columns, then redesign the plan so that it reaches behaviour and results, using the second table as a pattern. Finish by saying your two-sentence summary aloud, as you would to the sponsor: what the evidence shows so far, and what you will check next.

quiz.q: Name Kirkpatrick's four levels, and the common mistake in reading them.
quiz.a: Reaction, learning, behaviour and results. The mistake is to treat them as a causal chain, when liking a course relates only weakly to learning from it.

quiz.q: The feedback forms score 4.8 out of 5 and the client declares the course a success. What do you say?
quiz.a: The scores show people rated the day highly. They do not show learning. Propose a short scenario test several days later and a check with managers in six weeks.

quiz.q: A colleague proposes a knowledge quiz at the end of the day as proof the course worked. Using LTEM, what do you suggest instead?
quiz.a: A realistic decision or task, tested several days or more after the course. LTEM rates recall of facts as usually inadequate, and testing straight away as not fully adequate.

topics.tierReason: The warning not to read reaction scores as proof of learning is backed by meta-analyses in training and in university teaching, but the four levels themselves are a practitioner framework and the size of the link depends on what the form asks.

topics.title: Ask better questions on the feedback form

situation.text: The client's standard form has eleven questions. It asks "How would you rate the trainer?" and "Was the venue comfortable?" on a scale of one to five. You hand it out as people reach for their coats, most tick fours and fives in under a minute, and the average of 4.6 goes into a spreadsheet that nobody uses to change anything.

items: **Cut the form to five questions** that fit on one side of a page. Drop every question about enjoyment, the venue and the food unless someone will act on the answer.

**Ask what people can now do**, in specific terms, with answer choices that describe a level in words. For example: "I could not do it yet. I could do it with my notes. I could do it unaided. I could show a colleague how."
**Add one performance question** to pair with that confidence question: a short scenario with a right answer, written on the same form and marked by you afterwards.
**Ask what they will use, and when:** "Which conversation will you use this in first, and by what date?"
**Ask what would stop them**, with choices to tick and a blank line. The answers go to the sponsor as things to fix at work.
**Leave one open question:** "What one thing should we change before the next group?" Read every answer.

**Make the form anonymous.** Give it ten minutes in the room, before [the close](t:4.32), while people are still seated. Say why: "This is how the next group gets a better day, so please take the full ten minutes."
**Hand out both forms** if the client insists on their standard form. Agree beforehand what the scores will and will not be used for.

why.text: **Satisfaction scores relate weakly to learning.** They tell you more about the course and the trainer's style, and about people's confidence. A form can still be useful if it asks about understanding, intention to use and support at work.

why.title: What trainee reactions do and do not reflect
why.found: This meta-analysis found that reactions mainly reflect features of the course. The strongest predictors of reactions were the trainer's instructional style (rho = .66) and human interaction (rho = .56). Reactions predicted changes in motivation and confidence from before to after training.
why.means: Read reaction scores as feedback on delivery and on confidence, not as a measure of learning.

why.text: **Thalheimer asks about learning, not satisfaction.** Will Thalheimer argues for surveys that ask about learning effectiveness, such as understanding, realistic practice and motivation to apply, in place of satisfaction ratings. He proposes answer choices that describe a level in words. This is a practitioner's method. Even a well-written form is a hint, to be backed by a measure of what people can do.

**A confidence question records belief, not skill.** A question that begins "How able are you to" is a confidence item. It records what people believe they can do. A 2010 meta-analysis by Sitzmann and colleagues, covering education and workplace training, found that self-assessed knowledge related most strongly to motivation and satisfaction and only moderately to tested learning. Nearly a third of the evaluation studies it reviewed had treated self-assessment as evidence of learning. That is the reason for the pairing in step three. The two answers side by side show you where belief has run ahead of skill.

**Harder practice can lower your scores.** Be frank with yourself about one more thing. Many training companies and clients decide whether to rebook a trainer from these forms. If you swap recaps for recall and [make practice harder](t:1.3), the day may feel harder and score lower. There are ways to handle that. Tell the group why the harder practice is there. Ask your usefulness questions as well as the client's standard ones. Agree with your manager or client beforehand what the scores will and will not be used for.

try.text: Take a feedback form you have used or been given. Rewrite it to five questions, none of which asks whether people enjoyed the day. Then ask two colleagues to fill it in while saying aloud what they think each question means. Rewrite any question they read differently from you. Time them: the whole form should take under ten minutes.

try.title: A worked example: a five-question form for a day on giving feedback, for 12 new managers
lines: Anonymous. Ten minutes, filled in before we close.
1. How able are you to give corrective feedback using the model? Tick one. I could not do it yet. I could do it with my notes. I could do it unaided. I could show a colleague how.
2. A team member has missed two deadlines this month. Write the first two sentences you would say to them.
3. Which conversation will you use this in first, and by what date?
4. What is most likely to stop you? Tick any. No time in my one-to-ones. I am not sure my own manager backs this. I do not feel ready. Nothing will stop me. Something else, which is:
5. What one thing should we change before the next group?

try.title: A worked example: a confidence item paired with a performance item
lines: Confidence item: How able are you to give corrective feedback using the model? I could not do it yet. I could do it with my notes. I could do it unaided. I could show a colleague how.
Performance item: A team member has missed two deadlines this month. Write the first two sentences you would say to them.
Marking the performance item: one mark if it names the behaviour, one if it states the effect. Mark it yourself after the session.
Report the two side by side. Where confidence is high and marks are low, that is the gap to close.

items: **People answer politely**, and more so if you are standing over them. Make the form anonymous, step away from the tables, and have people drop it in a box by the door.
**A confidence score reported as learning.** Confidence is not competence. Label the item as confidence and report it beside the marks from the scenario question.
**The form cannot show behaviour change**, though it is asked to. It records intention on the day. Behaviour needs a later [check by someone other than the learner](t:6.4).

**The open answers are never read** because the scores are easier to average. Read them all the same evening, and sort them into things to change and things to keep. There is a guide to [sorting a large number with AI](t:7.8).
**The form goes out by email** the next day. Returns drop and the keenest people answer. Fill it in before the close, in the room.

quiz.a: Motivation and satisfaction. It related only moderately to tested learning.

quiz.q: On your form most people tick "I could do it unaided". Their answers to the scenario item score low. What do you report?
quiz.a: Both, side by side. High confidence with low marks is the gap to close, and the confidence figure alone would have misled the client.

quiz.q: You plan to make practice harder. The client decides whether to rebook you from feedback scores. What do you do before the day?
quiz.a: Agree with the client what the scores will and will not be used for, and add your own usefulness questions. On the day, tell the group why the practice is hard, and have the form filled in before the close, in the room.

topics.title: Measure what people do differently

situation.text: Eight weeks after a course for 24 customer support advisers, the head of support stops you in the corridor and asks, "Did it make a difference?" You have attendance figures and a feedback average. Complaints are down, but a new call script launched in the same month, and you cannot say whether one adviser handles a call differently.

items: **Name the behaviour** so that two people watching the same call would agree whether it happened. "Better listening" fails that test. "Says the customer's problem back in their own words before offering a fix" passes.
**Build an observation checklist** of four to six items. Each is a yes or no, with a note of what counts and what does not. Keep it to one page.
**Calibrate before you count.** Two observers score the same three calls separately, then compare. Rewrite any item they disagreed on.

**Observe a sample before the course** and again about six weeks after. Five calls per adviser is workable. Pick them by time slot, such as the first five after 10:00 on Tuesday, so nobody chooses their best ones.
**Add a second source** that is not the learner. Ask each team leader one question: "In the last two weeks, which of your advisers have you heard do this? Give me one example."
**Pull the result for the same weeks.** Use the one named in [the needs analysis](t:2.1), such as repeat contacts or complaints. Put the behaviour and the result on one page.
**Look for early signs** in the first fortnight, before the result can move: team leaders hearing the new step, or advisers asking for the job aid.
**List what else changed** over the same weeks. Then write the claim as contribution, not sole cause. You can [strengthen it with a comparison group](t:6.6).

why.text: **A modest claim is the one believed.** This is evaluation craft from the practitioner handbooks, not a tested procedure. Training rarely acts alone. Other things change at the same time: a new script, a price change, a quieter month. An honest, modest claim is believed. A large one is not, and overclaiming costs you the next project.

**Behaviour links the course to the result.** Behaviour is the link between the course and the result, which is why it is worth the effort of measuring. If complaints fall but advisers are doing nothing differently, the course did not cause the fall. If advisers have changed and complaints have not moved, either the result needs more time or the behaviour was the wrong one to train, and that sends you [back to the diagnosis](t:2.29). A result figure cannot tell you any of this without the behaviour count beside it.

**An outside observer beats self-report.** Self-report flatters. People describe what they intend to do and what they remember doing on a good day. A checklist in the hands of someone else is less kind and more useful. It has its own weakness: people perform for an observer. Recorded calls, or observations that team leaders already carry out as routine, reduce that.

**Compare groups where you can.** [A comparison group](t:6.6) strengthens the case where one is possible. For sales, product and retail training, there is a list of the [business measures](t:6.14) to pair with the behaviour count.

try.text: Pick one behaviour from a real programme. Write a checklist of four to six items for it. Then test it properly: you and a colleague each score the same recorded call, role-play or meeting without conferring, and compare item by item. Good looks like agreement on at least four items in five. Rewrite the rest. Finish by saying your contribution statement aloud in under thirty seconds.

try.title: Before and after: an honest contribution statement
lines: Before: "The course improved customer service."

After: "On observed calls, more advisers now say the problem back before offering a fix than did before the course. Team leaders gave examples from most advisers. Complaints fell over the same months. A new script launched too, so training is one contributor and we cannot say how large."
What makes the second one believable: it names the behaviour, it uses a source other than the advisers, and it puts the other cause on the page before the reader finds it.

items: **Your only evidence is self-report**, the learners' own survey answers. Self-report flatters. Add observation or a manager report.
**There is no count from before** because the measures are agreed after the course. Agree them at the start and [take the first count then](t:6.1).
**Observers score generously or differently** from each other. Calibrate on three shared calls first, and use the same observers before and after where you can.
**The checklist is used to appraise** individuals. Advisers then perform for it. Report results for the group, and say so before the first observation.
**You claim the whole fall** in complaints. Report the behaviour you observed, the result, and the other changes beside them.

quiz.q: Name three sources of evidence on behaviour.
quiz.a: Observation, manager reports and performance data.

quiz.q: Complaints fell in the months after your course. A new call script launched in the same period. What do you claim?

quiz.a: Rewrite the item with an example of what counts and what does not, then have them score three more calls. Counts from a checklist that observers read differently cannot be compared before and after.

topics.title: Go back later to see what stuck

situation.text: At 16:00 on the last afternoon, all fourteen store team leaders completed the incident report correctly with the guide open beside them. The retailer's operations manager wrote "100 per cent pass" in her update. Seven weeks later a real incident report arrives at head office with two sections blank.

items: **Put a date for a second check** in the plan before the course, and agree it with the sponsor. Four to twelve weeks is a common rule of thumb, not a research finding. Choose a date by which people will have had a chance to use the skill at work.
**Design the check to take ten minutes:** one realistic scenario, done from memory, marked against the same steps as on the day.
**Tell people a check will happen** and why, but do not tell them to revise and do not send the materials round again. You want to see what stuck.
**Run it somewhere people already are**, such as the first ten minutes of a team meeting, so that nobody has to make a special trip.
**Ask each manager one question** the same week: "Since the course, where have you seen this done, and where has it been missed?"
**Compare the two results step by step**, not as one total. The steps that dropped tell you what to fix.
**Send the gaps to whoever can act** on them: a reminder, [a job aid](t:5.7) or a change to the next run. There is more on [scheduling the follow-up itself](t:5.4).

why.text: **A delayed check shows what stuck.** [Performance at the end of a session](t:1.4) is a poor guide to what lasts. A delayed check shows what people kept and what they use.

why.title: Learning versus performance
why.found: This review of motor and verbal learning research concludes that performance during training is often an unreliable guide to lasting learning. Learning can happen with no visible gain at the time, and gains at the time can fade. People tend to mistake how well practice went for how much they learned.
why.means: Do not treat an end-of-course result as the measure of the course. Check again after a delay.

why.text: **A drop is normal and useful.** It tells you where follow-up is needed. The gap can run either way. Some methods that make the last afternoon look good produce little lasting learning, and some that make it look worse produce more. Only a later check tells you which you had.

**Test in the conditions of real use.** The rest is craft. The end-of-course result in the situation above was taken with the guide open, minutes after practice, in the room where the skill was taught. All three of those props are missing on the shop floor. The later check removes them on purpose, which is why it should be done from memory and unannounced in its detail. If the real job is always done with the guide to hand, test it with the guide to hand. The check should match the conditions of use, and the conditions on the last afternoon rarely do.

**The check can make people anxious.** There is a cost. A check that looks like an exam makes people anxious and can sour a course they liked. Keeping it short, saying it is a check on the course, and reporting only group results all help.

try.text: For one course you run, design the ten-minute check for six weeks later: the scenario, the marking steps, where it will happen and who marks it. Then say the announcement aloud, as you would to the group at the end of the course, until it takes under thirty seconds and does not sound like a threat. Use the wording below as a start.

lines: "One last thing before we close. In about six weeks I'll join your Tuesday team call for ten minutes."
"I'll give you a short scenario and ask you to fill in a report from it, no guide."
"It's a check on the course, not on you. I report the results for the group, never by name."
"Please don't revise for it. If steps have slipped by then, that tells me what to fix in the course and what reminders you need."

items: **Response rates fall with time.** Keep the check to ten minutes and run it where people already meet.
**The check feels like a test** and raises anxiety. Explain why you are doing it, report group results only, and keep managers from using it to rate individuals.
**The sponsor first hears of it** when the drop appears. Agree the check in advance, and say then that a drop is expected.
**You warn people to revise**, or resend the slides the day before. You then measure last night's reading. Announce that it will happen and leave the materials alone.
**You compare totals only.** "Down from 100 to 70 per cent" alarms people and fixes nothing. Compare step by step.

items.label: Soderstrom and Bjork (2015), Learning versus performance: an integrative review. Perspectives on Psychological Science.
Thalheimer (2018), The Learning-Transfer Evaluation Model: sending messages to enable learning effectiveness. Work-Learning Research report.

quiz.q: What does the Soderstrom and Bjork review conclude about performance during training?
quiz.a: It is often an unreliable guide to lasting learning. Gains seen at the time can fade, and learning can happen with no visible gain.

quiz.q: Everyone completed the task correctly on the last afternoon. The sponsor wants that reported as the result. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Report it as an end-of-course result, and book a short check four to twelve weeks later where people do the task from memory without being told to revise. Ask managers what they have seen.

quiz.q: At the six-week check, a third of the group miss the same two steps. The sponsor is alarmed. What do you say and do?
quiz.a: A drop is normal and shows where follow-up is needed. Turn the two missed steps into a reminder and a job aid, and use the result to improve the follow-up.

topics.tierReason: A large body of research shows performance during or just after training is an unreliable sign of lasting learning, but the timing of a follow-up check at work is a rule of thumb.

topics.title: Separate the effect of training from everything else

situation.text: Sales rose 8 per cent in the quarter after the sales course, and the slide for the board says so. Then the finance director points out that sales rose 7 per cent in the region that did not attend. The meeting moves on, and the course is not mentioned again.

items: **Ask one question before dates are fixed:** "Does everyone have to be trained in the same month?" Most roll-outs are staggered anyway because of room and trainer capacity. Use that.
**Split the groups into early and late** by the timetable, not by who is keen. Check that the two halves start from a similar place on the measure.

**Measure every group on the same dates:** once before anyone is trained, and once after the early groups have had time to use the skill and before the late groups start. The waiting groups are your comparison.
**Work out each half's change, then subtract.** The change in the trained groups minus the change in the waiting groups is the part you can link to the course.
**List what else changed over those weeks**, for each group: a price change, a new system, a new manager, a seasonal peak.

**Plot the measure month by month** where no comparison group is possible, for several months before the course and several after. A change in the trend at the point of training is stronger evidence than a single before and after pair.
**Make own estimates the last resort.** These are participants' and managers' own estimates of the share due to training. If you use them, label them as opinion and discount them.
**Say how sure you are and why** in the report, in plain words: "Fairly sure", "An indication only" or "We cannot tell", each with one sentence of reason.

why.text: **The change might have happened anyway.** Without a comparison, any change after training may have happened anyway. Markets move, seasons turn and new managers arrive. The waiting group lives through all of that too, so whatever those things did shows up in its figures, and subtracting it leaves a fairer estimate of what the course added. This is the reasoning of the practitioner handbooks on evaluation, not a new research finding.

**A staggered roll-out gives a cheap comparison.** A staggered roll-out is often the most practical way to get a comparison group. It costs almost nothing, because the stagger already exists. All you add is a second set of measuring dates. Nobody is denied the course. They receive it eight weeks later.

**Compare changes, because groups start unequal.** Comparing changes, not final scores, matters because groups differ before training. A depot that started with fewer errors will still have fewer afterwards, with or without you. The subtraction deals with a different starting level. It does not deal with a group that was already improving faster, which is why you check the starting point and let the timetable choose who goes first.

**Estimates from participants are weak evidence.** Use them as a last resort and say what they are. The trend method is weaker than a comparison group as well, because something else could have changed in the same month. It still beats one before and after pair, which cannot tell a real shift from an ordinary wobble.

try.text: For one real programme, write down the comparison you could set up at no extra cost: which groups go early, which wait, the measure, and the two measuring dates. If everyone must be trained together, ask the client for the monthly figure for the last six months and lay it out as in the second table. Then say your confidence statement aloud to a colleague and ask whether a finance director would accept it.

quiz.a: Without one, any change after training may have happened anyway.

quiz.q: Four depots need the same course and the client plans to train them all in March. How could you get a comparison at no extra cost?
quiz.a: Train two depots in March and two in May. Record error rates at all four in February and April. In April the May depots are the comparison. Let the timetable decide who goes first, and compare the change in each half.

topics.title: Do not mistake activity for learning

situation.text: The monthly learning dashboard for a retailer's 600 store staff shows 4,212 logins, 97 per cent completion of the returns module and an average of 11 minutes spent. The slide is headed "Training is working". On the shop floor, refunds are still being put through on the wrong code about as often as before.

items: **List every figure on the dashboard** in one column. Beside each, write one of three labels: activity, a record someone requires, or evidence of learning or behaviour.
**Apply the decision test to each one:** "If this number doubled or halved, what would we do differently, and who would do it?" If nobody can answer, take it off the report.

**Keep completion records** where a regulator, an auditor or a contract asks for them. Report them as [a record of who was trained](t:2.30), with the heading "Record", and put a measure of learning or behaviour beside them.
**Use activity data for its strength:** finding where people struggle or drop out. Look for the screen where most people leave, and the question most people get wrong at the first attempt.
**Send each of those findings** to the person who can fix it, with a date. A drop-off point goes to the designer. A team with low completion goes to its manager.
**Add at least one figure** from outside the platform: a spot check, [a scenario score after a delay](t:6.5) or [a manager's observation](t:6.4).
**Tell learners what you collect and why**, in two sentences at the start of the course. Check [your data protection duties](t:9.24) before you collect anything about them.

why.text: **Completion figures measure activity, not learning.** Completion and engagement figures are easy to get. They measure activity. They do not show learning or use. They turn into vanity metrics when they are offered as proof that the training worked. In [Thalheimer's LTEM](t:6.2), attendance and activity are the bottom two tiers, both described as inadequate for validating learning.

**A completion record still has a job.** In regulated training it is evidence the client may be asked to produce, and there is guidance on [how to keep the record](t:2.30). The mistake is to read the record as a result. A team can be at 98 per cent completion and still make the same error every month.

**Activity figures spread because they are free.** The reason dashboards fill with activity is that the platform produces it free. Time spent, logins and clicks arrive without anyone doing anything, while a spot check needs a person with a clipboard. So the report drifts towards what is cheap, and the cheap figures get asked to carry a claim they cannot support. The decision test is a way to push back without an argument about theory. You can check [what each tracking standard can record](t:3.14).

**Over-monitoring costs trust.** People who feel watched click through to satisfy the tracker. That is a judgement from practice. It is also why time spent is a poor figure to chase: once people know it is counted, a module left open in another tab looks like dedication.

try.text: Take a real set of analytics, from a learning platform or a webinar tool. Mark each figure as activity, a record someone requires, or evidence of learning or behaviour. Then mark the ones that tell you what to improve. Present the sorted version aloud to a colleague in two minutes, starting with the sentence "Here is what these figures can tell us, and here is what they cannot."

**The platform offers a prediction** of who will drop out. Treat any such prediction with caution. Use it as a prompt for a manager to have a conversation, never as a judgement on a person.
**Nobody acts on the dashboard**, though it is produced every month. A dashboard nobody acts on is decoration. Give each figure an owner or remove it.

**Completion is set as a target** for managers with nothing beside it. People click through to hit it. Pair it with a spot check so that the target is the behaviour.

quiz.q: What do completion figures show, and what do they not show?
quiz.a: They show activity: who started and finished. They do not show learning or use at work.

quiz.q: A client in a regulated sector reads that completions are a vanity metric and proposes to stop tracking them. What do you say?
quiz.a: Keep them. In regulated training [the completion record is evidence](t:2.30) the client may be asked to produce. Report it as a record, and add a behaviour measure such as spot checks beside it.

quiz.q: The dashboard shows most learners leaving the course part-way through module three. What do you do with that figure?
quiz.a: Send it to the designer, with a date, as a prompt to look at that module. Data like this is most useful for finding where the design is failing.

topics.title: Show the value in the client's own terms
topics.theory: Return on investment, return on expectations, and their honest limits

situation.text: Four months after a programme for twelve new managers, the finance director joins the review meeting for the first time and asks, "What did we get for our money?" The HR director talks about confidence and good feedback. The finance director nods, writes nothing down, and asks the same thing again in different words.

items: **Ask the sponsor to imagine success** at the scoping stage, before any design: "Imagine it is six months from now and you are telling your board this was money well spent. What are you pointing to?" Write the answer down word for word.
**Ask the follow-up twice:** "How would you know? Who would see it?" Stop when you reach something a person could count or observe.
**Find the sceptic early.** Ask, "Who else has to be convinced, and what will they ask?" If that is the finance director, get fifteen minutes with them now and put their test beside the sponsor's.

**Write each expectation as one line** with its evidence, who collects it and when. Send it back for agreement by email, so there is a dated record. There is more on the [wider conversation about what success looks like](t:9.6).

**Decide what will be priced**, line by line. Put a money value on a result only where the link from training to result is defensible and the client already counts it in money. Mark the others "reported, not priced".
**Set out the full cost** on the same page, including people's time away from work. Sponsors forget that line and finance directors never do.
**Use cautious assumptions and show them.** You can [work through the sums](t:6.15), and the Phillips method expects you to [separate the effect of training](t:6.6) from other causes first.
**Report against each agreed line** at the review, in the same order, including the ones that were missed and the benefits you could not price.

why.text: **Return figures persuade only with a clear link.** Return on investment compares the money value of results with the cost. It persuades where the link from training to result is clear, and misleads where it is not. An alternative is to agree in advance what the sponsor expects and report against that. It is often called return on expectations. Both come from the practitioner literature on evaluation, and choosing between them is a judgement about the client, not a research question.

**Value belongs to the person paying.** The reasoning for starting with expectations is that value is a judgement, and it belongs to the person paying. A percentage nobody asked for answers no question. A sponsor who said in January "I want new managers to handle a first absence conversation without calling HR" and is shown in June that most of them now do has had the question answered in the terms they set.

**Vague expectations will not survive a sceptic.** The approach has a weak point, and it helps to know it. Expectations can be vague or easy to meet, and the sponsor's expectations may not be the finance director's. A report that says "the sponsor is satisfied" does not survive a sceptic. That is the reason for steps two and three: push each expectation down to something countable, and collect the sceptic's test before the work starts.

**Price only what is already counted in money.** A return figure is only as good as the step before it. The Phillips method expects you to [separate the effect of training](t:6.6) from other causes before you put a price on anything. Where the result is already counted in money, such as agency spend, waste or sales, and you have a comparison, the sum is worth doing and you can follow [the steps for working it out](t:6.15). Where the benefit is a better conversation, pricing it invents a number, and a large invented number invites disbelief.

try.text: For one real programme, write the sponsor's test of value in one sentence, in their words, and the full cost including people's time. Then rehearse the opening question aloud with a colleague playing the sponsor. Ask them to give a vague first answer, such as "I just want them to be better managers", and practise the two follow-ups until you reach something countable.

items: **You present a large return figure.** It invites disbelief, and one challenged assumption can sink the whole report. Use cautious assumptions and show each one.
**Everything gets a price.** Not everything worth doing can be priced. Report confidence, retention of good people and similar benefits in words, under their own heading.
**The method is chosen late**, after the course. It then looks as if it was picked to suit the result. Agree the method before the course, in writing.
**The sponsor's test stays vague:** "better managers". Keep asking "How would you know?" until someone could count it.
**The cost leaves out people's time:** it shows fees and venue only. Finance will add the time away from work themselves and trust the rest of your page less. Put it in first.

quiz.a: The money value of results with the full cost, including people's time away from work.

quiz.q: A finance director asks what the organisation got for its money. The link from your course to revenue is weak. What do you report?
quiz.a: Results against the test of value the sponsor agreed in advance, in their words, with the full cost beside it. Do not put a money value on a link you cannot defend. List the benefits you could not price.

quiz.q: Your cost summary shows fees and venue. A colleague in finance says it is too low. What is missing?
quiz.a: People's time: the days away from work for every learner. It is part of the full cost.

topics.title: Feed the results back and make the case
topics.theory: Closing the loop and the business case

situation.text: The evaluation report for the first cohort was sent in June and filed. In September the second cohort of a software company's sales team sits through the same two days: same slides, same role-plays, same gap afterwards. The sponsor, asked whether to fund a third cohort, says she is not sure what the first two achieved.

items: **Book a 45-minute review** with the sponsor and one line manager before the course runs, dated for the week after the follow-up data arrives. A meeting already in the diary is much harder to skip.
**Open with the outcome** in the sponsor's language, in one sentence, set against [what was agreed at the start](t:6.8).
**State what the training contributed**, with its limits: what you measured, [what else changed](t:6.6), and how sure you are.

**Ask two questions about use:** "For the people who used it, what helped?" and "For those who did not, what got in the way?" Bring one case of each. [The Success Case Method](t:6.13) shows how to find them.
**Turn each finding into a change** with an owner and a date, and write them in a table during the meeting. Some will be changes to the course. Others will be for the client to make at work.
**Say what happens next** and ask for a decision: run again as changed, run a smaller version, or stop. If you recommend stopping part of it, say so plainly.
**Update the materials afterwards**, along with the facilitator guide, and [record the version](t:3.18). Add the lessons to [the close-out notes](t:9.26).

why.text: **Evaluation that changes nothing is wasted.** It is the input to the next version and to the next conversation with the sponsor. This is craft, and the reasoning is simple. Measuring costs the client time, and they will only keep giving that time if they see something done with it.

**Asking what helped gives something to change.** A common criticism of evaluation by levels is that it says whether training worked but not how to improve it. Asking what helped and what got in the way, for the people it worked for and the people it did not, gives you something to change. The answers are often not about the course at all. They are about what happened in the fortnight after it, which is the client's to fix and yours to point out.

**A report that admits limits is trusted.** Sponsors trust a report more when it says what it cannot show. A case that opens with its own limits has already answered the hardest question in the room. Conservative assumptions survive scrutiny, and a claim that survives is worth more to you than a bigger one that is picked apart.

**Bad news makes the next proposal believable.** There is a commercial tension here and it is better faced. The review is also the moment the client decides whether to buy more, so there is a pull towards showing only the good news. Reporting a failure, with the change that follows from it, is what makes the next proposal believable. The advice has a limit: if the findings say the course is the wrong answer to the problem, the next step is not a revised course, and there is more on [that conversation about reshaping the brief](t:9.29).

try.text: Take the results of one real programme. Fill in a findings table like the one below, with at least one change for you and one for the client. Then draft a one-page case for what should happen next: the outcome, the contribution, the limits and the decision you are asking for. Say the first four lines aloud as if opening the review meeting, and time them. Aim for under a minute.

**Failures are left out.** The sponsor usually knows about them already, and their absence costs you more than their presence. Report them with the change that follows.
**Every change lands on the trainer.** If the barrier was at work, such as no time to practise, name an owner on the client's side.
**The materials are not touched** once the findings table is written. Update the guide the same week and [record the version](t:3.18).
**The assumptions are generous.** Conservative assumptions survive scrutiny. Where you are choosing between two readings of the data, present the lower one.

topics.title: Report results people will read
topics.theory: Reporting and telling the story with data

situation.text: Your evaluation report runs to thirty pages. It opens with the background, then the method, and the main finding appears on page eleven. The operations director reads the first paragraph on her phone between meetings, learns that "this report describes the evaluation", and never opens it again.

items: **Write the finding first**, in one sentence of 25 words or fewer, with a number in it. "About half the shift leaders now use the handover checklist on every shift, up from 6 of 40."
**Put the recommendation second**, as an action with an owner: who should do what, by when.
**Show one or two charts**, each with [the claim as its headline](t:3.4) and [an honest axis](t:3.3). Before and after, or trained and waiting, side by side.
**Include one real case** in three or four sentences. Get [the person's consent](t:9.25) before you quote or name them, and say whether the case is typical or a best case.
**State what else changed** and what the data cannot show, in a section headed "Limits". Put the bad news in the body, not the appendix.
**Give the full cost in one line.** Claim a money value only if you have done [the cost and benefit work](t:6.15).
**Keep it to one page.** Method, full figures, the instruments and the comments go in an appendix that the page points to.
**Test it before you send it.** Read the first two sentences aloud to someone outside the programme and ask: "What happened, and what am I being asked to do?" If they cannot say, rewrite.

why.text: **Busy readers want the conclusion first.** A report is read by busy people who want to know what happened and what to do. Leading with the conclusion respects that. This is writing craft, not research. The [rules for honest charts](t:3.3) and for [putting the claim in the headline](t:3.4) apply here.

**The reader needs the reverse order.** The thirty-page report follows the order in which the work was done: background, method, results, conclusions. That order suits the writer, who lived it. The reader needs the reverse. A director who reads only the first two sentences should still leave with the finding and the decision, and everything below is there for the person who wants to check.

**One page also disciplines the claim.** With thirty pages you can hedge everywhere and commit to nothing. With one, you have to decide what you found. The limits section keeps that honest. A finance reader looks for the weak point first, and finding it already written down, in your words, is what makes the rest credible.

**A vivid case can outweigh the figures.** The case does a different job from the figures. Figures say how many, and a case shows what the change looks like on an ordinary shift. That is also the risk in it. A vivid story is remembered long after the figures are forgotten, so a best case with no label quietly becomes the result. There is a method for [choosing cases fairly](t:6.13). The one-page rule reverses for a regulator or an auditor, who may need the full record. Write the page anyway and attach the rest.

try.text: Take an evaluation summary you have written or received and rewrite it to one page in this order: finding, recommendation, evidence, case, limits, cost, next count. Then do the read-aloud test in step eight with someone who knows nothing about the programme. Good looks like this: after two sentences they can tell you what happened and what you want them to do.

try.title: A worked example: a one-page results report. Illustration with made-up figures
lines: Shift handover training: results at eight weeks. For the operations director. 40 shift leaders at a retailer's distribution site, trained over two weeks in March.
FINDING: About half the shift leaders (21 of 40) now use the handover checklist on every shift, up from 6 of 40 before the course.
RECOMMENDATION: Shift managers ask for the checklist at every shift change for the next eight weeks. Count again in July. Do not fund a second course yet.
WHAT WE MEASURED: Checklists filed per shift, from site records, for the four weeks before the course and for weeks 5 to 8 after it. Handover errors logged by the incoming shift, for the same weeks.
CHART 1, headline "Checklists are now filed on about half of shifts": 15 per cent of shifts before, 52 per cent in weeks 5 to 8.
CHART 2, headline "Handover errors fell by about a third": 34 logged in the four weeks before, 22 in weeks 5 to 8.
WHAT ELSE CHANGED: The new stock system went live in week 3 and also affects handover errors. Training is one contributor. We cannot say how large.

ONE CASE, shared with her consent: A night-shift leader keeps the checklist on a clipboard by the office door and walks it through with the incoming leader. Her shift logged no handover errors in weeks 5 to 8. This is the best case, not the average.
WHAT DID NOT WORK: 9 of the 40 have not used the checklist at all. Seven of them work on the two shifts whose managers missed the briefing.
LIMITS: Everyone was trained in the same fortnight, so there is no comparison group. Eight weeks is short. A filed checklist does not prove a good handover.
COST: £9,000 in fees and venue, plus half a day away from work for each of 40 people. No money value is claimed for the benefit.
NEXT COUNT: Weeks 13 to 16, pulled by the site analyst, reported in July.
APPENDIX: method, weekly figures by shift, the checklist, all form comments.

try.title: Before and after: the opening of a report
lines: Before: "This report describes the background, method and results of the evaluation."
After: "About half the team now use the handover checklist on every shift. We recommend a manager prompt at shift change to reach the rest."

items: **A case carries no label.** A case is not an average. Say which it is, in the same paragraph.
**Bad news is in the appendix.** Do not bury it. Put what did not work on the page, with what you propose to do about it.
**Someone is quoted or named** without being asked. Get [consent before quoting anyone](t:9.25), and offer to show them the wording.
**The chart flatters:** an axis that starts at 30, or percentages with no counts behind them. [Start the axis at zero](t:3.3) and give the numbers, as in "21 of 40".
**The page reports what was done**, such as sessions run and people trained, and calls it results. Those are [activity figures](t:6.7). Lead with what changed.

items.label: Brinkerhoff (2003), The Success Case Method: Find Out Quickly What's Working and What's Not.
BetterEvaluation, Success case method. Method guidance page.

quiz.q: What goes first in an evaluation report?
quiz.a: The finding, in one sentence, followed by what you recommend.

quiz.q: Your draft opens, "This report describes the background, method and results of the evaluation." How do you rewrite the opening?
quiz.a: Lead with the finding and the recommendation. For example: "About half the team now use the handover checklist on every shift. We recommend a manager prompt at shift change to reach the rest."

quiz.q: You want to include one adviser's story in the report, with her name. What do you do first, and what do you say about the story?
quiz.a: Get [her consent](t:9.25). In the report, say that it is one case and not the average.

parts.title: Go further with evaluation
parts.summary: How much to evaluate, getting the data, business measures and the money.

topics.title: Match the evaluation to the stakes

situation.text: A client runs forty programmes a year and asks you to "evaluate properly" a single half-day workshop. The evaluation you first sketch would cost more than the workshop.

items: **Ask three things before proposing anything:** what the programme costs in fees and people's time, how many people it reaches, and what decision the evaluation will inform.

**Sort it into one of three levels** of effort. Light for a one-off session. Standard for a programme reaching a few hundred people. Full for a company-wide programme, or one a senior sponsor is watching.

**For light, use a short form** with [a usefulness question and one scenario item](t:6.3). Four weeks later, send the sponsor one message asking what they have seen. Budget about an hour of your time.
**For standard, add four things:** [a baseline](t:6.1), [a delayed check](t:6.5) with a sample of people, a manager observation and one business measure tracked as a trend.
**For full, add four more things:** [a comparison built into the roll-out](t:6.6), data from the client's own analyst, success cases, and a cost and benefit case agreed with finance.
**Write the level and its price** into the proposal as a separate line. The client can then see what it buys and choose a lower level knowingly.
**Report operating measures under their own heading** when the client asks for them: cost per learner, fill rate and no-shows. Say that they describe efficiency and do not show learning.
**Move a programme up a level** if it will be repeated many times, or if a decision to scale depends on it.

why.text: **Evaluation effort should match the possible loss.** This is practitioner judgement. There is little research on how much evaluation a programme should get. The reasoning is about cost. Evaluation uses the client's money and people's time, so it should be in proportion to what is lost if the programme does not work.

**Phillips reserves return studies for big programmes.** The Phillips handbooks take the same line for their most demanding level. They reserve a return on investment study for programmes that are expensive, reach many people, drive business impact, have the attention of senior managers or are highly visible. They add that when you do go that far, you still report results at the lower levels.

**The right depth is easier to buy.** A learning team inside a large company runs hundreds of programmes and cannot fund deep work on each. A supplier who proposes the right depth, and says why, is easier to buy from than one who proposes the full treatment every time. Light does not mean nothing. Even a one-off workshop can end with one question that shows what people can do.

**Time to competence is nearer a result.** Time to competence is sometimes listed with the operating measures. It is closer to a result than the others. If the client reports it, ask how they define competent.

try.text: Take three pieces of work you know: a single workshop, a mid-sized programme and a large one. Give each a level and write one sentence defending it. Then say that sentence aloud, as you would to a sponsor who has asked for more.
