items: **Clients ask for the full treatment** and budget for light. Show the three levels with a price beside each and let them choose.
**Light evaluations add up** when repeated across fifty workshops. Pool the forms once a quarter and report on the set.
**Operating measures look precise** and get mistaken for results. Keep them under their own heading.
**Small programmes can carry high risk**, such as a safety task or a regulated one. Let the risk set the level, whatever the headcount.

items.label: Phillips and Phillips (2019), ROI Basics, chapter one. ATD Press. Copy on the ROI Institute's site.

quiz.q: Name two operating measures that describe efficiency and do not show learning.
quiz.a: Any two of: cost per learner, fill rate, no-shows.

quiz.q: A sponsor asks for a full return on investment study of one 90-minute session for twelve people. What do you do?
quiz.a: Propose the light level: one scenario item on the form and a message at four weeks. Explain that the study would cost more than the session, and offer the fuller level if the session is to be rolled out widely.

quiz.q: A course for eight warehouse staff covers a task where an error could injure someone. Headcount says light. What level do you choose?
quiz.a: Standard at least. Risk sets the level, so you check that each person can do the task after a delay and you ask the supervisor what they see.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement, with one handbook chapter on when a return on investment study is warranted.

topics.title: Get the data you need from the client

situation.text: Your plan says "compare complaint rates before and after". The course has run. The client's analyst has never heard of you, and the sponsor says the figures are "with HR".

items: **Ask the sponsor about each measure** in the plan, at proposal stage: who owns this figure, and who can pull it.
**Ask to be introduced to that person.** It is usually an analyst in sales operations, customer operations or HR. Explain the purpose in two lines and ask what is easy for them to produce.
**Request the least you need.** Team or store totals by month are usually enough. Ask for no names, no staff numbers and no free text.
**Offer the client its own analysis:** the option of running the comparison in its own systems and sending you a summary table. You then never hold individual records.
**Ask what minimum group size** the client applies before it shares a figure, and combine small teams to meet it.
**Write it into the statement of work:** the measures, the format, who supplies them, the dates for the baseline and the follow-up, and who may see the result.
**Allow weeks.** The request may need a data protection review, and the analyst has other work. Ask for the baseline before the first session.
**Switch to measures you can collect** yourself if the answer is no: an observation checklist, a scenario check, a short manager survey. Say in the report that business data was not available.

why.text: **Many evaluation plans fail on data access.** This is practitioner judgement about how client organisations work. A supplier has no access to a client's sales, quality or HR systems, and many evaluation plans fail here. The plan is sound and the data never arrives. Agreeing it before the work starts turns a favour into a commitment with a name and a date.

**Totals are safer, except in small teams.** Asking for totals makes the request easier to grant. The ICO's guidance on anonymisation says information is anonymous when the risk of identifying a person is sufficiently remote, and that removing obvious identifiers is not enough if someone can still be singled out or records can be linked. It mentions an NHS standard of five as one example of a minimum group size. Small teams are where this bites. A store with three staff and one complaint points at a person.

**Client data needs the same care.** There is guidance on [what you may collect and keep](t:9.24) about learners. The same care applies to anything the client sends you. This is general information, not legal advice.

**In-house analysis costs you some control.** When the client keeps the analysis in house, you give up some control over the method. Agree the comparison in writing first, so that the table you receive answers the question you asked.

try.text: Pick one programme and one business measure. Draft the request using the example below. Then make the ask aloud, as a two-minute request to a sponsor in a kick-off meeting, and time yourself.

try.title: A worked example: a data request to a client analyst
lines: Subject: Figures for the store launch training evaluation
Hello Sam. Priya suggested I contact you. I am evaluating the September launch training for store staff.
What I need: attach rate for the new accessory range, by store, by month.
Period: June to November, which is three months before the training and three after.
Level: store totals only. No names, staff numbers or till IDs.
Small stores: please combine any store with fewer than five staff into its area total.
Format: one spreadsheet, one row per store per month.
If it is easier, run the before and after comparison yourself and send me the summary table.
Dates: June to August figures by 5 September. September to November figures by 12 December.
Use: one summary chart in the report to the sponsor. I will delete the file when the report is signed off.
Who sees it: the sponsor, the learning team and me.
Is any of this hard to pull? If there is a simpler figure you already report, I would sooner use that.

items: **The analyst is never told**, though the sponsor agrees. Get the introduction in the kick-off meeting, with the sponsor present.
**You are sent individual records** you did not ask for. Do not work from them. Tell the client, delete the file and ask again for totals.
**The figures change layout each month.** Send a blank table with the columns you need.
**The client cannot share in writing.** Ask a client manager to talk you through the trend on a call and confirm the direction by email.
**The measure is defined differently** in each market. Ask for the definition with the first file.

items.label: Information Commissioner's Office, How do we ensure anonymisation is effective? (under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025).

quiz.q: When do you agree data access with a client?
quiz.a: Before the work starts, in the statement of work, with a named person and dates.

quiz.q: The analyst offers a file of every adviser's complaint count by name. You only need the team trend. What do you do?
quiz.a: Decline it and ask for team totals by month. You hold less personal data, and the request is easier for the client to approve.

quiz.q: Two weeks before the course, the client says no sales data can leave the building. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the client to run the comparison itself and share a summary. If that is refused too, collect your own measures, such as an observation checklist and a scenario check, and say so in the report.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement, with ICO guidance on when information counts as anonymous.

topics.title: Use the Success Case Method

situation.text: A customer service programme has run for 120 advisers. There is no comparison group. The sponsor wants to know whether it worked and what to change.

items: **Plan the study with the sponsor:** the decision it will inform, who will be surveyed, and when. Six to eight weeks after the programme is a workable point, as a rule of thumb.
**Write an impact model on one page.** It says what success would look like: the behaviour people would use at work and the result it should lead to.
**Send a short survey to everyone** who took part. Its only job is to find the people who used the training with most success and those who used it least. Three or four questions are enough.
**Pick a handful from each end.** As a working number, interview five or six of the most successful and three or four of the least.
**Interview each person** for 20 to 30 minutes. Ask what they did, what happened as a result, what helped and what got in the way.
**Confirm each success story** with someone who would know, such as the person's manager, or against a record. Report only what you can confirm.
**Report what the best cases achieved**, what was different for those who got nothing from it, and what to change. Include how many survey replies fell at each end.

why.text: **The method is Brinkerhoff's, in five steps.** Robert Brinkerhoff set out the method in a 2003 book. The publisher describes it as quicker and cheaper than other approaches, built on accounts of how people used an initiative, and able to find success even when it is rare. An evaluation guidance page lists five steps: plan the study, create an impact model, survey to find the best and worst cases, interview and document the cases, then communicate findings and recommendations.

**Study the two ends, not the average.** The logic is to study the two ends and leave the average alone. If a few people got a real result, their stories show what the programme can do and what made that possible. The people who got nothing show what blocked it. In practice the block is often a manager or a system, which is a judgement from experience and not a finding.

**The method has limits.** A success case is the best that happened. It does not tell you the typical result and it cannot stand in for [a comparison](t:6.6). It rests on people's own accounts, which is why the confirming step matters. One review of the book reports Brinkerhoff's test that a story should be able to stand up in court. The guidance page adds practical conditions. You need to reach participants and someone who can confirm what they say, and the work has to be planned and budgeted from the start.
This is a practitioner method. There is little independent testing of the method itself.

try.text: Write the impact model for one programme you know. Then run a practice interview aloud with a colleague playing a participant, using the questions below, and record it. Listen back for the moments where you suggested the answer.

try.title: A worked example: outline of a two-page success case study for a customer service programme

head: Section
What goes in it
rows: Purpose
Decide whether to run the call-handling programme for the next two intakes, and what to change first.
Who
All 120 advisers who completed it, surveyed seven weeks after their last session.
Impact model
Advisers confirm the customer's problem in their own words before offering a fix. Expected result: fewer repeat contacts about the same problem.
Survey
Four questions. Have you used the confirm step on live calls. How often. What happened as a result. May we talk to you.
Selection
Six advisers who report frequent use and a clear result. Four who report no use.
Interviews
25 minutes each by video call. What did you do, what happened, what helped, what got in the way.
Confirmation
The team leader confirms each success story. Where possible, check the adviser's repeat contact figures for the same weeks.
Report, page one
What the best cases achieved, in two short confirmed stories. How many survey replies fell at each end.
Report, page two
What blocked the others. Three changes for the next intake. What the study cannot show: the average effect.
Timetable
Survey in week seven. Interviews in weeks eight and nine. Report in week ten.

try.title: Words you can use: interview questions
lines: Tell me about one call where you used the confirm step. Talk me through it.
What did you do that you would not have done before?
What happened next, for the customer and for you?
How do you know that? Is there anything I could look at?
What made it possible? Who or what helped?
For someone who has not used it: what got in the way?
If we ran this again, what one thing should we change?

items: **Only the keen reply** to the survey. Send it through team leaders and keep it to two minutes.
**Success stories are presented as typical.** Put the number of replies at each end on the first page.
**A story cannot be confirmed.** Leave it out, however good it sounds.
**Interviews turn into blame** when they are with people who did not use it. Ask what got in the way, and report barriers by type with no names.
**You quote someone without asking.** Get [consent first](t:9.25).

items.label: Brinkerhoff (2003), The Success Case Method: Find Out Quickly What's Working and What's Not. Berrett-Koehler.
BetterEvaluation, Success case method. Method guidance page.
Tulloch, review of Brinkerhoff (2003), The Success Case Method. The Evaluation Exchange, Harvard Family Research Project.

quiz.q: What is the survey for in the Success Case Method?
quiz.a: To find the people who used the training with most success and those who used it least, so you can interview both.

quiz.q: An adviser tells you the training cut her repeat calls by half. Her team leader cannot confirm it and there is no record. What do you do?
quiz.a: Leave the claim out of the report. The method reports only what can be confirmed, which is what separates it from collecting anecdotes.

quiz.q: The sponsor reads your two success stories and says, "So this is what the programme does for people." What do you say?
quiz.a: That these are the best cases and not the typical result. Point to the number of replies at each end, and to what blocked the people who did not use it.

topics.title: Measure enablement by business results
topics.theory: Enablement measures for sales, product and retail training

situation.text: A technology client is launching a product in six markets. The contract says the training will be judged on "readiness". Nobody has said which figure that is.

items: **Ask the client which business figure** the training is meant to move, and write down its exact definition. Ramp time and win rate are defined differently from one company to the next.
**Pick one result measure.** Add one or two leading indicators you can observe yourself, such as a demo certification or a scored call.
**Find where each figure lives** and who owns it. Use the table below as a starting list, then follow the steps for [making the request to the client](t:6.12).
**Record the baseline** for the previous cohort or the previous quarter before the first session.
**List what else will move the figure** in the same period: price changes, promotions, the season, territory changes, the mix of new hires, stock.
**Report by cohort or by market**, as a trend. Add [a comparison where the roll-out allows one](t:6.6).
**State what you claim.** Certification and observation scores show what people can do. Business figures show what happened, with [training as one contributor](t:6.4).

why.text: **Sponsors accept figures they already use.** This topic is practitioner judgement, and there is little research on these measures as evidence of training. They are figures that sales, product and retail clients already use to run the business, which is why a sponsor accepts them more readily than a learning score.

**These figures move slowly and for many reasons.** Attribution is hard, and the reasons are worth saying to the client early. The figures respond to many things at once, and a launch usually arrives with a price, a campaign and new stock. They also lag. A win rate for a long sales cycle may not move for two quarters. Small groups swing widely too, so one large deal can change a whole market's figure.

**Pair a slow measure with a fast one.** That is the case for pairing a slow business measure with a fast one you control. A certification pass or a mystery shopping score will not prove revenue. It shows whether people can do what the training taught, soon enough to act on it.

**Keep completion, labelled as activity.** Completion by market still has a place, because many clients contract on it and some [need it as a record](t:2.30). [Report it as activity](t:6.7) and set it beside a measure of what people can do.

try.text: For one client, choose a result measure and a leading indicator from the table. Then explain the choice aloud in one minute, as you would to a sales operations lead. Record it and check that you defined each term.

quiz.q: What is an attach rate?
quiz.a: The share of sales of a main product that include a named add-on.

quiz.q: Win rate rose in the quarter after your sales course. A price cut landed in the same month. What do you report?
quiz.a: The trend, the price cut beside it, and training as one possible contributor. If any market had the price cut without the course yet, use it as the comparison.

quiz.q: A client with a nine-month sales cycle wants proof within six weeks of the course. What do you offer?
quiz.a: A leading indicator you can observe now, such as a scored demo or call, with the business measure to follow. Say plainly that the first shows capability and not revenue.

topics.title: Build the cost and benefit case
topics.theory: Cost and benefit analysis and the Phillips ROI formula

situation.text: The finance director has seen the proposal and asks for "the numbers". You have a fee and a hope.

items: **List every cost line:** needs analysis, design, delivery fees, venue and travel, platform and administration, evaluation. Then add learner time, which is days away from work multiplied by a daily cost.
**Ask the client's finance team** for the daily cost of a person's time and use their figure. Do the same for any unit value in the benefit. Finance should own the unit costs.

**Choose one benefit you can defend**, tied to [the measure agreed at the start](t:6.1). Write the chain in one sentence: the training changes this behaviour, which changes this figure, which is worth this much.
**Estimate the benefit three times:** low, mid and high. Count the first year only. Reduce each estimate for [the share that other causes could explain](t:6.6).
**Work out the break-even point first.** It is the size of improvement at which the benefit equals the cost. Ask the sponsor whether that improvement is plausible.

**Then calculate the two Phillips figures.** The benefit-cost ratio is programme benefits divided by programme costs. Return on investment, as a percentage, is net programme benefits divided by programme costs, multiplied by 100. Net benefits are benefits minus costs.
**Show the assumptions** on the same page as the result, and list the benefits you did not price.

why.text: **The formulas come from Jack and Patricia Phillips.** They define the benefit-cost ratio on gross benefits and return on investment on net benefits. They add a payback period, which is costs divided by benefits. Their guiding principles ask for the most conservative option where there is a choice, fully loaded costs, first-year benefits only for short-term programmes, and at least one method of isolating the programme's effect from other influences.

**Learner time is this site's addition.** Their list of costs names needs assessment, design, delivery and evaluation. Learner time is added here as this site's judgement, in line with the advice on [setting out the full cost](t:6.8). It is often the largest line, and a finance reader will look for it.

**The size of the change is uncertain.** A benefit estimate is only as honest as its weakest link. The value of a unit comes from finance. The size of the change comes from your evaluation and is uncertain. Three cases put that uncertainty on the page. Break-even reasoning often persuades more than a return figure, because it asks something the sponsor can judge from experience.
This is a practitioner framework with little independent testing.

**A benefit is priced too early**, before any change was measured. Call it a forecast, and replace it with measured figures after the follow-up.
**Learner time is left out** to make the case look better. Finance will add it back and trust the rest less.
**The same benefit is counted twice**, once as time saved and once as extra sales. Pick one.
**Illustration figures get quoted as real.** Label every draft.

items.label: Phillips and Phillips (2019), ROI Basics, chapter one. ATD Press. Copy on the ROI Institute's site.

quiz.q: How do Phillips and Phillips define return on investment as a percentage?
quiz.a: Net programme benefits divided by programme costs, multiplied by 100.

quiz.q: A programme cost £100,000 in total and the agreed first-year benefit is £150,000. What are the benefit-cost ratio and the return on investment?
quiz.a: The ratio is 1.5 and the return is 50%. The ratio uses the whole benefit, and the return uses the benefit after costs are taken off.

quiz.q: The sponsor wants a single return figure for the board and your three cases run from 0% to 200%. What do you do?
quiz.a: Give the break-even point and the low case first, then the range with its assumptions. A single high figure with hidden assumptions will not survive a finance question.

stages.name: Training in the AI era
stages.question: What does AI change about training, and what does it leave alone?

parts.title: AI in training
parts.summary: Using AI to build learning, judging the claims, and training people to work with it.

topics.title: Let AI draft, and keep a person accountable
topics.theory: Using AI to design and build learning

situation.text: A retailer wants a half-day course on its new returns policy for store staff, and wants it by Friday. An AI tool could write the whole thing by lunchtime and it would read well. You would not know which parts were wrong, and the client would not find out until a store manager spotted one in front of a customer.

items: **Write four decisions in your own words** before you open the tool: what the problem is, [whether training will fix it](t:2.29), what people [must be able to do at the end](t:2.11), and how you will know. These stay with you. Do not ask the tool to make them.

**Split the build into two lists.** Under "AI drafts" put first drafts of scenarios, question items, summaries of documents you supply, storyboards and alternative wordings. Under "I do" put the outline, what to leave out, every fact about the client's product, policy or the law, and the final wording of anything that is assessed.
**Brief the tool** with the objective, the audience and the constraints, and give it the client's source document so it is not working from memory. You can see [what a full brief looks like](t:7.6).

**Put the checking time in your plan** as its own line, with a date. Check every output for accuracy, bias and fit with the objective before a learner sees it. There is a [routine for checking AI output](t:7.7).

**Name the accountable person** on the project plan. A named, qualified person signs off what reaches learners, and can explain every line of it. Test it this way: point at any sentence and ask "Where does this come from?" If nobody can answer, the sentence comes out.
**Keep a short log** as you go: what the tool drafted, what you changed and who signed it off. You will need it when you tell the client and the learners [where AI was used](t:7.10).
**Check you have permission** before you paste in any client material, and check whether it contains personal data. You can read [the rules a team needs](t:7.3).

why.text: **AI drafts and a professional decides.** AI speeds up work you already know how to do well, because you can tell a good draft from a bad one. It cannot find out what the client's problem is, decide what to leave out, or judge whether a claim has evidence behind it. So the tool drafts and a professional decides.

**Tools with a teaching purpose tend to help.** A 2026 OECD review of the research points the same way for classrooms. Tools built or used with a clear teaching purpose tend to help. Getting a task done with a general chatbot does not by itself lead to learning. That is research about pupils and students. The rest of this page is professional craft.

**A tool cannot answer for the content.** The reason for a named person is simple. A client cannot ask a tool why line twelve says what it says, and a tool carries no responsibility when a learner acts on a wrong answer. Somebody has to be able to stand in front of the client and account for the content. If that is going to be you, you have to have read it.

**AI saves time only in subjects you know.** The time saved is real only for content you could have written yourself. In a subject you do not know, the advice reverses. You cannot tell a good draft from a bad one, so the draft costs more to check than it saved, and the safer route is to [start from a subject expert](t:3.17) and use the tool on what they give you.

try.text: Use an AI tool to draft one small asset, such as five quiz questions or a one-page handout, for an objective you have already written. Check it with [the routine for checking AI output](t:7.7). Note each change you made and why the tool could not have made it. Then hand the finished asset to a colleague, let them point at three lines, and say aloud where each one comes from.

items: **Plausible text can be wrong.** A fluent draft is no sign of an accurate one, so check against a source and not against how it reads.
**The deadline eats the check.** If time runs short, cut the amount of material and keep the check. Never send out a draft you have not read.
**You hand over the outline** as well as the drafting. The result is a generic course that fits no client. Write the outline yourself and give it to the tool.
**Where AI was used:** tell learners. One line on the material is enough, and there is [wording you can use](t:7.10).
**Confidential material:** do not paste it into a tool without permission. If the material includes personal data, data protection law applies. Check your organisation's rules before you use a tool.

quiz.a: Check each one against the objective and against a source. Keep, rewrite or bin them, and sign off what is left under your own name.

quiz.a: Do not paste it yet. Personal data brings data protection law into play, so check the organisation's rules and ask for an approved tool or a copy with names removed.

topics.title: Expect moderate gains from adaptive tools
topics.theory: Adaptive tutoring and the honest evidence

situation.text: A vendor's slide says its adaptive platform "doubles learning". The client's head of sales turns to you in the meeting and asks whether to buy it for 400 people. You have about a minute before the conversation moves on to price.

items: **Ask for the study behind the headline**, not the summary of it. Say: "Which study is that figure from, and can you send it to us?"

**Ask four questions in this order**: how big was the effect, what was it compared with, whose test measured it, and was anyone tested later without the tool. Each one is explained in [how to test a learning claim](t:1.11).
**Hold the answer against the reviews.** Expect moderate gains from well-designed systems. Treat very large figures as outliers and ask what the other studies found.
**Ask what produces the gain** in the design, such as feedback at each step, and what stops the tool handing over answers.
**Ask who was studied.** If it was school pupils or university students, say to the client that the size of any gain is untested for staff at work.
**Restate the claim for the client** in one plain sentence. Where the vendor could not answer a question, say so in the sentence.

**Propose a pilot** if the client still wants to buy, one that ends with a task done without the tool, for a group that used it and a group that did not. There is more on [using comparison groups](t:6.6).

why.text: **The gains are moderate, not two sigma.** Reviews of intelligent tutoring systems find real, moderate gains. These are programs that set problems and give feedback or hints as the learner works. Gains are reported in standard deviations, a measure of how spread out the scores are. One review of 50 controlled evaluations found a median gain of 0.66 standard deviations over conventional teaching, and the size depended heavily on the test used. As a rough guide, a gain of that size moves a middling learner to about the top quarter of the group. Another review found a gain of 0.42 over teacher-led classes and no significant difference from one-to-one human tutoring. The famous "two sigma" figure, the claim that one-to-one tutoring lifts learners by two standard deviations, has not held up. A 2011 review put human tutoring at about 0.79 against no tutoring, with step-based tutoring systems close behind at 0.76.
**Teaching design matters, not the label.** What produces the gain is how the tool is built to teach, such as feedback at each step. The word "adaptive" on the box tells you little.

**Evidence on AI tutors is thin and mixed.** Generative AI tutors are newer and the evidence is thinner. In one field experiment with nearly a thousand secondary school maths pupils, a plain chatbot raised practice grades, but those pupils then scored lower on a test without it than pupils who never had it. A version with teaching guardrails largely avoided the harm. In one university physics course, a carefully designed AI tutor beat an active-learning class on a short test. A 2026 OECD review draws the same line between general chatbots and tools built for teaching.

why.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning
why.found: In a field experiment with nearly a thousand secondary school maths pupils, a standard chatbot improved practice grades by 48% and a tutor version with guardrails by 127%. Once access was removed, pupils who had used the standard chatbot scored 17% lower than pupils who never had access. The guardrails largely prevented that drop.
why.means: Judge an AI learning tool by what people can do without it, and ask what in its design stops it handing over answers.

why.text: **Each question can shrink a headline.** The four questions matter because each one can shrink a headline. A gain measured against reading a manual says little about a gain against a good trainer. A test written by the vendor tends to fit the product. Scores taken while people still have the tool show performance, which is [a different thing from learning](t:1.4). One caution runs the other way. If the job will always be done with the tool to hand, what people can do with it may be exactly what the client is buying. That is a [design decision about working with AI](t:7.12), and it should be made on purpose.

try.text: Take three vendor claims for AI or virtual reality learning. For each, write down the size of the effect, what it was compared with, whose test was used and whether anyone was tested later without the tool. Then restate the claim in one plain sentence. Where the vendor cannot answer, say so in the sentence. Say each restated sentence aloud as you would to a client across a table, and time it. Good is under twenty seconds with no jargon.

lines: Vendor line: "Our adaptive platform doubles learning."

Restated after questions: "In one study, people using the platform scored moderately higher on the vendor's own test than a group who read a manual. No comparison with a good trainer. No follow-up test."

items: **Marketing quotes the best study.** Ask what the other studies found, and how many there were.

**Adaptive pacing helps some content more** than others. Ask which content the study used, and whether it looks like the client's.
**Better scores while using a tool** are not proof of learning. Test them without the tool.
**You sound like the person blocking** the purchase. Offer the pilot as the way to say yes safely, and put the four questions to the vendor in writing so the client sees the answers.

topics.title: Set the guardrails before you scale

situation.text: In a team meeting a colleague mentions that she used a chatbot to summarise last month's feedback comments, names and all. Three people nod. The team has been using AI tools for months, on different accounts, and nobody has written down what is allowed.

items: **Start from what is happening now.** Give the team ten minutes to list every tool they used last month and what material went into it. Say that nobody is in trouble, or the list will be short.
**List the risks for your own work**: wrong facts, bias, privacy and loss of trust. Write one real example beside each, taken from that list if you can.
**Require a named person to review** anything before it reaches a learner. They follow [the routine for checking AI output](t:7.7).
**Tell people where AI was used**: learners and clients, in a line on the material or in the joining note. There is [wording you can use](t:7.10).

**Set rules for learner data**: what may go into which tool, and what never does. A three-column table does it: approved tool, material allowed, material never allowed. There is more on [learner data and privacy under UK law](t:9.24).
**Say what AI may not decide**, such as who passes, who is put forward for a role, or who is reported to a manager.
**Name who is accountable for the policy**, and who people ask when a case is not covered. Put a date on the page and a date to review it.

**Read the page aloud with the team.** Ask each person for one case from last month that it does not cover, and add a line for each. The rule for [AI tools during live sessions](t:7.9) is a separate decision.

why.text: **Rules in advance beat deciding under deadline.** When AI use goes wrong in training, learners are harmed and you lose credibility with the client. Rules written in advance mean people do not have to decide case by case under deadline.
Bias in the data a tool learned from shows up in what it produces.

**Personal data brings UK law into play.** In the UK, data protection law applies whenever an AI tool handles personal data about learners. The ICO's guidance on AI covers accountability, transparency, lawfulness, accuracy, fairness and bias, security and data minimisation. It is under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, so read the current version. Significant decisions about a person made with no meaningful human involvement have their own rules and safeguards.

**The EU AI Act adds a literacy duty.** If you work with clients in the EU, the EU AI Act applies to organisations that provide or deploy AI systems. As of November 2026, the European Commission's pages say the following. Article 4 on AI literacy has applied since 2 February 2025, and national authorities have supervised it since 2 August 2026. An amending law, the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), entered into force on 27 July 2026. Since then, providers and deployers must take measures to support AI literacy among their staff and others who use AI systems on their behalf. No set level is required and no certificate is needed, and internal records of training are enough. The Commission lists AI used in education, such as scoring exams, and AI used to manage workers, such as software that sorts CVs, among high-risk uses. The rules for those uses now apply from 2 December 2027, a date moved back by the same amendment. If a tool you build or recommend scores learners or informs decisions about staff, raise it with the client's legal team early. This is general information, not legal advice.

**A page that bans everything gets ignored.** The shape of the policy is craft. Most teams write it after the tools are in use, which is why the first step is an honest list. Strictness has a cost. A page that bans everything gets ignored, and people carry on quietly with personal accounts where nobody can see what went in. Naming approved tools and a person to ask keeps the use in the open.

try.text: Draft a one-page policy for a learning team covering review, disclosure, data handling and what AI may not decide. Give it to a colleague and ask them to name one case from last month that it does not cover. Then read the page aloud as you would to the team, and time it. If it takes more than four minutes, it is too long to be remembered.

try.title: A worked example: a one-page AI policy for a learning team of six
lines: 1. Review. A named designer reviews every AI-drafted item before learners see it.
2. Disclosure. We tell learners where AI was used, in a line on the material or in the joining note.
3. Approved tools. Only the two tools the organisation has approved. No personal accounts for client work.
4. Data. No learner names, scores or free-text answers go into a tool the organisation has not approved.
5. Client material. Nothing confidential goes into any tool unless the client has agreed in writing.
6. Decisions. AI never decides who passes, who is put forward for a role or who is reported to a manager.
7. Monitoring. If a tool tracks what learners type or how long they take, we tell them, and say who sees it.
8. Accountable: the head of learning. Not sure about a case? Ask her before you use the tool, not after.
9. Written in November. Reviewed at the start of every new client or tool, and at least every six months.

items: **A policy nobody reads** protects nobody. Keep it to one page and go through it aloud with the team.
**The law is changing.** Check the current rules each time you start a new client or tool.
**Monitoring learners costs trust.** If a tool tracks what people type or how long they take, tell them, and say who sees it.
**The policy is so strict** that people work round it. Name the approved tools and a person to ask, so the easy route is also the allowed one.

**The page covers design work** and forgets everything else. Check it against the list from step one: [feedback analysis](t:7.8), [live sessions](t:7.9) and [practice tools for learners](t:7.11) all need a line.

topics.title: Train people to check the AI's work
topics.theory: Training people for an AI world

situation.text: The head of customer success at a software company shows you a renewal report that went to a customer with the wrong contract end date. It was pasted from an AI summary and nobody read it. She says it is not the first, and asks you for a one-hour session for her team of twelve.

items: **Ask the manager for three documents** two weeks before, ones the team knows well, such as a pricing policy, a product note and an account summary. Ask which AI tools the team uses and for what.

**Make an AI-written summary of each document.** Find or plant one confident error in each: a wrong number, a missing exception or a detail that is not in the source. Write down exactly where each one is.
**Open with ten minutes on the tools**: what they can and cannot do, using examples from the team's own work. Leave out the general talk about AI.

**Run the practice in pairs** for fifteen minutes. Give each pair the three summaries and say: "One of these has an error that would embarrass us with a customer. Mark what you would check before sending it, and how you would check it." Then reveal the errors and compare the checks people chose.

**Give the team a two-minute check**: every number, name, date and stated rule gets held against the source. It is the [same test as any claim](t:1.11), which is what the evidence is and compared with what. There is a fuller [routine you use on your own materials](t:7.7).
**Run a second round on live work.** Each person takes something they will send this week and applies the two-minute check while you walk the room.
**State the ownership rule** and have the manager say it too: whoever sends the report owns what is in it.
**Agree where the check sits** in the workflow as [a visible step](t:7.13), using the last ten minutes. Put tool-specific steps in [a job aid you can update](t:5.7).

why.text: **Judgement matters more when AI drafts.** As AI takes over some tasks, employers still ask for human skills such as communication, collaboration and leadership alongside AI skills. Judgement and critical evaluation matter more when a tool can produce plausible work on demand.

**Adverts and surveys show demand for AI skills.** Demand for AI skills shows up in job adverts. PwC's 2025 analysis of close to a billion adverts found that jobs asking for AI skills paid 56% more on average than similar jobs that did not, up from 25% a year earlier. It also reports the skills employers ask for changing 66% faster in the occupations most exposed to AI. An industry consortium found AI skills in 78% of the 50 technology roles it studied across the G7. In a survey commissioned by the UK government and published in January 2026, 97% of respondents named at least one AI skills gap.

**Treat these as signals and not as forecasts.** They come from job adverts and employer surveys, they show links and not causes, and two of the three come from firms that sell AI services or training. In the [school experiment on AI tutors](t:7.2), pupils who leaned on a plain chatbot did worse once it was taken away. That is the habit this training is meant to prevent.

**People catch errors only in familiar material.** The session design is craft. It uses documents the team knows well because people can only catch an error where they have the knowledge to notice it. On unfamiliar material the lesson they take away is that checking is impossible. Checking everything also has a limit. A rough internal note does not need the care a customer report does, so teach people to scale the check to what happens if the content is wrong.

try.text: For a real role, list the tasks AI may take over and the skills that gain value as a result. Sketch a one-hour session for the second list, built round practice like the plan below. Then run the fifteen-minute pairs exercise with two colleagues, giving the instruction aloud once. Good looks like this: they start within a minute, and at least one check they choose is one you had not thought of.

items: **Predictions about jobs are uncertain.** Say so when you quote one.
**Tools change faster than courses.** Teach the checking habit, which lasts, and keep tool-specific steps in [a job aid you can update](t:5.7).
**Fear gets in the way.** Make it safe to ask basic questions: start from the basics for everyone and take questions in pairs or in writing.
**The checking habit fades:** a session will not keep people checking for long. Build the check into the workflow as [a visible step](t:7.13).

topics.title: Plan reskilling around skills, not job titles
topics.theory: Reskilling at scale and skills-based organisations

situation.text: The operations director of a software company says half the roles in customer support will change within three years, and asks you for a reskilling plan by the end of next month. She slides a sheet across the table. It is a list of fourteen job titles.

items: **Ask which work is growing** and which is shrinking, and how sure the client is. Plan for two or three likely changes. Do not stake the plan on one prediction.

**List the skills the work will need** for each growing role, not the job titles. Write six to ten, each as something a person does: "sets up the product for a new customer", not "technical skills". There is more on [mapping roles and skills](t:9.13).
**Find out what skills people have now.** Use work samples, a manager's observation or a short practical task, not a self-rating form. Do this only for the people in the roles you are planning round.
**Find the adjacent moves**: the people who already have most of the skills a growing role needs. Put the skills in a table with a column for the evidence, and the gap shows itself.
**Build a route for each move**, with practice on real work and someone checking it. Say how many weeks it takes, who supervises and what counts as ready.
**Give people paid time to learn**, and a named role to move into at the end. Get both in writing from the sponsor before anything is announced to staff.
**Review the skills list and the routes** once a year, and sooner if one of the predicted changes does not arrive.

why.text: **Most organisations do not know their skills.** Planning around skills lets an organisation move people between roles as work changes. It depends on knowing what skills people have, which most organisations do not.
Forecasts of which jobs will change are uncertain. Plan routes for two or three likely changes and review them.

**Skills needs seem to be moving fast.** There are signs that skills needs are moving quickly. PwC's 2025 analysis of job adverts reports the skills employers ask for changing 66% faster in the occupations most exposed to AI. A 2026 UK survey for the government found that 88% of organisations rely on on-the-job training for AI skills in place of structured programmes. These figures come from job adverts and an employer survey, so read them as signals. The method on this page is craft.

**Job titles hide the overlap between roles.** Two titles in different departments can share most of their skills, and a title tells you nothing about what one person can do. Starting from an adjacent move keeps the new learning small, which makes the route short enough for the client to fund and for the person to finish. The named role matters for a practical reason: [a skill that is not used fades](t:5.17), so a route that ends with no job to do loses what it built.

**Finding out current skills is the cost.** The cost sits in finding out what people can do now. Work samples and observed tasks take time, which is why you do it for a few roles and not the whole organisation. Sometimes there is no adjacent move, and nobody has most of what the growing role needs. Say so plainly. That is a hiring decision or a long retraining, and calling it a route will not make it one.

try.text: For one role likely to change, list its skills and two roles those skills are close to. For the closer of the two, fill in a table like the one below, with the evidence you would accept for each skill. Then explain the move aloud to a colleague in two minutes, as you would to a sponsor, ending with what you need from them.

parts.title: Use AI in your own practice
parts.summary: Briefing a tool, checking what it gives you, sorting feedback, AI in the room, and an honest account of how you used it.

topics.title: Brief an AI tool well

situation.text: You type "write a one-day course on feedback for managers" and get a tidy, generic agenda that could be for anyone.

items: **State the task and your role** in one sentence, and say that you will check and rewrite the output.
**Give the context**: who the learners are, how many, where, for how long, and what they do now.
**Paste the source material**, such as your needs analysis notes. Tell the tool to use only that for facts about the client. [Remove names and anything confidential](t:7.1) first.
**State the objective** as something people will do. Add the constraints: timings, share of practice, room and kit.
**Show the format you want** with one example row or paragraph.
**Ask what it was unsure about**, as a list, and ask it to criticise its own draft as a sceptical trainer would.
**Read the draft against your notes.** Send one correction at a time, saying what was wrong and why.
**Keep the brief.** Next time, change the context and reuse the rest.

why.text: **A general tool knows nothing about your client.** Whatever you leave out, it fills with the most common answer, which is why a thin request returns a generic agenda.

**Brief the tool as you would a colleague.** One vendor's guidance for its own model makes the same points. Be explicit about the output and the constraints. Give the reason behind an instruction. Say what to do in place of what to avoid. Include examples, separate source material from instructions, and ask the model to check its work against your criteria. It offers a test worth borrowing: if a colleague with little context would be confused by your brief, the tool probably will be too.

**The method lasts, the specifics do not.** That guidance is product help from one company. Other tools differ in detail and all of them change. Treat the method as craft that carries across tools, and the specifics as temporary.
**A critique shows where to look first.** Asking for a critique does not make the output right. It gives you a list of places to look first. [The design decisions stay with you](t:7.1).

try.text: Take a real needs analysis with names removed. Write a brief using the example below as a pattern, and run it in a tool your organisation allows. Mark every line of the output that you cannot trace to your notes.

try.title: A worked example: a brief for a session outline
lines: I am a trainer. Help me draft a session outline. I will check and rewrite what you produce.
Context: 12 team leaders in a software company's customer support team, all promoted in the last year. In person, one day, 09:30 to 16:30, one trainer.
The need, from interviews with their manager and four team leaders: they avoid corrective feedback, and when they give it, it is vague.
The manager wants every team leader to give specific feedback in each fortnightly one-to-one.
My notes are pasted below under the heading NEEDS ANALYSIS. Use only those for facts about the team. If something is missing, ask me. Do not fill the gap.
Objective: by the end, each person can give two minutes of corrective feedback on a real case from their own team, naming the behaviour, its effect and the change they want.
Constraints: at least half the day is practice in threes. No input block longer than 15 minutes. Lunch 12:30 to 13:15. Two breaks.
Format: a table with clock time, what happens, who is talking, and the reason for the block. Plain UK English.
One row in the style I want: 10:15. Threes practise case one, observer uses the checklist. Participants talking. Reason: a first attempt before any model answer.
Before you finish, list three weaknesses in the outline as a sceptical trainer would see them, and anything you were unsure about.

**You paste a client document** with names in it. Strip personal and confidential details first, and use only an approved tool.
**You rewrite the whole brief** after each poor answer. Change one thing at a time so you learn what made the difference.
**The tool agrees with every correction.** Agreement is not evidence. Check the new draft as carefully as the first.

quiz.q: What test does the vendor guidance suggest for a brief?
quiz.a: If a colleague with little context would be confused by it, the tool probably will be too.

quiz.q: The tool's outline says the team "struggles with remote working". Your notes say nothing about that. What do you do?
quiz.a: Tell it to remove any statement about the team that is not in the needs analysis and to list what it removed. The tool filled a gap, and an invented fact about a client is the costliest kind of error.

quiz.q: Your first draft comes back generic. You are tempted to start again with a new prompt. What do you do?
quiz.a: Add the missing context or constraint and send one correction. Changing one thing at a time shows you what the tool needed.

topics.title: Check AI output before it reaches a learner

situation.text: An AI tool has drafted a handout with six statistics and four references. It looks finished. The session is tomorrow.

items: **Check the facts first.** Underline every factual claim and check each against a source you open yourself. Delete what you cannot confirm.
**Check the sources next.** Search for every reference by title. Confirm that it exists, that the authors and year are right, and that it says what the draft claims.
**Verify the numbers.** Trace each figure to its original page, with its unit, its date and what it was compared with. Redo any arithmetic.
**Look for bias.** Read the examples and the names. Look at who is shown as the manager, the customer, the expert and the problem. Rewrite anything that leans one way.
**Check the tone.** Read a paragraph aloud. Cut anything you would not say to this group, and anything that claims too much.
**Check the fit.** Hold each item against the objective and remove what does not serve it.
**Sign off.** The [named person who is accountable](t:7.1) records what was checked and the date. For technical or legal content, a subject expert signs as well.

why.text: **AI tools invent references that sound real.** Language tools produce text that sounds right, including references that do not exist. In a 2023 test, 55% of the citations written by one model and 18% of those written by its successor were fabricated, and many of the real ones contained errors. A 2025 experiment with a newer model found that about one in five citations could not be traced to a real source. Fabrication was more common on less familiar topics.

**Errors gather where public material is thin.** These are tests of particular models on particular dates, in academic writing. Tools that search the web may do better or fail in other ways. The figures above do not cover them. What carries over is the pattern. Errors gather where the subject is specialist and public material is thin, which describes most client-specific training content.

**Government guidance also says to test outputs.** The UK government's AI Playbook, written for civil servants, gives the same instruction in general terms. These systems are not guaranteed to be accurate, outputs need a process for testing, and people should validate high-risk decisions that AI has influenced.

**An invented reference does the most damage.** The order of the routine is craft. Facts and sources come first because an invented reference in a handout does most damage to your standing with a client.

why.title: Fabricated citations from a current model
why.found: The researchers asked a widely used model for six literature reviews on mental health topics and checked all 176 citations. Thirty-five (19.9%) could not be traced to a real source. Of the 141 real ones, 64 (45.4%) had at least one error, most often in the DOI. Fabrication ran at 6% for the most familiar topic and 28% to 29% for the two less familiar ones.
why.means: Look up every reference an AI tool gives you, and expect more errors the more specialist the topic.

try.text: Ask a tool for a one-page handout with five references, on a subject you know well. Run the routine and time it. Then tell a colleague aloud what you found, in one minute, without softening it.

items: **A reference has a working link**, so you assume it is sound. Open it and read the summary. Real papers get cited for things they do not say.
**You check the facts you doubt** and skip the ones you like. Check all of them.
**You ask the same tool** to verify its own output. Use it to find sources, then read them yourself.
**The deadline is tomorrow.** Cut the parts you could not verify. A shorter handout is safer than a wrong one.

items.label: Walters and Wilder (2023), Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT. Scientific Reports.
Linardon and colleagues (2025), Influence of topic familiarity and prompt specificity on citation fabrication in mental health research using large language models. JMIR Mental Health.
Government Digital Service (2025), Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government.

quiz.q: In the 2025 experiment, roughly what share of the model's citations could not be traced to a real source?
quiz.a: About one in five.

quiz.q: A handout draft cites a paper with a link that opens. You have ten minutes. What do you do?
quiz.a: Read the paper's summary and check that it supports the claim made. A real paper cited for something it does not say is as damaging as an invented one.

quiz.q: The night before a session you find that two of six statistics cannot be traced. What do you do?
quiz.a: Delete them and adjust the text. You sign for what reaches learners, and a shorter handout does less harm than a wrong figure.

topics.tierReason: Two experiments on fabricated citations and UK government guidance support the need to check. The routine itself is practitioner judgement.

topics.title: Use AI to sort and summarise feedback

situation.text: Three hundred people have answered "What would have made this more useful?" You have an afternoon.

items: **Check that you may.** Free-text comments can identify people. Confirm that the client agrees, that there is a lawful basis for this use, and that the tool is one the client has approved.
**Remove names, job titles, team names** and anything else that points to a person before the comments go anywhere.
**Read fifty comments yourself first** and note the themes you see. This is your check on the tool.
**Ask the tool for themes.** For each, ask for a one-line definition, a count, and three comments quoted exactly with their row numbers.
**Ask separately for two more lists**: comments that fit no theme, and the ten most critical.
**Verify the quotes and counts.** Find every quoted comment in your file. Recount two themes by hand. Compare the tool's themes with your own list.
**Write the summary yourself.** Give counts as approximate, say that a tool sorted the comments, and say how you checked.

why.text: **The tools are quick, the evidence thin.** Sorting comments by hand is slow, and these tools are quick at grouping similar wording. The evidence on how well they do it is recent and thin.

**Two studies found the tools missed things.** In a 2025 study by researchers at a large technology company, AI models judged whether theme summaries of more than 13,000 staff survey comments matched the comments. Agreement with human raters was moderate. The models sometimes passed summaries in which people found gaps in coverage or quotes that did not fit. A small 2026 study compared a chatbot's themes with human coding of answers from 134 people. The themes overlapped well, but the tool counted far fewer answers under one theme because it caught only simple statements. Its author treats the tool as a supplement to human coders.

**Distrust the counts and check the quotes.** So the counts are the weak part, and the quotes need checking against the file. Reading a sample first protects you from accepting a tidy list that missed what mattered.

**Removing names may not make comments anonymous.** On privacy, ICO guidance says you need a lawful basis whenever you process personal data, and that includes using an AI system. Its anonymisation guidance says removing obvious identifiers is not enough if a person can still be singled out. A comment that begins "as the only night manager in my region" identifies its author. There is more on [learner data and privacy under UK law](t:9.24). This is general information, not legal advice.

try.text: Take a set of comments you are allowed to use, or write thirty yourself. Run the steps. Then give a colleague a two-minute spoken summary, and have them ask how you know each count.

try.title: A worked example: a brief for sorting comments
lines: Below are 300 anonymous comments from a course feedback form, one per row, each with a row number.
The question was: What would have made this more useful?
Group them into no more than eight themes. Give each theme a name and a one-line definition.
For each theme, give the number of comments and three comments quoted exactly, with row numbers.
A comment may sit in more than one theme. Say how many do.
List separately any comments that fit no theme. Do not force them into one.
List the ten most critical comments, with row numbers.
Do not summarise, reword or correct the quotes. Do not guess who wrote anything.
Finish by telling me which themes you were least sure about, and why.

**Rare but serious comments vanish** into a theme. Read the unthemed list and the most critical list yourself.
**You paste raw comments** into a personal account. Use the client's approved tool, or sort by hand.
**The summary sounds more positive** than the comments. Compare its tone with your sample of fifty.

items.label: Bedemariam and colleagues (2025), Potential and perils of large language models as judges of unstructured textual data. Preprint.
Bartone (2026), Using AI for rapid and cost-effective identification of core themes in qualitative text data. Survey Practice.

quiz.q: What do you do before giving any comments to an AI tool?
quiz.a: Confirm the client's agreement, a lawful basis and an approved tool, and remove anything that identifies a person.

quiz.q: The tool reports "Pace too fast: 47 comments" with three quotes. You cannot find one of the quotes in your file. What do you do?
quiz.a: Drop that quote, recount the theme by hand and check the other quotes. An invented quote means the count cannot be trusted either.

quiz.q: A client sends 400 raw comments with names attached and asks for themes by tomorrow. Your only tool is a personal chatbot account. What do you do?
quiz.a: Do not paste them in. Ask for the client's approved tool or for the comments with names removed, and if neither is possible, sort a sample by hand and say so.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement, informed by two small studies of AI theme analysis and by ICO guidance.

topics.title: Set a rule for AI in the room

situation.text: Ten minutes into a workshop, one person is typing the exercise into a chatbot, another has a note-taking app recording, and the hands-on demo will not log in.

items: **Ask the client what is allowed** before the day: which AI tools staff may use, and whether sessions may be recorded or transcribed. Put the answer in the joining note.
**State the rule** in the first ten minutes, as part of how the group will work. Say which exercises are done with tools closed and why, and which will use them.
**Ask before anything records.** Say what will be captured, who will see it and when it will be deleted. If anyone says no, nothing records. Offer a written summary in its place.
**Give the reason when tools are closed**, in a sentence: the point is to practise the thinking, and the tool would do it for you.
**Ask people to show what they asked** and what they changed, in exercises that use a tool, so the group can compare.
**Prepare three fall-backs** for a hands-on AI session: a shared demo on your screen, pairs on one working account, and printed prompts with printed outputs to critique.
**Test logins on the client's network** the day before, with a participant's account and not your own.
**Say what was recorded** at the close, if anything, and where it will go.

why.text: **Tool use is a design choice.** This is practitioner judgement. Stating the rule at the start is easier than correcting someone halfway through an exercise, and it treats tool use as a design choice. Some practice only works unaided. In [one experiment on AI tutors](t:7.2), pupils who leaned on a plain chatbot during practice did worse once it was removed.

**Ask aloud before you record anyone.** Recording changes what people are willing to say, and a transcript of a session is personal data about the people in it. Product help for one widely used meeting tool says that all participants are notified when a recording starts, and that depending on where you are you may need everyone's permission before you record them. A notice on a screen is not agreement. Ask first, aloud, and accept a no without fuss. There is more on [the data protection duties](t:9.24).

**Access often fails before content does.** Hands-on sessions often fail on access before they fail on content. That is a common report from trainers, not a finding. Licences have not been assigned, the network blocks the site, or a login needs a phone that is in a locker. A fall-back prepared in advance keeps the learning going while someone fixes it.

try.text: Say the room rule aloud, standing, in under a minute, and record it. Then rehearse the recording request with a colleague who refuses, and practise accepting the no in one sentence.

try.title: Words you can use: the room rule and the recording request
lines: A word about AI tools before we start.
For the first two exercises, please keep them closed. I want you to do the thinking, and the tool would do it for you.
After the break we will use them on purpose. I will ask you to show what you asked and what you changed.
Nothing in this room is being recorded or transcribed.
If you use a note-taking app that records, please switch it off for today. I will send a written summary.
If we lose the tool this afternoon, we carry on in pairs with printed examples. You will not miss the point.
Is everyone happy to work that way?
If you do want a recording: I would like to record the last half hour so I can write up your actions.
Only I will hear it, and I will delete it on Friday.
If anyone would prefer I did not, say so now or tell me at the break, and I will take notes instead.

quiz.q: You ask to record the closing discussion. One person says they would prefer you did not. What do you do?

topics.title: Show how this site was made
topics.theory: Disclosing AI use in your own work

situation.text: Your manager asks how you built a whole learning site so quickly, and whether the content can be trusted.

items: **Say that an AI assistant was used**, plainly, and for what: planning, design and build.
**Say where the content came from**: your own source documents first, then research to fill the gaps.
**Say how it was checked.** The source material was reviewed and fact-checked, and claims that did not hold up were corrected or removed, including claims in your own sources.
**Say what a person signed off**, step by step: the content review, the site plan, the design, then the build.
**Say what is still weak.** Papers were read in summary and not in full, some on a university or index copy. A few topics have had no sources opened, and say so.
**Offer one page as a sample** and invite the listener to check any claim on it against its source.
**Keep the account to one minute** spoken, or one short page.

why.text: **A full account convinces more than silence.** This is practitioner judgement. You should already [tell learners where AI was used](t:7.1). The same applies to a manager or a client looking at your work. An account that names the tool's part, the checks and the limits is more convincing than silence, and more convincing than a claim that everything was verified.

**The limits are the part people remember.** Saying that papers were read in summary tells the reader how far to trust a citation and where to look harder. It also protects you. If someone finds an error, you have already said how the content was checked and where the gaps are.

**Describe only what was done.** Do not add checks that did not happen, and do not give a tally you cannot stand behind. The About page is the public version of this account. The example below is the same content arranged for a conversation.

try.text: Say the account below aloud to a colleague in one minute. Ask them for the first thing a sceptical manager would ask, and answer it without adding anything you did not do.

try.title: A worked example: the account of this site, for a manager
lines: I planned, designed and built this site with an AI assistant. I signed off each step: the content review, the site plan, the design, then the build.
The content started from three sources: a curriculum outline for trainers, a toolkit of methods, mechanics and session recipes, and a report on AI skills and training.
Where those had gaps, they were filled by research.
The source material was reviewed and fact-checked on 17 November 2026.
Claims that did not hold up were corrected or removed. Some of those were in my own sources.
The figures that held up are listed on the numbers page, each with its source.
Every practice carries an evidence rating, so you can see what rests on studies and what is craft.
The limits: papers were read in summary, not in full. Some were read on a university or index copy because the publisher's page would not open.
Nearly every topic has had its sources opened. The few that have not say so on the page.
Pick any claim and I will show you the source it rests on.

items: **You say "fact-checked"** and are asked what that means. Have the answer ready: sources opened and read in summary.
**You overstate your own part**, or the tool's. Say who did what.
**The account goes out of date** as the site changes. Date it, and review it when the content changes.
**You are asked how many claims** were corrected. If you did not count, say so.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: How were the papers behind this site read?
quiz.a: In summary, not in full, and some on a university or index copy.

quiz.q: A manager asks, "So the AI wrote it and you checked it?" What do you say?
quiz.a: Give the actual split: an AI assistant was used to plan, design and build, the source material was fact-checked, and you signed off each step. Then name the limits before you are asked.

quiz.q: A colleague finds a claim on the site that the cited paper does not support. What do you do?
quiz.a: Thank them, correct or remove the claim, and note the change. The account already says papers were read in summary, so the error is the kind you warned of.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement and on what this site's About page states.

parts.title: AI for learners at work
parts.summary: AI practice partners, assistants that answer the question during work, and the risk of people leaning on them too far.

topics.title: Use AI as a practice partner

situation.text: A sales director wants every seller to practise the new pricing conversation before launch. There are 200 sellers, six managers and two weeks.

items: **Teach the model of a good conversation** first, in ten minutes, with one worked example. Then send people to practise. This is the [show, practise and feedback pattern](t:2.34).
**Write the scenario** from the client's real work: the customer, the objection, the product. Give the AI partner a brief with a manner and a level of difficulty.
**Give people a rubric** of three or four behaviours before they start, so they know what good looks like.
**Limit feedback to two points** after each attempt: one thing to keep and one to change.
**Ask for a second attempt** on a different scenario. Getting better at the same scenario shows little.
**Bring a person in.** A peer or manager hears one conversation live, or reads one transcript, and debriefs for ten minutes.
**Judge the result outside the simulator**, with [an observed call or a manager's report](t:6.4).

why.text: **The controlled evidence is new and small.** In a 2026 experiment, 145 managers in the United States practised a difficult conversation with a text-based AI partner. They were randomly given practice only, practice with structured feedback, or both together with a short primer on a conversation model. Confidence rose, and scores improved from the first session to the second. On a new scenario that nobody had practised, the group with the primer and the feedback did better than the group that only practised.

**The paper is plain about its limits.** The conversations were typed. The scores came from an AI judge inside the same system. Nobody checked whether anything changed at work, or lasted. Confidence is also [the easiest thing to raise](t:6.3).

**AI feedback worked best through a manager.** Two other sources help with design. In interviews, 17 managers who tried a role-play prototype wanted scenarios from their own workplace and control over how hard the partner was. Many saw it as an addition to a human coach. A set of field experiments with sales agents at two financial technology firms looked at AI feedback on their customer conversations, which is coaching on real work and not role-play. Middle-ranked agents gained most. The lowest-ranked were swamped by the amount of feedback and did better when it was cut back, and the highest-ranked resisted it. Feedback from the AI passed on by a human manager beat either alone.
None of these studies shows an AI practice partner improving real sales results.

why.title: Practising difficult conversations with an AI partner
why.found: Managers were randomly assigned to practice only, practice with feedback, or a full version with a teaching primer. Confidence and scores rose after practice. On an unpractised scenario, the full version outperformed practice alone. Scoring was inside the text simulation, and lasting change at work was not tested.
why.means: Teach the model before the practice, add feedback, and test on a fresh scenario. Do not treat a simulator score as proof of skill at work.

quiz.q: In the 2026 experiment, which group did best on the scenario nobody had practised?
quiz.a: The group that had a short teaching primer and structured feedback as well as practice.

quiz.q: A vendor's dashboard shows your sellers' role-play scores up by a third in two weeks. The sales director asks if the training worked. What do you say?
quiz.a: That the scores show practice inside the tool, judged by the tool. You will know more when managers have observed real calls against the same rubric.

quiz.q: Your weakest sellers get a full page of AI feedback after each attempt and their scores are flat. What do you change?
quiz.a: Cut the feedback to one thing to keep and one to change. In the sales field experiments, the lowest-ranked agents were swamped by volume and did better with less.

topics.tierReason: One randomised experiment with managers, one interview study and one set of sales field experiments. None measured results at work from AI role-play.

topics.title: Design for AI in the flow of work
topics.theory: AI assistants and what is left to train

situation.text: A support team gets an AI assistant that suggests replies. The head of support asks whether the three-week product course for new starters is still needed.

items: **Pick one real workflow**, such as answering a billing query. Map its steps with someone who does the job.
**Mark who does each step**: the assistant does it, the assistant drafts and a person checks, or a person does it alone.
**Move content out of the course** for every step the assistant now answers, and into the tool or [a job aid](t:5.7).
**List what the person must still do.** It is usually judging whether the answer fits this case, checking it against a source, and deciding when to stop and ask someone.
**Train those with real cases**: good answers, wrong answers, and answers that are right in general and wrong for this customer.
**Teach what good looks like.** Show three strong replies and have people say what makes them strong, before they see any AI drafts.
**Redesign the work round the tool**, then train people on the redesigned work. Keep [a short unaided check](t:6.5) for new starters.

why.text: **An assistant lifted novices the most.** Two field studies show what an assistant changes. Among 5,179 customer support agents given an AI assistant in a staggered roll-out, issues resolved per hour rose by 14% on average and by 34% for novice and lower-skilled agents, with little change for the most experienced. The authors offer suggestive evidence that the tool spreads the habits of abler agents to newer ones. That supports cutting some product teaching for new starters, because the tool now carries it.

**Outside the tool's ability, people did worse.** The second study is the warning. In an experiment with 758 consultants, those using an AI model did more work, and better work, on tasks within its ability. On one task chosen to lie outside it, they were 19 percentage points less likely to reach the right answer than consultants working without it. The tool does not announce which kind of task it is facing.

**Train the part the tool cannot do.** What remains to train, then, is the part the tool cannot do for you: recognising a good answer, checking, and knowing where the tool's ability ends in your own work. That is a reading of the two studies and not a finding. Neither tested a training design.

**An assistant can be confidently wrong.** [A job aid is the answer](t:5.7) when people need help in the middle of a task. An assistant is a job aid that talks, and it can be confidently wrong. There is more on [the checking practice](t:7.4).
