quiz.q: In the customer support study, who gained most from the AI assistant?
quiz.a: Novice and lower-skilled agents, whose output rose by about a third.

quiz.q: An assistant now answers product questions for new support staff. The client wants to drop the product course entirely. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Cut the content the tool carries and use the time for judgement: real cases where the suggested answer is wrong or does not fit the customer. Keep a short unaided check so you know new starters can tell good from bad.

quiz.q: A team's AI drafts are usually right, so people have stopped reading them closely. One task type sits outside what the tool does well. What do you do?
quiz.a: Name that task type, show cases from it, and make the check a visible step for it. In the consultants' experiment, people using AI did worse than those without it on exactly that kind of task.

topics.tierReason: Two field studies of AI assistants at work support the reasoning. The training design itself was not tested in them.

topics.title: Guard against over-reliance

situation.text: Six months after an AI assistant arrived, a team leader notices that nobody questions its drafts any more. Two experienced people say they have forgotten how to do the task by hand.

items: **Decide which tasks to keep unaided**: the ones people must still be able to do without the tool. Keep the list short and write the reason beside each.
**Have people attempt first** on those tasks, and use the assistant second, while they are learning.
**Run an unaided check at intervals**, such as one task a quarter done without the tool. Judge skill by that.
**Build checking into the workflow** as a visible step: a field that says what was checked and against which source. Do not rely on a reminder to be careful.
**Give people time to check.** Checking is the first thing to go when several tasks compete.
**Plant a known error now and then** in practice material. Review it as a group, without blame.
**Ask people to rate their confidence** in themselves on the task and in the tool. Low in the first with high in the second is the pairing to watch.

why.text: **Instructions do not prevent automation bias.** A 2010 review of studies of people working with automated systems describes two linked problems. Complacency is monitoring the system too little, and it is most likely when people are handling several tasks at once. Automation bias is leaning on a decision aid, so that people miss problems the aid did not flag or act on advice that is wrong. The review reports that both affect experts as well as novices, and that automation bias is not prevented by training or instructions. That finding is the reason the steps above change the workflow and do not stop at a warning.

**Leaning on AI may weaken unaided work.** Three recent studies point the same way for AI tools. In the [school experiment on AI tutors](t:7.2), pupils who used a plain chatbot in practice scored lower once it was taken away. In a survey of 319 knowledge workers, higher confidence in the AI tool went with less critical thinking, and higher confidence in oneself went with more. In an observational study at four endoscopy centres in Poland, experienced clinicians' detection rate in procedures done without AI was lower after AI assistance had been introduced than before. The authors caution that other factors may explain it.

**None of this was tested in offices.** None of these is an experiment on adults in ordinary office work, and the survey rests on self-report. The steps are craft and were not tested. There is more on [teaching people to check](t:7.4).

why.title: Complacency and bias in human use of automation
why.found: This review treats complacency and automation bias as overlapping effects with attention at the centre. Complacency appears when manual tasks compete with watching the automation. Automation bias produces errors of omission and commission when a decision aid is imperfect. Both are found in novices and experts. Complacency is not overcome by simple practice.
why.means: Do not expect a warning to stop people leaning on an AI tool. Make checking a required, visible step with time allowed.

try.text: Choose one task your learners now do with an assistant. Write the unaided check for it. Then brief it aloud to a colleague as you would to a team, explaining why it is there, in under a minute.

items: **You answer with a warning slide.** The review found that instructions do not prevent automation bias. Change the workflow.
**Unaided checks feel like punishment.** Explain the reason, keep them short and keep the results out of performance ratings.
**Planted errors turn into a trap.** Tell people in advance that drills happen.
**You keep every manual skill alive** out of caution. Keep only those that matter when the tool is wrong or absent.

quiz.q: According to the 2010 review, does training or instruction prevent automation bias?
quiz.a: No. The review reports that it is not prevented by training or instructions, and that experts are affected as well as novices.

quiz.q: A manager wants to deal with over-reliance by adding a slide that says "Always check the AI's answer". What do you propose?
quiz.a: A change to the workflow: a required field recording what was checked, and time allowed for it. The review found instructions do not prevent the bias.

quiz.q: An experienced team says the unaided quarterly task is insulting. What do you do?
quiz.a: Explain that experts are affected too, keep the task short and keep results out of ratings. Then ask them which tasks matter most when the tool is wrong, and check those.

topics.tierReason: A review of automation research and three recent studies of AI tools support the risk. The design responses are practitioner judgement and were not tested.

parts.title: AI programmes for clients
parts.summary: Designing an AI literacy and adoption programme for a client's workforce, and answering the client's own questions about how you use AI.

topics.title: Design an AI literacy and adoption programme
topics.theory: AI literacy by role, safe use first, practice on real tasks, and measuring use

situation.text: A software company of 800 people bought an AI assistant for everyone six months ago. About a third use it each week. Security has found customer data pasted into a free tool, and the chief operating officer asks you for "AI training for everyone by spring".

items: **Start with what is approved.** Before you design, get three things from the client in writing: the list of approved tools, [the data rules](t:7.3) and the name of the person who owns them. If the rules do not exist, writing them is the client's first job.
**Sort the workforce** by what each group needs. Plan four strands: everyone, working teams, managers and senior leaders. Specialists who build AI systems are outside this programme.

**Run the safe-use session first**, for everyone, in under an hour. Cover which tools are approved, what must never go into them, how to [check an answer before using it](t:7.7) and who to ask. Record who completed it on the client's platform. Where the client operates in the EU, that record supports [the AI literacy duty](t:7.3).

**Choose use cases with each team.** With the manager and two people who do the job, pick two or three real tasks where the tool might help. There is a way to [map a workflow](t:7.12) and decide what the person still does.

**Run hands-on sessions on those tasks**, in the approved tool, with the team's own material. Allow 90 minutes for up to twelve people. Everyone leaves with [a saved prompt](t:7.6) and one output they have checked. There is more on [the rule for tools in the room](t:7.9). Build checking into every practice. Each exercise includes [one answer with a planted error](t:7.13), and people say what they would verify and how.

**Brief managers before their teams.** In 60 minutes cover what is allowed, what good use looks like in their team, and two questions to ask in one-to-ones. Ask them not to treat a usage count as a measure of a person's performance. There is more on [the manager's job around training](t:2.4).
**Recruit one volunteer in each team** to run a 30-minute clinic every month and keep a shared library of prompts that work.

**Measure use and quality separately.** For use, take weekly active users by team from the tool's own data. For quality, [score a sample of real work](t:6.4) against a short rubric before and after. Count reported incidents. If you collect self-reported time saved, label it as self-report. Name an owner on the client's side who reviews the content every quarter and whenever the tool changes.

why.text: **The design here is untested judgement.** The shape and timings here are practitioner judgement. No study opened for this topic tests a twelve-week design against another.

**Sorting people by need follows a UK framework.** The AI Skills for Business Competency Framework was developed by The Alan Turing Institute with Innovate UK's BridgeAI programme and is supported by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Version 3 is dated March 2026. The government's announcement of the draft described four groups: AI citizens, AI workers whose jobs are outside data and AI, AI professionals and AI leaders. The four strands above are this site's adaptation of that idea for one company.

**An OECD brief backs general literacy first.** An OECD policy brief from April 2025 supports putting general literacy first. It reports that about one in three job vacancies is in an occupation highly exposed to AI and that only about 1% of those ask for specialised AI skills. It concludes that most exposed workers need a general understanding.

why.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot experiment: cross-government findings report
why.found: About 20,000 UK civil servants had the tool for three months in late 2024. Users reported saving 26 minutes a day on average. That figure is self-reported, and the trial could not establish how the time was used. The report calls training essential to getting the benefits.
why.means: Usage data and self-reported time are worth collecting and are not proof of better work. Pair them with a check on the quality of real outputs, and plan training and support as part of the rollout.

try.text: Choose one team you know. Write the two or three tasks you would pick for its hands-on session, and for one of them write the planted error. Then run the first ten minutes of the safe-use session aloud to a colleague, with no slides.

quiz.q: What must the client supply before you design an AI literacy programme?
quiz.a: The list of approved tools, the data rules and the name of the person who owns them.

quiz.q: At week 12, weekly active use has risen from a third of staff to two thirds, and the sponsor wants to report that the programme "worked". What do you say?
quiz.a: Report the rise in use as a rise in use, and put the scored work sample beside it. Usage shows that people open the tool. Only the quality check says anything about the work, and without a comparison it cannot prove the cause.

quiz.q: A sales manager asks for a list of which of her sellers have not used the assistant this month. What do you do?
quiz.a: Explain that usage is reported by team, as agreed before launch, and offer her the team figure with two questions to ask in one-to-ones. Named usage lists turn a learning measure into surveillance and tell her nothing about the quality of anyone's work.

topics.title: Answer a client's questions about your own AI use
topics.theory: AI in supplier onboarding, security reviews and contracts

situation.text: The security questionnaire from a software client has a new section. "Do you or your subcontractors use generative AI tools in delivering services? List the tools, the data entered, where it is stored and how long it is kept." Your honest answer today would be "several, it depends, and I am not sure".

items: **List every AI tool you use** for client work. Include features inside ordinary software, such as meeting transcription, slide design helpers and image generators. For each one note whether it is a personal or a business account and what you use it for.

**Read the vendor's current data terms** for each tool, and write down three facts with the date you read them: whether what you enter is used to train models, where it is stored and how long it is kept. If you cannot find an answer, do not use that tool with client material.

**Set your data rule in three classes.** Public material may go into any tool on your list. Client confidential material goes only into tools the client has approved in writing, or into the client's own tools. Personal data about learners does not go in at all unless the client has approved it and there is a lawful basis. There is more on [learner data and privacy under UK law](t:9.24) and on [using AI on free-text comments](t:7.8).
**Write down who reviews.** A named person checks every AI-assisted item before it reaches the client or a learner, using [the method for checking AI output](t:7.7).
**Decide what you disclose and where.** Say in the proposal or statement of work which kinds of task AI assists. Offer a line on materials if the client wants one.

**Read the contract before you sign**, looking for [AI and ownership clauses](t:9.9). Clients commonly ask that their material stays out of unapproved tools, that AI-generated content is disclosed, and that you stand behind the deliverables as yours to hand over. Some ban AI-made images or voices. Ownership of AI-assisted material is a legal question this page does not answer. Tell the client where AI was used, keep your working files and take advice.

**Put it on one page**, date it, and keep it in [your onboarding folder with your policies](t:9.35). Review it every quarter and whenever you add a tool. [Bind your associates](t:9.20) to the same page. The questionnaire asks about subcontractors, and their habits are your answer.
**Answer any question about AI use truthfully** in a tender, including whether AI helped to write the bid.

why.text: **This rests on judgement and one source.** This is practitioner judgement. One official source shows what public buyers ask. Private clients write their own questions. This is general information, not legal advice.

**Your tools become part of the client's risk.** A large client asks these questions because your tools become part of its risk. If a designer pastes a product roadmap into a consumer chatbot, the client's confidential information has left its control through a supplier. Security teams therefore want the same facts from you that they demand of their own staff: which tools, what goes in, where it sits and who checks the output. A vague answer stalls the purchase order.

**Government suppliers may use AI in bids.** In UK central government the position is published. Procurement Policy Note 017, which applies to central departments, their executive agencies and non-departmental public bodies for procurements begun on or after 24 February 2025, says that suppliers are not prohibited from using AI to prepare bids. It gives buyers example disclosure questions. These ask whether AI tools were used in the tender and whether the output was checked for accuracy, and whether AI is part of the service to be supplied. The note marks those questions as for information only and not scored, though a buyer may add scored AI questions of its own if the tender documents say so. It also asks buyers to put controls in place so that confidential authority information is not used to train AI systems.

**Disclosure convinces more than silence.** The [reasoning on disclosure](t:7.10) is that an account that names the tool's part, the checks and the limits is more convincing than silence. Describe only what you do.

quiz.a: Whether what you enter is used to train models, where it is stored and how long it is kept, each with the date you read the vendor's page.

quiz.q: A client's onboarding form asks, "Do you use generative AI in delivering services?" You use an assistant for first drafts and nothing else. A colleague suggests ticking "no" to avoid delay. What do you do?
quiz.a: Tick yes and attach your one-page statement and tool register. A false answer can breach the contract, and a short, specific disclosure usually passes a security review faster than a follow-up investigation would.

quiz.q: Halfway through a project you realise an associate has pasted the client's draft pricing into a free chatbot. What do you do?
quiz.a: Tell the client's named contact within a working day, say what was entered and into which tool, and say what you have changed to prevent it. Then stop the associate using that tool and check your contract. Hiding it turns a mistake into a breach of trust.

topics.title: Promise the conditions, never the transformation

situation.text: You are finishing the proposal for a two-day leadership offsite for a software company's twelve team leads. The HR director has edited your headline. It now promises "a transformation of our management team", and the sponsor wants to sign this week.

items: **Start from the business result** the client is buying, such as a decision made or a skill people can use. Write it as one sentence. There is more on [how to agree it with the client](t:9.6).
**List the conditions you can control** and design those: time away from daily work, real cases from the business, practice with feedback, and a follow-up date.
**Write the promise in two parts**, the conditions you will provide and the work the group will finish. Put both in the proposal in plain words.
**Search the proposal and the marketing** for "transform", "life-changing" and any guarantee about how people will change. Take them out. There is more on [claims you can stand behind](t:9.7).
**Add a short list** headed "How you will know we delivered": the outputs the group produces, the practice rounds each person completes, and the date of the follow-up.
**Have your answer ready** for when the client asks for the big word back. The script below gives one.

**Report change as what participants said.** If they say afterwards that the event changed them, report it that way, next to the business result. There is more on what the evidence says [a retreat can and cannot do](t:8.8).

why.text: **Transformative learning means a deep shift.** One account, Jack Mezirow's, describes transformative learning as a deep shift in how someone makes sense of their experience, worked through by reflection.
**You cannot honestly promise this change.** People do report change of this kind. It is hard to measure, and no method produces it on demand, so you cannot honestly promise it to a client.

**The research behind the idea is mostly qualitative.** A 2007 review of 40 published studies found that interviews and case studies still dominated, with work on reflection, relationships and context. That is useful description. It is not proof that a programme can cause the change.

why.title: A review of research on transformative learning
why.found: The review covered 40 peer-reviewed studies published after the previous review in 1998. Research had moved towards how to encourage transformative learning, and qualitative designs still dominated.
why.means: Describe transformation as something some people report, and do not present it as a measured result of your programme.

why.text: **A measurable promise earns the second booking.** The rest is commercial craft. A promise you cannot measure is a promise you cannot show you kept. When the sponsor's budget is questioned six months later, "they were transformed" gives them nothing to point to. Conditions and finished work can be listed, counted and checked, which is what earns the second booking.

**A smaller promise may lose the sale.** There is a cost. A competitor's brochure will sound bigger than yours, and some buyers want the big word. You may lose that sale. The one place the word can appear is in a participant's own mouth: if someone says the event changed how they see their job and [agrees to be quoted](t:9.25), it is their report and you present it as that.

try.text: Take a real proposal or brochure, yours or someone else's. Underline every outcome it promises. Mark each one S for a skill or decision you could observe at work, or C for a change in how someone sees themselves. Rewrite every C as a condition you will provide. Then say your reply to the sponsor aloud, twice, until it sounds like you and takes under thirty seconds.

try.title: Words you can use: when the client wants the headline back
lines: "I understand why you want that line. It sounds like what you are hoping for."
"I can't promise that people will change, and nobody honestly can. Some may. I have no way to make it happen or to prove it did."
"What I can promise is on this page: the two days, the feedback, the practice and the plan. You will be able to see every one of them."
"If your managers tell you afterwards that it changed something for them, that will mean more coming from them than from my brochure."

items: **Clients like big promises**, and competitors make them. Offer a smaller promise you can show you kept: the work done, the practice completed, the follow-up held.
**Tears or a tense session** do not show that anything useful happened. Judge the event by what people do at work afterwards.
**Ordinary learning** is most of what a business needs from an offsite: a skill practised, a plan agreed. Do not treat that as second best.
**Personal change is not the product.** A business retreat is bought for a business result. Name that result and the conditions you will provide. Personal change may happen for some people.
**The big word creeps back in** through the invitation or the sponsor's opening speech. Send the sponsor two sentences they can use, and read the invitation before it goes out.

items.label: Taylor (2007), An update of transformative learning theory: a critical review of the empirical research (1999-2005). International Journal of Lifelong Education, 26(2).
Mezirow (1991), Transformative Dimensions of Adult Learning.

quiz.q: What does the 2007 review say about the research on transformative learning?
quiz.a: It is mostly qualitative: interviews and case studies. It describes change that people report and does not prove that a programme causes it.

quiz.q: A client's marketing lead rewrites your proposal headline as "Three days that will transform your managers". What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask for it to be changed back. Offer a line that names the conditions and the work, for example time away, feedback from peers and a plan tested in the first week back. Explain that no method produces deep change on demand.

quiz.q: After an offsite, the sponsor says two managers "seem like different people" and wants that quoted in your case study as the result. How do you report it?
quiz.a: As something two people reported, next to the business result you agreed at the start. Do not present it as an outcome the programme delivers.

topics.tierReason: Transformative learning is a theory studied mostly through qualitative research, and no checked source tests a method that produces it, so promising only the conditions is sound professional practice, not a tested technique.

topics.title: Design for absorption, not intensity

situation.text: The draft agenda for a 60-person sales kick-off is built around a dramatic high point: a raft race on the second afternoon, then an awards night. The new pitch, which is the reason the company is paying for two days away, has 45 minutes after lunch on day one.

items: **Give each activity one goal** the group can state in a sentence, for example "each pair delivers the new pitch in three minutes". If you cannot write the sentence, the activity is not ready.
**Build in feedback people get straight away:** a partner with a checklist, a facilitator at the table, or a result they can see for themselves.

**Offer two or three levels of difficulty** for the task so that new starters and old hands are both stretched. Describe each level by the task, such as a friendly customer, a customer with one objection and a customer who prefers a competitor. Let people choose their level.
**Give the block unbroken time.** As a craft rule, plan 60 to 90 minutes with phones away, no announcements and nobody pulled out for a call.
**Plan the high point of the event** as the moment people use the skill or make the decision the event exists for. There is more on [planning a peak and an ending](t:2.18).
**Debrief straight after**, using the steps for [debriefing an activity](t:4.28), and end the block with each person naming one thing they will change in real work.

**Test every other "big moment"** on the agenda with one question: what is it for. If nobody can link it to the business result, give the time to practice. There is more on [how to build the full timetable](t:8.10).

why.text: **You can invite flow, not guarantee it.** Flow is the name given to an absorbed state that people report when challenge and skill are balanced. You can set up conditions that make it more likely. You cannot guarantee it.
**Intensity does not prove learning.** People remember intense moments. That does not mean they learned anything they can use, so be wary of anyone selling "peak states".

**Challenge matched to skill is linked to flow.** A meta-analysis of 28 studies found a moderate link between the balance of challenge and skill and reported flow. Clear goals and a sense of control were linked to it as well. The link was weaker in work and education settings. Treat the balance as a helpful condition, not a switch.

why.title: Challenge-skill balance and flow: a meta-analysis
why.found: Across 28 studies, the balance of challenge and skill had a moderate relationship with flow. The relationship was weaker in work and education settings, and clear goals and a sense of control were also linked to flow.
why.means: Match the challenge to each person's skill and set clear goals, and do not promise that flow will follow.

why.text: **Levels balance challenge in a mixed room.** The steps above turn those conditions into a design, and that part is craft. Levels are how you balance challenge and skill in a mixed room, because one fixed task is too easy for some people and too hard for others. Letting people choose the level gives them some control. The one-sentence goal and the feedback at the table are the other conditions the studies name.

**A raft race looks better than practice.** Intensity is tempting for a plain reason. A raft race photographs well and a sponsor can see it happening, while a room of pairs working hard looks like nothing much from the door. Levels also cost you preparation, since you write three briefs where you used to write one. A shared, silly, high-energy moment still has a place on a retreat. Its job is play, which has [its own place on a retreat](t:8.6), and it should be planned and described as that.

try.text: Take one ninety-minute block from an offsite you know. Write the goal in one sentence, say where the feedback comes from, and set two levels of difficulty. Then say what the block has to do with the business result. Finish by giving the set-up instruction for the block aloud, standing, in under a minute. There is more on [giving instructions people can follow](t:4.24).

items: **Pushing for intensity** can hurt people. Physical challenges cause injuries, and pressure in front of colleagues causes distress. There is more on [the duty-of-care plan you need](t:8.5).
**A challenge too great for some** excludes them. Offer levels, and make the lowest level a respectable choice by having a senior person take it first.
**Without a debrief** people take home an anecdote and nothing to use. Debrief straight after, using the steps for [debriefing an activity](t:4.28).
**A high point without a purpose:** ask what it is for. If nobody can link it to the business result, give the time to practice.
**Everyone picks the easy level** to play safe. Say at the start that round two is a chance to move up, and keep scores and rankings out of it.

items.label: Fong, Zaleski and Leach (2015), The challenge-skill balance and antecedents of flow: a meta-analytic investigation. The Journal of Positive Psychology.
Csikszentmihalyi (1990, Harper Perennial edition 2008), Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience.

quiz.q: In the meta-analysis of 28 studies, was the link between challenge-skill balance and flow stronger or weaker in work and education settings?
quiz.a: Weaker. Treat the balance as a helpful condition. It does not guarantee anything.

quiz.q: A sponsor wants the second afternoon of the kick-off given to a raft race "to create a peak moment". What do you ask, and what do you offer?
quiz.a: Ask what the race is for and how it links to the business result. If nobody can say, offer a high point built on the real task, such as a pitch round with levels and feedback, and move the race to optional free time or drop it.

quiz.q: In a negotiation exercise the experienced account managers finish in ten minutes and look bored, while the new starters are lost. What do you change for the next round?
quiz.a: Run it at two or three levels of difficulty and let people choose. Give each level a clear goal and feedback straight after, so everyone is working at the edge of what they can do.

topics.tierReason: A meta-analysis links the balance of challenge and skill to flow, but the link is moderate, correlational and weaker in work and education settings, and nothing read shows that flow in a retreat leads to lasting learning.

topics.title: Build trust before you ask for openness

situation.text: On the first evening of a leadership offsite you ask people to share something personal. Some do. Several shut down, and one asks you afterwards, by the coffee, whether HR will hear what was said.

items: **Agree in writing what you will report** about individuals and what you will not, with the sponsor and before the event. Tell participants the rule in the first ten minutes, using words like those in the script below.
**Agree ground rules and confidentiality** at the start. There is a [four-minute way to do it](t:4.23).
**Go first, and keep it small** and about work: a mistake you made in a session, not a story from your private life. Thirty seconds is enough. The group will copy your depth and your length.
**Offer three questions** at different levels of depth, all about work, and let people choose one. Let them choose how much to share, and to pass without giving a reason.
**Start in pairs.** Move to fours or the whole room only on the second day, and only if the pairs went well.
**Keep your own voice and pace slow** and even. A room takes its cue from the facilitator.
**Watch for people who go quiet**, leave the room or stop joining in after a sharing exercise. Speak to them in private at the next break.

why.text: **People take risks when the group feels safe.** People take risks in a group more readily when they believe it is safe to do so. Researchers call that shared belief psychological safety, and studies of work teams link it to learning behaviour. There is more on [psychological safety and the error climate](t:1.17). The research is on teams at work, not on retreats.

why.title: Psychological safety in 51 work teams
why.found: In a field study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company, teams that shared a belief that it was safe to take interpersonal risks showed more learning behaviour. Learning behaviour in turn was linked to team performance.
why.means: Build safety first with ground rules, modest disclosure from you and a free choice to pass, and remember the evidence comes from work teams.

why.text: **A settling exercise needs no nervous-system claims.** Some retreat facilitators open with breathing or grounding exercises and explain them with claims about the nervous system. A business group does not need the claims. If you use an exercise like this, make it optional and say only that it helps people settle. A facilitator who is unhurried does most of that job anyway.

**State the reporting rule before any exercise.** What is particular to a business retreat is who is paying, and this part is craft. Everyone in the room is working out what will get back to their manager. Until that is answered out loud, people give safe answers or none. So the reporting rule comes before any exercise, and it has to be one the sponsor has already agreed, because a promise you break later costs more than no promise.

**Trust comes from what people see happen.** Order matters because trust is built by what people see happen. They watch you share something modest and nothing bad follows. They watch a colleague pass and nobody comments. The cost is time, since the first evening produces less than a sponsor might hope. A team that already works well together can move faster, but the questions still stay on the work.

try.text: Write the first thirty minutes of an offsite for a team you know: the confidentiality rule, what you will share first, and three questions at different levels of depth, all about work. Say the opening aloud and time it. Record it if you can, and listen for any line that sounds like pressure.

try.title: Words you can use: what goes back to the employer
lines: "Before we start, here is what your employer will and will not hear from me."
"I will send a short summary of what the group worked on and what you decided together."
"I will not report what any one of you said, or how any one of you got on in the practice."
"The exception is safety. If I think someone is at risk of harm, I will tell Jo, your host, and I will tell you first."
"What you say to each other stays in this room in the same way. Is everyone willing to work on that basis?"

items: **Pressure to share** is a breach of care. If a round is going past someone who has not spoken, move on without comment.
Confidentiality has limits. Say what they are.

**You are not a therapist.** If someone discloses something serious, listen, do not advise, and follow the steps for [when someone is upset](t:4.42). There is more on [your professional limits](t:4.16).

**Sponsors ask who struggled** or who was negative, because the employer is paying. Report themes and group progress. Do not report what a named person said or how they performed unless that was agreed beforehand and participants were told at the start. If a sponsor asks later, hold the rule: "We agreed I would report on the group. I can tell you what the group found hard." There is more on [the data protection side](t:9.24).

**Openness on a business retreat** means saying what is true about the work: a disagreement, a mistake, what is not working in the team. It does not mean childhood, health or home life. Set every sharing question at that level.

items.label: Edmondson (1999), Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. Administrative Science Quarterly, 44(2).
Frazier, Fainshmidt, Klinger, Pezeshkan and Vracheva (2017), Psychological safety: a meta-analytic review and extension. Personnel Psychology, 70.

quiz.q: Where does the main evidence on psychological safety come from?
quiz.a: From studies of teams at work, such as Edmondson's study of 51 teams in a manufacturing company. It does not come from retreats.

quiz.q: Two weeks after a leadership offsite the sponsor phones and asks which of the managers "struggled". What do you say?
quiz.a: Hold the rule agreed before the event: "We agreed I would report on the group. I can tell you what the group found hard." Give themes and group progress, with no names.

quiz.q: The client asks you to open the first evening with a round in which each person shares a personal challenge "to break down barriers". What do you propose?
quiz.a: A lighter opening. Agree confidentiality and its limits, share one small work mistake yourself, then let people pick from three questions about work, talk in pairs and pass if they wish. Trust comes first, and pressure to share is a breach of care.

topics.tierReason: Psychological safety is linked to learning behaviour in a field study and a large meta-analysis, but that research is on teams at work and is largely correlational, and the specific opening steps for a retreat have not been tested in the sources read.

topics.title: Take people out of their routine, and plan the return

situation.text: A leadership team of fourteen ends its two-day offsite with three agreed priorities and a round of applause. The offsite is a success at the venue. On Monday each of them opens a full inbox, and three weeks later the sponsor asks what happened to the priorities. Nobody has an answer.

items: **Mark the start clearly.** Phones go away, the sponsor says in two minutes why the group is here, and the first task begins within fifteen minutes of sitting down.
**Take people out of their usual setting** and loosen their usual roles: mixed groups, first names, and [senior people briefed beforehand to speak last](t:4.38).
**Use the setting once on purpose.** If the venue allows, put one paired conversation outdoors: 20 to 30 minutes, a written question to answer, and a time to be back.
**Mark the end as well.** Each person says one thing they will do, and the group finishes together before anyone leaves for a train. Check departure times and set the close before the earliest one.
**Give fifteen minutes to the return** before the close. Each person writes what they take back, who they will tell and what they will do in the first week.

**Book the follow-up meeting in calendars** while everyone is still in the room, and send line managers a note that day saying what to ask about on the first day back. There is a [full plan for the return](t:8.17), with the note to managers.

why.text: **The threshold idea is borrowed, not proven.** Anthropologists use the idea of a threshold, or liminal, stage for the in-between period in a rite of passage, when people have left one role and not yet taken up the next. Retreat designers borrow the idea when they take people out of their normal setting. Treat it as a design idea, not a proven mechanism of change.
**The return is the part most often neglected.** With no plan for it, people go back to the same desk and the same habits, and little of the work is used.

**Time outdoors has some support, from small studies.** In one, 36 city adults had lower stress hormone levels after spending time in nature, with 20 to 30 minutes the most efficient dose. In another, hikers tested about four days into a wilderness trip scored around half as much again on a creative reasoning test as hikers tested before setting off. Neither study could separate nature from rest, time off screens or who chose to take part.

**A marked start tells people the rules.** The practical reasoning is craft. A marked start tells people which rules apply for the next two days: who speaks first, whether the phone matters, whether rank counts. Without it they bring the office with them and behave as they do in the Monday meeting. A marked end does the opposite job. It hands people back to their normal roles with something decided, so the last thing they remember is a commitment and not a queue for taxis.

**Nobody owns the week after checkout.** The return gets neglected for a dull reason. The budget and the facilitator's contract usually end at checkout, so nobody owns the week after. Raise it when you scope the work. There is also a limit to stepping out of routine. For a decision that needs data, systems or people who are back at the office, distance gets in the way, and there is more on [whether to take people away at all](t:8.7).

try.text: For an offsite you know, write three lines: how it starts in the first fifteen minutes, how it ends in the last fifteen, and what each person does in the first five working days back. Add who will ask them about it. Then say the opening two minutes and the closing instruction aloud, as you would in the room.

items: **A ceremony can feel forced** in a work group, at the start or the end. Keep it plain, such as one sentence each, and let people pass.
**A good setting helps the work.** It does not replace it, so plan the sessions before you fall for the view.
**Tell line managers what to ask** about on the first day back. There is more on [the manager's part](t:2.4).
**Do not sell the setting** as science. The nature studies are small and say nothing about what people do back at work.

**The close gets squeezed** by an overrunning session and people drift off to trains. Protect the last 45 minutes in the timetable. There is detail on [the first week back](t:8.17) and on [the first-use plan](t:5.2).

Hunter, Gillespie and Chen (2019), Urban nature experiences reduce stress in the context of daily life based on salivary biomarkers. Frontiers in Psychology, 10, 722.
Atchley, Strayer and Atchley (2012), Creativity in the wild: improving creative reasoning through immersion in natural settings. PLOS ONE, 7(12).

quiz.q: What do anthropologists mean by a liminal stage?
quiz.a: The in-between period in a rite of passage, when people have left one role and not yet taken up the next. For a retreat it is a design idea. It has not been shown to cause change.

quiz.q: A venue's brochure says time in nature "is proven to boost creativity by 50 per cent". Your client wants the line in the invitation. What do you advise?
quiz.a: Leave it out. The studies are small and could not separate nature from rest, time off screens or who chose to take part. They say nothing about what people do back at work.

quiz.q: It is the last morning of an offsite and nothing has been planned for afterwards. What can you still do before people leave?
quiz.a: Use the last full block. Each person writes one thing to try, who they will tell and when. Book a short follow-up meeting in the calendars, and send line managers a note that day saying what to ask about on the first day back.

topics.tierReason: Liminality is an anthropological idea borrowed as a design principle, and the two nature studies read are small, uncontrolled and do not test retreats or the return to work.

topics.title: Write the duty-of-care plan first

situation.text: The plan for a three-day leadership residential is full of demanding exercises: feedback given in front of the group on day two, a role-play with an actor, a high-ropes afternoon. Sixteen managers are booked. Nobody has written down what happens if someone is distressed or hurt.

items: **Write the duty-of-care plan before the programme.** Use one page and five headings: who is in charge of safety, what participants are told beforehand, how to opt out of each exercise, who sits with someone in distress, and where you would send them for help.
**Tell participants in advance** what each day involves: the exercises, the hours, the overnight stay and anything physical. Ask them to agree to it, and read the note on consent below.

**Let people opt out of any exercise** without giving a reason, and with no report to their employer. Give each exercise a second role that is real work, such as observer with a checklist, so that opting out does not mean sitting alone.
**Know your limits.** Write down where you would send someone who needs more than you can give: 999 or NHS 111, the employer's assistance line if it has one, and their GP.
**Ask each person in advance, in private**, whether anything about the programme would be difficult for them, and adjust it. Do not run health screening of a client's employees yourself.

**Do a risk assessment:** identify the hazards, assess the risks, control them, record what you found and review it. Plan for incidents and emergencies, and count participants in when you assess first aid needs. There is more on [the risk assessment](t:9.19) and on [the incident plan](t:8.15).
**Give each delivery team member a copy** of the page and talk it through together before the first participant arrives.

why.text: **Your first duty is to the people.** Feedback in front of colleagues, role-play and physical challenges can all upset people. Your first duty as facilitator is to the people in the room, ahead of the programme. You are a trainer and not a therapist, so the plan has to say who is.

**Long days away add to the risk.** Long days away from home, with colleagues and managers present, add to the risk. People are tired, cannot easily leave, and are being watched by those who decide their pay and prospects.

**HSE says the organiser is responsible for safety.** In Great Britain, the Health and Safety at Work etc Act 1974 puts duties on employers towards their employees and towards members of the public. It also covers self-employed people whose work could put others at risk. HSE's guidance for events says the organiser has prime responsibility for the health and safety of workers, contractors and the people attending, and that planning should be in proportion to the scale and risk of the event. HSE guidance covers Great Britain. This page is general information, not legal advice.

**Consent is not fully free when employers choose.** On a business retreat the employer usually chooses who attends, so consent is not fully free. Agree with the client in writing that declining an exercise, or the overnight stay, carries no mark against anyone, and offer a non-residential alternative before invitations go out. There is detail on [planning for incidents](t:8.15) and on [people who cannot stay overnight](t:8.16).

**Writing the plan first changes the programme.** Writing the plan first is a craft choice, and it changes the programme. When you have to write the opt-out and the risk beside each exercise, you find the ones you cannot make safe while they are still cheap to cut. Written afterwards, the plan gets bent to fit a timetable the client has already approved. The cost is that some exercises lose their edge when people can step out. An exercise that only works if nobody is allowed to leave should not be in the programme.

try.text: Draft the one-page plan for a residential you know, using the five headings. Then talk a colleague through it aloud in three minutes, as you would brief a co-facilitator on the first morning, and ask them what they would still not know how to do at two in the morning.

What the plan says
rows: Who is in charge of safety
The lead facilitator, by name and mobile number. The co-facilitator covers when she is running a session. The venue duty manager is the contact for the building and for emergencies on site.
What participants are told beforehand

A two-page note three weeks ahead: each day's hours, every exercise in one line, the overnight stay, and the high-ropes afternoon with what it involves physically. It says anyone may decline any exercise.
Private question to each person
"Is there anything about this programme that would be difficult for you?" Asked by the client's HR contact. The facilitators are told only what to adjust.
Opt-out for each exercise

Feedback round: give feedback in pairs, or observe. Role-play with the actor: watch and take notes for a colleague. High ropes: ground crew, or a guided walk. No reasons asked and nothing reported to the employer.
Who sits with someone in distress
The co-facilitator leaves the room with them. The session carries on. The quiet room is next to reception.
Where we send people for help
999 in an emergency. NHS 111 for urgent advice. The employer's assistance line, number on the page. Their own GP. Nearest hospital and the venue's emergency contact are written on the page.
Agreed in writing with the client
Declining an exercise or the overnight stay carries no mark against anyone. A non-residential alternative is offered before invitations go out.

items: **Strong emotion by design:** do not design an exercise to provoke it, such as surprise feedback in front of the group or a staged confrontation.
**Check your insurance covers** an overnight event and each activity. There is more on [insurance for events](t:9.19) and on [the UK rules you work under](t:9.8).
**Facilitators work long hours** on a residential. Share the nights on call, as the guide to [staffing a residential](t:8.12) sets out.
**The opt-out exists on paper** and nobody dares use it with their manager watching. Say it aloud at the start of each exercise, and have the alternative role set up as a normal part of the task.
**The plan lives in one head.** Print it, give it to the whole delivery team and the venue contact, and keep a copy where the night cover can find it.

quiz.a: The event organiser. Planning should be in proportion to the scale and risk of the event.

quiz.q: A client says everyone must take part in the high-ropes afternoon "because it is a team event". What do you agree before invitations go out?
quiz.a: A written statement that anyone may decline an exercise with no mark against them, and an alternative task for those who do. The employer chose who attends, so consent is not fully free.

quiz.q: A sponsor asks you to send every participant a health questionnaire before the residential. What do you do instead?
quiz.a: Do not screen a client's employees yourself. Have each person asked in private whether anything about the programme would be difficult, and adjust the programme. There is more on [who collects and holds health information](t:8.15).

topics.title: Bring play into a retreat without losing the point

situation.text: The first night of a team offsite has a games evening, planned by the social committee: a drinking game at eight, then karaoke until midnight. Half the team of twenty has been looking forward to it for weeks. The other half is working out how early they can leave without it being noticed.

items: **Write one line for each playful activity** saying what it is for and how that serves the retreat's business result. There is more on [the purposes play can have](t:1.23). If the honest line is "so people enjoy the evening", write that. It is a fair purpose.
**Put light, low-risk play early**, while people are still getting to know each other. Keep anything that asks more of them for the second day.
**Run two or three things at once** so that nobody is the audience for one compulsory game. A quiz table, a building challenge and a quiet corner will do.
**Offer levels of involvement:** take part, help run it, or watch. Treat all three as normal, and say so when you introduce the evening.

**Give the evening a stated end time** that protects sleep, such as nine or half past, and make the soft drinks as good as the alcohol. Agree the evening rules with the client first, using the guide to [rules for evenings, alcohol and free time](t:8.14).
**Debrief any activity with a learning purpose** the same day or first thing next morning, using the steps for [debriefing an activity](t:4.28). One question is often enough.
**Leave free time.** Not everything needs a facilitator.

why.text: **Being away makes play easier.** A residential setting gives time and distance from work, which makes play easier. Shared play may help people get to know each other faster.
**Play can also exclude.** Physical challenges, alcohol and late nights leave some people out, and late nights cost sleep, and there is more on [protecting sleep on multi-day programmes](t:1.12).

**A compulsory game is a task.** This page is craft, and the central point is choice. Play only works when joining in is a choice. A game that people are told to join is a task with a smile on it, and the person told to "get stuck in" learns that the evening is being watched. Levels of involvement keep the choice real. Someone who keeps score or watches from the side is still in the room, and that counts.

**The purpose line helps you choose and cut.** The line of purpose is there to help you choose and to help you cut. An activity meant to mix people who do not know each other needs mixed teams and a low bar to entry. One meant to show a team how it works together needs a task with a result and a question the next morning. One that is purely for fun needs neither. The trouble comes from claiming a learning purpose for an evening that has none, and then running a debrief nobody believes.

**Optional means some people go to bed early.** Making everything optional has a cost, which is that some people will go to bed at half past eight. Let them. On a two-day event with a hard second day, that is a good outcome. A team that already knows each other well may need less organised play and more free time.

try.text: Review one retreat evening, past or planned. Say what each activity is for and who it might leave out. Then stand up and introduce the evening aloud in thirty seconds, as you would at the end of dinner, so that taking part, helping and watching all sound equally welcome.

parts.title: Design and run a business retreat
parts.summary: How to decide on, design, staff, cost and safely run a company offsite or residential course tied to a business result.

topics.title: Decide whether to take people away
topics.theory: The case for and against a residential

situation.text: A sales director at a software company asks for "three days away for the managers". The budget is approved. Nobody has asked what the three days are for, or whether four mornings in the office would do the same job.

items: **Ask the sponsor for the business result** first. Use these words: "Six months from now, what will these people be doing that they are not doing today?" Write the answer down and read it back.

**Sort the work into two piles.** One pile is skill that needs repeated practice over weeks. The other is work that needs the whole group together for long stretches: a hard decision, a plan, a relationship that has gone wrong.

**Price both options** before you recommend either. Cost the residential with the [method for the full cost](t:8.13), including people's time. Cost a spaced on-site version next to it, for example four half days over six weeks.

**Count who would be shut out** by an overnight stay. Ask the sponsor's HR contact how many of the group have caring duties, a disability or health condition, part-time hours or a faith practice that the dates or the venue would cut across.
**Run the decision test** below with the sponsor in the room. Read out each row and mark it together.

**Recommend the residential only on two conditions:** the together-for-long-stretches pile is the larger one and nobody is shut out without a real alternative. Otherwise recommend the spaced version, or a mix: one night away followed by three short sessions back at work.
**Put the recommendation in writing** with the result, the cost of each option and the follow-up dates.

why.text: **A residential buys time, togetherness and distance.** A residential buys three things an office programme struggles to give: long unbroken time, the whole group in one place, and distance from the inbox. Those claims are practitioner judgement. There is no published comparison that we know of between a residential and the same content spread out on site.

**Two findings from research pull the other way.** A review of spacing found that people recalled more when study was spread out than when it was packed together, with the same total study time. A meta-analysis of leadership training listed spaced sessions and an on-site location among the features of programmes with stronger results. There is more detail on [both findings, with their limits](t:8.8).

**So the test is about fit.** A decision that needs sixteen people to argue it through suits two days away. A skill such as coaching a sales call suits short sessions with practice at work in between. Many briefs contain both, and then the mixed option is usually the right recommendation.

try.text: Rehearse the conversation aloud with a colleague playing the sponsor. Your task is to recommend the cheaper spaced option to someone who wants the hotel. Record it on your phone. Listen for the moment you name the business result and the moment you give the two costs.

items: **The sponsor has already promised** the team a trip. Keep the trip and change its job: use it for the group work, and move the skill practice into sessions back at work.
**The "cost" you compared** leaves out people's time. Add it, because for senior groups it is often the largest line.
**You assume nobody minds staying away.** Ask through HR before dates are fixed, and treat the answers as private.
**The spaced option quietly dies** because no one protects the dates. Book all the sessions before the first one runs.
**The need may not be training** at all. If the managers already know how and something else stops them, no format will fix it. [Check it is a skill problem](t:1.20) before you compare formats.

items.label: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted and Rohrer (2006), Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: a review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3). Authors' copy.

Lacerenza, Reyes, Marlow, Joseph and Salas (2017), Leadership training design, delivery, and implementation: a meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 102(12). Abstract on the University of Central Florida repository.

quiz.q: Name two features that research links with better results and that a single block away does not give.
quiz.a: Practice spread over time, and for leadership training an on-site location.

quiz.q: A head of customer support wants a two-night retreat to teach 20 team leaders a new coaching routine. The leaders share one office. What do you recommend?
quiz.a: A spaced on-site programme, because the work is a skill that needs repeated practice and the group is already together. Offer one day away only if there is group work that needs it.

quiz.q: A leadership team of eight, spread across four countries, must agree next year's priorities and has failed twice on video calls. Residential or not?
quiz.a: A short residential fits: the work is a group decision that needs long unbroken time and the group never meets. Check first that everyone can travel and stay.

topics.tierReason: Rests on a spacing review and a leadership training meta-analysis opened for this build. The decision test itself is practitioner judgement and has not been tested.

topics.title: Know what the evidence says a retreat can and cannot do
topics.theory: Evidence for and against residential training

situation.text: You are pitching a three-day leadership residential. The client's head of learning asks: "What is the evidence that taking people away works better than training them here?"

items: **Give the short answer first:** "No study I have read compares a residential with the same programme run on site. There is evidence on three nearby questions, and some of it cuts against going away."

**State the spacing problem plainly.** A residential packs the practice into one block. Research on memory favours practice spread over time, as the guide to [spacing and mixing practice](t:5.14) explains.
**State the on-site finding.** A large review of leadership training lists an on-site location among the features of stronger programmes.
**State what the outdoor education evidence shows** and who it studied: long adventure programmes, with gains in how people see themselves.
**Say what you will do** about each one. Add spaced follow-up sessions after the event, bring real work into the venue, and promise no change in character.
**Keep setting claims out of the proposal.** Sell the time, the practice and the follow-up.
**Offer the sources.** Send the three links the same day.

why.text: **One block alone is a poor bet.** Spacing first. Cepeda and colleagues pooled 271 comparisons of massed and spaced study. All but 12 favoured spacing, and average recall was about 47 per cent for spaced items against about 37 per cent for massed ones. The best gap grew as the time to the final test grew. The studies were laboratory tests of verbal recall, mostly with young adults, and the authors say their findings do not settle the question for skill learning. A residential is not a memory experiment. Still, the direction is clear enough that one block with nothing after it is a poor bet.

**On-site training went with stronger effects.** Next, location. Lacerenza and colleagues pooled 335 samples of leadership training. They report that training worked on average and that several features went with stronger effects, among them spaced sessions, an on-site location and face-to-face delivery. Their published summary does not say why on-site training did better or how large the difference was. It is a pattern across many different programmes, not a trial of one design against another.

**Adventure gains were modest and from long programmes.** Then the outdoors. Hattie and colleagues pooled 96 studies of adventure programmes. The average gain at the end was 0.34, with a further 0.17 at follow-up. These figures are effect sizes, a standard measure of how far a group moved, and 0.34 is a modest gain. Effects varied a great deal between programmes and outcomes. They were larger for longer programmes and for older participants. The outcomes the review names are self-concept (how people see themselves), locus of control (how far people feel in charge of what happens to them) and leadership. A news report at the time described the participants as students and the typical programme as 20 to 26 days. That is a long way from two nights in a hotel for managers.

why.title: Spaced against massed study
why.found: Of 271 comparisons, 259 favoured spaced study over massed study with equal study time. The studies tested verbal recall, mostly in laboratories.
why.means: Do not let the residential be the whole programme. Plan practice after it.

why.title: What goes with stronger leadership training
why.found: Across 335 samples, leadership training improved reactions, learning, transfer and results. Needs analysis, feedback, several delivery methods with practice, spaced sessions, an on-site location and face-to-face delivery went with stronger effects.
why.means: Going off site is not an advantage in this evidence. Bring the workplace into the design.

why.title: Adventure programmes
why.found: Across 96 studies the average effect was 0.34 at the end and a further 0.17 later. Effects varied by programme and outcome and grew with programme length and participant age.
why.means: Evidence from long adventure courses does not transfer to a short business retreat. Do not cite it as proof for one.

try.text: Say it aloud. Set a timer for ninety seconds and answer the head of learning's question to a colleague, without notes. Then ask them which of the three findings they could repeat back. Do it again until all three survive.

items: **You quote 0.34** as if it applied to your event. It comes from programmes that mostly ran for weeks.
**You hide the on-site finding** because it is awkward. A client's sceptic will find it. Raise it first.
**You treat spacing as a rule** for every kind of learning. The review covers verbal recall, so apply it with care to group decisions and relationships.
**You overcorrect** and talk the client out of a retreat that suits the work. Use the [decision test for going away](t:8.7).
**You quote a review** as if you had read every page. If you know a paper only from its summary, say so when pressed.

quiz.q: In the Lacerenza meta-analysis, was an on-site or an off-site location linked with stronger leadership training?
quiz.a: On-site.

quiz.q: A venue's brochure says "research shows outdoor residentials build lasting leadership". Your client wants to quote it in the invitation. What do you do?
quiz.a: Advise against it. The main review covers long adventure programmes and measures such as self-concept, so it does not support a short business retreat.

quiz.q: A sponsor says the residential is the whole programme and there is no budget for anything after. What do you say?
quiz.a: That one packed block with no later practice goes against the spacing evidence. Shorten the residential by half a day and spend the saving on two short follow-up sessions.

topics.tierReason: Rests on one review read in full and two meta-analyses read as abstracts. None of them tests a business retreat directly.

topics.title: Choose the format

situation.text: A client says "we want an offsite". In the next ten minutes they describe a sales kick-off, a strategy session and a team social, all in the same two days.

items: **Ask one question to find the format:** "When people drive home, what must exist that did not exist when they arrived?" A decision, a plan, a skill and a relationship each point to a different format.
**Match the answer to the table** below. Read the "what it is for" column aloud and ask the sponsor to choose one.
**Set the group size from the work.** Decisions need a group small enough for everyone to speak. Skills practice needs groups of three with an observer or a facilitator close by.
**Set the length from the work** as well. Start with the shortest length in the table and add time only when you can name what the extra half day is for.
**Give each format its own block** if the sponsor wants two, with its own outcome and a break between them. A strategy morning and a skills afternoon can share a venue. They cannot share a session.
**Write the format in one sentence**, with the outcome, the group size and the length, and send it to the sponsor the same day.
**Check the sentence** against the [decision test for going away](t:8.7) before anyone books a venue.

why.text: **The formats below are practitioner judgement.** There is no research that compares one format with another, and the lengths and group sizes are working ranges that trainers and event teams commonly use. Treat them as a starting point for a conversation.

**Each format ends with a different product.** The reason to name a format is that each one has a different product at the end. A sales kick-off produces a sales team that knows the plan for the year and has practised the new pitch. A strategy offsite produces decisions with owners. When the format is left vague, the timetable fills with a little of everything and people leave with nothing finished.

**Size changes the craft.** Twelve people can hold one conversation. Eighty people cannot, so a large kick-off needs short sessions with everyone in one room and most of the time in small groups, with a facilitator or a briefed manager at each. There is more on [running a large kick-off](t:2.42). Size also changes [how you staff it](t:8.12) and [what it costs](t:8.13).

try.text: Ring a colleague and have them play a client who wants "a bit of everything". Ask the format question aloud and hold your ground until they pick one. Time it. If it takes more than five minutes, shorten your question.

**Two days of slides** are planned for a kick-off. Ask for half of every session to be practice in small groups, and offer to brief the managers who will lead them.
**A skills intensive sold without follow-up.** Apply the guide to [scheduling the follow-up](t:5.4) before you agree the dates.
**A leadership offsite drifts** into personal disclosure. Keep the work on how the team leads the business, and apply the advice on [building trust before asking for openness](t:8.3).
**The format you like running** is the one you design for. Let the sponsor's answer to the first question choose.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What single question helps you find the right format?
quiz.a: What must exist when people leave that did not exist when they arrived.

quiz.q: A chief executive wants a strategy offsite and invites all 45 managers "so everyone feels included". What do you do?
quiz.a: Explain that 45 people cannot make decisions in one conversation. Offer a decision group of about twelve, with a short session afterwards that shares the decisions with the other managers.

quiz.q: A sales leader wants a three-day kick-off with product presentations from nine to five each day. What do you suggest?
quiz.a: Cut the presentations and give at least half of each session to pitch practice in small groups. The format exists to send people home able to do something.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement. No research on retreat formats was opened.

topics.title: Build the timetable

situation.text: The draft agenda runs from 08:00 to 21:30 on both days, with a "fireside session" after dinner. The sponsor says people can sleep at the weekend.

items: **Fix the outcome for each day** before you fill a single slot. Write it at the top of the timetable.

**Start late on arrival day.** People have travelled and cleared their desks. On a two-night event begin after lunch and keep the first afternoon light: purpose, working agreement, one easy piece of real work.
**Use the first evening for dinner** and nothing else. No exercise, no speeches after 20:30, and say that leaving the table early is fine.
**Build each full day from work blocks** of about ninety minutes with a break between. Put the hardest work in the morning. Plan no more than four blocks a day.
**Give real free time in daylight**, at least ninety minutes on a full day, and put it in the printed timetable so it is not the first thing cut.
**Open each morning recalling the day before**, for fifteen to thirty minutes, as the guide to [protecting sleep on multi-day programmes](t:1.12) sets out.

**Finish before lunch on the last day**, or straight after it. People start leaving for trains from mid-afternoon whatever the agenda says. Put the plans for first use at work in the last full block, not in the final ten minutes.
**Print the clock times** and keep to them. Starting and ending on time is how the group learns that the free time is real.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. There is more on [the research on sleep](t:1.12). Nobody has tested one residential timetable against another.

**Energy and attention dip at known points.** The pattern comes from what trainers see on residentials. Energy is low on arrival and after lunch on the middle day. Attention falls quickly in a fifth or sixth work block. The last afternoon loses people to travel. A timetable that plans for these points gets more work done in fewer hours.

**Free time is part of the design.** It is when people talk over what happened, rest, ring home and deal with the email that would otherwise pull them out of a session. Evenings need the most care, and you can [set the rules for them](t:8.14).

**Both examples use the same group.** Both examples below are for the same group: 16 new managers at a software company, two facilitators, and one outcome. Each manager leaves able to open a difficult conversation and with a date to hold a real one.

**A block overruns** and free time shrinks. Cut content from the next block. Leave the break alone.

**Arrival day starts at 09:00** to "make the most of the venue". People arrive late and tired. Move the start, or add a night before.
**The timetable has no slack.** Leave one block on the middle day that you could drop without losing the outcome.

**An evening session** is what the whole outcome depends on. Anyone attending by day misses it. Keep all the work that counts inside the working day, as the guide to [including people who cannot stay overnight](t:8.16) sets out.

quiz.q: On a two-night residential, when should the programme start on arrival day?
quiz.a: After lunch, with a light first afternoon.

quiz.q: At 16:00 on the middle day you are forty minutes behind. The next items are a fourth work block and ninety minutes of free time. What do you do?
quiz.a: Shorten or drop the fourth block and keep the free time. Tired people get little from a late block, and cutting the break teaches the group that the timetable cannot be trusted.

quiz.q: The sponsor wants action plans written in the last fifteen minutes before the coaches leave. What do you change?
quiz.a: Move the plans into the last full work block of the morning so each person writes one, says it aloud and gets a question on it. Plans written in a rush at the door are forgotten.

topics.title: Choose and brief the venue
topics.theory: Venue selection and the site visit

situation.text: The client's assistant has found a country house hotel with good photographs. On the day, the main room turns out to be the bar with the tables pushed back, and a wedding party arrives at four.

items: **Write the brief before anyone searches:** dates, numbers, the outcome, how many rooms you need for work, bedrooms, access needs already known, and the longest travel time you will accept. For most groups aim for under two hours door to door.
**Shortlist two or three venues by phone.** Ask each the same first question: "Will we have the building, or our part of it, to ourselves?"

**Visit before you sign.** Go at the time of day you will be working and take the checklist below. If you cannot visit, ask for a video call walked through the rooms by the person who will be your contact.

**Stand in the main room** and test it. Check daylight, a flat floor, wall space for flipcharts, enough room for 16 chairs in a horseshoe and for groups of three to spread out. Play a phone at speaking volume from the far end.
**Walk a wheelchair user's route** from the car park to the main room, a breakout room, a bedroom, the dining room and a toilet. Do it yourself. Do not accept "mostly accessible".
**Test phone signal and wifi** where you will work, and find the spot where a mobile call to 999 would connect.

**Send the venue a written brief** two weeks ahead: the timetable with break and meal times, room layouts, dietary and access needs, who the venue contact is on each shift, and who may authorise extra spending.
**Walk the rooms again on arrival** with the venue contact before participants arrive.

why.text: **No research covers venue choice.** This is practitioner judgement, built from what goes wrong. There is no research on venue choice to draw on. There is more on [the risk assessment and insurance side](t:9.19) and on [room layout](t:4.5).

**Shared rooms and poor access undo the design.** The venue decides how much of your timetable survives. Shared public rooms mean interruptions and no privacy for hard conversations. One room with no breakouts means sixteen people practising in the same space and hearing each other. Poor access tells some participants they were an afterthought, and it may leave the employer short of its [duties to disabled staff](t:8.16).

**People need somewhere to be alone.** A quiet room matters more on a residential than on a training day. People are in company from breakfast until bedtime. Somewhere to sit alone, pray, take medication or make a private call makes it possible for more people to stay the course.
**The written brief outlasts a shift change.** The written brief exists because venue staff work shifts. The person who showed you round may not be there on the day.

try.text: Take the checklist to any hotel or conference venue near you and ask to see a meeting room. Walk the step-free route and ask the questions aloud to the duty manager. Twenty minutes of doing this once will teach you more than reading the list again.

**"Exclusive use"** covers only the meeting room. Ask about the bar, the lounge and the grounds.
**The accessible bedroom** is in an annexe across a gravel yard. Check the route in the dark as well.
**Twin rooms are offered** to save money. Adults at a work event should not be asked to share a bedroom.
**The sales office gets the brief** and it never reaches the duty manager. Hand a printed copy to your contact on arrival.

quiz.q: What is the first question to ask a venue on the phone?
quiz.a: Whether you will have the building, or your part of it, to yourselves.

quiz.q: On the site visit the manager says the house is "mostly accessible, just two steps into the dining room". One participant uses a wheelchair. What do you do?
quiz.a: Treat it as not accessible until there is a working ramp or another dining arrangement for the whole group. Ask for the solution in writing or choose another venue.

quiz.q: The venue you like has one large room and no breakouts. The programme is rehearsal in threes. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask for two more rooms or look elsewhere. Sixteen people rehearsing in one room cannot hear themselves, and private practice is the point of the event.

topics.title: Staff it
topics.theory: Roles and ratios on a residential

situation.text: You are quoted as the only facilitator for 16 people over two nights. At 22:40 on the first night a participant knocks on your door in tears, and you are due to open the morning session at 08:45.

items: **Set a floor of two facilitators** for any overnight event, whatever the group size. One person cannot run the room, look after someone who is unwell and stay fit to work the next day.

**Size the team from the practice.** For rehearsal in threes, plan one facilitator for every eight to twelve participants. A group of 16 needs two. Above 24, add a third or brief line managers to lead groups.
**Name a lead facilitator.** They hold the timetable, make the calls when the plan changes and are the one voice to the client.
**Ask the client for a host** who attends throughout: someone senior enough to make decisions about their own staff and to speak for the employer if a participant's conduct becomes a problem.
**Get one named venue contact** for each shift, with a mobile number, including overnight.
**Decide who holds the emergency contacts** and any health or access information, and who is on call each night. Write the names on one page. Share the nights between you.
**Hold a facilitator debrief each day**, fifteen minutes straight after the last session. Cover what happened, who you are concerned about and what changes tomorrow.
**Put the roles table in the proposal** so the client can see what the second fee pays for.

why.text: **These ratios are practitioner judgement.** Nobody has tested facilitator numbers on a residential, and other experienced trainers work to different figures. There is more on [group size and staffing for courses](t:2.33) in general.

**Two facilitators means nobody is left alone.** The case for two is about care as much as teaching. If someone is distressed or hurt, one facilitator stays with them and the other keeps the group working. With one facilitator, either the person or the group is left alone. A second facilitator also means nobody is alone with a participant late at night, which protects both of them.

**You have no authority over the client's staff.** The client host matters because you have no authority over the client's employees. You can ask someone to step out of a session. You cannot deal with a complaint between two colleagues or send someone home. The employer can, and its own policies apply.

**Shared nights keep you useful to the end.** Facilitators on a residential are on duty for long hours. Sharing the on-call nights and ending the facilitator debrief on time is how you are still useful on the last morning. There is more on [looking after yourself](t:4.16).

try.text: Run a fifteen minute facilitator debrief with a colleague after any session you deliver this month. Use three questions aloud: what happened, who are we concerned about, what changes tomorrow. Keep to time with a phone timer.
