**The participants' own boss** is the client host. People will hold back. Ask for an HR partner or a manager from another team.
**Both facilitators stay up** until the last person leaves the bar. Agree who is on duty and let the other go to bed.
**One person's phone** holds the emergency contact list. Keep a sealed paper copy with the second facilitator.
**An hour of stories** is what the debrief turns into. Three questions, fifteen minutes, then stop.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What is the minimum number of facilitators for an overnight event in this topic's advice?
quiz.a: Two.

quiz.q: A client wants you to run a two-night skills residential for 14 people alone, to save money. What do you say?
quiz.a: Decline to run it alone and explain why: practice groups need feedback, and one person cannot look after an unwell participant and run the room. Offer a shorter event with two facilitators.

quiz.q: During the second evening one participant tells you a colleague has been making comments she finds offensive. What is your first move?
quiz.a: Listen, note the time and what she said, and bring in the client host, because the employer's policy applies and you have no authority over its staff. Tell her that is what you are going to do before you do it.

topics.title: Cost it
topics.theory: The full cost of a residential

situation.text: The sponsor says the retreat will cost "about twelve thousand, that is what the hotel quoted". The hotel quote covers rooms and food. Nothing else has been counted.

items: **List every cost line** before you look at any quote: venue hire, bedrooms, food and drink, travel, facilitator fees, design time, materials, insurance and contingency.
**Count heads for each line.** Bedrooms and meals include the facilitators and the client host. Travel includes yours.
**Get the venue's price** as a day-delegate or 24-hour rate and ask exactly what it includes. Ask about minimum numbers and the cancellation scale.
**Add contingency as its own visible line.** Ten per cent of the cash subtotal is a common working figure. It covers a late dietary need, a taxi, an extra room.
**Cost people's time as a separate line** below the cash total. Ask the client's finance contact for an average daily cost for the group. Multiply by people and by days, including travel days.
**Show two totals:** cash, and cash plus time. Divide each by the number of participants.
**Cost the alternative** from the [decision test for going away](t:8.7) in the same table shape, so the sponsor compares like with like.
**State what is not included**, in a single line under the table.

why.text: **The cost layout is judgement, not research.** This is practitioner judgement about how to lay out a cost, with no research behind it. There is more on [scoping and pricing your own fee](t:9.4) and on [working out your day rate](t:9.28).

**Leave out time and a residential looks cheap.** The cash lines are the ones a sponsor expects. The line most often missing is time. Sixteen managers away for three days is 48 working days that the business pays for and gets no other work from. For senior groups it can be the largest single line. Leaving it out makes every residential look cheaper than a spaced programme, which uses hours instead of days.
**A visible contingency line is honest.** Without it, small extras either come out of your fee or arrive as a surprise invoice, and both damage trust.

**Use the shape, not the figures.** The figures below are made up and round, chosen so the sums are easy to follow. Real prices vary widely by region, season and venue. Use the shape and get real quotes for every line.

try.text: Talk a colleague through the table in two minutes, as if they were the sponsor. Say both totals aloud and the cost per head. Record it. If you hear yourself apologising for the time line, practise that sentence again.

**Your own design days are hidden** inside the delivery fee. Show them, or the client will expect the next design for nothing.

quiz.q: Which cost line is most often left out of a retreat budget?
quiz.a: The cost of people's time away from work.

quiz.q: A sponsor compares your £33,000 residential with a £9,000 quote for on-site sessions and says the retreat is "only" £24,000 more. What do you add?
quiz.a: The time line for both options. Three days away for 16 people costs far more in time than four half days, so the real gap is wider.

quiz.q: Two days before the event a participant tells the venue about a severe allergy and the kitchen charges for separate preparation. Where does the cost go?
quiz.a: Against the contingency line, which exists for this. Tell the client host the same day so the spend is no surprise.

topics.title: Set the rules for evenings, alcohol and free time

situation.text: It is 22:15 on the first night. The work went well. The sponsor has put a card behind the bar, three people have gone to bed, and a participant asks you to stay for "one more".

items: **Agree the rules with the client** before invitations go out. Put them in writing: what the employer pays for at the bar and until when, which policy applies to conduct, and who participants go to with a concern.

**Make everything after the last session optional**, and say so twice: in the invitation and in the opening. Include dinner if you can. If dinner is expected, say that leaving after the main course is fine.
**Make opting out easy.** Print the end time of each evening. Offer a second space that is not the bar, with good soft drinks and hot drinks. Never ask anyone why they are leaving.
**Set your own rule on alcohol** and keep it. A workable rule is none, or one drink with dinner and none after. You are at work until you close your bedroom door.
**Stay in public spaces.** Do not go to a participant's bedroom or invite one to yours. If someone needs a private talk at night, use a lounge and tell your co-facilitator where you are.
**Agree who is on duty each evening** with your co-facilitator, and what time that person leaves the bar. The other one goes to bed.
**Stay off personal social media with participants** during the event. Say you will connect on a work network afterwards.

why.text: **Trainers say incidents cluster late in the evening.** Most of this is practitioner judgement. Trainers who run residentials report that incidents cluster late in the evening, when people are tired, away from home and drinking with colleagues and managers. We know of no research that measures it.

**The conduct rules are the client's to set.** Two points come from official guidance. Acas says that from 30 October 2026 an employer is liable for harassment of its workers by third parties as well as by other workers, unless it has taken all reasonable steps to prevent it. Acas adds that being at work can include business travel, external training and office parties. A residential is an employer's event in that sense, which is why the conduct rules are the client's to set and yours to follow. You may be one of the third parties.

**Acas counts required training as working time.** Acas also says that training needed for the job counts as working time, and that workers are entitled to 11 hours of rest between working days. A timetable that expects people in the bar until midnight and in the room at eight sits badly with that. This is general information, not legal advice.

**Leave at ten and it becomes ordinary.** Your own conduct carries more weight than the written rules. People copy the facilitator. If you leave at ten with a soft drink in your hand, leaving at ten becomes ordinary.

try.text: Say the opening statement below aloud, standing, three times. Record the third. It should take under a minute and sound like information, not a warning. Then practise one sentence for declining a drink without making it awkward.

The company pays for drinks with dinner. The bar tab closes at 21:30.
A lounge with soft drinks, tea and coffee is open all evening as a second space.
The company's code of conduct applies for the whole event, including evenings and travel.
Concerns go to the client host or to either facilitator. Mobile numbers are on the back of the name badge.

"Dinner is at seven. Come if you would like to, and leave when you like. Nobody will ask."

And to the offer of one more: "Not for me, thanks. I am on at quarter to nine. See you at breakfast."

items: **The senior person stays late** and everyone feels they must. Ask the client host beforehand to leave by ten and say goodnight.
**"Optional" activities are noticed** by who does not come. Never report attendance at social events to the employer, and say so.
**The bar is the only space** in the evening. Book the lounge when you book the venue.
**A participant shares something personal** with you late at night. Listen, do not advise, and raise it with your co-facilitator in the morning without detail the person would not want passed on.

items.label: Acas, Harassment at work: preventing harassment.
Acas, Working time rules: understanding the Working Time Regulations.

quiz.q: According to Acas, can an employer's duty to prevent harassment cover external training and work social events?
quiz.a: Yes. Acas lists business travel, external training and office parties as examples of being in the course of employment.

quiz.q: The sponsor proposes a free bar until midnight "as a thank you". What do you suggest?
quiz.a: Drinks with dinner and a tab that closes at a stated time, with a second space that is not the bar. A long free bar raises the chance of an incident and makes it harder for people to opt out.

quiz.q: A participant you get on well with suggests carrying on a conversation in their room because the bar is closing. What do you do?
quiz.a: Decline and offer the lounge or breakfast. A facilitator stays in public spaces and is still at work.

topics.title: Plan for incidents

situation.text: At 23:30 a participant slips on the steps outside the hotel and cannot put weight on her ankle. Her manager is in bed, the night porter is new, and nobody knows who has her emergency contact.

items: **Name one incident lead and a deputy** for the event. On a small residential this is the lead facilitator with the second facilitator as deputy. Put both mobile numbers on the back of every name badge.

**Write the risk assessment** with the client and the venue, following the steps for [assessing the risks of an event](t:9.19). Add the residential risks: evenings, alcohol, paths in the dark, travel and distress.

**Agree in writing who collects information** about health, access and diet, and who sees it. The simplest route is that the employer collects it and passes on only what the venue and the facilitators must act on.

**Collect the minimum.** Ask what the person needs, not what their diagnosis is: "Is there anything we should know to keep you safe and comfortable, such as an allergy, an access need or medication that must be kept cold?"
**Prepare a one-page "who calls whom" sheet** and an incident log, both shown below. Carry them on paper.
**Find out the venue's first aid arrangements:** who the first aider or appointed person is on each shift, where the kit is, and how far the nearest emergency department is.
**Talk through three scenarios aloud** with the client host and venue contact before participants arrive: an injury at night, a person in distress, a complaint about another participant.
**Write the log entry the same day** after any incident, and tell the client host.

why.text: **Assess risk for visitors as well as employees.** HSE sets out [risk assessment as five steps](t:9.19), and says to consider visitors and members of the public as well as employees. Its first aid guidance says an employer must make arrangements that fit the workplace and its risks, with at least a stocked kit, an appointed person and information for employees. It adds that a first aider may give initial support to someone in acute mental distress if they know how to reach professional help.

**HSE asks for incident plans and named people.** HSE's event guidance says organisers need plans for incidents in proportion to the risk, with people appointed to carry them out. It suggests working through scenarios round a table beforehand.

**Health details are special category data.** Health details fall under the ICO's rules on special category data. You need a lawful basis and a separate condition, you must keep to the minimum needed, and the sensitivity of the data should shape how you secure it. The ICO says consent is usually not appropriate where power is unequal, and it names employers. Its example for the vital interests condition is sharing an unconscious employee's allergy details with an ambulance crew. Ask the client's data protection lead which basis fits your event.
The log and the named lead are practitioner judgement. This is general information, not legal advice.

try.text: Run the table-top with a colleague. One of you reads a scenario aloud: "It is 23:30, someone has fallen on the steps." The other says, out loud and in order, what they do and who they call, using the sheet. Swap, and mark every point where you had to guess.

try.title: A worked example: who calls whom
lines: Life at risk: anyone calls 999 first, then the incident lead.
Incident lead: Priya, lead facilitator. Deputy: Sam, second facilitator. Numbers on every badge.
Injury or illness: fetch the venue's first aider through reception. The incident lead stays with the person.
The deputy keeps the group working or closes the session calmly.
The incident lead tells the client host. The client host contacts the person's emergency contact and their manager.
Nobody goes to hospital alone. The client host or a facilitator goes with them, and the other facilitator runs the room.
Distress without injury: one facilitator sits with the person in the quiet room, door open, and asks what they need. We listen. We do not counsel.
If the person may be at risk of harm: 999, or NHS 111 for urgent advice, and tell the client host.
A complaint about another participant: listen, write down what was said, and take it to the client host. The employer's policy applies.
Health and contact details: one sealed paper copy with the client host, one with the incident lead. Shredded when the event ends.
Log every incident the same day.

quiz.q: In HSE's first aid guidance, what is the minimum an employer must provide?
quiz.a: A suitably stocked first aid kit, an appointed person and information for employees about the arrangements.

quiz.q: A client suggests you email all participants a form asking for medical conditions and medication, to be returned to you. What do you propose instead?
quiz.a: That the employer asks one question about what people need to be safe and comfortable, and passes on only what you and the venue must act on. Health details are special category data, so collect the minimum and agree who holds it.

quiz.q: At 07:30 a participant tells you he has not slept and cannot face the day. Your co-facilitator is setting up. What do you do?
quiz.a: Sit with him somewhere quiet, ask what he needs and offer the choice to rest, join later or go home, with no pressure. Tell your co-facilitator so the session can start, and involve the client host if he wants to leave.

topics.title: Include people who cannot or will not stay overnight
topics.theory: Inclusion and reasonable adjustments on residentials

situation.text: The invitation says attendance at the two-night offsite is "expected". One manager cares for a parent every evening. Another uses a wheelchair. A third does not want to be anywhere built round a bar. None of them has said anything yet.

items: **Raise overnight stays with the sponsor** before the format is fixed. Ask: "Who in this group might find two nights away difficult, and what will we offer them?"
**Have the invitation come from the employer** with a named, private contact, usually in HR, and a plain sentence that says adjustments are normal.
**Design a day-attendance version from the start.** Put all the work that leads to the outcome between 09:00 and 17:15, so someone who goes home each night misses nothing that counts.

**Offer options before people have to ask:** daily travel paid for, a single night, a ground-floor bedroom, a fridge for medication, a quiet room for prayer, food that meets religious and medical needs.
**Talk with each person raising a need** about what would help. Do not guess from a label and do not ask for a reason beyond what is needed to arrange it.
**Keep evening events free of work content** and decisions. If the team's plan is settled over drinks, the people who left are shut out of it.
**Agree an equivalent with the sponsor** if someone cannot attend at all: the same practice in two on-site sessions with a facilitator, and a place in the follow-up.

why.text: **Employers must make reasonable adjustments.** GOV.UK says employers must make reasonable adjustments so that workers with disabilities or health conditions are not substantially disadvantaged, and lists offering training opportunities among its examples. Acas says the duty applies when the employer knows, or could be expected to know, that someone is disabled, or when the person asks. The employer should talk with the person, avoid assumptions and pay for the adjustment.

**A rule for everyone can still discriminate.** Acas describes indirect discrimination as a rule that is the same for everyone and has a worse effect on some people because of a protected characteristic such as disability, religion or belief, or sex. Working hours are among the practices it lists. Such a rule can be lawful only if the employer shows a legitimate aim and a proportionate way of reaching it. On religion, Acas gives the example of a change to break times that disadvantaged staff who used them for prayer. It also warns against leaving someone out of an event because of an assumption about alcohol and their partner's faith.

**Your part is to raise the question early.** A compulsory overnight stay applies to everyone and may fall harder on some groups. Whether it is lawful in a given case is for the employer and its advisers. Your part is to see that the question is asked early and that a real alternative exists. This is general information, not legal advice.

**The guidance leaves out cost and preference.** The guidance above does not cover people who cannot afford the extra costs of being away, or who simply do not want to stay. Making room for both is practitioner judgement.

**Day attendance exists on paper** and the key session is after dinner. Move the session.
**A set of slides to read** is the alternative. Make it practice with a facilitator, or it is not equivalent.
**Dates are fixed before anyone checks** religious festivals and school holidays. Check first.

quiz.q: According to Acas, when does an employer's duty to make reasonable adjustments apply?
quiz.a: When the employer knows, or could reasonably be expected to know, that someone is disabled, or when a disabled person asks for adjustments.

quiz.q: A sponsor says: "Attendance is compulsory. If we let one person go home at night, half of them will." What do you say?
quiz.a: That a blanket rule can disadvantage carers, disabled staff and others, and the employer would need to justify it. Suggest designing the days so that going home costs nobody the outcome, and let HR handle individual requests.

quiz.q: A participant tells you on arrival that she fasts during the day this week and will eat after sunset. Dinner is at 19:00 and sunset is at 20:10. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask her what would help, then arrange with the venue for a meal to be kept or served later and a place to eat it. Do it quietly and do not single her out in the room.

topics.title: Plan the return to work

situation.text: The offsite ended on Thursday with real energy. On Monday each manager has 140 unread emails and a team asking what the "jolly" was like. By Friday nobody has tried anything.

items: **Design the first week back** before you design day one. Decide what each person will do, by when, and who will ask them about it.

**Brief the line managers two weeks ahead**, in a twenty minute call. Tell them the outcome, what their person will bring back and the one conversation you need from them. There is more on [the manager's job before, during and after](t:2.4).

**Have each participant write a first-use plan** in the last full work block of the event, in [the when-then form](t:5.2), with a date in the first five working days. Each one says it aloud to a partner.
**Book the follow-up session before people leave**, in their calendars. Three weeks out works well: long enough to have tried something, short enough to remember.
**Send the manager note** below on the afternoon the event ends, so it is waiting on the first morning back.
**Have each participant talk to their manager** on the first day back, in a fifteen minute conversation. Three questions, listed below.
**Run the follow-up session for sixty minutes** on a video call or on site. Open with recall, then each person reports what they tried and what happened. Rehearse the hard part again.
**After that, move to the schedule** for [spaced follow-up after the event](t:5.4).

why.text: **The residential plan itself is judgement.** This is practitioner judgement applied to a residential. The research behind [first-use plans](t:5.2) and [follow-up after the event](t:5.4) is set out elsewhere and is not repeated here.

**A residential makes the return harder.** The return is harder after a residential than after a training day. People have been away for longer, so the backlog is bigger. Their colleagues were not there and may be wary of it. Everything happened in one block, so nothing has yet been practised in the place where it will be used. The spacing evidence, part of [what the evidence says about retreats](t:8.8), points to later practice as the thing that makes the block worth having.

**The manager conversation does two jobs.** It tells the participant that the employer expects the new behaviour. It also clears a path: the manager can remove one obstacle on the spot. Without the briefing call, many managers ask "was it fun?" and the moment passes.

**Suppliers may not reach line managers.** If you are an external supplier, you may not have access to the line managers. Ask the sponsor to send the note in their own name, and write the follow-up session into the proposal so it is paid for.

try.text: Rehearse the manager conversation aloud with a colleague. Play the manager first, using only the three questions, and keep it to fifteen minutes. Then swap. Notice how hard it is not to fill the silences.

items: **Nobody mentions the plans again** once they are written. The practice partner message on day five is the cheapest fix.
**Managers are not briefed** and feel judged by the note. Hold the call first.
**The follow-up session is cancelled** because diaries are full. Book it before the event and name it in the proposal.
**Participants come back with private language** and in-jokes. Ask them at the close to agree one plain sentence that tells colleagues what they worked on.
**A holiday week or quarter end** is the first week back. Check the calendar when you choose the dates.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: When should the first-use plan be written on a residential?
quiz.a: In the last full work block, with a date in the first five working days back.

quiz.q: You are an external facilitator and the sponsor says line managers are too busy for a briefing call. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the sponsor to send the short manager note in their own name and keep the fifteen minute conversation. A note takes five minutes and tells managers the one thing you need from them.

quiz.q: Three weeks after the event, half the group say they have not held their planned conversation. How do you run the follow-up?
quiz.a: Without blame. Ask what got in the way, rehearse the opening again in pairs and have each person set a new date before the call ends.

parts.title: Facilitate a working offsite
parts.summary: How to prepare, run and follow up an offsite whose product is a decision, a plan or a team that works better, from the first interviews to the 30-day check.

topics.title: Find out what the offsite is really for

situation.text: The chief executive of a 120-person software company books you for a two-day strategy offsite with her leadership team of ten. Her brief is one line: "We need to agree next year's priorities." On your second call the finance director tells you the priorities were agreed in March and nobody followed them.

items: **Make interviews a condition of the work.** Say to the leader: "Before I design anything I talk to every person who will be in the room, for half an hour each. I report themes to you. I never report who said what." If the leader refuses, you are designing blind and should say so.
**Ask the leader to send the invitation** in their own name, with your promise about names in it. People believe the promise more when the boss has put it in writing.

**Book 30 minutes with each attendee** by video call, two to three weeks ahead. Interview the leader first, for 45 minutes. Ten people is about six hours of calls plus two hours to sort the notes. Charge for it as design time.

**Open every call with the same words:** "Nothing you say will be attached to your name. I will give the team a one-page summary of themes, and you will see the same page the boss sees." Then ask the same questions in the same order, from the list below.
**Take notes yourself and do not record.** After each call, write three lines: what this person thinks the offsite is for, what they think is in the way, and what they said with most feeling.

**Sort the notes into themes** when all the calls are done. Count how many people raised each one. A point becomes a theme when three or more people raised it without being asked. Reword every example so that no job title, project or turn of phrase points to one person.

**Play the themes back to the leader** on a 45 minute call, a week before the event. Send the page ten minutes before the call, not the night before. Start with what the team agrees on. Then ask: "Which of these surprises you?" and wait.
**Change the design to fit** what you heard, and tell the leader what you changed. Read the same page to the whole group in the first hour.

why.text: **Interviewing first is judgement, not research.** This is practitioner judgement. No study opened for this topic tests interviews before an offsite against going without them. There is more on [interviewing to find a training need](t:2.1) and on [the first conversation with a client](t:9.3). This topic is about a different question: what ten people each think they are coming to do.

**The stated question often hides another.** The leader's brief is one view out of ten. Facilitators commonly find that the stated question sits on top of another one. Here the team does not need new priorities. It needs to know why the last set did not hold. A design built on the brief alone would have produced a second list and the same result by the summer.

**The interviews also do work in the room.** People who have said the awkward thing once, privately, find it easier to say again. When you read out a theme that seven of ten raised, nobody has to be the first to raise it. That is the main reason for reporting counts and not names.

**The promise about names must survive pressure.** The promise about names is the whole value of the exercise, so it has to survive pressure. Leaders often ask who said a thing. Decide your answer before the call, and practise it.

try.text: Interview two colleagues or friends about a real team meeting they both attend, 20 minutes each, using the questions below. Write a half-page of themes. Then say the playback aloud to a third person who plays the leader and asks you, twice, who said it. Record the playback. Good looks like this: you start with what people agree on, every theme has a count, and you refuse the name without apologising.

try.title: The interview questions, in order (30 minutes)
lines: 1. What is your role, and how long have you been on this team?
2. In your own words, what is this offsite for?
3. If it goes well, what will exist at the end that does not exist now?
4. What has this team decided in the last year that held? What made it hold?
5. What has it decided that did not hold? What happened?
6. What does this team not talk about that it needs to?
7. What would make these two days a waste of your time?
8. What do you need from the chief executive in the room? And from me?
9. Is there anything I should know so that you can take a full part: access, health, timing, anything else?
10. What have I not asked that I should have?
Listen for: the same point from many people, a point made with heat by a few, and any gap between what the leader says the offsite is for and what everyone else says.

items: **The leader asks who said it.** Say: "I promised each of them I would not say, and I made you the same promise. What I can tell you is that six people raised it."
**Only one person could have raised** a theme, such as the only director based abroad. Leave it out of the page and raise it with that person: "Do you want this in the summary, and in what words?"
**Someone raises a matter for HR**, such as bullying. Say it is outside what the summary can handle, and ask what they would like to happen next. There is more on [your professional limits](t:4.16).
**You soften the page** because the leader is paying. The team will see the same page in the room and will know what was cut.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: How many people should raise a point before you report it as a theme, on a team of ten?
quiz.a: Three or more, without being prompted. Fewer than that and the point can be traced to a person.

quiz.q: On the playback call the chief executive says: "I think I know who said the thing about me having already decided. Was it the sales director?" What do you do?
quiz.a: Decline to confirm or deny, and give the count instead: six of ten raised it. The interviews are only useful while people believe the promise about names, and she will need that trust in the room.

quiz.q: A sponsor says there is no time or budget for interviews and asks you to send a ten-question survey instead. What do you say?
quiz.a: Offer a shorter version before you give up the calls: 20 minutes each with at least the leader and five others. A survey gives you answers without the follow-up question, and it is the follow-up that tells you what the offsite is really for.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement about preparing a facilitated offsite. No research was opened for it.

topics.title: Agree with the leader how decisions will be made
topics.theory: Decision rules and the leader's role in the room

situation.text: Ten leaders spend a day and a half working up three options for next year. At the end the chief executive thanks everyone and says she will think about it over the weekend. Half the room believed they were there to decide. They drive home feeling they were consulted for show.

items: **Hold a 45 minute call** with the leader at least two weeks before the offsite, after the interviews. Its only subject is how each decision will be made.
**List the decisions the offsite must produce**, one line each, as questions. "Which one of three growth bets do we fund next year?" is a decision. "Discuss growth" is not.

**Ask who decides, for each decision:** "When the discussion ends, who decides, and how?" Offer the four rules in the table below and let the leader choose one for each line. Different decisions on the same agenda can have different rules.

**Ask what is already decided.** Use these words: "Is there an answer you would not accept, whatever the team says?" If there is, that point is out of scope and you will say so in the opening. People forgive a fixed point. They do not forgive finding it out afterwards.

**Agree a fallback and a time.** "If we do not have consent by 10:45 on day two, you decide in the room, with your reasons." Without a fallback, a consent or consensus rule can run until the coaches leave.

**Agree how the leader behaves.** Ask for three things: they speak last in every round, they ask questions before giving views, and they say the decision rule aloud themselves in the opening. The advice on [a senior person who takes over](t:4.38) gives the wording for this call and for holding them to it in the room.
**Write the agreement on one page** the same day and send it to the leader. Ask for a reply that says "agreed". Bring it printed.
**Have the leader read the rule** for each decision on the day, before the block that produces it. Write it on a flipchart sheet that stays on the wall.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. The four rules are standard in the facilitation literature, and Kaner's guide, listed below, gives whole chapters to them. No study opened for this topic compares one rule with another, and the notes on when each suits are working guidance.

**Confusion over who decides damages trust.** The reasoning is about what people think they are doing. A team that believes it is deciding argues to win. A team that knows it is advising argues to inform, and can live with a decision that goes another way. Both are workable. What damages trust is a room where some people think one and some think the other. In the interviews for this team, six of ten were unsure who decides.

**The leader deciding is often right.** Most leadership teams are not democracies, and it is honest to say so. "The leader decides after hearing every view" is the commonest rule in practice and often the right one, because the leader carries the result. Consent is slower and gives stronger commitment, since each person has said aloud that they can support the choice. Full consensus is rare and expensive. A vote is quick and leaves a losing side, so keep it for small matters.

**A hidden fixed point wastes the event.** The fixed points matter as much as the rule. If the budget is set, saying so in the first ten minutes costs a moment of disappointment. Letting the team spend two hours on it costs the rest of the event.

try.text: Rehearse the call aloud with a colleague playing a leader who says "we will just see how it goes on the day". Your task is to leave with a rule and a fallback for each decision, in 15 minutes. Record it. Listen for the moment you ask what is already decided, and check that you waited for the answer.

try.title: A worked example: the pre-offsite agreement with the leader
lines: Strategy offsite, leadership team of ten. Agreed by phone and confirmed by email.
Decision 1: which one of three growth bets we fund next year. Rule: the chief executive decides after hearing every view, in the room on day two, with reasons.
Decision 2: what we stop doing to make room for it. Rule: consent. Fallback: if there is no consent by 12:00 on day two, the chief executive decides.
Decision 3: how a new priority gets added during the year. Rule: consent, same fallback.
Not for decision: the headcount budget is fixed for next year. The price rise in January goes ahead. The chief executive will say both in the opening.
In scope for comment, not decision: the sales team structure. Views will be recorded and taken to the board.
The chief executive will read each rule aloud before the block it applies to.
She will speak last in every round and ask questions before she gives a view.
If the facilitator thinks the room is waiting for her view, the facilitator will ask her to hold it. She has agreed to this.

Nothing said in the interviews or the room will be attributed to a person in the write-up.

items: **The leader says "consensus"** and means "I decide, and I would like them to agree". Ask what happens if one person still says no at four o'clock. The answer tells you the real rule.

**The leader has already decided** and wants the offsite to produce the same answer. Say plainly that you will not run a discussion with a fixed result. Offer a different event: the leader announces the decision, and the team works on how to carry it out.
**The leader forgets the agreed rule** under pressure. Point to the sheet on the wall: "We said consent for this one. Can I check with each person?"
**The leader speaks first** out of habit. Use the hold you agreed: "Rachel, I will come to you last, as we said."
**Someone not in the room** turns out to be needed for a decision. Record it as a recommendation with an owner and a date for taking it to that person.

items.label: Kaner (2014), Facilitator's Guide to Participatory Decision-Making, third edition. Jossey-Bass. The contents list includes chapters on decision rules.

quiz.q: Under a consent rule, what stops a proposal?
quiz.a: An objection that someone cannot live with. Preferring another option is not enough, and objections are used to improve the proposal.

quiz.q: A managing director tells you: "I want the team to feel they own the strategy, so let them decide. But it has to include the Germany launch." What do you do?
quiz.a: Take the Germany launch out of scope and have the director say so in the opening. Then agree a real rule for what is left, because a team that discovers a fixed answer halfway through stops trusting every other decision.

quiz.q: It is 11:50 on day two. The rule was consent, the fallback time is 12:00, and two people still object to the proposal. What do you do?
quiz.a: Name the time, ask each objector for the one change that would let them support it, and test that change with the room. If it does not land by 12:00, hand to the leader to decide with reasons, as agreed in advance.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement and standard facilitation practice. The one source is a practitioner book, checked from its description.

topics.title: Open a question up, then narrow it
topics.theory: Silent writing, grouping and narrowing to a shortlist

situation.text: You ask a leadership team of ten: "Where could next year's growth come from?" The sales director answers within three seconds. For the next forty minutes the group discusses her idea. Four people say nothing, and the flipchart holds one option and some objections to it.

items: **Write the question on the wall** before the block, as one sentence that starts with "How", "Where" or "What". Read it aloud and ask one person to say it back in their own words.
**Start in silence.** Each person writes alone for seven minutes, one idea on each sticky note, in thick pen, at least five notes. Say the number. People stop at three unless you ask for more.
**Put people in pairs** for five minutes to read their notes to each other and add any new ones. Nobody judges an idea yet.

**Collect the notes on the wall** one at a time, going round the room. Each person reads one note and sticks it up. Others with the same idea add theirs on top. Keep going until the hands are empty. The leader goes last in each round.
**Group in silence.** Everyone stands and moves the notes into clusters without talking, for five minutes. Then name each cluster together and write the name on a different-coloured note.
**Discuss the clusters, not the notes.** Take questions of understanding first: "What does this one mean?" Then give each cluster two minutes on what would have to be true for it to work.

**Narrow by a method you named** at the start. Use dots for a first cut: three dots each, placed at the same moment, the leader last. Use criteria when the shortlist will become a decision: score each cluster against the two or three tests agreed with the leader.

**Read the result aloud** and ask: "Is anything below the line that we would regret dropping?" Move one item up if someone makes the case. Write the shortlist on a clean sheet. Dots make a shortlist. The decision comes later, by the rule agreed with the leader.

why.text: The first half of this sequence rests on research. The second half is craft.

**Talking groups produce fewer ideas.** The research is about producing ideas. Mullen, Johnson and Salas pooled the earlier studies that compared a group brainstorming aloud with the same number of people working separately and having their ideas combined afterwards. The talking groups produced fewer ideas, and ideas of lower quality. The loss was larger in bigger groups, and larger when people spoke their ideas than when they wrote them. Diehl and Stroebe ran four experiments to find the cause. Fear of being judged and leaving the work to others each played a part, but the main cause was waiting: only one person can talk at a time.

why.title: Groups that brainstorm aloud
why.found: Across earlier studies, interacting groups produced fewer and poorer ideas than the same number of people working apart. The loss grew with group size.
why.means: Have people write alone before anyone speaks, above all in a group of ten.

why.text: **The studies support writing alone first.** These were laboratory studies of listing ideas, and neither summary says anything about leadership teams or strategy. They support one design choice strongly: have people write alone before anyone speaks. Writing removes the queue.

**The rest is practitioner judgement.** Facilitators find that the first idea spoken tends to become the subject of the meeting, and that it usually comes from the most senior or the quickest person. Collecting one note at a time spreads ownership of the wall. Placing dots at the same moment stops people copying the leader. None of this has been tested in a study opened for this topic. There is more on [working on flipcharts and walls](t:4.18).

try.text: Run the first 30 minutes of the run sheet with four or five colleagues or friends on a real question, such as "What could we do with the spare room at the office?" Give every instruction aloud, once, and keep the times with a visible timer. Good looks like this: nobody spoke during the writing, every person put up at least three notes, and you did not comment on any idea.

head: Minute

rows: Question on the wall. State how the block ends
"The question is: where could next year's growth come from? In an hour we will have a shortlist of three. We are not deciding today."

"Seven minutes on your own, in silence. One idea on each note, big enough to read from two metres. At least five. Go."
Pairs read notes to each other and add more
"Turn to your neighbour. Read your notes to each other. No judging. If a new idea comes, write it. Five minutes."
Notes go up one at a time, round the room
"One note each, read it out and stick it up. If you have the same one, put it on top. Rachel, I will come to you last each round."

"Everyone up. Move notes that belong together, without talking. If a note keeps moving, copy it and put it in both."

"First, is there any note you do not understand? Now, for each cluster: what would have to be true for this to work?"

"Three tests, agreed beforehand: it can show revenue within 12 months, we can staff it without new hires, and it fits larger customers."

"Three dots each. Choose in your seat first. No more than one dot on any cluster. Now everyone up and place them together."

"Four clusters have five dots or more. Is there anything lower down that we would regret dropping?"

"Our shortlist is these three. Who will lead the work on each one this afternoon?"

items: **The leader comments on notes** as they go up. Hold it lightly: "Views in the next step. For now we are only getting them on the wall."
**Someone refuses to write** and wants to "just talk it through". Keep the seven minutes and say why: "This is how we hear from all ten of you, and I will open it up straight after."
**Dots turn into the decision.** Say at the start and again at the end that dots make a shortlist. The decision is made by the rule agreed with the leader.
**A good idea with one dot** disappears. Ask the regret question every time, and keep a visible list of what was set aside.

items.label: Mullen, Johnson and Salas (1991), Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: a meta-analytic integration. Basic and Applied Social Psychology, 12(1). Abstract on Scilit.
Diehl and Stroebe (1987), Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: toward the solution of a riddle. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 53(3). Abstract on Scilit.

quiz.q: In Diehl and Stroebe's experiments, what explained most of the loss of ideas in groups that brainstormed aloud?
quiz.a: Having to wait for a turn to speak, known as production blocking. Fear of judgement and leaving the work to others explained less.

quiz.q: You have 25 minutes, not 60, and the chief executive says: "Skip the sticky notes, we are all adults, let us just discuss it." What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep the silent writing and shorten everything else: four minutes writing, notes straight to the wall, a quick grouping and one round of voices. Writing first is the part with research behind it, and it is what gets ten views out in place of two.

quiz.q: After the dots, the option the sales director argued for has one dot, and she says the method is childish. How do you respond?
quiz.a: Ask the regret question openly and invite her to make the case for moving it up, with a two minute limit. The dots are a first cut and not the decision, so a reasoned case can change the shortlist without anyone losing face.

topics.tierReason: Writing alone before talking rests on a meta-analysis and a set of experiments on brainstorming, read in summary. The grouping and narrowing steps are practitioner judgement.

topics.title: Record decisions, owners and dates on the wall
topics.theory: The live decision log and the parked list

situation.text: At 16:00 on day two the leadership team feels it has agreed a great deal. You ask each person to write down, alone, what was decided about the partner channel. You get four different answers, and two people have written "explore further".

items: **Put up two sheets before people arrive** that stay on the wall for the whole event. Head one "Decisions" with four columns: decision, owner, by when, first step. Head the other "Parked". The advice on [working on flipcharts and walls](t:4.18) covers writing so the back of the room can read it.
**Write decisions the moment they are made**, in front of the group, each in a full sentence that starts with "We will". Stop the conversation to do it. Say: "Let me write that down before we go on."
**Read the sentence back and test it.** Ask: "Who does what, by when?" If nobody can answer, you have a wish and not a decision. Either finish it or move it to the parked list.

**Put one name in the owner column.** A person, in the room, who says yes aloud. "The sales team" and "all of us" are not owners. If the natural owner is absent, the owner is the person who will brief them, with a date for that.
**Ask the owner for a real date** and a first step that can happen in the next ten working days. "Quarter two" is not a date.
**Add what stops.** For every decision that adds work, ask: "What will we stop or delay to make room?" Write the answer as its own line with its own owner.

**Use the parked list** for anything important that is off today's question. Write it in the speaker's words and say when you will come back to it. Clear the list in the last hour: each item becomes a decision, gets an owner and a date for a later meeting, or is dropped by agreement.
**Close the log** before the close of the event. Each owner reads their own lines aloud. The leader goes last and says "agreed". Photograph both sheets before anyone touches them.

why.text: **This rests on what facilitators see.** This is practitioner judgement, with no research opened for it. The reasoning comes from what facilitators see in the weeks after an offsite.

**People leave with different memories.** A discussion that felt like agreement often is not one. People leave the same conversation with different memories of it, each tilted towards what they hoped for. Writing the sentence where everyone can see it, and asking them to correct it, brings the differences out while the group is still together and able to settle them. Found a week later, the same differences look like bad faith.

**The test question does most of the work.** "Who does what by when" turns "we should improve onboarding" into a named person, an action and a date, or shows that the group is not ready to decide. Both are useful to know at 11:00. Neither is useful to learn in the write-up.

**Shared ownership is how decisions stall.** A single owner matters because shared ownership is how decisions stall: each of two owners waits for the other. The parked list has a different job. It lets you protect the question in hand without dismissing the person who raised something else.
**The wall is also your raw material.** [The record you send afterwards](t:8.24) is the log typed up, and it should contain nothing the group did not see on the day.

try.text: At the next meeting you attend, keep a decision log on a sheet of paper without telling anyone. Each time something seems decided, write it as a "We will" sentence and try to fill in the owner and the date. Count how many lines you could complete. Then practise the interruption aloud, ten times, until it sounds ordinary: "Let me write that down before we go on. Who does what, by when?"

items: **You write a summary** of the discussion in the decision column. If the line does not start with "We will", it is a note. Ask the group to turn it into a decision or park it.
**Every line carries the leader's name.** Ask after the third one: "Which of these could someone else own?"
**Someone accepts a line** and their face says no. Ask kindly: "Is that date real for you, with everything else you have on?"

**The parked list hides hard topics:** it becomes the place where they are sent to be forgotten. If the same item is parked twice, it probably belongs in the room. There is guidance on [holding the conversation the team is avoiding](t:8.22).

**A participant acts as scribe** and writes the log. They stop taking part, and the wording becomes theirs. You hold the pen, or a co-facilitator does, as the advice on [working as a pair](t:4.17) describes.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What question tests whether a line on the wall is a decision?
quiz.a: Who does what, by when. If nobody can answer, it is a wish and should be finished or parked.

quiz.q: The group agrees "we need to be more customer-focused" and people nod. The leader says, "Good, write that up." What do you do?
quiz.a: Write it, then ask who will do what by when as a result. If no action follows, say that it is a statement of intent and ask whether the group wants to turn it into one concrete decision or leave it out of the log.

quiz.q: With 30 minutes left there are nine items on the parked list and the room is tired. What do you do?
quiz.a: Go through them at one minute each with three choices only: decide now, give it an owner and a meeting date, or drop it. Anything left unsorted will be read later as a promise nobody kept.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement about recording decisions in a facilitated meeting. No research was opened for it.

topics.title: Hold the conversation the team has been avoiding
topics.theory: Facilitating a hard conversation, and the limits of the role

situation.text: It is 11:20 on day two. The product director is explaining the roadmap when the sales director says, quietly, "We have had this roadmap three times. It changes whenever one customer shouts." Nobody moves. The chief executive looks at you. In the interviews, five of ten people raised this, and it has never been said in a meeting.

items: **Know the signs that it has started.** The room goes still. People look at the table or at the leader. Someone makes a joke, or says "let us take that offline". When you see two of these together, stop following the agenda.

**Name it and ask permission**, in one breath: "I think something important has just been said. I would like to stay with it for twenty minutes before we go on. Is that all right with everyone?" Look at the leader last. Most groups say yes, with relief.
**Slow it down.** Sit down if you were standing. Ask the person who spoke for an example: "Can you tell us about one time it happened?" Examples can be worked on. General statements start fights.

**Hear one person at a time.** Say the rule: "One voice at a time, and I will make sure each of you is heard. Nobody has to speak." After each speaker, say back what you heard in one sentence and check: "Have I got that right?" This gives the speaker proof of being heard and everyone else a few seconds to think.
**Ask the other side to speak** for themselves, and about themselves. "What is it like on your side when that happens?" is better than "What do you say to that?"
**Bring in the rest of the room** once the two or three most involved have spoken: "One sentence each on how this affects your work. Pass if you want to." The leader speaks last, as agreed.

**Turn towards the future** before the time runs out. Ask: "What would each of you need, to do this differently from Monday?" Write the answers on the wall. If one becomes a decision, put it in the log with an owner and a date.
**Close it properly.** Say what was covered and what was not, and take a real break of fifteen minutes. Check quietly with the people most involved during it.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study opened for this topic tests these moves. There is [research on psychological safety](t:1.17), and the guidance on [building trust before asking for openness](t:8.3) applies it to retreats.

**The team learns whether speaking is safe.** Teams avoid a subject because raising it has felt more dangerous than living with it. An offsite changes the balance for a short time: there is a stranger in the room whose job is to keep order, and the interviews have shown that others feel the same. When the subject surfaces, the group watches what happens to the person who raised it. If the meeting moves on, or turns into an argument, they learn that it is still not safe.

**Your role has an edge.** You are there to help a team talk about its work. A personal dispute between two people, a complaint about someone's conduct, or distress that goes beyond the moment is outside it. Acas describes workplace mediation as a voluntary and confidential process run by a neutral mediator, used for relationship breakdowns and bullying, and generally not used for disputes about pay, dismissal or conduct. That is a separate service. When the conversation reaches that edge, stop it in the room and take it to the people whose job it is. There is separate guidance on [conflict between two participants](t:4.41), on [distress in an ordinary session](t:4.42) and on [your professional limits](t:4.16).

try.text: With two colleagues, set up a small real disagreement about work, such as how a shared document should be organised. They talk. You facilitate for ten minutes using only three moves: say back what you heard, ask for an example, and ask the other person what it is like on their side. Record it. Good looks like this: you spoke for less than a quarter of the time, you offered no opinion, and each of them says afterwards that you got their point right.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: To start: "I think something important has just been said. Can we stay with it for twenty minutes?"
To slow down: "Before anyone answers, let me check I heard that."
To say it back: "What I hear is that the roadmap has changed three times and you found out from a customer. Is that right?"
To get an example: "Can you tell us about one time it happened? What did you see?"
To the other side: "You do not need to defend it. What is it like on your side when that happens?"
To hold an interruption: "Hold that. I will come to you next, and I want to hear the end of this first."
To the leader, if they step in: "Rachel, I would like two more voices before yours, as we agreed."
To turn it: "What would each of you need, to do this differently from Monday?"
To stop when it turns personal: "I am going to pause us. This has moved from how the team works to something between two people, and this room is the wrong place for that."
To close: "We have covered how roadmap changes reach sales. We have not covered commission, and that is on the parked list. Fifteen minutes' break."
At the break, one to one: "That was a lot. How are you doing? Is there anything you need before we start again?"

try.title: Stay with it, or stop and take it outside the room

head: What you see
What you do
rows: A disagreement about how the work is done: priorities, handovers, who was told what
Stay with it. This is what the offsite is for
Strong feeling, a raised voice or tears, and the person wants to go on
Slow down, offer a pause and let them choose. Feeling is not a reason to stop
A remark about someone's character or ability, not their actions
Stop it at once. Restate the rule: we talk about what happened, not about what someone is like
An allegation of bullying, harassment or discrimination
Stop the discussion, say it will be taken seriously outside the room, and tell the sponsor and the HR contact the same day
Two people locked in an old dispute while eight others watch
End it in the room. Suggest to the leader afterwards that the two of them are offered a trained mediator
Someone discloses a health or personal crisis
Thank them, take a break, speak to them privately and follow [the incident plan](t:8.15)
The leader is the subject, and starts to answer every point
Call a break and speak to the leader alone. Ask them to listen for one full round before replying

items: **You open the subject yourself** because the interviews told you it was there. Bring the theme as a count on the page and let the group choose to pick it up. Forcing it breaks the choice that the guidance on [building trust before asking for openness](t:8.3) says people must have.
**You try to solve it.** Your job is that each side is heard and one next step is agreed. A problem that took two years to build will not be fixed before lunch.
**The person who raised it** is treated as a hero or a troublemaker afterwards. Say at the close that the point belonged to several people, which the interviews showed.
**You carry it home.** Talk it through with your co-facilitator the same evening.

items.label: Acas, Mediation at work: what mediation is and how it can help.

quiz.q: According to Acas, name two features of workplace mediation.
quiz.a: It is voluntary and confidential, and it is run by a neutral mediator who does not take sides.

quiz.q: The avoided subject comes up 25 minutes before lunch. The chief executive says, "Good point, let us pick that up another time," and reaches for the agenda. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the room, including her, for twenty minutes on it now. Moving on teaches the team that the subject is still not safe, and the interviews showed that half of them have been waiting for it.

quiz.q: During the conversation one director says to another: "The real problem is that you have never been up to this job." What do you do?
quiz.a: Stop it immediately and restate the rule that the group talks about actions and their effects, not about a person's worth. Take a break, check on both people separately, and tell the leader that anything further between those two belongs outside the room.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement. The description of mediation comes from an official Acas page.

topics.title: Run a strategy offsite and a team offsite
topics.theory: Timetables for an offsite whose product is a decision or a better way of working

situation.text: You have two bookings in the same month. One is a two-day strategy offsite for a leadership team of ten. The other is a day away for a customer support team of fourteen whose shift handovers keep going wrong. Your only worked timetables are for a skills course, with demonstrations and practice in threes. Neither group is there to learn a skill.

items: **Write the product of the event** as a list of things that will exist at the end. For a strategy offsite: the decisions, each with an owner and a date. For a team offsite: agreed goals, a page on who owns what, and one or two changes to how the team works.

**Give each product its own block** and work backwards. A decision needs three blocks before it: shared facts, options, and a worked-up shortlist. Put the decision itself on the morning of day two, after a night's sleep.

**Replace input with reading.** Where a skills day has a ten minute explanation, a working offsite has a two-page paper read in silence at the start of the block. Ask the owners of the facts to write these papers beforehand, and edit them.

**Use fewer, longer blocks** than a skills day. Ninety minutes is still the unit, as the guidance on [pacing a residential](t:8.10) sets out, but plan three blocks on a full day and leave slack after the one most likely to overrun.
**Start every block with people writing alone**, as in the [silent writing, grouping and narrowing](t:8.20) sequence. Keep the decision log in view all day.
**Leave the evening empty.** On a strategy offsite, post the worked-up options on the wall at 17:00 and decide nothing. People talk over dinner, and that is useful.
**Build the day on the work** for a team offsite: what the team is for, who does what, and one real problem solved together. Put any social activity at lunch or after the close and keep it optional.
**End with the log read aloud** and with what the group will tell colleagues, then a 20 minute close. Book the 30-day check before people leave.

why.text: The timetables are practitioner judgement. One piece of research bears on the team offsite.

**Pooled studies support a modest claim.** Klein and colleagues pooled studies of team building, defined by four components: goal setting, interpersonal relations, problem solving and role clarification. Their summary reports a moderate positive effect across the outcomes they looked at, strongest for how team members felt and how the team worked together. The summary says the paper examines each component and the effect of team size. It does not report which component did best, and the full paper was not read for this topic. So the research supports a modest claim, and nothing in it tests a one-day format or a day of games.

why.title: Does team building work?
why.found: Across 60 correlations, team building had a moderate positive effect on team outcomes, strongest for affective and process outcomes.
why.means: A structured team day is a reasonable thing to sell. Promise better working together, not better results.

why.text: **The team day works on real tasks.** The team day below uses three of the four components on real tasks. That choice is craft. Goals and roles produce pages the team can use on Monday, and solving a real problem together does more for working relations, in most facilitators' experience, than an exercise invented for the day.

**Here the output belongs to the group.** What differs from [the skills intensive timetable](t:8.10) follows from the product. There the output is in each person, so the day is built from demonstration, practice and feedback, and it ends with first-use plans. Here the output is on the wall and belongs to the group. Practice rounds give way to cycles of writing, discussing and deciding. The leader is a participant with a role agreed beforehand. You have no content to teach and should hold no view on the answer. Preparation moves as well: less time on materials, more on interviews and the agreement with the leader.

try.text: Take the strategy timetable and deliver the opening at 10:00 aloud, standing, to a colleague or a recording, in under 12 minutes: the purpose, the three decisions, the handover to the leader to read the decision rules, and the finish times. Then explain to your colleague, in one minute, why nothing is decided on day one. If you cannot say why, read the steps again.

items: **Fact papers arrive as 30-slide decks.** Send them back with a template: two pages, the three numbers that matter and what the author thinks they mean.

**Fixing one person** is what a team offsite is asked to do. That is a management conversation and not a group event. Say so to the sponsor, and use the method for [diagnosing what the problem is](t:2.29).
**You form a view** on the right strategy and start steering towards it. Give your process observations freely and keep your view on the answer to yourself.
**The decision comes on day one** because the room has energy at 16:45. Hold the plan. A choice that still stands after dinner and a night's sleep is worth more.

items.label: Klein, DiazGranados, Salas, Le, Burke, Lyons and Goodwin (2009), Does team building work? Small Group Research, 40(2). Abstract on the University of Central Florida repository.

quiz.q: In the summary of Klein and colleagues' meta-analysis, for which kinds of outcome was team building most strongly related?
quiz.a: Affective and process outcomes: how team members feel and how the team works together. The overall effect across outcomes was moderate and positive.

quiz.q: A head of support wants the team day to be "mostly fun, with an escape room and a nice lunch", because morale is low after a hard quarter. Interviews show the real complaint is unclear roles. What do you propose?
quiz.a: A working day on goals, roles and one real problem, with the escape room offered as an optional evening. Morale is low because of how the work is set up, and a day that fixes part of that will do more for it than a day that avoids it.

quiz.q: At 16:45 on day one of a strategy offsite the chief executive says, "I think we all know the answer. Let us decide now and finish early tomorrow." What do you say?
quiz.a: Suggest she holds the decision until 09:15 as planned, and ask everyone to write their choice alone first thing. If the answer is the same in the morning it has cost nothing, and anyone with doubts has had a chance to voice them.

topics.tierReason: The value of structured team building rests on one meta-analysis read in summary. The timetables and the comparison with a skills intensive are practitioner judgement.

topics.title: Send the write-up and keep the decisions alive
topics.theory: The record, the 30-day check and what to do when decisions stall

situation.text: The strategy offsite ended on Friday with seven lines in the decision log. Three weeks later you ring the chief executive. Two decisions have been carried out. One has been quietly reopened in a corridor. Nobody can find the photographs of the wall, and the sales director remembers the Germany decision differently.

items: **Block two hours in your diary** for the morning after the offsite, before you leave for it. The write-up goes out within two working days. After that people's memories have already started to differ, and the record reads as your version.

**Write two pages and no more.** Page one is the decision log, typed from the photographs, in the words on the wall. Page two holds the parked items and what happened to each, the message agreed for the rest of the company, and the dates of the next steps.
**Add nothing new.** No analysis, no recommendations, no account of who argued what. If a line on the wall was unclear, ring its owner and ask. Do not tidy it yourself.

**Send it to the leader first**, with one question: "Is this what you saw decided?" Give them until the end of the day. Then the leader sends it to the team in their own name, with the photographs attached.
**Hold the 30-day check with the leader.** Thirty minutes by video call, booked before the offsite ended. Go down the log line by line and mark each one done, moving, stalled or changed.

**Find out the kind of stall** for each stalled line, using the table below, and agree one action. Most stalls come from an owner with no time, a decision that was never really accepted, or facts that have changed.

**Put the log on the team's agenda:** ask the leader to make it the first item of the team's regular meeting for the next three months. Five minutes: each owner says done, moving or stuck. This is the leader's job, and it outlasts your contract.
**Send a three-line note after the check:** what is done, what is stuck, what the leader has agreed to do. Then [close out and hand over the work](t:9.26).

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. The two-day and 30-day timings are working conventions and no research opened for this topic supports either number. The same point applies to [follow-up dates for training](t:5.4), and there is more on [returning to work after a residential](t:8.17).

**A short record can be checked.** The write-up is short because of what it is for. It is a record that ten people can check against their own memory in five minutes, and that the rest of the company can be shown. A twenty-page report with your reflections is harder to check and easier to ignore. Sending it through the leader matters as well. A record from the facilitator is a consultant's document. The same record from the chief executive is what the team is working to.

**Decisions stall for ordinary reasons.** The owner went back to a full diary. Someone who went along with the decision in the room has since said, to one colleague at a time, that they never agreed. This is what happens to any decision without a routine behind it, and the regular agenda item is that routine.

**An outsider can only ask and notice.** As an outside supplier you can ask and you can notice. You cannot make anyone do anything. The 30-day check works because the leader hears the state of each line from someone with no stake in the answer. Write the check into the proposal so that it is paid for and expected. There is more on [keeping the relationship going after that](t:9.36).

try.text: Take the notes from any meeting you attended this week and write the record in the form below, in 30 minutes. Then rehearse the 30-day check aloud with a colleague playing a leader who says of one line: "That one has slipped, we have been busy." Your task is to find out which kind of stall it is with two questions, without sounding like an auditor. Record it and listen to your tone.

try.title: A worked example: the write-up, filled in
lines: Leadership offsite, 26 and 27 November. Record of decisions. Sent by the chief executive on Tuesday 1 December.
Who was there: all ten members of the leadership team. Facilitated by two outside facilitators.
What we set out to do: choose one growth bet for next year, agree what stops, and agree how a new priority gets added.
Decisions (full log with first steps attached): 1. Fund selling to larger customers. Owner: chief executive. 2. No Germany launch next year, review on 15 September. Owner: sales director.
3. Pause the partner pilot by 31 January. Owner: head of partnerships. 4. No custom features below the size threshold from 1 January. Owner: product director.
5. A new priority is added only when the team agrees what it replaces. Owner: chief executive. 6. Two engineers move to the larger-customer work by 1 February. Owner: engineering director.
Recommendation to the board on 14 January: change commission to favour larger deals. Owner: finance director.
How decisions were made: decision 1 by the chief executive after hearing all views. Decisions 2 to 6 by consent.
Parked and dealt with: pricing page (December meeting, marketing director). Monday meeting (now 45 minutes with written updates, from 7 December).
Out of scope: reporting line for customer success. The chief executive will take views one to one.

What we are telling the company: "Next year we are putting our growth effort into larger customers. To make room, the partner pilot pauses and Germany waits. You will hear what this means for your team from your director by 4 December."
Next dates: owners report at the leadership meeting on 7 December and monthly after that. Check with the facilitator on 7 January.
Attached: photographs of the decision log and the parked list as they stood at 13:00 on 27 November.

**The write-up names who said what.** It records decisions and owners only, as promised in the working agreement.
**The leader sits on the draft** for a week. Agree the two-day deadline in the pre-offsite agreement, and send a reminder with the draft pasted into the email.
**A decision is reversed privately** between the leader and one director. Say to the leader that the team will find out, and that a decision changed in the open costs less trust than one that fades.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: How long is the write-up, and what goes on page one?
quiz.a: Two pages. Page one is the decision log, typed in the words that were on the wall.

quiz.q: While typing the log you find a line that reads "Sort out onboarding. Owner: Helen. January." You are fairly sure you know what was meant. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ring the owner and ask for the full sentence, then use her words. Guessing puts your interpretation into a record that the team is meant to recognise as its own.

quiz.q: At the 30-day check the chief executive says the partner pilot was not paused after all, because the head of partnerships "made a good case" to her privately. What do you suggest?
quiz.a: That she takes the change to the next team meeting, says what new information changed her mind, and records it as a changed decision. The team agreed how priorities change, and a private reversal in the first month undoes that agreement.

parts.title: The commercial side of a retreat
parts.summary: Who signs with the venue, who carries the money risk, and how to price a retreat so your fee survives changes in cost and numbers.

topics.title: Know who signs the venue contract and who carries the risk
topics.theory: Venue contracts: deposits, minimum numbers, cancellation and who is liable

situation.text: A client loves the country house you found for their leadership offsite. The venue sends a contract for £14,000 with a 30 per cent deposit due in seven days, and asks whose name goes on it. The client says, "You deal with it, just add it to your invoice." You have been trading for four months.

items: **Decide who signs** before you talk about price. Either the client signs the venue contract and pays the venue direct while you advise and manage, or you sign, pay the venue and charge the client. Make the first route your default while your business is small.
**Stay useful if the client signs.** Read the contract for them, note the points below on one page, and be the venue's named contact. Charge for this as planning days.
**Write each money clause down** in plain words: the deposit and whether it is refundable, when the balance is due, the minimum numbers, and the last date to reduce numbers without charge.
**Find the attrition clause**, which says how far numbers can fall and what you pay for empty places. Ask for the right to reduce by 10 per cent up to four weeks before, in writing.
**Copy out the cancellation scale** as a table of dates and percentages. Put the dates in your diary and the client's.
**Ask what happens if the venue cancels** or double-books, and what its clause on events outside anyone's control covers. Do not assume it covers a client that changes its mind.

**Mirror every venue term if you sign**, in your own terms with the client, with dates seven days earlier than the venue's. Take the deposit from the client before you pay it. There is more on [your own cancellation wording](t:9.9).

**Take advice before you sign** your first venue contract, and before you sell bedrooms or travel inside your own price: a solicitor on the contract, an accountant on VAT, your insurer on cancellation cover. There is separate guidance on [event insurance](t:9.19).

why.text: **The steps are practitioner judgement about commercial risk.** The legal and tax points come from official UK pages opened for this topic. This is general information, not legal advice.

**Whoever signs owes the venue the money.** If the client cuts the group from sixteen to nine, or cancels three weeks out, the venue looks to the name on the contract. Signing also puts the cash through your account: you pay a deposit months ahead and wait for the client's payment run.

**Signing can change your legal position.** Government guidance on the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018 says a package is generally a combination of two or more different types of travel service for the same trip. Accommodation is one type and carriage of passengers is another. The trader who combines and sells a package is the organiser, is liable for the services in it and must hold insolvency protection. Business travellers are generally covered, though packages bought under a general agreement, such as a framework contract with a business travel agency, are outside the rules. The guidance does not deal expressly with conferences or training events. If you sell bedrooms together with a coach or flights at one price, find out whether the rules apply to you.

**VAT changes too.** HMRC's notice on the Tour Operators' Margin Scheme names a company organising conferences with delegate accommodation as an example of who it can cover. Accommodation or passenger transport that you buy in and resell in your own name falls within the scheme, and a business customer buying for its own use cannot be given a VAT invoice for it. A separate HMRC page says a cost counts as a disbursement only if conditions are met, among them that the client was responsible for paying the supplier and that you pass on the exact amount.

**Money already paid may be recoverable.** When an event becomes impossible, section 1 of the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943 says that under a frustrated contract governed by English law, money already paid can be recovered, though a court may let the other side keep some for expenses. Whether a contract is frustrated at all is a question for a solicitor.

"That way you get the venue's VAT invoice direct, and there is no handling charge on that part."

items: **The venue's reduction date passes** while the client is still confirming names. Send the client a reminder two weeks before each date, with the cost of missing it.
**Your terms are softer** than the venue's. If the venue charges 100 per cent inside four weeks and you charge the client 50 per cent, the gap is yours.
**You rely on this page.** Rules change, and contract wording decides most outcomes. Check the official pages below and take advice on your own facts.

GOV.UK, Package holidays: complying with regulations, guidance for businesses.

HM Revenue and Customs, VAT: costs or disbursements passed to customers.
