quiz.q: According to the government guidance on the package travel regulations, what generally makes a package?
quiz.a: A combination of two or more different types of travel service for the same trip, such as accommodation and carriage of passengers.

quiz.q: A client asks you to sign a £14,000 venue contract in your own name and invoice them afterwards on 30 day terms. The venue wants 30 per cent in seven days. What do you propose?
quiz.a: That the client signs and pays the venue direct while you manage the booking for a planning fee. If they insist, take the deposit from them before you sign and mirror the venue's terms in yours, because the venue will hold whoever signed to the full amount.

quiz.q: Five weeks before an offsite the client says six of sixteen people can no longer come. The client signed the venue contract. What do you do the same day?
quiz.a: Check the attrition clause and the reduction date, tell the client in writing what the six empty places will cost and by when numbers can still be cut, and ask the venue what it can offer. Then look at whether the design still works for ten.

topics.title: Price a retreat and protect your margin
topics.theory: Fees, pass-through costs, handling charges and payment stages

situation.text: You quote £18,000 all-in for a two-day strategy offsite. The venue comes in £1,500 higher than the first estimate, the client adds two people, and you spend three unplanned days on rooming lists and dietary forms. When the last invoice is paid you work out that you earned less per day than your floor rate.

items: **Split the quote into two parts** and never mix them. Fee is what you charge for your own work. Pass-through costs are what other suppliers charge for the event: venue, bedrooms, food, transport, outside providers, printing.

**Count every day of your own work** as fee, at a rate above the floor you worked out for [your day rate](t:9.28). Include the days that usually go unpaid: interviews, the site visit, venue liaison, the joining pack, travel the night before, the write-up and the 30-day check.
**List pass-through costs at the supplier's price**, with the quote attached. Where the client can pay a supplier direct, let them. That line then leaves your invoice and your risk.

**Charge openly for handling** what does pass through your books. Choose one method. A management fee is a stated percentage or fixed sum on top of the costs you handle. A mark-up is built into each line so the client sees one price. Say which you use. The worked example uses a visible management fee of 15 per cent, which is a made-up figure.
**Add contingency on the pass-through costs** as its own line, as the [full cost of a residential](t:8.13) does, and say what happens to it: unspent contingency is returned or never invoiced.

**Tie payment stages to the dates** you must pay others. The client's first payment lands before the venue deposit leaves your account. The second lands before the venue balance is due. Only your delivery fee waits until after the event.
**State what changes the price:** numbers up or down after a named date, extra interviews, a change of venue, a second site visit. Give the day rate that applies.
**Reconcile within two weeks after the event.** Send the client the actual pass-through costs against the estimate, with receipts, and return what is owed.

why.text: **This is practitioner judgement and arithmetic.** No research sits behind it, and every figure below is invented. There is more on [scoping and pricing in general](t:9.4), and a separate breakdown lays out [the full cost of a residential](t:8.13) from the client's side. This topic is about your side of the same event.

**Supplier price rises eat a blended fee.** An all-in price hides two different things in one number. Your fee is yours to set and to protect. The venue's price is not. When they are blended, every rise in a supplier's cost comes out of your earnings, and the client cannot see why the total is what it is. Splitting them means a higher venue quote is a conversation about the venue.

**A visible fee beats a hidden mark-up.** Handling other people's invoices is work and carries risk. You chase quotes, check bills, pay ahead and stand between the client and the supplier when something goes wrong. A management fee charges for that in plain sight. A hidden mark-up earns the same money until the client sees the venue's own price list. Some clients forbid mark-ups in their purchasing terms, part of [how large organisations buy](t:9.35).

**Paying the deposit yourself is a loan.** Payment stages protect a small business more than any other line. A venue deposit paid from your own account, with the client paying 60 days later, is a loan from you to a larger company. You can check [the rules on late payment](t:9.9).

**Tax sits outside this sum.** How VAT applies to costs you pass on, and to bedrooms or travel you resell, depends on who contracts with the supplier. The official pages are listed with the guidance on [who signs the venue contract](t:8.25). Ask an accountant before your first quote.

try.text: Take a retreat you might run and build the quote in the table shape below, with your own rate from [working out your day rate](t:9.28). Then present it aloud to a colleague playing a client who says: "Why am I paying you 15 per cent on top of the hotel?" Answer in three sentences without lowering the figure. Record it. Offer the alternative once: the client pays the venue direct and the fee falls away.

**You leave out the planning days** because they feel like overhead. On a residential they can equal the delivery days. Show them as a line.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a mark-up and a management fee?
quiz.a: A mark-up is built into the price of each cost, so the client sees one figure. A management fee is shown as a separate percentage or sum for handling those costs.

quiz.q: A client asks for "one simple price per person" for a retreat of sixteen. Three weeks before the event, the group drops to eleven. How should your quote have been built?
quiz.a: With a fixed fee for your work and per-person lines only for the venue and food. Your design and facilitation days do not shrink when five people drop out, so a per-head price would have cut your earnings by almost a third.

quiz.q: The venue wants a 30 per cent deposit on signing, and the client's payment terms are 60 days. You are holding the venue contract. What do you do?
quiz.a: Make the first payment stage a condition of booking: the deposit reaches you before you sign. If the client cannot pay ahead, ask them to contract with the venue direct.

stages.name: Work with clients
stages.question: How do we win the work, shape it with the client, and run it well?

parts.title: Win and scope the work
parts.summary: Who buys training, the brief, the price, the proposal and what success means.

topics.title: Know who buys training, and what they are buying
topics.theory: The learning and development industry: roles, budgets and buyers

situation.text: A learning partner at a software company liked your talk and said, "Send me something on handling difficult customer calls." You sent a two-page outline. Three weeks later you have heard nothing, and you realise you do not know whether she has a budget, who asked her for anything, or how her company buys from a new supplier.

items: **Draw three boxes on a page** before the next call: the buyer (holds the budget and signs), the sponsor (has the problem and uses the result, usually the learners' manager or director) and the learner. Put a name or a question mark in each.
**Ask who holds the budget.** "If this went ahead, whose budget would it come from: the learning team's, the business unit's or HR's?"

**Ask what they are buying:** a skill, a compliance record, an event, or a change in results. "When this is finished, what do you need to be able to show? That people attended, that they can do something new, or that a number has moved?"
**Ask about the calendar.** "When does your budget year start, and when is next year's plan fixed?" Put both dates in your diary and get in touch a couple of months before the plan is fixed.

**Ask how they buy:** through procurement, from a list of approved suppliers, or on a manager's purchase order. There is more on [how large organisations buy](t:9.35). "What does a new supplier have to provide, and how long does that usually take?"

**Speak to the person with the problem** as well as the person who signs, and ask for it. "Could I have twenty minutes with the support director? I will design a better day if I hear it from her." Ask through your contact and invite her to join.
**Write what each person wants**, one line for each of the three people, in their own words. Fill any gap with a [discovery conversation](t:9.3) before you propose anything.

why.text: **Buyer, sponsor and learner want different things.** In most organisations the buyer, the sponsor and the learner are different people with different aims. A learning team often buys on behalf of a business unit that has the real problem. If you speak only to the learning team, you design for a second-hand account of that problem.

**Ask what is bought before you outline.** What is being bought shapes what counts as success. A team buying a record of attendance wants something different from a director buying a change in performance. The same one-day course can be right for one and a disappointment to the other, which is why the question comes before the outline.

**A UK survey shows busier learning teams.** The CIPD's Learning at work 2023 survey gives a UK view of the people who buy. It reported that learning budgets and headcount had recovered, and that 53% of learning staff said their team's workload had grown. Survey figures describe the people who answered. They do not measure the whole market.

**You need both buyer and sponsor.** The rest of this page is craft. In practice the buyer's aims decide whether the work is bought and the sponsor's decide whether it is bought again, so you need both. The trade-off is your contact's position: going round her to reach the director can cost you the relationship, so ask through her. In a small company the founder may be buyer and sponsor at once, and one conversation covers both. Inside a large client the buyer is several people: a learning team with its own roles, and procurement, IT and HR beside it. You can map who they are and [what each one cares about](t:9.34).

try.text: Take one prospective client. Fill in the three boxes with names, what each person wants and what you still need to ask. Then say your budget, calendar and buying questions aloud twice, so they come out plainly on the call. Good looks like this: no box holds a guess presented as a fact, and you know the date next year's plan is fixed.

**You assume learners want the course.** They often want something narrower than their director does. Write their aim down as well, because it decides how the day has to open.

quiz.q: Which three people in a client organisation usually have different aims?
quiz.a: The buyer, the sponsor and the learner.

quiz.q: A learning manager holds the budget and asks you for a negotiation course. The sales director is the one who asked her for it. What do you do before you propose anything?
quiz.a: Ask to speak to the sales director, because the director has the problem. Find out what result the director wants, then write down what the manager, the director and the sales staff each want.

quiz.q: In October a prospect says they like your course but there is no money for it. What do you ask?
quiz.a: When the budget year starts and when next year's plan is fixed. Budgets are set months ahead, so ask to be considered in that round and find out how they buy.

topics.tierReason: This is business practice about how training is bought. Industry surveys describe it, and no experiments test it.

topics.title: Sell and run a public course
topics.theory: Open courses where the learner is the buyer: motivation, pricing, drop-out and proof of value

situation.text: You plan a six-week evening course on presenting at work, with twelve places, open to anyone who books. People will pay with their own card. No employer is sending them, and nobody will chase them when work gets busy in week three.

items: **Describe the course in their words:** who it is for and what they will be able to do. Read the description to two people who fit it and ask, "Is this you?" Rewrite until they say yes without a pause.

**Price it against the alternatives:** what they would otherwise spend to get the same result, such as a rival course, a book or a few hours of coaching. Write those alternatives down with their prices and place yours among them.

**Test the price** by selling a small first run at full price and counting who pays. Eight places is enough. Do not fill it with friends at a discount, because that tells you nothing. This is craft, not research.
**Make joining easy:** one page, one payment step, and a confirmation within the hour giving the dates, the times, the address or link and what to bring.

**Give the first session a usable result.** Make sure people leave it with something they can use, as [an early win](t:1.18). On a presenting course that could be a 60-second opening for their next real talk, said aloud twice.

**Build in contact and deadlines** to keep people: a live session each week, a small task of about fifteen minutes due before it, and a partner from week one. Message anyone who misses a session within a day: "We missed you on Tuesday. Here is the one thing to do before next week. Are you still in?"
**Say what you do not promise**, plainly, on the page.
**Collect evidence of results, with consent.** In the last session ask each person what they can do now that they could not do in week one, and ask in writing [before you use anyone's words](t:9.25).

why.text: **Drop-out is the main risk.** When the learner is the buyer, they chose to come and they bear the cost. Motivation is usually higher at the start. Nobody at work is making them finish, so drop-out is the main risk.

**Follow-up must be part of the product.** There is no manager to reinforce the learning, so follow-up and peer contact have to be part of the product. Research on public, self-funded courses is thinner than on workplace training, and this page rests on practice.

**You stand in for the employer.** The reasoning behind the steps is about what replaces the employer. At work, a manager supplies the deadline, the reason and the question afterwards. On an open course you supply all of them: the weekly task is the deadline, the partner is the person who notices, and your message after a missed session is the manager's question. The first session matters most because it is the last point at which staying costs nothing.

**Homework that feels like school backfires.** There is a trade-off. Adults paying with their own money and evenings will resent homework that feels like school, so keep each task small and tied to something they have to do at work anyway. A one-off workshop reverses part of this advice. It needs no plan for keeping people, but it still needs the usable result before they leave.

try.text: Write the course page for one open course: who it is for, what they will be able to do, what you do not promise. Read it aloud to one person who fits the description and watch where they frown. Then write the message you will send to someone who misses week two.

Who it is for: people who present at work a few times a year and dread it for a week beforehand.

What you will be able to do: open a talk without notes, structure ten minutes around one message, and handle a question you cannot answer.
Between sessions: one task of about fifteen minutes each week, and a partner to try it out on.
What we do not promise: to remove nerves. Most people are still nervous. You will have a plan for what to do with them.
Who it is not for: people who need to present to large conferences, or who want one-to-one coaching.
If you miss a session: we send the task and a short note of what was covered, and your partner will expect to hear from you.

quiz.a: Drop-out. They chose to come, but nobody at work is making them finish.

quiz.q: A third of the people on your six-week open course stop turning up after week two. What do you change for the next run?
quiz.a: Build contact and deadlines into the product: a task due before each session, peer contact between sessions and a message to anyone who misses one. There is no manager to do the follow-up, so it has to be yours.

quiz.q: A participant emails to say the course was the best they have done. You want the line on your course page. What do you do?

topics.title: Run a discovery conversation with a client

situation.text: The head of people at a software company rings on a Tuesday. "We need a two-day leadership course for twelve team leads. What would you charge?" You could answer in one sentence. If you do, you will have priced a course before you know what it is for.

items: **Give a price range** and ask for thirty minutes, if they want a price first. "I can give you a range today. Two days for twelve usually lands between X and Y with design and follow-up. To narrow it I need half an hour of questions. Is now good, or Thursday?"
**Open with how the call will run.** "I will ask questions for about twenty minutes, play back what I have heard, and then we agree what happens next."
**Ask what is happening** that made them call, and what it is costing them. "What has happened that made leadership the priority now?" Say nothing about your product yet.
**Ask what they want to be different**, and how they would know. "By spring, what would you see team leads doing that they are not doing today?"
**Ask what has been tried** and what happened to it.
**Ask who else has a view**, and whether you can speak to them. "Who else would notice if this worked? Could I have twenty minutes with one of them and with two of the team leads?"
**Listen more than you talk.** As a working target, speak for less than a third of the call. Write down their exact phrases, and wait three seconds after an answer before you ask the next question.

**Play back what you heard** in under a minute and agree the next step with a date. "So: six people promoted last year, two resignations where the exit interview named the manager, and you want hard conversations happening early. I will send a one-page summary by Thursday. Have I got that right?"

why.text: **The request is an untested diagnosis.** A discovery conversation tests the request before you price it. It is the [needs analysis](t:2.1) done with the client in the room. The request for a two-day course is the client's own diagnosis, made before anyone looked closely, and the call is where you find out what it rests on.

**Once you describe your course, discovery stops.** Ask about the situation and what it is costing them before you say anything about your product. Once you describe your course, the client starts judging the course and stops describing the problem.

**More practitioners say they diagnose first.** The CIPD's Learning at work 2023 survey found that 57% of learning practitioners said they identify the performance issue before recommending a solution, up from 32% in 2021. The CIPD Profession Map asks people professionals to question a problem to find its underlying causes and to listen carefully to a range of views.

**Give a range, hold your diagnosis.** The rest is craft. Give the range because refusing to name any price sounds evasive and loses the call. Hold your diagnosis because one person's account in the first twenty minutes is thin evidence, and the full method is a [performance diagnosis](t:2.29). The record matters as much as the call: a one-page summary in the client's words is the first thing of yours they forward, and it becomes [the opening of the proposal](t:9.5). The advice reverses when the client has already done a proper diagnosis. Then ask to see it and test it with a few questions. Do not make them repeat it.

try.text: Write eight questions for a first client conversation. None may mention your course. Then ask a colleague to play a client who wants a price, and run the call aloud for twenty minutes with a recording on. Listen back and time how long you spoke. Good looks like this: under a third of the talking was yours, you played back in under a minute, and the call ended with a dated next step. Write the record within the hour.

try.title: A worked example: the first minutes of the call
lines: Client: We need a two-day leadership course for twelve team leads. What would you charge?
You: I can give you a range today, and I will. First, what has happened that made leadership the priority now?
Client: We promoted six engineers to team lead last year. Two people have left since, and both exit interviews mentioned their manager.
You: What did the interviews say, as closely as you remember?
Client: That problems were left to drift. Nobody told them where they stood until the review.
You: What is that costing you, apart from the two people?
Client: Replacing an engineer takes us months. And the team leads' own managers are stepping in to have the conversations for them.
You: By spring, what would you see team leads doing that they are not doing today?
Client: Raising a problem in the week it happens. Holding a proper one-to-one every month.
You: What has been tried so far?
Client: An online management course. Most of them finished it. Nothing changed.
You: Who else would notice if this worked, and could I speak to one of them and to two of the team leads?
Client: The engineering director. I can set that up.
You: Let me play that back, then I will give you the range and send a one-page summary by Thursday.

**Do not diagnose** in the first five minutes. If what you hear suggests training is the wrong answer, there is more on [saying so and reshaping the brief](t:9.29).
**Free consulting has a limit.** Decide yours before the call, for example one conversation and a one-page summary, with any further diagnosis paid for. This is craft.

quiz.q: What does a discovery conversation test?
quiz.a: The request, before you price it.

quiz.q: A caller opens with, "We need a two-day leadership course. What would you charge?" What do you say?
quiz.a: Give a price range and ask for thirty minutes. Then ask what happened that made them call, what they want to be different and how they would know.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes into a first call you are fairly sure the real problem is managers avoiding feedback. What do you do next?
quiz.a: Hold the diagnosis. Play back what you heard, ask who else has a view and whether you can speak to them, and agree the next step.

topics.title: Scope and price the work so it can succeed

situation.text: You quote two days of delivery at your day rate for a programme for twelve new managers. The client accepts within the hour. Over the next month you design the programme, travel to two planning meetings, rewrite the materials three times and run a follow-up call. All of it comes out of your own time, because the quote had one line.

items: **List everything the work includes**, one line each: discovery, design, materials, delivery, follow-up, evaluation.

**Estimate the time for each line** in days or half days. If you have logged past jobs, use your own ratio of design time to delivery time. If you have not, estimate line by line and start logging now.
**Include what the work needs to succeed.** Add a one-hour briefing for the participants' managers before the course and [a follow-up session after it](t:5.4), as lines with their own days.
**State what is not included**, and what changes cost. "One round of changes to the outline is included. Further rounds are charged at the day rate. Travel and accommodation are charged at cost."
**Price the whole piece of work** as one figure, shown line by line. Use your [floor rate for a day](t:9.28) as the least you will accept for a day.
**Work out the same price two ways**, as a day rate and as a price per head, before you send it, so you can answer when a buyer compares you with another supplier.
**Put it in writing** and send it before any design work starts, with [your terms on expenses and cancellation](t:9.9).

why.text: **A one-line quote invites assumptions.** Scope is the agreement about what will and will not be done. Unclear scope is a common cause of work that loses money or disappoints. A one-line quote leaves the client free to assume everything is included, and they are not being unreasonable when they do.

**Without follow-up the event will likely fade.** A price that leaves out follow-up sells an event that is likely to fade. No market rates are given here because they vary widely. There is [a method for finding your own floor](t:9.28), and the quote below shows the arithmetic with made-up figures.

**One view: charge for value, not time.** One well-known view, from the consultant Alan Weiss, is to set the fee by the value of the result to the client and not by the time you spend. He argues against billing by the day. Track your hours anyway so you know what the work costs you.

**Buyers compare by day rate or head.** Training is sold in four common ways: by the day, as a fixed price for a programme, per head and on a retainer. The table below says when each suits. Most corporate buyers compare suppliers by day rate or by price per head, so be ready to show your price in either form even when you quote a fixed price. This is practitioner knowledge, not research.

why.title: Four pricing models and when each suits

With seven lines, they can choose what to do without, and you can say what each cut will cost them. The approach reverses for [associate work through an agency](t:9.32), where the agency holds the scope and you are usually paid a day rate for delivery. Read what the day is expected to include before you accept it.

items: **A routine discount request** often comes from a buyer in a large organisation. Do not take offence, and do not simply cut the price. Trade scope for price: remove a line, shorten the design or agree a lower rate for more volume. Keep the follow-up in.

**Design usually takes longer than delivery**, often much longer. Log your design hours for every job. After a few programmes you will know your own ratio of design time to delivery time, and you can quote from it.
Agree [expenses and cancellation terms](t:9.9).

**The scope grows by small favours:** an extra call, a second version of the slides for another team. Name each one when it is asked for, say whether it is inside the quote, and give the cost before you start.

**You quote before discovery.** Give a range on the first call and a line-by-line price only after you know the group, the problem and who has to approve it, which [a discovery conversation](t:9.3) tells you.

quiz.q: Name the four common ways training is priced.
quiz.a: By the day, as a fixed price for a programme, per head and on a retainer.

quiz.q: A client asks for "just the two delivery days" from your quote, to save money. What do you do?
quiz.a: Explain that the design days are what make the two days fit their people, and offer to cut scope somewhere else, such as reusing their case studies. Keep the follow-up, because without it the two days are likely to fade.

quiz.q: After you send a fixed price, the client asks for a third round of changes to the materials. What do you do?
quiz.a: Point to the line that says one round is included and further rounds are charged at the day rate, then give the cost before you start. Scope stated in writing is what makes this an easy conversation.

topics.title: Write a proposal the client can say yes to

situation.text: Your proposal for a retailer's new team leaders runs to nine pages. The first three are about your company, your method and your past clients. The operations manager who asked for it finds the price on page eight, cannot see her own problem anywhere, and forwards it to her director with the note "Bit long. Thoughts?"

items: **Write only after a conversation**, the [discovery conversation with the client](t:9.3), and send within two or three working days while their words are fresh. Have your notes from the call open as you write.
**Open with the client's situation** in their words: three or four sentences, using phrases from your notes. Your name does not appear until after it.
**State the result they want** in one sentence, with a date and [how it will be judged](t:9.6).
**Describe what you will do**, in numbered steps with rough dates: the calls, the design, the review point, the delivery days, the follow-up.

**Say what you need from them:** managers' time, data, access to people, a named contact, a room. Give hours and dates. "Each area manager gives one hour in the week of 12 January to brief their team leaders."

**Offer two or three options** of different sizes and say which you recommend. For example: the core programme with its follow-up, the same with coaching for managers, and the same again with an evaluation report. Make the smallest option one you would be glad to deliver.
**Give the price, dates and terms**, and say how long the price holds. The price comes from [the scope you priced](t:9.4) and the terms from [what you put in writing](t:9.9).

**Keep it short.** Two to four pages is enough for most jobs. This is craft, not a rule. Put a short paragraph about you last, and offer to talk it through: "Could I take you through it in fifteen minutes on Thursday?"

why.text: **A proposal confirms a conversation.** It should show you understood the problem before it describes the solution. The person you spoke to will usually pass it to someone you have not met, so the first page has to make their case for them in words they recognise.

**Options replace yes or no.** Options let the client choose how much to buy, not whether to buy. With a single price the only answers are yes and no. With three sizes the discussion becomes which one, and a request to spend less has somewhere to go that does not involve cutting your rate.

**Say what only the client can supply.** All of this is craft, drawn from consulting practice such as Peter Block's writing on contracting with a client. The reasoning for stating what you need from them is that a training programme depends on things only the client can supply. If the proposal is silent on those, you have promised a result while leaving out half of what produces it.

**Options have a cost.** Three sizes take longer to write and can look like indecision, so recommend one and say why in a sentence. Do not include a small option you expect to fail, because clients do pick it. The advice changes for [a formal tender](t:9.35): use the buyer's format and answer their questions in their order. [As an associate](t:9.32), the agency writes the proposal and you may only be asked for a paragraph.

try.text: Rewrite the first page of a proposal so the client's problem appears before your name. Then write the options as a table with a recommendation. Read the first page aloud to someone outside the work and ask them to tell you what the client's problem is. If they cannot, rewrite the opening.

**A proposal sent without a conversation** is a weak bet. Talk first.
**A client may rely** on what your proposal says. Write only what you can deliver, and have your terms checked by someone qualified.
**You email it and wait.** Ask for fifteen minutes to walk through it, and ask who else will read it and what they will look for.
**The cheapest option** leaves out the follow-up. Keep it in every option, so that whichever one they choose can work.

quiz.q: What does a good proposal open with?
quiz.a: The client's situation, in their words.

quiz.q: A prospect you have never spoken to emails: "Send us a proposal by Friday." What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask for a short call first. A proposal sent without a conversation is a weak bet, because you cannot open with their situation or show you understood the problem.

quiz.q: The client asks you to add a line saying the course will cut staff turnover by 10%. What do you do?
quiz.a: Decline to promise it, because you cannot influence turnover on your own and the client may rely on what the proposal says. Write what you will deliver and what people will be able to do, and agree how success will be judged.

topics.title: Agree what success looks like before you start

situation.text: Three months after a programme for a retailer's store managers, the operations director says, "This is not what we expected. Staff turnover in those stores has not moved." Nobody had said turnover was the measure. You look back through the emails, and the only description of success anyone wrote down is "better people management".

items: **Write down what success looks like** before you start, and [how it will be judged](t:6.1): what people will be doing, by when, and who will check. If the client talks about value in broad terms, settle [what value means](t:6.8) first.
**Say what training can and cannot change**, on the same page. "We cannot promise lower staff turnover. Pay, rotas and recruitment affect it and are outside this work."
**Name what the client must do**, with names, hours and dates. "Each area manager gives one hour before the course to brief their store managers."

**Agree what will be reported** about individual participants and what will not. For example: attendance and completion by name, and nothing about what anyone said or how they did in practice. Tell participants this at the start of the first session, as part of [handling learner data and privacy](t:9.24).

**Send it as one page** and ask for an answer. "Please reply to confirm, or tell me what to change, by Friday." If nothing comes back, phone. Ask the sponsor to confirm as well as your day-to-day contact.
**Agree check-in points** and put them in both diaries now: twenty minutes with the sponsor after the first delivery, and again at six weeks.

**Raise problems early**, within a day or two of seeing them, with the cost and a suggestion. "Four of the twelve managers were not briefed. They arrived unsure why they were there. I suggest a fifteen-minute call with their area manager this week."
**Record changes to the brief** by email the same day, with the change to the price or the dates, and get a reply before you do the extra work.

why.text: **Unstated expectations often end in disappointment.** Disappointment often comes from expectations that were never stated. Writing them down exposes differences while they are cheap to fix. Two people in the same client can each be certain what the programme is for and mean different things, and neither knows until a page makes them choose words.
**State the limits, or the course gets blamed.** Being clear about limits is part of the service. A client who expected a course to fix a management problem will blame the course.

**The client may have no evaluation method.** Do not assume the client already has a way to judge success. In the CIPD's Learning at work 2023 survey, almost half of respondents lacked a systematic approach to evaluating learning.

**The written page outlasts the people.** That survey figure is the only research here. The rest is craft. The page earns its keep when people change: [sponsors move on mid-programme](t:9.36), and a successor inherits a budget line with no memory of the conversation behind it. Naming limits can feel like talking yourself down while you are trying to win the work. In practice it does the opposite, because it shows you know what produces the result. The one case for a lighter touch is a single short session, where a paragraph in the confirming email does the job of the page.

try.text: For one project, write three lines: what success is, what you cannot promise, what the client must do. Then say the limits sentence aloud, as you would to a director, until it sounds matter-of-fact and not apologetic. Send the page to the sponsor and note how long a reply takes. Good looks like this: a written yes from the sponsor, and two check-in dates in the diary.

try.title: A worked example: the one-page agreement, sent in week one
lines: Programme: managing people day to day, for 12 store managers. Two days in March, follow-up in May.
Success: by the end of June, each store manager holds a monthly one-to-one with each of their team leaders.
How it will be judged: a five-question staff survey in the 12 stores in February and again in June, and what area managers see on store visits.
We cannot promise: lower staff turnover. Pay, rotas and recruitment affect it and are outside this work.
You will: give each area manager one hour before the course to brief their store managers, and ask them to raise one-to-ones at every store visit until June.
You will also: release all 12 managers for both days, with cover arranged.
What we report about individuals: attendance and completion, by name. Nothing about what anyone said or how they did in practice. Participants are told this at the start of day one.
Check-ins: 20 minutes with the operations director in the week after the course, and in the week of the follow-up.
Changes: anything added to this brief is agreed by email first, with its effect on price or dates.
Please reply to confirm, or tell me what to change, by Friday.

items: **Different people hold different expectations** in the client. Send the page to the sponsor and the buyer together, and ask each to confirm.
**Silence is not agreement.** If nobody replies, phone before the first session.
**Changes to the brief** need a change to the price or the dates. Agree it before you do the extra work.
**A sponsor may ask who struggled** afterwards. Go back to what was agreed. Do not name anyone unless participants were told at the start that you would.
**Writing a measure you cannot see.** If success is judged by a survey or by store visits, agree who runs it and when you will be sent the result.

topics.title: Market your training without overclaiming

situation.text: You are writing the home page for your new training business. A competitor's website promises "guaranteed transformation" and "brain-based learning that boosts retention by 80%". Your own draft says you run practical courses for new managers, and beside theirs it looks flat. The temptation is to borrow a number.

items: **Describe what people will do** and be able to do. Use verbs you could watch. "You will plan and hold a feedback conversation" and not "you will become a confident leader".
**List every claim** on your site, brochure and profile in a table: the claim, whether it is a fact or an opinion, the evidence you hold, and what you will do with it.
**Quote only results you can evidence.** For each one, keep the document that supports it in a folder, dated, before the claim goes live.
**Name the source of any figure** next to the figure. Trace it to the original first, the way you would [test any learning claim](t:1.11). If you cannot find one, take the figure out.
**Avoid brain language you cannot support.** Replace "brain-based" or "backed by neuroscience" with the method itself, such as "spaced practice and regular quizzing".
**Use real cases**, [gathered with consent](t:9.25).
**Say who it does not suit.** "This course is not for experienced managers, or for anyone who needs employment law training."

why.text: **Inflated claims lose informed buyers.** Buyers who know the field distrust inflated claims, and you owe every buyer the truth in any case. Test your own marketing the way you would [test any learning claim](t:1.11).

**Hold the evidence before you publish.** In the UK, the CAP Code says marketing must not materially mislead. You must hold documentary evidence for any objective claim before you publish it, and you must not overstate what a product can do. This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.
**Testimonials alone rarely prove a claim.** A happy customer's words are not evidence that a course works. ASA advice says testimonials alone are unlikely to be enough to support a factual claim.

**Specifics sell where superlatives cannot.** What follows is craft. A plain page looks quieter than a competitor's, and with some buyers that will cost you the first glance. What you gain is that every line survives a question. Specifics do the selling that superlatives cannot: the group size, what people practise, how long the follow-up runs, who the course is wrong for. A learning manager who has been let down by a "transformation" before reads those details as a sign that you have done the work.

try.text: Audit your own website for claims. For each, write the evidence or remove it. Then read your rewritten home page aloud to someone who buys training and ask which sentence they would challenge. Good looks like this: every figure has a named source beside it, and you can open the evidence for each factual claim within a minute.

items: **A statistic repeated across the industry** may have no source. Trace it before you use it, and leave it out if you cannot.
**Testimonials must be genuine.** Keep proof that each one is real, keep the person's contact details, and ask their permission. A factual claim inside a testimonial still needs evidence.
**"Evidence-based" is itself a claim.** Be ready to say which evidence.
**Fake reviews**, and paid reviews that hide the payment, have been banned in sales to consumers since 6 April 2025. Take care with the word "guarantee" too. The CAP Code has rules on it.
**Permission and wording** for case studies and testimonials are covered under [gathering proof with consent](t:9.25).

quiz.a: Documentary evidence for it.

quiz.q: You want to write "learners retain 80% more" on your site because several training companies quote it. What do you do?
quiz.a: Look for the source. A figure repeated across the industry may have none. If you cannot name a source and have not measured it yourself, leave it out and describe what the course does.

quiz.q: A happy client offers the testimonial, "This course doubled our sales." Can you publish it?
quiz.a: Not on its own. A factual claim inside a testimonial still needs evidence, and a testimonial alone is unlikely to be enough. Keep proof it is genuine, their contact details and their permission, and use only what you can support.

topics.title: Know the UK bodies and rules you work under
topics.theory: UK context: CIPD, LPI, Skills England, accessibility and data law

situation.text: A public sector client sends a supplier questionnaire. Question 4 asks, "Is the provider accredited?" Question 5 asks, "Does the course meet the regulations?" Each has a yes or no box and no space to explain. Ticking yes would be easy, and you are not sure what either question means.

items: **Ask what they mean** before you answer. "Which accreditation do you have in mind, and which regulations?" Buyers often mean a qualification, insurance, data protection or accessibility.

**Know the professional bodies:** CIPD for people professionals, the Learning and Performance Institute for learning practitioners. Be able to say in one sentence what you hold from each, if anything.
**Know who oversees skills policy** in England, so you can answer when a client asks whether levy funds will pay for your course.

**Know the laws that touch your work:** equality, [data protection](t:9.24), [health and safety](t:9.19), [consumer rights](t:9.2). Keep a one-page list with the official page for each and the date you last read it.
**Check each on its official site** before you rely on it. Read the pages again before any tender, and at least twice a year.
**Ask which accessibility standard the contract names** at the start with a public sector client, and [build to it from the first draft](t:3.15).
**Say what your accreditation covers** and what it does not. Write the answer once, say it aloud, and use the same wording on forms and on calls.

why.text: **Training in the UK is mostly unregulated.** Anyone can call themselves a trainer. Professional bodies offer membership, qualifications, accreditation and published standards. The CIPD has its Profession Map, which includes learning and development as a specialist area. The Learning and Performance Institute has its Capability Map. Some fields have regulators of their own.

**The laws that matter most are general ones.** Data protection law is the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, both amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. The ICO says all of that Act's data protection changes were in force by 19 June 2026. One of them applies to every organisation that handles personal data: give people a clear way to complain and acknowledge a complaint within 30 days. Details change, so check the official page. There is more on [what this means for learner data](t:9.24).

**Levy funds do not pay for general training.** Skills England oversees apprenticeship standards in England. It became an executive agency on 2 June 2025 and took on the work of the Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education. It is now sponsored by the Department for Work and Pensions. The growth and skills levy builds on the apprenticeship levy. Since 1 August 2026 levy funds can pay for apprenticeships, foundation apprenticeships and short apprenticeship units in a set list of subjects. They do not pay for training in general.

**Public sector contracts carry accessibility rules.** Public sector clients must make their websites, apps, intranets and documents meet WCAG 2.2 level AA under the Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018. They stay responsible when they buy from a supplier, so expect the requirement in your contract. The government's guidance also says every UK service provider has a duty under the Equality Act 2010 to consider reasonable adjustments for disabled people.

**An exact answer beats a broad yes.** The practical point is craft. Because the field is mostly unregulated, "accredited" has no single meaning, and a buyer who asks is usually looking for reassurance on something specific. An exact answer about what you hold is more convincing than a broad yes, and it is the only answer you can stand behind if someone later checks.

try.text: List the bodies and laws that apply to your next project. Find the official page for each and note the date you read it. Then say your answer to "Are you accredited?" aloud three times, until it takes under twenty seconds and does not sound defensive.

"I hold a CIPD Level 5 diploma and I am a member of a professional body."
"The course itself is not accredited by anyone."
"Here is how we handle data and accessibility. I can send our one-page summary today."
On a form with only a yes or no box: tick neither until you have asked, or tick no and attach the four sentences above.

topics.title: Put the terms in writing
topics.theory: Contracts: who owns the materials, cancellation and liability

situation.text: You agree a two-day programme for a software company's team leads in an email thread: the dates, the price and "looking forward to it". Two days before the first session the client cancels because of a product launch. A month later you hear that your slides are on their intranet and that a sister company has run the session without you.

items: **Use a written agreement for every job.** For a small one, a two-page letter that the client confirms by email before work starts is enough to settle the six points below.
**Say who owns the materials** and what the client may do with them. If you want them to use the materials but not own them, write a licence that says who may use them, for what and for how long.
**Set cancellation and postponement terms:** a sliding charge by length of notice, and a line saying a postponement counts as a cancellation unless a new date is agreed within a set period.
**Set payment terms:** when you invoice, how many days the client has to pay, and that you need the purchase order number before work starts.
**State the limits of your liability** and hold suitable insurance. Before you quote, ask the client what cover they require and ask your insurer what your activities need.
**Cover confidentiality and data:** what you will keep private, [what you will hold about participants](t:9.24) and for how long.

**Ask early whose terms will apply.** [Large clients usually contract on their own](t:9.35). Read theirs for the ownership clause first, and ask for a licence in its place if it claims everything you make.
**Get your own standard agreement checked** once by a solicitor, then reuse it.

why.text: **Ownership, cancellation and payment cause most trouble.** A written agreement protects both sides by settling the awkward questions before they arise. The ones that cause most trouble are ownership of materials, cancellation and payment.

**A freelancer's materials stay theirs by default.** By default, the person who creates a work is the first owner of the copyright. If you are a freelancer, the materials you make for a client stay yours unless you agree otherwise in writing. Staff are different. An employer owns what an employee makes as part of the job. A transfer of copyright needs a written, signed contract. Without one, the client may have only a limited right to use the work for the purpose it was made for. Get the agreement checked.

**You can charge interest on late payment.** GOV.UK sets out the position on late payment between businesses. If no payment date was agreed, a payment is late 30 days after the customer gets the invoice, or after you provide the service if that is later. A date agreed between two businesses should usually fall within 60 days, and a longer period must be fair to both. You can charge statutory interest on a late business payment at 8% plus the Bank of England base rate, and a fixed sum of £40, £70 or £100 depending on the size of the debt. If your contract sets a different interest rate, you cannot claim the statutory rate. Send a new invoice if you add interest.

**Raise terms before anyone has a grievance.** The timing is craft. Terms are easiest to agree at the start, when both sides want the work to happen and nobody has a grievance. The same clause raised after a cancellation reads as an accusation. Sending terms can feel heavy-handed for a small job with a friendly client, and that is the trade-off. A short letter in plain words is usually taken as a sign that you run a proper business. Your position differs if you are not contracting directly: [as an associate](t:9.32) the agency's terms with the client govern the materials, and if you are employed, [your employment contract](t:9.33) does.

try.text: List the six points above. For your last job, mark which were written down, and where. For each gap, write the sentence you would add next time. Then say aloud how you would raise terms with a client you like: "Before we start, I will send a two-page agreement so we both know where we stand on dates, payment and the materials."

items: This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.
**A client's standard terms** may claim ownership of everything you make. Large clients usually [contract on their own terms](t:9.35), not yours, so read that clause first.

**Insurers set conditions.** Read them. Clients often ask for proof of professional indemnity and public liability insurance. Ask what cover they require before you quote, and ask your insurer what your activities need.
**Postponing with no new date** lets a client avoid a cancellation fee. Say in the agreement that a postponement counts as a cancellation unless a new date is agreed within a set period.

quiz.a: 8% plus the Bank of England base rate, unless the contract sets a different rate.

quiz.q: Ten days before a workshop the client emails: "We need to postpone, dates to follow." Your agreement has a sliding cancellation scale and a postponement clause. What do you do?
quiz.a: Reply the same day, point to the clause and offer dates inside the agreed period. If no new date is agreed in time, the cancellation charge for that notice period applies.

quiz.q: A client's learning team shares your slides with a sister company. Your agreement says nothing about materials. Where do you stand, and what do you change?
quiz.a: By default the copyright is yours and the client probably has only a limited right to use the materials for the purpose they were made for, so raise it calmly and take advice. From now on, put a licence in every agreement that says who may use the materials and for what.

topics.title: Plan your own qualifications

situation.text: You have run workshops for eight years and clients ask you back. A tender for a management programme arrives, and section 3 says: "The lead trainer must hold a recognised training qualification. Attach certificates." You have references and a portfolio. You have no certificate, and the deadline is in three weeks.

items: **List what clients in your market request.** Collect the exact wording from three tenders, supplier forms or agency associate forms, and put them side by side.
**Ask the buyer what they accept.** "What would count as a recognised qualification for this tender, and do you accept equivalent experience with references?" Ask before the clarification deadline.
**Look at the routes:** professional body qualifications, teaching awards, facilitation and coaching credentials.
**Check each route's level, cost and time** on the provider's own site, and put them in one table. Add the renewal or membership fee for each year after.
**Ask who assesses you and how** before you pay: written assignments, observed delivery, or attendance only.
**Choose for what you will learn** as well as the letters. Write down two gaps in your own practice first, and check each route's content against them.
**Build evidence alongside any study:** a recording of you delivering, two references who will take a call, and [a case study gathered with consent](t:9.25).
**Keep a record of your development** each year. One page will do: the date, what you did and what you changed in your practice because of it.

why.text: **A qualification is a signal, not proof.** A qualification signals a baseline to buyers who cannot judge your work. It does not prove you can run a room.

**The routes differ by body and level.** CIPD offers a Level 3 Foundation Certificate in People Practice, a Level 5 Associate Diploma in Organisational Learning and Development and a Level 7 Advanced Diploma in Strategic Learning and Development. The Learning and Performance Institute offers membership grades, a free skills self-assessment and its own certificates in online facilitation and online learning design. There are also teaching awards for the further education sector. Titles and levels change, so check the provider's site.

**Only the higher diplomas specialise in learning.** The CIPD Level 3 certificate covers people practice as a whole, with learning and development as one part of one unit. The Level 5 and Level 7 diplomas are the specialist learning and development routes. CIPD says the Level 7 diploma typically takes 16 to 24 months.

**A certificate matters most with new buyers.** The reasoning that follows is craft. A procurement officer scoring twenty bids cannot watch you train, so a certificate stands in for the judgement they cannot make. That is why it matters more with new buyers than with clients who have seen your work. The trade-off is time and money spent on a signal when the same months could go on evidence: observed delivery, references and results. Asking the buyer first tells you which one this market wants. The balance tips towards study when you are moving into a field where nobody knows you, or when the gaps you wrote down are real and a course would close them.

try.text: Write down three tenders or clients you want. Note what each asks for, in their words, and what they said when you asked what they accept. Then fill in the comparison table for two routes from the providers' own sites. Say the question to the buyer aloud before you send it, so it sounds like a clarification and not an apology.

parts.title: Set the strategy
parts.summary: Running the strategy workshop and tying training to what the organisation needs.

topics.title: Run a training strategy workshop

situation.text: A people director at a software company of 300 emails you: 'Can you run a workshop to set our training strategy for next year? We have a half day with the leadership team on the 14th.' Attached is last year's course catalogue, 42 lines long. If you start from that list, eight senior people will spend the morning adding to it.

items: **Hold a 30-minute call with the sponsor** two weeks before. Ask for the organisation's goals for the year, the current training list with its cost, and any data they hold, such as staff turnover or customer complaints. Ask what money and how many days away from work are available.
**Check who will be in the room.** You need the budget holder, the heads of the teams affected and two or three line managers who see the work every day. Six to ten people is workable.

**Send one page three days ahead:** the goals, the limit on money and time, and the question for the day written as a decision. For example: 'Which five capability gaps will we fund next year, who owns each, and how will we judge them?'
**Open with the organisation's goals:** what it is trying to do. Put the goals on a flipchart and ask the group to choose the three that depend most on what people can do. Allow 30 minutes.

**Map the gaps** between those goals and what people can do now. Each person writes alone for ten minutes, one gap per sticky note, in this form: 'To hit this goal, [who] need to [do what], and at the moment [what happens].' Then group the notes under each goal on the wall.

**Sort the gaps** into training and something else. For each note, ask the [quick test for a skill problem](t:1.20): could these people do it if their job depended on it. If they could, the note goes on the 'something else' list with a named owner beside it. There is a [full diagnosis](t:2.29) for any gap the group argues over.
**Prioritise with the group.** One way that works: give each person three votes, then discuss the five gaps with the most votes and put them in order. This is craft. Rank inside the stated budget.

**Agree an owner**, a date for the first step and how success will be judged for each of the five. Send a one-page summary within two days: the priorities in order, what was left out and why, owners and dates.

why.text: **The room must own the list.** A strategy workshop is a facilitated decision, not a presentation. Its output is a short list of priorities that the people in the room own. A list ranked by the people who must release the staff and the money is hard for them to disown in March. A list you wrote for them is easy to drop.

**Start from goals, not from courses.** The order matters: goals, then gaps, then causes, then priorities. Starting from a list of courses produces a catalogue, because every course has a supporter in the room. Starting from goals gives the group a test for everything that follows. People write alone first because, once the most senior person has spoken, the notes that follow tend to agree with them.

**Votes show popularity, not judgement.** All of this is practitioner craft, and nobody has tested this agenda against another one. Votes show what is popular, so the discussion of the top five is where the judgement happens. A half day also allows only a rough sort of causes. Mark any gap the group disagreed about as 'cause not confirmed' and check it afterwards.

**No stated goals, no workshop yet.** The advice reverses when the organisation has no stated goals for the year. Agree them with the sponsor first and run the workshop later. Two other topics do the detailed work. One covers [linking each programme to a goal](t:9.12), and the other covers [choosing what to leave out](t:9.14).

Good looks like this: every output is something you could photograph, and the voting instruction takes under 40 seconds.

items: **The decision-maker is missing.** Without them in the room, nothing is decided. Move the date, or have them join for the prioritising and the close.
**Groups list everything.** Force a ranking, and finish with five in order.
**A strategy with no budget** is a wish. Ask before the day what money and time are available, and rank within that.
**The gaps block overruns** and the owners block is lost. Protect the last 50 minutes. Cut the gaps discussion short and photograph the wall.
**The 'something else' list is forgotten** because it is nobody's training project. Include it in the summary, with the owners' names.

quiz.q: In what order does a strategy workshop work?
quiz.a: Goals, then gaps, then causes, then priorities.

quiz.q: The day before the workshop you hear that the director who holds the budget cannot come. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask to move the date, or to have the director join for the prioritising and the close. Without the decision-maker in the room, nothing is decided.

quiz.q: By mid-morning the group has listed 25 gaps and says all of them matter. What do you do?
quiz.a: Force a ranking. Sort out the gaps training would not fix, give each person three votes on the rest, and discuss the top five into an order with owners and dates.

topics.title: Tie training to what the organisation is trying to do

situation.text: The head of people at a software company sends you next year's training plan to 'sense-check'. It has fourteen lines: presentation skills, resilience, advanced spreadsheets, a new manager programme. Attendance was good last year, which is why they are all back. You ask which business goal each one serves, and the line goes quiet.

items: **Get the organisation's goals in writing** for the year: the business plan, the board's objectives or the sponsor's own targets. You want three to five goals, each with a number and a date. If you are handed values or slogans, ask what the measure is.

**Ask what must change for each goal.** Put it to the people who run the work: 'What must people do differently for this to happen?' Push for something you could watch. 'Better communication' is not an answer. 'Bid teams rehearse before every tender presentation' is.
**Ask what stops people now**, for each behaviour. Write down every answer you hear: no time, a slow tool, no reason to, nobody has shown them, they have never practised.

**Plan learning for skill obstacles only.** Use the [quick test for a skill problem](t:1.20), and the [performance diagnosis](t:2.29) where the cause is disputed. Pass the other obstacles in writing to whoever can fix them.
**Write one line for each programme:** goal, behaviour, obstacle, programme, measure. Choose a measure the business already tracks for that goal. There is more on [choosing what to measure](t:6.1).
**Write the goal beside each item** as you go down the existing plan. Mark anything with no goal as an orphan. List training that is required by law separately, because it stays whatever the goals.

**Take the orphans to the sponsor** with a recommendation for each: drop it, or name the goal it serves and redesign it around the behaviour. Review the sheet at mid-year and whenever the goals change.

why.text: **Goal to behaviour to skill narrows the work.** Training earns its budget by helping the organisation do what it is trying to do. The link runs from goal, to behaviour, to the skill behind it. Each step narrows the work. A goal on its own could justify almost any course. A behaviour you could watch justifies only a few, and an obstacle that turns out to be skill justifies practice in one specific thing.

**Choose actions first, content last.** One practitioner method works this way. It starts from a measurable goal and works back to the actions people must take, before any content is chosen. Content comes last on purpose. Once an expert has listed what people 'need to know', the list grows and nobody can say what to cut. Starting from actions supplies the test: content that does not help someone carry out one of the actions is left out. This is craft, not a research finding.

**The link is often weak in practice.** In the CIPD's Learning at work 2023 survey, learning practitioners were less likely than in 2021 to agree that their learning strategy supports business priorities. The CIPD Profession Map treats understanding the organisation's strategy and priorities as core knowledge for people professionals.

**A strict goals test can starve slow work.** There is a trade-off. A strict goals test favours this year's targets and can starve slower work, such as preparing next year's managers. If the sponsor wants that work, ask them to state it as a goal with a measure, so that it is chosen in the open. Popular courses are the hardest to cut, because good attendance looks like evidence. It tells you people liked the course. It does not tell you the goal moved.

try.text: Take a real training plan, your client's or your own employer's. Write the business goal next to each item, or mark it as an orphan. Then choose one orphan and say aloud, in under a minute, what you would tell the sponsor: what the item is, why it has no goal, and what you recommend. Record it and listen back. Good looks like this: you name a goal or say plainly that there is none, you offer a choice, and you do not apologise for asking.

items: **Goals change mid-year.** Review. Put a date in the diary at six months, and look again after any reorganisation.
**Some training is required by law** whatever the goals. List it separately and leave it out of the goals test.
**Leaders may not have clear goals.** Help them state one. Ask what they most need to be different a year from now and how they would measure it.

**A goal is written in afterwards** to save a favourite course, such as 'supports our people strategy'. If a goal would fit every line on the plan, it is not doing any work. Ask for the measure and the behaviour.

**You say nothing** when you find the obstacle is not skill, because there is no course in it. Report it to the sponsor with a recommendation. There is more on [turning that finding into work that helps](t:9.29).

quiz.q: What is the chain that links strategy to training?
quiz.a: Goal, to behaviour, to the skill behind it.

quiz.q: A client's plan includes 'Presentation skills, two days, open to all'. Nobody can say which goal it serves. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask which goal it supports and what people must do differently for that goal. If it links to nothing, recommend dropping it, or redesign it around a named behaviour.

quiz.q: You have traced a goal to a behaviour, and found that people already know how to do it but the system makes it slow. What do you plan?
quiz.a: No course. Learning is planned only where skill is the obstacle, so recommend a fix to the system and pass it in writing to whoever owns it.

topics.title: Map roles and skills before you plan courses

situation.text: A software company wants 'a curriculum for customer support' by the end of the quarter. You ask who does what and receive three job descriptions written four years ago. In your first interview an adviser says, 'Refunds? Only one of the seniors can do those. When she's on holiday we ask customers to wait.'

items: **Explain the purpose** before you ask anyone what they do. Check with the sponsor what is true, then have the team's manager say it: 'We are planning next year's training and need to understand the work. This is not a review of jobs or headcount.'

**Draw how the work flows** and who does each part. Take the team's main piece of work, such as a customer ticket from arrival to closed, and draw it with two or three people who do it. Five to ten boxes, left to right, with a role written under each. Allow 45 minutes.
**List the roles as people perform them.** Where a job description and the drawing disagree, trust the drawing.

**List tasks and the skills behind them**, for each role. A task is what gets done: 'issue a refund'. A skill is what a person must be able to do: 'judge a claim against the refund policy and use the billing tool'. Eight to fifteen tasks a role is enough.

**Make a grid** with tasks down the side and roles across the top. In each cell, write how many people can do the task alone today. Ask people, then check the answers with the team lead. Mark where skills are missing or held by one person.
**Decide how to close each gap:** build the skill by training the people you have, buy it by hiring, borrow it from a contractor or another team, or redesign the role so the skill is not needed.

**Ask if they have a skills framework.** If they do, match each skill on your map to the framework's own wording and levels before you name any session. Where the framework has no matching skill, tell its owner. Do not invent a level.
**Then plan learning**, and only for the gaps marked 'build'.

why.text: **A map shows where the need is.** Training fills gaps in skill. Gaps are visible only against a picture of the roles and the work. A curriculum written from job titles sends everyone to everything on the list. A map shows which cells hold the real need. Sometimes the answer is to change the role, not to train the person.

**The map exposes skills one person holds.** The map also finds risks that no training request would raise. Nobody asks for a course in something a colleague handles well, so a skill held by one person stays hidden until she is on holiday. The fix for a single point of failure is rarely a course for the whole team. It is usually a written procedure and a second person trained on the job.

**This is organisation design at its simplest.** Larger redesigns are specialist work. The CIPD Profession Map describes both halves of this. Organisation design covers who does what and how the work is done. Learning and development includes capability analysis, which means defining the capability needs of people, teams and the organisation.

**Check self-ratings and stay with one team.** The method itself is craft, and it has limits. People may rate their own skills generously, which is why the team lead checks the grid. Keep it to one team. A skills database for a whole company is a different project. The advice reverses when the client already keeps role profiles and a framework up to date. Then check a sample against the real work and build on what exists. Their appraisals and grades use the framework's words, so your programme should too.

try.text: For one team, map the work, the roles and the skills. Mark one gap and one single point of failure. Do the flow drawing live with two people who do the work, at a wall or on a shared screen, and say your opening explanation aloud before you begin. Good looks like this: each task on your grid has a skill beside it, and you can name the decision for each gap.

items: **Job descriptions** are often out of date. Ask people what they do.
**Mapping can alarm people**, who may read it as a step towards job cuts. Explain why you are doing it before you ask anyone what they do.
**Know when a specialist is needed.** Changes to reporting lines, grades or headcount are organisation design work, not training work.

quiz.a: A skill held by only one person.

quiz.q: A client hands you the job descriptions and asks for a curriculum. What do you do first?

quiz.q: Your map of a support team shows that one senior alone can issue refunds. What do you recommend?

topics.title: Decide what not to train
topics.theory: Prioritising, and when training is the wrong answer

situation.text: It is November. The learning manager at a retailer shares a spreadsheet of forty training requests collected from department heads. The budget covers about eight. The head of buying has emailed twice this week about her negotiation course, and the sponsor asks you to 'help us pick'.

items: **Take compliance training out** of the list first. Some of it may be fixed by law or by a regulator. Cost it, and see what budget is left for the rest.

**Get three facts for every remaining request**, in a 15-minute call or a short form to the requester: which goal it serves, how many people are affected and how far they are from what is needed, and what stops them now.

**Score each request on three tests** from 0 to 2. [Link to a goal](t:9.12): 0 for none, 1 for indirect, 2 for a direct link with a measure. Size of the gap: 0 for small or few people, 2 for large or costly. [Whether skill is the cause](t:1.20): 0 for no, 1 for partly or unknown, 2 for yes. The scale is a working tool, not a researched one.
**Remove every request scoring 0 on cause**, whatever its total. Training is not the answer there. Write one line saying what is, and who should hear it.
**Rank the rest with the sponsor** in a 60-minute meeting. Start from the totals. The sponsor may move an item, and you record the reason beside it.

**Cost each programme in full**, with the manager briefing, the practice and [the scheduled follow-up](t:5.4) included. Draw the line where the money runs out. Fund the top few properly, even if that means six programmes where you had hoped for eight.
**Tell people what was not chosen** and why. Each requester gets a reply within a week of the ranking: the decision, the three scores and the alternative.

why.text: **Saying no is part of strategy.** Eight programmes done well, with follow-up, do more than forty events. That is a practitioner judgement and nobody has measured it for you. The reasoning is about where the money goes. A fixed budget spread across forty requests pays for forty sessions and leaves nothing for practice, manager support or follow-up, which are the parts that carry a skill into the work.

**Training is one fix among several.** Requests where skill is not the cause should go back with a different recommendation. The test of whether skill is the cause comes from performance analysis. Mager and Pipe's method starts by finding why people are not doing what they should, before any fix is chosen. Training is one possible fix among several. You can [walk through the diagnosis](t:2.29), and there is more on [the conversation with the client](t:9.29).

**The scores make your reasons visible.** They are not precise. A request on 5 is not better than a request on 4 in any way you could defend, so treat the totals as bands and let the sponsor's discussion settle the order inside a band. The cause test works as a veto because of what training can do. However important the goal and however large the gap, a course will not close a gap caused by staffing or a broken tool.

**With forty requests, the scale protects you.** Scoring costs each requester a little time, and that is the trade-off. With five requests and one sponsor, skip the scale and ask the three questions aloud. With forty, the scale protects you: the decision no longer depends on who asks most often, and a requester who sees the scores can argue with a reason and not with you.

try.text: Take ten training requests, from a client or from your own organisation's plan. Score each on the three tests and rank them. Then choose one you removed and say the reply to the requester aloud in under a minute. Record it. Good looks like this: you give the decision in your first two sentences, you say which test it failed, and you finish with what you have done about the real cause.

lines: Thanks for making the time. I want to tell you where your request landed, and why, before the list goes round.

items: **The loudest requester** is not the highest priority. Rank by the scores with the sponsor, and hide the requester's name while you score.
**Compliance training may be fixed** by law or by a regulator. Take it out of the ranking first, so you can see what budget is left for the rest.
**A no without an alternative** is a brush-off. Every removed request leaves with a recommendation and a named person to take it to.
**The scores are adjusted** until a favourite gets through. Score before the ranking meeting, and write down every change the sponsor makes with the reason.
**All eight are funded thinly**, with no follow-up for any. Cut the list to six and say which two are waiting for next year.
