topics.title: Plan the change, not only the course

situation.text: A sales director books you to train 60 account managers on a new customer system. It goes live on Monday the 3rd, and the training sits in the diary three weeks earlier 'to get it out of the way'. In the first session a rep folds her arms and says, 'Nobody has told us why we're losing the old one. My whole pipeline is in it.'

items: **Find out what is changing**, for whom, and what they lose. Ask the sponsor and three or four users. For each group write three columns: what they gain, what they lose, what they need besides training. Losses are often small and real: a shortcut, a personal spreadsheet, being the expert in the old way.

**Make sure leaders have explained why.** Ask the sponsor: 'Who has told the teams why this is happening, when, and in what words?' If nobody has, ask for five minutes from the director, live, before any training runs. Offer to draft it.
**Involve the people affected** in how it is done. Ask for two or three users to test the training on real tasks, choose the examples and decide what goes on the one-page guide.
**Train close to when people need it**, in go-live week or the week before. If the dates cannot move, add a 20-minute refresher on go-live day and put the one-page guide on every desk.
**Build the session on real tasks:** the five to eight people will do in their first week, using their own accounts or records where the system allows it.

**Support the first weeks**, with someone on hand to answer questions where the work happens. Agree named people, a daily 15-minute drop-in and one place to post questions. Have the supporters' time released by their managers in advance.

**Listen for resistance** and treat it as information. Sort what you hear into three piles: people who do not know why, people who think the new way is worse and can say where, and people who cannot yet do it. The first goes to the leader, the second to the project team, and the third is yours.

why.text: **Training is one part of a change.** People also need to know why, to see leaders act on it, and to have the means to work the new way. A course can supply knowledge and practice and nothing else on that list. When the reason is missing, the room argues the decision with you, and you cannot answer.

**Change models are checklists, not laws.** Kotter's eight steps and Prosci's ADKAR (awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, reinforcement) are practitioner models. Use them as checklists, not as proven laws. The commonly quoted figure that 70 per cent of change efforts fail has no solid source. A 2011 review of five works that state it found no valid evidence behind it.

why.title: Do 70 per cent of change initiatives really fail?
why.found: Hughes reviewed five published works that state a 70 per cent failure rate for organisational change. He found no valid and reliable empirical evidence behind the figure.
why.means: Leave the 70 per cent figure out of proposals and slides, and question it when a client quotes it.

why.text: **Timing is where the trainer has most influence.** Training given too early is forgotten by go-live, and a new system is mostly procedures with many steps, the kind of [skill that fades fastest without use](t:5.17). Clients book early because go-live week is busy. Offer short sessions near the date before you accept long ones far from it.

**Loud objectors often know the work best.** Treating resistance as information is craft. The people who object loudest often know the work best, and some of their complaints will be faults in the set-up that can still be fixed. A small change, such as one new field on a form, needs a note and a guide, not a plan. And you do not own the change. Your part is to ask the questions and report what you hear.

try.text: For one change, real and current if you can, list what people gain, what they lose and what they need besides training. Then rehearse aloud the two-minute conversation with the sponsor in which you ask who has explained the reason and propose moving the training nearer to go-live. Record it. Good looks like this: you ask before you advise, and you name one loss in the users' own words.

head: Group
What they gain
What they lose

items: **Training too early** is forgotten by go-live. Move it, or add a refresher and a guide on the day.
**The 70 per cent figure:** do not quote it. If the client quotes it, say that a 2011 review found no valid evidence behind it.

**An unannounced change:** you cannot train people into a change they were not told about. If the room does not know why, pause the content, note the questions and take them to the sponsor the same day.
**You end up defending a decision** you did not make. Say: 'I can't answer that. I'll take it to the director and you'll hear back by Friday.' Then make sure they do.
**Floor support fades after two days** because the supporters have their own targets. Agree their released time with their managers before go-live, in writing.

quiz.q: A new system goes live in three weeks and the client wants all the training done now to get it out of the way. What do you advise?
quiz.a: Move the training close to go-live, because training given too early is forgotten by then. Plan support for the first weeks as well, and if the dates cannot move, add a short refresher and a one-page guide on the day.

quiz.q: In a system training session people are angry and say nobody told them why the change is happening. What do you do?
quiz.a: Treat the resistance as information. Take it to the sponsor and ask leaders to explain the reason, because you cannot train people into a change they were not told about.

topics.title: Design a custom course for a client, end to end

situation.text: A client has signed off a bespoke one-day course for 40 team leaders. You have six weeks until the first delivery, and three people at the client each expect to approve it: the operations director who is paying, the HR partner and the head of support. On the first call, each describes a different course.

items: **Week 1: discover.** Run the [discovery conversation](t:9.3) with the sponsor, then talk to two or three learners and one of their managers. Come away with [the need](t:2.1), a picture of [the learners' working day](t:2.10) and the constraints: dates, room, budget and anything that cannot be said. If training looks like the wrong answer, stop and run a [performance diagnosis](t:2.29).
**Ask the sponsor to name one decision-maker** on the same call: "Three of you have a view, and I want all three. Who makes the final call when you disagree?" Every draft goes to that person.
**End of week 1: write the objectives**, three or four [the client could observe](t:2.11), and [how success will be judged](t:9.6). Send both on one page and get a yes in writing.

**Week 2: sketch the outline** on one page. Show the timings, what learners do in each block and which objective each block serves. Talk the client and two learners through it for 30 minutes each. Ask what is missing and what they would cut.

**Still in week 2, build one section** as a rough version, the one you are least sure of. Plain slides, the activity instructions and the handout are enough. Try it on two or three people, or walk the client through it, before you build more.

**Weeks 3 and 4: build the rest** to the same pattern, using the client's own examples. Write [the session plan](t:4.33) as you go, and [a facilitator guide](t:3.20) if someone else will deliver. Agree a freeze date at the end of week 4. After it, only the pilot changes the content.

**Week 5: pilot with a small group** of real learners. If that is not possible, run the first cohort as the pilot and tell the client so. Note the real timings, where people got stuck and what they asked. Keep three or four working days free afterwards to make the changes, and agree them with the decision-maker first.
**Week 6: deliver.** [Book the follow-up](t:5.4) before the day. Afterwards, [review the results with the client](t:6.9) against the measures you agreed and [hand over the materials](t:9.26).

why.text: **Show the client something while change is cheap.** A custom course follows the same path as any design, with the client involved at each decision. Clients often cannot say what they want until they see something. An outline shown in week 2 takes an hour to change. A finished deck shown in week 5 can cost you the week.

**The cheapest decisions to change come first.** So the five decisions run in order of what is cheapest to change. Objectives cost a page, the outline an hour, and one rough section a day. The freeze protects the client as much as you, since a course rewritten in week 5 is a course nobody has rehearsed. Rough work can worry an anxious client, so say in advance what they will see and what kind of comment you want.

**Short rounds come from the SAM model.** Working in short rounds with the client is the idea behind the Successive Approximation Model (SAM). Allen proposed it as an alternative to finishing each design stage before starting the next. There is more on [using design models as checklists](t:2.12). The six-week timings here are craft. When legal or compliance wording needs formal approval, plan a longer review and show fuller drafts earlier. When you are adapting a course you have run before, skip the rough section and keep the pilot.

**This topic is the route map.** Each step is taught in full elsewhere: [finding the real need](t:2.1), [writing observable objectives](t:2.11), [sequencing and scaffolding](t:2.13) and [pacing and energy](t:2.14), materials in Stage 3, delivery in Stage 4, [transfer as a design problem](t:5.1) and [planning the evaluation](t:6.1).

try.text: Lay out a six-week plan for a custom one-day course and mark each point where the client decides something. A plan like this usually has five client decisions: the objectives and success measure (week 1), the outline (week 2), the rough section (week 2), the content freeze (week 4) and the changes after the pilot (week 5). Put a date and one name against each.

lines: On the first call: "Three of you have a view, and I want all three. Who makes the final call when you disagree?"

With the outline: "This is a sketch. I need to know if it is the right course, not whether it looks finished. What is missing? What would you cut?"
With the rough section: "Every other section will follow this pattern. If you want it different, now is the cheap moment."
At the freeze: "After Friday, the only thing that changes the content is what we learn in the pilot."
When a topic is added late: "We can add that. The day is full, so which block should come out to make room?"

items: **Three sets of comments conflict.** Send every draft to the one decision-maker named in week 1, and let that person settle it.
**Client examples take weeks to arrive** and may need approval. Ask for three real cases in the first meeting, and check what you may name.
**The pilot is booked** for the day before delivery, so nothing can change. Leave three or four working days between them.
**The scope grows with each review.** When the client adds a topic, ask which one comes out, and go back to [what was agreed in the scope](t:9.4).
**The client goes quiet between decisions.** Put the review dates in their diary at the start, as part of [planning the programme's dates](t:9.18), and send a short update every Friday.

quiz.q: Three managers at the client send conflicting comments on your outline. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the sponsor to name one decision-maker and let that person settle it. Do not try to satisfy all three in the design.

topics.title: Run the client process for a custom retreat or offsite
topics.theory: The client side of a retreat: brief, proposal, sign-offs and who decides what

situation.text: The chief executive of a 120-person software company emails you: "We want two days away for the leadership team in March, to bond and think about the future. Can you send a proposal by Friday?" There are eight people in the team, and her assistant is already ringing venues.

items: **Hold a 45-minute brief call** with the sponsor before you write anything. Ask: "What will be decided or different on the Monday after?" and "What is still open, and what have you already decided?" If the answer could be reached in a meeting room at the office, say so. There is more on [deciding whether to take people away](t:8.7).

**Agree in writing who decides what**, with one name for each. The sponsor decides outcomes, attendance and budget. A named organiser handles venue, travel and forms. You decide the methods and the timetable inside the agreed hours. Each participant decides what they opt out of.

**Send a two-page proposal** within three working days, using the guidance on [writing a proposal](t:9.5). Give the outcomes in the sponsor's own words, what you will do before, during and after, the three sign-off dates, the price and what it covers, drawing on [how to scope and price the work](t:9.4) and [the full cost of a residential](t:8.13), and what you do not promise, since you [promise the conditions, never the transformation](t:8.1).
**Get sign-off 1 on outcomes and attendance**, before any venue is booked. Agree one or two outcomes you could check, and the list of names.

**Phone each participant for 20 minutes** and ask what the group avoids talking about. Agree with the sponsor beforehand what you will and will not pass on, usually themes with no names, and tell each person at the start of their call.

**Get sign-off 2 on the outline** and the venue brief, about four weeks before. Walk the sponsor through one page showing the shape of the two days, the hours, and the rules for evenings and free time, all designed with the guidance that runs from [choosing the format](t:8.9) to [setting the rules for evenings](t:8.14). Tell her the themes from the calls and what they changed.

**Get sign-off 3 on the duty-of-care plan**, about two weeks before, and before the programme is confirmed to participants. It says who is responsible for what, what the risks are, what people can opt out of, and what happens if someone is ill, hurt or distressed. Use the guidance on [writing the duty-of-care plan](t:8.5), [planning for incidents](t:8.15) and [assessing the risks of the event](t:9.19). On the same call, ask the sponsor to speak last in the room. There is more on [the senior person who takes over](t:4.38).

**Close the loop.** Send the decisions and their owners in writing before people leave, book a 45-minute check-in for the following week as part of [planning the return to work](t:8.17), and review the outcomes with the sponsor.

why.text: **The purpose has to justify the cost.** An offsite takes people out of routine, which makes some conversations possible. It also costs a great deal of senior time, so the purpose has to justify it. The main risks are [intensity without follow-up](t:8.4), [pressure to disclose](t:8.3) and [long days](t:1.12). You can read what the evidence says [a retreat can and cannot do](t:8.8).

**This page handles the client, not the design.** This topic is the client-facing route through Stage 8. For the design, go from [deciding whether to take people away](t:8.7) through to [planning the return to work](t:8.17). The sign-offs, timings and scripts here are craft.

**The sponsor is client and participant at once.** The sponsor of a retreat is usually in the room, and is usually the most senior person there. She is your client and one of your participants at once. So you settle three things with her before the event: what you report from the private calls, what is still open for the group to decide, and how she will behave when the hard conversation starts.

**The sign-offs follow what is costly to undo.** The three sign-offs run in order of what is costly to undo: outcomes and names before a venue deposit, the outline before travel is booked, the duty-of-care plan before participants are told what they are coming to. The private calls carry a trade-off. They tell you things the sponsor does not know, and your promise to participants limits what you can tell the person who is paying. Agree that limit first, or do not make the calls. When the event is a celebration with no decisions to make, drop the calls and the outline sign-off, and keep the duty-of-care plan.

try.text: Take a real or likely retreat enquiry and write its decision table: each decision, the one person who makes it, when, and what they are shown. Then rehearse the brief call aloud with a colleague playing a sponsor who keeps answering "we just want to bond". Good looks like this: inside ten minutes you have one outcome you could check on the Monday after.

items: **"Bonding" is accepted as the outcome.** It is not one. Ask what would be different, and write the answer into sign-off 1.

**The venue is booked** before the outcomes are agreed, and the design has to fit a room chosen from a brochure. Ask the organiser to hold off, and send the [venue brief](t:8.11) straight after sign-off 1.
**The sponsor announces a decision** already made, using the offsite to do it. Ask beforehand what is still open, and tell the group at the start.

**Some of the group is excluded** by an activity or an evening. Have the organiser send an access and dietary form to every participant, check each activity against who is coming, and offer a real alternative. Confirm your insurance and the venue's in writing well before the date. Both are covered under [inclusion and reasonable adjustments](t:8.16) and [event insurance and risk assessment](t:9.19).

quiz.q: What are the three sign-offs in the client process for a retreat, in order?
quiz.a: Outcomes and attendance, before a venue is booked. Then the outline and venue brief. Then the duty-of-care plan, before the programme is confirmed to participants.

quiz.q: A sponsor tells you the outcome of the offsite is "for the team to bond". What do you ask?
quiz.a: Ask what will be decided or different on the Monday after. Agree one or two outcomes you could check, such as three priorities for next year with a named owner each.

quiz.q: After your private calls with the leadership team, the sponsor asks which of them is unhappy with her plan. What do you say?
quiz.a: Remind her of what you agreed before the calls: themes, no names. Give her the theme and what you have changed in the outline because of it, since naming one person would end honest answers from all of them.

parts.title: Run the programme
parts.summary: The plan, the tracking, the tools and the close.

topics.title: Plan the programme: scope, roles, risks and dates

situation.text: The programme has twelve cohorts, four trainers and three venues, and it lives in your head and your inbox. On Tuesday the client's coordinator asks who is booking the room for cohort 3. You each thought the other was doing it, and the session is nine days away.

items: **Write the scope in five lines**: what is in, what is out, and what the client provides. Write the "out" line with as much care as the "in" line, for example "Out: booking participants' travel, loading materials onto the client's platform."

**List every piece of work**, broken down until each item takes a week or less. Put one person's name against each. "The client" and "the team" are not names. If two people share an item, pick one and make the other a helper.

**Put the work in order with dates**, working back from the first session. Next to each item write what it needs before it can start, for example "Invitations: needs venue confirmed." Those are your dependencies.
**List five risks to the programme**, each with a response and an owner. The [event risk assessment](t:9.19) for each day is a separate document.

**Agree who can approve a change** to scope or dates: one named person at the client and one on your side. Start a change log with four columns: date, what changed, who approved it, and the effect on dates and fee.
**Agree how and when you report**: a fixed day and one page. There is more on [tracking and reporting progress](t:9.21).
**Keep one plan that everyone can see**, in one shared file. Name the person who updates it and the day they do it, for example "Sam, every Thursday by 4pm."

**Hold a 30 minute call** with the client before work starts. Read out each item with its owner and date, and get a yes from each owner. Say "Cohort 3 venue, booked by the 14th, that is with you, Priya. Is that right?"

why.text: **Every method rests on the same basics.** A programme is a set of related projects and other work, managed together towards a shared aim. Missed handoffs and unclear ownership are common ways for it to go wrong. The basics are the same in every method: scope, owners, dates, risks and a single shared plan. The steps above are practitioner craft built on those basics, not a tested procedure.

**Gaps open where work changes hands.** A plan in your head works for one workshop because you are the only person doing the work. A programme moves work between people, and the gaps open where it changes hands. One name per item closes the commonest gap, which is two people each assuming the other has it. Reading the names aloud on a call matters more than it looks. People agree to a document without reading it, and they rarely agree to their own name spoken to them without thinking about it.

**One late item delays everything after it.** Dependencies are where a small delay becomes a large one. A venue confirmed a week late delays the invitations, which shortens the notice people get, which lowers attendance. Writing "needs" beside each item lets you see that chain before it starts moving.

**Unlogged extra requests become unpaid work.** The "out" line and the change log are there for the day the client asks for more. Without them every extra request is a favour, and by the eighth cohort you are doing a different job for the same fee. The trade-off is time. All of this is too much for a single workshop, which needs a checklist and a confirmation email.

try.text: For one programme you are running or about to run, write the scope in five lines and name one owner for each piece of work. Then phone or meet the client's coordinator and read the owner list aloud, item by item. Good looks like this: every item has one person's name, every date has a "needs" beside it or the word "nothing", and the coordinator has corrected you on one or two items. A correction now is the point of the call.

quiz.a: A set of related projects and other work, managed together towards a shared aim.

topics.title: Plan the logistics and assess the risks
topics.theory: Event logistics, venue, insurance and risk assessment

situation.text: The venue is booked from its website, and the photographs look fine. Nobody has asked about step-free access, the fire procedure or what happens if the trainer wakes up ill on the morning. The event is three weeks away and sixteen people have accepted.

items: **Visit the venue**, or get a full description. If you cannot go, ask for a floor plan, photographs of the actual room, and a 20 minute video call in which someone walks from the front door to the room.

**Check access, travel, food, equipment and connectivity**, one question at a time. Ask about the step-free route and the nearest accessible toilet. Ask for the walking time from the station, the serving times for food, which connectors the screen takes, and whether you can test the guest wifi.

**Ask participants about dietary and access needs** in the invitation, at least two weeks ahead. Use the wording from [collecting only the learner data you need](t:9.24), which asks what would help and does not ask for a diagnosis.
**Write a risk assessment**, one line per risk: what could cause harm, to whom, how likely and how serious, and what you will do. Add an owner to each line. Five lines is usual for a classroom day.
**Check insurance for the event** and the activities, yours and the venue's, alongside the [liability terms in your contract](t:9.9). Send your insurer the list of activities and ask what they need.
**Name who is in charge** on the day. Put that person's mobile number at the top of the running sheet, and tell the venue and the client who it is.
**Back up the trainer and the technology.** A second trainer holds the slides and the plan. The slides are also on a memory stick as a PDF, and you know which parts of the day run from a flipchart.
**Review the assessment when something changes**, such as the venue, the group or the activity.

why.text: **Write the risk assessment down, whatever your size.** Logistics decide whether people can attend and attend to the content. A risk assessment means identifying what could cause harm, judging how likely and how serious it is, and deciding what you will do about it. Employers with five or more employees must record the significant findings. Write yours down whatever your size, so that others can follow it.

**Health and safety duties depend on the event.** Employers and organisers have legal duties for health and safety. What applies depends on the event. This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.

**Most employers must hold liability insurance.** Employers' liability insurance is required by law for most employers, with cover of at least £5 million from an authorised insurer. Venues and clients often set their own insurance conditions as well. Read the contract and ask your insurer what the activities need. If you are self-employed with no staff, health and safety law still applies where your work could put other people at risk.

**Match the effort to the risk.** The rest is craft. Writing each risk as a line with a likelihood and a seriousness shows you where to spend effort. An unlikely event that would be serious, such as a trainer falling ill, earns a prepared response. A likely event that is minor, such as the projector failing to connect, earns a spare cable and a plan B. The amount of paper should match the day. A classroom session needs five lines on one page, and a day with a physical activity needs a separate assessment from the people qualified to run it.

topics.title: Brief and check the people you bring in

situation.text: You have won more work than you can deliver, and two dates clash next month. A colleague recommends an associate you met once at a conference. The easy route is to send the slides the night before and hope.

items: **Watch them work, or see evidence** such as a recording or a reference from someone who has, before you put them in front of a client. Twenty minutes is enough if it includes them running an activity and taking a question.

**Hold a 30 minute briefing call** at least a week before the date. Cover the client, the aims and the reasons behind the design. For each activity say what it is for: "The role-play at 11:00 is the only time they practise, so it stays even if we run late."
**Agree what may be adapted** and what may not. Go through the session plan together and mark each block fixed or flexible.
**Ask them to talk the day back** to you. Say "Walk me through the afternoon as you would run it." You will hear the misunderstandings before the client does.
**Put terms in writing** before the first delivery: fees, materials, confidentiality, contact with the client. You can read [the same terms from the associate's side](t:9.32).
**Send a one-page brief** together with the [facilitator guide](t:3.20). Observe the first delivery, or the first hour of it, and swap notes the same day.
**Get feedback after each delivery**, from the client and from the associate. Ask the associate two questions: "What did you change, and why?" and "What would you change in the design?"
**Brief venues, caterers and activity providers** in writing too, with times, numbers and the name of the [person in charge on the day](t:9.19).

why.text: **An associate delivers under your name.** The client judges you by them. The same holds for venues, caterers and activity providers. Briefing and checking take time and cost less than a poor day. This is practitioner craft, and no study on this page tests it.

**The reasons tell a trainer what to cut.** The reasons behind the design are the part people leave out, and they do most of the work. Every session runs off its plan at some point, and the associate then has to cut something with nobody to ask. A trainer who knows only the running order cuts whatever looks optional, which is usually the practice, and keeps the slides. A trainer who knows that the practice is the purpose of the day cuts slides.

**Three or four fixed points is usually enough.** Marking blocks as fixed or flexible is a trade-off. Fix everything and a good trainer becomes stiff and reads your script. Fix nothing and the client gets a different course each time. Three or four fixed points in a day is usually enough: the practice, the client's own cases, the close and anything the sponsor asked for by name.
**The advice loosens with experience of each other.** An associate who has run the session five times needs a ten minute call about this client and this group, not the full brief again.

try.text: Write a one-page brief for an associate on one session: aims, audience, what is fixed, what is flexible. Then give it aloud to a colleague in ten minutes, as if they were delivering next week, and ask them to tell you what is fixed and why. Good looks like this: they can name the fixed points and the reason for each without looking at the page.

The aim: each person can respond to "it's too expensive" by asking two questions before they mention price.

Fixed: the 11:00 practice in threes, because it is the only time they do the skill. Feedback order as in [running a role-play](t:4.29).
Fixed: the afternoon uses their own live deals, because the sponsor asked for it by name.
Fixed: the close at 16:10, where each person writes the first call they will try it on.
Flexible: the opening exercise, the examples you use, the order of the two morning inputs, your own stories.

**Employment status** decides how an associate is taxed. If they work through their own limited company, the off-payroll working rules (IR35) may apply. topics.title: Track progress where everyone can see it

situation.text: The sponsor stops you after a meeting and asks how the programme is going. You say "fine, I think" and then spend an afternoon pulling attendance from three emails and a notebook to send a proper answer. Next month the same question will cost you the same afternoon.

items: **Choose a few things to track**: sessions run, attendance, actions, risks, results. Keep the tracker to eight columns or fewer. Test each one by asking yourself what decision would change if it moved. If none would, leave it out.
**Keep them in one place** the client can see. Send a link to the tracker, not a copy of it.
**Update on a fixed day** and name who does it, for example "Jo updates it every Thursday by 4pm."
**Agree what counts as off track** with the sponsor, before the first session. For example: attendance below 10 of 12, an action more than a week late, or any date at risk.
**Report by exception**: what is off track and what you are doing. Give each item an action, an owner and the date of the next decision.
**Keep the report to a page.** Open with one line of totals, such as "Sessions run: 6 of 12. Attendance on plan." Leave out everything else that is on plan.
**Report a problem in the week** you learn of it, with the action, even when it is not yet solved.
**Ask the sponsor once a month** which parts of the report they use and remove a line they do not.

why.text: **A tracker only helps if it is current.** Visible progress builds trust and brings problems out early. A tracker is useful only if it is current and someone looks at it. Track only what would change a decision. The same rule applies to [learning data](t:6.7). All of this is practitioner craft, taken from how projects are usually reported.

**The sponsor has only a few minutes.** Reporting by exception works because a sponsor has a few minutes for your programme each week. A page of green rows hides the one amber row, so the report shows only what needs their attention. Agreeing the thresholds beforehand matters for a less obvious reason. When cohort 4 loses its venue, you will be tempted to hold the status at green until you have fixed it. A rule agreed in a calm week makes the decision for you.

**A hidden problem costs more than the problem.** Bad news that arrives with an action reads as control. The same news found out later reads as concealment, and the sponsor then doubts every green status you have sent. That is why one hidden problem costs more than the problem itself.

**Exception reports never show what went well.** The trade-off is that a report of exceptions never shows what went well. One line of totals covers that. The advice also bends for a new or nervous client, who may want a fuller report for the first month. Give it, then agree a date to move to one page.

try.text: Set up a tracker for one programme with no more than eight columns. Then stand up, start a timer and give this week's report aloud in 60 seconds, as if the sponsor had asked you in a corridor. Good looks like this: you open with the totals, name what is off track, and give the action, the owner and the date without checking the screen.

items: **A green status hiding a problem** destroys trust. Report it as off track in the week you learn of it, with the action.
**Two trackers** means neither is right. If the client's coordinator keeps her own sheet, agree which one stays and close the other.
**People's personal data:** do not track it without need, under the rule to [collect only what you need](t:9.24). Attendance by name may be needed. Notes on individuals rarely are.
**A tracker updated only when asked** is always out of date. Keep the fixed day even in a quiet week, and write "no change".
**Columns grow.** When someone asks for a new one, ask what decision it would change, and remove one if you add one.

quiz.q: The client's coordinator keeps her own attendance spreadsheet and it disagrees with yours. What do you do?
quiz.a: Agree one tracker, in one place the client can see, updated on a fixed day. Two trackers means neither is right.

topics.title: Run a programme in Google Workspace

situation.text: You run programmes with files across email, a laptop and three people's drives. The associate asks for the latest session plan and you send the wrong one. The feedback responses from cohort 2 are in a folder that the whole client team can open.

items: **Create one shared folder per programme**, with the same structure each time. Number the subfolders so they sort the same way, for example 01 Plan and tracker through to 06 Final versions.
**Use a spreadsheet for plan and tracker**, one tab for each: the [programme plan](t:9.18) and the [tracker everyone can see](t:9.21).
**Write briefs and session plans in documents**, with comments for review. When you need an answer from one person, assign the comment to them.
**Use forms for sign-up, needs and feedback.** Send the responses to a linked spreadsheet.
**Keep form responses in a separate folder**, outside the programme folder, shared only with the two or three named people who need them.
**Put sessions in a shared calendar** with joining details. For an online session, add the Google Meet link to the event.

**Set sharing permissions deliberately.** Decide for each folder who can view, who can comment and who can edit, and write the decision down. Leave general access on Restricted unless you have a reason to change it.

**Hold the programme in a shared drive** on a work account, so the files belong to the team and stay when someone leaves. Ask the client in the first week whether their staff can open files from outside the company, which is part of [working inside the client's tools](t:9.30).

why.text: **The method outlasts the tool.** Google Workspace gives you documents, spreadsheets, forms, a calendar, storage and video calls that work together. Its strength is several people editing the same file. The method is the same as any programme: one plan, named owners, one place for files. That method carries over if the tool changes.

**The steps rest on a few Workspace features.** In Drive you share a file or folder with named people as Viewer, Commenter or Editor, and set general access to Restricted or to anyone with the link. On a work or school account, a shared drive holds files that belong to the team and stay when someone leaves. Forms can send responses to a linked spreadsheet. Comments in Docs can be assigned to a person. A Calendar event can carry a Google Meet link.

**Everyone finds files without asking.** The same structure every time is craft, and it pays back on the third programme. You, an associate and a client coordinator can each find the session plan without asking, because it is where it was last time. Numbered folders also show what is missing. An empty 02 Briefs folder two weeks before delivery is a prompt.

**Ease of sharing is also the hazard.** A file takes on the access of the folder it sits in, so one sharing decision made for a folder applies to everything you later drop into it. That is convenient for session plans and wrong for feedback, which is why responses live apart from the programme folder. For a single workshop with one client contact, this set-up is more than you need. One folder and one document will do.

Then ask a colleague who is not on the list to try to open the feedback folder, and to tell you what they see. topics.title: Run a programme in Notion

situation.text: You want one place for the plan, the sessions, the people and the notes, and a spreadsheet is straining. It now has a tab by date, a tab by trainer and a tab of tasks. Last week you changed a venue on one tab and not on the other two.

items: **Make a database of sessions** with five properties: date, cohort, trainer, venue, status. Enter every session once, including the ones without a venue yet.
**Make a database of tasks**, linked to sessions with a relation property. Each task has an owner and a due date, as in [planning the programme](t:9.18).
**Add views**: a calendar for dates, a board for status, a table for detail. Give each view its own filter where it helps, such as the table showing only the next four weeks.
**Keep a page per programme** that pulls these together, with [the scope](t:9.18) at the top and the views beneath it.
**Save a database template** for a standard session, so each new one starts the same way. Put your usual checklist in it: room confirmed, invitations sent, materials shipped, trainer briefed.
**Ask the client about Notion accounts** before you share anything: whether they have them and are willing to use them.
**Share the programme page with the client** as a guest, with Can view access.
**Do a test export of the page** in the first week, so you know you can send a PDF to someone who will not open Notion.

why.text: **Notion shows the same sessions several ways.** Notion combines pages with databases that can be linked and shown in different views. That suits a programme, where the same sessions need to be seen by date, by owner and by status. It takes more set-up than a spreadsheet and some clients will not use it. A guest needs their own Notion account to open a page you share with them.

**A relation property ties tasks to sessions.** A relation property links items in one database to items in another, which is how tasks attach to sessions. Notion offers table, board, calendar, timeline, list, gallery and chart layouts, and each view keeps its own filters and sorts. The calendar layout needs a date property.

**A database holds each session once.** The reasoning is craft. The spreadsheet strains because each new way of looking at the sessions becomes a new tab with the same rows copied in, and the copies drift apart. That is the [two-trackers problem](t:9.21) inside one file. A database holds each session once and the views are different windows onto it, so a change of venue shows everywhere.

**It costs set-up time and another tool.** The cost is set-up time and one more tool for other people to learn. For a programme of three sessions a spreadsheet is quicker and nobody needs an account. When the client will not open Notion, keep it as your own working tool and send them the [one-page report](t:9.21) as an export.

topics.title: Collect only the learner data you need
topics.theory: Learner data and privacy under UK law

situation.text: You copy last year's sign-up form for a new programme. It asks for date of birth, home address and "any medical conditions". Nobody on the team can say what the date of birth was ever used for, and forty people are about to fill it in.

items: **List what you need** to run the programme, and collect only that. Go through the form field by field and write what you will do with each answer. If you cannot say, remove the field.
**Tell people what you collect**, why, and how long you keep it. Put it in three or four plain lines at the top of the form, and state your lawful basis in your privacy information.
**Take extra care with health** and similar information. Ask "Is there anything we can do to help you take part?" in place of a question about medical conditions.
**Limit who can see it.** Name the people, and keep it in a [folder only they can open](t:9.22).
**Decide how long you need** each kind of data and write down your reason. Delete or anonymise it when you no longer need it, and put the deletion date in your calendar on the day you collect it.
**Agree in writing with the client** who decides what is collected, who holds it and who deletes it.
**Give people a way to complain** to you about how you use their data, such as a named contact on the form. Decide who acknowledges a complaint, so that it is done within 30 days.
**Tell people before they take part** if individual results will go to managers, and agree it with the client first, when you [agree what success looks like](t:9.6).

why.text: **UK law limits what you collect and keep.** UK data protection law sets principles that include collecting only what is needed, using it for a stated purpose and keeping it no longer than necessary. You also need a lawful basis before you collect anything, and your privacy information must state it. Some kinds of information, called special category data, get extra protection. Health data is one of them.
**Feedback, assessment results and attendance are personal data.** This is general information, not legal advice. Check the current rules or ask a solicitor.

**The law was amended, not replaced.** The law is the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 amended both and did not replace them. Among its changes, you must give people a way to complain to you about how you use their data and acknowledge a complaint within 30 days. The law sets no fixed retention periods. You decide how long you need the data and must be able to justify it.

**The cheapest data is data never collected.** The practical reasoning is craft. Forms grow by inheritance: each one is copied from the last, and fields survive long after anyone remembers why they were added. Every field you keep is something to store, restrict and later delete, so the cheapest data to look after is the data you never asked for. The access question is also the more useful one for a trainer. A diagnosis does not tell you what to change in the room. "I need to sit near the front and have the slides the day before" does.

try.text: Take one of your forms. For each field, write why you need it, or remove it. Then write the note that goes at the top: what you collect, why, how long you keep it and who to contact. Good looks like this: every remaining field has a use you could explain to a participant in one sentence, and the note gives a deletion point you have put in your calendar.

topics.title: Gather proof with consent
topics.theory: Case studies and testimonials, gathered honestly

situation.text: You want a case study for your website. The programme went well and the client is pleased. One anonymous feedback form has a line so good that you have already pasted it into the homepage draft.

items: **Ask permission in writing**, from the organisation and from anyone named or quoted. Say what you will publish, where it will appear and how to withdraw. The [close-out review](t:9.26) is a natural moment to raise it.
**Use their words** and do not improve them. If you shorten a quote, show them the shortened version.
**Report what happened, including the limits.** Give the number of people, the length of the programme, and what you did not or could not measure.

**Claim contribution, not sole cause.** Other things changed at the same time as your programme. Name one of them in the case study. There is more on [separating the effect of training](t:6.6) from everything else.
**Let them see it** before it is published. Send the whole page as it will appear, with the headline and any photograph, and wait for a yes.
**File what you hold for each testimonial**: the original words, the contact details of the person who gave them, and their permission.
**Remove it if they ask.** Tell them at the start how to ask and how quickly you will act, for example within two working days.

why.text: **A case study must be true and typical.** A case study is evidence only if it is true and typical of what you say it shows. A hand-picked success presented as the norm misleads. Consent protects the people involved and your relationship with the client.

**UK advertising rules say the same.** Under the CAP Code you must hold evidence that a testimonial is genuine, contact details for whoever gave it, and their permission to use it. A testimonial must not be edited or taken out of context in a way that misleads.

**Praise on a feedback form was private.** The rest is craft judgement. The person who wrote a kind line on a feedback form was talking to you, privately, about the day. Putting it on a homepage changes the audience and the purpose without asking them, and they may be recognisable to colleagues even without a name. Asking takes one email and usually gets a yes.

**Stating the limits costs you a stronger headline.** In return, the claim can survive a question from a careful buyer, who will know that a pricing change or a new manager also moves a sales figure. The other cost is that some organisations will refuse to be named. Ask whether an unnamed version, such as "a software company's sales team", would be acceptable, and show them that version too.

try.text: Draft a consent request for a case study. Say what you will publish, where, and how to withdraw. Then say the request aloud in 30 seconds, as you would on a call with the client, and record it. Good looks like this: you name the exact quote, say where it will appear, and make it easy to say no.

topics.title: Close out and hand over
topics.theory: Closing a programme and keeping the lessons

situation.text: The last session ends on a Thursday. By Monday the trainers are on other work and the client's coordinator has a new project. Six months later you start the next programme and book a venue late again, because the lesson from cohort 4 was never written down.

items: **Put the review in diaries** when the programme starts, for a date within two weeks of the last session. Allow 60 minutes with the client and the team.
**Send three questions two days before**: what worked, what did not, and what to change. Bring the lessons you noted while the programme ran.

**Hold the review.** Open by saying what it is for: "This hour is about what we would do differently next time. It is not about who got what wrong." Take what happened first, then the three questions.
**Report results against what was agreed** at the start, when you [agreed what success looks like](t:9.6). Use the same measures and the same words, including any that were missed.
**Turn each lesson into a change** with an owner. "Venues were a problem" is a complaint. "Confirm all venues before invitations go out, owned by Jo" is a lesson.
**Hand over materials, data and open actions**, with owners. File the final versions in one place and remove the drafts.
**Delete the learner data** you no longer need, on a stated date, and record that you did. There is more on [how long to keep learner data](t:9.24).
**Agree any follow-up and who does it**, with a date. Then thank people by name, in writing, for something specific they did.

why.text: **Without a review, mistakes come round again.** A proper close leaves the client holding what it paid for, and gives you the lessons from the work. Without a review, the same mistakes come round again. A structured review after a project is a form of debrief, and debriefs have been studied.

why.title: Do team and individual debriefs enhance performance?
why.found: A meta-analysis of 46 samples compared people and teams who held debriefs with controls who did not. Debriefs improved later performance by roughly 20 to 25 per cent (d = 0.67), with similar results for teams and individuals.
why.means: Hold a structured review that looks at what happened and what to change, and keep it about learning, not blame.

why.text: **Lessons noted along the way are more reliable.** That finding is about debriefs in general. Using it for the review at the end of a training programme is a reasonable inference, and the steps above are craft. The reasoning for them is about timing and memory. At the end of a programme people remember the last cohort and the worst day, which is why lessons noted along the way are more reliable than lessons recalled in the room.

**Blame silences the person who knows most.** Blame shuts a review down for a practical reason. The person who knows most about what went wrong with cohort 4 is the one who was there, and they stop talking the moment the hour turns into a verdict on them. Asking "what happened" and "what would we change" keeps them contributing. The limit of any end review is that it comes too late for this programme, so do not save every lesson for it.

try.text: Write a one-page close-out for a finished programme: results, lessons, handover. Then stand up and say the first two minutes of the review aloud, including the sentence about what the hour is for, and record it. Good looks like this: every lesson on your page has an owner, every follow-up has a date, and your opening names the purpose before anyone can start on blame.

try.title: A worked example: a one-page close-out
lines: New managers programme, twelve cohorts, January to June. Close-out agreed at the review on 2 July.

Results against the three measures agreed at the start: attendance, met. Managers observed holding a feedback conversation within four weeks, met for nine cohorts of twelve. Sponsor's measure of fewer escalations to HR, not yet known, client to report in September.
Lesson 1: confirm every venue before invitations go out. Owner: Jo.
Lesson 2: participant lists arrived late for four cohorts. Next time the sponsor names a contact in each team at the start. Owner: Priya.
Lesson 3: the afternoon practice ran short in the first three cohorts. The session plan now protects 50 minutes for it. Owner: Sam.
Handed over: final slides, workbook and facilitator guide, in the 06 Final versions folder. Drafts removed.
Data: attendance records passed to the client on 2 July. Learner feedback responses deleted on 31 July.
Open action: two people missed their cohort. Priya decides by 15 July whether they join the autumn run.
Follow-up: one 90 minute session for all managers on 18 September, run by Sam, booked by Priya.
Thanks sent to the three associates and the venue coordinators on 3 July.

items: **A review that looks for blame** teaches nothing. When someone starts on a person, bring it back to what happened and what to change.
**Learner data you no longer need:** delete it. Feedback forms left on a drive are the usual leftover. There is more on [collecting only the learner data you need](t:9.24).
**Follow-up promised at close-out** needs a date and an owner, or it will not happen once everyone has moved on.
**Every lesson saved for the end.** Note lessons as the programme runs and give each one an owner.
**A lesson with no owner** is a comment. Before the hour ends, read the lessons back with the names attached.

quiz.a: Bring it back to what happened and what to change. A review that looks for blame teaches nothing. Write the lesson down and give it an owner.

quiz.q: The programme has ended. Feedback forms and attendance sheets are still on your drive. What do you do?
quiz.a: Hand over what the client is due, such as attendance data, and delete the learner data you no longer need on a stated date. Record both in the close-out.

parts.title: Rates, briefs and working across borders
parts.summary: Working out a rate, reshaping a brief, and working in other people's tools and languages.

topics.title: Deliver across countries and languages

situation.text: One programme has to run in nine countries and five languages within the same fortnight. The English deck changed twice last week, and the German team says the examples make no sense for their customers.

items: **Freeze the source before anything is translated.** Give the frozen version a number and date. Changes after the freeze go into a log and are released together as the next version.

**Build a glossary first.** List product names, feature names and key terms with the approved wording in each language and a note on which stay in English. The client's local marketing team usually owns these.

**Mark each piece of content** as translate or adapt. Instructions and product facts are translated. Examples, customer stories, role-play cases, names, currencies and humour are adapted by someone in the market.
**Get an in-market review** from a person who does the learners' job or manages them. Ask them three things: is it accurate, would a customer here say it this way, and what would embarrass us.
**Name one person per market** who signs off, and a date. Without a named sign-off, review comments arrive for ever.

**Cascade through local facilitators.** That means you train them and they deliver in their own language. Give them a facilitator guide with timings, the exact instructions, the reason for each activity, and what may and may not be changed. Sign each one off by watching them teach a section back, following the method for [teaching others to train](t:5.10).
**Plan live sessions by time zone.** Keep every session inside the learners' working day. Run the same session two or three times instead of once at a bad hour, and state every time with its zone.
**Set the update cycle.** Decide how a change to the source reaches every language, who checks it and how old versions are withdrawn.

why.text: This is professional practice from localisation and programme management. There is little published research on localising training programmes.

**Survey translation guidelines offer a borrowed model.** The closest formal guidance comes from another field. Guidelines for translating questionnaires in cross-national surveys recommend a team approach: more than one translator, a review meeting, a named adjudicator who signs off, a pretest with real respondents and written records of every decision. They advise translating from the source, not from another translation. They no longer recommend back translation as a check. Back translation means translating the new text back into the source language and comparing the two. The guidelines say that comparison can mislead, and they say to assess the translated text directly. Survey questions are not training materials, so treat this as a borrowed model.

**Every late change multiplies across languages.** The freeze matters because every late change is multiplied by the number of languages. The glossary matters because inconsistent product terms are the error local teams notice first. A translator can render an instruction faithfully and should not be asked to invent a believable customer in another country. There is more on [preparing content so it can be translated](t:3.16) and on [the mix of cultures in one room](t:4.7).
Local facilitators carry the quality. A guide that explains why each activity is there lets them adapt well.

try.text: Take a session you have run and mark every item as translate or adapt. Then, on a call with someone who works in another country, ask the three in-market review questions aloud about one example.

quiz.q: Why freeze the source before translation starts?
quiz.a: Every later change has to be made again in each language, so late changes multiply cost and errors.

quiz.q: The French reviewer says the role-play customer, a chain of American diners, means nothing to her sellers. The translator rendered it accurately. What do you do?
quiz.a: Treat the case as content to adapt, and ask the reviewer to supply a believable local customer with the same problem. Translation carries the words across, and examples have to be rebuilt for the market.

quiz.q: Head office wants one live launch briefing at 16:00 UK time for every market, including teams in east Asia and the west coast of the United States. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Two or three runs of the same briefing, each inside local working hours, with the same facilitator guide. A session at midnight for one region will be skipped or watched half asleep, and a recording gives them no practice.

topics.title: Work out your day rate
topics.theory: Building a rate from income, costs and sellable days

situation.text: A client asks, "What is your day rate?" You take your last salary, divide it by the working days in a year and say the answer. Six months later you are busy and short of money.

items: **Write down your target income** for the year: what you need to take out of the business before tax, including pension contributions.
**Add up a year of business costs**: insurance, accountant, software, equipment, memberships, your own training, marketing and travel you cannot recharge.
**Count the days.** Start with 260 weekdays. Take off holiday and bank holidays, and an allowance for illness.
**Take off working days you cannot sell**: finding and proposing work, administration and finance, your own learning, and gaps left by cancellations.
**Divide the money by the days** that remain. That is your floor rate for each day you sell. Below it, you are paying to do the work.

**Decide what a sold day is** in your market. If design and preparation are charged as separate lines, the floor applies to each of those days. If clients pay only for delivery days, count the unpaid days behind each one and raise the rate to carry them.
**Check the floor against value.** Ask what the result is worth to the client. You can read about [pricing by value](t:9.4) and the four ways training is sold.

**Check it against the market.** Ask three people who buy or sell similar work what range they see, and note which of your own quotes were accepted. Move up from the floor when the checks allow it. Do not go below it.

why.text: The method is arithmetic and practitioner judgement. No research sits behind it.

**The salary sum fails for two reasons.** An employee is paid on days they do not work. GOV.UK says almost all workers are entitled to 5.6 weeks of paid holiday a year, which is 28 days on a five-day week, and that self-employed people get no holiday or sick pay. You fund those days yourself. The second reason is larger. Much of a working week in a small business goes on selling, quoting, invoicing and learning, and nobody pays for that directly.
**No market rates are given here.** They vary widely with the sector, the size of the client and the kind of work, and your floor does not depend on them.

**The same sum explains an agency's rate card.** An employed trainer's salary and share of overheads are spread across the days the agency can bill for them. That is why your billable days matter to an employer. Tax and VAT sit outside this sum. Ask an accountant how they apply to you.

try.text: Run the sum with your own figures. Then say your rate aloud to a colleague and stop talking. Have them reply, "That is more than we expected." Practise answering by changing the scope and leaving the rate alone. Record it.

**You forget the unpaid days** behind a delivery day. The guidance on [scoping and pricing the work](t:9.4) says design usually takes longer than delivery. Charge for it as a line, or carry it in the rate.
**You set the rate once** and never revisit it. Rerun the sum each year with your logged hours and actual costs.
**You quote an associate rate** to a direct client. An [associate fee](t:9.32) leaves out selling and administration because the training company does them. Direct work has to pay for both.
**You treat these figures as typical.** They are invented to show the arithmetic.

items.label: GOV.UK, Holiday entitlement.
GOV.UK, Employment status: self-employed and contractor.

quiz.q: What do you divide by what to get a floor day rate?
quiz.a: Target income plus business costs, divided by the days you can realistically sell.

quiz.q: Your floor is £500 per sold day. A client will pay only for two delivery days, and the job needs three days of design. What do you do?
quiz.a: Price all five days, either as separate design and delivery lines or as a higher delivery rate that carries the design. Quoting two days at the floor means three days unpaid.

quiz.q: Your floor of £500 assumed 120 sold days and £60,000 to earn. After three months of logging your time, you are on course to sell 96 days. What do you do?
quiz.a: Rerun the sum with the real figure. £60,000 divided by 96 is £625, so that is the new floor. Quote from it on new work, and look at which unsold days you could cut or charge for.

topics.tierReason: Arithmetic and practitioner judgement. The holiday and self-employment points report GOV.UK pages, and the figures are invented.

topics.title: Reshape the brief when training is the wrong answer
topics.theory: Turning a training request into work that will help

situation.text: A retailer's operations manager asks for a half-day customer service course for 200 store staff. Two store managers tell you on a call that staff know what good service looks like. The queue builds because a refund takes eleven screens on the till.

items: **Find the cause before you answer** the request. There is a [full method for diagnosing the cause](t:2.29). If you are external and not yet paid, use the small version: a 30-minute call with two of the people who do the job and one of their managers.
**Say the cause back to the client** in their own words, with what you saw or heard as evidence. "Three people told me the refund takes eleven screens."
**Match the cause** to a piece of work, using the table below. Most causes that training cannot fix still have work in them that a learning person does well.

**Offer the reshaped brief as options**, set out as you would when [writing a proposal](t:9.5). One addresses the cause. One adds a short session if skill is part of the problem. One is the original request, with a plain statement of what it will and will not change.
**Price the new work properly.** Diagnosis, a job aid and a manager guide are design days, and belong in [how you scope and price the work](t:9.4).
**Say what lies outside your skill** and who should do it. System changes, staffing and pay are the client's. Recommend the change and say plainly that you cannot make it.

**Choose whether to deliver or decline** if the client still wants the original course and you believe it will not help. Deliver it with the limits written down, as part of [agreeing what success looks like](t:9.6), or decline and suggest someone else. If you are employed or an associate, take it to the account lead. The decision is theirs.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement, built on the performance analysis tradition behind [running a performance diagnosis](t:2.29) and [deciding what not to train](t:9.14).

**Declining is the last move.** The guidance on [checking it is a skill problem](t:1.20) says to be ready to decline work that will not help. The guidance on [deciding what not to train](t:9.14) says to send back requests where skill is not the cause. Both are right, and declining is the last move. The client has a real problem and a deadline. Walking away leaves them with both, and often with a supplier who will run the course without asking anything.

**Non-training fixes still use a trainer's skills.** Much of what fixes a non-training cause is work a trainer already knows how to do. A job aid is a design task. A manager coaching guide is a short piece of curriculum. A change message is clear writing for a defined audience. Offering these keeps you useful and keeps the client's money pointed at the cause.

**Selling every fix means you have stopped diagnosing.** There is a risk on the other side. If every cause turns into something you sell, you have stopped diagnosing. Some rows in the table end with a recommendation and a small fee, or none. Leave them that way.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play the operations manager who wants the course. Aloud, in five minutes, play back the cause, offer two options and say what you cannot fix. Record it. Check whether you blamed anyone and whether you gave a price for the reshaped work.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: "I spoke to two of your store managers. Can I tell you what I heard before we talk about the course?"
"They said the team knows what good service is. What slows them down is the refund process."
"A course would cost you 200 half-days and the queue would still be there."
"Here is what I can do: a one-page refund guide for the till, tested in two stores, and a short session with whoever owns the till system."
"If you still want the course after that, I will run it, and I will put in writing what I expect it to change."

items: **You announce the diagnosis** as a correction. The client asked in good faith. Present what you heard and let them reach the conclusion.
**You offer work beyond your skill.** Process redesign and communications each have specialists. Bring one in or hand it over.
**You do the diagnosis free** and the client takes it to someone cheaper. Keep [free discovery](t:9.3) short and price anything beyond it.
**You reshape a brief** that belongs to your employer's account. Tell the account lead what you found and let them take it to the client.
**You never say no.** Reshape first, and decline when no version of the work would help.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Name two kinds of paid work, other than a course, that can address a performance problem.
quiz.a: Any two of: a job aid, a process workshop with evidence, manager coaching, communications, a written standard.

quiz.q: A sales leader wants negotiation training. Two reps tell you they give discounts because approval for anything else takes a week. What do you propose?
quiz.a: Play back the cause with the evidence, and offer a session with whoever owns approvals plus a one-page guide to what reps can agree alone. Offer the course as a second option, with its limits stated.

quiz.q: You are an associate and discover on a briefing call that the course you have been booked to deliver will not fix the client's problem. What do you do?
quiz.a: Tell the account lead at the company what you heard and what you would suggest. The client and the decision are theirs, and you deliver what they agree.

topics.title: Work inside the client's tools
topics.theory: Guest access, the client's learning platform and their security rules

situation.text: You build the programme tracker in your own workspace and send a link. The client's laptops block it. Their learning partner, your contact in [the client's learning team](t:9.34), then asks you to record attendance in the company's learning platform, which you cannot log in to.

items: **Ask which collaboration suite the client uses**, in week one. That means its software for chat, files and meetings, such as Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace. Ask how suppliers get in: guest access, a client account or a client laptop. Ask who requests it and how long it takes. Start the request that day.
**Use one identity**, the email address they invite. Open the shared space and a file before your first meeting.
**Keep each working file's current version** in the client's space. Drafts can stay with you.
**Ask the platform owner** how content gets on to the learning platform: who loads it, which formats it accepts and the lead time.
**Treat their platform as the record** of attendance and completion. Do not keep a rival register. Send attendance in the format they ask for on the day of the session.
**Ask about file rules**: their slide template, size limits, and whether video and outside links play on their network.

**Ask the security questions** before you plan activities. Can participants reach outside polling or whiteboard sites from work devices? May sessions be recorded? May you use your own laptop, or outside tools, with their material?

**Test inside their environment a week ahead.** Ask one participant to open the deck, play the video and join the poll from a work device. At the end, move final files to the agreed place and ask for your access to be removed, as part of [closing out and handing over](t:9.26).

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. The guest access details come from Microsoft's documentation.

**A large client has already chosen its tools.** There are guides to running a programme in tools you choose, [in Google Workspace](t:9.22) and [in Notion](t:9.23). A large client has already chosen. Its staff work in one suite, and its learning platform holds the official record of who completed what. A second attendance list creates two versions of the truth and a [data protection question](t:9.24).

**Guest access takes time.** Microsoft's documentation for Teams is one example. A guest is someone outside the organisation who is given access to teams, channel files, chats and meetings. The client's administrators switch guest access on or off for the whole organisation. A guest account is created in the client's directory, and access can take up to 12 hours to appear after you are added. Leaving a team does not delete the account. An administrator has to remove it. Other suites have their own rules, so ask the client's administrator how theirs works.
**Security rules change the design.** The security questions come first because they change the design. An activity built round an outside whiteboard fails in a company that blocks it.

try.text: Take a session you have already built. Assume the client blocks every outside site and accepts only its own slide template. Rework one activity so it runs with what is left, then run that activity aloud with a colleague as participant.

try.title: Week one questions about the client's tools
lines: Which suite do you use for chat, files and meetings?
How do suppliers get access, who requests it and how long does it take?
Where should programme files live, and who else can see that space?
Who owns the learning platform, and who loads content?
Which file formats does the platform accept, and what is the lead time?
How is attendance recorded, by whom, and by when do you need it?
Is there a slide template, and which software version do people use?
Do video and outside links play on your network?
Can participants use outside polling or whiteboard sites on work devices?
May sessions be recorded, and where are recordings kept?
May I use my own laptop? Which tools are not allowed with your material?
What happens to my access and the files when the programme ends?

items: **You ask for access too late**, in the week before delivery. Ask on day one.
**You get round a block** by emailing files to a personal address or carrying them on a memory stick. Ask for the approved route.
**You keep your own copy** of the attendance list "just in case". It is personal data you no longer need. Send it, confirm it arrived and delete it.
**You assume the room has internet** of the kind your activity needs. Test from a work device on the client's network.
**You leave guest accounts open** after the programme. Ask the client to remove them and note the date in your close-out.

items.label: Microsoft Learn, Guest access in Microsoft Teams.

quiz.q: On a client programme, which system is the record of attendance and completion?
quiz.a: The client's learning platform.

quiz.q: Your design uses an outside whiteboard site. A week before delivery you learn the client blocks it. What do you do?
quiz.a: Rebuild the activity with a tool the client has approved, or with paper, and test it from a work device. Do not ask participants to use personal phones to get round the block.

quiz.q: The client's laptops cannot open the tracker in your own workspace. What do you do?
quiz.a: Move the tracker into the client's shared space and keep the current version there. A tracker the client cannot open is no use to them, and two copies drift apart.

parts.title: Work inside an agency or as an associate
parts.summary: Delivering someone else's design, associate terms, your own contract, the client's learning team, how large organisations buy and looking after an account.

topics.title: Deliver someone else's design
topics.theory: Delivering to a brief you did not write

situation.text: The agency sends you 140 slides and a facilitator guide on Thursday. On Tuesday you deliver it to a client's sales team. You did not design the day and you have never met the client.

items: **Ask before you say yes**, using the questions in the list below.
**Ask for the full pack** five working days ahead: facilitator guide, slides, participant materials, the timed plan and the original brief. Ask for 30 minutes with the designer.
**Read for intent first.** Beside each block write one line: what people should be able to do after it. Where you cannot, you have a question for the designer.

**Sort the day into fixed and flexible.** Fixed, unless you are told otherwise: the objectives, any assessed activity, the client's product facts and policy wording, the branding, and timings shared with another room. Flexible: your own stories, how you form groups, your wording of instructions and the order of your debrief questions.
**Rehearse aloud the three parts** most likely to go wrong: the first ten minutes, the hardest activity to set up and the section you understand least.
**Raise any design problem before the day**, in writing, with whoever owns the design. State the problem, the risk and one fix that fits the same time. Then deliver what they decide.
**Make the smallest change** that protects the objective if something fails on the day. Note the time and what you did.
**Send a one-page delivery report** within 24 hours: what ran to time, what you changed and why, questions the materials could not answer, and anything the client said about future work.

why.text: **The design carries promises to the client.** This is practitioner judgement. No study tests it. The design carries promises you were not there to hear. Somebody agreed the objectives with the client, and the assessed activities are often what the client paid for, so those parts are fixed. Your stories and your way with a group are yours.

**Ask for the reasons behind the design.** The guidance on [briefing the people you bring in](t:9.20) tells the hirer to brief the reasons behind the design. From the other chair, you ask for them. A facilitator who knows what an activity is for can shorten it well when the room runs late.

**Raising a problem early moves you towards collaborator.** Peter Block describes three roles a consultant can take: expert, pair of hands and collaborator. Delivering another person's design starts as pair of hands. Raising a problem early, with a fix, moves you towards collaborator. Raising it on the day does the opposite. Nobody can approve a change at 09:15, and the client sees a supplier arguing with itself.

try.text: Take a session plan someone else wrote. Mark each block fixed or flexible. Then deliver the opening and the first activity set-up aloud to a colleague, in your own words. Ask them what the objective was. If they cannot say, you changed more than the wording.

try.title: Questions to ask before you accept the booking
lines: Who is the end client, and who is my contact on the day?
What should people be able to do by the end, and how will anyone know?
Who is in the room: roles, how many, how long in the job, and what were they told about why they are coming?
Has this design run before? What happened, and what was changed afterwards?
When do I get the full pack, and can I speak to the designer?
What may I adapt, and what must stay exactly as written?
Who do I tell if I see a problem with the design, and by what date?
Is preparation time paid, and how much is expected?
Room or platform, equipment, co-facilitator or producer: who provides each and who sets up?
Will senior people or the client's learning team be in the room?
What gets reported afterwards about the session, and about individuals?
What do I say if someone asks me about further work?

try.title: Words you can use: raising a design problem before the day
lines: "I have been through the pack for Tuesday and I have one concern and a suggestion."
"The role-play at 11:15 gives each pair eight minutes. With 16 people and one of me, I can observe two pairs at most."
"The risk is that most people practise the call with nobody watching and repeat their old habits."
"Could we run it in threes with an observer using the checklist on page 12? It fits the same 40 minutes."
"If you would rather keep pairs, I will run it as written. Could you let me know by Friday noon?"

items: **You rewrite the day** because you would have designed it differently. If the objective is not at risk, deliver it as written and put your idea in the report.
**The pack arrives the night before.** Tell the agency that evening which sections you can deliver as designed and which you will simplify.
**You distance yourself in the room** with a line such as "I did not write this slide". Present the content as yours for the day.
**You improve the client's product facts** or policy wording. Deliver them exactly and report any that looked wrong.
**You send no report.** The designer's only view of the room is yours, and agencies rebook the people who make the next run better.

items.label: Block (2023), Flawless Consulting: A Guide to Getting Your Expertise Used. Fourth edition. Wiley.

quiz.q: Name three things that are normally fixed when you deliver someone else's design.
quiz.a: Any three of: the objectives, assessed activities, the client's product facts and policy wording, the branding, timings shared with another room.

quiz.q: Four days before delivery you see that an activity cannot work with the group size. What do you do?
quiz.a: Write to the person who owns the design with the problem, the risk and one fix that fits the same time, and ask for a decision by a date. Then deliver what they decide, because the change is theirs to approve.

quiz.q: At 14:00 the day is running 25 minutes late and the last block is the assessed practice. What do you do?
quiz.a: Protect the assessed practice and shorten something flexible, such as a discussion or an energy break. Note the time and the change, and put it in your report the same day.
