topics.title: Work as an associate
topics.theory: Associate terms: bookings, day rates and whose client it is

situation.text: A training company emails: "Are you free on the 14th and 15th? Software firm, new managers, our design, usual day rate." You have never seen their associate agreement and you do not know what the usual rate covers.

items: **Ask for the associate agreement** before the first booking and read it while no date depends on it.

**Know which of three states** a booking is in. An enquiry asks if you are free. A provisional hold, often called a pencil, reserves the date with no commitment. A confirmed booking is in writing with dates, place and fee. Give every hold a release time.
**Ask what the day rate includes**, line by line. Use the table below. Anything nobody mentions is unpaid.
**Agree expenses before you travel**: what is repaid, any limits, and who books.
**Read cancellation in both directions**: what you are paid if the client cancels late, and what notice you must give to withdraw.

**Read the clauses about the client.** Expect to represent the company's brand, to pass on every enquiry about further work, and not to approach its clients for a period. Check how long, and which clients.
**Check the materials clause.** Their materials stay theirs. If you bring a handout of your own, say in writing beforehand that it stays yours.
**Ask how you get paid**: when to invoice, what reference to quote, and whether you are paid on fixed terms or only once the client has paid the company. Invoice the day after delivery.

why.text: Most of this is practitioner judgement. The tax and payment points come from GOV.UK.

**You trade a lower fee for found work.** An associate is a freelance trainer who delivers a training company's work to its clients, under its name. The arrangement is a trade. The company finds the client, wins the work and carries the risk. You accept a lower fee than you would charge direct, and the client stays theirs. The clauses that stop you approaching its clients, often called non-solicitation clauses, protect what the company spent to win them. You can read about [the same arrangement from the hirer's side](t:9.20).

**Count the unpaid days behind the rate.** A day rate means little until you know how many unpaid days sit behind it. Divide the fee by every day the booking takes and compare the answer with your floor, the figure from [working out your day rate](t:9.28).

**Your rights come from the contract.** GOV.UK says self-employed people get no holiday or sick pay and have the rights their contract with the client gives them. So the agreement is your protection. If you work through your own limited company, the off-payroll working rules (IR35) may apply. GOV.UK says the client decides your employment status for tax where it is in the public sector or is a medium or large private business. Where the client is small and outside the public sector, your own company decides. Agencies in the chain have responsibilities whatever their size. If the rules apply, tax and National Insurance are deducted from the fee before it reaches your company. This is general information, not legal advice.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play the company's resourcing manager. Aloud, in three minutes, ask what the rate includes, when the hold is released and how you get paid. Record it and listen for apologies.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: On a hold: "Happy to pencil those in. I will hold them until Friday at five and release them if I have not heard."
On the rate: "Before I confirm, can you tell me what the rate covers? I am thinking of preparation, the briefing call and travel."
On payment: "When should I invoice, and what reference do you need on it?"
When a participant asks if you run courses yourself: "I am here with the team at the company today, so they are the right people to ask. I will pass your name on this afternoon."

items: **A pencil with no release date.** You turn down paid work for a hold that quietly lapses.
**The client offers you direct work.** Name your contact at the company and pass it on the same day. Taking it may break your agreement.

**Paid when paid.** Ask for fixed terms. GOV.UK says that where no date is agreed, a business payment is late 30 days after the invoice or the service, whichever is later. You can read about [interest on late payment](t:9.9).
**Blurring the brands.** Showing your own logo, or connecting with participants from your business profile, may breach the agreement. Ask.

quiz.q: Under the off-payroll working rules, who decides your employment status for tax when the client is a large private company?
quiz.a: The client.

quiz.q: A company asks you to pencil in three dates next month. Another client offers confirmed work on one of them. What do you do?
quiz.a: Tell the first company you have a confirmed offer and ask them to confirm or release by a set time today. A hold with no release time costs you paid work.

quiz.q: During a break, the client's sales director asks for your card so she can book you direct. What do you do?
quiz.a: Thank her, say you are there with the company and give her your contact there, then tell the company the same day. The client is theirs, and your agreement almost certainly says so.

topics.title: Know your contract before you build your own thing
topics.theory: Employment terms on intellectual property, outside interests and restrictions after leaving

situation.text: You work for a training company. In the evenings you are building a website, a set of templates and a plan for a business of your own. Nobody at work knows yet.

items: **Gather the documents**: your employment contract, any letters that changed it, the staff handbook and the policies on intellectual property, conflicts of interest and company equipment.
**Find the intellectual property clause.** Note what it claims. Some cover only work done as part of your job. Others reach anything connected with the employer's business.
**Find the clause on outside interests**, which may be headed exclusivity or conflicts of interest. Note whether you need written consent before you start a business or take other paid work.
**Find the confidentiality clause.** Note what it covers and whether it continues after you leave.
**Find the restrictions after leaving.** For each one write down how long it lasts, which clients or colleagues it covers and any area it names.

**Keep the two bodies of work apart** from today. Use your own laptop, accounts and time. Keep dated records of what you made. Copy nothing from your employer or its clients, even as a starting point.
**Tell your manager about the second business** early and in writing. Ask for a written reply that says what is agreed, including who owns any named piece of work.
**Take advice from an employment solicitor** before you rely on your own reading or sign anything new.

why.text: This is general information, not legal advice.

**Employers usually own work made in the job.** The Intellectual Property Office says the person who creates a work is usually the first owner of the copyright. The exception is work an employee creates in the course of employment. There the employer is the first owner, unless an agreement says otherwise. The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 does not define "in the course of employment". The Office's guidance says courts have asked whether the person worked under a contract of service, as an employee, or a contract for services, as a freelancer. The guidance does not say where the line falls for something you make at home that is close to your day job. That depends on your contract and the facts, which is why you take advice. You can read about [who owns the materials](t:9.9) when you are the freelancer.

**Contract terms can bind you after you leave.** Acas says an employer may include terms that limit what you do. An exclusivity clause stops you working for another employer, or requires consent first. Restrictive covenants apply after you leave. Acas lists four kinds: not competing, not disclosing confidential information, not encouraging colleagues to leave with you, and not trying to win the former employer's clients. It says an employer usually cannot enforce these unless they are clear, specific and limited in time, and it calls this area of law complex.

**A declared side business costs less trust.** Telling your manager early is practitioner judgement. Nothing in the official guidance requires it, though your contract may. A side business found out later costs more trust than one that was declared.

items: **You assume evening work** is automatically yours. The official guidance gives the default and does not settle your case. The contract may reach further. Read it and ask.
**You use the work laptop** or work accounts to draft your own materials. Move nothing across in either direction.
**You reuse a client example** or an activity you built at work. Rebuild from your own sources or leave it out.
**You rely on something spoken**, a "that is fine". Managers move on. Get it in an email.
**You sign a new contract** or a promotion letter without rereading these clauses. Terms often change at that moment.

items.label: Intellectual Property Office, Ownership of copyright works.
Acas, Terms restricting a worker's actions.

quiz.q: According to the Intellectual Property Office, who is the first owner of copyright in work an employee creates in the course of employment?
quiz.a: The employer, unless an agreement says otherwise.

quiz.q: You are employed and want to register a company for a future retreat business. Your contract has a clause headed "Other business interests". What do you do?
quiz.a: Read what the clause requires, ask for consent in writing before you register and keep the reply. If the wording is unclear, take advice from an employment solicitor before you act.

quiz.q: You built a useful session plan at work for a client and want it in your own toolkit. What do you do?
quiz.a: Leave it where it is. Work made as part of the job belongs to the employer by default, so build your own version from your own sources in your own time.

topics.tierReason: Reports what the Intellectual Property Office and Acas pages say. The advice to declare early is practitioner judgement.

topics.title: Know the client's learning function
topics.theory: Who sits in and around a large client's learning team

situation.text: The sales director who wants the programme says, "Just send me the proposal." Two weeks later an email arrives from a learning partner you have never heard of. She asks why she found out about the programme from procurement.

items: **Ask any sponsor two questions** in the first conversation: "Who in your learning team should know about this?" and "How does a new supplier get set up here?"
**Draw the stakeholder map** in the first week. Use the table below. Put one name against each role, or write "not known yet" and find out.
**Meet the learning team early** and come with questions. What already exists on this subject? Which models and terms do people here already use? What else is on the calendar for this audience?
**Ask how their year runs**: when budgets are set, when the plan is fixed, and which weeks are closed to training. For a sales team that is often quarter end. For store staff it is peak trading.
**Ask what the head of learning reports** upward, and shape your own reporting to feed it.
**Agree in writing who does what.** Cover bookings, messages to participants, loading content to the platform, attendance records and contact with line managers.
**Send the same one-page update** to the sponsor and the learning team on the same day, using the [one-page progress report](t:9.21). Neither should hear news from the other.

why.text: **Treat the table as questions to ask.** This is practitioner knowledge of how large organisations tend to be arranged. Titles and structures vary, so treat the table as questions to ask.

**The buyer is several people.** The guide to [who buys training](t:9.1) separates the buyer, the sponsor and the learner. In a large company the buyer is itself several people. A head of learning sets priorities and answers for the budget. Learning partners each look after one part of the business and are the usual way in. Specialists design and run programmes. Somebody owns the learning platform. Beside the team sit HR business partners, who know the managers and the people issues, and procurement, IT and security, who decide whether you can be paid and what you can connect to.

**Each of them is judged on something different.** The sponsor wants a result in their team. The head of learning has to defend spend and avoid duplication. Procurement wants a compliant supplier at a fair price. Security wants no new risk. A proposal that pleases the sponsor and ignores the rest stalls for reasons the sponsor cannot see.

**Going round the learning team costs your place.** Going round the learning team is the usual way suppliers lose their place. You duplicate what exists, you use different words for the same idea, and you ask for things only the learning team can give. Meeting them first costs an hour.

items: **The sponsor says not to bother** the learning team. Say you will keep it light, and tell them anyway. They control the platform, the calendar and often the purchase order.

**You ask the learning team** for access to line managers as if they could grant it. Often they cannot. Ask who can, which is usually the sponsor or the HR partner.

quiz.q: Name four roles in or beside a large client's learning function, other than the sponsor.
quiz.a: Any four of: head of learning, learning partner, HR business partner, procurement, IT and security, platform owner.

quiz.q: A business sponsor says, "Do not involve the learning team, they slow everything down." What do you do?
quiz.a: Say you will keep their involvement short, and still tell the learning partner what is planned. They control the platform, the calendar and often the purchase order, and they will find out anyway.

quiz.q: In week one you learn the client already teaches a feedback model different from the one in your design. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the learning team which model people use and rebuild your activity round theirs. Two models for one skill confuse learners and set you against the internal team.

topics.title: Understand how large organisations buy
topics.theory: Supplier onboarding, tenders, contracts and purchase orders

situation.text: A technology company's enablement lead says yes on a call in March. The first session runs in June. The weeks between went on forms, a security questionnaire, a contract and a purchase order.

items: **Ask about supplier set-up** at the first sign of interest: "Are we already set up as a supplier? If not, what does it involve and how long does it usually take?"

**Prepare for supplier onboarding.** Expect a form asking for company and bank details, insurance certificates and policies on data protection, security and equality. Keep current copies in one folder.

**Read a tender's scoring before its questions.** If the work goes to tender, suppliers bid in writing against published questions and are scored. Note the criteria, the weight on each, the word limits and the deadline for clarification questions. Answer under their headings, in their order.

**Learn the two contract documents.** A master agreement sets the general terms once: ownership of materials, confidentiality, liability, data and payment. A statement of work then describes each job: what is delivered, dates, named people and price.

**Read the ownership clause** against the guidance on [who owns the materials](t:9.9). Large clients often expect to own what they pay for. Ask to keep the material you brought with you and license it to them.
**Answer the security and data questionnaire** truthfully and briefly. "Not applicable, we hold none of your data" is a complete answer.
**Get the purchase order number** before any work starts. Put it on every invoice and send the invoice where the order says.
**Read the payment terms** and plan your cash for the gap. Put every buying step on [the programme plan](t:9.18) with a date.

why.text: **Wanting and paying sit with different people.** The steps above describe common practice, and each organisation has its own version. A large organisation separates the person who wants something from the people who commit money and accept risk. For you that means time. The sponsor's yes begins a second process.

**Public bodies must publish how they score.** For UK public bodies the position is set by the Procurement Act 2023, whose rules took effect on 24 February 2025. The government's guide for suppliers says you register free on the central digital platform, Find a Tender, and store your business details once for reuse across bids. Official guidance says a public contract is awarded to the most advantageous tender, meaning the best tender when assessed against the published award criteria and assessment method. The authority must set out the criteria and their relative importance. Awarding on price alone is possible, and the guidance says it is unlikely to suit most contracts. Suppliers whose tenders were assessed receive an assessment summary. The supplier guide also says 30-day payment terms will reach more public sector contracts. This is general information, not legal advice.

**Private companies set their own rules.** GOV.UK publishes reports from large businesses showing the average time they take to pay suppliers and the share of payments made late. On security, some buyers ask suppliers to hold Cyber Essentials, which the National Cyber Security Centre describes as a government certification scheme against common cyber attacks.

try.text: Pick one large organisation you would like to work for. Look up its payment report on GOV.UK. Then build your onboarding folder: insurance certificates, policies and a one-page company summary.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a master agreement and a statement of work?
quiz.a: The master agreement sets the general terms once. A statement of work describes one piece of work under it: what is delivered, dates, people and price.

quiz.q: A sponsor says, "Procurement will catch up, can you start design on Monday?" What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask for the purchase order number first, or written confirmation of who will pay if it is delayed. Work done before the order exists may be impossible to invoice.

quiz.q: A tender gives 30% to approach and 25% to price, with a two-page limit per answer. How do you spend your effort?
quiz.a: Put most of it into the approach answer, written under their heading and inside the limit, because that is where most marks are. Then give a complete price in their format.

topics.title: Look after an account
topics.theory: Service reviews, changes of sponsor, budget freezes and renewals

situation.text: The programme is in month four of nine. Your sponsor emails to say she is moving to another division and her successor will be in touch. In the same week the client's finance team freezes discretionary spending.

items: **Hold a service review**, a regular meeting with the sponsor about how the work is going, on a fixed rhythm: monthly for the first three months, then quarterly. Keep it to 45 minutes and use the same agenda each time.
**Bring evidence.** Show what ran, who attended, what participants and managers reported, what is off track and what you propose to change. There is more on [tracking and reporting progress](t:9.21).
**Ask a leaving sponsor for two things** before they go: a call with you and the successor, and a short written note of what was agreed and why.
**Meet the new sponsor within two weeks.** Start with their priorities. Then [confirm the success measures in writing](t:9.6) again, because they did not agree the first set.

**Do not argue with a freeze** when it lands. Read your contract's pause and cancellation terms first. Then offer options in writing: pause with dates held, cut to the part tied most closely to the business result, spread the remaining sessions over a longer period, or [stop cleanly with a handover](t:9.26).

**Agree who owns what** where other suppliers or an internal team work with the same people. Share your calendar and use the terms the client already uses. If two programmes teach clashing models, take it to the learning team with a proposal.

**Start the renewal conversation** three months before the end. Ask what the sponsor would need to see to continue. Bring results against the agreed measures, and one recommendation that makes the work smaller somewhere.
**Write a short account note** after every meeting, so that a colleague could take over tomorrow.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement from client work. There is little research on it.

**Programmes are seldom lost in the classroom.** They end when the person who wanted them leaves, when money tightens, or when the supplier has become hard work. A regular review gives small problems somewhere to go before they grow. It also means a successor finds a record.

**A new sponsor did not choose you.** They inherit a cost they will be asked to defend, and they have plans of their own. Opening with your history asks them to honour someone else's decision. Opening with their priorities lets them make it theirs.

**A freeze is rarely about you.** Offering options keeps you in the conversation and shows you can tell which parts of the programme matter most. Recommending less work now and then has the same effect at renewal. The client learns that your advice is not always an invoice.

try.text: Ask a colleague to play a new sponsor who has inherited your programme and is unsure about it. Run the first ten minutes of that call aloud. Record it and count how many minutes passed before you asked about their priorities.

try.title: Words you can use
lines: To a new sponsor: "Before I tell you anything about the programme, what are you being asked to deliver this year?"
"Here is one page on what was agreed and what has happened so far. Tell me what no longer fits."
On a freeze: "Understood. I do not want to add to the pressure. Can I send you four options by Thursday, from a pause to a clean stop?"
"If only one part carries on, I would keep the manager sessions. They are the part tied to the result you named."
On another supplier's model: "Your leadership course uses a different feedback model. I suggest we adopt theirs so people hear one thing."

items: **You have one relationship.** When that person leaves, so does the account. Keep at least two, and make one of them the learning team.
**A review with only good news.** The first hidden problem that surfaces costs you the client's belief in every earlier report.
**A pause treated as a cancellation:** you send the invoice. Check the contract, then talk. A client who is helped through a freeze usually comes back.
**You criticise another supplier** to the client. It reads as selling. Raise a clash as a problem for learners and offer a fix.
**Renewal left to the last month.** Budgets are set earlier than that. There is more on [how training budgets and buyers work](t:9.1).

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: How long before the end of a programme should the renewal conversation start?
quiz.a: About three months.

quiz.q: Your sponsor is leaving in two weeks. What do you ask her for?
quiz.a: A call with you and her successor, and a short written note of what was agreed and why. Then meet the successor within two weeks and confirm the success measures again.

quiz.q: Finance freezes spending halfway through a programme. The sponsor sounds embarrassed. What do you do?
quiz.a: Check your pause and cancellation terms, then send written options from a pause to a clean stop, and say which part you would keep. Options keep you part of the decision.

parts.title: Start your own practice
parts.summary: Setting up and finding work for your own training and retreat business: the offer, the first clients, a pipeline, the business form, tax registration, insurance and associate work.

topics.title: Decide what you offer and to whom
topics.theory: Choosing a first market and a single clear offer

situation.text: A former colleague asks what your new business does. You say, "Leadership training, team days, retreats, facilitation, some coaching, workshop design, that sort of thing." She says it sounds great and wishes you luck. She could have introduced you to two people that week, and she had nothing she could repeat to them.

items: **List the people you already know** who could buy from you or introduce you: former managers and colleagues, people who have moved to other companies, past clients, people you trained with. Aim for thirty names. If you are employed, read about [what your employment contract restricts](t:9.33) first, because your contract may limit who you can approach.

**Sort the names** by the kind of organisation they work in. Your first market is the group where you have the most names and already understand the work. For many people that is the sector they have just left.

**Ring five people in that group** for fifteen minutes each. Ask what they last took a team away for or trained a team in, who organised it, what was hard about it and what it cost in time. Do not pitch. You are looking for a problem they already spend money on.
**Choose one offer:** one buyer, one format and one result. Write down who signs it off, how many people attend, how long it lasts and what exists at the end that did not exist before.

**Write the offer as one sentence** of under thirty words: "I run [format] for [who], so that [result in their words]." Promise what people will do or leave with. There are reasons [why you never promise a transformation](t:8.1), and guidance on [claims you can support](t:9.7).

**Say the sentence to three people** from that market and then ask, "Who do you know with this problem?" If they name someone, the sentence works. If they say "that sounds interesting" and name nobody, make it narrower.
**Add a rough shape and price range** beside it, built from [the floor for your day rate](t:9.28), so that you can answer "what does that cost" on the spot.

**Lead with the one offer** for six months or ten buyer conversations, whichever comes first. Take other work that arrives if you can do it well. Then review what people asked for and rewrite the sentence.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study compares a new training business with one offer against one with a menu, and some people do well as generalists because one large client keeps them busy.

**People pass on a sentence, not a list.** The reasoning is about what other people can do with your description. Most early work comes through someone who knows you talking to someone who does not. That person needs a sentence short enough to repeat and specific enough that the listener recognises their own problem in it. A list of seven services gives them nothing to pass on.

**One offer is also easier to run.** You can price it, because you know the shape. You get better at it quickly, because the third time you run a two-day leadership offsite you are reusing a timetable you have already fixed twice. And you can show a sample of it before you have a single case study.

**Known contacts stand in for a track record.** Starting from people you know is a substitute for a track record. A stranger has to trust your website. A former colleague has seen you work. The common fear is that a narrow offer turns work away. In practice people still ask for other things once they know you.
**Two lines need two sentences.** If you run two lines, such as retreats and one-day training, give each its own sentence and its own buyer. Open any one conversation with only one of them.

try.text: Write your sentence, then say it aloud to three people this week, one of them outside your field. Record yourself on the third. Good looks like this: it takes under fifteen seconds, the listener can say it back to you an hour later, and at least one of the three names a person you should talk to. If the person outside your field cannot say what you do, take out the trade words.

Rewritten

No buyer, no format and no result. Nobody can think of a person to pass it to.
"I run one-day feedback courses for newly promoted managers in software companies. Each manager practises twice on a real case of their own."
"Transformational retreats that reconnect your team and reignite their purpose."
It promises a change inside people that nobody can deliver to order, and it does not say what happens.
"I plan and run two-day offsites for leadership teams of eight to twelve. You leave with next year's three priorities agreed, each with a named owner."
"Training, facilitation, coaching, team days, workshop design and e-learning."
It is a menu. The listener has to work out which item fits them, and most will not.
"I help customer support teams in technology companies handle angry calls. It is a half-day in the room with recorded practice, and a follow-up a month later."

items: **You pick the most interesting market** and know nobody in it. Start where your names are. Move later, with paid work behind you.
**Your sentence describes you:** your method, your years, your values. Rewrite it so the subject is the client's team and the end is what they leave with.
**You change the offer** after every conversation. One person's reaction is weak evidence. Hold it steady for ten conversations and then look for the pattern.

**You promise what you cannot control:** an outcome such as higher sales or lower staff turnover. Promise the work and what people will produce in the room, and [agree measures with the client](t:9.6).

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What three things does a single clear offer name?
quiz.a: One buyer, one format and one result, written as a sentence of under thirty words.

quiz.q: You say your sentence to a former colleague. She says, "That sounds really interesting," and changes the subject. What do you do?
quiz.a: Treat it as a sign the sentence is too general, and narrow the buyer or the result until a listener can name a person with that problem. Polite interest with no name attached means nobody recognised themselves in it.

quiz.q: Your offer is two-day offsites for leadership teams. A contact asks whether you could run a half-day on presentation skills for her sales team next month. What do you do?
quiz.a: Say yes if you can do it well and it clears your floor rate. The offer decides what you lead with in new conversations, and paid work with someone who trusts you is how a first-year business gets its evidence.

topics.title: Win your first three clients
topics.theory: Finding paid work with no track record

situation.text: Your website has been live for six weeks. You have posted four times and had no enquiry. You have no client logos and no case studies, and you are waiting to feel ready before you contact anyone you know.

items: **Write a list of twenty names** from [the market you chose](t:9.37). Use people who have seen you work. Beside each, write whether they could buy, could introduce you or could only advise. Leave out clients of an employer or of a training company you work through. The guides to [whose client it is as an associate](t:9.32) and [what your employment terms restrict](t:9.33) explain why they are not yours to approach.
**Send five personal messages a week,** each written to one person. Ask for twenty minutes of their view. Do not attach a brochure. The wording is below.

**Run the conversation in three parts.** Spend the first twelve minutes on their situation, using the [questions for a discovery conversation](t:9.3). Then say your one-sentence offer and ask, "Is that a problem here, or for anyone you know?" Use the last three minutes to agree a next step with a date and to ask who else you should speak to.

**Propose a small paid first job** when someone has a need: a half-day for one team, a ninety-minute session at a team meeting, or the facilitation of one day of an offsite they have already booked. Give a fixed price and [written terms](t:9.9).

**If you reduce the price, say so** and say what you want in return: "This is a first-client price. In return I would like a thirty-minute review call afterwards and, if you are pleased, a short testimonial." There are rules on [consent for using their words](t:9.25). Do not work for nothing.

**Show the work** in place of case studies. Send a one-page outline written for their situation, a sample timetable (like the [session plan for a training day](t:4.33) or the [timetable for a residential](t:8.10)) and a three-minute recording of you running part of a session. Offer two people who have watched you teach or facilitate, even if that was inside a previous job.
**Follow up once after a week** and once more two weeks later. Then stop, and note a date three months on to try again.
**Plan for it to be slow.** Expect months between a first conversation and a first paid day. Keep other income while you build, such as [getting on to an associate list](t:9.43).

why.text: **This is practitioner judgement, including the numbers.** Five messages a week and three months are working assumptions, not findings.

**A small first job lowers the buyer's risk.** A buyer who hires an unknown trainer is taking a risk with their own reputation. People who know your work carry less of that risk, and a small first job reduces it further. A half-day is easy to approve, and it gives you a paying client, a session you can describe and someone who can speak for you.

**A sample answers the buyer's real question.** Showing a sample works because it answers the buyer's real question, which is whether you can do this for their team. Never fill the gap with an invented client, a made-up result or a testimonial from a friend posing as a customer. You can read [the rules on reviews](t:9.25).

**One legal point applies to outreach.** The Information Commissioner's Office says the marketing rules also cover messages sent to businesses. On its page, promotional email to a company address does not need prior consent under the electronic marketing rules, but you must say who you are and give a valid way to opt out. Sole traders and some partnerships are treated as individuals, so you need their consent or a narrow exception that applies to your own past customers. A named person's work email is personal data, and that person can object to marketing at any time. The page says it is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act. This is general information, not legal advice.

try.text: Write the list of twenty today. Then rehearse the conversation aloud with a friend playing a busy head of department: twelve minutes of questions, your sentence, the ask, the next step. Record it. Good looks like this: you talk for less than a third of the time, you say the offer once without apologising, and the call ends with a date. Send the first five messages before the end of the week.

try.title: Words you can use: a first message and a follow-up

"Hi Dan. I have set up on my own, running two-day offsites for leadership teams in software companies."
"I am not selling you anything. I would value twenty minutes of your view on how your team plans its away days and what tends to go wrong."
"Could you do a call on Tuesday or Thursday next week? If now is a bad time, say so and I will leave you in peace."
Follow-up, one week later:
"Hi Dan. A quick nudge on my note last week, in case it got buried. Twenty minutes any day this fortnight would be a real help."
Second follow-up, two weeks after that, with something useful:
"Hi Dan. I have written a one-page checklist for planning a leadership offsite and thought of you. Here it is, no reply needed. I will try you again in the new year."
After a good conversation:
"Thank you for today. You said the January planning day usually ends without owners for the actions. I will send a one-page outline for that day by Friday, with a fixed price."

**You work free "for the exposure".** Free work is treated as worth what it cost, and it rarely turns into paid work. Charge a small fixed price and name what you want in return.

**You approach participants or clients** you met through a training company. That may break your agreement and it will end the relationship. Pass every such enquiry to the company, as the [terms of associate work](t:9.32) say.

items.label: Information Commissioner's Office, Business-to-business marketing.

quiz.q: According to the Information Commissioner's Office, what must a promotional email to a company address always include?
quiz.a: Who you are and a valid way to opt out. Sole traders and some partnerships are treated as individuals and have stronger protection.

quiz.q: A former manager says, "We might need something for the team in the spring. Send me your case studies." You have none. What do you do?
quiz.a: Say plainly that the business is new, and send a one-page outline written for her team, a sample timetable and a short recording, with two people who have watched you work. A tailored sample answers her real question, and an invented case study would be dishonest.

quiz.q: A contact offers you a first job if you will do the day for nothing, "to get your name known". What do you do?
quiz.a: Offer a stated first-client price for a small fixed piece of work, in return for a review call and a testimonial if they are pleased. A paid job gives you a real client to describe, and unpaid work is rarely valued or repeated.

topics.title: Keep a simple pipeline
topics.theory: Tracking possible work from first conversation to signed job

situation.text: In September you had three warm conversations. It is now November. One person was waiting for an outline from you, one was going to speak to her director, and you cannot remember what the third agreed. You have been busy delivering and nothing new has come in.

items: **Keep one table** with one row for each possible piece of work. A spreadsheet is enough. A row is a person with a possible job, so a contact with no possible job stays on your list of names.

**Use six stages** and move each row through them. Name: on your list, not yet spoken to. Conversation: you have talked. Need confirmed: they have told you the problem, a rough date and who decides. [Proposal sent](t:9.5). Agreed in words. Signed: you hold a [signed agreement or written order](t:9.9), and with a large client a [purchase order](t:9.35).
**Give every live row a next step,** an owner and a date. If the next step is theirs, set your own date to check. A row with no dated next step is not live.
**Add a rough value and the month** the work might happen. This is for your own planning. Until a row is signed, do not count it as income.

**Hold a thirty-minute pipeline session** at the same time every week, such as Friday at 09:00. Use the order in the routine below. Keep the slot in weeks when you are delivering, even if you cut it to fifteen minutes.
**Count three numbers each month:** first conversations held, proposals sent and jobs signed. After six months, divide one by the next to find your own ratios.

**Plan on about ten real conversations** for three proposals and one signed job, until you have your own figures. That is a working assumption from practitioner judgement, stated so you can plan, and your numbers will differ.
**Park any row with no reply** for ninety days, checking once a month. Give it a date to get back in touch and take it out of your totals.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. Nobody has tested this table against another one, and the ten, three and one figures are an assumption. They are not a statistic about the training market.

**The table exists because of a delay.** Work you deliver this month came from conversations you had some months ago. When you are busy in the room you stop having conversations, and the gap shows up later as an empty diary. Freelancers call this feast and famine. A fixed weekly slot is the usual defence, because it keeps a small amount of selling going in the weeks you least feel like it.

**A dated next step matters most.** The stages matter less than the rule that each row has a dated next step. Most possible work is lost through neither side following up, and far less of it through a refusal. Writing "send outline, me, Friday" turns a pleasant chat into a commitment you will see again in a week.

**A spoken yes is not income.** Keeping "agreed in words" apart from "signed" protects your cash. A sponsor can say yes and still lose the budget. There is more on [budget freezes and changes of sponsor](t:9.36). Your [sellable days](t:9.28) should be filled from the signed column only.
**Twenty rows need no special software.** You do not need customer relationship software for twenty rows. If the table takes more than half an hour a week, it is too elaborate.

try.text: Build the table today with real rows, however few. Then talk a friend through it aloud: one sentence per row, saying the stage, the next step and the date. Record it. Good looks like this: every live row has a date within the next three weeks, you can say who decides for each row at "Need confirmed" or beyond, and nothing is described as "probably happening".

quiz.a: A next step, an owner and a date.

quiz.q: A sponsor tells you on a call, "Yes, let's do it in March." Another client asks for the same March dates. What do you do?
quiz.a: Tell the first sponsor you have a second request for those dates and ask for the signed terms by a set day. Agreed in words is not signed, and budgets and sponsors change.

quiz.q: You are delivering four days a week for the next six weeks and think of pausing all selling until it is over. What do you do?
quiz.a: Keep a fifteen-minute weekly slot and still send five messages. Work arrives months after the conversations that caused it, so a six-week pause now becomes an empty diary later.

topics.title: Choose a business form
topics.theory: Sole trader or limited company in the UK: what each involves

situation.text: Your first client says yes and asks, "Who do we make the purchase order out to?" You have a business name, a logo and a bank account in your own name. You have not decided what the business legally is.

items: **Know the two usual forms.** GOV.UK says most businesses register as a sole trader or a limited company, and that other structures exist, such as a partnership. It says the form you choose affects how you pay tax and what your legal responsibilities are.

**Read what being a sole trader involves.** GOV.UK describes it as the simplest form to set up. You are self-employed and you keep the profits after tax. You are personally responsible for all the debts of the business, which the page calls unlimited liability.

**Note how a sole trader registers.** GOV.UK says you can start trading without registering. You must register for Self Assessment with HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) if you earn more than £1,000 in a tax year, which runs from 6 April to 5 April. You must keep records from the day you start.

**Read what a limited company involves.** GOV.UK says it is legally separate from the people who own it, and that owners are responsible for its debts only up to the value of their investment. It is run by one or more directors. Directors must keep company and accounting records, confirm through a confirmation statement that the details Companies House holds are correct, prepare and file accounts and a Company Tax Return, and pay Corporation Tax. They can hire an accountant for these tasks and stay legally responsible.

**Note how a company registers.** It must be registered with Companies House before it trades. You need at least one director and one shareholder, who can be the same person. You may need to verify your identity with GOV.UK One Login first. The page read on 17 November 2026 gave a fee of £100 online and said companies are usually registered within 24 hours.

**Note how money comes out** of a company. GOV.UK says directors must follow rules: a salary through payroll, dividends paid from profit with a recorded decision and a voucher, or a director's loan that must be recorded.

**Ask the people who will pay you.** Some large clients and training companies set their own rules about the kind of supplier they will contract with. This is practitioner knowledge, not an official statement. If you work through your own company, read the off-payroll working paragraph in the guide to [working as an associate](t:9.32).

**See an accountant before you register,** taking the comparison and your own figures. GOV.UK says you can change form later, and that moving from sole trader to limited company is usually easier than the reverse.

why.text: **Every statement here comes from GOV.UK.** This is general information, not legal or tax advice. Every statement about the two forms above comes from GOV.UK pages read on 17 November 2026. This page does not say which form to choose.

**The forms differ in who owes the debts.** The official pages set out the differences as duties. A sole trader and the business are the same legal person, so the business's debts are the owner's. A company is a separate legal person. GOV.UK says that may protect you if things go wrong, and adds that you may still need business insurance in either form. A company carries more formal duties in return.

**Tax is handled differently too.** A sole trader's profit is reported on a Self Assessment return, and HMRC uses it to work out Income Tax and National Insurance. A company pays Corporation Tax on its profit, and the people who take money out may then pay tax on what they take. Which of these costs you less depends on your profit, your other income and your plans. That is a calculation for an accountant with your figures.

**You sign terms as that legal person.** Your [written terms with a client](t:9.9) are signed in the name of whichever legal person you are. There is a guide to [the registrations each form brings](t:9.41).

try.text: Read the two GOV.UK step-by-step guides in full, which takes about forty minutes. Then book thirty minutes with an accountant who works with small service businesses and ask the questions below aloud. Good looks like this: you leave knowing which form you will register, what it will cost each year in fees and time, and the first three dates you must not miss.

topics.title: Register for the taxes that apply
topics.theory: Self Assessment, Corporation Tax and VAT for a new UK training business

situation.text: Your first invoice has been paid and £3,000 is sitting in your current account. You do not know how much of it is yours to spend, when any tax is due, or whether you should have added VAT.

items: **Register for Self Assessment** if you are a sole trader. GOV.UK says you must register once you earn more than £1,000 in a tax year. The deadlines page read on 17 November 2026 covered the 2025 to 2026 tax year: tell HMRC by 5 October 2026, then send the online return and pay by 31 January 2027. Check the page for the dates for your first year.

**Plan for payments on account.** GOV.UK says these are advance payments towards the next bill, each half of the previous year's bill, due on 31 January and 31 July. In GOV.UK's own example, a first bill of £3,000 means paying £4,500 by 31 January.

**Check Making Tax Digital for Income Tax** and whether it applies. HMRC said on 5 October 2026 that it has been mandatory since 6 April 2026 for sole traders with income over £50,000, will apply over £30,000 from 6 April 2027, and over £20,000 from April 2028. Income here means before expenses.

**Check the Corporation Tax registration** if you have a limited company. GOV.UK says this usually happens when you register with Companies House. Otherwise a company must tell HMRC within three months of the start of its accounting period.

**Know no Corporation Tax bill is sent.** The company works out, reports and pays the tax itself. For taxable profits up to £1.5 million, GOV.UK gives the payment deadline as nine months and one day after the end of the accounting period. A late Company Tax Return brings a penalty even when no tax is owed. A company that pays anyone a salary must also register as an employer.

**Watch your turnover for VAT every month.** On 17 November 2026 GOV.UK gave the registration threshold as £90,000 of taxable turnover. You must register if your taxable turnover for the last twelve months goes over it, or if you expect to go over it in the next thirty days alone. Below it you can register voluntarily.
**Add "plus VAT if it applies"** to every price you quote, as the [example on scoping and pricing](t:9.4) does.

why.text: **Thresholds and dates change, so check.** This is general information, not legal or tax advice. Every rule and figure above comes from a GOV.UK page read on 17 November 2026. Thresholds and dates change, so check the page before you rely on it.

**The VAT rule looks back and forward.** GOV.UK says that if you pass the threshold over the last twelve months, you must register within thirty days of the end of the month in which you passed it, and your registration starts on the first day of the second month after. Register late and you owe the VAT from the date you should have registered, and may get a penalty.

**VAT raises your price for unregistered buyers.** For pricing, GOV.UK says the standard rate is 20% and applies to most goods and services. A registered business adds VAT to its prices, and pays HMRC the difference between the VAT it charged and the VAT it paid on purchases. A client that is itself registered generally gets the VAT back through its own return. A buyer who is not registered, such as an individual on [a public course](t:9.2), bears the whole 20%. So registering changes little for most corporate clients and raises your price for the others.

**Two points need an accountant's answer.** First, on a residential the venue bill may pass through your invoice, as in the [cost table for a residential](t:8.13). Ask how that counts towards the threshold, because one event can be a large share of £90,000. Second, do not assume training is exempt. HMRC's notice on education says profit-making commercial providers are unlikely to be eligible bodies, and that their vocational training is exempt only where an approved government scheme funds it.

try.text: Add up your invoices for the last twelve months and write the total where you will see it each month. Put the dates that apply to you in your diary. Then rehearse aloud, with a friend playing a client's finance contact, your answer to "Is that price plus VAT?" for both cases: registered and not registered. Good looks like this: a one-sentence answer, with no apology.

topics.title: Get the insurance you need
topics.theory: What UK law requires, what contracts ask for and what a retreat adds

situation.text: A client's new supplier form arrives with three boxes: employers' liability, public liability and professional indemnity. Each asks for a certificate and a level of cover. The offsite is in five weeks and you hold none of the three.

items: **Start with what the law requires.** GOV.UK says you must have employers' liability insurance as soon as you become an employer, with cover of at least £5 million from an authorised insurer. It gives a fine of £2,500 for each day without it.

**Check the exemptions.** GOV.UK says you do not need it if you employ only close family members or only people based abroad. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) guide adds that the family exemption does not cover a family business that is a limited company, and that a company is exempt if its only employee is its owner and that person holds 50% or more of the shares.

**Work out who counts as an employee** among the people who help you. The HSE guide says the title you give someone and how they are taxed do not settle it. What counts is the real relationship and how much control you have. Its signs include whether you decide where, when and how they work and whether they can send someone in their place. This matters when you bring in an assistant or a second facilitator, whether you are [staffing a residential](t:8.12) or [briefing people you bring in](t:9.20).
**Tell your motor insurer.** The government's business guidance says motor insurance is required by law if you use a vehicle in the business, including your own car.

**Treat public liability as a contract requirement.** The HSE guide says it is generally voluntary. The government's guidance says almost all businesses need it, for instance when a contract requires it. Venues and clients commonly ask for it.

**Treat professional indemnity the same way.** The government's guidance describes it as cover for claims that your advice, work or services caused a client financial loss, needed if you give professional advice or a regulator requires it. No official page read for this topic makes it a legal requirement for trainers. Clients' contracts often do.

**Add what a retreat brings.** Ask a broker about event cancellation cover, about your liability under the venue contract, about activities run by outside providers and about equipment you carry. These points are practitioner knowledge, not from an official page.

**Speak to a broker before you sign** a venue contract or a client's terms. GOV.UK points to the British Insurance Brokers' Association to find one, and says to check that an insurer is authorised on the Financial Conduct Authority register.

why.text: This is general information, not legal advice. The statements about what is compulsory come from GOV.UK, the HSE and the government's business guidance site, all read on 17 November 2026.

**Only two kinds of cover are compulsory.** Only two kinds of cover were described as legally required on the pages read: employers' liability once you employ someone, and motor insurance for a vehicle used in the business. Everything else is a commercial decision or a condition someone else sets. For a trainer that is usually a client's supplier form or a venue's hire terms, both covered under [putting terms in writing](t:9.9) and [how large organisations buy](t:9.35).

**More of a residential is yours to insure.** A residential changes the answer because more of the event is yours. You may have signed for bedrooms and meals, paid a deposit and promised minimum numbers, as the guides to [choosing and briefing the venue](t:8.11) and [costing a residential](t:8.13) describe. People are in your care in the evening, which is why you [set rules for evenings and alcohol](t:8.14) and [plan for incidents](t:8.15). An activity may be run by a provider you chose. An insurer needs to know all of this, because a policy bought for classroom training may not have been written with it in mind.

**One further legal point belongs with an adviser.** Government guidance on the package travel regulations says that combining two or more kinds of travel service for the same trip, such as transport and accommodation, can create a package, and that the organiser of a package has duties including protecting customers' money if the organiser fails. The guidance, dated 28 October 2026, lists exemptions, including business travel bought under a general agreement. If you sell places on a retreat with accommodation, ask whether these rules reach you.

topics.title: Get on to an associate list
topics.theory: How training companies find, try out and keep freelance trainers

situation.text: Your diary has gaps and you have heard that training companies use freelance associates. You send your CV to six "info@" addresses with a covering note. A month later you have one automatic reply. The guide to [working as an associate](t:9.32) starts when the booking email arrives. This topic is about getting that email.

items: **Understand when a company adds people.** It needs associates when it wins more work than its own trainers can deliver, or work in a subject, place or language it cannot cover. So it looks in a hurry, and it looks first among people it already knows.

**Find the person who books trainers.** In a small company it is often the founder. In a larger one the title may be resourcing manager, delivery manager or head of faculty. A CV sent to a general address rarely reaches them.
**Get introduced.** Ask every trainer you know which companies they work for and whether they would pass your profile to the booker. An introduction from a current associate is the usual way in.
**Choose five to eight companies** whose work matches yours in subject, client sector and format. Be ready to name two of their courses you could deliver.

**Send a one-page profile** in place of a CV. The example below shows what goes in it. Add a link to a three-minute recording of you running part of a session, and two people who have watched you deliver.

**Prepare for a trial.** Common forms are a teach-back, where you deliver fifteen to twenty minutes of the company's own material to two of its people, a day shadowing one of its trainers, or a first delivery alongside a lead trainer. Ask which it will be, how long and whether it is paid.

**Deliver their design as written** in the trial, using the guide to [delivering someone else's design](t:9.31). [Give one instruction](t:4.24) and run one short activity so they see more than your talking. [Finish on time](t:4.31). When they give feedback, write it down and thank them.

**Ask for the associate agreement** and what the day rate covers before the first booking, using the notes on [associate terms and day rates](t:9.32). Then make yourself easy to book: answer every enquiry the same day, even with a no, and send your free dates at the start of each month.

why.text: This is practitioner judgement. No study or official source describes how training companies recruit associates, and companies differ.

**The booker's name is on the programme.** The reasoning follows the booker's position. They have sold a programme to a client and their name is on it. A trainer they have not seen is a risk to that client relationship. An introduction from someone they trust lowers the risk, and a trial lowers it further. That is why the trial tests whether you will deliver their material faithfully, keep to time and take direction. Your own best material is beside the point.

**The booker is matching, not hiring.** A one-page profile works better than a CV because the booker is matching, not hiring. They are asking whether you can deliver this subject, to this kind of group, in this place, on these dates. Give an honest count of the days you have delivered. Some companies will start a newer trainer on co-delivery.

**Reliability keeps you on the list.** Staying on the list is mostly about being reliable. Bookers return to people who reply quickly, turn up early, deliver the design, pass on every lead and cause no surprises. Send a short note after each delivery saying what went well and what the client mentioned.

**Associate work has a cost.** The fee is lower than your direct rate because the company does the selling, as the warning on [working out your day rate](t:9.28) explains, and the agreement will stop you approaching its clients. It also gives you delivery days and feedback from experienced people. Asking three companies what they pay associates gives you a market check for your own rate.

try.text: Borrow fifteen minutes of someone else's material, such as a section of a colleague's session plan. Deliver it standing up to two people and a timer. Ask them to play quiet participants and to give you two minutes of feedback. Record it. Good looks like this: you finish within thirty seconds of the time, the listeners do something for at least four of the fifteen minutes, you add no content of your own, and you answer the feedback with "thank you" and one question.

items: **You show your own material** in the trial. They need to know you will deliver theirs. Keep to the guide, and offer suggestions afterwards if asked.
**You inflate your experience.** The first observed day will show the truth. State your real count and ask to co-deliver first.
**You hand out your business card** on a company's delivery. The client is theirs. Pass every enquiry on the same day.
**Associate work fills the year.** Your own clients then never arrive. Keep the [weekly pipeline session](t:9.39) in every month.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: What is a teach-back?
quiz.a: A trial in which you deliver a short section of the company's own material, often fifteen to twenty minutes, to one or two of its people, and then take feedback.

quiz.q: In a teach-back you see a better way to run the activity in the company's guide. You have twenty minutes. What do you do?
quiz.a: Run it as written and keep to time. The trial tests whether you will deliver their design faithfully, so mention your idea afterwards only if they ask what you would change.

quiz.q: A training company's booker asks how many days you have delivered. The honest answer is fourteen, most of them co-delivered. What do you say?
quiz.a: Give the real number and what the days were, then offer to co-deliver or be observed on a first booking. An inflated answer is exposed on the first day, and a plain one lets them place you where you will do well.

parts.title: Inside the client's learning function
parts.summary: What a large client's learning team is trying to do across its year: plan and spend a budget, report to leaders and build skills, so that a supplier can be useful to it.

topics.title: Understand how a learning function plans and spends its year
topics.theory: The annual cycle: business planning, the budget, mandatory and discretionary spend

situation.text: In February a head of learning at a software company tells you she likes your idea and has no money for it until next year. In October another supplier brought her something similar. It is now a line in her plan.

items: **Ask about the calendar** in your first proper conversation with the learning team. "When does your financial year start, and when does next year's learning plan get fixed?" Do not assume January. Many UK companies run April to March.

**Learn the four stretches of their year.** Planning comes three to four months before the year starts: the business sets its goals and the learning partners collect requests from each division. Budgeting follows, when the plan is costed, challenged and cut. Then comes delivery. Part way through there is a reforecast, when finance takes money back or releases it.

**Ask how the budget splits.** "How much of next year is committed before you choose anything?" Platform and content licences, mandatory training and running programmes such as onboarding usually come first. Leadership, enablement and skills programmes are planned on top. A small sum is often held back for requests during the year.

**Ask where the money sits.** Some of it is in the central learning budget. Some sits with business units. A sales director often pays for sales enablement from her own budget, and the learning team may only co-ordinate it.

**Bring ideas in the planning window.** At that point a one-page outline is enough: the business goal it serves, who it is for, a rough shape and a round cost. The [full proposal](t:9.5) comes later. After the budget is approved, a new idea has to fit an existing line or the held-back sum.

**Know what a reforecast cuts first.** Work that is discretionary, has not started, has no signed contract and serves no named business goal goes first. Travel and venues follow. Mandatory training and licences survive. So [tie your work to a named goal](t:9.12) and sponsor, get the contract signed early, and offer it in phases so that a first phase can survive alone.

**Ask about the end of the year.** Some functions find unspent money in the last quarter that will be lost if it is not used. Keep one small piece of work ready that can be delivered and invoiced before their cut-off date. Ask procurement what that date is.

why.text: **Every company runs its own version.** This is practitioner knowledge of how large organisations tend to run. No study was found that tests it, and every company has its own version. Treat the calendar below as a set of questions.

**The head of learning has little free budget.** The guide to [the client's learning function](t:9.34) tells you to ask how the client's year runs. This topic shows what a typical answer looks like, so that you can hear what the head of learning is telling you. Her freedom is smaller than it looks from outside. Much of her budget is spoken for before she chooses anything, because licences run on contracts of a year or more and mandatory training has to happen. What is left is shared between programmes that each have a senior sponsor. She decides between them as a portfolio, which is part of [deciding what not to train](t:9.14).

**Money is committed early in her year.** That explains the timing. In the planning window she is looking for good ideas with rough costs, and a supplier who helps her build the plan becomes part of it. Four months later the same idea is a request for money she does not have. It also explains what protects a programme. At a reforecast, finance asks which lines can be stopped without breaking a promise or a contract. A programme with a named goal, a sponsor who will argue for it and work already under way is hard to stop. There is advice on [what to do when a freeze lands](t:9.36) anyway.

try.text: Pick one client or employer. Draw their year as twelve boxes and write in what you know: year start, planning, budget, reforecast, closed weeks. Circle the gaps. Then say aloud, to a colleague playing a learning partner, the three questions you would ask to fill them. Record it.

items: **You pitch a large new programme** in the first quarter. The answer is no for reasons that have nothing to do with quality. Ask whether a small first phase could come from the held-back sum or the sponsor's own budget, and bring the full idea back in the planning window.
**Nothing is signed before the reforecast** and your programme is planned for the second half. It is the easiest line to cut. Ask to contract it, or to start a first phase, before that date.
**Year-end money treated as a windfall:** you sell something you would not otherwise recommend. The client remembers what it bought, not why it was in a hurry.

deeper.text: This page is practitioner craft. No study tests it directly.

quiz.q: Which lines of a learning budget are usually committed before the head of learning makes any choice?
quiz.a: Platform and content licences and mandatory training, often with running programmes such as onboarding.

quiz.q: In February a head of learning says she likes your programme and has no budget until next year. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask whether a small first phase could be paid for from the sum held back for requests or from the sponsor's own budget, and ask when next year's planning starts. Then bring a one-page outline with a round cost into that window, when she is building the plan.

quiz.q: Your programme is due to start in September. In May you learn that the client reforecasts in June, and no contract is signed. What do you do?
quiz.a: Ask the sponsor to sign the contract or start a first phase before the reforecast, and send a short note tying the work to the named business goal. Work that has not started and has no contract is the first to be cut.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement about how large organisations plan and budget. No study tests it and each client's calendar differs.

topics.title: Know what a learning function reports upward
topics.theory: Reporting to the executive: how much, how well and what changed

situation.text: You send a twelve-page end-of-programme report you are proud of. The head of learning thanks you and asks for three figures by Friday, in her template. Her quarterly report to the executive committee is one page, and your programme is one row on it.

items: **Ask to see her report** in the first month. "Could I see last quarter's report to the executive, with the figures taken out if you need to? I want ours to drop straight into it."

**Sort what you see into three kinds** of measure. How much: people trained, hours, spend against budget, cost per learner. How well: ratings, pass rates, whether people and their managers say it is being used. What changed: the business measure a priority programme was meant to move.

**Expect leaders to want few numbers.** The usual ones are spend against budget, completion of mandatory training, progress on the two or three programmes tied to this year's goals, and one or two people measures such as time to competence for new starters or retention after a leadership programme.

**Know what a finance director will challenge,** and check your own figures for it first. Costs that leave out learner time. A benefit [claimed with no comparison](t:6.6). A percentage with no count beside it. Self-reported confidence or time saved presented as a result. A measure that changed between quarters. There is a guide to [the cost method finance expects](t:6.15).

**Agree definitions in week one** and use theirs. Ask what counts as a completion, which headcount the percentage is taken from, which dates the quarter covers and on which day the figures are frozen.

**Send your figures early, in her format:** five working days before her deadline. Add one sentence of finding and one stated limit, written as the guide to [reporting results people will read](t:6.10) describes.
**Give a status in her words,** usually on track, at risk or off track. If your row is at risk, tell her before the report is due and bring a proposed fix.
**Offer one short case she can quote,** [gathered with consent](t:9.25). Say that it is one case and not an average.

why.text: **No research was found on reporting formats.** This is practitioner judgement, with one practitioner standard behind the three kinds of measure. No research was found that tests one reporting format against another.

**The three kinds are a convention.** The three kinds come from the Talent Development Reporting Principles, an effort led by people in the profession to standardise how learning is measured and reported. A summary on the Association for Talent Development's site describes efficiency measures that answer how much, effectiveness measures that answer how well, and outcome measures that show the result for the organisation's goals. It also describes a summary report for the chief executive and governing bodies that shows how learning lines up with their goals. It is a convention, and your client may use other names.

**Mismatched figures get reworked or left out.** Your programme report and her report do different jobs. Yours explains one programme to the people who commissioned it, and the guide to [reporting results people will read](t:6.10) is the home for writing it. Hers answers a room that is deciding where money goes next year. If your figures use a different definition of completion, a different quarter or a different headcount, she has to rework them or leave them out. A supplier whose numbers arrive early and in her template makes her job easier in a way she will remember when next year's plan is built.

**A completion shows activity, not learning.** Completions deserve a plain word. As the guides to [not mistaking activity for learning](t:6.7) and [doing compliance training properly](t:2.30) say, a completion figure shows activity and is not proof of learning, and in regulated training it is still a record the company must hold. Leaders ask for it for that reason. Report it without apology, and put a better measure beside it for the programmes that matter most.

try.text: Take a programme you have run or studied. Write its one row for the report below: the measure, the plan, the actual figure with its count, a status and a comment of no more than fifteen words. Then give it aloud to a colleague playing a finance director, and ask them to challenge one figure. Good looks like this: you answer with the count, the definition and the limit, and you do not reach for an adjective.

lines: Measure: managers holding a one-to-one with each team member every month, from your team survey.
Definition: a manager counts if at least three in four of their team answer yes.

After, June survey: 28 of 40 managers, 70%. Your plan was 80%.
Status: at risk.
Finding: more managers are holding one-to-ones, and twelve still are not.

Proposed fix: the twelve managers get a 30-minute call with their own manager in July.

items: **You report percentages only.** Finance asks "of how many?" and the room loses confidence in the page. Put the count beside every percentage.
**You change the measure halfway through** because the new one looks better. Keep the first measure and add the second beside it.
**Figures sent on her deadline day.** She has already written the row from what she had. Agree the date and beat it by a week.
**Made-up figures from a draft** get copied into a real report. Label every illustration in its title, as here.

items.label: Association for Talent Development (2021), A better framework for L&D measurement and analytics. Describes the Talent Development Reporting Principles set out by Vance and Parskey.

quiz.q: What are the three kinds of measure in the Talent Development Reporting Principles?
quiz.a: Efficiency (how much), effectiveness (how well) and outcome (what changed for the organisation's goals).

quiz.q: A finance director reads your row, "cost to date £45,000", and asks whether that includes the managers' time away from their teams. It does not. What do you say?
quiz.a: Say plainly that it does not, and offer to add learner time using finance's own daily cost figure, as the [cost and benefit method](t:6.15) sets out. A cost that leaves out learner time will be corrected by finance anyway, and the rest of your figures will be trusted less.

quiz.q: You have counted a completion as attending any session. The client's platform counts it only when all four sessions and the assessed task are done. Your figure is 95% and theirs is 80%. Which do you report?
quiz.a: Theirs, with the count beside it. Her report can only use one definition, and two figures for the same thing invite the question of which is true.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement. The three kinds of measure come from a practitioner reporting standard, read in summary on a professional body's page.

topics.title: Work with a client's skills strategy
topics.theory: Skills frameworks, skills data, and build, buy, borrow or redesign

situation.text: You are presenting a programme for customer success managers. The learning partner asks, "Which skills in our framework does this build, and to what level?" You have never seen their framework.

items: **Ask for the framework before you design.** "Do you have a skills framework for this job family? Could I see the skills, the level descriptions and who owns it?" A skills framework is a list of named skills, each described at several levels, with a note of which level each role needs.

**Ask how the company knows people's skills** as they stand now. The usual sources are self-rating in a skills platform, a manager's rating, assessments and certificates, and software that infers skills from job history. Ask which of these the learning team trusts.
**Treat self-ratings as a first sketch.** For the skills your programme targets, ask for a second source: a manager's rating against the level description, or [an observed task](t:2.25).

**Ask what the company has decided** to do about each gap. There are four choices. Build means developing current staff. Buy means hiring. Borrow means using contractors or partners. Redesign means [changing the work or the role](t:9.13) so the gap closes another way. Your programme belongs only where the answer is build.

**Map your programme to their skills,** no more than six and in their words. For each, write the level the role needs, the level most people are at now, the part of the programme where people practise it, and the evidence at the end. Use their wording exactly, and leave out any skill that is only mentioned. A programme that claims twenty skills has usually practised three.

**Be honest about levels.** A short programme with practice at work can move most people up one level in a few skills. It cannot take a group from beginner to expert. Say which skills will move and which will only be introduced.

**Agree what feeds their skills record** and who enters it. Evidence from an assessed task is fair. Your private view of a person is not, and any record about a named learner follows [the rules on learner data](t:9.24).

why.text: Most of this is practitioner judgement. One part rests on research: the weakness of self-rating.

why.title: Do people have insight into their abilities? A metasynthesis
why.found: The authors combined 22 earlier meta-analyses that compared people's ratings of their own ability with measures of their performance. The average correlation was .29, which they describe as moderate insight. Ratings were more accurate for specific skills than for broad ones, and when the task was familiar, objective or simple.
why.means: A skills record built only on self-rating is a rough guide. If you must use self-ratings, ask about narrow, familiar tasks in the framework's own level wording, and check the skills that matter against a second source.

why.text: **A framework gives skills a shared language.** A large learning function cares about skills for reasons beyond courses. It wants to know which skills the business will need, where they are thin, who could move into a growing role, and who could succeed a senior person. You can read about [planning reskilling round skills and adjacent moves](t:7.5), and about how to [map roles and skills for one team](t:9.13). A framework gives all of that a shared language. It also organises the client's systems. Content on the learning platform is often tagged by skill, and a programme that carries no tags is hard to find and hard to report.

**SFIA shows the usual pattern.** Frameworks vary. Some companies write their own. Many technology firms adapt a public one. SFIA, a widely used framework for digital roles, shows the usual pattern. Its official site describes seven levels of responsibility, from "follow" at level one to "set strategy, inspire, mobilise" at level seven. Each skill has a name, a code, a description and level descriptions, and not every skill is defined at all seven levels.

try.text: Find a public skills framework for a field you know, or ask a client for theirs. Choose one programme you have designed and map it to six skills using the table below as a pattern. Then explain the map aloud to a colleague in two minutes, including one skill you decided not to claim and why.

try.title: Words you can use when the level asked for is more than the programme can give
lines: "Your framework asks for level 3 on renewal objections. Most of this group are at 1 or 2."
"Three days and six weeks of practice will get most of them to a solid 2, and some to 3."
"If you need the whole group at 3, the route is more observed calls with their managers after we finish. I can design that part with you."
"I would sooner tell you that now than tag the programme at level 3 and have the data say otherwise."

items: **You bring your own competency model.** The client already has one. Ask first and use theirs.
**You tag the programme too widely,** to every skill it touches. The catalogue fills with weak matches and the learning team stops trusting your tags. Claim what is practised and assessed.
**Progress measured by self-rating:** you ask people to rate themselves before and after. Ratings often rise with confidence alone. Use an observed task for the skills that matter.
**A framework level becomes a grade** on a person. Record evidence against the task, tell people what is recorded, and keep to [the rules on learner data](t:9.24).

items.label: Zell and Krizan (2014), Do people have insight into their abilities? A metasynthesis. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 9(2), 111 to 125. Index record.
SFIA Foundation, How SFIA works: levels of responsibility and skills.

quiz.q: What are the four choices for closing a skills gap?
quiz.a: Build (develop current staff), buy (hire), borrow (use contractors or partners) and redesign (change the work or the role).

quiz.q: A client's skills platform shows that 80% of the support team rate themselves "advanced" at troubleshooting. The head of support says the escalation rate suggests otherwise. You are asked to design training. What do you do first?
quiz.a: Ask for a second source on the skill, such as a manager's rating against the level description or an observed task on real tickets. Self-ratings give only moderate insight into ability, so they should not set the starting level alone.

quiz.q: A learning partner asks you to tag your two-day programme to fourteen skills so that it appears in more searches. What do you say?
quiz.a: Offer the four to six skills that people practise and are assessed on, and list the others as mentioned and not built. Tags that overclaim make the skills data wrong and cost you the learning team's trust.

topics.tierReason: Rests on practitioner judgement, with one research synthesis on self-rating read in summary and one framework's official page.
